claims.claim: Law is a form of structured being-with.
claims.source_quote: Law as Structured Being-With
claims.note: This is a section heading that names the author's positive ontological thesis about the nature of law, asserting a relational/structural ontological category.

claims.claim: Obligations are entities with an ontological status.
claims.source_quote: The Ontological Status of Obligation
claims.note: Section heading commits the author to treating obligation as having a determinate ontological status, i.e., as a real kind of entity.

claims.claim: Recognition is an ontological event.
claims.source_quote: Recognition as Ontological Event
claims.note: Section heading asserts that recognition belongs to the category of events in the ontological sense.

claims.claim: Legal reality is created and can become extinct.
claims.source_quote: The Creation and Extinction of Legal Reality
claims.note: Section heading asserts that legal reality is the kind of thing that comes into and goes out of existence.

claims.claim: Institutions are role networks.
claims.source_quote: Institutions as Role Networks
claims.note: Section heading directly asserts a subkind/compositional ontological claim: institutions are constituted by networks of roles.

claims.claim: Legal roles are relational entities.
claims.source_quote: Roles as relational entities
claims.note: Section heading asserts that roles belong to the ontological category of relational entities.

claims.claim: Roles are not reducible to behavior.
claims.source_quote: Roles Are Not Reducible to Behavior
claims.note: Section heading asserts a negative ontological claim about the nature of roles—they are not identical to or definable by behavior.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant.
claims.source_quote: Property as Relational Continuant
claims.note: Section heading asserts that property belongs to the ontological category of relational continuants.

claims.claim: Value is ontologically dependent on other entities.
claims.source_quote: The Dependence of Value
claims.note: Section heading asserts an ontological dependence relation for value, committing to its dependent ontological status.

claims.claim: Ownership requires institutional maintenance.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Maintenance of Ownership
claims.note: Section heading asserts a functional/relational claim that ownership depends on institutions for its continuation.

claims.claim: Legal facts are procedurally realized.
claims.source_quote: Procedural Realization of Facts
claims.note: Section heading asserts that legal facts bear a realization relation to procedures.

claims.claim: Hart's secondary rules stand in a relation of ontological dependence.
claims.source_quote: Hart's Secondary Rules and Ontological Dependence
claims.note: Section heading commits the author to secondary rules bearing ontological dependence relations.

claims.claim: Justice is the structural integrity of legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: Justice as Structural Integrity
claims.note: Section heading directly asserts an ontological identification of justice with structural integrity.

claims.claim: Justice is a relational coherence of legal structure.
claims.source_quote: Justice as relational coherence
claims.note: Sub-heading asserts justice has the property of relational coherence as its defining feature.

claims.claim: Repair is the ethical core of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: Repair as the System's Ethical Core
claims.note: Sub-heading asserts a functional/role claim about repair within the legal system.

claims.claim: Obligations arise from recognition.
claims.source_quote: How obligations arise from recognition
claims.note: Sub-heading asserts a generative ontological relation between recognition (as event) and obligations.

claims.claim: Obligations are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Dependent continuants that shape the field of legal possibility
claims.note: Sub-heading categorizes obligations (and claims/permissions) as dependent continuants in the BFO sense.

claims.claim: Institutions are aggregations with recognitive powers.
claims.source_quote: Institutions as aggregations with recognitive powers
claims.note: Sub-heading asserts both the compositional nature of institutions (aggregations) and their dispositional property (recognitive powers).

claims.claim: Coherence is the condition of justice.
claims.source_quote: Coherence as the Condition of Justice
claims.note: Sub-heading asserts that coherence is a necessary ontological condition for justice.

claims.claim: The law does not act; people act in roles.
claims.source_quote: The Law Does Not Act, People Do, in Roles
claims.note: Section heading asserts that agency belongs to persons occupying roles, not to law as such—an ontological claim about agency.

claims.claim: Legal roles differ ontologically from bearer-independent functions.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Roles vs. Bearer-Independent Functions
claims.note: Section heading asserts an ontological distinction between two kinds of functional entities.

claims.claim: Smart contracts compress ontological structure and lose the recognition relation.
claims.source_quote: Smart Contracts: Ontological Compression and the Loss of Recognition
claims.note: Sub-heading asserts a specific ontological defect of smart contracts: compression that eliminates the recognition relation.

claims.claim: Algorithmic adjudication produces pseudo-recognition and norm drift.
claims.source_quote: Algorithmic Adjudication: Pseudo-Recognition and Norm Drift
claims.note: Sub-heading asserts that algorithmic adjudication instantiates a deficient form of recognition and causes norm instability.

claims.claim: Legal structure is composed of obligations, from which institutions arise, which in turn ground justice.
claims.source_quote: From Obligation to Institution to Justice: Law as the Architecture of Being-With
claims.note: Section heading asserts a hierarchical ontological architecture linking obligation, institution, and justice.

claims.claim: Roles are relational positions within legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: Roles as relational positions
claims.note: Sub-heading directly asserts the ontological character of roles as positional and relational.

claims.claim: Roles are distinct from their bearers.
claims.source_quote: Bearers vs. roles
claims.note: Sub-heading asserts an ontological distinction between the role and the individual who bears it.

claims.claim: Roles persist continuously and stably across different bearers.
claims.source_quote: Continuity and stability across roles
claims.note: Sub-heading asserts that roles have the property of continuity and stability, an ontological claim about their persistence.

claims.claim: Law is a structured domain of social reality.
claims.source_quote: many of its central debates, about validity, obligation, and authority, could be clarified if we treated law as a structured domain of social reality.
claims.note: The author asserts this as his own positive view, not merely a methodological proposal.

claims.claim: Law is a real system of interdependent entities.
claims.source_quote: a way of understanding, and of teaching others to understand, law as a real system of interdependent entities.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature of law as a kind of entity-system.

claims.claim: Roles, institutions, and obligations are parts of a coherent architecture.
claims.source_quote: to grasp how roles, institutions, and obligations fit together as parts of a coherent architecture.
claims.note: Asserts a part-whole and structural relation among legal entities.

claims.claim: Law is a structured field of relations sustained by recognition, obligation, and repair.
claims.source_quote: The approach developed here encourages students and readers to see law as a structured field of relations, sustained by recognition, obligation, and repair.
claims.note: Author's own positive characterization of law's ontological nature.

claims.claim: Law's authority arises from the ontological coherence of its structures.
claims.source_quote: Law's authority, on this view, is not mysterious; it arises from the ontological coherence of its structures and the stability of the recognitions that sustain them.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding relation: authority has its source in ontological coherence and recognition.

claims.claim: Law's authority arises from the stability of the recognitions that sustain its structures.
claims.source_quote: Law's authority, on this view, is not mysterious; it arises from the ontological coherence of its structures and the stability of the recognitions that sustain them.
claims.note: Asserts a second grounding relation: recognition-stability as a sustaining condition for legal structures.

claims.claim: Law is a human institution that persists, fails, and repairs itself.
claims.source_quote: meant for students of philosophy, law, and social theory who want to understand law's reality as a human institution, how it persists, fails, and repairs itself.
claims.note: Asserts that law is a kind of human institution with properties of persistence, failure, and self-repair.

claims.claim: Rights, contracts, and judgments are entities that have a determinate kind of reality.
claims.source_quote: What sort of reality do laws and institutions have? What is a right, a contract, or a judgment, in the most literal sense?
claims.note: The author presents these questions as the genuine ontological gap in jurisprudence, implying commitment that these are real entities whose nature can be specified; medium because posed as questions the book answers rather than direct assertion.

claims.claim: Jurisprudence lacks an account of law's being.
claims.source_quote: what was missing in jurisprudence was not another moral or linguistic theory, but an account of law's being.
claims.note: Asserts a property (a lack) of the domain of jurisprudence as a discipline.

claims.claim: Law is a real domain of social being.
claims.source_quote: The chapter proposes a structural ontological approach that treats law as a real domain of social being constituted by relations of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: The author endorses this view as the book's central thesis, asserting law's mode of existence as a real social domain.

claims.claim: Law is constituted by relations of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: treats law as a real domain of social being constituted by relations of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive relational structure of law — a direct ontological claim about what law is made of.

claims.claim: Law is structured being-with.
claims.source_quote: Law is defined as structured being-with: an architecture of dependent relations that persists through institutional recognition and repair.
claims.note: The author explicitly defines law as a kind of entity — structured being-with — making this a direct ontological classification claim.

claims.claim: Law is an architecture of dependent relations.
claims.source_quote: Law is defined as structured being-with: an architecture of dependent relations that persists through institutional recognition and repair.
claims.note: The author asserts that law's structure consists of dependent relations, an ontological claim about the composition of law.

claims.claim: Law persists through institutional recognition and repair.
claims.source_quote: an architecture of dependent relations that persists through institutional recognition and repair.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for law as an entity — an ontological claim about the conditions under which law continues to exist.

claims.claim: Traditional jurisprudential approaches have left law's mode of existence under-examined.
claims.source_quote: traditional jurisprudential approaches, including natural law, legal positivism, and legal realism, have focused on law's authority, content, or social effects while leaving its mode of existence under-examined.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a substantive claim about the state of prior theories, implying law has a mode of existence that is a genuine ontological feature requiring examination.

claims.claim: Law is a structure of organized continuities of human recognition and participation.
claims.source_quote: They are structures, organized continuities of human recognition and participation that give shape to social reality.
claims.note: Author asserts what law is as a kind of entity—a structure of organized continuities.

claims.claim: Legal systems are composed of interdependent entities, roles, obligations, processes, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: It is to study law not as a set of texts or behaviors but as a system of interdependent entities, roles, obligations, processes, and institutions, that form a coherent architecture.
claims.note: Author asserts the composition of legal systems—what kinds of entities compose them.

claims.claim: Legal entities endure, interact, and change in lawful ways.
claims.source_quote: They endure, interact, and change in lawful ways. Their being cannot be reduced to words on paper or the fleeting intentions of their makers.
claims.note: Author asserts properties of legal entities—endurance, interaction, change.

claims.claim: The being of legal entities cannot be reduced to words on paper or the intentions of their makers.
claims.source_quote: Their being cannot be reduced to words on paper or the fleeting intentions of their makers.
claims.note: Author asserts a negative ontological claim about the irreducibility of legal entities.

claims.claim: Legal phenomena arise from acts of recognition and persist as structured continuants within the social world.
claims.source_quote: Applied to law, these distinctions reveal how legal phenomena arise from acts of recognition and persist as structured continuants within the social world.
claims.note: Author asserts both the causal origin and ontological category of legal phenomena.

claims.claim: An obligation is a specific relation between agents that constrains possibilities of action.
claims.source_quote: An obligation is a specific relation between agents that constrains possibilities of action.
claims.note: Author directly asserts what kind of entity an obligation is and its relational structure.

claims.claim: A court is an institutional node that realizes functions through role-bearing persons.
claims.source_quote: a court is an institutional node that realizes functions through role-bearing persons.
claims.note: Author asserts what kind of entity a court is and how it realizes its functions.

claims.claim: Justice is the coherence achieved when legal relations are harmonized.
claims.source_quote: justice is the coherence achieved when these relations are harmonized.
claims.note: Author asserts what justice is as an ontological property or state of legal relations.

claims.claim: Obligation, authority, institution, and justice name real structures of dependence.
claims.source_quote: Terms such as obligation, authority, institution, and justice are not only moral or linguistic constructs; they name real structures of dependence.
claims.note: Author asserts that these terms refer to real ontological structures, not merely linguistic or moral constructs.

claims.claim: Legal systems include socially sustained continuants that depend on collective recognition but maintain integrity once established.
claims.source_quote: They point to the existence of socially sustained continuants, entities that depend on collective recognition but maintain integrity once established.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of a specific kind of entity—socially sustained continuants—within legal systems.

claims.claim: Socially sustained continuants in law fall under the BFO category of specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: This continuity, captured in the BFO category of specifically dependent continuants, allows law to have both temporal depth and structural stability.
claims.note: Author asserts that legal continuants belong to the ontological category of specifically dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Law has both temporal depth and structural stability.
claims.source_quote: This continuity...allows law to have both temporal depth and structural stability.
claims.note: Author asserts properties of law as an entity—temporal depth and structural stability.

claims.claim: Law is part of the real world.
claims.source_quote: It treats law as part of the real world, subject to analysis in the same way we analyze biological organisms or technical systems.
claims.note: Author asserts that law has the property of being a real-world entity.

claims.claim: Law is the most visible architecture of human coexistence and coordination.
claims.source_quote: Law is the most visible architecture of that coexistence.
claims.note: Author asserts a property and role of law within the broader ontology of social being.

claims.claim: Law exists within the broader ontology of being-with—the field of relations through which persons coexist and coordinate.
claims.source_quote: it restores that significance by situating law within the broader ontology of being-with, the field of relations through which persons coexist and coordinate their actions.
claims.note: Author asserts that law is situated within a broader ontological field called being-with.

claims.claim: Being-with is the field of relations through which persons coexist and coordinate their actions.
claims.source_quote: the broader ontology of being-with, the field of relations through which persons coexist and coordinate their actions.
claims.note: Author defines being-with as a real ontological field of relations among persons.

claims.claim: Legal norms, roles, and institutions interact to form a coherent system capable of repair, collapse, and rebirth.
claims.source_quote: Its goal is to describe the architecture of legal being: how norms, roles, and institutions interact to form a coherent system capable of repair, collapse, and rebirth.
claims.note: Author asserts the relational structure and properties of the legal system as an entity.

claims.claim: A rule must be a kind of entity capable of existing and exerting causal or normative force.
claims.source_quote: the ontologist asks what sort of entity a 'rule' must be to exist and exert causal or normative force.
claims.note: Author frames this as what ontology asks, but commits to the view that rules must be entities with causal/normative force.

claims.claim: Legal systems cannot be fully understood as artifacts of language, will, or power alone.
claims.source_quote: legal systems cannot be fully understood as artifacts of language, will, or power alone.
claims.note: Author asserts a negative ontological claim about the nature of legal systems—they are not reducible to language, will, or power.

claims.claim: Natural law theory presupposes that moral facts exist independently of human decree.
claims.source_quote: It presupposes that moral facts exist independently and that law's reality depends on their recognition.
claims.note: The author is characterizing what natural law theory presupposes; the author attributes this ontological commitment to the view as a way of critiquing it, implying endorsement of the characterization as accurate.

claims.claim: On the natural law view, law's reality depends on the recognition of independent moral facts.
claims.source_quote: It presupposes that moral facts exist independently and that law's reality depends on their recognition.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a structural feature of natural law ontology, characterizing a dependence relation between legal reality and moral facts.

claims.claim: The natural law view collapses law into ethics.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this collapses law into ethics.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts this as their own ontological verdict on the natural law position.

claims.claim: Natural law confuses the conditions for legitimacy with the conditions for existence.
claims.source_quote: Natural law's strength, its moral confidence, is thus its weakness as ontology: it confuses the conditions for legitimacy with the conditions for existence.
claims.note: Direct authorial assertion about a category error in natural law theory—ontological claim about misidentified conditions.

claims.claim: Unjust yet effective legal systems persist despite moral condemnation.
claims.source_quote: It fails to account for the persistence of unjust yet effective legal systems, or for the brute social fact that legal institutions endure even when morality recoils from their acts.
claims.note: The author asserts as a fact that unjust legal systems have persistence—an ontological claim about the endurance of legal entities.

claims.claim: Legal institutions endure even when morality condemns their acts.
claims.source_quote: for the brute social fact that legal institutions endure even when morality recoils from their acts.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a 'brute social fact'—an ontological claim about the persistence of institutional entities.

claims.claim: Positivism does not explain what kind of entity a norm must be in order to exist.
claims.source_quote: Positivism describes how norms are validated, but not what kind of thing a norm must be to exist at all. Its focus on criteria of validity obscures the deeper question of ontological constitution.
claims.note: Author asserts that positivism has a genuine explanatory gap regarding the ontological constitution of norms.

claims.claim: Realism deprives law of ontological depth by reducing it to behavior or expectation.
claims.source_quote: Realism, for all its descriptive power, deprives law of ontological depth. It mistakes the manifestations of legal order for its underlying form.
claims.note: Author asserts that legal realism fails to capture law's ontological structure—a claim about what law has (depth, underlying form).

claims.claim: Law has an underlying form that is distinct from its manifestations.
claims.source_quote: It mistakes the manifestations of legal order for its underlying form.
claims.note: Author commits to law having an underlying form distinguishable from observable manifestations.

claims.claim: Structural realism holds that relations are more real than individual objects of experience.
claims.source_quote: it holds that what is most real are not the individual objects of experience but the relations that connect them.
claims.note: Author endorses structural realism and its core ontological thesis about relations.

claims.claim: Entities derive their identity from their place within a structure of dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Entities derive their identity from their place within a structure of dependencies.
claims.note: Directly asserted structural-realist ontological claim about the identity conditions of entities.

claims.claim: Rights, obligations, and institutions exist as interrelated continuants sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: structural realism suggests that rights, obligations, and institutions exist not as isolated facts but as interrelated continuants sustained by recognition.
claims.note: Author endorses the structural realist account—asserts the mode of existence of legal entities.

claims.claim: A statute has meaning because it stands in determinate relations to other norms, institutional roles, and social acts of acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: A statute has meaning because it stands in determinate relations to other norms, to institutional roles, and to social acts of acknowledgment.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational constitution claim about statutes—their meaning is grounded in relational position.

claims.claim: A court's authority is a stable node in a network of relational dependencies.
claims.source_quote: A court's authority is real not as a psychological disposition or moral ideal but as a stable node in this network of relational dependencies.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological nature of a court's authority as a structural node—entity-property claim.

claims.claim: Recognition, obligation, and institutional function are ontological categories.
claims.source_quote: The answer lies in the interplay of recognition, obligation, and institutional function. These are not abstractions but ontological categories.
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts these are ontological categories, not mere abstractions.

claims.claim: Recognition, obligation, and institutional function are specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: specifically dependent continuants that emerge when agents acknowledge one another's capacities and duties within organized systems.
claims.note: Author asserts these legal categories are a specific ontological type (dependent continuants) within BFO-style ontology.

claims.claim: The legal world is composed of patterns of recognition instantiated in enduring institutional forms.
claims.source_quote: The legal world is thus composed of patterns of recognition instantiated in enduring institutional forms.
claims.note: Author asserts the compositional ontology of the legal world.

claims.claim: Law's persistence depends on the coherence of relational patterns rather than on any particular actor's will.
claims.source_quote: Its persistence depends on the coherence of these relations rather than on the will of any particular actor.
claims.note: Ontological claim about what sustains legal entities over time.

claims.claim: Legal entities are relations rather than substances.
claims.source_quote: Because its entities are relations rather than substances, legal order can evolve without ceasing to be itself.
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts the ontological category of legal entities as relations, not substances.

claims.claim: Legal institutions adapt as roles and obligations are reconfigured while structural integrity persists.
claims.source_quote: Institutions adapt as roles and obligations are reconfigured, yet the structural integrity of law persists so long as the network of recognition remains coherent.
claims.note: Ontological claim about how institutional entities change while maintaining identity through relational coherence.

claims.claim: Law is distinguished from mere custom or habit by its capacity for repair and reestablishing order.
claims.source_quote: This capacity for repair, for reestablishing order after disruption, is what distinguishes law from mere custom or habit.
claims.note: Author asserts a distinguishing property of law as a kind, differentiating it from custom/habit.

claims.claim: Law is a real, evolving architecture of human coexistence.
claims.source_quote: what it is, a real, evolving architecture of human coexistence.
claims.note: Author directly asserts law's ontological nature as a real structure.

claims.claim: Roles, obligations, and institutions function as interlocking continuants within a dynamic system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: we will map how roles, obligations, and institutions function as interlocking continuants within a dynamic system of recognition.
claims.note: Author endorses this as the correct account, though framed as a research program; the ontological commitment is clear from context.

claims.claim: Law is one of the world's enduring structures.
claims.source_quote: we recover law's reality as one of the world's enduring structures.
claims.note: Author asserts law belongs to the category of enduring structures in the world—an ontological kind claim.

claims.claim: Roles, obligations, and institutions are interlocking continuants within a dynamic system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: we will map how roles, obligations, and institutions function as interlocking continuants within a dynamic system of recognition.
claims.note: The author asserts that roles, obligations, and institutions are a specific kind of entity (continuants) bearing interlocking relations within a system.

claims.claim: Law is a real, evolving architecture of human coexistence.
claims.source_quote: what it is, a real, evolving architecture of human coexistence. By situating jurisprudence within ontology, we recover law's reality as one of the world's enduring structures.
claims.note: The author positively asserts law's ontological status as a real, evolving architecture.

claims.claim: Law is one of the world's enduring structures.
claims.source_quote: we recover law's reality as one of the world's enduring structures.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about law's ontological character as an enduring structure.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and permissions are dependent entities.
claims.source_quote: distinguishing between enduring continuants and transient occurrents, between independent entities like persons and institutions and dependent ones like rights, duties, or permissions.
claims.note: The author classifies rights, duties, and permissions as dependent entities, asserting a subkind relation.

claims.claim: Persons and institutions are independent entities.
claims.source_quote: between independent entities like persons and institutions and dependent ones like rights, duties, or permissions.
claims.note: The author asserts that persons and institutions are independent entities (a property/classification).

claims.claim: Law is a structured domain of being.
claims.source_quote: revealing it as a structured domain of being rather than a mere aggregation of texts and practices.
claims.note: The author positively asserts law's ontological status as a structured domain of being.

claims.claim: Continuants are entities that persist through time while maintaining their identity.
claims.source_quote: continuants, entities that persist through time while maintaining their identity, and occurrents, entities that unfold in time, such as processes or events
claims.note: The author asserts a defining property of continuants as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Occurrents are entities that unfold in time, such as processes or events.
claims.source_quote: occurrents, entities that unfold in time, such as processes or events
claims.note: The author asserts a defining property of occurrents as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: A person is a continuant.
claims.source_quote: A person, an institution, or a statute are continuants; a trial, a vote, or a contract signing are occurrents.
claims.note: The author asserts that a person is an individual of the kind 'continuant'.

claims.claim: An institution is a continuant.
claims.source_quote: A person, an institution, or a statute are continuants; a trial, a vote, or a contract signing are occurrents.
claims.note: The author asserts that an institution is an individual of the kind 'continuant'.

claims.claim: A statute is a continuant.
claims.source_quote: A person, an institution, or a statute are continuants; a trial, a vote, or a contract signing are occurrents.
claims.note: The author asserts that a statute is an individual of the kind 'continuant'.

claims.claim: A trial is an occurrent.
claims.source_quote: a trial, a vote, or a contract signing are occurrents.
claims.note: The author asserts that a trial is an individual of the kind 'occurrent'.

claims.claim: Legal systems persist as networks of continuants.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems persist as networks of continuants that are enacted, interpreted, and revised through occurrents.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal systems have the property of persisting as networks of continuants.

claims.claim: Legal systems are enacted, interpreted, and revised through occurrents.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems persist as networks of continuants that are enacted, interpreted, and revised through occurrents.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational property between legal systems (continuants) and occurrents.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, powers, and immunities are specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Obligations, rights, powers, and immunities are all specifically dependent continuants: they exist because certain relations among agents, institutions, and norms obtain.
claims.note: The author classifies these entities as a subkind of continuants (specifically dependent).

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, powers, and immunities exist because certain relations among agents, institutions, and norms obtain.
claims.source_quote: they exist because certain relations among agents, institutions, and norms obtain.
claims.note: The author asserts a dependency relation grounding the existence of these legal entities.

claims.claim: When a contract is signed, new obligations come into being.
claims.source_quote: When a contract is signed, new obligations come into being; when a verdict is rendered, new legal statuses are instantiated.
claims.note: The author asserts that contract signing is an event that brings obligations (entities) into existence.

claims.claim: When a verdict is rendered, new legal statuses are instantiated.
claims.source_quote: when a verdict is rendered, new legal statuses are instantiated.
claims.note: The author asserts that verdict-rendering is an event that brings new legal statuses (entities) into existence.

claims.claim: The creation of obligations and legal statuses constitutes real ontological events.
claims.source_quote: These are not metaphors but ontological events, the creation of real entities that alter what agents can or cannot do.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts that these creations are real ontological events, not merely metaphorical.

claims.claim: Obligations and legal statuses are real entities that alter what agents can or cannot do.
claims.source_quote: the creation of real entities that alter what agents can or cannot do.
claims.note: The author asserts that obligations/statuses are real entities with causal/normative efficacy.

claims.claim: A legal case is a complex occurrent involving continuant participants.
claims.source_quote: A 'legal case' can be understood as a complex occurrent involving continuant participants, judge, plaintiff, defendant, each bearing specific roles.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological kind of a legal case as a complex occurrent.

claims.claim: A judge, plaintiff, and defendant are continuant participants in a legal case, each bearing specific roles.
claims.source_quote: continuant participants, judge, plaintiff, defendant, each bearing specific roles.
claims.note: The author asserts that these individuals are continuants bearing the property of specific roles.

claims.claim: A legal judgment is a dependent continuant that is an information artifact.
claims.source_quote: The judgment produced at its conclusion is a new dependent continuant, an information artifact that modifies the network of obligations in which the parties stand.
claims.note: The author asserts that a legal judgment is a subkind of dependent continuant and also an information artifact.

claims.claim: A legal judgment modifies the network of obligations in which the parties stand.
claims.source_quote: an information artifact that modifies the network of obligations in which the parties stand.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational property: a judgment bears a modifying relation to the network of obligations.

claims.claim: Hart's rule of recognition functions as a higher-order dependency relation.
claims.source_quote: His rule of recognition functions as a higher-order dependency relation: a collectively sustained practice that confers validity on other norms.
claims.note: The author endorses and asserts an ontological characterization of the rule of recognition as a dependency relation.

claims.claim: Hart's rule of recognition is a collectively sustained practice that confers validity on other norms.
claims.source_quote: a collectively sustained practice that confers validity on other norms.
claims.note: The author positively asserts properties of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Hart's rule of recognition operates as an institutional function of a legal system.
claims.source_quote: this rule operates as an institutional function, a realized capacity of a legal system to generate, modify, and validate obligations.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological role/function of the rule of recognition within a legal system.

claims.claim: Primary rules govern agents directly.
claims.source_quote: primary rules govern agents directly, while secondary rules govern the processes by which norms themselves come into being.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/function of primary rules in relation to agents.

claims.claim: Secondary rules govern the processes by which norms come into being.
claims.source_quote: secondary rules govern the processes by which norms themselves come into being.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/function of secondary rules in relation to norm-generating processes.

claims.claim: Principles are abstract relational constraints that ensure consistency within the legal structure.
claims.source_quote: Principles in this sense are not psychological commitments but abstract relational constraints that ensure consistency within the legal structure.
claims.note: The author asserts an ontological characterization of legal principles as abstract relational constraints.

claims.claim: Principles are meta-level dependencies that guide the realization of rules and decisions within a unified structure.
claims.source_quote: principles appear as meta-level dependencies that guide the realization of rules and decisions within a unified structure of meaning.
claims.note: The author asserts an ontological role for principles as meta-level dependencies.

claims.claim: Law is a relational architecture of continuants and occurrents sustained through recognition.
claims.source_quote: to describe law as a relational architecture of continuants and occurrents sustained through recognition.
claims.note: The author positively asserts the ontological character of law as a relational architecture.

claims.claim: Law is a living structure of relations sustained by shared recognition.
claims.source_quote: it is neither an abstraction imposed from above nor a mere reflection of moral sentiment, but a living structure of relations sustained by shared recognition.
claims.note: The author makes a positive ontological assertion about law's nature as a structure of relations.

claims.claim: Law is one of the most visible architectures through which human coexistence takes form.
claims.source_quote: Law does not stand apart from human life; it is one of the most visible architectures through which human coexistence takes form.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/role of law as an architecture of human coexistence.

claims.claim: Every act of governance, every contract, every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Every act of governance, every contract, every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment, of who counts as an agent, what rol
claims.note: The author asserts a dependency relation: legal acts presuppose a network of mutual acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Legal entities such as obligations, promises, and rights are social objects that come into being through acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: His A Priori Foundations of the Civil Law (1913) argued that legal entities such as obligations, promises, and rights are social objects, entities that come into being through acts of recognition among persons.
claims.note: The author presents Reinach's view but endorses it as the basis for 'a realist ontology of law,' indicating commitment; medium confidence because it is framed as Reinach's view being endorsed.

claims.claim: Dependent continuants exist only insofar as they inhere in or are recognized by other entities.
claims.source_quote: These are entities that exist only insofar as they inhere in or are recognized by other entities.
claims.note: The author asserts a defining property of dependent continuants as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Law is a living structure of relations sustained by shared recognition.
claims.source_quote: law is neither an abstraction imposed from above nor a mere reflection of moral sentiment, but a living structure of relations sustained by shared recognition.
claims.note: The author positively asserts what law is—a structure of relations—distinguishing it from other characterizations.

claims.claim: Law is a framework for being-together.
claims.source_quote: law is a framework for being-together, a structured field of interdependence in which individual and institutional existence are mutually constituted.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature/role of law as a structured field.

claims.claim: Law is a structured field of interdependence.
claims.source_quote: law is a framework for being-together, a structured field of interdependence in which individual and institutional existence are mutually constituted.
claims.note: Author asserts law has the property of being a structured field of interdependence.

claims.claim: Individual and institutional existence are mutually constituted within law.
claims.source_quote: a structured field of interdependence in which individual and institutional existence are mutually constituted.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive relation between individual existence and institutional existence mediated by law.

claims.claim: Every act of governance presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Every act of governance, every contract, every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment, of who counts as an agent, what roles they bear, and what obligations or immunities accompany those roles.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: governance acts depend on (presuppose) a network of mutual acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Every contract presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Every act of governance, every contract, every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment, of who counts as an agent, what roles they bear, and what obligations or immunities accompany those roles.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between contracts and a network of mutual acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Every act of governance, every contract, every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment, of who counts as an agent, what roles they bear, and what obligations or immunities accompany those roles.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between judgments and a network of mutual acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Roles bear obligations and immunities.
claims.source_quote: what roles they bear, and what obligations or immunities accompany those roles.
claims.note: Asserts that roles have the property of being accompanied by obligations and immunities.

claims.claim: Institutions are the primary loci of law's relational structure.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are the primary loci of this relational structure.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the role/location of institutions within the relational structure of law.

claims.claim: Natural law, positivism, and realism fail to explain law's mode of existence.
claims.source_quote: The introduction situates the discussion within the failures of natural law, positivism, and realism to explain law's mode of existence.
claims.note: The author asserts a property (failure to explain law's mode of existence) of these three jurisprudential traditions, committing to a claim about their ontological inadequacy.

claims.claim: Legal systems are organized continuities of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: It then articulates the need for a structural realist approach that treats legal systems as organized continuities of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: The author endorses this characterization of legal systems as part of the book's framework, asserting a structural property of legal systems.

claims.claim: Law is structured being-with.
claims.source_quote: It concludes by defining law as structured being-with, a term that encapsulates its relational ontology.
claims.note: The author explicitly defines law as structured being-with, asserting what kind of entity law is.

claims.claim: Law has a relational ontology.
claims.source_quote: It concludes by defining law as structured being-with, a term that encapsulates its relational ontology.
claims.note: The author asserts that law's ontology is relational, a direct property claim about law's mode of being.

claims.claim: Law is a structured being-with, embodying a relational ontology.
claims.source_quote: It concludes by defining law as structured being-with, a term that encapsulates its relational ontology.
claims.note: Author directly asserts a definition of law as a kind of entity with a specific ontological character.

claims.claim: Legal entities are continuants dependent on recognition.
claims.source_quote: a realist ontology that treats legal entities as continuants dependent on recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind and dependence relation of legal entities.

claims.claim: Obligations are specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: It defines obligations as specifically dependent continuants that emerge from acts of recognition between agents and persist until realized or nullified.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind of obligations.

claims.claim: Obligations emerge from acts of recognition between agents.
claims.source_quote: obligations as specifically dependent continuants that emerge from acts of recognition between agents and persist until realized or nullified.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/generative relation between recognition acts and obligations.

claims.claim: Obligations persist until they are realized or nullified.
claims.source_quote: obligations as specifically dependent continuants that emerge from acts of recognition between agents and persist until realized or nullified.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of obligations concerning their temporal persistence.

claims.claim: Recognition is the ontological act that animates law.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is described as the ontological act that animates law, turning ephemeral social gestures into enduring structures.
claims.note: Author asserts the role/function of recognition in constituting law.

claims.claim: Recognition turns ephemeral social gestures into enduring structures.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is described as the ontological act that animates law, turning ephemeral social gestures into enduring structures.
claims.note: Author asserts that recognition has a transformative ontological function.

claims.claim: Courts, legislatures, and other bodies are repair nodes that stabilize relational fields.
claims.source_quote: treating courts, legislatures, and other bodies as repair nodes that stabilize relational fields.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological role/function of legal institutions.

claims.claim: Law operates through role-bearing individuals whose actions instantiate institutional functions.
claims.source_quote: law operates through role-bearing individuals whose actions instantiate institutional functions.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational claim about how law functions via individuals and roles.

claims.claim: Status functions are dependent continuants that arise from institutional processes.
claims.source_quote: how status functions, Searle's notion that 'X counts as Y in context C', can be modeled ontologically as dependent continuants that arise from institutional processes.
claims.note: Author endorses this ontological modeling as the correct account, committing to status functions being dependent continuants; slightly hedged by 'can be modeled'.

claims.claim: Property rights are relational continuants maintained by legal recognition.
claims.source_quote: showing how property rights are realized as relational continuants maintained by legal recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind and sustaining relation of property rights.

claims.claim: Trials, testimony, and artifacts are processes that produce and sustain juridical truth.
claims.source_quote: mapping how trials, testimony, and artifacts function as processes that produce and sustain juridical truth.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind and function of evidentiary legal processes.

claims.claim: Every judgment or transaction modifies the structure of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: revealing how every judgment or transaction modifies the structure of legal reality.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational/causal claim about judgments and legal reality.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt is the accumulation of unresolved conflicts within a legal system.
claims.source_quote: the concept of contradiction debt is introduced to describe the accumulation of unresolved conflicts within a legal system.
claims.note: Author introduces and asserts this ontological concept as part of their own framework.

claims.claim: Justice is the restoration of structural coherence within the architecture of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Justice is defined not as abstract fairness but as the restoration of structural coherence within the architecture of recognition.
claims.note: Author directly defines justice, asserting its ontological character.

claims.claim: Justice is not an external ideal imposed upon law but law's internal measure of coherence.
claims.source_quote: It argues that justice is not an external ideal imposed upon law but the internal measure of its coherence.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of justice in relation to law.

claims.claim: A just law or institution maintains the integrity of recognition and obligation within its structure.
claims.source_quote: To say that a law or institution is just is to say that it maintains the integrity of recognition and obligation within its structure.
claims.note: Author asserts what it means for a legal entity to have the property of being just.

claims.claim: Persons, institutions, and obligations co-constitute the social world through a network of relations.
claims.source_quote: the network of relations through which persons, institutions, and obligations co-constitute the social world.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological relation among persons, institutions, and obligations.

claims.claim: Law is an ontological structure that stabilizes human coexistence through recognition, obligation, and repair.
claims.source_quote: law is an ontological structure that stabilizes human coexistence through recognition, obligation, and repair.
claims.note: Author explicitly states the book's central thesis, asserting the kind and function of law.

claims.claim: Law endures because it is built to be repaired.
claims.source_quote: It endures because it is built to be mended.
claims.note: Author asserts a disposition/property of law that explains its persistence.

claims.claim: Law is an architecture of social being, not a linguistic or moral construct.
claims.source_quote: By treating law as an architecture of social being rather than as a linguistic or moral construct
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind of law, distinguishing it from linguistic or moral constructs.

claims.claim: Law is an architecture of social being, not merely a linguistic or moral construct.
claims.source_quote: By treating law as an architecture of social being rather than as a linguistic or moral construct, we can understand both its necessity and its fragility.
claims.note: The author positively asserts what law is ontologically—an architecture of social being—contrasting it with rival characterizations.

claims.claim: Law has an enduring framework of being-with that allows justice to take form in the world.
claims.source_quote: the enduring framework of being-with that allows justice to take form in the world.
claims.note: The author asserts that this framework exists and has the function of allowing justice to take form—an ontological claim about law's constitutive structure.

claims.claim: Law endures because it is built to be mended.
claims.source_quote: It endures because it is built to be mended.
claims.note: The author asserts a dispositional property of law—its capacity for repair—as the ground of its endurance.

claims.claim: Law has both necessity and fragility as properties.
claims.source_quote: we can understand both its necessity and its fragility.
claims.note: The author implies law genuinely possesses necessity and fragility; the claim is endorsed as what understanding reveals, not merely a methodological point.

claims.claim: The divergence of moral and formal senses of law marks the beginning of the modern crisis of legal meaning.
claims.source_quote: The divergence of these two senses of law, one moral, the other formal, marks the beginning of the modern crisis of legal meaning.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/role of a historical event (the divergence) as constituting the origin of a crisis — an ontological claim about the nature and origin of the crisis.

claims.claim: The shift from Recht to Gesetz was both the symptom and consequence of loss of metaphysical unity.
claims.source_quote: The shift from Recht to Gesetz, from moral right to enacted statute, was both the symptom and the consequence of this loss of metaphysical unity.
claims.note: The author asserts a causal/relational property of a historical transformation, committing to its ontological status as symptom and consequence.

claims.claim: Kelsen's pure theory reduced law to an abstract system of validity relations without explaining what makes norms real.
claims.source_quote: it reduced law to an abstract system of validity relations without explaining what makes those norms real. The Grundnorm functioned as a logical postulate, not an entity in the world.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of Kelsen's theory (ontological weakness) and asserts that the Grundnorm is a logical postulate, not an entity — an ontological claim.

claims.claim: The Grundnorm is a logical postulate, not an entity in the world.
claims.source_quote: The Grundnorm functioned as a logical postulate, not an entity in the world.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the kind of thing the Grundnorm is — a postulate, not a real-world entity.

claims.claim: Once moral realism was removed from law, the ontological status of law itself evaporated.
claims.source_quote: Once the last trace of moral realism was removed, the ontological status of law itself evaporated. Law became a self-referential structure, complete, formal, and hollow.
claims.note: The author asserts that law's ontological status depends on moral realism — an ontological claim about law's mode of being.

claims.claim: Law became a self-referential structure that is formal and hollow.
claims.source_quote: Law became a self-referential structure, complete, formal, and hollow.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of law under positivism: it is a self-referential, hollow structure — an ontological characterization.

claims.claim: The disjunction between Recht and Gesetz mirrors the split between being and value that characterizes modernity.
claims.source_quote: The disjunction of these terms mirrors the split between being and value, between fact and norm, that characterizes modernity.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational claim: the linguistic disjunction mirrors an ontological split between being and value.

claims.claim: Law has lost its ontological anchor, floating between metaphysical idealism and empirical formalism.
claims.source_quote: The crisis of legal meaning arises precisely from this impasse: law has lost its ontological anchor, floating uneasily between metaphysical idealism and empirical formalism.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of law (loss of ontological anchor) and identifies this as the source of the crisis — a direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: Morality without institutional embodiment is impotent.
claims.source_quote: Morality without institutional embodiment remains impotent; institutions without moral orientation become unintelligible.
claims.note: The author asserts a dispositional property of morality (impotence without institutional embodiment) — an ontological claim about morality's dependence relation.

claims.claim: Institutions without moral orientation are unintelligible.
claims.source_quote: institutions without moral orientation become unintelligible.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of institutions lacking moral orientation — an ontological claim about their intelligibility condition.

claims.claim: The crisis of legal meaning is not primarily semantic or moral but ontological.
claims.source_quote: The crisis of legal meaning, the chapter concludes, is not primarily semantic or moral, but ontological.
claims.note: The author directly asserts the kind/nature of the crisis — an ontological claim about what kind of crisis it is.

claims.claim: Legal entities are real but dependent continuants sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: the chapter prepares the ground for a structural account of law that treats legal entities as real but dependent continuants sustained by recognition.
claims.note: The author endorses this as the view being argued for, committing to legal entities being a subkind of dependent continuants sustained by recognition.

claims.claim: The debates over meaning, validity, and obligation implicitly rely on unarticulated ontological assumptions.
claims.source_quote: The analysis shows that debates over meaning, validity, and obligation implicitly rely on ontological assumptions that remain unarticulated.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational property of jurisprudential debates — they bear a dependence relation to ontological assumptions.

claims.claim: Under the scholastic model, legitimacy is a matter of participation in divine reason.
claims.source_quote: Under the scholastic model, legitimacy was a matter of participation in divine reason; under positivism, it became a matter of compliance with procedure.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of legitimacy under scholasticism (participation in divine reason) as part of an ontological contrast he is drawing and endorsing.

claims.claim: Under positivism, legitimacy is a matter of compliance with procedure.
claims.source_quote: under positivism, it became a matter of compliance with procedure.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of legitimacy under positivism as part of an endorsed contrast.

claims.claim: Positivism replaced the ontological question about law's being with an epistemic question about valid rules.
claims.source_quote: The ontological question, what kind of being does law have?, was replaced by an epistemic one, how can we know which rules are valid?
claims.note: The author asserts a relation of substitution between two kinds of questions, committing to the ontological/epistemic distinction as real.

claims.claim: Jurisprudence was narrowed into an analysis of sources, texts, and commands by this substitution.
claims.source_quote: This substitution narrowed jurisprudence into an analysis of sources, texts, and commands, leaving untouched the deeper issue of how such entities can exist and exert normative force.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/effect of the substitution on jurisprudence as a discipline.

claims.claim: There is a deeper issue of how legal entities exist and exert normative force.
claims.source_quote: leaving untouched the deeper issue of how such entities can exist and exert normative force.
claims.note: The author asserts the existence of a genuine ontological issue concerning law's existence and normative force.

claims.claim: Kelsen's 'purity' is, ontologically speaking, a form of abstraction.
claims.source_quote: What Kelsen called 'purity' was, ontologically speaking, a form of abstraction that cut law off from the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of Kelsen's pure theory: it is a form of abstraction in the ontological sense.

claims.claim: Kelsen's abstraction cut law off from the structures of social reality.
claims.source_quote: a form of abstraction that cut law off from the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author asserts a relation: Kelsenian abstraction severs law from social reality structures.

claims.claim: Structures of social reality give law its life.
claims.source_quote: the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/causal relation: social reality structures are what sustain law's existence or efficacy.

claims.claim: Kelsen's 'purity' was, ontologically, an abstraction that severed law from social reality.
claims.source_quote: What Kelsen called 'purity' was, ontologically speaking, a form of abstraction that cut law off from the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author directly asserts a property of Kelsen's purity—it is an abstraction that severs law from social reality.

claims.claim: Social reality has structures that give law its life.
claims.source_quote: What Kelsen called 'purity' was, ontologically speaking, a form of abstraction that cut law off from the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author commits to social reality having structures that sustain law's existence.

claims.claim: Holmes's view dissolves legality into prediction and psychology.
claims.source_quote: To say, as Holmes did, that law is 'the prophecy of what courts will do in fact' was to dissolve legality into prediction and psychology.
claims.note: The author endorses this characterization as a genuine ontological consequence of Holmes's view.

claims.claim: The Holmes view leaves no room for law's persistence beyond immediate human action.
claims.source_quote: The being of law disappeared into behavior, leaving no room for understanding law's persistence beyond immediate human action.
claims.note: Author asserts this as an ontological deficit of behaviorist legal realism.

claims.claim: Natural law retains moral substance but lacks social grounding.
claims.source_quote: Natural law retained moral substance but lacked social grounding.
claims.note: Author's own summary assessment, attributing a property to natural law as a tradition.

claims.claim: Positivism achieves procedural clarity but loses existential depth.
claims.source_quote: Positivism achieved procedural clarity but lost existential depth.
claims.note: Author's own evaluative claim attributing properties to positivism as a tradition.

claims.claim: Realism captures practice but abandons structure.
claims.source_quote: Realism captured practice but abandoned structure.
claims.note: Author's own property-attribution to legal realism.

claims.claim: Modern jurisprudence became epistemology without ontology.
claims.source_quote: Jurisprudence had become epistemology without ontology.
claims.note: Author directly asserts this characterization of modern jurisprudence's ontological status.

claims.claim: The crisis of legal meaning has a double origin: historical and conceptual.
claims.source_quote: The crisis of legal meaning thus has a double origin: historical and conceptual.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence and dual nature of the crisis of legal meaning.

claims.claim: The medieval unity of moral and legal order dissolved historically.
claims.source_quote: Historically, it arose from the dissolution of the medieval unity of moral and legal order, a unity symbolized by the harmony of Recht and Gesetz.
claims.note: Author asserts a historical ontological fact about the dissolution of a prior unity.

claims.claim: Modern theories of law oscillate between severed poles of moral and procedural order.
claims.source_quote: Conceptually, it persists because modern theories of law continue to oscillate between these severed poles.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational/structural property of modern legal theories.

claims.claim: Law is the relational architecture that makes both command and moral ideal possible.
claims.source_quote: …the redefinition of law not as command or ideal, but as the relational architecture that makes both possible.
claims.note: Author positively asserts a definition/ontological characterization of law.

claims.claim: Moral, procedural, and institutional dimensions of law coexist as parts of a single structure of recognition.
claims.source_quote: …by showing how moral, procedural, and institutional dimensions coexist as parts of a single structure of recognition.
claims.note: Author endorses this as the task's grounding claim—a direct ontological assertion about law's structure.

claims.claim: An unjust law continues to exist as a social entity even when it violates the moral order.
claims.source_quote: It denies the existence of legal entities that clearly operate within the social world, even when they violate the moral order.
claims.note: Author asserts that unjust laws are real existing entities operating in the social world.

claims.claim: The maxim 'lex iniusta non est lex' functions as a moral verdict, not an ontological description.
claims.source_quote: Thus, the maxim lex iniusta non est lex ('an unjust law is no law at all') functions more as a moral verdict than as an ontological description.
claims.note: Author directly asserts the ontological status—or lack thereof—of this maxim.

claims.claim: Injustice deprives law of legitimacy, not of existence.
claims.source_quote: It asserts that injustice deprives law of legitimacy, not of existence.
claims.note: Author endorses this distinction between legitimacy and existence as an ontological claim.

claims.claim: The moral and the ontological are two distinct orders of inquiry.
claims.source_quote: But in making legitimacy the criterion of being, it confuses two distinct orders of inquiry: the moral and the ontological.
claims.note: Author asserts the distinctness of the moral and ontological orders.

claims.claim: Natural law theory confuses moral evaluation with ontological description by making legitimacy the criterion of being.
claims.source_quote: But in making legitimacy the criterion of being, it confuses two distinct orders of inquiry: the moral and the ontological. The question 'is it right?' becomes indistinguishable from 'is it real?'
claims.note: Author directly asserts that natural law commits a category error with ontological consequences.

claims.claim: Finnis's natural law theory cannot explain what law is when it fails to be just.
claims.source_quote: It can tell us what law ought to be, but not what it is when it fails.
claims.note: Author asserts a descriptive/ontological inadequacy of Finnis's theory.

claims.claim: Unjust legal systems exist and function as legal systems, contradicting accounts that deny their legality.
claims.source_quote: Either they are not truly law, contradicting empirical observation, or they are law but only defectively so, inviting an unstable distinction between 'real' and 'deficient' being.
claims.note: Author implies unjust legal systems genuinely exist and function; the 'contradicting empirical observation' clause signals the author's endorsement of this premise.

claims.claim: Apartheid statutes, segregation laws, and Nazi racial statutes were real legal entities.
claims.source_quote: These regimes generated vast bodies of law, codified, enforced, and institutionally recognized... They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: The author asserts ontological reality of these laws, explicitly committing to their existence as law despite moral bankruptcy.

claims.claim: Apartheid, segregation, and Nazi statutes organized power.
claims.source_quote: They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/relational property of these legal regimes — they organized power.

claims.claim: Apartheid, segregation, and Nazi statutes distributed rights and duties.
claims.source_quote: They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional property of these legal regimes — they distributed rights and duties.

claims.claim: Apartheid, segregation, and Nazi statutes structured daily life.
claims.source_quote: They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/relational property of these legal regimes — they structured daily life.

claims.claim: Natural law theory cannot adequately describe law that fails morally.
claims.source_quote: It can tell us what law ought to be, but not what it is when it fails.
claims.note: The author asserts a property (descriptive inadequacy) of natural law theory as a kind of legal theory.

claims.claim: Denying legal status to morally bankrupt statutes does violence to ontology.
claims.source_quote: To say that their statutes were 'not law' may satisfy moral conscience but does violence to ontology.
claims.note: The author asserts that classifying these statutes as non-law is ontologically incorrect, committing to their status as law.

claims.claim: Law is a form of structured being-with others.
claims.source_quote: Law as Structured Being-With
claims.note: Section heading used in author's own framework signals an ontological claim about the nature of law as a mode of being-with.

claims.claim: Obligations are entities with an ontological status.
claims.source_quote: The Ontological Status of Obligation
claims.note: Section heading in author's own framework asserts obligations have ontological status, implying they are real entities.

claims.claim: Recognition is an ontological event.
claims.source_quote: Recognition as Ontological Event
claims.note: Section heading in author's framework asserts recognition is a type of ontological event.

claims.claim: Legal reality is created and can be extinguished.
claims.source_quote: The Creation and Extinction of Legal Reality
claims.note: Section heading asserts that legal reality undergoes creation and extinction, implying it is a real, temporally bounded entity.

claims.claim: Institutions are networks of roles.
claims.source_quote: Institutions as Role Networks
claims.note: Section heading in the author's own framework directly asserts an ontological claim about the nature of institutions.

claims.claim: Law does not act; people act in roles.
claims.source_quote: The Law Does Not Act, People Do, in Roles
claims.note: Explicit ontological claim about agency: law lacks agency; persons acting in roles are the agents.

claims.claim: Institutional roles differ from bearer-independent functions.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Roles vs. Bearer-Independent Functions
claims.note: Section heading asserts an ontological distinction between two kinds of entity.

claims.claim: Roles are relational entities.
claims.source_quote: Roles as relational entities
claims.note: Section heading in author's framework directly asserts an ontological claim about roles.

claims.claim: Roles are not reducible to behavior.
claims.source_quote: Roles Are Not Reducible to Behavior
claims.note: Explicit ontological claim about the irreducibility of roles.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant.
claims.source_quote: Property as Relational Continuant
claims.note: Section heading in author's framework directly asserts an ontological classification of property.

claims.claim: Value is ontologically dependent.
claims.source_quote: The Dependence of Value
claims.note: Section heading asserts value has ontological dependence on other entities.

claims.claim: Legal facts are procedurally realized.
claims.source_quote: Procedural Realization of Facts
claims.note: Section heading asserts legal facts come into being through procedural realization.

claims.claim: Hart's secondary rules involve ontological dependence.
claims.source_quote: Hart's Secondary Rules and Ontological Dependence
claims.note: Section heading asserts an ontological relation (dependence) pertaining to Hart's secondary rules, endorsed by the author.

claims.claim: Obligations arise from acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: How obligations arise from recognition
claims.note: Section heading in author's framework asserts a generative ontological relation between recognition and obligations.

claims.claim: Obligations and claims are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Dependent continuants that shape the field of legal possibility
claims.note: Author classifies obligations, claims, and permissions as dependent continuants in the BFO sense.

claims.claim: Institutions have recognitive powers and function as aggregations.
claims.source_quote: Institutions as aggregations with recognitive powers
claims.note: Author's own framework asserts two ontological properties of institutions: they are aggregations and they have recognitive powers.

claims.claim: Justice is the structural integrity of legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: Justice as Structural Integrity
claims.note: Section heading in author's framework asserts an ontological identification of justice with structural integrity.

claims.claim: Justice is relational coherence.
claims.source_quote: Justice as relational coherence
claims.note: Author directly asserts an ontological characterization of justice as relational coherence.

claims.claim: Repair is an ontological process.
claims.source_quote: Ontology of Repair as a Process
claims.note: Author classifies repair as a process in his ontological framework.

claims.claim: Smart contracts involve ontological compression and loss of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Smart Contracts: Ontological Compression and the Loss of Recognition
claims.note: Author asserts ontological properties specific to smart contracts within his framework.

claims.claim: Algorithmic adjudication involves pseudo-recognition and norm drift.
claims.source_quote: Algorithmic Adjudication: Pseudo-Recognition and Norm Drift
claims.note: Author asserts ontological properties of algorithmic adjudication within his framework.

claims.claim: Roles are relational positions within legal structures.
claims.source_quote: Roles as relational positions
claims.note: Author directly asserts a classification of roles as relational positions.

claims.claim: Roles are distinct from their bearers.
claims.source_quote: Bearers vs. roles
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological distinction between role bearers and roles themselves.

claims.claim: Roles exhibit continuity and stability across different bearers.
claims.source_quote: Continuity and stability across roles
claims.note: Author asserts a dispositional/structural property of roles: they persist continuously across bearer changes.

claims.claim: Law is an articulated field of relations.
claims.source_quote: Law as an Articulated Field of Relations
claims.note: Author directly asserts an ontological characterization of law as a relational field.

claims.claim: Coherence is the condition of justice.
claims.source_quote: Coherence as the Condition of Justice
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological dependency: justice depends on coherence as its necessary condition.

claims.claim: Moral and legal obligations differ at the structural level.
claims.source_quote: The difference between moral and legal obligations at a structural level
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological distinction between two kinds of obligation.

claims.claim: Law is a structured domain of social reality.
claims.source_quote: many of its central debates, about validity, obligation, and authority, could be clarified if we treated law as a structured domain of social reality.
claims.note: The author asserts this as the basis of his framework, not merely as a hypothesis to consider.

claims.claim: Law is a real system of interdependent entities.
claims.source_quote: a way of understanding, and of teaching others to understand, law as a real system of interdependent entities.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature of law.

claims.claim: Roles, institutions, and obligations are parts of a coherent architecture.
claims.source_quote: to grasp how roles, institutions, and obligations fit together as parts of a coherent architecture.
claims.note: Asserts a part-of or compositional relation among legal entities.

claims.claim: Law is a structured field of relations sustained by recognition, obligation, and repair.
claims.source_quote: The approach developed here encourages students and readers to see law as a structured field of relations, sustained by recognition, obligation, and repair.
claims.note: Positive ontological characterization of law's nature and what sustains it.

claims.claim: Law's authority arises from the ontological coherence of its structures.
claims.source_quote: Law's authority, on this view, is not mysterious; it arises from the ontological coherence of its structures and the stability of the recognitions that sustain them.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding relation: authority is produced by structural ontological coherence.

claims.claim: Law's authority arises from the stability of the recognitions that sustain its structures.
claims.source_quote: Law's authority, on this view, is not mysterious; it arises from the ontological coherence of its structures and the stability of the recognitions that sustain them.
claims.note: Asserts that recognitions play a sustaining role in law's authority—a relational ontological claim.

claims.claim: Law persists, fails, and repairs itself as a human institution.
claims.source_quote: understand law's reality as a human institution, how it persists, fails, and repairs itself.
claims.note: Asserts that law is a human institution with properties of persistence, failure, and self-repair.

claims.claim: Law is a human institution.
claims.source_quote: understand law's reality as a human institution
claims.note: Direct assertion that law belongs to the kind 'human institution'.

claims.claim: Jurisprudence lacks an adequate account of law's being.
claims.source_quote: what was missing in jurisprudence was not another moral or linguistic theory, but an account of law's being.
claims.note: Asserts a property (absence of ontological account) of the discipline of jurisprudence.

claims.claim: Law is a real domain of social being.
claims.source_quote: The chapter proposes a structural ontological approach that treats law as a real domain of social being constituted by relations of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: The author asserts law's mode of existence as a real domain of social being, an ontological claim about what law is.

claims.claim: Law is constituted by relations of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: treats law as a real domain of social being constituted by relations of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive relational structure that defines law's being—an ontological claim about law's composition.

claims.claim: Law is structured being-with.
