claims.source_quote: Law is defined as structured being-with: an architecture of dependent relations that persists through institutional recognition and repair.
claims.note: The author explicitly defines law as a kind of entity ('structured being-with'), asserting its ontological character.

claims.claim: Law is an architecture of dependent relations.
claims.source_quote: Law is defined as structured being-with: an architecture of dependent relations that persists through institutional recognition and repair.
claims.note: Asserts that law's structure consists of dependent relations—a claim about law's ontological composition.

claims.claim: Law persists through institutional recognition and repair.
claims.source_quote: an architecture of dependent relations that persists through institutional recognition and repair.
claims.note: Asserts a property/disposition of law regarding the conditions of its persistence—an ontological claim about law's mode of continuity.

claims.claim: Traditional jurisprudential approaches have left law's mode of existence under-examined.
claims.source_quote: traditional jurisprudential approaches, including natural law, legal positivism, and legal realism, have focused on law's authority, content, or social effects while leaving its mode of existence under-examined.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a substantive finding about the state of jurisprudence, implying law has a mode of existence that is a genuine ontological matter requiring examination.

claims.claim: Nazi racial statutes were real structures that organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.source_quote: They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological reality of unjust legal regimes as structures with functional properties.

claims.claim: A morally defective law does not vanish from social reality.
claims.source_quote: A morally defective law may lack legitimacy, but it does not vanish from the fabric of social reality.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the persistence of unjust law in social reality.

claims.claim: An unjust law persists as a malformed but effective structure—an ontological pathology.
claims.source_quote: It persists as a malformed but effective structure, an ontological pathology.
claims.note: Author asserts that unjust law is a kind of entity with a determinate ontological status: a pathological structure.

claims.claim: Injustice is a distortion within being itself, not an absence of being.
claims.source_quote: Its existence is not negated by injustice; rather, injustice appears as a distortion within being itself, a contradiction within the structure of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: Direct claim about the ontological character of injustice as distortion rather than nonexistence.

claims.claim: Moral failure does not entail ontological nullity.
claims.source_quote: To grasp this distinction is to see that moral failure does not entail ontological nullity.
claims.note: Explicit ontological claim asserting independence of existence from moral status.

claims.claim: Unjust law is a misalignment—a breakdown in the coherence of recognition—not an absence.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological perspective, unjust law is not an absence but a misalignment, a breakdown in the coherence of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological character of unjust law as misalignment rather than nonexistence.

claims.claim: Unjust law continues to function as law because institutions and agents acknowledge it as binding.
claims.source_quote: It continues to function as law because institutions and agents still acknowledge it as binding.
claims.note: Ontological claim about the condition sustaining unjust law's existence and function.

claims.claim: Injustice is the persistence of law under conditions of disordered recognition.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, injustice is the persistence of law under conditions of disordered recognition.
claims.note: Author provides an explicit ontological definition of injustice.

claims.claim: Law is oriented toward justice and fulfills its function only when it accords with right reason.
claims.source_quote: It concedes to Aquinas and Finnis that law is oriented toward justice, that it fulfills its function only when it accords with right reason.
claims.note: Author concedes this point as part of his own endorsed position, even while rejecting the further inference; constitutes an endorsed ontological-teleological claim.

claims.claim: Injustice is an ontological failure of alignment in which the structure of law remains intact but internally inconsistent.
claims.source_quote: Instead, it treats injustice as an ontological failure of alignment, a condition in which the structure of law remains intact but internally inconsistent.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological status of injustice as misalignment within a persisting structure.

claims.claim: Law can be both real and wrong simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Law, in this sense, can be both real and wrong.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim asserting the co-possibility of existence and moral defect in law.

claims.claim: Law's power derives from its structure as an institution of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: Law's power, for good or ill, derives from its structure as an institution of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: Author asserts a structural-ontological claim about the source of law's power.

claims.claim: Even immoral laws are woven into the social ontology they corrupt.
claims.source_quote: To understand that structure is to see that even immoral laws are woven into the social ontology they corrupt.
claims.note: Author asserts that immoral laws bear a constitutive relation to social ontology.

claims.claim: Law is an institution of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: Law's power, for good or ill, derives from its structure as an institution of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: Implicit kind-claim: law is a kind of institution defined by recognition and obligation.

claims.claim: Positivism reduced law to an artifact of will, habit, or linguistic convention.
claims.source_quote: It reduced law to an artifact of will, habit, or linguistic convention, something that exists only because people behave as if it does.
claims.note: Author is characterizing positivism critically, endorsing this as an accurate (and deficient) ontological reduction; used to support his own positive ontological view.

claims.claim: Positivism's conception of law is ontologically thin, explaining rule recognition without explaining what kind of being rules are.
claims.source_quote: The result is a conception of law that is analytically clear but ontologically thin: a model that explains how rules are recognized without ever explaining what kind of being rules are.
claims.note: Author endorses this as a genuine ontological deficiency of positivism, making a claim about the ontological inadequacy of positivist accounts.

claims.claim: Hart's rule of recognition describes how legal actors identify valid law but does not explain what law is.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition describes how legal actors know what valid law is; it does not explain what law is.
claims.note: Author asserts a distinction between epistemological description and ontological explanation, endorsing this as a genuine gap in Hart's account.

claims.claim: The positivist separation thesis is primarily an ontological omission, not a moral claim.
claims.source_quote: The positivist separation thesis, that the existence of law is one thing and its merit another, has been widely misunderstood as a moral claim, but it is primarily an ontological omission.
claims.note: Author explicitly classifies the separation thesis ontologically, asserting its nature as an omission.

claims.claim: If law is merely convention, the distinction between its existence and its value collapses.
claims.source_quote: If law is nothing more than a convention or a practice, then the distinction between its existence and its value collapses: conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.note: Author endorses this as a genuine ontological consequence of the positivist reduction.

claims.claim: Conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.source_quote: conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.note: Author asserts this as an ontological fact about conventions, used to ground his critique of positivism.

claims.claim: If law is a convention or practice, its existence and value cannot be distinguished.
claims.source_quote: If law is nothing more than a convention or a practice, then the distinction between its existence and its value collapses: conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.note: The author asserts an ontological consequence: conventions lack independent reality, so existence/value collapse for law-as-convention.

claims.claim: Conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.source_quote: conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the mode of existence of conventions.

claims.claim: If law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality, its being cannot be separated from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.source_quote: if law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality, then its being cannot be divorced from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.note: The author presents this as a conditional, but asserts it as a genuine ontological implication he endorses in his critique of positivism.

claims.claim: Positivist deflation of law's ontology undermines positivism's own analytic aims.
claims.source_quote: The positivist deflation of law's ontology thus undermines its own analytic aims.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts a relational/functional claim about positivism's ontological commitments and their self-defeating character.

claims.claim: Positivism explains validity at the cost of existence.
claims.source_quote: It explains validity at the cost of existence.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim: positivism's account of legal validity fails to account for legal existence, asserting a trade-off between two ontological categories.

claims.claim: Legal systems are structures: organized continuities of human recognition and participation.
claims.source_quote: They are structures, organized continuities of human recognition and participation that give shape to social reality.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the kind of entity legal systems are.

claims.claim: Legal entities (statutes, rights, courts) endure, interact, and change in lawful ways.
claims.source_quote: They endure, interact, and change in lawful ways. Their being cannot be reduced to words on paper or the fleeting intentions of their makers.
claims.note: Author asserts properties of legal entities: endurance, interaction, lawful change.

claims.claim: The being of legal entities cannot be reduced to words on paper or makers' intentions.
claims.source_quote: Their being cannot be reduced to words on paper or the fleeting intentions of their makers.
claims.note: Ontological claim about the irreducibility of legal entities.

claims.claim: Law is a system of interdependent entities, roles, obligations, processes, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: It is to study law not as a set of texts or behaviors but as a system of interdependent entities, roles, obligations, processes, and institutions, that form a coherent architecture.
claims.note: Author asserts the composition and kind of law as a system.

claims.claim: Legal phenomena arise from acts of recognition and persist as structured continuants in the social world.
claims.source_quote: Applied to law, these distinctions reveal how legal phenomena arise from acts of recognition and persist as structured continuants within the social world.
claims.note: Asserts the origin and mode of persistence of legal phenomena as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: An obligation is a specific relation between agents that constrains possibilities of action.
claims.source_quote: An obligation is a specific relation between agents that constrains possibilities of action.
claims.note: Direct ontological definition of obligation as a relational entity with a constraining property.

claims.claim: A court is an institutional node that realizes functions through role-bearing persons.
claims.source_quote: a court is an institutional node that realizes functions through role-bearing persons.
claims.note: Asserts what kind of entity a court is and how it realizes its functions.

claims.claim: Justice is the coherence achieved when legal relations among agents, norms, and institutions are harmonized.
claims.source_quote: justice is the coherence achieved when these relations are harmonized.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological characterization of justice as a property or state of a relational structure.

claims.claim: Obligations, authority, institutions, and justice name real structures of dependence.
claims.source_quote: Terms such as obligation, authority, institution, and justice are not only moral or linguistic constructs; they name real structures of dependence.
claims.note: Author asserts these are real entities (structures of dependence), not merely linguistic or moral constructs.

claims.claim: Legal systems include socially sustained continuants that depend on collective recognition but maintain integrity once established.
claims.source_quote: They point to the existence of socially sustained continuants, entities that depend on collective recognition but maintain integrity once established.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of a specific kind of entity (socially sustained continuants) in legal systems.

claims.claim: Legal continuants fall under the BFO category of specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: This continuity, captured in the BFO category of specifically dependent continuants, allows law to have both temporal depth and structural stability.
claims.note: Author endorses classifying legal continuants as specifically dependent continuants, asserting a subkind relation.

claims.claim: Law is part of the real world, analyzable as a coherent system capable of repair, collapse, and rebirth.
claims.source_quote: It treats law as part of the real world, subject to analysis in the same way we analyze biological organisms or technical systems.
claims.note: Asserts law's ontological status as part of the real world with specific properties.

claims.claim: Law is the most visible architecture of the coexistence of persons.
claims.source_quote: Law is the most visible architecture of that coexistence.
claims.note: Asserts a property and role of law relative to social being-with.

claims.claim: Legal systems exist as identifiable structures that persist through time.
claims.source_quote: still leave us unable to say in what sense legal systems exist, or why they persist as identifiable structures through time.
claims.note: Author treats this as the target explanandum, implicitly asserting that legal systems do persist as identifiable structures.

claims.claim: Norms, roles, and institutions interact to form a coherent system that composes law.
claims.source_quote: Its goal is to describe the architecture of legal being: how norms, roles, and institutions interact to form a coherent system capable of repair, collapse, and rebirth.
claims.note: Asserts compositional and relational claims about what law is built from.

claims.claim: Natural law theory presupposes that moral facts exist independently of human decree.
claims.source_quote: It presupposes that moral facts exist independently and that law's reality depends on their recognition.
claims.note: The author attributes this presupposition to natural law theory as part of his own critical analysis, asserting it as a genuine ontological commitment that theory makes.

claims.claim: Natural law theory makes law's reality depend on the recognition of independently existing moral facts.
claims.source_quote: It presupposes that moral facts exist independently and that law's reality depends on their recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a structural feature of natural law theory's ontology, committing to it as an accurate characterization.

claims.claim: Natural law theory collapses law into ethics ontologically.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this collapses law into ethics.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts this as his own ontological verdict on natural law theory, not merely reporting another's view.

claims.claim: Natural law theory blurs the boundary between what is and what ought to be.
claims.source_quote: this view blurs the boundary between what is and what ought to be.
claims.note: The author endorses this criticism (introduced via 'critics from Hobbes onward') as his own assessment of the theory's ontological defect.

claims.claim: Conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.source_quote: conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the mode of existence of conventions.

claims.claim: Law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality.
claims.source_quote: if law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality, then its being cannot be divorced from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a conditional whose consequent he endorses; the antecedent is stated approvingly to criticize positivism.

claims.claim: Law's being cannot be divorced from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.source_quote: if law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality, then its being cannot be divorced from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.note: Ontological claim about the constitutive role of normative relations in law's existence.

claims.claim: Legal systems survive the death of rulers and the replacement of officials.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems survive the death of rulers and the replacement of officials; statutes remain binding long after their authors are forgotten.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of legal systems as entities.

claims.claim: Statutes remain binding long after their authors are forgotten.
claims.source_quote: statutes remain binding long after their authors are forgotten.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the temporal persistence and binding property of statutes.

claims.claim: Acceptance is a relational act that depends on structures of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: Acceptance is itself a relational act that depends on structures of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: Ontological claim about the relational nature and dependency structure of acceptance.

claims.claim: Commands and rules are nodes within a network of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Commands and rules are not isolated events but nodes within a network of dependent continuants, obligations, roles, institutions, that together constitute the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and relational structure of commands and rules.

claims.claim: Obligations, roles, and institutions together constitute the legal domain.
claims.source_quote: nodes within a network of dependent continuants, obligations, roles, institutions, that together constitute the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts that these kinds of entities are constituents of the legal domain.

claims.claim: When a court issues a judgment, it brings into being new relational entities.
claims.source_quote: When a court issues a judgment, it does more than produce sounds or marks on paper; it brings into being new relational entities: rights, duties, and statuses that persist across time.
claims.note: Asserts the creative ontological function of judicial acts and the existence of resulting entities.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and statuses are relational entities that persist across time.
claims.source_quote: it brings into being new relational entities: rights, duties, and statuses that persist across time.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and temporal persistence of rights, duties, and statuses.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and statuses are not reducible to the psychological states of those who recognize them.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not reducible to the psychological states of those who recognize them.
claims.note: Asserts an irreducibility claim about these legal entities' ontological status.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and statuses have a structured mode of existence analogous to corporations or marriages.
claims.source_quote: They have a structured mode of existence analogous to other social continuants, like corporations or marriages.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership and structural property of legal entities.

claims.claim: The obligation to follow rules arises from a network of relational dependencies.
claims.source_quote: The obligation to follow rules is not generated by belief or habit; it arises from the network of relational dependencies that make those rules what they are.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological ground of legal obligation in relational structure.

claims.claim: Legal obligation is not generated by belief or habit.
claims.source_quote: The obligation to follow rules is not generated by belief or habit; it arises from the network of relational dependencies that make those rules what they are.
claims.note: Negative ontological claim about the source of legal obligation.

claims.claim: Rule-following by officials is possible only because law already exists as a structured domain of recognition.
claims.source_quote: such rule-following is possible only because law already exists as a structured domain of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts ontological priority of law's structured existence over official practice.

claims.claim: Law exists as a structured domain of recognition.
claims.source_quote: law already exists as a structured domain of recognition.
claims.note: Direct assertion of law's ontological status and character.

claims.claim: Legal realism reduces law to observable behavior and subjective judgment.
claims.source_quote: by reducing law to observable behavior and subjective judgment, realism ultimately erased the very structure it set out to explain.
claims.note: Author's characterization of legal realism's ontological move, stated critically as true.

claims.claim: Legal realism cannot account for the persistence, coherence, or ontology of law.
claims.source_quote: realism ultimately erased the very structure it set out to explain. What began as a critique of abstraction ended as a theory that could not account for the persistence, coherence, or ontology of law at all.
claims.note: Author's own negative assessment of realism's ontological adequacy.

claims.claim: Legal realism leaves law ontologically hollow by reducing norms to psychological or linguistic effects.
claims.source_quote: Such theories anticipated later linguistic and performative turns in philosophy but left law ontologically hollow.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of law-as-conceived-by-realism: ontological hollowness. This is an ontological claim about the status of law under that framework, endorsed by the author.

claims.claim: When norms are reduced to psychological or linguistic effects, their durability and coherence become inexplicable.
claims.source_quote: Once norms are reduced to psychological or linguistic effects, their durability and coherence become inexplicable.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational/property claim: norms have durability and coherence that cannot be explained if reduced to mere effects. This implies norms have genuine ontological structure.

claims.claim: Legal realism sacrifices an account of law's structure.
claims.source_quote: Legal realism's behaviorism achieved valuable clarity about how law functions in practice, but it did so by sacrificing an account of law's structure.
claims.note: The author asserts that law has a structure, and that legal realism fails to account for it — a positive ontological commitment to law having structure.

claims.claim: Natural law presupposes that moral facts exist independently of human recognition.
claims.source_quote: It presupposes that moral facts exist independently and that law's reality depends on their recognition.
claims.note: The author attributes this presupposition to natural law and treats it as a genuine ontological commitment being analyzed critically.

claims.claim: Unjust legal systems persist as effective institutions even when morality rejects their acts.
claims.source_quote: It fails to account for the persistence of unjust yet effective legal systems, or for the brute social fact that legal institutions endure even when morality recoils from their acts.
claims.note: The author asserts the existence and persistence of unjust yet effective legal institutions as a brute social fact.

claims.claim: Legal institutions are brute social facts.
claims.source_quote: the brute social fact that legal institutions endure even when morality recoils from their acts.
claims.note: The author characterizes legal institutions' persistence as a brute social fact, asserting their ontological status.

claims.claim: Natural law confuses the conditions for legitimacy with the conditions for existence.
claims.source_quote: Natural law's strength, its moral confidence, is thus its weakness as ontology: it confuses the conditions for legitimacy with the conditions for existence.
claims.note: The author directly asserts this as a flaw in natural law's ontology.

claims.claim: Positivism describes how norms are validated but not what kind of thing a norm must be to exist.
claims.source_quote: Positivism describes how norms are validated, but not what kind of thing a norm must be to exist at all.
claims.note: The author asserts a genuine ontological gap in positivism's account.

claims.claim: Legal realism deprives law of ontological depth by reducing it to observable behavior or psychological expectation.
claims.source_quote: Realism, for all its descriptive power, deprives law of ontological depth. It mistakes the manifestations of legal order for its underlying form.
claims.note: The author asserts that law has ontological depth distinct from its behavioral manifestations.

claims.claim: Law has an underlying form distinct from its behavioral or psychological manifestations.
claims.source_quote: It mistakes the manifestations of legal order for its underlying form.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal order has an underlying form, an ontological claim about law's constitution.

claims.claim: Law has an architecture that is not captured by natural law, positivism, or realism alone.
claims.source_quote: Each of these traditions, in its way, has described the appearance of law but not its architecture.
claims.note: The author asserts law has an architecture, implying a real structural constitution beyond appearances.

claims.claim: Structural realism holds that what is most real are the relations connecting entities, not the individual objects themselves.
claims.source_quote: it holds that what is most real are not the individual objects of experience but the relations that connect them. Entities derive their identity from their place within a structure of dependencies.
claims.note: The author endorses structural realism and its core ontological claim about relations being primary.

claims.claim: Entities derive their identity from their place within a structure of dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Entities derive their identity from their place within a structure of dependencies.
claims.note: The author asserts this as the correct ontological account of entity identity, endorsing structural realism.

claims.claim: Rights, obligations, and institutions exist as interrelated continuants sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: structural realism suggests that rights, obligations, and institutions exist not as isolated facts but as interrelated continuants sustained by recognition.
claims.note: The author endorses this ontological characterization of legal entities as part of the structural realist framework.

claims.claim: A statute has meaning because it stands in determinate relations to other norms, institutional roles, and social acts of acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: A statute has meaning because it stands in determinate relations to other norms, to institutional roles, and to social acts of acknowledgment.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational ontological account of statutory meaning.

claims.claim: A court's authority is a stable node in a network of relational dependencies.
claims.source_quote: A court's authority is real not as a psychological disposition or moral ideal but as a stable node in this network of relational dependencies.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological status of judicial authority as a relational node.

claims.claim: Recognition, obligation, and institutional function are ontological categories.
claims.source_quote: These are not abstractions but ontological categories, specifically dependent continuants that emerge when agents acknowledge one another's capacities and duties within organized systems.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts these are ontological categories, not mere abstractions.

claims.claim: Recognition, obligation, and institutional function are specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: specifically dependent continuants that emerge when agents acknowledge one another's capacities and duties within organized systems.
claims.note: The author asserts a specific ontological kind (dependent continuants) for these legal categories.

claims.claim: The legal world is composed of patterns of recognition instantiated in enduring institutional forms.
claims.source_quote: The legal world is thus composed of patterns of recognition instantiated in enduring institutional forms.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological composition of the legal world.

claims.claim: Law's persistence depends on the coherence of relational structures rather than on any particular actor's will.
claims.source_quote: Its persistence depends on the coherence of these relations rather than on the will of any particular actor.
claims.note: The author asserts what grounds legal persistence ontologically.

claims.claim: Legal entities are relations rather than substances.
claims.source_quote: Because its entities are relations rather than substances, legal order can evolve without ceasing to be itself.
claims.note: The author directly asserts the ontological kind of legal entities.

claims.claim: Institutions adapt as roles and obligations are reconfigured while the structural integrity of law persists.
claims.source_quote: Institutions adapt as roles and obligations are reconfigured, yet the structural integrity of law persists so long as the network of recognition remains coherent.
claims.note: The author asserts the conditions under which structural legal identity persists through change.

claims.claim: Law is distinct from mere custom or habit by its capacity for repair and reestablishment of order.
claims.source_quote: This capacity for repair, for reestablishing order after disruption, is what distinguishes law from mere custom or habit.
claims.note: The author asserts a property that distinguishes law as a kind from custom or habit.

claims.claim: Law is a real, evolving architecture of human coexistence.
claims.source_quote: what it is, a real, evolving architecture of human coexistence.
claims.note: The author asserts what law is ontologically.

claims.claim: Law is one of the world's enduring structures.
claims.source_quote: By situating jurisprudence within ontology, we recover law's reality as one of the world's enduring structures.
claims.note: The author asserts that law is an enduring structure in the world, an ontological claim about its status.

claims.claim: Roles, obligations, and institutions function as interlocking continuants within a dynamic system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Using the categories of BFO, we will map how roles, obligations, and institutions function as interlocking continuants within a dynamic system of recognition.
claims.note: The author presents this as the framework to be deployed, implying ontological commitment, though framed partly as a methodological program.

claims.claim: Legal facts are dependent continuants produced through structured processes.
claims.source_quote: Legal facts are modeled as dependent continuants produced through structured processes rather than mere descriptions of reality.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of legal facts as a kind of entity (dependent continuants).

claims.claim: Law transforms events, utterances, and actions into facts with normative and institutional significance.
claims.source_quote: Law operates by transforming the raw material of the social world (events, utterances, and actions) into structured facts that possess normative and institutional significance.
claims.note: Asserts a relation (transformation) between brute occurrences and legally salient entities.

claims.claim: These transformations require recognition, authority, and institutional process.
claims.source_quote: These transformations do not occur spontaneously; they require the mediation of recognition, authority, and institutional process.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition (property/relation) for the ontological transformation to legal facts.

claims.claim: A brute fact becomes a legal fact only when incorporated into the network of recognition constituting the legal domain.
claims.source_quote: What begins as a brute fact, a physical or social event apprehensible by perception, becomes a legal fact only when it is incorporated into the network of recognition that constitutes the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological condition for a brute fact's transition to a legal fact.

claims.claim: A signed document, spoken verdict, and legislative decree begin as brute occurrences in space and time.
claims.source_quote: A signed document, a spoken verdict, a legislative decree, all begin as brute occurrences in space and time, yet each acquires the status of a fact of law through a structured sequence of ontological transitions.
claims.note: Asserts the initial ontological kind of these entities.

claims.claim: A signed document, spoken verdict, and legislative decree each acquire the status of a legal fact through ontological transitions.
claims.source_quote: A signed document, a spoken verdict, a legislative decree, all begin as brute occurrences in space and time, yet each acquires the status of a fact of law through a structured sequence of ontological transitions.
claims.note: Asserts a property (legal fact status) borne by these entities after transformation.

claims.claim: From a BFO standpoint, transformation from brute to legal fact consists in adding a dependent continuant to an independent entity or process.
claims.source_quote: From the standpoint of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), the transformation from brute to legal fact can be described as the addition of a dependent continuant, a relational property sustained by recognition, to an independent entity or process.
claims.note: The author endorses this BFO-based ontological description as the framework of the chapter.

claims.claim: The dependent continuant added in legal transformation is a relational property sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: the transformation from brute to legal fact can be described as the addition of a dependent continuant, a relational property sustained by recognition, to an independent entity or process.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the dependent continuant: it is relational and sustained by recognition.

claims.claim: A brute fact, as a physical or social occurrence, is an independent continuant or occurrent.
claims.source_quote: The brute fact, as a physical or social occurrence, is an independent continuant or occurrent: it exists regardless of social acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of brute facts within BFO.

claims.claim: Brute facts exist regardless of social acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: The brute fact, as a physical or social occurrence, is an independent continuant or occurrent: it exists regardless of social acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts a property (independence from recognition) of brute facts.

claims.claim: When occurrences are recognized within an institutional framework, they acquire properties such as legality, validity, and enforceability.
claims.source_quote: When these occurrences are recognized within an institutional framework, they acquire new properties such as legality, validity, and enforceability, that depend on ongoing recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition confers new properties on entities.

claims.claim: Legal properties such as legality, validity, and enforceability depend on ongoing recognition.
claims.source_quote: they acquire new properties such as legality, validity, and enforceability, that depend on ongoing recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between legal properties and recognition.

claims.claim: Recognition does not change the underlying physical structure but creates a new ontological layer.
claims.source_quote: The act of recognition does not change the underlying physical structure but supervenes upon it, creating a new ontological layer.
claims.note: Asserts a supervenience relation and the existence of an additional ontological layer.

claims.claim: The legal status function is what makes an entity part of the legal domain.
claims.source_quote: This additional layer, the legal status function, is what makes the entity part of the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts the role/function of the legal status function in constituting legal domain membership.

claims.claim: A signature's transformation into a legal fact introduces a new dependent continuant: the status of being a valid signature.
claims.source_quote: This recognition introduces a new dependent continuant, the status of being a valid signature, which inheres in the physical mark and depends on the network of recognition that defines the relevant legal context.
claims.note: Asserts that a specific dependent continuant (valid signature status) is created and inheres in the physical mark.

claims.claim: The status of being a valid signature inheres in the physical mark.
claims.source_quote: a new dependent continuant, the status of being a valid signature, which inheres in the physical mark
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between the dependent continuant and the physical substrate.

claims.claim: The valid signature status depends on the network of recognition that defines the legal context.
claims.source_quote: which inheres in the physical mark and depends on the network of recognition that defines the relevant legal context.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between the legal status and the recognition network.

claims.claim: The valid signature status can persist even if the original signatory is absent or deceased, as long as sustaining institutional relations remain intact.
claims.source_quote: That status can persist even if the original signatory is absent or deceased, as long as the institutional relations that sustain it remain intact.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of this dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The legal fact 'this document is signed' refers to the relational structure of recognition granting the lines their institutional meaning.
claims.source_quote: The legal fact 'this document is signed' thus refers not to the physical lines themselves but to the relational structure of recognition that grants those lines their institutional meaning.
claims.note: Asserts what legal facts refer to: a relational structure of recognition.

claims.claim: A verdict is a legal occurrent: an event that alters the configuration of dependent continuants by modifying recognition relations.
claims.source_quote: The verdict is a paradigmatic legal occurrent: an event that alters the configuration of dependent continuants within the legal system by modifying recognition relations.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of a verdict and its functional role in modifying dependent continuants.

claims.claim: A verdict transforms the ontological state of the accused, creating or dissolving obligations and rights.
claims.source_quote: the utterance acquires the status of a legal fact: it transforms the ontological state of the accused, creating or dissolving obligations and rights.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive relation between the verdict and changes in obligations and rights.

claims.claim: Once entered into the record, a verdict becomes an enduring legal fact and persistent part of the institutional ontology.
claims.source_quote: Once entered into the record, it becomes an enduring legal fact, a persistent part of the institutional ontology that defines a person's status.
claims.note: Asserts that verdicts have persistence as enduring parts of institutional ontology.

claims.claim: The enactment of a statute creates new dependent continuants: norms and obligations depending on continued recognition of the decree's authority.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, this marks the creation of new dependent continuants, norms and obligations, that depend on the continued recognition of the decree's authority.
claims.note: Asserts that norms and obligations are dependent continuants created by legislative enactment.

claims.claim: Norms and obligations depend on the continued recognition of the decree's authority.
claims.source_quote: new dependent continuants, norms and obligations, that depend on the continued recognition of the decree's authority.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between norms/obligations and ongoing recognition.

claims.claim: The ontological transformation from brute event to legal fact proceeds in stages: brute event, recognized act, institutional continuant, and enduring component of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The ontological transformation thus proceeds in stages: from brute event to recognized act, from recognized act to institutional continuant, and from institutional continuant to enduring component of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts the staged ontological structure of the transformation process.

claims.claim: Recognition functions as the operator that generates new levels of dependence and coherence in legal transformation.
claims.source_quote: At each stage, recognition functions as the operator that generates new levels of dependence and coherence.
claims.note: Asserts the functional role of recognition in the ontological transformation.

claims.claim: Each legal fact involves a substrate (brute fact or object), a status function (institutional property conferred), and a field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Each legal fact involves at least three entities: – A substrate (the brute fact or object), – A status function (the institutional property conferred), and – A field of recognition (the network of agents and institutions that sustain the status).
claims.note: Asserts the ontological composition of legal facts: three constituent entities/components.

claims.claim: The field of recognition is a network of agents and institutions that sustain the status function.
claims.source_quote: A field of recognition (the network of agents and institutions that sustain the status).
claims.note: Asserts what the field of recognition is and its sustaining role.

claims.claim: A trial is a process that realizes enduring entities such as judgments, rights, and obligations.
claims.source_quote: A trial, for example, is not just a series of behaviors, it is a process that realizes enduring entities such as judgments, rights, and obligations.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature of a trial and what entities it realizes.

claims.claim: Judgments, rights, and obligations are continuants that persist beyond the moment of decision.
claims.source_quote: These continuants persist beyond the moment of decision and shape future behavior.
claims.note: Asserts persistence and the kind (continuant) of legal entities.

claims.claim: Law's authority arises from a structure of recognition that operates independently of any individual's psychology.
claims.source_quote: Its authority is not reducible to belief but arises from a structure of recognition that operates independently of any individual's psychology.
claims.note: Asserts a relational structure as the source of legal authority, an ontological claim about law's grounding.

claims.claim: A court's jurisdiction, a contract's validity, and a statute's force depend on stable intersubjective recognition of relations embedded in institutional contexts.
claims.source_quote: A court's jurisdiction, a contract's validity, or a statute's force do not depend on how participants feel about them. They depend on the stable, intersubjective recognition of relations embedded in institutional contexts.
claims.note: Asserts relational dependencies constituting legal entities and their properties.

claims.claim: Legal institutions persist through changing participants.
claims.source_quote: Behavior changes, judges retire, societies transform, yet legal institutions persist.
claims.note: Asserts the persistence of legal institutions as a fact about their nature.

claims.claim: Relational structures, roles, obligations, and institutional continuants persist through changing participants.
claims.source_quote: It implies the existence of relational structures, roles, obligations, and institutional continuants, that persist through changing participants.
claims.note: Explicit existential assertion of relational structures and their persistence as continuants.

claims.claim: These institutional structures are components of social reality, not mental states.
claims.source_quote: These structures are not mental states but components of social reality, instantiated in practices, artifacts, and shared recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and location of institutional structures.

claims.claim: Legal actions are occurrents—events through which enduring structures are realized.
claims.source_quote: Legal actions are occurrents, events through which enduring structures are realized.
claims.note: Asserts that legal actions belong to the ontological kind 'occurrent' and bear a realization relation to structures.

claims.claim: Institutions are continuants that persist through events, maintaining coherence over time.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are continuants that persist through those events, maintaining coherence over time.
claims.note: Asserts that institutions are a subkind (continuants) with the property of persistence.

claims.claim: Rules, obligations, and rights are dependent continuants that exist because of sustained patterns of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Rules, obligations, and rights are dependent continuants, entities that exist because of sustained patterns of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of rules, obligations, and rights and their dependence relation.

claims.claim: Law is a relational field that both grounds and exceeds the actions of officials.
claims.source_quote: ...to see law not as the psychology of officials but as the relational field that both grounds and exceeds their actions.
claims.note: Asserts that law is a relational field with grounding and transcending relations to official actions.

claims.claim: Law is a system of socially sustained meanings—a world of entities that exist because of continual recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law, in this sense, is a system of socially sustained meanings, a world of entities that exist because we participate in their continual recognition.
claims.note: Explicit existential and relational assertion about the ontological nature of law.

claims.claim: Legal meaning is a relational property emerging at the intersection of linguistic expression, institutional competence, and social acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Legal meaning, therefore, is a relational property: it emerges at the intersection of linguistic expression, institutional competence, and social acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts that legal meaning has the property of being relational and specifies its constitutive relations.

claims.claim: Without recognition, there is no law.
claims.source_quote: Without recognition, there is no law, only language.
claims.note: Direct existential claim: law's existence depends on recognition.

claims.claim: A rule of recognition is a collectively maintained practice of acknowledgment among officials.
claims.source_quote: A rule of recognition is not a text or command; it is a collectively maintained practice of acknowledgment among officials.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind (collective practice) of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Recognition is a relational act that brings a legal fact into being.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is not an opinion but a relational act that brings a legal fact into being.
claims.note: Asserts recognition as a relational act with a constitutive function for legal facts.

claims.claim: When a judge renders a verdict or a legislature enacts a law, those acts create entities that persist beyond the immediate consciousness of the actors.
claims.source_quote: When a judge renders a verdict or a legislature enacts a law, those acts create entities that persist beyond the immediate consciousness of the actors involved.
claims.note: Asserts that legal acts create persistent entities—an ontological claim about the effects of legal actions.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, statuses, and precedents exist as dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: These entities, rights, duties, statuses, precedents, exist as dependent continuants: they depend for their existence on continuing patterns of recognition within the community.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind (dependent continuants) of rights, duties, statuses, and precedents.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, statuses, and precedents depend for their existence on continuing patterns of recognition but are not identical with any particular act of acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: ...they depend for their existence on continuing patterns of recognition within the community but are not identical with any particular act of acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation and a non-identity claim for these legal entities.

claims.claim: Law is a social practice rather than a transcendent order.
claims.source_quote: In the end, legal realism's greatest contribution was its recognition that law is a social practice rather than a transcendent order.
claims.note: The author endorses this realist insight while building on it, indicating commitment to law's nature as social practice.

claims.claim: Meaning, validity, and obligation are sustained through a web of intersubjective acts that confer reality upon them.
claims.source_quote: Meaning, validity, and obligation are not properties of texts or commands alone; they are sustained through a web of intersubjective acts that confer reality upon them.
claims.note: Asserts a relational grounding for legal meaning, validity, and obligation in intersubjective acts.

claims.claim: Law's existence does not depend solely on moral content, formal procedure, or observed behavior, but on the structure of being that makes those possible.
claims.source_quote: ...that law's existence depends either on moral content, formal procedure, or observed behavior, but never on the structure of being that makes those possible.
claims.note: The author identifies this as a shared erroneous presupposition, implying the positive claim that law depends on a deeper structure of being.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, statuses, and precedents are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: These entities, rights, duties, statuses, precedents, exist as dependent continuants: they depend for their existence on continuing patterns of recognition within the community but are not identical with any particular act of acknowledgment.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of a kind of entity as a subkind (dependent continuants).

claims.claim: Rights, duties, statuses, and precedents depend for their existence on continuing patterns of community recognition.
claims.source_quote: they depend for their existence on continuing patterns of recognition within the community but are not identical with any particular act of acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependence relation between these entities and patterns of recognition.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, statuses, and precedents are not identical with any particular act of acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: they depend for their existence on continuing patterns of recognition within the community but are not identical with any particular act of acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts a non-identity relation, which is an ontological claim about distinctness of kinds.

claims.claim: Legal systems persist beyond the immediate consciousness of the actors involved.
claims.source_quote: e entities that persist beyond the immediate consciousness of the actors involved.
claims.note: Asserts a property (persistence beyond immediate consciousness) of legal-system entities.

claims.claim: The U.S. Constitution persists as a structure of ongoing recognition, not as parchment or memory.
claims.source_quote: The U.S. Constitution, for instance, persists not as parchment or memory but as a structure of ongoing recognition instantiated in courts, legislatures, and citizens.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature and persistence conditions of the U.S. Constitution as an individual.

claims.claim: The U.S. Constitution is instantiated in courts, legislatures, and citizens.
claims.source_quote: The U.S. Constitution, for instance, persists not as parchment or memory but as a structure of ongoing recognition instantiated in courts, legislatures, and citizens.
claims.note: Asserts an instantiation relation between the Constitution and specific social institutions.

claims.claim: The reality of the U.S. Constitution lies in the intersubjective fabric that sustains it.
claims.source_quote: Its reality lies in the intersubjective fabric that sustains it.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive/grounding relation between the Constitution's reality and the intersubjective fabric.

claims.claim: Roles, obligations, and institutions are interlocking continuants within a dynamic system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: we will map how roles, obligations, and institutions function as interlocking continuants within a dynamic system of recognition.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological status and interrelation of roles, obligations, and institutions.

claims.claim: Law is a real, evolving architecture of human coexistence.
claims.source_quote: what law means or commands but what it is, a real, evolving architecture of human coexistence.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts law's ontological character as a real, evolving architecture.

claims.claim: Law is one of the world's enduring structures.
claims.source_quote: we recover law's reality as one of the world's enduring structures.
claims.note: Direct assertion about law's ontological status as an enduring structure.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and permissions are dependent entities.
claims.source_quote: distinguishing between enduring continuants and transient occurrents, between independent entities like persons and institutions and dependent ones like rights, duties, or permissions.
claims.note: The author asserts the dependent ontological status of rights, duties, and permissions.

claims.claim: Persons and institutions are independent entities (continuants).
claims.source_quote: between independent entities like persons and institutions and dependent ones like rights, duties, or permissions.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological independence of persons and institutions.

claims.claim: Law is a structured domain of being.
claims.source_quote: revealing it as a structured domain of being rather than a mere aggregation of texts and practices.
claims.note: The author asserts law's nature as a structured domain of being, not merely texts and practices.

claims.claim: Continuants are entities that persist through time while maintaining their identity.
claims.source_quote: continuants, entities that persist through time while maintaining their identity, and occurrents, entities that unfold in time, such as processes or events.
claims.note: The author endorses and employs this BFO definition as an ontological claim about continuants.

claims.claim: Occurrents are entities that unfold in time, such as processes or events.
claims.source_quote: occurrents, entities that unfold in time, such as processes or events.
claims.note: The author endorses and employs this BFO definition as an ontological claim about occurrents.

claims.claim: A person is a continuant.
claims.source_quote: A person, an institution, or a statute are continuants; a trial, a vote, or a contract signing are occurrents.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of a person as a continuant.

claims.claim: An institution is a continuant.
claims.source_quote: A person, an institution, or a statute are continuants.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of an institution as a continuant.

claims.claim: A statute is a continuant.
claims.source_quote: A person, an institution, or a statute are continuants.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of a statute as a continuant.

claims.claim: A trial is an occurrent.
claims.source_quote: a trial, a vote, or a contract signing are occurrents.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of a trial as an occurrent.

claims.claim: A vote is an occurrent.
claims.source_quote: a trial, a vote, or a contract signing are occurrents.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of a vote as an occurrent.

claims.claim: A contract signing is an occurrent.
claims.source_quote: a trial, a vote, or a contract signing are occurrents.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of a contract signing as an occurrent.

claims.claim: Legal systems persist as networks of continuants enacted and revised through occurrents.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems persist as networks of continuants that are enacted, interpreted, and revised through occurrents.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure and persistence conditions of legal systems.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, powers, and immunities are specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Obligations, rights, powers, and immunities are all specifically dependent continuants: they exist because certain relations among agents, institutions, and norms obtain.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of obligations, rights, powers, and immunities as specifically dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Obligations exist because certain relations among agents, institutions, and norms obtain.
claims.source_quote: they exist because certain relations among agents, institutions, and norms obtain.
claims.note: Asserts the dependency conditions for the existence of obligations and related legal entities.

claims.claim: When a contract is signed, new obligations come into being.
claims.source_quote: When a contract is signed, new obligations come into being; when a verdict is rendered, new legal statuses are instantiated.
claims.note: Asserts that contract signing is an ontological event that creates new entities (obligations).

claims.claim: When a verdict is rendered, new legal statuses are instantiated.
claims.source_quote: when a verdict is rendered, new legal statuses are instantiated.
claims.note: Asserts that verdict rendering is an ontological event that instantiates new legal statuses.

claims.claim: The creation of obligations and legal statuses constitutes real ontological events.
claims.source_quote: These are not metaphors but ontological events, the creation of real entities that alter what agents can or cannot do.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts these are real ontological events, not merely metaphorical descriptions.

claims.claim: A legal case is a complex occurrent involving continuant participants.
claims.source_quote: A 'legal case' can be understood as a complex occurrent involving continuant participants, judge, plaintiff, defendant, each bearing specific roles.
claims.note: The author endorses this ontological classification of a legal case.

claims.claim: A judge, plaintiff, and defendant each bear specific roles within a legal case.
claims.source_quote: A 'legal case' can be understood as a complex occurrent involving continuant participants, judge, plaintiff, defendant, each bearing specific roles.
claims.note: Asserts that participants in a legal case bear specific roles, an ontological property claim.

claims.claim: A legal judgment is a dependent continuant that is an information artifact.
claims.source_quote: The judgment produced at its conclusion is a new dependent continuant, an information artifact that modifies the network of obligations in which the parties stand.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of a judgment as a dependent continuant and information artifact.

claims.claim: A legal judgment modifies the network of obligations in which parties stand.
claims.source_quote: an information artifact that modifies the network of obligations in which the parties stand.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/functional property of judgments with respect to the obligation network.

claims.claim: Legal entities such as obligations, promises, and rights are social objects.
claims.source_quote: His A Priori Foundations of the Civil Law (1913) argued that legal entities such as obligations, promises, and rights are social objects, entities that come into being through acts of recognition among persons.
claims.note: The author endorses Reinach's view as providing the ontological realism foundational to the project; attributed but endorsed.

claims.claim: Legal obligations and rights come into being through acts of recognition among persons.
claims.source_quote: entities that come into being through acts of recognition among persons.
claims.note: The author endorses Reinach's account as foundational to the project's ontological realism.

claims.claim: Dependent continuants are entities that exist only insofar as they inhere in or are recognized by other entities.
claims.source_quote: These are entities that exist only insofar as they inhere in or are recognized by other entities.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a defining ontological property of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Hart's rule of recognition is a higher-order dependency relation sustained collectively.
claims.source_quote: His rule of recognition functions as a higher-order dependency relation: a collectively sustained practice that confers validity on other norms.
claims.note: The author endorses this ontological characterization of Hart's rule of recognition as part of his own framework.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is an institutional function that is a realized capacity of a legal system.
claims.source_quote: this rule operates as an institutional function, a realized capacity of a legal system to generate, modify, and validate obligations.
claims.note: The author endorses this ontological characterization, applying BFO categories to Hart's concept.

claims.claim: Primary rules govern agents directly.
claims.source_quote: primary rules govern agents directly, while secondary rules govern the processes by which norms themselves come into being.
claims.note: Endorsed by the author as an ontological distinction about what primary rules relate to.

claims.claim: Secondary rules govern the processes by which norms come into being.
claims.source_quote: secondary rules govern the processes by which norms themselves come into being.
claims.note: Endorsed by the author as an ontological claim about what secondary rules govern.

claims.claim: Principles are abstract relational constraints that ensure consistency within a legal structure.
claims.source_quote: Principles in this sense are not psychological commitments but abstract relational constraints that ensure consistency within the legal structure.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological nature of legal principles as abstract relational constraints.

claims.claim: Principles are meta-level dependencies that guide the realization of rules and decisions.
claims.source_quote: principles appear as meta-level dependencies that guide the realization of rules and decisions within a unified structure of meaning.
claims.note: The author asserts this ontological characterization of principles when applying BFO to Dworkin.

claims.claim: Law is a relational architecture of continuants and occurrents sustained through recognition.
claims.source_quote: to describe law as a relational architecture of continuants and occurrents sustained through recognition.
claims.note: Direct assertion of law's ontological nature as a relational architecture.

claims.claim: Law is a living structure of relations sustained by shared recognition.
claims.source_quote: it is neither an abstraction imposed from above nor a mere reflection of moral sentiment, but a living structure of relations sustained by shared recognition.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about law's nature as a structure of relations.

claims.claim: Every act of governance presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment among agents.
claims.source_quote: Every act of governance, every contract, every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment, of who counts as an agent, what rol...
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation: acts of governance depend on a network of mutual acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Law is a living structure of relations sustained by shared recognition.
claims.source_quote: a living structure of relations sustained by shared recognition.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the nature of law as a relational structure with a property (being sustained by shared recognition).

claims.claim: Law is neither an abstraction imposed from above nor a mere reflection of moral sentiment.
claims.source_quote: it is neither an abstraction imposed from above nor a mere reflection of moral sentiment, but a living structure of relations sustained by shared recognition.
claims.note: Author positively asserts what law is not, constituting a claim about law's nature/properties.

claims.claim: Every act of governance presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Every act of governance, every contract, every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment, of who counts as an agent, what roles they bear, and what obligations or immunities accompany those roles.
claims.note: Asserts a relational presupposition that governance, contracts, and judgments bear to networks of mutual acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Every contract presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Every act of governance, every contract, every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about what contracts presuppose (relational dependency).

claims.claim: Every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Every act of governance, every contract, every judgment presupposes a network of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about what judgments presuppose (relational dependency).

claims.claim: Law is a framework for being-together.
claims.source_quote: law is a framework for being-together, a structured field of interdependence in which individual and institutional existence are mutually constituted.
claims.note: Positive assertion about the nature and role of law as a framework (functional/relational claim).

claims.claim: Law is a structured field of interdependence.
claims.source_quote: a structured field of interdependence in which individual and institutional existence are mutually constituted.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the kind of entity or structure law is.

claims.claim: Individual and institutional existence are mutually constituted within law.
claims.source_quote: a structured field of interdependence in which individual and institutional existence are mutually constituted.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive relation between individual existence and institutional existence within the legal field.

claims.claim: Institutions are the primary loci of the relational structure of law.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are the primary loci of this relational structure.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion assigning a role/property (being primary loci) to institutions with respect to the relational structure.

claims.claim: Networks of mutual acknowledgment include recognition of who counts as an agent.
claims.source_quote: a network of mutual acknowledgment, of who counts as an agent, what roles they bear, and what obligations or immunities accompany those roles.
claims.note: Asserts that agenthood is a component of the network of mutual acknowledgment, an ontological claim about the constituents of that network.

claims.claim: Agents bear roles that carry obligations or immunities.
claims.source_quote: what roles they bear, and what obligations or immunities accompany those roles.
claims.note: Asserts that roles are properties borne by agents, and that obligations/immunities are properties accompanying roles.

claims.claim: Each legal fact involves at least three entities: a substrate, a status function, and a field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Each legal fact involves at least three entities: – A substrate (the brute fact or object), – A status function (the institutional property conferred), and – A field of recognition (the network of agents and institutions that sustain the status).
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological composition of legal facts.

claims.claim: A substrate is a brute fact or object.
claims.source_quote: – A substrate (the brute fact or object),
claims.note: Asserts what kind of entity a substrate is.

claims.claim: A status function is an institutional property conferred on a substrate.
claims.source_quote: – A status function (the institutional property conferred),
claims.note: Asserts the nature and kind of status functions.

claims.claim: A field of recognition is a network of agents and institutions that sustain a status.
claims.source_quote: – A field of recognition (the network of agents and institutions that sustain the status).
claims.note: Asserts what a field of recognition is.

claims.claim: The dependency relation between substrate and status function is asymmetric.
claims.source_quote: This dependency relation is asymmetric and specifically dependent: the status cannot exist without the substrate and the field, but the substrate can exist without the status.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of the dependency between substrate and status.

claims.claim: The status function cannot exist without both the substrate and the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: the status cannot exist without the substrate and the field, but the substrate can exist without the status.
claims.note: Asserts an existence dependency of status functions.

claims.claim: The substrate can exist without the status function.
claims.source_quote: the status cannot exist without the substrate and the field, but the substrate can exist without the status.
claims.note: Asserts that substrates are ontologically independent of status functions.

claims.claim: The legal fact 'this verdict is final' involves the coexistence of a brute event, a status, and a sustaining field.
claims.source_quote: The legal fact 'this verdict is final' thus involves the coexistence of a brute event (the utterance), a status (finality), and a sustaining field (the judicial system that recognizes the verdict as binding).
claims.note: Asserts the ontological composition of a specific legal fact.

claims.claim: Legal facts are systematically embedded in hierarchical networks of recognition.
claims.source_quote: What distinguishes legal facts from other institutional facts is their systematic embedding in hierarchical networks of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a distinguishing property of legal facts.

claims.claim: The legal system provides a meta-field of recognition that organizes and stabilizes lower-level recognitions.
claims.source_quote: The legal system provides a meta-field of recognition that organizes and stabilizes lower-level recognitions.
claims.note: Asserts a role and function of the legal system as an entity.

claims.claim: Each act of legal recognition draws its validity from a higher-order institutional structure.
claims.source_quote: Each act of legal recognition (signing, declaring, adjudicating) draws its validity from this higher-order structure.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between legal recognition acts and higher-order structure.

claims.claim: Legal facts possess a distinctive ontological robustness through multiply mediated dependence.
claims.source_quote: Consequently, legal facts possess a distinctive kind of ontological robustness: their dependence is multiply mediated, sustained through layers of institutional coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal facts.

claims.claim: Legal facts persist even when individual recognitions falter, sustained by the institutional field.
claims.source_quote: This layered dependence is what allows law to persist even when individual recognitions falter; the institutional field maintains the continuity of legal facts across time and circumstance.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of legal facts and the sustaining role of the institutional field.

claims.claim: Brute facts are instantaneous or transient, while legal facts endure.
claims.source_quote: Brute facts are instantaneous or transient; legal facts endure.
claims.note: Asserts temporal properties distinguishing brute facts from legal facts.

claims.claim: The legal reality of a verdict persists indefinitely unless annulled.
claims.source_quote: The utterance of a verdict lasts seconds, but its legal reality persists indefinitely unless annulled.
claims.note: Asserts a temporal property of legal facts (verdicts).

claims.claim: Dependent continuants generated by recognition are temporally extended and inhere in enduring institutions.
claims.source_quote: This persistence arises because the dependent continuants generated by recognition are temporally extended: they inhere in institutions that endure.
claims.note: Asserts properties of dependent continuants and their inherence relation.

claims.claim: Legal facts are temporally thickened versions of brute facts, sustained by ongoing recognition.
claims.source_quote: Thus, legal facts are temporally thickened versions of brute facts, they retain a connection to their originating events but are sustained by ongoing recognition rather than physical continuity.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind/property relationship between legal facts and brute facts, and the basis of their persistence.

claims.claim: Legal systems externalize recognition through documents, registries, and databases, creating durable artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems externalize recognition through documents, registries, and databases, creating durable artifacts that embody the continuity of legal facts.
claims.note: Asserts a function and product of legal systems.

claims.claim: Legal documents, registries, and records function as physical anchors for institutional memory.
claims.source_quote: A court transcript, a land title, or a legislative record functions as a physical anchor for institutional memory.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of legal artifacts.

claims.claim: Legal artifacts serve as bearers for dependent continuants representing recognized legal relations.
claims.source_quote: These artifacts serve as bearers for dependent continuants representing recognized legal relations.
claims.note: Asserts a bearing relation between artifacts and dependent continuants.

claims.claim: A physical legal document carries the institutional relation of recognition that constitutes ownership.
claims.source_quote: we mean that the physical document carries the institutional relation of recognition that constitutes ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between a physical document and an institutional relation.

claims.claim: Ownership and important legal statuses are established by a system of institutional and social recognition.
claims.source_quote: Ownership and other important legal statuses are established by a system of institutional and social recognition itself.
claims.note: Asserts what establishes ownership and legal statuses as entities.

claims.claim: Documents act as enduring proof, carrying official authority to counter opposing claims.
claims.source_quote: Documents act as enduring proof, carrying official authority to counter any opposing claims.
claims.note: Asserts a property and function of legal documents.

claims.claim: Law's objectivity arises from the stability of recognition across time, not from metaphysical independence.
claims.source_quote: Law's objectivity arises from the stability of recognition across time, not from metaphysical independence.
claims.note: Asserts the source of law's objectivity as a property.

claims.claim: A legal fact is real because it is recognized, recorded, and publicly reproduced within structured institutional networks.
claims.source_quote: The legal fact is real precisely because it is recognized, is often recorded, and publicly reproduced within the structured network of institutions that define the legal world.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions for the reality of legal facts.

claims.claim: The truth conditions of legal facts are relational, depending on alignment of recognition among institutions.
claims.source_quote: The truth conditions of legal facts are thus relational: they depend on the alignment of recognition among institutions rather than on direct empirical correspondence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal facts regarding their truth conditions.

claims.claim: A brute fact such as physical occupancy does not constitute ownership without institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: a brute fact, such as A's physical occupancy of the land, does not constitute ownership without institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: ownership requires institutional recognition beyond brute facts.

claims.claim: Each recognition act generates a new dependent continuant inhering in an institutional continuant.
