claims.source_quote: It endures because it is built to be mended.
claims.note: This is a direct ontological assertion about the property (repairability) that explains law's persistence.

claims.claim: Law has the property of fragility.
claims.source_quote: By treating law as an architecture of social being rather than as a linguistic or moral construct, we can understand both its necessity and its fragility.
claims.note: The author commits to law having fragility as a real property, not merely as a rhetorical point.

claims.claim: Law has the property of necessity.
claims.source_quote: we can understand both its necessity and its fragility.
claims.note: The author commits to law having necessity as a real property alongside fragility.

claims.claim: Bindingness is a structural relation, not a moral feeling.
claims.source_quote: When we say that a law 'binds,' we are describing a structural relation, not a moral feeling.
claims.note: Author directly asserts the ontological character of bindingness as a structural relation.

claims.claim: Bindingness arises from the configuration of recognition and obligation connecting agents to institutions.
claims.source_quote: Bindingness arises from the configuration of recognition and obligation that connects agents to institutions.
claims.note: Author asserts the relational source of bindingness as an ontological claim.

claims.claim: The existence of the binding relation is ontological.
claims.source_quote: Moral judgment may inform whether such bindingness is justified, but the existence of the relation itself is ontological.
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts the ontological status of the binding relation.

claims.claim: The law binds because it is part of a structure that makes binding possible.
claims.source_quote: The law binds because it is part of a structure that makes binding possible.
claims.note: Author asserts a structural explanation for legal bindingness.

claims.claim: Corruption, contradiction, or collapse in legal systems are structural breakdowns.
claims.source_quote: When corruption, contradiction, or collapse occur, they can be analyzed as structural breakdowns, interruptions in the network of dependencies that constitute legality.
claims.note: Author asserts that legal failures are ontologically structural breakdowns.

claims.claim: Legality is constituted by a network of dependencies.
claims.source_quote: interruptions in the network of dependencies that constitute legality
claims.note: Author asserts that legality is constituted by dependency relations.

claims.claim: Repair of legal systems is the reestablishment of coherent relations among recognition, obligation, and authority.
claims.source_quote: Repair, therefore, is not merely political or moral reform but ontological restoration: the reestablishment of coherent relations among recognition, obligation, and authority.
claims.note: Author asserts that legal repair is ontologically a restoration of relations.

claims.claim: Law's structural resilience is the deepest sense in which law is real.
claims.source_quote: That capacity, its structural resilience, is the deepest sense in which law is real.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of law (structural resilience) as the basis of its reality.

claims.claim: Law is the architecture of recognition through which human beings organize their coexistence.
claims.source_quote: To understand law as structure is to understand it as what it has always been: the architecture of recognition through which human beings organize their coexistence.
claims.note: Author asserts what law is—its nature and function as an ontological claim.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, and permissions are real components of the world.
claims.source_quote: It was Adolf Reinach... who first treated these entities not as abstract norms or social conventions, but as real components of the world.
claims.note: Author endorses Reinach's view that legal entities are real components of the world.

claims.claim: Social acts such as promising, commanding, and transferring create enduring entities that outlast the acts themselves.
claims.source_quote: certain forms of human interaction create enduring entities that outlast the acts themselves. When one person promises another... something new comes into existence, a relation that persists after the words have been spoken.
claims.note: Author endorses Reinach's claim about the ontological productivity of social acts.

claims.claim: A promise creates a new relational entity: an obligation.
claims.source_quote: In promising, for example, the promisor binds themselves to the promisee, creating a new relational entity: the obligation.
claims.note: Author asserts that promising produces an obligation as a relational entity.

claims.claim: A command creates a duty.
claims.source_quote: In commanding, an authority creates a duty
claims.note: Author asserts that commanding produces a duty as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: A transfer causes a right of ownership to pass from one bearer to another.
claims.source_quote: in transferring, a right of ownership passes from one bearer to another.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational transfer of a right as an ontological event.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, and duties are ontologically real relations structuring human coexistence.
claims.source_quote: These entities do not exist in the mind or in language alone; they are ontologically real relations that structure the field of human coexistence.
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts the ontological reality and relational nature of these entities.

claims.claim: The structures of social acts are a priori and do not depend on empirical circumstances or legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: Reinach's central claim is that these structures are a priori, they do not depend on empirical circumstances or legal institutions.
claims.note: Author endorses Reinach's a priori claim about social act structures.

claims.claim: The act of promising gives rise to an obligation even without positive law.
claims.source_quote: Even in a state of nature, the act of promising gives rise to an obligation; even before any positive law, the act of transfer generates ownership.
claims.note: Author asserts the pre-institutional ontological productivity of promising.

claims.claim: A promise becomes binding because of the relational essence of the act itself.
claims.source_quote: The promise does not become binding because society declares it so; it becomes binding because of the relational essence of the act itself.
claims.note: Author asserts the intrinsic relational basis of promising's binding force.

claims.claim: An obligation is not identical with the act that gives rise to it.
claims.source_quote: As Reinach put it, 'An obligation is not identical with the act that gives rise to it; it is something new that comes into being through that act.'
claims.note: Author endorses Reinach's claim by presenting it as an 'insight' and core to the argument.

claims.claim: An obligation is something new that comes into being through the act of promising.
claims.source_quote: 'An obligation is not identical with the act that gives rise to it; it is something new that comes into being through that act.'
claims.note: Author endorses this claim from Reinach as foundational to the ontological account.

claims.claim: A social act is an occurrent that gives rise to a continuant persisting through time.
claims.source_quote: A social act is an occurrence, a temporal event, but it gives rise to a continuant, an entity that persists through time.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological distinction between social act (occurrent) and its product (continuant).

claims.claim: A promise, once made, continues to exist until it is fulfilled or annulled.
claims.source_quote: The promise, once made, continues to exist until it is fulfilled or annulled.
claims.note: Author asserts the temporal persistence of the promise as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: An obligation's existence depends on the relation itself, sustained through mutual recognition.
claims.source_quote: Its existence depends not on the promisor's ongoing mental state but on the relation itself, sustained through mutual recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the relational and recognition-dependent basis of obligation's existence.

claims.claim: An obligation inheres in the debtor; a right inheres in the creditor; authority inheres in the officeholder.
claims.source_quote: An obligation inheres in the debtor, a right in the creditor, an authority in the officeholder.
claims.note: Author asserts the inherence relations between legal entities and their bearers.

claims.claim: Legal continuants have no independent substance; they exist only because certain relational conditions hold.
claims.source_quote: These continuants have no independent substance, they exist only because certain relational conditions hold, but they are nonetheless real.
claims.note: Author asserts dependent existence of legal continuants as an ontological property.

claims.claim: Legal continuants are real even though their being is sustained by recognition rather than belief.
claims.source_quote: Their being is sustained by recognition, not by belief. Even if one party forgets or denies the promise, the obligation persists.
claims.note: Author asserts that recognition (not belief) sustains the being of legal continuants.

claims.claim: An obligation persists until the relational conditions that created it are properly dissolved.
claims.source_quote: Even if one party forgets or denies the promise, the obligation persists until the relational conditions that created it are properly dissolved.
claims.note: Author asserts a persistence condition for obligations as an ontological claim.

claims.claim: Social acts are occurrents that generate and modify continuants within a network of dependence relations.
claims.source_quote: the ontology of social acts anticipates the later formal categories of Basic Formal Ontology: occurrents that generate and modify continuants within a network of dependence relations.
claims.note: Author endorses the classification of social acts as occurrents and legal entities as continuants.

claims.claim: Each social act can be represented as a process linking agents and resulting in new dependent entities: obligations, permissions, or rights.
claims.source_quote: each act can be represented as a process (an occurrent) linking two or more agents and resulting in new dependent entities: obligations, permissions, or rights.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological structure of social acts as processes producing dependent entities.

claims.claim: Positive law formalizes what the ontology of social acts already makes possible.
claims.source_quote: Positive law merely formalizes what the ontology of social acts already makes possible.
claims.note: Author asserts a dependence relation between positive law and the ontology of social acts.

claims.claim: Beneath the variety of legal doctrines lies a constant relational grammar, an a priori structure of human interaction.
claims.source_quote: beneath the variety of legal doctrines lies a constant relational grammar, an a priori structure of human interaction that the law merely articulates.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of a universal a priori relational structure underlying all legal systems.

claims.claim: The divergence of moral law and formal law marks the beginning of the modern crisis of legal meaning.
claims.source_quote: The divergence of these two senses of law, one moral, the other formal, marks the beginning of the modern crisis of legal meaning.
claims.note: The author asserts a historical-ontological fact about the origin of a crisis, attributing a property to a historical event.

claims.claim: The crisis of legal meaning is ontological, not primarily semantic or moral.
claims.source_quote: The crisis of legal meaning, the chapter concludes, is not primarily semantic or moral, but ontological.
claims.note: The author directly asserts a property of the crisis of legal meaning.

claims.claim: Law has lost its ontological anchor.
claims.source_quote: The crisis of legal meaning arises precisely from this impasse: law has lost its ontological anchor, floating uneasily between metaphysical idealism and empirical formalism.
claims.note: The author asserts a property (loss of ontological anchor) of law as an entity.

claims.claim: Legal entities are real but dependent continuants sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: The chapter prepares the ground for a structural account of law that treats legal entities as real but dependent continuants sustained by recognition.
claims.note: The author endorses this characterization as the target of his own structural account, committing to it as his view.

claims.claim: Debates over meaning, validity, and obligation implicitly rely on unarticulated ontological assumptions.
claims.source_quote: The analysis shows that debates over meaning, validity, and obligation implicitly rely on ontological assumptions that remain unarticulated.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of jurisprudential debates—that they have hidden ontological commitments.

claims.claim: Natural law theory fails to explain how law maintains identity and authority amid moral disagreement and political change.
claims.source_quote: Through critical examination of natural law theory, legal positivism, and legal realism, the chapter argues that each fails to explain how law maintains identity and authority amid moral disagreement and political change.
claims.note: The author asserts a deficiency (a property) of natural law theory as a kind of jurisprudential entity.

claims.claim: Legal positivism fails to explain how law maintains identity and authority amid moral disagreement and political change.
claims.source_quote: Through critical examination of natural law theory, legal positivism, and legal realism, the chapter argues that each fails to explain how law maintains identity and authority amid moral disagreement and political change.
claims.note: The author asserts a deficiency of legal positivism.

claims.claim: Legal realism fails to explain how law maintains identity and authority amid moral disagreement and political change.
claims.source_quote: Through critical examination of natural law theory, legal positivism, and legal realism, the chapter argues that each fails to explain how law maintains identity and authority amid moral disagreement and political change.
claims.note: The author asserts a deficiency of legal realism.

claims.claim: Kelsen's pure theory reduced law to an abstract system of validity relations without explaining what makes those norms real.
claims.source_quote: Kelsen's 'pure theory of law' defined law as a hierarchy of norms… its weakness was ontological: it reduced law to an abstract system of validity relations without explaining what makes those norms real.
claims.note: The author asserts a property (ontological weakness) of Kelsen's theory as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: The Grundnorm functioned as a logical postulate, not an entity in the world.
claims.source_quote: The Grundnorm functioned as a logical postulate, not an entity in the world.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological status of the Grundnorm.

claims.claim: Law became a self-referential structure that is complete, formal, and hollow under Kelsenian positivism.
claims.source_quote: Once the last trace of moral realism was removed, the ontological status of law itself evaporated. Law became a self-referential structure, complete, formal, and hollow.
claims.note: The author asserts properties of law under the positivist framework he is critically analyzing, committing to this description of what positivism produces.

claims.claim: Morality without institutional embodiment is impotent.
claims.source_quote: Morality without institutional embodiment remains impotent; institutions without moral orientation become unintelligible.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational property: morality has a disposition (impotence) when lacking institutional embodiment.

claims.claim: Institutions without moral orientation are unintelligible.
claims.source_quote: Morality without institutional embodiment remains impotent; institutions without moral orientation become unintelligible.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of institutions lacking moral orientation.

claims.claim: The disjunction of Recht and Gesetz mirrors the split between being and value that characterizes modernity.
claims.source_quote: The disjunction of these terms mirrors the split between being and value, between fact and norm, that characterizes modernity.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational (mirroring) property between two conceptual divergences.

claims.claim: The ontological question of what kind of being law has was replaced by the epistemic question of which rules are valid.
claims.source_quote: The ontological question, what kind of being does law have?, was replaced by an epistemic one, how can we know which rules are valid?
claims.note: The author asserts a historical substitution—one kind of question replacing another—as a fact about jurisprudence.

claims.claim: A procedural act (trial, filing, enactment) is an occurrent through which a legal fact is created.
claims.source_quote: Occurrent: The procedural act (trial, filing, enactment) through which a fact is created.
claims.note: Asserts that procedural acts are occurrents and have the function of creating legal facts.

claims.claim: A legal relation or status (right, obligation, decision) is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: Dependent Continuant: The legal relation or status generated (right, obligation, decision).
claims.note: Asserts that legal relations and statuses are a subkind of dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The material or digital bearer that embodies a legal relation is an information artifact.
claims.source_quote: Information Artifact: The material or digital bearer that embodies the dependent continuant.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of the bearer of legal dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The court, registry, or agency that maintains recognition of an artifact is an institutional continuant.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Continuant: The system (court, registry, agency) that maintains recognition of the artifact.
claims.note: Asserts that institutional systems are a subkind of institutional continuant.

claims.claim: Legal facts endure by linking transient events to enduring material supports within stable institutions.
claims.source_quote: This chain ensures the endurance of legal facts by linking transient events to enduring material supports within stable institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of the ontological chain described.

claims.claim: Digital artifacts are continuants that bear information content entities.
claims.source_quote: digital artifacts are continuants bearing information content entities; their legal significance arises from institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and property of digital artifacts.

claims.claim: The legal significance of digital artifacts arises from institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: digital artifacts are continuants bearing information content entities; their legal significance arises from institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between legal significance and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: A digital signature or electronic court order is as ontologically real as its physical counterpart.
claims.source_quote: A digital signature or electronic court order is no less real than its physical counterpart because its being depends on the same structure of dependencies, authority, recognition, record.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property (reality/status) of digital legal artifacts.

claims.claim: Law's reality resides in the relations that confer and sustain recognition of artifacts, not in the artifacts' substance.
claims.source_quote: law's reality resides not in the substance of its artifacts but in the relations that confer and sustain their recognition.
claims.note: Asserts where law's ontological reality is located.

claims.claim: Procedures create a shared temporal ontology for law by standardizing temporal conditions of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Procedures standardize the temporal conditions under which these recognitions become effective, creating a shared temporal ontology for law.
claims.note: Asserts that procedures have a constitutive role in creating temporal ontology for law.

claims.claim: Filing deadlines, effective dates, and statutes of limitation are temporal constraints that ensure coherence across the system's occurrents.
claims.source_quote: Filing deadlines, effective dates, and statutes of limitation are not arbitrary technicalities; they are temporal constraints that ensure coherence across the system's occurrents.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature and function of legal temporal rules.

claims.claim: Temporal order is an ontological principle of law, realized through procedural regulation.
claims.source_quote: Temporal order, in this sense, is an ontological principle of law, realized through procedural regulation.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law: temporal order is an ontological principle realized procedurally.

claims.claim: Procedures connect local acts of recognition to the broader architecture of law.
claims.source_quote: They connect local acts of recognition to the broader architecture of law, ensuring that new entities are properly instantiated and aligned.
claims.note: Asserts a relational function of procedures within legal ontology.

claims.claim: An improperly filed motion may not exist as a legal entity.
claims.source_quote: an improperly filed motion may not exist as a legal entity, even if its content is known.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological consequence of procedural defect on the existence of a legal entity.

claims.claim: A verdict rendered by an unauthorized tribunal lacks the status of a legal fact.
claims.source_quote: a verdict rendered by an unauthorized tribunal lacks the status of a legal fact, regardless of its substantive accuracy.
claims.note: Asserts that procedural authority is necessary for a verdict to be a legal fact.

claims.claim: Ontological validity of legal entities depends on procedural realization.
claims.source_quote: Ontological validity depends on procedural realization, because only through procedure does recognition acquire enduring institutional form.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between ontological validity and procedural realization.

claims.claim: Legal procedural processes realize the functions of legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: In biology, physiological processes realize the functions of organs; in law, procedural processes realize the functions of institutions.
claims.note: Author endorses this parallel as a positive ontological claim about law.

claims.claim: Legal functions depend on recognition rather than causal mechanisms.
claims.source_quote: Biological functions depend on causal mechanisms, while legal functions depend on recognition. Yet both are real and equally necessary for the persistence of their respective systems.
claims.note: Asserts a distinctive ontological property of legal functions.

claims.claim: Law is ontologically alive: it endures through the continuous realization of its structures in procedural time.
claims.source_quote: Law, therefore, is not metaphorically but ontologically alive: it endures through the continuous realization of its structures in procedural time.
claims.note: Asserts a positive ontological property of law.

claims.claim: The archive of law is ontological memory that sustains the continuity of legal facts across temporal gaps.
claims.source_quote: The archive of law, the cumulative record of trials, decrees, filings, and decisions, is not merely historical; it is ontological memory. It sustains the continuity of legal facts across temporal gaps.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological role and property of legal archives.

claims.claim: Each procedural occurrent generates continuants such as records, judgments, and statutes.
claims.source_quote: Each procedural occurrent generates continuants that populate the legal world, such as records, judgments, statutes.
claims.note: Asserts a generative relation between procedural occurrents and legal continuants.

claims.claim: Each legal continuant becomes the substrate for further procedural realizations.
claims.source_quote: each of these continuants, in turn, becomes the substrate for further realizations.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/functional property of legal continuants.

claims.claim: Information artifacts serve as vehicles ensuring recognition survives the passage of time.
claims.source_quote: Information artifacts serve as the vehicles of this recursive process, ensuring that recognition survives the passage of time.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of information artifacts in legal ontology.

claims.claim: The procedural domain is the temporal field in which recognition becomes legal reality.
claims.source_quote: The procedural domain is thus the engine of legal being: the temporal field in which recognition becomes reality.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property/role of the procedural domain.

claims.claim: Primary rules impose duties; secondary rules confer powers specifying how primary rules may be recognized, altered, or adjudicated.
claims.source_quote: Primary rules impose duties, prescribing what must or must not be done, while secondary rules confer powers, specifying how primary rules may be recognized, altered, or adjudicated.
claims.note: Author endorses Hart's distinction as a positive ontological claim about kinds of legal rules.

claims.claim: Secondary rules form the infrastructure of legal being.
claims.source_quote: Secondary rules form the infrastructure of legal being; they are the mechanisms by which norms acquire, retain, and lose their validity within a system of interdependent recognition.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological role/property of secondary rules.

claims.claim: Secondary rules are mechanisms by which norms acquire, retain, and lose their validity within a system of interdependent recognition.
claims.source_quote: Secondary rules form the infrastructure of legal being; they are the mechanisms by which norms acquire, retain, and lose their validity within a system of interdependent recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the functional role of secondary rules in the validation of legal norms.

claims.claim: Secondary rules correspond to structural continuants that define conditions of existence for legal obligations, rights, and facts.
claims.source_quote: secondary rules correspond to the structural continuants that define the conditions of existence for dependent entities such as obligations, rights, and legal facts.
claims.note: Asserts that secondary rules are (or correspond to) structural continuants with a specific ontological function.

claims.claim: Secondary rules establish recognition and validation dependencies among entities in the legal domain.
claims.source_quote: they establish the recognition and validation dependencies among the entities that populate the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts a relational function of secondary rules.

claims.claim: Secondary rules function as meta-level dependent continuants that inhere in institutions and relations among them.
claims.source_quote: Within the Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) framework, secondary rules function as meta-level dependent continuants: they inhere not in individual agents but in institutions and in the relations among them.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and bearer of secondary rules.

claims.claim: The secondary rule is an ontological operator that defines dependence relations determining when and how legal entities can exist.
claims.source_quote: The secondary rule is thus an ontological operator; it defines the dependence relations that determine when and how legal entities can exist.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property/function of secondary rules.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition specifies the ultimate criteria by which legal norms are validated within a system.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition specifies the ultimate criteria by which legal norms are validated within a system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/ontological property of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition defines the top-level dependencies in the network of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It is the meta-structure that delineates the boundary of legal reality itself: what counts as law, and what does not. In effect, it defines the top-level dependencies in the network of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/relational property of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: All legal entities (statutes, contracts, judgments, obligations) derive their ontological status from alignment with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Everything that exists within a legal system - statutes, contracts, judgments, obligations - derives its ontological status from alignment with this rule.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between legal entities and the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition functions as the system's ontological anchor, ensuring coherence across institutions and roles.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition functions as the system's ontological anchor, ensuring coherence by maintaining a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of the rule of recognition in legal ontology.

claims.claim: Promises, commands, and transfers are processes (occurrents) linking two or more agents.
claims.source_quote: each act can be represented as a process (an occurrent) linking two or more agents and resulting in new dependent entities: obligations, permissions, or rights.
claims.note: The author asserts this in his own voice as a characterization of these acts in formal ontological terms, though framed partly as modeling ('can be represented').

claims.claim: Obligations, permissions, and rights are dependent entities.
claims.source_quote: each act can be represented as a process (an occurrent) linking two or more agents and resulting in new dependent entities: obligations, permissions, or rights.
claims.note: The author characterizes obligations, permissions, and rights as a kind of entity (dependent entities), which is an ontological claim about their nature.

claims.claim: Obligations, permissions, and rights enter into higher-order relations within institutions, courts, legislatures, and contracts.
claims.source_quote: These entities then enter into higher-order relations within institutions, courts, legislatures, contracts, that govern their creation and dissolution.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts that these entities stand in higher-order relations within social structures.

claims.claim: Institutions, courts, legislatures, and contracts govern the creation and dissolution of obligations, permissions, and rights.
claims.source_quote: These entities then enter into higher-order relations within institutions, courts, legislatures, contracts, that govern their creation and dissolution.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the governing function of these social structures over legal entities.

claims.claim: Law is a dynamic system in which acts continually generate and transform enduring entities.
claims.source_quote: Law becomes a dynamic system in which acts continually generate and transform enduring entities.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts this as an ontological characterization of law as a kind of system with a particular dynamic property.

claims.claim: A procedural act (trial, filing, enactment) is an occurrent through which a legal fact is created.
claims.source_quote: Occurrent: The procedural act (trial, filing, enactment) through which a fact is created.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership and functional role for procedural acts as occurrents.

claims.claim: A legal relation or status (right, obligation, decision) is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: Dependent Continuant: The legal relation or status generated (right, obligation, decision).
claims.note: Asserts that legal relations and statuses are a subkind of dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The material or digital bearer of a dependent continuant is an information artifact.
claims.source_quote: Information Artifact: The material or digital bearer that embodies the dependent continuant.
claims.note: Asserts a kind and a bearing/embodiment relation between artifacts and dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The court, registry, or agency that maintains recognition of an artifact is an institutional continuant.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Continuant: The system (court, registry, agency) that maintains recognition of the artifact.
claims.note: Asserts that legal institutions are institutional continuants with a maintenance relation to artifacts.

claims.claim: Legal facts endure by linking transient events to enduring material supports within stable institutions.
claims.source_quote: This chain ensures the endurance of legal facts by linking transient events to enduring material supports within stable institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of legal facts: their endurance depends on this chain of dependencies.

claims.claim: Digital artifacts are continuants that bear information content entities.
claims.source_quote: digital artifacts are continuants bearing information content entities; their legal significance arises from institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership (continuant) and a bearing relation for digital artifacts.

claims.claim: The legal significance of digital artifacts arises from institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: digital artifacts are continuants bearing information content entities; their legal significance arises from institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: legal significance depends on institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Law's reality resides in the relations that confer and sustain recognition of artifacts, not in the substance of the artifacts themselves.
claims.source_quote: law's reality resides not in the substance of its artifacts but in the relations that confer and sustain their recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law's reality: grounded in recognition relations, not material substance.

claims.claim: Filing deadlines, effective dates, and statutes of limitation are temporal constraints on legal occurrents.
claims.source_quote: Filing deadlines, effective dates, and statutes of limitation are not arbitrary technicalities; they are temporal constraints that ensure coherence across the system's occurrents.
claims.note: Asserts that these legal instruments have the property of being temporal constraints on occurrents.

claims.claim: Temporal order is an ontological principle of law, realized through procedural regulation.
claims.source_quote: Temporal order, in this sense, is an ontological principle of law, realized through procedural regulation.
claims.note: Asserts that temporal order is a property/principle of law and is realized by procedural regulation.

claims.claim: Procedures connect local acts of recognition to the broader architecture of law.
claims.source_quote: They connect local acts of recognition to the broader architecture of law, ensuring that new entities are properly instantiated and aligned.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/functional property of procedures within legal ontology.

claims.claim: An improperly filed motion may not exist as a legal entity.
claims.source_quote: an improperly filed motion may not exist as a legal entity, even if its content is known.
claims.note: Asserts a condition of non-existence for legal entities; medium confidence due to 'may not'.

claims.claim: A verdict rendered by an unauthorized tribunal lacks the status of a legal fact.
claims.source_quote: a verdict rendered by an unauthorized tribunal lacks the status of a legal fact, regardless of its substantive accuracy.
claims.note: Asserts that procedural authorization is necessary for a verdict to be a legal fact.

claims.claim: Ontological validity of legal entities depends on procedural realization.
claims.source_quote: Ontological validity depends on procedural realization, because only through procedure does recognition acquire enduring institutional form.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between ontological validity and procedural realization.

claims.claim: Legal procedural processes realize the functions of legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: In biology, physiological processes realize the functions of organs; in law, procedural processes realize the functions of institutions.
claims.note: Author endorses this structural parallel as a positive claim about legal ontology.

claims.claim: Legal functions depend on recognition, not causal mechanisms.
claims.source_quote: Biological functions depend on causal mechanisms, while legal functions depend on recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a distinctive dependence property of legal functions.

claims.claim: Law endures through the continuous realization of its structures in procedural time.
claims.source_quote: Law, therefore, is not metaphorically but ontologically alive: it endures through the continuous realization of its structures in procedural time.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law's persistence: ontologically realized through procedural processes.

claims.claim: The archive of law is ontological memory that sustains continuity of legal facts across temporal gaps.
claims.source_quote: The archive of law, the cumulative record of trials, decrees, filings, and decisions, is not merely historical; it is ontological memory. It sustains the continuity of legal facts across temporal gaps.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/ontological property of the legal archive.

claims.claim: Obligations and rights persist beyond the lives of their creators through information artifacts.
claims.source_quote: allowing obligations and rights to persist beyond the lives of their creators. Through these artifacts, law maintains its presence as a living structure of recognition extended through material and informational continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of obligations and rights enabled by artifacts.

claims.claim: Each procedural occurrent generates continuants such as records, judgments, and statutes.
claims.source_quote: Each procedural occurrent generates continuants that populate the legal world, such as records, judgments, statutes.
claims.note: Asserts that procedural occurrents generate dependent continuants as legal entities.

claims.claim: Information artifacts serve as vehicles of the recursive process by which recognition survives the passage of time.
claims.source_quote: Information artifacts serve as the vehicles of this recursive process, ensuring that recognition survives the passage of time.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of information artifacts in the legal ontology.

claims.claim: Hart's secondary rules are meta-level dependent continuants inhering in institutions and relations among them.
claims.source_quote: Within the Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) framework, secondary rules function as meta-level dependent continuants: they inhere not in individual agents but in institutions and in the relations among them.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership and an inherence relation for secondary rules.

claims.claim: Secondary rules provide the schema through which legal facts, norms, and authorities are organized.
claims.source_quote: They provide the schema through which legal facts, norms, and authorities are organized.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/organizational function of secondary rules.

claims.claim: The secondary rule is an ontological operator that defines dependence relations determining when legal entities can exist.
claims.source_quote: The secondary rule is thus an ontological operator; it defines the dependence relations that determine when and how legal entities can exist.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role (ontological operator) for secondary rules and their relation to legal entities.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition specifies the ultimate criteria by which legal norms are validated within a system.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition specifies the ultimate criteria by which legal norms are validated within a system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition defines the top-level dependencies in the network of recognition.
claims.source_quote: In effect, it defines the top-level dependencies in the network of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property (top-level dependency definition) of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Every legal entity within a system derives its ontological status from alignment with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Everything that exists within a legal system - statutes, contracts, judgments, obligations - derives its ontological status from alignment with this rule.
claims.note: Asserts a universal dependence relation between legal entities and the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition functions as the system's ontological anchor.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition functions as the system's ontological anchor, ensuring coherence by maintaining a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of the rule of recognition in the legal ontology.

claims.claim: Under scholasticism, legal legitimacy is a matter of participation in divine reason.
claims.source_quote: Under the scholastic model, legitimacy was a matter of participation in divine reason
claims.note: The author presents this as a historical characterization, but asserts it as a fact about the scholastic model's ontological grounding of legitimacy.

claims.claim: Under legal positivism, legitimacy is a matter of compliance with procedure.
claims.source_quote: under positivism, it became a matter of compliance with procedure.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a characterization of positivism's account of legitimacy, stated as fact.

claims.claim: Positivist jurisprudence narrowed law's study to sources, texts, and commands.
claims.source_quote: This substitution narrowed jurisprudence into an analysis of sources, texts, and commands, leaving untouched the deeper issue of how such entities can exist and exert normative force.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts this as a consequence of the epistemic substitution in jurisprudence.

claims.claim: Law has the capacity to exert normative force.
claims.source_quote: leaving untouched the deeper issue of how such entities can exist and exert normative force.
claims.note: By framing this as a 'deeper issue' left untouched, the author implicitly asserts that law does exist and exert normative force as a genuine ontological matter.

claims.claim: Kelsen's 'purity' is ontologically a form of abstraction.
claims.source_quote: What Kelsen called 'purity' was, ontologically speaking, a form of abstraction that cut law off from the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author asserts in his own voice that Kelsenian purity is ontologically an abstraction.

claims.claim: Kelsenian abstraction cuts law off from the social structures that give it life.
claims.source_quote: a form of abstraction that cut law off from the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts that Kelsen's abstraction severs law from the social reality that sustains it.

claims.claim: Structures of social reality give law its life (sustaining existence and normative force).
claims.source_quote: the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author asserts that social reality structures are the source of law's vitality, an ontological relational claim.

claims.claim: Statutes, contracts, judgments, and obligations derive their ontological status from alignment with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Everything that exists within a legal system - statutes, contracts, judgments, obligations - derives its ontological status from alignment with this rule.
claims.note: Direct assertion that legal entities have their ontological status grounded in the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition functions as the ontological anchor of a legal system.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition functions as the system's ontological anchor, ensuring coherence by maintaining a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/role property of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition maintains a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.source_quote: ensuring coherence by maintaining a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property and function the rule of recognition has.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition provides law with closure as a self-sustaining field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It provides law with its closure as a self-sustaining field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of the rule of recognition relative to law.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.source_quote: its ontological status is more precise: it is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts the ontological kind/nature of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Direct assertion placing the rule of recognition in an ontological category (dependent continuant).

claims.claim: The rule of recognition inheres in the system of institutions collectively, not in any single agent.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Asserts a relation of inherence between the rule of recognition and the collective institutional system.

claims.claim: Statutes, contracts, judgments, and obligations derive their ontological status from alignment with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Everything that exists within a legal system - statutes, contracts, judgments, obligations - derives its ontological status from alignment with this rule.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the source of ontological status for legal entities.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition functions as the ontological anchor of a legal system.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition functions as the system's ontological anchor, ensuring coherence by maintaining a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.note: The author asserts a role/function of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition maintains a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.source_quote: ensuring coherence by maintaining a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of the rule of recognition regarding institutional relations.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition provides law with its closure as a self-sustaining field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It provides law with its closure as a self-sustaining field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law and a function of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Law is a self-sustaining field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It provides law with its closure as a self-sustaining field of recognition.
claims.note: The author characterizes law's nature as a self-sustaining field; implied ontological claim about what law is.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.source_quote: its ontological status is more precise: it is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological nature of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition exists as a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Explicit ontological categorization of the rule of recognition as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition inheres in the system of institutions collectively, not in any one agent.
claims.source_quote: it is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions. It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Asserts a relation of inherence between the rule of recognition and the collective institutional system.

claims.claim: Kelsen's 'purity' was ontologically a form of abstraction that cut law off from social reality.
claims.source_quote: What Kelsen called 'purity' was, ontologically speaking, a form of abstraction that cut law off from the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author directly asserts a property of Kelsen's concept—it is an abstraction with a specific ontological character.

claims.claim: Social reality has structures that give law its life.
claims.source_quote: a form of abstraction that cut law off from the structures of social reality that give it life.
claims.note: The author implicitly asserts that social reality has structures capable of grounding law's existence and normativity.

claims.claim: Holmes's view dissolved legality into prediction and psychology.
claims.source_quote: To say, as Holmes did, that law is 'the prophecy of what courts will do in fact' was to dissolve legality into prediction and psychology.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/consequence of Holmes's conception—legality is reduced to prediction and psychology.

claims.claim: The being of law disappeared into behavior under realist conceptions.
claims.source_quote: The being of law disappeared into behavior, leaving no room for understanding law's persistence beyond immediate human action.
claims.note: The author asserts an ontological consequence of legal realism: law's being was dissolved into behavior.

claims.claim: Natural law retained moral substance but lacked social grounding.
claims.source_quote: Natural law retained moral substance but lacked social grounding.
claims.note: The author attributes a property (moral substance without social grounding) to natural law as a theory.

claims.claim: Positivism achieved procedural clarity but lost existential depth.
claims.source_quote: Positivism achieved procedural clarity but lost existential depth.
claims.note: The author attributes properties (procedural clarity, lack of existential depth) to positivism.

claims.claim: Realism captured practice but abandoned structure.
claims.source_quote: Realism captured practice but abandoned structure.
claims.note: The author attributes a property to legal realism—it captures practice but lacks structural account.

claims.claim: Jurisprudence had become epistemology without ontology.
claims.source_quote: Jurisprudence had become epistemology without ontology.
claims.note: The author directly asserts a characterization of the kind of discipline jurisprudence became.

claims.claim: The crisis of legal meaning has both a historical and a conceptual origin.
claims.source_quote: The crisis of legal meaning thus has a double origin: historical and conceptual.
claims.note: The author asserts that the crisis of legal meaning is a real phenomenon with two kinds of causes.

claims.claim: The medieval unity of moral and legal order dissolved historically.
claims.source_quote: Historically, it arose from the dissolution of the medieval unity of moral and legal order, a unity symbolized by the harmony of Recht and Gesetz.
claims.note: The author asserts a historical ontological fact: a prior unity between moral and legal order existed and was dissolved.

claims.claim: Modern legal theories continue to oscillate between severed poles of moral and procedural conceptions.
claims.source_quote: Conceptually, it persists because modern theories of law continue to oscillate between these severed poles.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of modern legal theories—they oscillate between poles rather than unifying them.

claims.claim: Law is the relational architecture that makes both command and ideal possible.
claims.source_quote: beginning with the redefinition of law not as command or ideal, but as the relational architecture that makes both possible.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts what law is—a relational architecture—as his own positive ontological claim.

claims.claim: Moral, procedural, and institutional dimensions coexist as parts of a single structure of recognition.
claims.source_quote: by showing how moral, procedural, and institutional dimensions coexist as parts of a single structure of recognition.
claims.note: The author asserts that these dimensions are parts of a single structure—a mereological-ontological claim.

claims.claim: Unjust laws continue to exist even when they violate the moral order.
claims.source_quote: It denies the existence of legal entities that clearly operate within the social world, even when they violate the moral order.
claims.note: The author asserts that unjust laws are real legal entities that exist and operate in the social world.

claims.claim: Unjust laws persist as entities that are applied, enforced, and suffered under.
claims.source_quote: it continues to be applied, enforced, and suffered under. People are imprisoned or executed in its name; institutions operate by reference to it.
claims.note: The author asserts that unjust laws have social existence and causal efficacy—an ontological claim about their being.

claims.claim: Denying the being of unjust laws would deny the experiences of those subject to them.
claims.source_quote: To deny its being would be to deny the experiences of those subject to it.
claims.note: The author asserts a relation between the being of unjust laws and the reality of subjects' experiences.

claims.claim: The maxim 'lex iniusta non est lex' functions as a moral verdict, not an ontological description.
claims.source_quote: the maxim lex iniusta non est lex ('an unjust law is no law at all') functions more as a moral verdict than as an ontological description.
claims.note: The author directly asserts a property/function of the maxim—it is moral, not ontological in character.

claims.claim: Injustice deprives law of legitimacy, not of existence.
claims.source_quote: It asserts that injustice deprives law of legitimacy, not of existence.
claims.note: The author asserts a distinction between two properties of law—legitimacy and existence—and which injustice affects.

claims.claim: The moral and ontological orders of inquiry are distinct.
claims.source_quote: in making legitimacy the criterion of being, it confuses two distinct orders of inquiry: the moral and the ontological.
claims.note: The author asserts that the moral and ontological are two distinct orders—an ontological claim about the structure of inquiry.

claims.claim: Finnis's theory encounters an ontological problem regarding unjust legal systems.
claims.source_quote: Yet it encounters the same ontological problem. If the reality of law depends on its orientation toward moral goods, then the existence of unjust legal systems becomes paradoxical.
claims.note: The author asserts that Finnis's theory has a genuine ontological problem—the existence of unjust systems is paradoxical within it.

claims.claim: Natural law theory cannot account for what law is when it fails to be just.
claims.source_quote: It can tell us what law ought to be, but not what it is when it fails.
claims.note: The author asserts a limitation of natural law theory regarding the ontological status of unjust law.

claims.claim: Obligations, permissions, and rights are entities that exist within legal systems.
claims.source_quote: es: obligations, permissions, or rights. These entities then enter into higher-order relations within institutions, courts, legislatures, contracts, that govern their creation and dissolution.
claims.note: Author asserts that obligations, permissions, and rights are entities that enter into relations—a direct ontological commitment.

claims.claim: Legal acts are transient; the entities they create are enduring relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: transient acts producing enduring relational continuants. The implications of this insight extend far beyond contract or private law.
claims.note: Author asserts a distinction in temporal ontology between acts and their outcomes, endorsing this as law's structural pattern.

claims.claim: Law is a dynamic system in which acts continually generate and transform enduring entities.
claims.source_quote: Law becomes a dynamic system in which acts continually generate and transform enduring entities.
claims.note: Direct ontological characterization of law as a system of entities generated by acts.

claims.claim: A commander's order creates an obligation of obedience within a structure of roles.
claims.source_quote: A commander's order binds subordinates, not because of coercion, but because the social act of command creates an obligation of obedience recognized within a structure of roles.
claims.note: Author asserts that commanding produces a real obligation entity—an ontological claim about the outcome of the social act.

claims.claim: Transferring generates ownership through mutual acknowledgment of a change in rights.
claims.source_quote: Transferring generates ownership, not by physical exchange, but through mutual acknowledgment of a change in rights.
claims.note: Author asserts that the act of transferring produces a real change in rights/ownership—an ontological claim about relational change.

claims.claim: A relational structure comes into being through intentional interaction sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: In each case, a relational structure comes into being through intentional interaction, sustained by recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts that relational structures are real entities that come into being via recognition—ontological claim about the genesis of legal entities.

claims.claim: Social acts have a mode of being as real as physical objects.
claims.source_quote: For him, social acts have a mode of being as real as physical objects.
claims.note: Author endorses Reinach's view here as part of the structural realism developed in the book, attributing it approvingly rather than merely reporting it.

claims.claim: A promise is a metaphysical possibility grounded in the structure of personhood.
claims.source_quote: A promise is not a convention but a metaphysical possibility grounded in the structure of personhood.
claims.note: Author endorses this as part of the structural realism of the book, not merely reporting Reinach.

claims.claim: Social reality has an a priori order that is objective.
claims.source_quote: It reveals that social reality has an a priori order no less objective than the natural world.
claims.note: Author endorses this claim as part of his own structural realist position, not merely describing Reinach.

claims.claim: Legal systems are historical elaborations of the a priori order of social acts.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems, in turn, are historical elaborations of that order, cultural architectures built upon the ontological bedrock of the social act.
claims.note: Author asserts a relation between legal systems and the ontological structure of social acts.

claims.claim: An unjust command still generates an obligation of a kind.
claims.source_quote: An unjust command still generates an obligation of a kind, though it may later be annulled or condemned.
claims.note: Author endorses this as a feature of the ontology being developed—law's being is independent of moral worth.

claims.claim: Law's being is independent of its moral worth.
claims.source_quote: the idea that law's being is independent of its moral worth, grounded instead in the coherence and persistence of recognition relations.
claims.note: Author explicitly endorses this as his own structural realism—direct ontological commitment about the nature of legal being.

claims.claim: Law's being is grounded in the coherence and persistence of recognition relations.
claims.source_quote: law's being is independent of its moral worth, grounded instead in the coherence and persistence of recognition relations.
claims.note: Author asserts this as the basis of legal ontology in his structural realist account.

claims.claim: Acts of communication instantiate processes that create new dependent continuants such as obligations, rights, and authorities.
claims.source_quote: Acts of communication instantiate processes that create new dependent continuants, obligations, rights, authorities, that populate the legal world.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological mechanism: communication produces dependent continuants—direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, and authorities are dependent continuants that populate the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Acts of communication instantiate processes that create new dependent continuants, obligations, rights, authorities, that populate the legal world.
claims.note: Author categorizes legal entities as dependent continuants—a subkind claim within formal ontology.

claims.claim: Every obligation, right, and institution ultimately originates in social acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Every obligation, every right, every institution ultimately originates in such acts, moments of recognition that generate the fabric of legal being.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal-ontological relation between social acts and all legal entities.

claims.claim: Hart's primary rules connect agents through obligations and permissions.
claims.source_quote: A primary rule connects agents directly through obligations and permissions: 'You shall not steal' establishes a relation of duty between potential offenders and victims.
claims.note: Author's own ontological reinterpretation asserts that primary rules are relational entities connecting agents—ontological claim.

claims.claim: Hart's secondary rules are relations among relations.
claims.source_quote: A secondary rule, by contrast, connects rules to one another, it is a relation among relations.
claims.note: Author asserts a specific ontological character for secondary rules—they are higher-order relations.

claims.claim: Both primary and secondary rules are continuants that endure through time by virtue of ongoing recognition.
claims.source_quote: Both levels of rule are continuants, structures that endure through time by virtue of ongoing recognition within a community.
claims.note: Author classifies legal rules as continuants—a subkind claim in formal ontology.

claims.claim: Legal rules are not ideas in the minds of officials but patterns of interrelation realized in institutions.
claims.source_quote: They are not ideas in the minds of officials, but patterns of interrelation realized in institutions and sustained by practice.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological locus of legal rules—realized in institutions, not mental states.

claims.claim: A legal rule is an enduring relation that transcends its author and persists independently of the individuals who created it.
claims.source_quote: A rule, in Hart's sense, is an enduring relation that transcends its author. Once recognized, it continues to exist independently of the individuals who created it.
claims.note: Author asserts the persistence and independence of rules as ontological entities—direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: A rule's being depends on the structural network that sustains it, not on the intentions of its creators.
claims.source_quote: Its being depends not on their intentions but on the structural network that sustains
claims.note: Author asserts what grounds the existence of a rule—a claim about ontological dependence.

claims.claim: Hart's rules and Dworkin's principles are relational continuants that persist through recognition within institutions.
claims.source_quote: both Hart's rules and Dworkin's principles reveal themselves not as mere linguistic or normative propositions but as relational continuants: entities that persist and exert force through the recognition of agents within institutions.
claims.note: Author's own ontological reinterpretation categorizes these entities as relational continuants—direct subkind and property claim.

claims.claim: The statutes of unjust regimes were real in every practical sense.
claims.source_quote: To say that their statutes were 'not law' may satisfy moral conscience but does violence to ontology. They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: The author directly asserts ontological reality of these statutes, contra natural law dismissal.

claims.claim: Unjust legal regimes organized power.
claims.source_quote: They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/relational property of these regimes as part of their ontological reality.

claims.claim: Unjust legal regimes distributed rights and duties.
claims.source_quote: They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational/functional property of these regimes.

claims.claim: Unjust legal regimes structured daily life.
claims.source_quote: They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional property of these regimes as part of their ontological character.

claims.claim: The statutes of apartheid, segregation, and Nazi racial laws were codified, enforced, and institutionally recognized.
claims.source_quote: These regimes generated vast bodies of law, codified, enforced, and institutionally recognized, yet their moral bankruptcy is beyond dispute.
claims.note: The author asserts properties (codified, enforced, institutionally recognized) of these legal bodies as ontological facts.

claims.claim: Natural law theory cannot adequately describe what law is when it fails morally.
claims.source_quote: It can tell us what law ought to be, but not what it is when it fails.
claims.note: The author asserts a limitation (a property of inadequacy) in natural law theory's descriptive power—an ontological claim about the theory's scope.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.source_quote: its ontological status is more precise: it is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the nature/kind of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition exists as a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Explicit assertion of the ontological kind of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition inheres in the system of institutions collectively, not in any one agent.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between the rule of recognition and a collective institutional system.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is realized whenever institutions recognize one another's acts as legally valid.
claims.source_quote: Its realization occurs whenever institutions recognize one another's acts as legally valid, when a court accepts a statute as binding, or when a legislature enacts a rule recognized by the judiciary.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between institutional acts and the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Each act of mutual institutional recognition realizes the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Each act of mutual recognition realizes the rule of recognition and thereby reinforces its persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between mutual recognition acts and the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition's being is distributed and recurrent.
claims.source_quote: The rule's being is thus distributed and recurrent; it exists as long as its network of realizations continues across time.
claims.note: Asserts a property (distributed, recurrent) of the rule of recognition's mode of existence.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition exists as long as its network of realizations continues across time.
claims.source_quote: it exists as long as its network of realizations continues across time.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition (ontological dependence on ongoing realizations) for the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Primary rules depend on secondary rules for their validity and normative persistence.
claims.source_quote: Primary rules depend on secondary rules for their validity and for the persistence of their normative force.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between primary and secondary rules.

claims.claim: Without secondary rules, primary norms cannot exist as components of a coherent legal system.
claims.source_quote: Without secondary rules, primary norms could exist as moral or customary directives but not as components of a coherent legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for primary norms to have the property of being legal-system components.

claims.claim: Secondary rules provide the relational architecture that binds primary norms into an integrated legal structure.
claims.source_quote: Secondary rules provide the relational architecture that binds primary norms into an integrated structure.
claims.note: Asserts a structural role/function of secondary rules in relation to primary norms.

claims.claim: Secondary rules determine which norms are valid and how they may be created, interpreted, and repealed.
claims.source_quote: They determine not only which norms are valid but also how they may be created, interpreted, and repealed.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/dispositional property of secondary rules.

claims.claim: Secondary rules are the meta-conditions of legal being that make norms real within a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: They are the meta-conditions of legal being, the relations that make norms real within a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a foundational ontological role of secondary rules for the existence of norms.

claims.claim: A primary norm is a dependent continuant that inheres in an institution or agent role.
claims.source_quote: Primary Norm (Dependent Continuant) inheres in — Institution or Agent Role.
claims.note: Explicit ontological categorization and inherence relation asserted in the author's formal schema.

claims.claim: A secondary rule is a dependent continuant that depends on a system of institutions for realization.
claims.source_quote: Secondary Rule (Dependent Continuant) depends on — System of Institutions for realization.
claims.note: Explicit ontological categorization and dependence relation in the author's formal schema.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a meta-level continuant that organizes dependencies among all other rules.
claims.source_quote: Rule of Recognition (Meta-level Continuant) organizes dependencies among all other rules.
claims.note: Explicit ontological categorization and relational role asserted in the author's formal schema.

claims.claim: Institutional processes are occurrents that realize the dependencies defined by secondary rules.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Processes (Occurrents) realize the dependencies defined by secondary rules through enactment, adjudication, or amendment.
claims.note: Explicit ontological categorization and realization relation in the author's formal schema.

claims.claim: The validity of a primary norm is the result of its alignment with the system's dependency structure.
claims.source_quote: The validity of a primary norm, then, is not a property it possesses in isolation but the result of its alignment with this dependency structure.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property (validity) as relationally constituted.

claims.claim: A statute's validity is an ontological condition, not merely a sociological one.
claims.source_quote: The statute's validity is an ontological condition, not merely a sociological one, it exists within the system because its dependencies are coherently satisfied.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of a norm's validity property.

claims.claim: A statute exists as law because its dependencies trace back through institutions and secondary rules to the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: To say that a statute 'is law' is to say that it participates in a chain of dependence that traces back, through institutions and secondary rules, to the rule of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a participation/dependence relation constitutive of a norm's legal existence.

claims.claim: The rule of change defines the temporal dependencies of legal entities, governing how one set of norms can succeed another.
claims.source_quote: It specifies the temporal dependencies of legal entities, how one set of norms can succeed another without disrupting institutional continuity.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the rule of change regarding temporal ontological relations.

claims.claim: The rule of adjudication defines the repair dependencies that allow the legal system to maintain coherence.
claims.source_quote: It defines the repair dependencies that allow the system to maintain coherence in the face of contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of the rule of adjudication.

claims.claim: Secondary rules enable law's self-maintenance through time.
claims.source_quote: Together, these secondary rules enable law's self-maintenance through time.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional/functional property of secondary rules collectively.

claims.claim: Legal systems are stratified networks of dependency with the rule of recognition at the apex.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems are stratified networks of dependency, with the rule of recognition at the apex.
claims.note: Asserts the kind (stratified network of dependency) and structural position of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Constitutions, statutes, regulations, and decisions each derive validity from the levels above them in the hierarchy.
claims.source_quote: Constitutions, statutes, regulations, and decisions all occupy different levels within this hierarchy, each deriving validity from the levels above.
claims.note: Asserts dependence relations among legal entities at different hierarchical levels.

claims.claim: Validity is a relational property: a norm is valid if it exists within the appropriate dependency network.
claims.source_quote: Validity is not an empirical property but a relational one: a norm is valid if it exists within the appropriate dependency network.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind/nature of the property of validity.

claims.claim: When a norm ceases to align with the rule of recognition, it loses its ontological grounding within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The moment a norm ceases to align with the rule of recognition, for instance, when a court declares a statute unconstitutional, it loses its ontological grounding within the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a consequence (loss of ontological grounding) when a dependence relation is broken.

claims.claim: A norm declared unconstitutional may still exist as a historical artifact but no longer exists as law.
claims.source_quote: The norm may still exist as a historical artifact, but it no longer exists as law.
claims.note: Asserts a distinction in the mode of existence of an invalidated norm.

claims.claim: When a norm ceases to exist as law, its dependent continuants—obligations, rights, permissions—are extinguished or transformed.
claims.source_quote: Its dependent continuants, obligations, rights, permissions, are extinguished or transformed.
claims.note: Asserts that obligations, rights, and permissions are dependent continuants of norms, and that they are destroyed when the norm loses legal existence.

claims.claim: Invalidity is the dissolution of recognition that sustains an entity's existence within the legal field.
claims.source_quote: invalidity is a kind of ontological death: the dissolution of recognition that sustains an entity's existence within the legal field.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of invalidity as a form of existential dissolution.

claims.claim: Physical and social events (signing, voting, declaring) serve as the substrates of recognition in law.
claims.source_quote: At the base are physical and social events (signing, voting, declaring) that serve as the substrates of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of physical and social events within the legal ontological structure.

claims.claim: Rules, rights, and duties are dependent continuants that inhere in institutions.
claims.source_quote: above them are dependent continuants (rules, rights, duties) that inhere in institutions.
claims.note: Asserts ontological categorization and inherence relation for rules, rights, and duties.

claims.claim: Secondary rules are meta-level continuants that define and coordinate dependencies among lower-level legal entities.
claims.source_quote: above these are meta-level continuants (secondary rules) that define and coordinate the dependencies among lower levels.
claims.note: Asserts ontological categorization and relational function of secondary rules.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition occupies the highest level as the organizing principle of the entire legal structure.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition occupies the highest level as the organizing principle of the entire structure.
claims.note: Asserts a structural position and functional role of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: A new norm is created through an institutional process that realizes a secondary rule.
claims.source_quote: Generation: A new norm (N?) is created through an institutional process (P?) that realizes a secondary rule (R?).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between institutional processes, secondary rules, and norm generation.
