claims.claim: A norm becomes a legal fact when recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Validation: N? becomes a legal fact when it is recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition (R?).
claims.note: Asserts a condition for a norm to have the property of being a legal fact.

claims.claim: A norm persists as long as the dependencies linking it to the institutional process, secondary rule, and rule of recognition remain coherent.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance: The norm persists as long as the dependencies linking N?, P?, R?, and R? remain coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for norms as dependent on a coherent dependency network.

claims.claim: When a norm's dependencies are broken, it ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.source_quote: Termination: When these dependencies are broken, through repeal, invalidation, or loss of recognition, the norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.note: Asserts that breakage of dependency relations causes a norm to lose its status as a legal continuant.

claims.claim: A command is a transient act.
claims.source_quote: A command, as Hobbes and Austin conceived it, is a transient act, a momentary expression of will that obliges only while power or fear persists.
claims.note: The author characterizes commands as transient acts; presented as a property of commands, though attributed to Hobbes and Austin's conception, the author uses it as a foil accepted for contrast.

claims.claim: A command is a momentary expression of will.
claims.source_quote: A command, as Hobbes and Austin conceived it, is a transient act, a momentary expression of will that obliges only while power or fear persists.
claims.note: Property claim about commands; used as accepted background contrast, medium confidence since it is attributed to Hobbes/Austin but endorsed as contrast.

claims.claim: A rule is an enduring relation that transcends its author.
claims.source_quote: A rule, in Hart's sense, is an enduring relation that transcends its author.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a positive ontological characterization of rules, using it to build the argument.

claims.claim: A rule continues to exist independently of the individuals who created it.
claims.source_quote: Once recognized, it continues to exist independently of the individuals who created it.
claims.note: Direct existence claim about the ontological independence of rules from their creators.

claims.claim: A rule's being depends on the structural network that sustains its validity.
claims.source_quote: Its being depends not on their intentions but on the structural network that sustains its validity.
claims.note: Explicit ontological claim about what grounds the existence of a rule.

claims.claim: A rule is a specifically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: In the language of Basic Formal Ontology, a rule is a specifically dependent continuant.
claims.note: Explicit kind-membership claim: rules belong to the BFO category of specifically dependent continuants.

claims.claim: A rule exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.source_quote: it exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.note: Ontological grounding claim: the existence of a rule depends on collective relational maintenance by a community.

claims.claim: Laws can survive the death of their creators.
claims.source_quote: This explains why laws can survive the death of their creators.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a fact to be explained, committing to it as true.

claims.claim: A legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.source_quote: why a legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.note: Existence/persistence claim about legal systems; asserted as a fact to be explained by the ontological account.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a shared structural dependency organizing relations among institutions.
claims.source_quote: its ontological status is more precise: it is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological nature of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition exists as a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Explicit ontological classification of the rule of recognition as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition inheres in the system of institutions collectively, not in any one agent.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Asserts a specific inherence relation for the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is realized whenever institutions mutually recognize one another's acts as legally valid.
claims.source_quote: Its realization occurs whenever institutions recognize one another's acts as legally valid, when a court accepts a statute as binding, or when a legislature enacts a rule recognized by the judiciary.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between institutional acts and the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Each act of mutual recognition realizes the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Each act of mutual recognition realizes the rule of recognition and thereby reinforces its persistence.
claims.note: Asserts that particular acts bear a realization relation to the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition's being is distributed and recurrent.
claims.source_quote: The rule's being is thus distributed and recurrent; it exists as long as its network of realizations continues across time.
claims.note: Asserts a property (distributed and recurrent being) of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition exists as long as its network of realizations continues across time.
claims.source_quote: it exists as long as its network of realizations continues across time.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Primary rules depend on secondary rules for their validity and normative force.
claims.source_quote: Primary rules depend on secondary rules for their validity and for the persistence of their normative force.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between primary rules and secondary rules.

claims.claim: Without secondary rules, primary norms could exist only as moral or customary directives, not as legal system components.
claims.source_quote: Without secondary rules, primary norms could exist as moral or customary directives but not as components of a coherent legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a conditional existence condition for primary norms' legal status.

claims.claim: Secondary rules provide the relational architecture that binds primary norms into an integrated structure.
claims.source_quote: Secondary rules provide the relational architecture that binds primary norms into an integrated structure.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/functional role of secondary rules.

claims.claim: Secondary rules determine which norms are valid and how they may be created, interpreted, and repealed.
claims.source_quote: They determine not only which norms are valid but also how they may be created, interpreted, and repealed.
claims.note: Asserts functional properties of secondary rules.

claims.claim: Secondary rules are the meta-conditions of legal being that make norms real within a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: They are the meta-conditions of legal being, the relations that make norms real within a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological role/function for secondary rules.

claims.claim: A primary norm is a dependent continuant that inheres in an institution or agent role.
claims.source_quote: Primary Norm (Dependent Continuant) inheres in ? Institution or Agent Role.
claims.note: Formal ontological classification and relation asserted in the author's schematic.

claims.claim: A secondary rule is a dependent continuant that depends on a system of institutions for realization.
claims.source_quote: Secondary Rule (Dependent Continuant) depends on ? System of Institutions for realization.
claims.note: Formal ontological classification and dependence relation asserted in the author's schematic.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a meta-level continuant that organizes dependencies among all other rules.
claims.source_quote: Rule of Recognition (Meta-level Continuant) organizes dependencies among all other rules.
claims.note: Formal ontological classification and relational role asserted in the author's schematic.

claims.claim: Institutional processes are occurrents that realize the dependencies defined by secondary rules.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Processes (Occurrents) realize the dependencies defined by secondary rules through enactment, adjudication, or amendment.
claims.note: Asserts classification of institutional processes as occurrents and their realization relation.

claims.claim: The validity of a primary norm is a relational property resulting from its alignment with the dependency structure.
claims.source_quote: The validity of a primary norm, then, is not a property it possesses in isolation but the result of its alignment with this dependency structure.
claims.note: Asserts the relational ontological nature of legal validity.

claims.claim: A statute's validity is an ontological condition, not merely a sociological one.
claims.source_quote: The statute's validity is an ontological condition, not merely a sociological one, it exists within the system because its dependencies are coherently satisfied.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological (not merely sociological) character of a statute's validity.

claims.claim: The rule of change defines the temporal dependencies governing how one set of norms can succeed another.
claims.source_quote: It specifies the temporal dependencies of legal entities, how one set of norms can succeed another without disrupting institutional continuity.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the rule of change involving temporal dependencies.

claims.claim: The rule of adjudication defines the repair dependencies that allow the legal system to maintain coherence amid contradiction.
claims.source_quote: It defines the repair dependencies that allow the system to maintain coherence in the face of contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of the rule of adjudication.

claims.claim: Secondary rules collectively enable law's self-maintenance through time.
claims.source_quote: Together, these secondary rules enable law's self-maintenance through time.
claims.note: Asserts a systemic function of secondary rules.

claims.claim: Legal systems are stratified networks of dependency with the rule of recognition at the apex.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems are stratified networks of dependency, with the rule of recognition at the apex.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure and organization of legal systems.

claims.claim: Constitutions, statutes, regulations, and decisions each derive validity from the levels above them in the hierarchy.
claims.source_quote: Constitutions, statutes, regulations, and decisions all occupy different levels within this hierarchy, each deriving validity from the levels above.
claims.note: Asserts a hierarchical dependence relation among legal entities.

claims.claim: Validity is a relational property: a norm is valid if it exists within the appropriate dependency network.
claims.source_quote: Validity is not an empirical property but a relational one: a norm is valid if it exists within the appropriate dependency network.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature of legal validity.

claims.claim: When a norm ceases to align with the rule of recognition, it loses its ontological grounding within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The moment a norm ceases to align with the rule of recognition, for instance, when a court declares a statute unconstitutional, it loses its ontological grounding within the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a condition under which an entity loses a relational property (ontological grounding).

claims.claim: An invalidated norm may still exist as a historical artifact but no longer exists as law.
claims.source_quote: The norm may still exist as a historical artifact, but it no longer exists as law.
claims.note: Asserts that invalidation changes the ontological kind of a norm's existence.

claims.claim: When a norm loses legal existence, its dependent continuants—obligations, rights, permissions—are extinguished or transformed.
claims.source_quote: Its dependent continuants, obligations, rights, permissions, are extinguished or transformed.
claims.note: Asserts what happens to entities ontologically dependent on an invalidated norm.

claims.claim: Invalidity is a kind of ontological death: the dissolution of recognition sustaining an entity's legal existence.
claims.source_quote: invalidity is a kind of ontological death: the dissolution of recognition that sustains an entity's existence within the legal field.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological characterization of invalidity as cessation of existence within the legal domain.

claims.claim: Physical and social events such as signing, voting, and declaring serve as substrates of recognition.
claims.source_quote: At the base are physical and social events (signing, voting, declaring) that serve as the substrates of recognition
claims.note: Asserts that physical and social events have the functional role of substrates in the legal ontology.

claims.claim: Rules, rights, and duties are dependent continuants that inhere in institutions.
claims.source_quote: above them are dependent continuants (rules, rights, duties) that inhere in institutions
claims.note: Asserts ontological classification and inherence relation for rules, rights, and duties.

claims.claim: Secondary rules are meta-level continuants that define and coordinate dependencies among lower-level legal entities.
claims.source_quote: above these are meta-level continuants (secondary rules) that define and coordinate the dependencies among lower levels.
claims.note: Asserts ontological classification and relational role of secondary rules.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the organizing principle of the entire legal structure, occupying its highest level.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition occupies the highest level as the organizing principle of the entire structure.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function and positional property of the rule of recognition within the legal ontology.

claims.claim: A new norm is created through an institutional process that realizes a secondary rule.
claims.source_quote: Generation: A new norm (N?) is created through an institutional process (P?) that realizes a secondary rule (R?).
claims.note: Asserts the generative ontological process by which norms come into existence.

claims.claim: A norm becomes a legal fact when recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Validation: N? becomes a legal fact when it is recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition (R?).
claims.note: Asserts the condition under which a norm acquires the status of legal fact.

claims.claim: A norm persists as long as the dependencies linking it to the institutional process, secondary rule, and rule of recognition remain coherent.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance: The norm persists as long as the dependencies linking N?, P?, R?, and R? remain coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for legal norms in terms of dependency coherence.

claims.claim: When its dependencies are broken, a norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.source_quote: Termination: When these dependencies are broken, through repeal, invalidation, or loss of recognition, the norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.note: Asserts a termination condition for legal norms' existence as legal continuants.

claims.claim: Nazi racial statutes were real legal structures that organized power and structured daily life.
claims.source_quote: They were real in every practical sense: they organized power, distributed rights and duties, and structured daily life.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological reality and structural properties of unjust legal regimes.

claims.claim: A morally defective law persists as a malformed but effective structure in social reality.
claims.source_quote: A morally defective law may lack legitimacy, but it does not vanish from the fabric of social reality. It persists as a malformed but effective structure, an ontological pathology.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the persistence and nature of unjust law.

claims.claim: Unjust law is an ontological pathology—a malformed structure, not an absence.
claims.source_quote: It persists as a malformed but effective structure, an ontological pathology. Its existence is not negated by injustice; rather, injustice appears as a distortion within being itself.
claims.note: Author positively asserts a specific ontological category for unjust law.

claims.claim: Injustice is a distortion within being, a contradiction within the structure of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: Injustice appears as a distortion within being itself, a contradiction within the structure of recognition and obligation that constitutes the legal order.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological nature of injustice as a structural distortion.

claims.claim: Moral failure does not entail ontological nullity; law can exist wrongly.
claims.source_quote: To grasp this distinction is to see that moral failure does not entail ontological nullity. Law can exist wrongly.
claims.note: Author asserts a relationship (non-entailment) between moral and ontological status.

claims.claim: Unjust law is a misalignment—a breakdown in the coherence of recognition.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological perspective, unjust law is not an absence but a misalignment, a breakdown in the coherence of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological character of unjust law as misalignment.

claims.claim: Unjust law continues to function as law because institutions and agents acknowledge it as binding.
claims.source_quote: It continues to function as law because institutions and agents still acknowledge it as binding.
claims.note: Author asserts what sustains the legal being of unjust law—a relational/functional claim.

claims.claim: Injustice is the persistence of law under conditions of disordered recognition.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, injustice is the persistence of law under conditions of disordered recognition.
claims.note: Author offers a positive ontological definition of injustice.

claims.claim: Injustice is an ontological failure of alignment, where law's structure remains intact but internally inconsistent.
claims.source_quote: It treats injustice as an ontological failure of alignment, a condition in which the structure of law remains intact but internally inconsistent.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological nature of injustice as structural misalignment.

claims.claim: Law can be both real and wrong simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Law, in this sense, can be both real and wrong.
claims.note: Author asserts a fundamental ontological duality of law.

claims.claim: Law's power derives from its structure as an institution of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: Law's power, for good or ill, derives from its structure as an institution of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: Author asserts what kind of entity law is and what accounts for its causal power.

claims.claim: Even immoral laws are woven into the social ontology they corrupt.
claims.source_quote: Even immoral laws are woven into the social ontology they corrupt.
claims.note: Author asserts that immoral laws are part of social ontology—a claim about their mode of existence.

claims.claim: Legal positivism reduced law to an artifact of will, habit, or linguistic convention.
claims.source_quote: It reduced law to an artifact of will, habit, or linguistic convention, something that exists only because people behave as if it does.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a characterization of positivism's ontological commitment, which he then criticizes; asserted as a description of what positivism holds and implicitly rejects.

claims.claim: Positivism produced a conception of law that is ontologically thin.
claims.source_quote: The result is a conception of law that is analytically clear but ontologically thin: a model that explains how rules are recognized without ever explaining what kind of being rules are.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of positivism's conception of law—its ontological thinness.

claims.claim: Hart's rule of recognition is epistemological rather than ontological in character.
claims.source_quote: Even his model remained epistemological rather than ontological. The rule of recognition describes how legal actors know what valid law is; it does not explain what law is.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological character (or lack thereof) of Hart's rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Hart's social practice account leaves unexplored the nature of the entities that patterns of behavior sustain.
claims.source_quote: Hart's 'social practice' account locates legality in patterns of behavior and acceptance, but it leaves unexplored the nature of the entities those patterns sustain.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological gap in Hart's account—the nature of legal entities is unaddressed.

claims.claim: The positivist separation thesis is primarily an ontological omission, not merely a moral claim.
claims.source_quote: The positivist separation thesis, that the existence of law is one thing and its merit another, has been widely misunderstood as a moral claim, but it is primarily an ontological omission.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological character of the separation thesis.

claims.claim: If law is nothing more than convention or practice, its existence collapses into the judgments and habits that sustain it.
claims.source_quote: If law is nothing more than a convention or a practice, then the distinction between its existence and its value collapses: conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a consequence of the positivist position, indicating conventions have no independent reality—an ontological claim the author endorses as showing positivism's inadequacy.

claims.claim: The legal order is constituted by a structure of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: A contradiction within the structure of recognition and obligation that constitutes the legal order.
claims.note: Author asserts what constitutes the legal order—a claim about its ontological makeup.

claims.claim: A legal norm becomes a legal fact when recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Validation: N? becomes a legal fact when it is recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition (R?).
claims.note: Direct assertion about the conditions under which a legal norm acquires the status of legal fact—an ontological claim about entity existence and recognition.

claims.claim: A legal norm persists as long as its dependencies among norm, power, primary rule, and secondary rule remain coherent.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance: The norm persists as long as the dependencies linking N?, P?, R?, and R? remain coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for a legal norm as an entity, grounding its continued existence in relational dependencies.

claims.claim: A legal norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant when its dependencies are broken.
claims.source_quote: Termination: When these dependencies are broken, through repeal, invalidation, or loss of recognition, the norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.note: Asserts that the norm is a legal continuant whose existence is terminated by the dissolution of specific ontological dependencies.

claims.claim: Law's validity is a dynamic equilibrium sustained by ontological dependencies among rules and institutions.
claims.source_quote: law's validity is a dynamic equilibrium sustained by ontological dependencies among rules and institutions.
claims.note: The author endorses this as what Hart 'intuited but did not formalize'—a positive ontological assertion about the nature of legal validity.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the organizing principle that coordinates dependencies across the legal system's processes.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition is the organizing principle that coordinates these dependencies across the system's processes of creation, adjudication, and change.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function for the rule of recognition within the legal system—an ontological claim about its function.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the metaphysical condition of legality itself.
claims.source_quote: the rule of recognition is not merely a sociological convention but the metaphysical condition of legality itself.
claims.note: Explicit positive assertion by the author about the ontological status of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the structure that allows law to exist as a self-identifying domain of reality.
claims.source_quote: It is the structure that allows law to exist as a self-identifying domain of reality, a world of norms sustained by recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property and function of the rule of recognition in enabling law's existence as a domain.

claims.claim: The authority of the rule of recognition derives from ontological coherence, not from force or moral obligation.
claims.source_quote: Its authority derives not from force or moral obligation but from ontological coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the rule of recognition—the source of its authority—as an ontological rather than normative or causal matter.

claims.claim: When the rule of recognition collapses, law disintegrates.
claims.source_quote: When the rule of recognition collapses, when institutions no longer share a unified structure of validation, law disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: law's existence is conditioned on the rule of recognition's coherence.

claims.claim: A constitutional crisis is the dissolution of the meta-structure that sustains legal being.
claims.source_quote: This is the ontological meaning of A constitutional crisis: the dissolution of the meta-structure that sustains legal being.
claims.note: The author defines a constitutional crisis ontologically as the breakdown of the meta-structure—asserting what kind of event it is.

claims.claim: The restoration of law occurs when a new rule of recognition emerges and reorganizes the dependencies of the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: the restoration of law occurs when a new rule of recognition emerges, reorganizing the dependencies that define the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts conditions under which law as an entity is restored—an ontological claim about law's existence and conditions for it.

claims.claim: Law's reality consists in the dependencies that bind its rules together, not in the commands it issues.
claims.source_quote: It implies that law's reality consists not in the commands it issues but in the dependencies that bind its rules together.
claims.note: The author endorses this implication as part of his own structural ontology—an assertion about what constitutes law's reality.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition, as meta-structure, embodies the highest level of ontological dependence in the legal world.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition, as meta-structure, embodies the highest level of ontological dependence in the legal world, it is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a property and role of the rule of recognition within the ontological hierarchy of the legal system.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.source_quote: it is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of the rule of recognition—an ontological claim about what it is for law as a system.

claims.claim: Law is an evolving ontological system: a network of roles, rules, and processes that continually realizes itself through the maintenance of its dependencies.
claims.source_quote: we can see law as an evolving ontological system: a network of roles, rules, and processes that continually realizes itself through the maintenance of its dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind that law belongs to and describes its constitutive structure and mode of existence.

claims.claim: A fact-making failure occurs when the dependencies required for the existence of a legal fact are not satisfied.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, a fact-making failure occurs when the dependencies required for the existence of a legal fact are not satisfied, or when incompatible dependencies coexist without repair.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological definition of fact-making failure—a claim about what kind of situation it is in terms of dependency relations.

claims.claim: A fact-making failure corresponds to a breakdown in the chain linking occurrents to dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: In the Basic Formal Ontology framework, this corresponds to a breakdown in the chain that links occurrents (procedural events) to dependent continuants (recognized relations and statuses).
claims.note: Asserts an ontological identification of fact-making failure in terms of BFO categories—a relational ontological claim.

claims.claim: A pseudo-entity is an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The result is a pseudo-entity: an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Introduces and defines a kind of entity (pseudo-entity) and asserts its property of lacking ontological integrity—an ontological claim.

claims.claim: Law's existence is continuously contingent on the proper functioning of its institutional and relational machinery.
claims.source_quote: law's existence is neither metaphysically secure nor automatically self-sustaining, but continuously contingent on the proper functioning of its institutional and relational machinery.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law's existence—its contingency on institutional functioning—a direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: Law's validity is a dynamic equilibrium sustained by ontological dependencies among rules and institutions.
claims.source_quote: law's validity is a dynamic equilibrium sustained by ontological dependencies among rules and institutions. The rule of recognition is the organizing principle that coordinates these dependencies across the system's processes of creation, adjudication, and change.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the nature of legal validity as an ontological property.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the organizing principle coordinating dependencies across legal processes.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition is the organizing principle that coordinates these dependencies across the system's processes of creation, adjudication, and change.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/structural role for the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the metaphysical condition of legality itself.
claims.source_quote: the rule of recognition is not merely a sociological convention but the metaphysical condition of legality itself.
claims.note: Author plainly asserts this in his own voice, contrasting it with the 'merely sociological' view.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the structure that allows law to exist as a self-identifying domain of reality.
claims.source_quote: It is the structure that allows law to exist as a self-identifying domain of reality, a world of norms sustained by recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/enabling property of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The authority of the rule of recognition derives from ontological coherence.
claims.source_quote: Its authority derives not from force or moral obligation but from ontological coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property (source of authority) of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: When the rule of recognition collapses, law disintegrates.
claims.source_quote: When the rule of recognition collapses, when institutions no longer share a unified structure of validation, law disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: law's existence depends on the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: A constitutional crisis is the dissolution of the meta-structure that sustains legal being.
claims.source_quote: This is the ontological meaning of A constitutional crisis: the dissolution of the meta-structure that sustains legal being.
claims.note: Asserts what kind of thing a constitutional crisis is ontologically.

claims.claim: The restoration of law occurs when a new rule of recognition emerges.
claims.source_quote: the restoration of law occurs when a new rule of recognition emerges, reorganizing the dependencies that define the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a condition for the re-existence of law.

claims.claim: Law's reality consists in the dependencies that bind its rules together, not in the commands it issues.
claims.source_quote: It implies that law's reality consists not in the commands it issues but in the dependencies that bind its rules together.
claims.note: Author endorses this as the implication of his structural ontology.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition embodies the highest level of ontological dependence in the legal world.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition, as meta-structure, embodies the highest level of ontological dependence in the legal world, it is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a property (highest ontological dependence) of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.source_quote: it is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.note: Directly asserts a functional/ontological role for the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Law is an evolving ontological system: a network of roles, rules, and processes.
claims.source_quote: we can see law as an evolving ontological system: a network of roles, rules, and processes that continually realizes itself through the maintenance of its dependencies.
claims.note: Author asserts what kind of entity law is.

claims.claim: Law continually realizes itself through the maintenance of its dependencies.
claims.source_quote: a network of roles, rules, and processes that continually realizes itself through the maintenance of its dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional/functional property of law as an ontological system.

claims.claim: A fact-making failure occurs when dependencies required for a legal fact are not satisfied.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, a fact-making failure occurs when the dependencies required for the existence of a legal fact are not satisfied, or when incompatible dependencies coexist without repair.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of fact-making failures in terms of dependency satisfaction.

claims.claim: A fact-making failure also occurs when incompatible dependencies coexist without repair.
claims.source_quote: a fact-making failure occurs when the dependencies required for the existence of a legal fact are not satisfied, or when incompatible dependencies coexist without repair.
claims.note: Asserts a second ontological condition constituting fact-making failure.

claims.claim: Fact-making failures correspond to breakdowns in the chain linking occurrents to dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: In the Basic Formal Ontology framework, this corresponds to a breakdown in the chain that links occurrents (procedural events) to dependent continuants (recognized relations and statuses).
claims.note: Author asserts what fact-making failures are in BFO ontological terms, endorsed as his framework.

claims.claim: A pseudo-entity is an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The result is a pseudo-entity: an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts what kind of entity a pseudo-entity is and what property it has (lack of ontological integrity).

claims.claim: Law's existence is continuously contingent on the proper functioning of its institutional and relational machinery.
claims.source_quote: law's existence is neither metaphysically secure nor automatically self-sustaining, but continuously contingent on the proper functioning of its institutional and relational machinery.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law's mode of existence: contingency on institutional functioning.

claims.claim: A norm persists as long as the dependencies linking it, its power, and its rules remain coherent.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance: The norm persists as long as the dependencies linking N?, P?, R?, and R? remain coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for norms, a direct ontological claim about norm existence.

claims.claim: When its dependencies are broken, a norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.source_quote: Termination: When these dependencies are broken, through repeal, invalidation, or loss of recognition, the norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.note: Asserts a termination condition for the existence of a norm qua legal continuant.

claims.claim: A norm becomes a legal fact when recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Validation: N? becomes a legal fact when it is recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition (R?).
claims.note: Asserts the condition under which a norm acquires the status of legal fact.

claims.claim: A rule is a specifically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: In the language of Basic Formal Ontology, a rule is a specifically dependent continuant, it exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.note: Direct ontological categorization of rules as a subkind of specifically dependent continuant.

claims.claim: A rule exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.source_quote: a rule is a specifically dependent continuant, it exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.note: Asserts the dependence relation: rules depend on collective maintenance of instantiating relations.

claims.claim: Laws can survive the death of their creators.
claims.source_quote: This explains why laws can survive the death of their creators, and why a legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.note: Asserts a property of laws: persistence beyond their creators.

claims.claim: A legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.source_quote: This explains why laws can survive the death of their creators, and why a legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of legal systems: temporal persistence through social change.

claims.claim: Primary rules depend on the recognition of agents within specific contexts of application.
claims.source_quote: Primary rules depend on the recognition of agents within specific contexts of application, citizens, officials, litigants.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between primary rules and agent recognition.

claims.claim: Secondary rules depend on the recognition of institutions as authoritative arbiters of validity.
claims.source_quote: secondary rules depend on the recognition of institutions as authoritative arbiters of validity.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between secondary rules and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the meta-relation that coordinates all other relations within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition stands at the apex of this hierarchy: it is the meta-relation that coordinates all other relations within the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts the relational role/function of the rule of recognition within the legal ontological hierarchy.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the structural backbone of legality.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological standpoint, the rule of recognition is the structural backbone of legality, the mechanism by which coherence is maintained within the field of relational continuants that constitute law.
claims.note: Assigns a structural role/property to the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Law is constituted by a field of relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: the mechanism by which coherence is maintained within the field of relational continuants that constitute law.
claims.note: Asserts that law's constituents are relational continuants—a claim about the ontological makeup of law.

claims.claim: Dworkin's principles are structural constraints within the network of relational continuants that make up law.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological perspective, Dworkin's 'principles' can be understood as structural constraints within the network of relational continuants that make up law.
claims.note: Author endorses this reinterpretation as his own positive ontological claim, not merely reported as Dworkin's view.

claims.claim: Principles are internal conditions of coherence that govern how relations among rules, obligations, and institutions hold together.
claims.source_quote: They are not external moral appeals imposed from outside the legal system, but internal conditions of coherence that govern how relations among rules, obligations, and institutions hold together.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of principles within the legal ontological structure.

claims.claim: A principle such as equality before the law is a structural requirement ensuring consistency of the relational web constituting legality.
claims.source_quote: A principle such as equality before the law is not merely an ethical ideal; it is a structural requirement that ensures the consistency of the relational web that constitutes legality.
claims.note: Asserts that a specific principle has the property of being a structural requirement, not merely an ethical ideal.

claims.claim: Rules and principles are relational continuants within the same network of dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Ontology unites them by showing that both rules and principles are relational continuants within the same network of dependencies.
claims.note: Directly categorizes both rules and principles as relational continuants sharing the same ontological network.

claims.claim: Rules define the connections within the legal network.
claims.source_quote: Rules define the connections; principles regulate the integrity of those connections.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of rules within the relational legal structure.

claims.claim: Principles regulate the integrity of the connections within the legal network.
claims.source_quote: Rules define the connections; principles regulate the integrity of those connections.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of principles within the relational legal structure.

claims.claim: Rules give law its durable form.
claims.source_quote: Rules give law its durable form; principles allow it to evolve while remaining coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of rules: providing durable form to law.

claims.claim: Principles allow law to evolve while remaining coherent.
claims.source_quote: Rules give law its durable form; principles allow it to evolve while remaining coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of principles: enabling coherent evolution of law.

claims.claim: Principles preserve the legal system's capacity for self-correction.
claims.source_quote: They are the means by which law repairs itself ontologically. In this way, principles fulfill a structural rather than a moral role: they preserve the system's capacity for self-correction.
claims.note: Asserts a structural function of principles: preserving self-corrective capacity.

claims.claim: A legal system is legitimate when its network of rules and principles forms a coherent whole.
claims.source_quote: A legal system is legitimate when its network of rules and principles forms a coherent whole, when obligations align with recognitions and institutions operate within their structural constraints.
claims.note: Asserts a condition (property) of legitimacy for legal systems in ontological terms.

claims.claim: Illegitimacy is a form of ontological contradiction—a misalignment among continuants.
claims.source_quote: Illegitimacy, by contrast, is a form of ontological contradiction: a misalignment among continuants that undermines the system's capacity for self-sustaining order.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological identity: illegitimacy is a misalignment among continuants.

claims.claim: Norms are real entities that occupy specific ontological categories.
claims.source_quote: the recognition that norms themselves are entities, real components of the world that occupy specific ontological categories.
claims.note: Explicitly asserts the existence and ontological categorization of norms.

claims.claim: A norm is a realizable dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: A norm is neither a fact nor a statement about facts; it is a realizable dependent continuant, a relational structure that exists in virtue of being recognized and capable of being realized through action.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of norms as a subkind of realizable dependent continuant.

claims.claim: A norm is a relational structure that exists in virtue of being recognized and capable of being realized through action.
claims.source_quote: it is a realizable dependent continuant, a relational structure that exists in virtue of being recognized and capable of being realized through action.
claims.note: Asserts the mode of existence and relational nature of norms.

claims.claim: Norms are potentials embedded within social reality.
claims.source_quote: In other words, norms are potentials embedded within social reality.
claims.note: Asserts a property of norms: they are potentials located within social reality.

claims.claim: Norms exist as enduring possibilities whose realization continuously shapes law and social order.
claims.source_quote: They exist not as abstract ideals but as enduring possibilities whose realization continuously shapes the fabric of law and social order.
claims.note: Asserts the mode of existence of norms and their causal/structural role.

claims.claim: Primary and secondary rules constitute the structural skeleton of law.
claims.source_quote: Primary and secondary rules constitute the structural skeleton; principles form the tensile fabric that holds it together.
claims.note: Asserts the structural role of primary and secondary rules within the legal ontology.

claims.claim: Principles form the tensile fabric that holds the legal structure together.
claims.source_quote: Primary and secondary rules constitute the structural skeleton; principles form the tensile fabric that holds it together.
claims.note: Asserts the structural role of principles within the legal ontology.

claims.claim: Law's validity and meaning arise from the stability of the relations connecting rules and principles.
claims.source_quote: law's validity and meaning arise not from will or morality alone but from the stability of the relations that connect them, a structure at once normative, institutional, and ontological.
claims.note: Asserts a claim about the ontological source of law's validity and meaning.

claims.claim: If law is a convention or practice, its existence and value cannot be separated.
claims.source_quote: If law is nothing more than a convention or a practice, then the distinction between its existence and its value collapses: conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.note: The author asserts an ontological consequence: for conventions, existence and value are inseparable, because conventions lack reality independent of sustaining judgments and habits.

claims.claim: Conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.source_quote: conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the mode of existence of conventions: their reality is constituted by judgments and habits.

claims.claim: If law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality, its being cannot be divorced from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.source_quote: if law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality, then its being cannot be divorced from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.note: The author presents this as a conditional but endorses the underlying ontological point—law's being is constituted by normative relations—as part of the argument against positivism.

claims.claim: Positivist deflation of law's ontology undermines its own analytic aims.
claims.source_quote: The positivist deflation of law's ontology thus undermines its own analytic aims. It explains validity at the cost of existence.
claims.note: The author asserts that positivism's ontological stance is self-defeating, which is an ontological claim about the relationship between positivism's account of validity and existence.

claims.claim: Positivist accounts explain validity at the cost of existence.
claims.source_quote: It explains validity at the cost of existence.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion: positivism's account of legal validity sacrifices an account of law's existence.

claims.claim: The separation thesis is primarily an ontological omission, not a moral claim.
claims.source_quote: has been widely misunderstood as a moral claim, but it is primarily an ontological omission. It refuses to specify what sort of thing law must be for the separation even to make sense.
claims.note: The author asserts the nature of the separation thesis: it is an ontological omission—a claim about what kind of entity law is (or fails to specify).

claims.claim: A realizable dependent continuant is an entity that inheres in a bearer and is fulfilled or manifested under certain conditions.
claims.source_quote: A realizable dependent continuant, in the framework of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), is an entity that inheres in a bearer and is fulfilled or manifested under certain conditions.
claims.note: Direct ontological definition asserting what kind of entity a realizable dependent continuant is and what properties it has.

claims.claim: A legal norm exists insofar as it possesses the capacity to structure behavior and recognition within an institutional framework.
claims.source_quote: A legal norm "exists" insofar as it possesses the capacity to structure behavior and recognition within an institutional framework.
claims.note: The author asserts a positive ontological claim about what constitutes the existence of a legal norm and what property it has.

claims.claim: A legal norm continues to exist as a potential for realization even when unfulfilled.
claims.source_quote: It does not vanish when unfulfilled; rather, it continues to exist as a potential for realization, ready to be instantiated when the relevant conditions arise.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal norms: they persist as unrealized potentials rather than ceasing to exist when not instantiated.

claims.claim: The capacity of a statute to obligate and of a right to empower are ontological parallels to natural realizable dispositions.
claims.source_quote: In the legal world, the capacity of a statute to obligate or of a right to empower operates in precisely the same way. These are not metaphors but ontological parallels.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts these are ontological parallels, not merely analogies, committing to a shared ontological structure between legal and natural dispositions.

claims.claim: A statute has the capacity to obligate.
claims.source_quote: the capacity of a statute to obligate or of a right to empower operates in precisely the same way.
claims.note: Asserts a property (capacity to obligate) of a specific legal entity (statute).

claims.claim: A right has the capacity to empower.
claims.source_quote: the capacity of a statute to obligate or of a right to empower operates in precisely the same way.
claims.note: Asserts a property (capacity to empower) of a specific legal entity (right).

claims.claim: Institutionalization continuously shapes the fabric of law and social order.
claims.source_quote: ization continuously shapes the fabric of law and social order.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive relation between institutionalization and law/social order; medium confidence due to partial text.

claims.claim: Misrecognition produces a false positive: a dependent continuant instantiated without necessary structural support.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this produces a false positive: a dependent continuant (the supposed legal fact) instantiated without the necessary structural support.
claims.note: Author directly asserts an ontological result of misrecognition in terms of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Entities created by misrecognition are ontologically unstable and exist in a state of suspended legitimacy.
claims.source_quote: Such misrecognition creates entities that are ontologically unstable, they exist in a state of suspended legitimacy, subject to annulment or correction once the error is discovered.
claims.note: Author asserts a property (ontological instability, suspended legitimacy) of entities created by misrecognition.

claims.claim: In ontological defect, the legal fact itself fails to exist within the legal field.
claims.source_quote: in ontological defect, the fact itself fails to exist within the legal field.
claims.note: Author asserts a distinction about existence of legal facts, committing to when a legal fact fails to exist.

claims.claim: An impostor's signing lacks the necessary dependencies of intention, authority, and recognized identity.
claims.source_quote: Yet the necessary dependencies (intention, authority, and recognized identity) are absent. The act does not instantiate a genuine legal obligation, even if it temporarily appears to.
claims.note: Author asserts that an act without these dependencies fails to instantiate a legal obligation—an ontological claim about dependency conditions.

claims.claim: A void act is a non-being clothed in the appearance of law.
claims.source_quote: It is not merely voidable but void: a non-being clothed in the appearance of law.
claims.note: Author asserts that void acts are non-beings—a direct ontological claim about their mode of existence.

claims.claim: Misrecognition generates entities without the dependencies required for their persistence.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition, then, is the ontological equivalent of a false creation, an act that generates entities without the dependencies required for their persistence.
claims.note: Author asserts that misrecognition generates a certain kind of entity lacking required dependencies.

claims.claim: Fraudulent legal entities are dependent continuants without proper grounding.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, such entities are dependent continuants without proper grounding: they borrow their apparent being from genuine institutional processes but lack alignment with the system's rule of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological classification of fraudulent entities as improperly grounded dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Fraudulent entities are ontologically parasitic, depending on concealment of their own invalidity.
claims.source_quote: Fraud operates by manipulating recognition processes to produce entities that appear valid but are ontologically parasitic. A fraudulent deed or forged judicial order... creates a phantom legal entity that depends on the concealment of its own invalidity.
claims.note: Author asserts a property (ontological parasitism) and a dependency relation of fraudulent entities.

claims.claim: When fraud is exposed, no legal entity ever truly existed.
claims.source_quote: Once exposed, their recognition collapses, revealing that no legal entity ever truly existed.
claims.note: Author asserts that fraudulent entities lack genuine existence—a direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: The nullification of fraud is an ontological repair restoring coherence in the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The nullification of fraud, therefore, is not merely a moral correction but an ontological repair: the restoration of coherence in the field of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts that nullification of fraud has the ontological role/function of repair and coherence restoration.

claims.claim: Periods during which fraudulent entities are treated as real constitute temporary zones of incoherence.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, these moments constitute temporary zones of incoherence in which contradiction is tolerated.
claims.note: Author asserts that certain temporal periods have the ontological property of incoherence/contradiction.

claims.claim: Jurisdictional voids are situations of non-recognition where no competent institution exists to confer recognition.
claims.source_quote: A third form of failure arises in jurisdictional voids, where recognition cannot attach because no competent institution exists to confer it. These are not cases of misrecognition but of non-recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the nature and defining condition of jurisdictional voids as a distinct ontological category.

claims.claim: Acts in jurisdictional voids exist in a liminal state called recognitional indeterminacy.
claims.source_quote: They exist in a liminal state between legality and non-being, a condition we might call recognitional indeterminacy.
claims.note: Author names and asserts a liminal ontological condition, though the label is introduced with 'we might call', slightly hedged.

claims.claim: When institutional domains fail to overlap or are contested, the ontological field of law fragments.
claims.source_quote: When these domains fail to overlap or are contested, the ontological field of law fragments. The result is not merely political uncertainty but ontological discontinuity.
claims.note: Author asserts that contested domains produce ontological fragmentation—a claim about the structure of legal ontology.

claims.claim: Creating new legal spaces is an act of ontological reconstruction establishing boundaries for recognition.
claims.source_quote: Creating new legal spaces is an act of ontological reconstruction, it establishes the boundaries within which recognition can once again attach to brute facts, converting chaos into order.
claims.note: Author asserts a role/function for the creation of new legal spaces: ontological reconstruction.

claims.claim: Misrecognition corrupts the referential alignment between recognition and its object.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition corrupts the referential alignment between recognition and its object; fraud subverts the dependency structure itself; jurisdictional voids eliminate the conditions of recognition altogether.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational property of misrecognition regarding alignment between recognition and object.

claims.claim: Fraud subverts the dependency structure of legal fact-making.
claims.source_quote: fraud subverts the dependency structure itself
claims.note: Author asserts a property/action of fraud with respect to dependency structures.

claims.claim: Jurisdictional voids eliminate the conditions of recognition altogether.
claims.source_quote: jurisdictional voids eliminate the conditions of recognition altogether.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of jurisdictional voids: elimination of conditions of recognition.

claims.claim: Unresolved contradiction debt leads to systemic fragility and eventual collapse.
claims.source_quote: If left unresolved, such debt accumulates, leading to systemic fragility and eventual collapse.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/dispositional property of unresolved contradiction debt.

claims.claim: Procedural correctness is an ontological, not merely formal, requirement for legal facts.
claims.source_quote: Anomalies in fact-making also clarify why procedural correctness is an ontological, not merely formal, requirement. Procedural errors are not trivial technicalities but breaches in the chain of recognition that sustains law's being.
claims.note: Author asserts that procedural correctness has an ontological status, not merely formal—a claim about its nature and function.

claims.claim: A judgment rendered without jurisdiction cannot exist as a valid legal entity.
claims.source_quote: A judgment rendered without jurisdiction, even if substantively just, cannot exist as a valid legal entity because it fails to satisfy its dependency conditions.
claims.note: Author asserts an existence condition for legal entities: jurisdictional dependency.

claims.claim: A contract without consent lacks the recognition necessary to instantiate obligation.
claims.source_quote: Similarly, a contract without consent lacks the recognition necessary to instantiate obligation.
claims.note: Author asserts a dependency condition: consent is required for a contract to instantiate obligation.

claims.claim: The act of legal correction modifies the structure of recognition in the present rather than undoing past brute events.
claims.source_quote: The act of correction does not travel backward in time to undo the brute events; rather, it modifies the structure of recognition in the present, redefining which entities are acknowledged as valid continuants.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of legal correction regarding its temporal and ontological mode of operation.

claims.claim: When a fraudulent deed is annulled, its dependent continuants—ownership, rights, obligations—are extinguished.
claims.source_quote: The fraudulent deed, once annulled, remains as a historical artifact, a record of misrecognition, but its dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) are extinguished.
claims.note: Author asserts that annulment extinguishes specific dependent continuants, with ontological commitment to these entities and their cessation.

claims.claim: Law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality.
claims.source_quote: In this way, law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality: what once seemed real may persist as record but not as law.
claims.note: Author asserts a distinction internal to legal ontology between two modes of persistence.

claims.claim: Recognition is always localized within a network of institutions defining territorial or functional domains.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is always localized within a network of institutions that define territorial or functional domains.
claims.note: Author asserts a structural property of recognition: its localization within institutional networks.

claims.claim: A pseudo-entity is an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The result is a pseudo-entity: an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence and defining property of a pseudo-entity as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.source_quote: conventions have no reality apart from the judgments and habits that sustain them.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological status of conventions.

claims.claim: Law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality.
claims.source_quote: if law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality, then its being cannot be divorced from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.note: The author presents this as a conditional but treats it as capturing law's actual nature, contrasting it with positivism's failure.

claims.claim: Law's being cannot be divorced from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.source_quote: if law is a structure of recognition embedded in social reality, then its being cannot be divorced from the normative relations that constitute it.
claims.note: The author endorses this as following from law's nature; it is an ontological claim about constitutive relations.

claims.claim: Legal systems survive the death of rulers and the replacement of officials.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems survive the death of rulers and the replacement of officials; statutes remain binding long after their authors are forgotten.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal systems: temporal persistence beyond their creators.

claims.claim: Statutes remain binding long after their authors are forgotten.
claims.source_quote: statutes remain binding long after their authors are forgotten.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of statutes regarding their continued normative force.

claims.claim: Acceptance is a relational act that depends on structures of recognition and obligation.
claims.source_quote: Acceptance is itself a relational act that depends on structures of recognition and obligation.
claims.note: Asserts that acceptance bears a dependency relation to structures of recognition and obligation.

claims.claim: Commands and rules are nodes within a network of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Commands and rules are not isolated events but nodes within a network of dependent continuants, obligations, roles, institutions, that together constitute the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and relational structure of commands and rules.

claims.claim: Obligations, roles, and institutions together constitute the legal domain.
claims.source_quote: nodes within a network of dependent continuants, obligations, roles, institutions, that together constitute the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive relation between obligations, roles, institutions, and the legal domain.

claims.claim: When a court issues a judgment, it brings into being new relational entities.
claims.source_quote: When a court issues a judgment, it does more than produce sounds or marks on paper; it brings into being new relational entities: rights, duties, and statuses that persist across time.
claims.note: Asserts that judicial judgments are causally responsible for the existence of new entities.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and statuses are relational entities that persist across time.
claims.source_quote: it brings into being new relational entities: rights, duties, and statuses that persist across time.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind (relational entities) and property (temporal persistence) of rights, duties, and statuses.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and statuses are not reducible to psychological states of those who recognize them.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not reducible to the psychological states of those who recognize them.
claims.note: Asserts an irreducibility claim about the ontological status of legal entities.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and statuses have a structured mode of existence analogous to other social continuants.
claims.source_quote: They have a structured mode of existence analogous to other social continuants, like corporations or marriages.
claims.note: Asserts that legal entities share an ontological mode with social continuants such as corporations and marriages.

claims.claim: Corporations and marriages are social continuants.
claims.source_quote: analogous to other social continuants, like corporations or marriages.
claims.note: Asserts that corporations and marriages are instances of the kind 'social continuant'.

claims.claim: Legal obligation arises from the network of relational dependencies that make rules what they are.
claims.source_quote: The obligation to follow rules is not generated by belief or habit; it arises from the network of relational dependencies that make those rules what they are.
claims.note: Asserts the causal/ontological ground of legal obligation.

claims.claim: Legal obligation is not generated by belief or habit.
claims.source_quote: The obligation to follow rules is not generated by belief or habit
claims.note: Asserts a negative ontological claim about the source of legal obligation.

claims.claim: Rule-following by officials is possible only because law already exists as a structured domain of recognition.
claims.source_quote: the ontologist replies that such rule-following is possible only because law already exists as a structured domain of recognition.
claims.note: The author voices this as the ontologist's position, which he endorses throughout the passage.

claims.claim: Law exists as a structured domain of recognition.
claims.source_quote: law already exists as a structured domain of recognition.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about what law is.

claims.claim: Legal entities persist, interact, and exert force.
claims.source_quote: he cannot explain why legal entities persist, interact, and exert force.
claims.note: The author asserts these as genuine properties of legal entities that require explanation.

claims.claim: Legal realism reduces law to observable behavior and subjective judgment.
claims.source_quote: by reducing law to observable behavior and subjective judgment, realism ultimately erased the very structure it set out to explain.
claims.note: Author's characterization and critique of legal realism's ontological reduction.

claims.claim: Legal realism cannot account for the persistence, coherence, or ontology of law.
claims.source_quote: ended as a theory that could not account for the persistence, coherence, or ontology of law at all.
claims.note: Author asserts a deficiency of realism implying that law does have persistence, coherence, and ontology.

claims.claim: Cases of legal invalidity constitute a pseudo-entity: an apparent legal fact lacking ontological integrity.
claims.source_quote: The result is a pseudo-entity: an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Direct assertion that a certain kind of entity (pseudo-entity) exists and has a specific property (lacking ontological integrity).

claims.claim: Misrecognition is the most basic form of fact-making failure.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition is the most basic form of fact-making failure.
claims.note: Asserts a property/role of misrecognition within a taxonomy of failure types.

claims.claim: Misrecognition occurs when recognition is extended to an entity that does not satisfy the conditions of the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It occurs when recognition is extended to an entity, act, or role that does not satisfy the conditions set by the rule of recognition.
claims.note: Defines the conditions under which misrecognition obtains; an ontological claim about when a particular failure-kind is instantiated.

claims.claim: Misrecognition produces a false positive: a dependent continuant instantiated without the necessary structural support.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this produces a false positive: a dependent continuant (the supposed legal fact) instantiated without the necessary structural support.
claims.note: Asserts a kind of entity (dependent continuant) exists and has a property (lacking necessary structural support).

claims.claim: Entities created by misrecognition exist in a state of suspended legitimacy.
claims.source_quote: Such misrecognition creates entities that are ontologically unstable, they exist in a state of suspended legitimacy, subject to annulment or correction once the error is discovered.
claims.note: Asserts a property (suspended legitimacy, ontological instability) of a kind of entity (products of misrecognition).

claims.claim: In epistemic error, the fact exists but our understanding is mistaken.
claims.source_quote: In epistemic error, the fact exists, but our understanding of it is mistaken; in ontological defect, the fact itself fails to exist within the legal field.
claims.note: Asserts distinct ontological statuses for epistemic error vs. ontological defect.

claims.claim: In ontological defect, the legal fact fails to exist within the legal field.
claims.source_quote: in ontological defect, the fact itself fails to exist within the legal field.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the non-existence of a legal fact in cases of ontological defect.

claims.claim: An act performed by an impostor does not instantiate a genuine legal obligation.
claims.source_quote: Yet the necessary dependencies (intention, authority, and recognized identity) are absent. The act does not instantiate a genuine legal obligation, even if it temporarily appears to.
claims.note: Asserts that a particular kind of act lacks a relational property (instantiating legal obligation).

claims.claim: An impostor's signing act is not merely voidable but void: a non-being clothed in the appearance of law.
claims.source_quote: It is not merely voidable but void: a non-being clothed in the appearance of law.
claims.note: Asserts ontological status (void, non-being) of a specific kind of act.

claims.claim: Misrecognition generates entities without the dependencies required for their persistence.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition, then, is the ontological equivalent of a false creation, an act that generates entities without the dependencies required for their persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of entities generated by misrecognition (lacking persistence dependencies).

claims.claim: Fraud creates phantom legal entities that depend on the concealment of their own invalidity.
claims.source_quote: it creates a phantom legal entity that depends on the concealment of its own invalidity.
claims.note: Asserts existence and a dependency relation of a particular kind of entity (phantom legal entity).

claims.claim: Fraudulent entities are dependent continuants without proper grounding in the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, such entities are dependent continuants without proper grounding: they borrow their apparent being from genuine institutional processes but lack alignment with the system's rule of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a kind (dependent continuant) and a property (lacking proper grounding) of fraudulent legal entities.

claims.claim: When fraud is exposed, no legal entity ever truly existed.
claims.source_quote: Once exposed, their recognition collapses, revealing that no legal entity ever truly existed.
claims.note: Asserts the non-existence of genuine legal entities in fraud cases.

claims.claim: The nullification of fraud is an ontological repair: a restoration of coherence in the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The nullification of fraud, therefore, is not merely a moral correction but an ontological repair: the restoration of coherence in the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the nature/function of fraud nullification as ontological repair.

claims.claim: Fraudulent continuants exist temporarily as zones of incoherence where contradiction is tolerated.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, these moments constitute temporary zones of incoherence in which contradiction is tolerated.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status (temporary zones of incoherence) of fraud-sustained entities.

claims.claim: Ontological purification strips away false continuants and reaffirms the integrity of the dependency structure.
claims.source_quote: the process of correction operates as an act of ontological purification, stripping away the false continuant and reaffirming the integrity of the dependency structure.
claims.note: Asserts a function and effect of the correction process on continuants and dependency structures.

claims.claim: Without ontological repair, law would lose its capacity for coherence and drift into systemic contradiction.
claims.source_quote: Without it, law would lose its capacity for ontological repair and drift into systemic contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of law (needing repair to avoid contradiction); slightly conditional but endorsed by the author.

claims.claim: Jurisdictional voids are cases of non-recognition, not misrecognition.
claims.source_quote: These are not cases of misrecognition but of non-recognition, situations in which brute events that could be legally significant occur outside any established field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a classificatory distinction between two kinds of ontological failure.

claims.claim: Acts in jurisdictional voids exist in a liminal state between legality and non-being: recognitional indeterminacy.
claims.source_quote: They exist in a liminal state between legality and non-being, a condition we might call recognitional indeterminacy.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological status for a class of acts; 'we might call' slightly hedges the label but the ontological status is asserted.

claims.claim: Recognition is always localized within a network of institutions that define territorial or functional domains.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is always localized within a network of institutions that define territorial or functional domains.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of recognition as an entity/process.

claims.claim: When institutional domains fail to overlap, the ontological field of law fragments into discontinuity.
claims.source_quote: When these domains fail to overlap or are contested, the ontological field of law fragments. The result is not merely political uncertainty but ontological discontinuity.
claims.note: Asserts a consequence (ontological discontinuity) affecting the ontological field of law.

claims.claim: Creating new legal spaces is an act of ontological reconstruction establishing conditions for recognition.
claims.source_quote: Creating new legal spaces is an act of ontological reconstruction, it establishes the boundaries within which recognition can once again attach to brute facts.
claims.note: Asserts a nature/function of creating legal spaces as ontological reconstruction.

claims.claim: Misrecognition corrupts the referential alignment between recognition and its object.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition corrupts the referential alignment between recognition and its object.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/structural property of misrecognition.

claims.claim: Fraud subverts the dependency structure itself.
