claims.source_quote: Validity and existence are thus intertwined: to exist legally is to be coherently recognized.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between two legal properties.

claims.claim: Legal institutions are structured continuities of acknowledgment, not arbitrary conventions.
claims.source_quote: legal institutions are not arbitrary conventions but structured continuities of acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal institutions—what kind of entities they are.

claims.claim: A law exists when recognized by those authorized to recognize it within a structure existing by shared recognition.
claims.source_quote: A law exists when it is recognized by those authorized to recognize it, within a structure that itself exists by virtue of shared recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions of existence for a law—an ontological existence claim.

claims.claim: The recursive relation of recognition at multiple levels is the ontological core of legality.
claims.source_quote: This recursive relation is the ontological core of legality: law is the ongoing realization of recognition at multiple levels.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legality—its ontological core.

claims.claim: Law is the ongoing realization of recognition at multiple levels.
claims.source_quote: law is the ongoing realization of recognition at multiple levels.
claims.note: Direct definition of law as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: The legal world is populated by structures of dependence between agents, roles, institutions, obligations, and acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The answers lie not in texts or motives but in structures of dependence, between agents and roles, roles and institutions, obligations and acts of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the kinds of entities and relations that populate the legal world.

claims.claim: Law's meaning is a mode of being sustained through relation.
claims.source_quote: Law's meaning, in this view, is neither an interpretive product nor a moral essence but a mode of being sustained through relation.
claims.note: Asserts what kind of entity/property law's meaning is.

claims.claim: Law is a real system of socially sustained meanings.
claims.source_quote: Law is not an illusion or an ideal but a real system of socially sustained meanings, one that operates through acts of recognition woven into the fabric of institutional life.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim asserting law's existence as a real system.

claims.claim: Law operates through acts of recognition woven into the fabric of institutional life.
claims.source_quote: one that operates through acts of recognition woven into the fabric of institutional life.
claims.note: Asserts a property/mode of operation of law.

claims.claim: Roles, obligations, and institutions form the architecture of law as a structured domain of social reality.
claims.source_quote: to map how roles, obligations, and institutions form the architecture of law as a structured domain of social reality.
claims.note: Asserted as the content of what formal ontology will reveal—author commits to this ontological structure, though presented as a program.

claims.claim: Ownership does not inhere in the physical object alone but in a network of recognition linking object to owner.
claims.source_quote: Ownership can change bearers because it does not inhere in the physical object alone but in the network of recognition that links the object to an owner.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological locus of ownership—a property/relation claim.

claims.claim: A transfer of ownership is a reconfiguration of the recognition network surrounding an object.
claims.source_quote: A transfer occurs when this network is reconfigured, when recognition is withdrawn from one agent and extended to another.
claims.note: Asserts what a transfer is ontologically—a relational reconfiguration.

claims.claim: Legal formalities (signature, delivery, registration, notarization) are procedural realizations through which recognition is reoriented.
claims.source_quote: signature, delivery, registration, or notarization are procedural realizations through which recognition is reoriented.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/realizing role for legal formalities—an ontological claim about their function.

claims.claim: Without legal formalities, a transfer of ownership is ontologically incomplete.
claims.source_quote: Without these formalities, the transfer remains ontologically incomplete; the relation cannot shift coherently within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological status (incompleteness) of transfers lacking formalities.

claims.claim: Intangible property has no physical substrate; its object is an information content entity.
claims.source_quote: Here, there is no physical substrate to anchor the relation; the object of ownership is an information content entity, a generically dependent continuant that can exist on multiple bearers.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership (information content entity, generically dependent continuant) for intangible property objects.

claims.claim: An information content entity is a generically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: the object of ownership is an information content entity, a generically dependent continuant that can exist on multiple bearers.
claims.note: Asserts subkind relation: information content entity is a generically dependent continuant.

claims.claim: Copyright is a legally recognized relation between an author (or assignee) and a work's expression.
claims.source_quote: the copyright to a novel... is... the legally recognized relation between the author (or assignee) and the work's expression.
claims.note: Asserts what copyright is ontologically—a relational continuant.

claims.claim: Copyright persists across copies and translations as long as the institutional structure defining and enforcing it remains in place.
claims.source_quote: This relation persists across copies and translations, as long as the institutional structure that defines and enforces copyright remains in place.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for a relational continuant—ontological claim about duration/dependence.

claims.claim: Ownership of a digital token, blockchain entry, or virtual good consists solely in recognized control within an institutionalized computational system.
claims.source_quote: ownership of a digital token, blockchain entry, or virtual good consists solely in recognized control within an institutionalized computational system.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological constitution of digital asset ownership.

claims.claim: Property is an architecture of recognition sustained by informational and procedural continuants.
claims.source_quote: property, far from being tied to material substance, is increasingly an architecture of recognition sustained by informational and procedural continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a structural ontological characterization of property.

claims.claim: In collective ownership, each right and obligation is a dependent continuant inhering in specific configurations of agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Each right and obligation in this arrangement is a dependent continuant inhering in specific configurations of agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership and inherence relation for rights and obligations.

claims.claim: A legal entity such as an association is a higher-order continuant maintaining coherence among property relations.
claims.source_quote: The legal entity 'association' serves as a higher-order continuant maintaining coherence among these relations.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership and functional role for legal entities—ontological claim.

claims.claim: Collective ownership is a more complex configuration of dependencies, not a different kind of property.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, collective ownership is not a different kind of property but a more complex configuration of dependencies: multiple agents jointly recognized as bearers of rights and obligations relative to shared objects.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological classification claim about collective ownership.

claims.claim: When recognition lapses through expropriation or legal collapse, ownership ceases to exist.
claims.source_quote: When recognition lapses, through expropriation, nationalization, or legal collapse, ownership ceases to exist.
claims.note: Asserts an existence condition for ownership—ontological claim about dependence.

claims.claim: Property is as fragile as the institutions that sustain it; its being is conditional on legal system coherence.
claims.source_quote: property is as fragile as the institutions that sustain it, its being is always conditional on the coherence of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between property's existence and institutional coherence.

claims.claim: Registers, cadasters, and ledgers are information artifacts that distribute recognition over time and space.
claims.source_quote: Registers, cadasters, and ledgers serve as information artifacts that distribute recognition over time and space.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership and functional role for registration systems.

claims.claim: Registration converts private ownership relations into public facts.
claims.source_quote: They convert private relations into public facts, enabling third parties to orient their behavior accordingly.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative ontological function of registration.

claims.claim: Registration transforms property from a bilateral relation between owner and object into a multilateral relation encompassing all potential recognizers.
claims.source_quote: This publicity transforms property from a bilateral relation between owner and object into a multilateral relation encompassing all potential recognizers within the system.
claims.note: Asserts a relational ontological transformation produced by registration.

claims.claim: Value does not reside in things themselves but in the structure of relations that law sustains.
claims.source_quote: The value of property does not reside in things themselves but in the structure of relations that law sustains.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological locus of value—a relational rather than intrinsic property.

claims.claim: Property is a fundamental ontological mechanism through which law gives stable relational form to value.
claims.source_quote: Property is thus not only a legal category but a fundamental ontological mechanism: it is how law gives stable relational form to value.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/ontological role for property.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant—a structured dependency among agents, institutions, and things persisting through recognition.
claims.source_quote: property... is not a substance but a relational continuant, a structured dependency among agents, institutions, and things that persists through recognition.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership and structural characterization of property.

claims.claim: Value emerges only within networks of exchange and assessment; it is not intrinsic to objects.
claims.source_quote: Just as ownership exists only within a field of recognition, so too does value emerge only within networks of exchange and assessment. A piece of land, a painting, or a patent possesses no intrinsic worth.
claims.note: Asserts a relational existence condition for value, denying intrinsic worth.

claims.claim: Value is the evaluative correlate of property's relational form, acquired through collective acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Value is the evaluative correlate of property's relational form, the symbolic and economic magnitude that property acquires through collective acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts what value is and how it is constituted—an ontological characterization.

claims.claim: Within BFO, value belongs to the class of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Within the framework of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), value belongs to the class of dependent continuants, but of a distinctive sort.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership of value within an ontological framework the author endorses.

claims.claim: Value is a relational disposition that exists only insofar as certain interactions (market exchange, legal transfer, institutional appraisal) are possible.
claims.source_quote: it is a relational disposition that exists only insofar as certain kinds of interactions, like market exchange, legal transfer, or institutional appraisal, are possible.
claims.note: Asserts the existence conditions and dispositional character of value—ontological claim.

claims.claim: The ontological condition for value is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.source_quote: The ontological condition for value, therefore, is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence/grounding relation between value and legal institutional capacity.

claims.claim: Obligation is the entity through which recognition becomes durable across time.
claims.source_quote: It is the entity through which recognition becomes durable, through which a social act transforms from an event in time into a structure that endures across time.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the nature and function of obligation as an entity.

claims.claim: Obligation is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, an obligation is a dependent continuant: it cannot exist on its own but only through the relations that sustain it.
claims.note: Explicit ontological categorization of obligation.

claims.claim: Obligation cannot exist independently but only through the relations that sustain it.
claims.source_quote: it cannot exist on its own but only through the relations that sustain it.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency property of obligation as an entity.

claims.claim: Obligation depends on the agents and institutions that recognize it.
claims.source_quote: Likewise, an obligation depends on the agents and institutions that recognize it.
claims.note: Asserts a relational dependency between obligation and recognizing agents/institutions.

claims.claim: Obligation inheres in the debtor and is directed toward the creditor.
claims.source_quote: It inheres in the debtor and is directed toward the creditor, but it also depends on the broader system of recognition that sustains its validity.
claims.note: Asserts two structural relations that obligation bears to agents.

claims.claim: Obligation persists as long as the necessary conditions of recognition remain.
claims.source_quote: The obligation does not vanish when ignored or denied; it persists as long as the necessary conditions of recognition remain.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for obligation as an entity.

claims.claim: Obligation modifies the topology of the agent's possible actions.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, the obligation modifies the topology of the agent's possible world. It alters the configuration of potential actions, marking certain outcomes as inconsistent with the state of affairs that constitutes the relation.
claims.note: Asserts a property/effect of obligation on the agent's action space.

claims.claim: A contract, once enacted, creates a relational entity that endures beyond the event of its creation.
claims.source_quote: The contract, once enacted, creates a relational entity that endures beyond the event of its creation.
claims.note: Asserts that contracts generate a new enduring relational entity.

claims.claim: Legal obligations are specifically dependent continuants that arise from acts of recognition between agents.
claims.source_quote: It defines legal obligations as specifically dependent continuants that arise from acts of recognition between agents and persist until fulfilled, extinguished, or repaired.
claims.note: Explicit ontological categorization and origin-claim for legal obligations.

claims.claim: Legal obligations persist until fulfilled, extinguished, or repaired.
claims.source_quote: legal obligations as specifically dependent continuants that arise from acts of recognition between agents and persist until fulfilled, extinguished, or repaired.
claims.note: Asserts the persistence conditions and termination conditions of legal obligations.

claims.claim: Obligations attach to roles rather than to persons.
claims.source_quote: The chapter explains how obligations attach to roles rather than persons and how their creation and extinction constitute changes in legal reality.
claims.note: Asserts that roles, not persons, are the bearers of obligations.

claims.claim: The creation and extinction of obligations constitute changes in legal reality.
claims.source_quote: how their creation and extinction constitute changes in legal reality.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between obligation events and legal reality as an ontological domain.

claims.claim: Recognition is the ontological event that transforms social interactions into enduring legal structures.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is analyzed as the ontological event that transforms social interactions into enduring legal structures.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and causal role of recognition.

claims.claim: Consent is an ontological generator through which new dependent continuants enter the world.
claims.source_quote: Consent is therefore not merely a psychological state or moral approval; it is an ontological generator, a process through which new dependent continuants enter the world.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological role and productive function of consent.

claims.claim: When two parties consent, they generate a new entity—an obligation—that neither could produce alone.
claims.source_quote: When two parties consent to exchange goods or services, they generate a new entity, an obligation, that neither could produce alone.
claims.note: Asserts that consent produces a new obligation entity with specific relational origin.

claims.claim: Legal obligations are embedded within structured systems of recognition that include roles, procedures, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Legal obligations, by contrast, are embedded within structured systems of recognition that include roles, procedures, and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of legal obligations distinguishing them from moral ones.

claims.claim: Legal obligations are re-recognizable: capable of being invoked, enforced, and repaired through formal processes.
claims.source_quote: They are not only recognized but re-recognizable: capable of being invoked, enforced, and repaired through formal processes.
claims.note: Asserts a distinctive dispositional property of legal obligations.

claims.claim: Each obligation stands in a triadic relation among debtor, creditor, and institutional context.
claims.source_quote: each obligation can be represented as a triadic relation among debtor, creditor, and institutional context.
claims.note: Asserts the relational structure of obligation as involving three relata.

claims.claim: Obligation depends on the institutional structure that recognizes and enforces it.
claims.source_quote: depends_on (institutional structure that recognizes and enforces)
claims.note: Formal ontological assertion of a dependency relation between obligation and institution.

claims.claim: Obligation is realized in processes of performance or enforcement.
claims.source_quote: realized_in (processes of performance or enforcement)
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between obligation and processes.

claims.claim: A breached contract still exists as an unfulfilled relation.
claims.source_quote: A breached contract still exists as an unfulfilled relation; the law's role is to mediate its realization or repair.
claims.note: Asserts that a breached contract persists as a real relational entity.

claims.claim: Obligation occupies an intermediate zone between moral intention and institutional structure.
claims.source_quote: legal obligation occupies an intermediate zone between moral intention and institutional structure, binding them through enduring relational form.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological position/role for legal obligation relative to two other domains.

claims.claim: Obligation and recognition are the fundamental building blocks of legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: The analysis establishes obligation and recognition as the fundamental building blocks of legal ontology and as prerequisites for institutional coherence.
claims.note: Asserts the foundational ontological status of obligation and recognition.

claims.claim: Obligation and recognition are prerequisites for institutional coherence.
claims.source_quote: obligation and recognition as the fundamental building blocks of legal ontology and as prerequisites for institutional coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/structural role of these entities relative to institutions.

claims.claim: Ownership does not inhere in the physical object alone but in the network of recognition linking object to owner.
claims.source_quote: Ownership can change bearers because it does not inhere in the physical object alone but in the network of recognition that links the object to an owner.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological locus of ownership — a property/relation claim.

claims.claim: A transfer of ownership occurs when the network of recognition is reconfigured.
claims.source_quote: A transfer occurs when this network is reconfigured, when recognition is withdrawn from one agent and extended to another.
claims.note: Asserts what constitutes a transfer event — an ontological claim about the nature of ownership transfer.

claims.claim: Legal formalities (signature, delivery, registration, notarization) are procedural realizations through which recognition is reoriented.
claims.source_quote: signature, delivery, registration, or notarization are procedural realizations through which recognition is reoriented.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between legal formalities and recognition — ontological claim about the role/function of legal procedures.

claims.claim: Without legal formalities, a transfer of ownership is ontologically incomplete.
claims.source_quote: Without these formalities, the transfer remains ontologically incomplete; the relation cannot shift coherently within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological status (incompleteness) of informal transfers — a property claim.

claims.claim: The object of ownership in intangible property is an information content entity.
claims.source_quote: the object of ownership is an information content entity, a generically dependent continuant that can exist on multiple bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a kind membership claim — intangible property objects are information content entities.

claims.claim: An information content entity is a generically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: the object of ownership is an information content entity, a generically dependent continuant that can exist on multiple bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation between information content entity and generically dependent continuant.

claims.claim: A copyright is a legally recognized relation between the author (or assignee) and the work's expression.
claims.source_quote: the copyright to a novel...is...the legally recognized relation between the author (or assignee) and the work's expression.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of copyright as a relational entity.

claims.claim: Copyright persists across copies and translations as long as the institutional structure defining and enforcing it remains in place.
claims.source_quote: This relation persists across copies and translations, as long as the institutional structure that defines and enforces copyright remains in place.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for a relational entity — ontological claim about continuant persistence.

claims.claim: Ownership of a digital token consists solely in recognized control within an institutionalized computational system.
claims.source_quote: ownership of a digital token, blockchain entry, or virtual good consists solely in recognized control within an institutionalized computational system.
claims.note: Asserts what digital ownership consists in — an ontological constitution claim.

claims.claim: Property is an architecture of recognition sustained by informational and procedural continuants.
claims.source_quote: property, far from being tied to material substance, is increasingly an architecture of recognition sustained by informational and procedural continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a property/constitution claim about the ontological nature of property.

claims.claim: In collective ownership, the property relation involves multiple bearers on the owning side.
claims.source_quote: In these cases, the property relation involves multiple bearers on the owning side.
claims.note: Asserts a structural feature of collective ownership relations.

claims.claim: Each right and obligation in a collective ownership arrangement is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: Each right and obligation in this arrangement is a dependent continuant inhering in specific configurations of agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership — rights and obligations are dependent continuants.

claims.claim: A legal entity such as an 'association' is a higher-order continuant maintaining coherence among property relations.
claims.source_quote: The legal entity 'association' serves as a higher-order continuant maintaining coherence among these relations.
claims.note: Asserts that a legal entity is a higher-order continuant — kind membership and functional role claim.

claims.claim: Collective ownership is a more complex configuration of dependencies, not a different kind of property.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, collective ownership is not a different kind of property but a more complex configuration of dependencies: multiple agents jointly recognized as bearers of rights and obligations relative to shared objects.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological identity/classification claim about collective ownership.

claims.claim: When recognition lapses through expropriation or legal collapse, ownership ceases to exist.
claims.source_quote: When recognition lapses, through expropriation, nationalization, or legal collapse, ownership ceases to exist.
claims.note: Asserts an existence condition — ownership existence is dependent on recognition.

claims.claim: Property is as fragile as the institutions that sustain it.
claims.source_quote: property is as fragile as the institutions that sustain it, its being is always conditional on the coherence of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between property's being and institutional coherence.

claims.claim: Property's being is always conditional on the coherence of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: its being is always conditional on the coherence of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency — property existence depends on legal system coherence.

claims.claim: Registers, cadasters, and ledgers are information artifacts that distribute recognition over time and space.
claims.source_quote: Registers, cadasters, and ledgers serve as information artifacts that distribute recognition over time and space.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership and functional role of registration systems.

claims.claim: Registration converts private property relations into public facts.
claims.source_quote: They convert private relations into public facts, enabling third parties to orient their behavior accordingly.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative function of registration — a functional/relational ontological claim.

claims.claim: Registration transforms property from a bilateral relation between owner and object into a multilateral relation encompassing all potential recognizers.
claims.source_quote: This publicity transforms property from a bilateral relation between owner and object into a multilateral relation encompassing all potential recognizers within the system.
claims.note: Asserts a structural transformation of the property relation — ontological claim about relational structure.

claims.claim: The value of property does not reside in things themselves but in the structure of relations that law sustains.
claims.source_quote: The value of property does not reside in things themselves but in the structure of relations that law sustains.
claims.note: Asserts a negative and positive ontological location of value — relational ontology claim.

claims.claim: Property is a node in a larger field of social coordination where value is expressed through recognition.
claims.source_quote: Property is not merely a relation among agents and objects but a node in a larger field of social coordination where value, economic, symbolic, and moral, is expressed through recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/relational role of property within a broader ontological field.

claims.claim: Property is a fundamental ontological mechanism by which law gives stable relational form to value.
claims.source_quote: Property is thus not only a legal category but a fundamental ontological mechanism: it is how law gives stable relational form to value.
claims.note: Asserts a kind and functional role for property — ontological mechanism claim.

claims.claim: Ownership is neither absolute nor metaphysical but contingent and revisable.
claims.source_quote: To treat property as relational is to acknowledge that ownership is neither absolute nor metaphysical but contingent and revisable.
claims.note: Asserts properties (contingency, revisability) of ownership — a property claim.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant — a structured dependency among agents, institutions, and things that persists through recognition.
claims.source_quote: property...is not a substance but a relational continuant, a structured dependency among agents, institutions, and things that persists through recognition.
claims.note: Direct assertion of the ontological kind and constitution of property.

claims.claim: Value emerges only within networks of exchange and assessment.
claims.source_quote: Just as ownership exists only within a field of recognition, so too does value emerge only within networks of exchange and assessment.
claims.note: Asserts an existence condition and relational dependency for value.

claims.claim: A piece of land, painting, or patent possesses no intrinsic worth; its value is a manifestation of recognition distributed across social and institutional relations.
claims.source_quote: A piece of land, a painting, or a patent possesses no intrinsic worth; its value is the manifestation of recognition distributed across social and institutional relations.
claims.note: Asserts a negative intrinsic property and a positive relational account of value.

claims.claim: Within BFO, value belongs to the class of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Within the framework of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), value belongs to the class of dependent continuants, but of a distinctive sort.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership of value within a formal ontological framework the author endorses.

claims.claim: Value is a relational disposition that exists only insofar as certain kinds of interactions are possible.
claims.source_quote: it is a relational disposition that exists only insofar as certain kinds of interactions, like market exchange, legal transfer, or institutional appraisal, are possible.
claims.note: Asserts that value is a relational disposition — a kind and existence-condition claim.

claims.claim: The ontological condition for value is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.source_quote: The ontological condition for value, therefore, is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation — value's existence depends on the legal system's sustaining capacity.

claims.claim: Stability and recognition transform material or informational objects into participants in the social field of exchange.
claims.source_quote: Stability and recognition transform material or informational objects into participants in the social field of exchange.
claims.note: Asserts a property/role transformation: objects acquire the property of being participants in exchange through stability and recognition.

claims.claim: The ontological condition for value is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.source_quote: The ontological condition for value, therefore, is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding/dependency relation: value ontologically depends on the legal system's sustaining of property relations.

claims.claim: Property depends on recognition: without institutional acknowledgment, ownership cannot exist.
claims.source_quote: On the first level, property depends on recognition: without institutional acknowledgment, ownership cannot exist.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation between property/ownership and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Value depends on property: without stable, recognized ownership, there can be no coherent field for valuation.
claims.source_quote: On the second level, value depends on property: without stable, recognized ownership, there can be no coherent field for valuation.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation: value (or the field of valuation) depends on stable, recognized property.

claims.claim: Recognition and value-dependence-on-property together form a hierarchy of ontological dependence.
claims.source_quote: Together, these layers form a hierarchy of ontological dependence.
claims.note: Asserts that the two dependency relations constitute a structured hierarchical ontological relation.

claims.claim: Stability and recognition transform material or informational objects into participants in the social field of exchange.
claims.source_quote: Stability and recognition transform material or informational objects into participants in the social field of exchange.
claims.note: Asserts a property/relation: objects acquire the role of participants in exchange through stability and recognition.

claims.claim: The legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants is the ontological condition for value.
claims.source_quote: The ontological condition for value, therefore, is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.note: Asserts that value has an ontological condition, identifying that condition as the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations.

claims.claim: Property depends on institutional recognition; without institutional acknowledgment, ownership cannot exist.
claims.source_quote: On the first level, property depends on recognition: without institutional acknowledgment, ownership cannot exist.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between property/ownership and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Value depends on property; without stable, recognized ownership, there can be no coherent field for valuation.
claims.source_quote: On the second level, value depends on property: without stable, recognized ownership, there can be no coherent field for valuation.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between value and property.

claims.claim: Recognition and value-dependence-on-property together form a hierarchy of ontological dependence.
claims.source_quote: Together, these layers form a hierarchy of ontological dependence.
claims.note: Asserts that the two tiers constitute a hierarchical ontological structure.

claims.claim: Law is a system of relations, not a collection of discrete rules or acts.
claims.source_quote: law is not a collection of discrete rules or acts, but a system of relations. Its meaning and validity depend on the underlying relational forms that connect persons, norms, and institutions.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature of law as relational rather than discrete.

claims.claim: Law's meaning and validity depend on relational forms connecting persons, norms, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Its meaning and validity depend on the underlying relational forms that connect persons, norms, and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between law's properties and underlying relational forms.

claims.claim: Recognition is a relational entity involving at least two agents and a shared object of acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: recognition itself is relational, it involves at least two agents and a shared object of acknowledgment.
claims.note: Ontological characterization of recognition as a relation with specific relata.

claims.claim: Legal validity involves a network of dependencies among legislators, courts, and citizens.
claims.source_quote: When we say that a law is 'valid,' we invoke a network of dependencies: between legislators and their procedures, between courts and the texts they interpret, between citizens and the authorities they obey.
claims.note: Asserts that legal validity is constituted by specific ontological dependency relations.

claims.claim: Dependencies among legislators, courts, and citizens are ontological conditions for law's existence.
claims.source_quote: These dependencies are not merely sociological; they are ontological conditions for law's existence.
claims.note: Explicit assertion that these relations are ontological conditions, not merely sociological facts.

claims.claim: Law is a structure, a pattern of relational continuities holding together diverse agents and acts.
claims.source_quote: Law is thus not a substance but a structure, a pattern of relational continuities that holds together diverse agents and acts.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim denying law is a substance and asserting it is a structure.

claims.claim: A contract generates an enduring dependent continuant that persists until fulfilled or extinguished.
claims.source_quote: This recognition generates an enduring relation, a dependent continuant, that persists until fulfilled or extinguished.
claims.note: Asserts that contracts are dependent continuants with temporal persistence.

claims.claim: A contract is a network of relational entities linking persons through obligations and expectations.
claims.source_quote: The contract is a small-scale instance of law's general form: a network of relational entities linking persons through obligations and expectations.
claims.note: Ontological characterization of what a contract is.

claims.claim: Statutes and judgments are information artifacts that record and transmit meaning.
claims.source_quote: Some entities, like statutes or judgments, are information artifacts, documents that record and transmit meaning.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation: statutes and judgments are a kind of information artifact.

claims.claim: Institutions and offices are continuants that persist through time.
claims.source_quote: Others, like institutions and offices, are continuants, structures that persist through time.
claims.note: Asserts that institutions and offices belong to the ontological category of continuants.

claims.claim: Trials and legislative sessions are occurrents, events through which legal reality is realized.
claims.source_quote: Still others, like trials or legislative sessions, are occurrents, events through which legal reality is realized.
claims.note: Asserts that trials and legislative sessions belong to the ontological category of occurrents.

claims.claim: A law's meaning depends on its recognition by officials.
claims.source_quote: A law's meaning depends on its recognition by officials; an obligation depends on the continued existence of the institution that issued it.
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological dependency relation between law's meaning and official recognition.

claims.claim: An obligation depends on the continued existence of the institution that issued it.
claims.source_quote: an obligation depends on the continued existence of the institution that issued it; an institution depends on recurring processes that renew its legitimacy.
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological dependency relation between obligations and institutions.

claims.claim: An institution depends on recurring processes that renew its legitimacy.
claims.source_quote: an institution depends on recurring processes that renew its legitimacy.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between institutions and renewal processes.

claims.claim: Obligations and rights are dependent entities, existing only because certain relations among independent entities obtain.
claims.source_quote: a dependent entity, such as an obligation or right, exists only because certain relations among independent entities obtain.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category membership and dependency conditions for obligations and rights.

claims.claim: A right depends on its holder.
claims.source_quote: A right depends on its holder; an office depends on the institution that defines it; an obligation depends on the recognition of both debtor and creditor.
claims.note: Asserts a specific dependency relation between a right and its bearer.

claims.claim: An office depends on the institution that defines it.
claims.source_quote: an office depends on the institution that defines it
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation between an office and its defining institution.

claims.claim: An obligation depends on the recognition of both debtor and creditor.
claims.source_quote: an obligation depends on the recognition of both debtor and creditor.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological conditions (dependency) for the existence of an obligation.

claims.claim: Legal entities are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Because legal entities are dependent continuants, they can survive the turnover of individuals and the passage of time.
claims.note: Asserts that legal entities belong to the ontological category of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The office of 'judge' persists even as individual judges come and go.
claims.source_quote: The office of 'judge' persists even as judges come and go; the obligation created by a contract persists until it is fulfilled.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of the office as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The obligation created by a contract persists until it is fulfilled.
claims.source_quote: the obligation created by a contract persists until it is fulfilled
claims.note: Asserts the temporal persistence of contractual obligations.

claims.claim: Legal entities depend not on particular people but on the ongoing realization of defining relations.
claims.source_quote: These entities depend not on particular people but on the ongoing realization of relations that define them.
claims.note: Asserts what legal entities ontologically depend upon.

claims.claim: Law's endurance is an emergent property of the network of dependencies that sustains it.
claims.source_quote: Law's endurance is structural, not personal. It is an emergent property of the network of dependencies that sustains it.
claims.note: Asserts that persistence/endurance is an emergent property arising from the dependency network.

claims.claim: A court's ruling modifies the network of dependencies by creating or dissolving relations of obligation and right.
claims.source_quote: A court's ruling does not merely predict future behavior; it modifies the network of dependencies by creating or dissolving relations of obligation and right.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/causal role for court rulings in altering the ontological network.

claims.claim: Invalidity is a form of ontological failure: a disruption in the pattern of dependence.
claims.source_quote: Invalidity, conversely, is a form of ontological failure: a disruption in the pattern of dependence.
claims.note: Asserts that invalidity has an ontological character as structural incoherence.

claims.claim: A usurped office, unconstitutional statute, or contradictory judgment is ontologically incoherent.
claims.source_quote: A usurped office, an unconstitutional statute, or a contradictory judgment are not merely wrong in the normative sense, they are incoherent in the ontological sense. Their dependencies do not hold together.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property (incoherence) of specific legal entities under specific conditions.

claims.claim: Law is grounded in institutional recognition rather than linguistic convention or moral truth.
claims.source_quote: Law is modeled as a structure of dependent continuants grounded in institutional recognition rather than linguistic convention or moral truth.
claims.note: Direct ontological grounding claim from the abstract, asserting what law depends upon.

claims.claim: Obligations, powers, and rights arise from social acts and persist through recognized roles and procedures.
claims.source_quote: The chapter shows how obligations, powers, and rights arise from social acts and persist through recognized roles and procedures.
claims.note: Asserts the causal origin and persistence conditions of obligations, powers, and rights.

claims.claim: Legal norms can be objectively real without being morally absolute or socially arbitrary.
claims.source_quote: the chapter articulates how legal norms can be objectively real without being morally absolute or socially arbitrary.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal norms (objective reality) while denying two alternative characterizations.

claims.claim: When a law 'binds,' this describes a structural relation rather than a moral one.
claims.source_quote: When we say that a law 'binds,' we are describing a structural relation, not a mora[l one].
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of the binding relation as structural, not moral.

claims.claim: Property depends on recognition for its existence.
claims.source_quote: On the first level, property depends on recognition: without institutional acknowledgment, ownership cannot exist.
claims.note: Direct assertion of an ontological dependence relation between property and recognition.

claims.claim: Value depends on property for its existence.
claims.source_quote: On the second level, value depends on property: without stable, recognized ownership, there can be no coherent field for valuation.
claims.note: Direct assertion of an ontological dependence relation between value and property.

claims.claim: Recognition is a social/institutional continuant.
claims.source_quote: Level 1: Recognition (social/institutional continuants).
claims.note: The author categorizes recognition as a kind of entity (social/institutional continuant).

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: Level 2: Property (relational continuants sustained by recognition).
claims.note: The author categorizes property as a subkind of relational continuant with a sustaining relation to recognition.

claims.claim: Value consists of relational dispositions realized through exchange.
claims.source_quote: Level 3: Value (relational dispositions realized through exchange).
claims.note: The author categorizes value as relational dispositions, asserting both its nature and the process through which it is realized.

claims.claim: Each ontological level presupposes the coherence of the level below it.
claims.source_quote: Each level presupposes the coherence of the one below it. When recognition fails, property dissolves; when property collapses, value disappears.
claims.note: Asserts a hierarchical dependence structure among the three ontological levels.

claims.claim: Economic crises and legal ruptures are ontological failures of recognition cascaded through the dependence hierarchy.
claims.source_quote: economic crises and legal ruptures alike can be understood as ontological failures of recognition cascaded through the hierarchy of dependence.
claims.note: Author asserts this as an ontological characterization, though 'can be understood as' introduces slight qualification.

claims.claim: Exchange is a realization occurrent that brings relational capacities embedded in property to manifestation.
claims.source_quote: exchange is not merely the transfer of goods or titles but a realization occurrent: a process that brings to manifestation the relational capacities embedded in property.
claims.note: The author positively categorizes exchange as a realization occurrent and asserts its function/role.

claims.claim: Exchange reconfigures the network of ownership relations through mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: When two agents exchange property, each recognizes the other's entitlement and, through mutual acknowledgment, reconfigures the network of ownership relations.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/relational claim about what exchange does to ownership relations.

claims.claim: Exchange is a realization of recognition symmetry.
claims.source_quote: Exchange, therefore, is a realization of recognition symmetry.
claims.note: Direct assertion identifying exchange with a specific ontological category (realization of recognition symmetry).

claims.claim: Exchange creates value by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: It does not merely measure value; it creates it by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.note: Asserts that exchange has the property/function of creating value, not merely measuring it.

claims.claim: Markets are ontological engines of equivalence that produce and stabilize value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: markets are ontological engines of equivalence, continuously producing and stabilizing value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property and function of markets as entities that produce and stabilize value.

claims.claim: Law's continuity depends on the interplay of change and coherence within its relational architecture.
claims.source_quote: law's continuity depends on the interplay of change and coherence within its relational architecture.
claims.note: Direct assertion about a dependency relation between law's continuity and its relational structure.

claims.claim: Dependence relations explain the normative dimension of law without reducing it to morality.
claims.source_quote: Dependence relations likewise explain the normative dimension of law without reducing it to morality.
claims.note: Author's own positive claim about the explanatory role of dependence relations regarding law's normativity.

claims.claim: Bindingness is a structural relation, not a moral feeling.
claims.source_quote: When we say that a law 'binds,' we are describing a structural relation, not a moral feeling.
claims.note: Author asserts a property/kind claim about what bindingness is ontologically.

claims.claim: Bindingness arises from the configuration of recognition and obligation connecting agents to institutions.
claims.source_quote: Bindingness arises from the configuration of recognition and obligation that connects agents to institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive relation: bindingness has its source in a specific structural configuration.

claims.claim: The existence of the binding relation itself is ontological.
claims.source_quote: the existence of the relation itself is ontological.
claims.note: Direct assertion that the binding relation has ontological (not merely moral or evaluative) existence.

claims.claim: Law binds because it is part of a structure that makes binding possible.
claims.source_quote: The law binds because it is part of a structure that makes binding possible.
claims.note: Asserts a part-of relation between law and a structure, and attributes a function (making binding possible) to that structure.

claims.claim: Moral judgment may inform whether bindingness is justified, but does not constitute the relation itself.
claims.source_quote: Moral judgment may inform whether such bindingness is justified, but the existence of the relation itself is ontological.
claims.note: Author draws an ontological/normative distinction, asserting moral judgment is separate from the existence of the binding relation.

claims.claim: Property depends on recognition for its existence.
claims.source_quote: On the first level, property depends on recognition: without institutional acknowledgment, ownership cannot exist.
claims.note: Direct assertion of ontological dependence: recognition is a necessary condition for property.

claims.claim: Value depends on property for its existence.
claims.source_quote: On the second level, value depends on property: without stable, recognized ownership, there can be no coherent field for valuation.
claims.note: Direct assertion of ontological dependence: property is a necessary condition for value.

claims.claim: Recognition is a social/institutional continuant.
claims.source_quote: Level 1: Recognition (social/institutional continuants).
claims.note: Classifies recognition as a kind of entity (social/institutional continuant).

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: Level 2: Property (relational continuants sustained by recognition).
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and dependence relation of property.

claims.claim: Value consists of relational dispositions realized through exchange.
claims.source_quote: Level 3: Value (relational dispositions realized through exchange).
claims.note: Classifies value as a kind of entity (relational dispositions) with a realization relation to exchange.

claims.claim: Recognition, property, and value form a hierarchy of ontological dependence.
claims.source_quote: Together, these layers form a hierarchy of ontological dependence.
claims.note: Asserts the existence and structure of a hierarchical ontological dependence relation among these kinds.

claims.claim: When recognition fails, property dissolves.
claims.source_quote: When recognition fails, property dissolves; when property collapses, value disappears.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation: property ceases to exist when recognition fails.

claims.claim: When property collapses, value disappears.
claims.source_quote: When recognition fails, property dissolves; when property collapses, value disappears.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation: value ceases to exist when property collapses.

claims.claim: Economic crises and legal ruptures are ontological failures of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Economic crises and legal ruptures alike can be understood as ontological failures of recognition cascaded through the hierarchy of dependence.
claims.note: Author asserts this with slight hedging ('can be understood as') but presents it as the correct ontological characterization.

claims.claim: Exchange is a realization occurrent.
claims.source_quote: Exchange is not merely the transfer of goods or titles but a realization occurrent: a process that brings to manifestation the relational capacities embedded in property.
claims.note: Classifies exchange as a specific ontological kind (realization occurrent).

claims.claim: Exchange brings to manifestation the relational capacities embedded in property.
claims.source_quote: A realization occurrent: a process that brings to manifestation the relational capacities embedded in property.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/realization relation between exchange and the relational capacities of property.

claims.claim: Exchange reconfigures the network of ownership relations.
claims.source_quote: When two agents exchange property, each recognizes the other's entitlement and, through mutual acknowledgment, reconfigures the network of ownership relations.
claims.note: Asserts that exchange has the property of reconfiguring ownership relation networks.

claims.claim: Exchange is a realization of recognition symmetry.
claims.source_quote: Exchange, therefore, is a realization of recognition symmetry.
claims.note: Classifies exchange by its realization relation to recognition symmetry.

claims.claim: Exchange creates value by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: It does not merely measure value; it creates it by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive relation: exchange produces value through coherence generation.

claims.claim: Markets are ontological engines of equivalence.
claims.source_quote: In this sense, markets are ontological engines of equivalence, continuously producing and stabilizing value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of markets: they produce and stabilize value via recognition.

claims.claim: Markets continuously produce and stabilize value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Markets are ontological engines of equivalence, continuously producing and stabilizing value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that markets have the function/disposition of producing and stabilizing value via recognition.

claims.claim: Obligations inhere in the debtor.
claims.source_quote: inheres_in (obligation, debtor)
claims.note: The author formalizes this as an ontological relation the obligation bears to the debtor.

claims.claim: Obligations are directed toward the creditor.
claims.source_quote: directed_toward (obligation, creditor)
claims.note: Explicitly stated as an ontological relation in the author's own formal schema.

claims.claim: Obligations are realized in processes of performance or enforcement.
claims.source_quote: realized_in (processes of performance or enforcement)
claims.note: Author's own ontological schema asserts this realization relation.

claims.claim: Obligations depend on institutional structures that recognize and enforce them.
claims.source_quote: depends_on (institutional structure that recognizes and enforces)
claims.note: Explicitly stated dependency relation in the author's ontological schema.

claims.claim: Obligations exist both within agents and within the larger legal architecture.
claims.source_quote: This schema captures how obligations exist both within agents and within the larger legal architecture.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the mode of existence of obligations.

claims.claim: Obligations are simultaneously subjective and objective, personal and institutional.
claims.source_quote: They are simultaneously subjective and objective, personal and institutional.
claims.note: Author's own positive assertion about the ontological character of obligations.

claims.claim: Obligations have lifecycles: they come into being, persist, and are extinguished.
claims.source_quote: Obligations have lifecycles: they come into being, persist, and are extinguished.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the temporal structure of obligations as entities.

claims.claim: Obligations are continuants in BFO terms.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, the obligation is the continuant, and these acts are occurrents that realize or terminate it.
claims.note: Author explicitly categorizes obligations as continuants within BFO ontology.

claims.claim: Acts such as signing, performing, breaching, or discharging are occurrents that realize or terminate obligations.
claims.source_quote: these acts are occurrents that realize or terminate it.
claims.note: Author's own ontological categorization of legal acts as occurrents.

claims.claim: The law's temporal dimension emerges from the interaction between continuants and occurrents.
claims.source_quote: The law's temporal dimension thus emerges from the interaction between continuants and occurrents.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the source of law's temporality.

claims.claim: Time is an intrinsic feature of law's ontology, not a mere background dimension.
claims.source_quote: Time, for law, is not a background dimension but an intrinsic feature of its ontology.
claims.note: Explicit assertion about the ontological status of temporality in law.

claims.claim: Responsibility is an ontological condition of persistence within a structure of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Responsibility, therefore, is not simply an ethical posture but an ontological condition of persistence within a structure of recognition.
claims.note: Author positively asserts the ontological character of responsibility.

claims.claim: Responsibility describes the endurance of the relation that binds an agent to an obligation.
claims.source_quote: It describes the endurance of the relation that binds the agent to the obligation.
claims.note: Direct claim about what responsibility is as a relational ontological entity.

claims.claim: A breach of an obligation modifies its state from active to violated, creating new entities such as liabilities and penalties.
claims.source_quote: The breach of an obligation does not annihilate it; rather, it modifies its state from active to violated, creating new entities, liabilities, penalties, that extend the structure forward in time.
claims.note: Author asserts that breach changes the state of an obligation and generates new dependent entities.

claims.claim: Obligation originates in lived acts of recognition but persists as a formal continuant within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: It originates in lived acts of recognition but persists as a formal continuant within the legal system.
claims.note: Author's own claim about the dual origin and ontological persistence of obligation.

claims.claim: Obligation is the ontological key to understanding legal reality.
claims.source_quote: obligation is not merely a topic within jurisprudence but the ontological key to understanding legal reality itself.
claims.note: Author's positive assertion about the fundamental ontological role of obligation.

claims.claim: Enforcement presupposes creation: there must first be an obligation for coercion to make sense.
claims.source_quote: The ontological analysis shows that enforcement presupposes creation, there must first be an obligation for coercion to make sense.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological priority relation between obligation-creation and enforcement.

claims.claim: Law's authority rests on its capacity to create and sustain enduring relations of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law's authority, therefore, rests not on force but on its capacity to create and sustain these enduring relations of recognition.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological ground of legal authority.

claims.claim: Law's power is ontogenetic before it is punitive.
claims.source_quote: Its power is ontogenetic before it is punitive.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of law's power regarding its primary ontological function.

claims.claim: Obligation is the medium through which law exists as a structured reality.
claims.source_quote: Obligation is the medium through which law exists as a structured reality, binding persons into networks of mutual accountability that persist through time, language, and institutional change.
claims.note: Direct claim about the ontological role obligation plays in constituting law.

claims.claim: Recognition is an ontological event, a real occurrence that transforms the structure of social reality.
claims.source_quote: It is not an attitude, belief, or habit, but an ontological event, a real occurrence that transforms the structure of social reality.
claims.note: Author plainly asserts the ontological category of recognition.

claims.claim: Recognition brings into existence entities such as obligations, authorities, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Recognition brings into existence entities that could not exist without it: obligations, authorities, institutions.
claims.note: Direct claim that recognition has creative ontological power producing specific kinds of entities.

claims.claim: Recognition is not internal assent but participation in a relational structure.
claims.source_quote: Recognition, unlike belief, is not internal assent but participation in a relational structure.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological nature of recognition by distinguishing it from epistemic states.

claims.claim: Recognition, once established, becomes part of the social ontology.
claims.source_quote: Recognition, once established, becomes part of the social ontology, a structure that can be reactivated, repaired, or contested.
claims.note: Author asserts that recognition has a persistent ontological status within social reality.

claims.claim: Recognition creates and maintains enduring relations, unlike mere habit.
claims.source_quote: Habits describe repeated behaviors; recognition creates and maintains enduring relations.
claims.note: Direct ontological contrast: recognition has generative and sustaining ontological function.

claims.claim: Recognition brings into existence new dependent continuants by altering relations among agents.
claims.source_quote: As an ontological event, recognition is creative. It brings into existence new dependent continuants by altering the configuration of relations among agents.
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts recognition's creative ontological function in BFO terms.

claims.claim: When two persons recognize a contract, a new obligation arises between them.
claims.source_quote: When two persons recognize a contract, a new obligation arises between them.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological consequence of a specific act of recognition.

claims.claim: When citizens recognize a constitution, a political entity—the state—comes into being.
claims.source_quote: When citizens recognize a constitution, a political entity, the state, comes into being.
claims.note: Author asserts a specific ontological consequence of collective recognition.

claims.claim: Recognition is the formative cause of law.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is not simply a prerequisite for law but its formative cause.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal-ontological relation between recognition and law's existence.

claims.claim: Law is constructed through human acts of recognition yet generates enduring entities that constrain future possibilities.
claims.source_quote: Law is constructed in the sense that it arises through human acts of recognition; it is real in the sense that those acts generate enduring entities that constrain future possibilities.
claims.note: Author asserts dual ontological character of law: constructed yet real.

claims.claim: Institutions achieve temporal endurance through recursive recognition rather than physical permanence.
claims.source_quote: Institutions thus achieve temporal endurance not through physical permanence but through recursive recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological mechanism by which institutions persist over time.

claims.claim: Institutions are repositories of recognition that stabilize momentary acts of obligation-creation in durable structures.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are the repositories of recognition. They stabilize the fragile, momentary acts through which obligations and authorities are created, embedding them in durable structures that outlast their founders.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological function and role of institutions.

claims.claim: An institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes that continually reaffirm its place in the social ontology.
claims.source_quote: The institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes, elections, sessions, rulings, that continually reaffirm its place in the ontology of the social world.
claims.note: Author asserts how institutional being is sustained ontologically.

claims.claim: Institutions act as memory for recognition, preserving its effects across time.
claims.source_quote: Institutions thus act as memory for recognition, preserving its effects across time.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional-ontological property of institutions regarding temporal persistence of recognition.

claims.claim: Exchange is a realization of recognition symmetry.
claims.source_quote: Exchange, therefore, is a realization of recognition symmetry. It does not merely measure value; it creates it by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological nature of exchange as a realization relation.

claims.claim: Exchange creates value by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: It does not merely measure value; it creates it by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.note: Positive assertion about value creation through relational coherence.

claims.claim: Markets are ontological engines that produce and stabilize value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: markets are ontological engines of equivalence, continuously producing and stabilizing value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological role and function of markets.

claims.claim: Property consists of dependent continuants that receive recognition.
claims.source_quote: the dependent continuants that constitute property are subject to variations in the density and stability of recognition they receive.
claims.note: Asserts that property is constituted by dependent continuants bearing a recognition relation.

claims.claim: Market value is a dependent continuant sustained by a field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Economic volatility is thus ontological volatility: a fluctuation in the field of recognition that sustains the dependent continuant 'market value.'
claims.note: Explicitly identifies market value as a dependent continuant with recognition as its sustaining condition.

claims.claim: Economic volatility is ontological volatility in the recognition field.
claims.source_quote: Economic volatility is thus ontological volatility: a fluctuation in the field of recognition that sustains the dependent continuant 'market value.'
claims.note: Asserts an identity/equivalence between two kinds of volatility, making an ontological claim.

claims.claim: Price is the quantification of recognition.
claims.source_quote: price appears as the quantification of recognition. It is the numerical form in which the degree of collective acknowledgment is expressed.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about what price is ontologically.

claims.claim: Price is not identical to value but represents the equilibrium achieved through exchange.
claims.source_quote: A price is not identical to value but a representation of the equilibrium achieved through exchange.
claims.note: Asserts a non-identity and a representational relation between price and value.

claims.claim: Price is a public signal of recognition coherence.
claims.source_quote: It serves as a public signal of recognition coherence, a token indicating that, within the current configuration of property and institution, a given object is acknowledged as possessing a specific relational worth.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/role property of price.

claims.claim: Value belongs to the domain of ontology.
claims.source_quote: while price belongs to the domain of measurement, value belongs to the domain of ontology.
claims.note: Direct categorical assertion about the domain of value.

claims.claim: Price is an information artifact; value is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: The two are related as information artifact to dependent continuant: the former records the latter's realization in a form transmissible across agents and systems.
claims.note: Asserts ontological kinds for price and value and a recording/realization relation between them.

claims.claim: Value arises from socially sustained recognition.
claims.source_quote: Because value arises from socially sustained recognition, it is susceptible to asymmetry and exclusion.
claims.note: Direct causal-ontological claim about the origin of value.

claims.claim: The ontology of value is inseparable from the politics of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Thus, the ontology of value is inseparable from the politics of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive dependency relation between value ontology and recognition politics.

claims.claim: Redistribution, market regulation, and cultural change are processes of ontological recalibration.
claims.source_quote: Redistribution, market regulation, and even cultural change are, at their core, processes of ontological recalibration, attempts to reshape the dependencies that produce and maintain value.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological kind-membership for social/political processes.

claims.claim: When agents lack a shared field of recognition, exchange is ontologically impossible.
claims.source_quote: When two agents do not share a coherent field of recognition, when their systems of property, currency, or obligation do not align, exchange becomes ontologically impossible.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for exchange as an ontological matter.

claims.claim: Failed exchanges lack ontological closure because no shared recognition field exists.
claims.source_quote: The exchange lacks ontological closure: no shared field exists in which value could inhere.
claims.note: Asserts a property (lack of ontological closure) of failed exchange situations.

claims.claim: Markets depend on law for the very existence of value as a stable relation.
claims.source_quote: Markets depend on law not merely for enforcement but for the very existence of value as a stable relation among agents and goods.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between markets/value and law.

claims.claim: Use-value is a realization of property's relational capacities within a single agent's recognition horizon.
claims.source_quote: Use-value corresponds to the realization of a property relation within a single agent's horizon of recognition, an owner's capacity to employ an object's functions.
claims.note: Asserts what use-value is ontologically—a realization of relational capacity.

claims.claim: Exchange-value is a realization of property's relational capacities across multiple agents.
claims.source_quote: Exchange-value corresponds to realization across multiple agents, mediated by institutional structures of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts what exchange-value is ontologically.

claims.claim: Use-value and exchange-value are different modes of relation, not different substances.
claims.source_quote: The two are not different substances but different modes of relation: one internal, the other intersubjective.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological classification of the distinction between use- and exchange-value.

claims.claim: Value is the institutional realization of phenomenological potential.
claims.source_quote: Thus, value is the institutional realization of phenomenological potential. It is the structured possibility of meaningful interaction among things, sustained not by individual consciousness but by collective recognition encoded in law.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about what value is ontologically.

claims.claim: Property transforms subjective intentionality into objective social reality.
claims.source_quote: In this respect, property transforms subjective intentionality into objective social reality.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative function/role of property as an ontological process.

claims.claim: Digital assets and immaterial entities possess value because they are embedded in networks of institutional and social recognition.
claims.source_quote: Digital assets, trademarks, data sets, and even social media 'influence' possess value because they are embedded in networks of institutional and social recognition that assign and sustain rights over them.
claims.note: Asserts that immaterial entities have value and identifies its relational ground.

claims.claim: The worth of immaterial entities is relational, not intrinsic.
claims.source_quote: Their worth is not intrinsic but relational, deriving from the coherence and scope of the recognition field that supports them.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological character of immaterial entities' worth.

claims.claim: When recognition falters, dependent continuants dissolve and value dissipates.
claims.source_quote: When recognition falters, when a platform collapses or legal rights expire, the value dissipates. Ontologically, such collapses are not mysterious market events but the dissolution of dependent continuants no longer sustained by institutional acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts what happens ontologically when recognition fails—dissolution of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Value is not an emergent property of matter but of relation.
claims.source_quote: value is not an emergent property of matter but of relation.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological category from which value emerges.

claims.claim: The economic system is an ontological extension of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The economic system is thus not an independent sphere but an ontological extension of the legal system, a dynamic field in which law's structures of recognition generate, distribute, and sustain value.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/ontological relation between the economic and legal systems.

claims.claim: Property is a foundational mechanism through which social value is generated and maintained.
claims.source_quote: Property is not merely a juridical category but a foundational mechanism through which social value is generated and maintained.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role for property as an ontological mechanism.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant that exists across material, informational, and digital layers of reality.
claims.source_quote: Property, as a relational continuant, is not confined to a single ontological domain. It exists across multiple layers of reality, including material, informational, and digital, each with its own modes of recognition, realization, and persistence.
claims.note: Asserts ontological kind-membership and cross-domain existence of property.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for a class of entities.

claims.claim: An institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes such as elections, sessions, and rulings.
claims.source_quote: The institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes, elections, sessions, rulings, that continually reaffirm its place in the ontology of the social world.
claims.note: Direct assertion about what sustains the existence of an institution — an ontological claim about institutional being.

claims.claim: Institutions have a place in the ontology of the social world.
claims.source_quote: The institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes, elections, sessions, rulings, that continually reaffirm its place in the ontology of the social world.
