claims.note: The author asserts that institutions are genuine constituents of social reality.

claims.claim: Institutions act as memory for recognition, preserving recognition's effects across time.
claims.source_quote: Institutions thus act as memory for recognition, preserving its effects across time.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of institutions in relation to recognition — an ontological claim about institutional function.

claims.claim: Recognition explains the continuity of law through historical transformation.
claims.source_quote: Recognition also explains the continuity of law through historical transformation.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition bears an explanatory/causal relation to legal continuity — an ontological claim about the relation between recognition and law.

claims.claim: Legal systems survive revolutions, reforms, and reinterpretations.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems survive revolutions, reforms, and reinterpretations because certain core structures of recognition persist even as their material forms change.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal systems — their persistence through transformation.

claims.claim: Core structures of recognition persist even as their material forms change.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems survive revolutions, reforms, and reinterpretations because certain core structures of recognition persist even as their material forms change.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition structures have a property of persistence distinct from their material instantiation.

claims.claim: The office of 'judge' is a recognized role whose existence endures through functional changes.
claims.source_quote: The office of 'judge,' for instance, may evolve in function or authority, but its existence as a recognized role endures.
claims.note: Asserts that the judge-role is a kind of recognized entity with persistent existence — an ontological claim about a social role.

claims.claim: Recognition links past, present, and future acts into a coherent temporal chain.
claims.source_quote: Recognition links past, present, and future acts into a coherent temporal chain.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of recognition — it binds temporally distinct acts together — an ontological claim about recognition's causal/constitutive role.

claims.claim: Modern legal systems increasingly operate within domains where ownership attaches to intangible or virtual entities.
claims.source_quote: modern legal systems increasingly operate within domains where ownership attaches to intangible or virtual entities.
claims.note: Asserts a property of modern legal systems regarding the domain of ownership.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities are not material objects but structures of information and code.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim: virtual/intangible entities are structures of information and code, not material objects.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional/relational property of intangible entities regarding their mode of persistence.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.source_quote: that are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between intangible/virtual entities and material forms.

claims.claim: Ownership is a recognized dependency relation.
claims.source_quote: the same relational form, ownership as a recognized dependency, adapts across these layered domains of being.
claims.note: Asserts a characterization of ownership as a relational form constituted by recognized dependency.

claims.claim: Tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.source_quote: At the most fundamental level, tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-domain membership claim: tangible property belongs to the ontological domain of material continuants.

claims.claim: Exchange is a realization of recognition symmetry.
claims.source_quote: Exchange, therefore, is a realization of recognition symmetry. It does not merely measure value; it creates it by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.note: Author plainly asserts a relational/ontological identity between exchange and recognition symmetry.

claims.claim: Exchange creates value by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: It does not merely measure value; it creates it by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/constitutive role for exchange in producing value.

claims.claim: Markets are ontological engines of equivalence that produce and stabilize value.
claims.source_quote: markets are ontological engines of equivalence, continuously producing and stabilizing value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts a property/function of markets as entities.

claims.claim: Value fluctuates because recognition is neither uniform nor static.
claims.source_quote: Since recognition is neither uniform nor static, the dependent continuants that constitute property are subject to variations in the density and stability of recognition they receive.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological ground of value fluctuation.

claims.claim: Property is constituted by dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: the dependent continuants that constitute property are subject to variations in the density and stability of recognition they receive.
claims.note: Author asserts a constitutive relation between dependent continuants and property.

claims.claim: Market value is a dependent continuant sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: Economic volatility is thus ontological volatility: a fluctuation in the field of recognition that sustains the dependent continuant 'market value.'
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind of market value and its dependence relation.

claims.claim: Economic volatility is ontological volatility in the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Economic volatility is thus ontological volatility: a fluctuation in the field of recognition that sustains the dependent continuant 'market value.'
claims.note: Author asserts an identity between economic and ontological volatility.

claims.claim: Price is the quantification of recognition.
claims.source_quote: price appears as the quantification of recognition. It is the numerical form in which the degree of collective acknowledgment is expressed.
claims.note: Author asserts what price is ontologically.

claims.claim: Price is not identical to value but a representation of the equilibrium achieved through exchange.
claims.source_quote: A price is not identical to value but a representation of the equilibrium achieved through exchange.
claims.note: Author asserts a distinction and relation between price and value.

claims.claim: Price serves as a public signal of recognition coherence.
claims.source_quote: It serves as a public signal of recognition coherence, a token indicating that, within the current configuration of property and institution, a given object is acknowledged as possessing a specific relational worth.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional role for price.

claims.claim: Value belongs to the domain of ontology; price belongs to the domain of measurement.
claims.source_quote: while price belongs to the domain of measurement, value belongs to the domain of ontology.
claims.note: Author asserts domain membership for both value and price.

claims.claim: Price is an information artifact; value is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: The two are related as information artifact to dependent continuant: the former records the latter's realization in a form transmissible across agents and systems.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kinds of price and value.

claims.claim: Value arises from socially sustained recognition.
claims.source_quote: Because value arises from socially sustained recognition, it is susceptible to asymmetry and exclusion.
claims.note: Author asserts the generative dependence of value on social recognition.

claims.claim: Recognition is never evenly distributed; it reflects existing structures of power and institutional priority.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is never evenly distributed; it reflects existing structures of power and institutional priority.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of recognition as an entity.

claims.claim: Differential recognition translates into differential value.
claims.source_quote: Certain forms of property, like land, labor, and intellectual creations, gain recognition more readily than others, and this differential recognition translates into differential value.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/constitutive link between recognition distribution and value distribution.

claims.claim: The ontology of value is inseparable from the politics of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Thus, the ontology of value is inseparable from the politics of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts a necessary relational bond between value ontology and recognition politics.

claims.claim: Redistribution, market regulation, and cultural change are processes of ontological recalibration.
claims.source_quote: Redistribution, market regulation, and even cultural change are, at their core, processes of ontological recalibration, attempts to reshape the dependencies that produce and maintain value.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind of these social processes.

claims.claim: When agents lack a coherent shared field of recognition, exchange is ontologically impossible.
claims.source_quote: When two agents do not share a coherent field of recognition, when their systems of property, currency, or obligation do not align, exchange becomes ontologically impossible.
claims.note: Author asserts a necessary condition for the ontological possibility of exchange.

claims.claim: Without reciprocal recognition, no value is realized in a transfer.
claims.source_quote: no value is realized because the transfer lacks reciprocal recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts that reciprocal recognition is necessary for value realization.

claims.claim: Failed exchanges lack ontological closure because no shared recognition field exists.
claims.source_quote: The exchange lacks ontological closure: no shared field exists in which value could inhere.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of failed exchanges.

claims.claim: Markets depend on law for the very existence of value as a stable relation.
claims.source_quote: Markets depend on law not merely for enforcement but for the very existence of value as a stable relation among agents and goods.
claims.note: Author asserts a constitutive dependence of value on law.

claims.claim: Use-value and exchange-value are both realizations of property's relational capacities.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, however, both are realizations of property's relational capacities.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind of both forms of value.

claims.claim: Use-value is the realization of a property relation within a single agent's horizon of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Use-value corresponds to the realization of a property relation within a single agent's horizon of recognition, an owner's capacity to employ an object's functions.
claims.note: Author asserts what use-value is ontologically.

claims.claim: Exchange-value is realization across multiple agents mediated by institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Exchange-value corresponds to realization across multiple agents, mediated by institutional structures of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts what exchange-value is ontologically.

claims.claim: Use-value and exchange-value are different modes of relation, not different substances.
claims.source_quote: The two are not different substances but different modes of relation: one internal, the other intersubjective.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological distinction between these modes.

claims.claim: Value is the institutional realization of phenomenological potential.
claims.source_quote: Thus, value is the institutional realization of phenomenological potential.
claims.note: Author asserts what value is ontologically in relation to phenomenological potential.

claims.claim: Value is the structured possibility of meaningful interaction among things, sustained by collective recognition encoded in law.
claims.source_quote: It is the structured possibility of meaningful interaction among things, sustained not by individual consciousness but by collective recognition encoded in law.
claims.note: Author asserts a definition/property of value.

claims.claim: Property transforms subjective intentionality into objective social reality.
claims.source_quote: In this respect, property transforms subjective intentionality into objective social reality.
claims.note: Author asserts a function/role of property.

claims.claim: Digital assets, trademarks, and data sets possess value because they are embedded in networks of institutional and social recognition.
claims.source_quote: Digital assets, trademarks, data sets, and even social media 'influence' possess value because they are embedded in networks of institutional and social recognition that assign and sustain rights over them.
claims.note: Author asserts the ground of value for immaterial entities.

claims.claim: The worth of immaterial entities is relational, not intrinsic.
claims.source_quote: Their worth is not intrinsic but relational, deriving from the coherence and scope of the recognition field that supports them.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of immaterial entities' value.

claims.claim: When recognition falters, value dissipates.
claims.source_quote: When recognition falters, when a platform collapses or legal rights expire, the value dissipates.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/constitutive dependence: value dissolution follows recognition dissolution.

claims.claim: Collapses of digital value are dissolutions of dependent continuants no longer sustained by institutional acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, such collapses are not mysterious market events but the dissolution of dependent continuants no longer sustained by institutional acknowledgment.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind of such value collapses.

claims.claim: Value is an emergent property of relation, not of matter.
claims.source_quote: value is not an emergent property of matter but of relation.
claims.note: Author asserts value's ontological ground.

claims.claim: The world of value is the world of recognized dependency among institutions, agents, norms, and things.
claims.source_quote: The world of value is the world of recognized dependency: of institutions maintaining coherence among agents, norms, and things.
claims.note: Author asserts a characterization of value's ontological domain.

claims.claim: Law furnishes the conditions for value's realization.
claims.source_quote: Law does not create value ex nihilo, but it furnishes the conditions for its realization.
claims.note: Author asserts the role of law in relation to value.

claims.claim: Law renders property capable of functioning as a bearer of value through recognition, registration, and enforcement.
claims.source_quote: Through recognition, registration, and enforcement, law renders property capable of functioning as a bearer of value.
claims.note: Author asserts law's functional effect on property.

claims.claim: The economic system is an ontological extension of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The economic system is thus not an independent sphere but an ontological extension of the legal system, a dynamic field in which law's structures of recognition generate, distribute, and sustain value.
claims.note: Author asserts a subkind/extension relation between economic and legal systems.

claims.claim: Property is a foundational mechanism through which social value is generated and maintained.
claims.source_quote: Property is not merely a juridical category but a foundational mechanism through which social value is generated and maintained.
claims.note: Author asserts a property/function of property as an entity.

claims.claim: Economy is one of law's most intricate ontological expressions.
claims.source_quote: the economy, far from existing outside law, is one of its most intricate ontological expressions.
claims.note: Author asserts a relation between economy and law.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant that exists across multiple ontological layers.
claims.source_quote: Property, as a relational continuant, is not confined to a single ontological domain. It exists across multiple layers of reality, including material, informational, and digital.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind and multi-domain existence of property.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.note: Author asserts a dependence relation for intangible entities.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities are structures of information and code.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation and that are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.note: The author positively asserts what kind of thing intangible/virtual entities are: structures of information and code.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation and that are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/condition of existence for these entities: dependence on institutional and technological mediation.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation and that are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.note: The author asserts a realization relation between intangible entities and material forms.

claims.claim: Ownership is a recognized dependency relation.
claims.source_quote: one must trace how the same relational form, ownership as a recognized dependency, adapts across these layered domains of being.
claims.note: The author characterizes ownership ontologically as a relational form constituted by recognized dependency.

claims.claim: Tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.source_quote: At the most fundamental level, tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.note: The author asserts that tangible property belongs to the ontological category of material continuants.

claims.claim: Being is structured in layered domains.
claims.source_quote: one must trace how the same relational form, ownership as a recognized dependency, adapts across these layered domains of being.
claims.note: The phrase 'layered domains of being' commits the author to an ontology with distinct, hierarchically organized domains of being.

claims.claim: Promises, commands, and transfers are processes (occurrents) linking two or more agents.
claims.source_quote: each act can be represented as a process (an occurrent) linking two or more agents and resulting in new dependent entities: obligations, permissions, or rights.
claims.note: The author asserts this in his own voice as a positive ontological characterization, though 'can be represented' introduces slight hedging.

claims.claim: Obligations, permissions, and rights are dependent entities.
claims.source_quote: each act can be represented as a process (an occurrent) linking two or more agents and resulting in new dependent entities: obligations, permissions, or rights.
claims.note: The author positively classifies obligations, permissions, and rights as dependent entities, an ontological kind claim.

claims.claim: Obligations, permissions, and rights are results of social acts such as promises, commands, and transfers.
claims.source_quote: each act can be represented as a process (an occurrent) linking two or more agents and resulting in new dependent entities: obligations, permissions, or rights.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/generative relation between social acts and the dependent entities they produce.

claims.claim: Obligations, permissions, and rights enter into higher-order relations within institutions, courts, legislatures, and contracts.
claims.source_quote: These entities then enter into higher-order relations within institutions, courts, legislatures, contracts, that govern their creation and dissolution.
claims.note: Direct assertion of a relational property: these entities participate in higher-order institutional relations.

claims.claim: Institutions, courts, legislatures, and contracts govern the creation and dissolution of obligations, permissions, and rights.
claims.source_quote: These entities then enter into higher-order relations within institutions, courts, legislatures, contracts, that govern their creation and dissolution.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/dispositional role for these institutional entities: they govern creation and dissolution of normative entities.

claims.claim: Law is a dynamic system in which acts continually generate and transform enduring entities.
claims.source_quote: Law becomes a dynamic system in which acts continually generate and transform enduring entities.
claims.note: The author positively asserts a property of law as a kind: it is a dynamic system with a generative function over enduring entities.

claims.claim: Core structures of recognition persist through legal revolutions and reforms.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems survive revolutions, reforms, and reinterpretations because certain core structures of recognition persist even as their material forms change.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the persistence of a structural entity (recognition) through change—an ontological claim about endurance.

claims.claim: The office of 'judge' exists as a recognized role that endures through functional evolution.
claims.source_quote: The office of 'judge,' for instance, may evolve in function or authority, but its existence as a recognized role endures.
claims.note: Asserts that a specific entity (the office of judge) has the property of enduring existence as a recognized role.

claims.claim: Recognition links past, present, and future acts into a coherent temporal chain.
claims.source_quote: Recognition links past, present, and future acts into a coherent temporal chain.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of recognition—it connects acts across time.

claims.claim: The continuity of law is the maintenance of recognition across generations.
claims.source_quote: The continuity of law is thus an ontological achievement: the maintenance of recognition across generations.
claims.note: Identifies the ontological character of legal continuity as constituted by recognition maintenance.

claims.claim: Recognition creates institutions.
claims.source_quote: Recognition creates institutions, and institutions, in turn, sustain recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a generative causal-ontological relation between recognition and institutions.

claims.claim: Institutions sustain recognition.
claims.source_quote: Recognition creates institutions, and institutions, in turn, sustain recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a sustaining relation from institutions back to recognition.

claims.claim: When recognition fails, entities that depended on those relations begin to lose their being.
claims.source_quote: When recognition fails, when citizens cease to acknowledge legitimacy or institutions lose their capacity to command acknowledgment, the system decays... the entities that depended on those relations begin to lose their being.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency: the being of certain entities depends on recognition relations.

claims.claim: A constitution unrecognized ceases to exist as law and becomes a historical artifact.
claims.source_quote: A constitution unrecognized ceases to exist as law; it becomes a historical artifact.
claims.note: Asserts a change in ontological status of a specific kind of entity when recognition is withdrawn.

claims.claim: Ontological repair—restoration of coherence in the field of recognition—is the condition for legal renewal.
claims.source_quote: Ontological repair, the restoration of coherence within the field of recognition, is the condition for renewal.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition relation: ontological repair (a process) is required for renewal.

claims.claim: Recognition is an occurrent—a process that realizes the potential of agents to enter mutual acknowledgment relations.
claims.source_quote: Recognition's ontological role can also be expressed in BFO terms. It is an occurrent, a process that realizes the potential of agents to enter relations of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim: recognition is an occurrent (a process), and it realizes a potential.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, and offices are dependent continuants that persist after recognition events.
claims.source_quote: The entities created, obligations, rights, offices, are dependent continuants that persist after the event.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation: obligations, rights, offices are dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Institutions are independent continuants that house and stabilize dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are independent continuants that house and stabilize these dependents.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership (institutions are independent continuants) and a functional/relational property.

claims.claim: The structure of law is a dynamic interplay between occurrents of recognition and the continuants they produce and sustain.
claims.source_quote: The entire structure of law can thus be understood as a dynamic interplay between occurrents of recognition and the continuants they produce and sustain.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological constitution of legal structure in terms of process-continuant relations.

claims.claim: Recognition is the generative event of law.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is the generative event; institution is the enduring vessel; obligation is the relational product.
claims.note: Assigns a specific ontological role/function to recognition.

claims.claim: Institution is the enduring vessel of law.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is the generative event; institution is the enduring vessel; obligation is the relational product.
claims.note: Assigns a specific ontological role/function to institution.

claims.claim: Obligation is the relational product of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is the generative event; institution is the enduring vessel; obligation is the relational product.
claims.note: Assigns a specific ontological character (relational product) to obligation.

claims.claim: Recognition operates through patterned acknowledgment distributed across agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: It operates through patterned acknowledgment, not unanimous belief. In large-scale societies, recognition is distributed: officials, citizens, and institutions acknowledge one another's roles through countless localized interactions.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of recognition as distributed and patterned.

claims.claim: Law's durability reflects the density and regularity of recognition relations.
claims.source_quote: Law's durability, therefore, reflects the density and regularity of these recognition relations, not the purity of collective belief.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law (durability) and grounds it in recognition relations.

claims.claim: Recognition is the foundation of normativity.
claims.source_quote: From a phenomenological standpoint, recognition is also the foundation of normativity.
claims.note: Asserts a foundational ontological relation between recognition and normativity.

claims.claim: Constraints of respect, reciprocity, and non-harm are built into the ontology of personhood.
claims.source_quote: These constraints are not moral ideals layered onto social life; they are built into the ontology of personhood.
claims.note: Asserts that normative constraints are intrinsic properties of personhood as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: Normativity emerges from being rather than being imposed upon it.
claims.source_quote: Normativity, in this sense, is not imposed upon being but emerges from it.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological claim about the source and mode of existence of normativity.

claims.claim: Recognition is the point where the descriptive and the prescriptive converge and ontology generates obligation.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is the point where the descriptive and the prescriptive converge, where ontology generates obligation.
claims.note: Asserts a relational and generative property of recognition with respect to obligation.

claims.claim: Institutions stabilize recognition through time by embedding acknowledgment in procedures and artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Institutions thus function as stabilizers of recognition through time. They do so by embedding acts of acknowledgment within procedures and artifacts that outlast individual participants.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of institutions with respect to recognition.

claims.claim: Statutes, court records, treaties, and constitutions are material anchors for recognition.
claims.source_quote: Statutes, court records, treaties, and constitutions serve as material anchors for recognition, ensuring that it can be reactivated by new generations.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of specific legal artifacts.

claims.claim: Legal artifacts preserve the conditions under which law can continue to exist.
claims.source_quote: These artifacts do not contain law by themselves; they preserve the conditions under which law can continue to exist.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of legal artifacts distinct from containing law itself.

claims.claim: Law is a living archive of recognition that endures through renewal.
claims.source_quote: Law, therefore, is a living archive of recognition, a structure that endures through renewal.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological characterization of law as a recognition-archive with the property of renewal-dependent endurance.

claims.claim: Every legal act is a crystallization of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Every legal act, legislation, judgment, contract, is a crystallization of recognition, a moment when the fabric of relations thickens and takes shape.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological characterization of legal acts as instances/crystallizations of recognition.

claims.claim: Obligations attach to roles rather than directly to individual agents.
claims.source_quote: Obligations, in turn, inhere in roles rather than directly in agents.
claims.note: Asserts a specific inherence relation: obligations inhere in roles, not individuals.

claims.claim: A role is a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in an agent but depends on an institutional structure.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, a role is a specifically dependent continuant, an entity that inheres in an agent but depends on an institutional structure for its existence.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership and inherence/dependence relations for roles.

claims.claim: The role of 'judge' depends on the institution of the judiciary for its existence.
claims.source_quote: The role of 'judge' depends on the institution of the judiciary; the role of 'buyer' depends on the institution of exchange; the role of 'citizen' depends on the political community that recognizes it.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation between a specific role and its institutional host.

claims.claim: The role of 'buyer' depends on the institution of exchange for its existence.
claims.source_quote: The role of 'buyer' depends on the institution of exchange.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation between a specific role and its institutional host.

claims.claim: The role of 'citizen' depends on the political community that recognizes it.
claims.source_quote: The role of 'citizen' depends on the political community that recognizes it.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation between a specific role and its recognizing community.

claims.claim: Roles are relational entities, not psychological identities.
claims.source_quote: These roles are not psychological identities but relational entities.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership (relational entities) and negative characterization for roles.

claims.claim: To occupy a role is to inhabit a position within a network of recognition carrying powers, responsibilities, and expectations.
claims.source_quote: To occupy a role is to inhabit a position within a network of recognition, one that carries with it certain powers, responsibilities, and expectations.
claims.note: Asserts properties and relations constitutive of role-occupancy.

claims.claim: Legal obligations persist despite turnover in personnel because they belong to roles, not individuals.
claims.source_quote: This is why legal obligations persist despite turnover in personnel. When one official retires and another takes office, the obligation does not disappear; it transfers seamlessly because it belongs to the role, not the individual.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal obligations (persistence) grounded in their inherence in roles rather than persons.

claims.claim: Moral obligations attach directly to persons as moral agents.
claims.source_quote: Moral obligations attach to persons directly, insofar as they are moral agents; legal obligations attach to them derivatively, insofar as they occupy roles within institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a direct inherence relation between moral obligations and persons.

claims.claim: Legal obligations attach to persons derivatively, insofar as they occupy institutional roles.
claims.source_quote: Legal obligations attach to them derivatively, insofar as they occupy roles within institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a derivative inherence relation between legal obligations and persons via roles.

claims.claim: A judge's authority derives from institutional relations defining her position, not from personal conviction.
claims.source_quote: Her decision's authority derives from the institutional relations that define her position, not from her personal conviction.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological ground of juridical authority in institutional relations.

claims.claim: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.source_quote: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.note: Asserts two relations: inherence (role in agent) and participation (agent in institution).

claims.claim: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.source_quote: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.note: Asserts inherence (obligation in role) and dependency (obligation on institution) relations.

claims.claim: A role inheres in an agent.
claims.source_quote: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts the inheres_in relation between role and agent as part of the ontological representation.

claims.claim: An agent participates in an institution.
claims.source_quote: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts the participates_in relation between agent and institution.

claims.claim: An obligation inheres in a role.
claims.source_quote: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts the inheres_in relation between obligation and role.

claims.claim: An obligation depends on an institution for its continuing validity.
claims.source_quote: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts the depends_on relation between obligation and institution.

claims.claim: The relation between agent, role, and institution forms a chain of ontological dependencies.
claims.source_quote: The relation between agent, role, and institution can be represented ontologically as a chain of dependencies.
claims.note: The author asserts this as the ontological structure, though framed as 'can be represented'; the subsequent formal listing confirms endorsement.

claims.claim: Law functions through roles rather than through the fluctuating intentions of individuals.
claims.source_quote: llows law to function objectively, to speak through roles rather than through the fluctuating intentions of individuals.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/dispositional property of law: it operates via roles, not individual intentions. Slight qualification from fragmentary context.

claims.claim: Tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.source_quote: At the most fundamental level, tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of tangible property within a domain of being.

claims.claim: Material continuants are independent continuants that exist regardless of recognition.
claims.source_quote: These are independent continuants in BFO terms: physical objects that exist regardless of recognition, though their status as property depends on it.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the kind 'independent continuants': existence independent of recognition.

claims.claim: Land, buildings, and artifacts are paradigmatic cases of tangible property.
claims.source_quote: Land, buildings, and artifacts are paradigmatic cases.
claims.note: Asserts that specific entities are instances of a kind (tangible property).

claims.claim: The property relation links owner, object owned, and institutional framework that sustains recognition.
claims.source_quote: The property relation here links the agent (owner), the object (thing owned), and the institutional framework that sustains recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the relational structure of property as having three relata.

claims.claim: A physical entity persists even if recognition of it as property lapses.
claims.source_quote: even if recognition lapses, the physical entity remains available for reappropriation and is susceptible to occupation or physical control.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of physical entities independent of institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Tangible property provides the ontological baseline where law's relational structure engages the material world.
claims.source_quote: Tangible property thus provides the ontological baseline: the domain where law's relational structure most visibly engages the material world.
claims.note: Asserts a foundational ontological role for tangible property.

claims.claim: Intangible property occupies the domain of informational and conceptual continuants.
claims.source_quote: Intangible property, by contrast, occupies the domain of informational and conceptual continuants, entities that exist not as physical things but as structured content or form.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of intangible property.

claims.claim: Copyrights, patents, trademarks, and debts are information content entities embedded in institutional recognition structures.
claims.source_quote: Copyrights, patents, trademarks, and debts are not objects in the material sense but information content entities (ICEs) embedded in institutional recognition structures.
claims.note: Asserts that specific kinds of intangible property are instances of ICEs with a particular embedding relation.

claims.claim: Intangible property exists only through systems that encode and sustain it, such as registries and databases.
claims.source_quote: They exist only through the systems that encode and sustain them: registries, ledgers, databases, and enforcement mechanisms.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between intangible property and sustaining systems.

claims.claim: A patent inheres in the institutional continuant of the patent office and the legal system.
claims.source_quote: A patent, for example, exists as a recognized right to exclude others from using a specific innovation; it inheres in the institutional continuant of the patent office and the legal system that enforces it.
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between a patent and an institutional continuant.

claims.claim: A patent's being depends on recognition distributed across institutions and realized through procedural occurrents.
claims.source_quote: Its being depends on recognition distributed across these institutions, realized through procedural occurrents such as filing, examination, and granting.
claims.note: Asserts ontological dependence of a patent on distributed recognition and procedural occurrents.

claims.claim: When recognition ceases, intangible property ceases to exist as law.
claims.source_quote: When recognition ceases, through lapse, expiration, or legal invalidation, the intangible property ceases to exist as law, though its informational substrate may remain.
claims.note: Asserts a conditional cessation of existence for intangible property.

claims.claim: Digital property includes software licenses, cryptocurrency tokens, domain names, and virtual goods.
claims.source_quote: Digital property includes software licenses, cryptocurrency tokens, domain names, and virtual goods in online environments.
claims.note: Asserts that specific entities are instances of the kind 'digital property'.

claims.claim: Digital property entities are computational continuants sustained by technological and institutional dependencies.
claims.source_quote: they are computational continuants, structured states of digital systems sustained by both technological and institutional dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts a kind classification and dependency relations for digital property entities.

claims.claim: Digital property entities are generically dependent continuants realized through coordinated functioning of hardware, software, and institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, they are generically dependent continuants realized through the coordinated functioning of hardware, software, and institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts ontological kind and realization relation for digital property.

claims.claim: A digital token exists only as long as the blockchain encoding it remains operational and recognized as authoritative.
claims.source_quote: A digital token, for instance, exists only as long as the blockchain that encodes it remains operational and recognized as authoritative.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between a digital token's existence and its sustaining blockchain.

claims.claim: Ownership of a digital token is defined by control over cryptographic credentials.
claims.source_quote: Its ownership is defined by control over cryptographic credentials, which serve as procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive relation between ownership and cryptographic credential control.

claims.claim: Cryptographic credentials are procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.source_quote: control over cryptographic credentials, which serve as procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between cryptographic credentials and recognition.

claims.claim: Technical recognition achieves legal reality only when acknowledged by institutional systems.
claims.source_quote: this technical recognition only achieves legal reality when it is acknowledged by institutional systems, when courts, regulators, or markets accept blockchain records as evidence of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between technical recognition and legal reality.

claims.claim: The ontological chain for digital assets runs from algorithmic recognition to institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: The ontological chain thus runs from algorithmic recognition to institutional recognition, forming a hybrid system of dependence.
claims.note: Asserts a relational structure linking two types of recognition in a chain of dependence.

claims.claim: Law and technology together sustain the being of digital assets.
claims.source_quote: Law and technology together sustain the being of digital assets, each contributing distinct but interlocking layers of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a joint sustaining relation between law, technology, and digital asset existence.

claims.claim: A software program is both a work of authorship (intangible property) and a functional system (digital property).
claims.source_quote: A software program is both a work of authorship (intangible property protected by copyright) and a functional system (digital property realized through execution on computational hardware).
claims.note: Asserts dual ontological classification of software.

claims.claim: The same software entity exists simultaneously across different ontological layers, each sustained by its own recognition structure.
claims.source_quote: The same entity exists simultaneously across different ontological layers, each sustained by its own recognition structure.
claims.note: Asserts multi-layer simultaneous existence for a single entity.

claims.claim: Ownership of software involves a complex network of recognitions including author's rights, licensee's usage rights, and institutional rules.
claims.source_quote: Ownership of software therefore involves a complex network of recognitions: the author's moral and economic rights, the licensee's usage rights, and the institutional rules defining the permissible scope of execution.
claims.note: Asserts the relational composition of software ownership.

claims.claim: Data are information artifacts: structured representations of entities, events, or relations.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, data are information artifacts, structured representations of entities, events, or relations.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of data as a kind.

claims.claim: Data are generically dependent continuants that can exist in multiple copies simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Because data are generically dependent continuants that can exist in multiple copies simultaneously, property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.note: Asserts ontological kind and a property of data (multiple simultaneous copies).

claims.claim: The owner of data is the agent recognized as controlling its flow within institutional systems.
claims.source_quote: The owner of data is, in effect, the agent recognized as controlling its flow within these systems.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive claim about what data ownership consists in.

claims.claim: Data ownership is a right to control relational configurations rather than physical possession.
claims.source_quote: The legal innovation of data ownership thus consists in redefining property as a right to control relational configurations rather than physical possession.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of data ownership as distinct from traditional property.

claims.claim: Virtual property arises entirely within artificial worlds governed by programmed ontologies.
claims.source_quote: Here, property arises entirely within artificial worlds governed by programmed ontologies.
claims.note: Asserts the domain of origin and governance structure for virtual property.

claims.claim: A virtual object exists only as an aggregation of code instantiated within a software platform.
claims.source_quote: A virtual sword or parcel of digital land exists only as an aggregation of code instantiated within a software platform.
claims.note: Asserts the constitutive basis of virtual objects.

claims.claim: Within its platform, a virtual object functions as property: it can be owned, transferred, and valued.
claims.source_quote: Yet within that platform, it functions as property: it can be owned, transferred, and valued.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of virtual objects within their platform.

claims.claim: Virtual property exemplifies nested recognition: recognition within one ontological layer sustained by another.
claims.source_quote: Virtual property therefore exemplifies nested recognition: an entity recognized within one ontological layer (the virtual environment) whose reality is further sustained by another (the legal system).
claims.note: Asserts a structural ontological feature (nested recognition) instantiated by virtual property.

claims.claim: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is their relational form, not their substance.
claims.source_quote: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is not their substance but their relational form.
claims.note: Asserts a unifying ontological feature across property kinds.

claims.claim: In all property domains, ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object, and a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: In each case, ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object (physical, informational, or virtual), and a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the universal relational structure of ownership across property kinds.

claims.claim: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is their relational form, not their substance.
claims.source_quote: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is not their substance but their relational form.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the unifying feature of different property types—an ontological claim about what kind of thing property fundamentally is.

claims.claim: Ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object, and a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: In each case, ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object (physical, informational, or virtual), and a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the relational structure constitutive of ownership—an ontological claim about what ownership is.

claims.claim: The persistence and transfer of property depend on the stability of these dependencies.
claims.source_quote: The persistence and transfer of property depend on the stability of these dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property's persistence/transfer and the stability of its constitutive relational structure.

claims.claim: The transition to software and data does not alter property's ontological nature.
claims.source_quote: The transition from land and goods to software and data does not alter property's ontological nature; it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Positive assertion about property's ontological invariance across domains.

claims.claim: The transition to software and data multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.source_quote: it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Asserts that new domains add new kinds of continuants bearing property relations—an ontological claim about the extension of property.

claims.claim: Ownership has a stratified ontology spanning multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.source_quote: The result is a stratified ontology of ownership, in which legal recognition spans multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.note: Asserts that ownership's ontology is stratified across material and immaterial layers—a direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: Legal recognition spans multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.source_quote: in which legal recognition spans multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between legal recognition and multiple ontological layers (material and immaterial).

claims.claim: Law has the capacity to extend its ontology across heterogeneous domains of being.
claims.source_quote: te law's capacity to extend its ontology across heterogeneous domains of being.
claims.note: The author presents this as a real feature of law's structure; slightly qualified because the sentence is fragmentary but clearly posited as a real capacity.

claims.claim: Obligations, permissions, and rights are entities that exist within legal systems.
claims.source_quote: es: obligations, permissions, or rights. These entities then enter into higher-order relations within institutions, courts, legislatures, contracts, that govern their creation and dissolution.
claims.note: The author asserts these are entities that enter into relations, committing to their existence.

claims.claim: Institutions, courts, legislatures, and contracts are entities within which legal entities enter into higher-order relations.
claims.source_quote: These entities then enter into higher-order relations within institutions, courts, legislatures, contracts, that govern their creation and dissolution.
claims.note: The author asserts the existence and relational role of these institutional entities.

claims.claim: Legal acts are transient; the entities they create are enduring relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: transient acts producing enduring relational continuants.
claims.note: The author asserts a categorical distinction between the ontological status of acts and their outcomes.

claims.claim: A legal act occurs in time, while the entities it creates persist across time.
claims.source_quote: An act occurs in time; the entities it creates persist across time. This explains how legal systems can have history and continuity.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the temporal properties of acts versus their outcomes.

claims.claim: Obligations and rights accumulate and interact within legal systems.
claims.source_quote: Each new promise or judgment adds to the growing network of obligations and rights, which accumulate and interact, sometimes harmoniously, sometimes in contradiction.
claims.note: The author asserts that obligations and rights are entities that accumulate and stand in relations to one another.

claims.claim: Institutions exist to manage the accumulation of obligations and rights.
claims.source_quote: Institutions arise to manage this accumulation, to repair conflicts and ensure coherence.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/relational property of institutions.

claims.claim: The social act of command creates an obligation of obedience recognized within a structure of roles.
claims.source_quote: A commander's order binds subordinates, not because of coercion, but because the social act of command creates an obligation of obedience recognized within a structure of roles.
claims.note: The author endorses this as an ontological claim about how commanding generates obligations.

claims.claim: Transferring generates ownership through mutual acknowledgment of a change in rights.
claims.source_quote: Transferring generates ownership, not by physical exchange, but through mutual acknowledgment of a change in rights.
claims.note: The author asserts a mechanism by which ownership (an entity) comes into being through a relational process.

claims.claim: A relational structure comes into being through intentional interaction and is sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: In each case, a relational structure comes into being through intentional interaction, sustained by recognition.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the origin and sustaining condition of relational structures.

claims.claim: Law is the systematic elaboration of elementary ontological mechanisms across the social field.
claims.source_quote: Law is thus the systematic elaboration of these elementary ontological mechanisms across the entire social field.
claims.note: The author asserts what law is as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: Social acts have a mode of being as real as physical objects.
claims.source_quote: For him, social acts have a mode of being as real as physical objects.
claims.note: The author attributes this to Reinach but endorses it as part of his own structural realism, though the immediate attribution is to Reinach; context shows endorsement.

claims.claim: A promise is a metaphysical possibility grounded in the structure of personhood.
claims.source_quote: A promise is not a convention but a metaphysical possibility grounded in the structure of personhood.
claims.note: Stated in Reinach's voice but endorsed by the author as part of his own structural realism framework.

claims.claim: Social reality has an a priori order that is no less objective than the natural world.
claims.source_quote: It reveals that social reality has an a priori order no less objective than the natural world.
claims.note: Author endorses this as part of the structural realist framework being developed.

claims.claim: Legal systems are historical elaborations of the ontological order of the social act.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems, in turn, are historical elaborations of that order, cultural architectures built upon the ontological bedrock of the social act.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological grounding and character of legal systems.

claims.claim: An unjust command still generates an obligation of a kind.
claims.source_quote: An unjust command still generates an obligation of a kind, though it may later be annulled or condemned.
claims.note: The author endorses this as part of his ontological framework's explanatory power.

claims.claim: Law's being is independent of its moral worth and is grounded in the coherence and persistence of recognition relations.
claims.source_quote: the idea that law's being is independent of its moral worth, grounded instead in the coherence and persistence of recognition relations.
claims.note: The author presents this as his own structural realism, asserting a property of law's being.

claims.claim: Acts of communication instantiate processes that create new dependent continuants such as obligations, rights, and authorities.
claims.source_quote: Acts of communication instantiate processes that create new dependent continuants, obligations, rights, authorities, that populate the legal world.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the mechanism of legal reality generation and the kinds of entities produced.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, and authorities are dependent continuants that populate the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Acts of communication instantiate processes that create new dependent continuants, obligations, rights, authorities, that populate the legal world.
claims.note: The author explicitly categorizes these legal entities as dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Promising, commanding, and transferring are the archetypes of legal creation.
claims.source_quote: Promising, commanding, and transferring are not just examples; they are the archetypes of legal creation.
claims.note: The author asserts a categorical/functional property of these act types.

claims.claim: Every obligation, right, and institution originates in acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Every obligation, every right, every institution ultimately originates in such acts, moments of recognition that generate the fabric of legal being.
claims.note: The author asserts a universal claim about the origin relation between recognition acts and legal entities.

claims.claim: The promise, command, and transfer are ontological engines producing enduring relations that make law possible.
claims.source_quote: The promise, the command, and the transfer are not metaphors but ontological engines, producing the enduring relations that make law possible.
claims.note: The author asserts these acts have a real causal/generative ontological role.

claims.claim: Hart's primary and secondary rules are relational continuants that persist through ongoing recognition within a community.
claims.source_quote: Both levels of rule are continuants, structures that endure through time by virtue of ongoing recognition within a community.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological category and persistence condition of legal rules.

claims.claim: A primary rule connects agents through obligations and permissions.
claims.source_quote: A primary rule connects agents directly through obligations and permissions: 'You shall not steal' establishes a relation of duty between potential offenders and victims.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational ontological characterization of primary rules.

claims.claim: A secondary rule is a relation among relations, connecting rules to one another.
claims.source_quote: A secondary rule, by contrast, connects rules to one another, it is a relation among relations.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological type of secondary rules as higher-order relations.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition specifies dependencies among norms that constitute a legal system.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition, for instance, specifies the dependencies among norms that constitute a legal system: which procedures, texts, or authorities generate valid law.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/relational property of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Legal rules are patterns of interrelation realized in institutions and sustained by practice.
claims.source_quote: They are not ideas in the minds of officials, but patterns of interrelation realized in institutions and sustained by practice.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological nature and location of legal rules.

claims.claim: A legal rule is an enduring relation that transcends its author and exists independently of the individuals who created it.
claims.source_quote: A rule, in Hart's sense, is an enduring relation that transcends its author. Once recognized, it continues to exist independently of the individuals who created it.
claims.note: The author asserts a persistence property and independence condition for legal rules.

claims.claim: The being of a legal rule depends on the structural network that sustains it, not on the intentions of its creators.
claims.source_quote: Its being depends not on their intentions but on the structural network that sustains
claims.note: The author asserts the dependence relation for the existence of legal rules.

claims.claim: A command is a transient act that obliges only while power or fear persists.
claims.source_quote: A command, as Hobbes and Austin conceived it, is a transient act, a momentary expression of will that obliges only while power or fear persists.
claims.note: The author endorses this contrast as part of his ontological framework distinguishing rules from commands.

claims.claim: Tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.source_quote: At the most fundamental level, tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of tangible property within a domain of being.

claims.claim: Material continuants are independent continuants in BFO terms.
claims.source_quote: These are independent continuants in BFO terms: physical objects that exist regardless of recognition, though their status as property depends on it.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-relation between material continuants and BFO independent continuants.

claims.claim: Physical objects exist regardless of recognition.
claims.source_quote: These are independent continuants in BFO terms: physical objects that exist regardless of recognition, though their status as property depends on it.
claims.note: Asserts a property of physical objects (existence independent of recognition).

claims.claim: The status of physical objects as property depends on recognition.
claims.source_quote: physical objects that exist regardless of recognition, though their status as property depends on it.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property status and recognition.

claims.claim: Land, buildings, and artifacts are paradigmatic cases of tangible property.
claims.source_quote: Land, buildings, and artifacts are paradigmatic cases.
claims.note: Asserts that these entities are instances of tangible property.

claims.claim: The property relation links the owner, the object owned, and the institutional framework sustaining recognition.
claims.source_quote: The property relation here links the agent (owner), the object (thing owned), and the institutional framework that sustains recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the relational structure of the property relation with three relata.

claims.claim: Tangible property has distinctive stability due to the persistence of the object's material substrate.
claims.source_quote: The persistence of the object's material substrate gives tangible property a distinctive stability.
claims.note: Asserts a property (stability) of tangible property and its grounding cause.

claims.claim: Even if recognition lapses, the physical entity remains available for reappropriation.
claims.source_quote: even if recognition lapses, the physical entity remains available for reappropriation and is susceptible to occupation or physical control.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of physical entities independent of recognition.

claims.claim: Intangible property occupies the domain of informational and conceptual continuants.
claims.source_quote: Intangible property, by contrast, occupies the domain of informational and conceptual continuants, entities that exist not as physical things but as structured content or form.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of intangible property.

claims.claim: Informational and conceptual continuants exist as structured content or form, not as physical things.
claims.source_quote: entities that exist not as physical things but as structured content or form.
claims.note: Asserts a property distinguishing this kind of entity from physical objects.

claims.claim: Copyrights, patents, trademarks, and debts are information content entities embedded in institutional recognition structures.
claims.source_quote: Copyrights, patents, trademarks, and debts are not objects in the material sense but information content entities (ICEs) embedded in institutional recognition structures.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership and relational embedding for these entities.

claims.claim: Intangible property entities exist only through the systems that encode and sustain them.
claims.source_quote: They exist only through the systems that encode and sustain them: registries, ledgers, databases, and enforcement mechanisms.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency relation between intangible property and institutional systems.

claims.claim: A patent inheres in the institutional continuant of the patent office and the legal system.
claims.source_quote: it inheres in the institutional continuant of the patent office and the legal system that enforces it.
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between a patent and institutional continuants.

claims.claim: A patent's being depends on recognition distributed across institutions.
claims.source_quote: Its being depends on recognition distributed across these institutions, realized through procedural occurrents such as filing, examination, and granting.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of a patent on distributed institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Filing, examination, and granting are procedural occurrents that realize patent recognition.
claims.source_quote: realized through procedural occurrents such as filing, examination, and granting.
claims.note: Asserts that these processes are occurrents that serve a realization function.

claims.claim: When recognition of intangible property ceases, the intangible property ceases to exist as law.
claims.source_quote: When recognition ceases, through lapse, expiration, or legal invalidation, the intangible property ceases to exist as law, though its informational substrate may remain.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency such that cessation of recognition entails cessation of legal existence.

claims.claim: Digital property includes software licenses, cryptocurrency tokens, domain names, and virtual goods.
claims.source_quote: Digital property includes software licenses, cryptocurrency tokens, domain names, and virtual goods in online environments.
claims.note: Asserts membership of these entities in the kind 'digital property'.

claims.claim: Digital property entities are computational continuants sustained by technological and institutional dependencies.
claims.source_quote: they are computational continuants, structured states of digital systems sustained by both technological and institutional dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership and a sustaining dependency relation for digital property entities.

claims.claim: Digital property entities are generically dependent continuants realized through coordinated functioning of hardware, software, and institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, they are generically dependent continuants realized through the coordinated functioning of hardware, software, and institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts BFO classification and realization relation for digital property entities.

claims.claim: A digital token exists only as long as its blockchain remains operational and recognized as authoritative.
claims.source_quote: A digital token, for instance, exists only as long as the blockchain that encodes it remains operational and recognized as authoritative.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of a digital token on blockchain operationality and recognition.

claims.claim: Ownership of a digital token is defined by control over cryptographic credentials.
claims.source_quote: Its ownership is defined by control over cryptographic credentials, which serve as procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.note: Asserts that cryptographic credential control constitutes/defines digital token ownership.

claims.claim: Cryptographic credentials serve as procedural realizations of recognition within digital systems.
claims.source_quote: which serve as procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/realization role for cryptographic credentials.

claims.claim: In cryptocurrencies, recognition is distributed algorithmically across a network of validators.
claims.source_quote: In the case of cryptocurrencies, recognition is distributed algorithmically across a network of validators rather than concentrated in a centralized legal authority.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of cryptocurrency recognition.

claims.claim: Technical recognition achieves legal reality only when acknowledged by institutional systems.
claims.source_quote: Yet this technical recognition only achieves legal reality when it is acknowledged by institutional systems, when courts, regulators, or markets accept blockchain records as evidence of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between technical recognition and legal reality.

claims.claim: Law and technology together sustain the being of digital assets.
claims.source_quote: Law and technology together sustain the being of digital assets, each contributing distinct but interlocking layers of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a joint sustaining relation between law, technology, and digital assets' existence.

claims.claim: The durability of digital property depends on the continued coherence of both the legal and technological systems.
claims.source_quote: The durability of such property depends on the continued coherence of both systems; a disruption in either loss of network consensus or legal disavowal, can dissolve ownership entirely.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency of digital property durability on dual-system coherence.

claims.claim: A software program is both a work of authorship and a functional system realized through execution on computational hardware.
claims.source_quote: A software program is both a work of authorship (intangible property protected by copyright) and a functional system (digital property realized through execution on computational hardware).
claims.note: Asserts dual ontological status and realization relation for software.

claims.claim: The same software entity exists simultaneously across different ontological layers, each sustained by its own recognition structure.
claims.source_quote: The same entity exists simultaneously across different ontological layers, each sustained by its own recognition structure.
claims.note: Asserts multi-layer simultaneous existence as a property of software entities.

claims.claim: Ownership of software involves a complex network of recognitions including author's rights, licensee's rights, and institutional rules.
claims.source_quote: Ownership of software therefore involves a complex network of recognitions: the author's moral and economic rights, the licensee's usage rights, and the institutional rules defining the permissible scope of execution.
claims.note: Asserts the composite recognition structure constituting software ownership.

claims.claim: Property in software is a model of ontological interdependence.
claims.source_quote: Property in software is thus a model of ontological interdependence.
claims.note: Asserts a characterizing property of software property relations.

claims.claim: Data are information artifacts that are structured representations of entities, events, or relations.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, data are information artifacts, structured representations of entities, events, or relations.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership and a defining property for data.

claims.claim: The property relation over data attaches not to the data themselves but to their organization, access, and control within institutional systems.
claims.source_quote: The property relation here attaches not to the data themselves but to their organization, access, and control within institutional systems.
claims.note: Asserts the specific relatum of the property relation in data contexts.

claims.claim: Databases, cloud infrastructures, and privacy frameworks are the continuants that sustain recognition of data property.
claims.source_quote: Databases, cloud infrastructures, and privacy frameworks serve as the continuants that sustain recognition.
claims.note: Asserts these entities are continuants with a sustaining function for data property.

claims.claim: Data are generically dependent continuants that can exist in multiple copies simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Because data are generically dependent continuants that can exist in multiple copies simultaneously, property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership and a distinctive property of data.

claims.claim: Property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.source_quote: property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.note: Asserts a defining property of the data property relation.

claims.claim: Data ownership consists in a right to control relational configurations rather than physical possession.
claims.source_quote: The legal innovation of data ownership thus consists in redefining property as a right to control relational configurations rather than physical possession.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of data ownership rights.

claims.claim: A virtual sword or digital land parcel exists only as an aggregation of code instantiated within a software platform.
claims.source_quote: A virtual sword or parcel of digital land exists only as an aggregation of code instantiated within a software platform.
claims.note: Asserts the constitutive basis and existential dependency of virtual property entities.

claims.claim: Virtual property can be owned, transferred, and valued within its platform.
claims.source_quote: Yet within that platform, it functions as property: it can be owned, transferred, and valued.
claims.note: Asserts functional properties of virtual property entities.

claims.claim: Virtual property is sustained by both internal recognition (game code and user community) and external recognition (contracts, markets, courts).
claims.source_quote: The recognition that sustains it is both internal (within the game's code and user community) and external (through contracts, markets, and sometimes courts).
claims.note: Asserts dual sustaining recognition structures for virtual property.

claims.claim: Virtual property exemplifies nested recognition: an entity recognized within one ontological layer whose reality is further sustained by another.
claims.source_quote: Virtual property therefore exemplifies nested recognition: an entity recognized within one ontological layer (the virtual environment) whose reality is further sustained by another (the legal system).
claims.note: Asserts a structural property (nested recognition) characterizing virtual property.

claims.claim: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is their relational form, not their substance.
claims.source_quote: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is not their substance but their relational form.
claims.note: Asserts that relational form, not substance, is the unifying property across property kinds.

claims.claim: Ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object, and a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: In each case, ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object (physical, informational, or virtual), and a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure of ownership as a three-place dependency relation.

claims.claim: The persistence and transfer of property depend on the stability of the recognition system.
claims.source_quote: The persistence and transfer of property depend on the stability of the
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property persistence/transfer and recognition system stability.

claims.claim: A command is a transient act.
