claims.source_quote: A command, as Hobbes and Austin conceived it, is a transient act, a momentary expression of will that obliges only while power or fear persists.
claims.note: The author characterizes what a command is ontologically (a transient act), though the framing references Hobbes and Austin; the author appears to endorse this characterization as accurate.

claims.claim: A command is a momentary expression of will.
claims.source_quote: A command, as Hobbes and Austin conceived it, is a transient act, a momentary expression of will that obliges only while power or fear persists.
claims.note: Asserts a property/nature of commands as entities; author endorses this as a correct account.

claims.claim: A rule is an enduring relation that transcends its author.
claims.source_quote: A rule, in Hart's sense, is an enduring relation that transcends its author.
claims.note: Asserts what kind of entity a rule is (an enduring relation) and a key property (transcending its author); author endorses Hart's account.

claims.claim: A rule continues to exist independently of the individuals who created it.
claims.source_quote: Once recognized, it continues to exist independently of the individuals who created it.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the independence of a rule's existence from its creators.

claims.claim: A rule's existence depends on the structural network that sustains its validity.
claims.source_quote: Its being depends not on their intentions but on the structural network that sustains its validity.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: a rule's being is grounded in a structural network, not in intentions.

claims.claim: A rule is a specifically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: In the language of Basic Formal Ontology, a rule is a specifically dependent continuant.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of rules as a subkind of specifically dependent continuant.

claims.claim: A rule exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.source_quote: it exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological ground of a rule's existence: collective maintenance of instantiating relations by a community.

claims.claim: Laws can survive the death of their creators.
claims.source_quote: This explains why laws can survive the death of their creators.
claims.note: Asserts a property of laws as entities: persistence beyond their creators' deaths.

claims.claim: A legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.source_quote: why a legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of legal systems as entities.

claims.claim: Tangible, intangible, and digital property are unified by their relational form, not their substance.
claims.source_quote: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is not their substance but their relational form.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the nature of the unifying feature of property types—an ontological claim about what property kinds share.

claims.claim: Ownership exists as a dependency relation linking an agent, an object, and a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: In each case, ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object (physical, informational, or virtual), and a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure of ownership as a dependency relation with specific relata.

claims.claim: The persistence and transfer of property depend on the stability of agent-object-recognition dependencies.
claims.source_quote: The persistence and transfer of property depend on the stability of these dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property's persistence/transfer and relational stability—an ontological claim.

claims.claim: The transition to software and data as property objects does not alter property's ontological nature.
claims.source_quote: The transition from land and goods to software and data does not alter property's ontological nature; it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Directly asserts a claim about the invariance of property's ontological nature across domain transitions.

claims.claim: The transition to digital property multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations attach.
claims.source_quote: it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological claim about continuants and their relation to property relations.

claims.claim: Ownership has a stratified ontology spanning multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.source_quote: The result is a stratified ontology of ownership, in which legal recognition spans multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.note: Asserts that ownership's ontology is stratified and encompasses both material and immaterial layers—a direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: A role inheres in an agent.
claims.source_quote: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.note: Direct assertion of an ontological relation (inheres_in) between role and agent.

claims.claim: An agent participates in an institution.
claims.source_quote: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.note: Direct assertion of a participation relation between agent and institution.

claims.claim: An obligation inheres in a role.
claims.source_quote: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.note: Direct assertion of an inheres_in relation between obligation and role.

claims.claim: An obligation depends on an institution for its continuing validity.
claims.source_quote: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.note: Direct assertion of a dependency relation between obligation and institution.

claims.claim: An agent's legal identity is constituted through roles they occupy and institutions that recognize them.
claims.source_quote: The agent's legal identity is therefore not primitive but mediated, it is constituted through the roles they occupy and the institutions that recognize them.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive ontological relation between legal identity, roles, and institutions.

claims.claim: An agent's legal identity is not a primitive entity.
claims.source_quote: The agent's legal identity is therefore not primitive but mediated.
claims.note: Asserts a property (non-primitiveness) of legal identity as an entity.

claims.claim: Roles and institutions are ontological intermediaries that allow obligations to be generalized and standardized.
claims.source_quote: Roles and institutions serve as ontological intermediaries, allowing obligations to be generalized and standardized.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of roles and institutions in legal ontology.

claims.claim: A corporation is an institutional continuant that aggregates multiple roles.
claims.source_quote: A corporation, for example, functions as an institutional continuant that aggregates multiple roles, executive, shareholder, employee, each carrying distinct obligations and powers.
claims.note: Asserts the kind (institutional continuant) and a property (aggregates roles) of a corporation.

claims.claim: The obligations of a corporation are borne by institutional roles and realized through the actions of their occupants.
claims.source_quote: The obligations of the corporation itself, such as to pay taxes or comply with regulation, are borne by institutional roles and realized through the actions of their occupants.
claims.note: Asserts realization and bearer relations among corporate obligations, roles, and agents.

claims.claim: Norms define what roles entail, and roles realize norms by embodying them in practice.
claims.source_quote: Norms define what roles entail; roles realize norms by embodying them in practice.
claims.note: Asserts a reciprocal ontological relation (definition and realization) between norms and roles.

claims.claim: The relation between role and norm is one of mutual dependence.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this relation is one of mutual dependence: the norm provides the capacity, the role provides the bearer. Neither can exist in isolation.
claims.note: Directly asserts mutual existential dependence as an ontological relation between norm and role.

claims.claim: A norm provides capacity, while a role provides the bearer.
claims.source_quote: the norm provides the capacity, the role provides the bearer.
claims.note: Asserts distinct functional properties of norms and roles within their mutual dependence relation.

claims.claim: Institutions persist through time because their roles can be filled successively by different agents without altering the structure.
claims.source_quote: Institutions persist through time because their roles can be filled successively by different agents without altering the structure.
claims.note: Asserts a property (persistence) of institutions and its basis in role-occupancy succession.

claims.claim: An office (role) remains continuous across different occupants because the role is defined by stable relations.
claims.source_quote: The office of 'president,' for instance, remains continuous across administrations because the role itself is defined by stable relations, constitutional rules, expectations, and powers.
claims.note: Asserts the continuity property of a role entity and its ontological basis.

claims.claim: Obligations associated with an office transfer automatically to the next occupant.
claims.source_quote: Obligations associated with that office transfer automatically to the next occupant, preserving the coherence of the system.
claims.note: Asserts a transfer relation between obligations and successive role occupants.

claims.claim: A corporation is an institutional entity, not a natural person.
claims.source_quote: A corporation, for example, is not a natural person but an institutional entity that can bear roles and obligations.
claims.note: Asserts the kind of entity a corporation is.

claims.claim: A corporation can bear roles and obligations.
claims.source_quote: an institutional entity that can bear roles and obligations.
claims.note: Asserts a disposition/capacity of a corporation as an institutional entity.

claims.claim: Corporate personhood is an ontological extension of the principle that obligations attach to roles.
claims.source_quote: corporate personhood is not a fiction but an ontological extension of the principle that obligations attach to roles.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status of corporate personhood and its grounding.

claims.claim: Authority is a relational structure connecting roles within an institution.
claims.source_quote: Authority is not a metaphysical property possessed by individuals but a relational structure connecting roles within an institution.
claims.note: Asserts the kind and nature of authority as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: Authority is not a metaphysical property possessed by individuals.
claims.source_quote: Authority is not a metaphysical property possessed by individuals but a relational structure connecting roles within an institution.
claims.note: Asserts a negative ontological property claim about authority.

claims.claim: Authority is an emergent feature of the web of dependencies among roles, agents, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Authority, like obligation, is thus an emergent feature of the web of dependencies among roles, agents, and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts emergence as a property of authority and its relational basis.

claims.claim: Every act of law is the realization of a role's capacity to instantiate a norm within an institutional framework.
claims.source_quote: Every act of law, from a judgment to a signature, is the realization of a role's capacity to instantiate a norm within an institutional framework.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation constituting every legal act.

claims.claim: Legal processes such as legislation, adjudication, agreement, performance, and repeal are ontological transitions.
claims.source_quote: These processes - legislation, adjudication, agreement, performance, and repeal - are not merely procedural moments but ontological transitions.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of legal processes.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, and statuses are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: They mark the genesis, transformation, and dissolution of dependent continuants such as obligations, rights, and statuses.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category (dependent continuant) of obligations, rights, and statuses.

claims.claim: Law's being is fundamentally dynamic; it exists through time by virtue of the processes that realize and modify its structures.
claims.source_quote: Law's being, therefore, is fundamentally dynamic: it exists through time by virtue of the processes that realize and modify its structures.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental ontological property (dynamism) of law's being.

claims.claim: A promise, contract, or statute transforms a transient event (occurrent) into a continuing relational structure (a dependent continuant).
claims.source_quote: A promise, contract, or statute transforms a transient event (an occurrent in BFO terms) into a continuing relational structure (a dependent continuant).
claims.note: Asserts an ontological transformation relation from occurrent to dependent continuant effected by legal acts.

claims.claim: An obligation persists beyond the act that produced it.
claims.source_quote: This entity persists beyond the act that produced it. The signature fades, the utterance ceases, but the relation remains.
claims.note: Asserts persistence as a property of obligations as entities.

claims.claim: An obligation endures until it is fulfilled, extinguished, or invalidated by another recognized process.
claims.source_quote: An obligation does not vanish because it is ignored or denied; it endures until it is fulfilled, extinguished, or invalidated by another recognized process.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions for the persistence and extinction of obligation as an entity.

claims.claim: Legal continuity is a function of ongoing recognition, not material permanence.
claims.source_quote: Legal continuity, therefore, is not a function of material permanence but of ongoing recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition, not materiality, is the ontological basis of legal continuity.

claims.claim: Every legal creation is the bringing-into-being of new relational continuants through the medium of recognition.
claims.source_quote: every legal creation is a kind of social ontogenesis, the bringing-into-being of new relational continuants through the medium of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that legal creation produces new relational continuant entities via recognition.

claims.claim: A legal obligation endures until it is fulfilled, extinguished, or invalidated by another recognized process.
claims.source_quote: it endures until it is fulfilled, extinguished, or invalidated by another recognized process.
claims.note: Asserts a property/disposition of legal obligations: their persistence conditions.

claims.claim: Legal continuity is a function of ongoing recognition, not material permanence.
claims.source_quote: Legal continuity, therefore, is not a function of material permanence but of ongoing recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/constitutive claim about what grounds legal continuity.

claims.claim: A debt recorded in a creditor's records is part of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: The debt that endures in the creditor's records, the statute still in force in a codex, the contract clause unperformed, all remain parts of legal reality because they continue to be acknowledged within the institutional system.
claims.note: Asserts that debts (when acknowledged) are parts of legal reality—a part-of relation.

claims.claim: A statute still in force in a codex is part of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: the statute still in force in a codex, the contract clause unperformed, all remain parts of legal reality because they continue to be acknowledged within the institutional system.
claims.note: Asserts that statutes in force are parts of legal reality.

claims.claim: An unperformed contract clause is part of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: the contract clause unperformed, all remain parts of legal reality because they continue to be acknowledged within the institutional system that sustains them.
claims.note: Asserts that unperformed contract clauses are parts of legal reality.

claims.claim: Legal entities persist as parts of legal reality because they are acknowledged within an institutional system.
claims.source_quote: all remain parts of legal reality because they continue to be acknowledged within the institutional system that sustains them.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding relation: institutional acknowledgment is what sustains legal entities in legal reality.

claims.claim: There exists an institutional system that sustains legal entities.
claims.source_quote: the institutional system that sustains them.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of an institutional system with the function of sustaining legal entities.

claims.claim: The persistence of legal entities can be modeled as a temporal relation among entities.
claims.source_quote: This persistence can be modeled formally as a temporal relation among entities.
claims.note: Asserts that legal persistence is (formally representable as) a temporal relation—ontological claim about the structure of legal persistence, though 'can be modeled' introduces slight hedging.

claims.claim: The transition from land to software does not alter property's ontological nature.
claims.source_quote: The transition from land and goods to software and data does not alter property's ontological nature; it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological nature of property across different substrates.

claims.claim: The transition from land to software multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.source_quote: it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/extensional property of property relations in ontological terms.

claims.claim: Ownership exists as a stratified ontology spanning multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.source_quote: The result is a stratified ontology of ownership, in which legal recognition spans multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.note: Asserts that ownership has a stratified ontological structure.

claims.claim: Law is an ontological system with adaptive capacity.
claims.source_quote: The proliferation of digital and informational property also reveals law's adaptability as an ontological system.
claims.note: Asserts that law is a kind of ontological system with a dispositional property (adaptability).

claims.claim: New technologies continually generate new entities such as cryptographic assets, AI models, and virtual personas.
claims.source_quote: New technologies continually generate new entities, including cryptographic assets, artificial intelligence models, and virtual personas, that challenge traditional categories.
claims.note: Asserts existence of new kinds of entities generated by technology.

claims.claim: Cryptographic assets, AI models, and virtual personas are entities.
claims.source_quote: New technologies continually generate new entities, including cryptographic assets, artificial intelligence models, and virtual personas
claims.note: Asserts that these digital items are genuine entities (existential claim).

claims.claim: Law responds to new entities by extending recognition through analogy and formal innovation.
claims.source_quote: Yet law responds not by abandoning its framework but rather by extending recognition to these entities through analogy and formal innovation.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/functional property of law regarding novel entities.

claims.claim: Law expands the range of what can exist as property by encompassing novel continuants.
claims.source_quote: law reconfigures its network of recognition to encompass novel continuants, thereby expanding the range of what can exist as property.
claims.note: Asserts that law performs an ontological function of expanding the domain of property.

claims.claim: The extension of property to new entities is an expansion of recognition fields, not creation of new categories.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this is not the creation of new categories but the expansion of recognition fields, a process through which law continuously refines its map of social and material reality.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of a process.

claims.claim: Property is a manifestation of relational dependence at every layer.
claims.source_quote: At every layer, property remains a manifestation of relational dependence.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental ontological property of property.

claims.claim: Ownership exists only through the coordinated interplay of agents, institutions, and media of recognition.
claims.source_quote: ownership exists only through the coordinated interplay of agents, institutions, and media of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary relational condition for ownership's existence.

claims.claim: The ontology of property mirrors the ontology of law itself.
claims.source_quote: The ontology of property thus mirrors the ontology of law itself: a hierarchy of dependent continuants sustained by networks of recognition that evolve with the structures of social life.
claims.note: Asserts a structural similarity between two ontological domains.

claims.claim: Law and property consist in a hierarchy of dependent continuants sustained by networks of recognition.
claims.source_quote: a hierarchy of dependent continuants sustained by networks of recognition that evolve with the structures of social life.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure of law/property using BFO categories.

claims.claim: Law's fundamental vocation is to stabilize relations across an ever-expanding field of being.
claims.source_quote: law reveals its fundamental vocation: to stabilize relations across an ever-expanding field of being, translating new forms of existence into enduring forms of order.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/dispositional property of law.

claims.claim: Property persists only through the stable functioning of institutional mechanisms that maintain recognition over time.
claims.source_quote: Property persists only through the stable functioning of institutional mechanisms that maintain and reaffirm recognition over time.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for property's persistence.

claims.claim: Ownership exists solely within a web of continuous institutional affirmation.
claims.source_quote: ownership exists solely within a web of continuous institutional affirmation.
claims.note: Direct existential claim about the conditions of ownership's existence.

claims.claim: Institutions serve as ontological stabilizers of property.
claims.source_quote: Institutions, in this sense, serve as ontological stabilizers of property: they ensure that the dependencies linking agents, objects, and rights remain coherent, traceable, and enforceable within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of institutions in the ontology of property.

claims.claim: Property relations are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Property relations, as dependent continuants, require persistent bearers in both agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind/classification claim using BFO ontology.

claims.claim: Property relations require persistent bearers in both agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Property relations, as dependent continuants, require persistent bearers in both agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary relational/structural property of property relations.

claims.claim: The registry, contract, and court are institutional continuants.
claims.source_quote: The registry, the contract, and the court each function as institutional continuants, entities whose role is to instantiate and help maintain the relations that define ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a classification of legal institutions as a kind of entity (institutional continuant).

claims.claim: The registry, contract, and court have the role of instantiating and maintaining ownership relations.
claims.source_quote: entities whose role is to instantiate and help maintain the relations that define ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/role property of these institutional continuants.

claims.claim: Recording, verifying, adjudicating, and enforcing are occurrents that realize and reaffirm the dependent continuants of ownership.
claims.source_quote: They do so through a series of occurrents, procedural acts such as recording, verifying, adjudicating, and enforcing, which continually realize and reaffirm the dependent continuants of ownership and entitlement.
claims.note: Asserts that procedural acts are occurrents that bear a realization relation to ownership continuants.

claims.claim: Without recurring realizations by institutions, property would collapse back into mere possession.
claims.source_quote: Without these recurring realizations, property would collapse back into mere possession and fragile memories, its ontological stability lost with the withdrawal of formal recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for property's ontological stability.

claims.claim: A land registry, corporate register, or patent database is an institutional continuant.
claims.source_quote: A land registry, corporate register, or patent database is not merely a repository of information but an institutional continuant helping to hold together the network of recognition itself.
claims.note: Asserts classification of specific institutions as institutional continuants.

claims.claim: Each registry entry represents a recorded dependent continuant sustained by institutional memory.
claims.source_quote: Each entry in such a registry represents a recorded dependent continuant, a legal fact sustained by institutional memory and procedural validation.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status of registry entries as dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The act of registration transforms transient recognition into a persistent institutional fact.
claims.source_quote: The act of registration transforms transient recognition (the acknowledgment of a transaction or ownership claim) into a persistent institutional fact.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative ontological function of registration.

claims.claim: Once entered into a registry, ownership becomes part of the legal system's enduring ontology.
claims.source_quote: Once entered into the registry, ownership becomes part of the legal system's enduring ontology, capable of surviving changes in agents, institutions, or physical conditions.
claims.note: Asserts a change in ontological status that results from registration.

claims.claim: Titles, deeds, and certificates are information artifacts embedded in institutional structures.
claims.source_quote: This persistence is achieved through the embedding of information artifacts, titles, deeds, certificates, within an institutional structure that ensures their ongoing validity.
claims.note: Asserts classification of legal documents as information artifacts and their relation to institutional structures.

claims.claim: The registry transforms recognition from an occurrent into an enduring relation between institutional continuants and information artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Recognition, initially a social or procedural occurrent, becomes encoded as an enduring relation between institutional continuants and information artifacts.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological transformation performed by the registry.

claims.claim: The registry is the metaphysical anchor of modern property systems.
claims.source_quote: The registry is thus the metaphysical anchor of modern property systems, law's apparatus for making recognition permanent.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental ontological role/function of the registry.

claims.claim: Ownership survives through the persistence of its representation in institutional memory.
claims.source_quote: ownership survives through the persistence of its representation in institutional memory.
claims.note: Asserts a condition for the persistence of ownership as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: A contract is an information artifact that records the creation of dependent continuants including rights, obligations, and transfers.
claims.source_quote: A contract is an information artifact that records the creation of dependent continuants, including rights, obligations, and transfers, whose validity depends on institutional acceptance.
claims.note: Asserts a classification of contracts and a functional/relational property.

claims.claim: Rights, obligations, and transfers are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: A contract is an information artifact that records the creation of dependent continuants, including rights, obligations, and transfers
claims.note: Asserts subkind classification of rights, obligations, and transfers as dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The signing of a contract is an occurrent that realizes both the agents' roles and the institution's role.
claims.source_quote: The signing of a contract is an occurrent that realizes both the agents' roles (as parties) and the institution's role (as guarantor of recognition).
claims.note: Asserts ontological classification of contract-signing and its realization relations.

claims.claim: Enforcement processes are repair occurrents that restore coherence to the structure of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Enforcement processes (litigation, execution, repossession) are repair occurrents: temporal events that restore coherence by reaffirming the underlying structure of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts classification of enforcement processes as a type of occurrent with a restorative function.

claims.claim: Theft, fraud, and systemic corruption are ontological disruptions in the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Failures in institutional maintenance, such as theft, fraud, or systemic corruption, represent ontological disruptions in the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a classification of certain events as ontological disruptions.

claims.claim: Theft displaces the realization of recognition without transferring the dependent continuant of ownership.
claims.source_quote: it temporarily displaces the realization of recognition. The thief possesses the object but not the dependent continuant of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological asymmetry between possession and ownership as dependent continuant.

claims.claim: A stolen object remains ontologically owned as long as the institutional relations defining ownership persist.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the object remains 'owned' as long as the institutional relations that define ownership persist.
claims.note: Asserts that ownership as a dependent continuant persists independently of physical possession.

claims.claim: Ownership ceases to exist only if recognition collapses through destruction of the registry or disintegration of the legal order.
claims.source_quote: Only if recognition collapses, if the registry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim, does ownership cease to exist.
claims.note: Asserts necessary conditions for the cessation of ownership as an entity.

claims.claim: An object remains owned as long as the institutional relations defining ownership persist.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the object remains 'owned' as long as the institutional relations that define ownership persist.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the conditions for ownership's existence.

claims.claim: Ownership ceases to exist when recognition collapses or the legal order disintegrates.
claims.source_quote: Only if recognition collapses, if the registry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim, does ownership cease to exist.
claims.note: Asserts conditions under which ownership (a kind of entity or relation) ceases to exist.

claims.claim: Property has both a physical aspect and a legal aspect.
claims.source_quote: Theft thus illustrates the duality of property's being: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts that property has two ontologically distinct aspects (physical and legal).

claims.claim: The legal aspect of property remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.source_quote: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts a property/disposition of the legal aspect of property.

claims.claim: Fraud involves the fabrication of recognition through false appearances.
claims.source_quote: Fraud introduces a subtler form of disruption: the fabrication of recognition through false appearances.
claims.note: Asserts what fraud is as an ontological kind—a fabrication of recognition.

claims.claim: A rule is a specifically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: In the language of Basic Formal Ontology, a rule is a specifically dependent continuant, it exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of rules as a kind of entity (specifically dependent continuant).

claims.claim: A rule exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.source_quote: a rule is a specifically dependent continuant, it exists because a community of agents collectively maintains the relations that instantiate it.
claims.note: Asserts the dependency relation that grounds the existence of rules.

claims.claim: Laws can survive the death of their creators.
claims.source_quote: This explains why laws can survive the death of their creators, and why a legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.note: Asserts a property of laws (persistence beyond creators' deaths).

claims.claim: A legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.source_quote: why a legal system can persist across centuries of social change.
claims.note: Asserts a property (persistence) of legal systems as entities.

claims.claim: Primary rules depend on the recognition of agents within specific contexts of application.
claims.source_quote: Primary rules depend on the recognition of agents within specific contexts of application, citizens, officials, litigants.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between primary rules and agent recognition.

claims.claim: Secondary rules depend on the recognition of institutions as authoritative arbiters of validity.
claims.source_quote: secondary rules depend on the recognition of institutions as authoritative arbiters of validity.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between secondary rules and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a meta-relation that coordinates all other relations within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition stands at the apex of this hierarchy: it is the meta-relation that coordinates all other relations within the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of the rule of recognition as a kind of entity (meta-relation).

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the structural backbone of legality.
claims.source_quote: the rule of recognition is the structural backbone of legality, the mechanism by which coherence is maintained within the field of relational continuants that constitute law.
claims.note: Asserts a structural role/property of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Coherence within the legal system is maintained by the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: the mechanism by which coherence is maintained within the field of relational continuants that constitute law.
claims.note: Asserts a functional relation between the rule of recognition and systemic coherence.

claims.claim: Law is constituted by relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: the field of relational continuants that constitute law.
claims.note: Asserts that law's constituents are relational continuants—an ontological composition claim.

claims.claim: Dworkin's principles are structural constraints within the network of relational continuants that make up law.
claims.source_quote: Dworkin's 'principles' can be understood as structural constraints within the network of relational continuants that make up law.
claims.note: Author endorses this ontological reinterpretation of Dworkin's principles.

claims.claim: Principles are internal conditions of coherence that govern how relations among rules, obligations, and institutions hold together.
claims.source_quote: They are not external moral appeals imposed from outside the legal system, but internal conditions of coherence that govern how relations among rules, obligations, and institutions hold together.
claims.note: Asserts a property and role of principles as entities within the legal system.

claims.claim: A principle such as equality before the law is a structural requirement ensuring consistency of the relational web of legality.
claims.source_quote: A principle such as equality before the law is not merely an ethical ideal; it is a structural requirement that ensures the consistency of the relational web that constitutes legality.
claims.note: Asserts that a specific principle has the property of being a structural requirement.

claims.claim: Violation of a structural constraint causes the network's coherence to falter.
claims.source_quote: When this constraint is violated, the network's coherence falters, producing contradiction and systemic strain.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/relational property of structural constraints within the legal network.

claims.claim: Principles are the ontological counterparts of design tolerances in engineering systems.
claims.source_quote: Principles, in this sense, are the ontological counterparts of what engineers call design tolerances, the boundaries within which a system can maintain integrity.
claims.note: Author endorses this analogy as an ontological characterization of principles; medium because it is partly analogical.

claims.claim: The principle of fairness ensures reciprocal recognition between citizen and state.
claims.source_quote: The principle of fairness, for instance, ensures reciprocal recognition between citizen and state.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of the principle of fairness.

claims.claim: The principle of equality ensures the substitutability of persons within the system's logic of rights and duties.
claims.source_quote: the principle of equality ensures the substitutability of persons within the system's logic of rights and duties.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the principle of equality.

claims.claim: Both rules and principles are relational continuants within the same network of dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Ontology unites them by showing that both rules and principles are relational continuants within the same network of dependencies.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of rules and principles as relational continuants.

claims.claim: Rules define connections within the legal network; principles regulate the integrity of those connections.
claims.source_quote: Rules define the connections; principles regulate the integrity of those connections.
claims.note: Asserts distinct roles/functions of rules and principles as entities.

claims.claim: Rules give law its durable form; principles allow it to evolve while remaining coherent.
claims.source_quote: Rules give law its durable form; principles allow it to evolve while remaining coherent.
claims.note: Asserts functional properties of rules and principles respectively.

claims.claim: Illegitimacy is a form of ontological contradiction—a misalignment among continuants.
claims.source_quote: Illegitimacy, by contrast, is a form of ontological contradiction: a misalignment among continuants that undermines the system's capacity for self-sustaining order.
claims.note: Asserts what illegitimacy is, classifying it ontologically.

claims.claim: A legal system is legitimate when its network of rules and principles forms a coherent whole.
claims.source_quote: A legal system is legitimate when its network of rules and principles forms a coherent whole, when obligations align with recognitions and institutions operate within their structural constraints.
claims.note: Asserts a condition (property) that constitutes legitimacy for a legal system.

claims.claim: Norms are entities—real components of the world that occupy specific ontological categories.
claims.source_quote: the recognition that norms themselves are entities, real components of the world that occupy specific ontological categories.
claims.note: Direct assertion that norms exist as entities of a particular kind.

claims.claim: A norm is a realizable dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: A norm is neither a fact nor a statement about facts; it is a realizable dependent continuant, a relational structure that exists in virtue of being recognized and capable of being realized through action.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of norms as a subkind of entity (realizable dependent continuant).

claims.claim: A norm is a relational structure that exists in virtue of being recognized.
claims.source_quote: it is a realizable dependent continuant, a relational structure that exists in virtue of being recognized and capable of being realized through action.
claims.note: Asserts the mode of existence and dependence relation of norms.

claims.claim: Norms are potentials embedded within social reality.
claims.source_quote: In other words, norms are potentials embedded within social reality.
claims.note: Asserts a property/mode of being of norms—they are potentials located in social reality.

claims.claim: Norms exist not as abstract ideals but as enduring possibilities whose realization shapes law and social order.
claims.source_quote: They exist not as abstract ideals but as enduring possibilities whose realization continuously shapes the fabric of law and social order.
claims.note: Asserts the mode of existence and causal role of norms.

claims.claim: Primary and secondary rules constitute the structural skeleton of law.
claims.source_quote: Primary and secondary rules constitute the structural skeleton; principles form the tensile fabric that holds it together.
claims.note: Asserts a compositional/structural role of primary and secondary rules within the legal system.

claims.claim: Principles form the tensile fabric that holds the legal structure together.
claims.source_quote: principles form the tensile fabric that holds it together.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/functional role of principles as entities within law.

claims.claim: Law's validity and meaning arise from the stability of the relations that connect rules and principles.
claims.source_quote: law's validity and meaning arise not from will or morality alone but from the stability of the relations that connect them, a structure at once normative, institutional, and ontological.
claims.note: Asserts a relational ground for law's validity and meaning—an ontological claim about dependence.

claims.claim: A realizable dependent continuant inheres in a bearer and is fulfilled under certain conditions.
claims.source_quote: A realizable dependent continuant, in the framework of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), is an entity that inheres in a bearer and is fulfilled or manifested under certain conditions.
claims.note: Author endorses this BFO definition as the ontological category to which norms belong; counts as asserting properties of this kind.

claims.claim: Persistence of legal entities is a function of ongoing recognition, not material permanence.
claims.source_quote: not a function of material permanence but of ongoing recognition.
claims.note: Author plainly asserts a property of legal persistence: it depends on recognition, not material permanence.

claims.claim: A debt enduring in creditor's records remains part of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: The debt that endures in the creditor's records... remain parts of legal reality because they continue to be acknowledged within the institutional system that sustains them.
claims.note: Author asserts that debts are parts of legal reality, an ontological claim about membership in a domain.

claims.claim: A statute still in force remains part of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: the statute still in force in a codex... remain parts of legal reality because they continue to be acknowledged within the institutional system that sustains them.
claims.note: Author asserts statutes in force are parts of legal reality.

claims.claim: An unperformed contract clause remains part of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: the contract clause unperformed... remain parts of legal reality because they continue to be acknowledged within the institutional system that sustains them.
claims.note: Author asserts unperformed contract clauses are parts of legal reality.

claims.claim: Legal entities persist because they are acknowledged within an institutional system.
claims.source_quote: they continue to be acknowledged within the institutional system that sustains them.
claims.note: Author asserts a grounding relation: acknowledgment within an institutional system is what sustains legal entities.

claims.claim: Creation (C) is an occurrent through which a dependent continuant comes into existence.
claims.source_quote: Creation (C): an occurrent through which a dependent continuant (e.g., obligation) comes into existence.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind of the creation event (occurrent) and its relation to dependent continuants.

claims.claim: An obligation is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: a dependent continuant (e.g., obligation) comes into existence.
claims.note: Author classifies obligation as a subkind (dependent continuant), an atomic ontological claim about kind membership.

claims.claim: Maintenance (M) is the phase during which a dependent continuant exists.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance (M): the phase during which the continuant exists, sustained by recognition and institutional context.
claims.note: Author asserts that maintenance is a phase (a kind of temporal entity) in which the continuant exists.

claims.claim: A dependent continuant's existence during maintenance is sustained by recognition and institutional context.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance (M): the phase during which the continuant exists, sustained by recognition and institutional context.
claims.note: Author asserts a sustaining relation between recognition/institutional context and the continuant's existence.

claims.claim: Extinction (E) is the process that terminates a dependent continuant's existence.
claims.source_quote: Extinction (E): the process that terminates the continuant's existence, either through fulfillment, repeal, or invalidation.
claims.note: Author asserts extinction is a process (kind of occurrent) and that it bears a termination relation to the continuant.

claims.claim: Fulfillment, repeal, and invalidation are modes through which extinction occurs.
claims.source_quote: either through fulfillment, repeal, or invalidation.
claims.note: Author asserts these are the ways extinction is brought about, an ontological claim about the relation between these processes and extinction.

claims.claim: The transition from land/goods to software/data does not alter property's ontological nature.
claims.source_quote: The transition from land and goods to software and data does not alter property's ontological nature; it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological nature of property across different substrates.

claims.claim: The transition from land to software multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations attach.
claims.source_quote: it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Asserts a property/relation of property relations with respect to continuants.

claims.claim: There is a stratified ontology of ownership spanning multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.source_quote: The result is a stratified ontology of ownership, in which legal recognition spans multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of a stratified ontological structure of ownership.

claims.claim: Law is an ontological system with adaptive capacity.
claims.source_quote: The proliferation of digital and informational property also reveals law's adaptability as an ontological system.
claims.note: Asserts that law has the property of being an ontological system.

claims.claim: Cryptographic assets, AI models, and virtual personas are new entities that challenge traditional legal categories.
claims.source_quote: New technologies continually generate new entities, including cryptographic assets, artificial intelligence models, and virtual personas, that challenge traditional categories.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of these novel entities and their challenging relation to traditional categories.

claims.claim: Law extends recognition to novel entities through analogy and formal innovation.
claims.source_quote: law responds not by abandoning its framework but rather by extending recognition to these entities through analogy and formal innovation.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of law: extending recognition to new continuants.

claims.claim: Law's response to novel entities is an expansion of recognition fields, not creation of new categories.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this is not the creation of new categories but the expansion of recognition fields, a process through which law continuously refines its map of social and material reality.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of law's adaptive process.

claims.claim: Property is a manifestation of relational dependence.
claims.source_quote: At every layer, property remains a manifestation of relational dependence.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental property/nature of property.

claims.claim: Ownership exists only through the coordinated interplay of agents, institutions, and media of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Whether it concerns land or software, data or virtual goods, ownership exists only through the coordinated interplay of agents, institutions, and media of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological conditions of existence for ownership.

claims.claim: The ontology of property mirrors the ontology of law: a hierarchy of dependent continuants sustained by networks of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The ontology of property thus mirrors the ontology of law itself: a hierarchy of dependent continuants sustained by networks of recognition that evolve with the structures of social life.
claims.note: Asserts a structural identity/similarity between property's ontology and law's ontology.

claims.claim: Law's fundamental vocation is to stabilize relations across an ever-expanding field of being.
claims.source_quote: law reveals its fundamental vocation: to stabilize relations across an ever-expanding field of being, translating new forms of existence into enduring forms of order.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/disposition of law.

claims.claim: Property persists only through stable institutional mechanisms that maintain and reaffirm recognition over time.
claims.source_quote: Property persists only through the stable functioning of institutional mechanisms that maintain and reaffirm recognition over time.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological dependency of property on institutional mechanisms.

claims.claim: Ownership exists solely within a web of continuous institutional affirmation.
claims.source_quote: ownership exists solely within a web of continuous institutional affirmation.
claims.note: Asserts the necessary ontological condition for ownership's existence.

claims.claim: Institutions serve as ontological stabilizers of property.
claims.source_quote: Institutions, in this sense, serve as ontological stabilizers of property: they ensure that the dependencies linking agents, objects, and rights remain coherent, traceable, and enforceable within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological role/function of institutions with respect to property.

claims.claim: Property relations are dependent continuants requiring persistent bearers in both agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Property relations, as dependent continuants, require persistent bearers in both agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts that property relations are a subkind of dependent continuant and have a dependency relation to agents and institutions.

claims.claim: The registry, contract, and court each function as institutional continuants.
claims.source_quote: The registry, the contract, and the court each function as institutional continuants, entities whose role is to instantiate and help maintain the relations that define ownership.
claims.note: Asserts that these entities are instances of institutional continuants with a specific role.

claims.claim: Recording, verifying, adjudicating, and enforcing are occurrents that realize and reaffirm the dependent continuants of ownership.
claims.source_quote: They do so through a series of occurrents, procedural acts such as recording, verifying, adjudicating, and enforcing, which continually realize and reaffirm the dependent continuants of ownership and entitlement.
claims.note: Asserts that these procedural acts are occurrents bearing a realization relation to dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Without recurring institutional realizations, property would collapse into mere possession.
claims.source_quote: Without these recurring realizations, property would collapse back into mere possession and fragile memories, its ontological stability lost with the withdrawal of formal recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological dependency of property on recurring institutional realization.

claims.claim: A land registry or patent database is an institutional continuant that holds together the network of recognition.
claims.source_quote: A land registry, corporate register, or patent database is not merely a repository of information but an institutional continuant helping to hold together the network of recognition itself.
claims.note: Asserts that registries are institutional continuants with the function of maintaining the recognition network.

claims.claim: Each registry entry is a recorded dependent continuant sustained by institutional memory and procedural validation.
claims.source_quote: Each entry in such a registry represents a recorded dependent continuant, a legal fact sustained by institutional memory and procedural validation.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of registry entries as dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Registration transforms transient recognition into a persistent institutional fact.
claims.source_quote: The act of registration transforms transient recognition (the acknowledgment of a transaction or ownership claim) into a persistent institutional fact.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative ontological function of the act of registration.

claims.claim: Once registered, ownership becomes part of the legal system's enduring ontology.
claims.source_quote: Once entered into the registry, ownership becomes part of the legal system's enduring ontology, capable of surviving changes in agents, institutions, or physical conditions.
claims.note: Asserts that registered ownership has a persistence property within the legal ontology.

claims.claim: The registry bridges temporal scales by transforming ephemeral acts of acknowledgment into durable components of the legal order.
claims.source_quote: The registry thereby bridges temporal scales: it transforms ephemeral acts of acknowledgment into durable components of the legal order.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of the registry connecting temporal scales.

claims.claim: The registry is the metaphysical anchor of modern property systems.
claims.source_quote: The registry is thus the metaphysical anchor of modern property systems, law's apparatus for making recognition permanent.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of the registry within property systems.

claims.claim: A contract is an information artifact that records the creation of dependent continuants including rights, obligations, and transfers.
claims.source_quote: A contract is an information artifact that records the creation of dependent continuants, including rights, obligations, and transfers, whose validity depends on institutional acceptance.
claims.note: Asserts that contracts are a subkind of information artifact and records of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The signing of a contract is an occurrent that realizes both the agents' roles and the institution's role as guarantor.
claims.source_quote: The signing of a contract is an occurrent that realizes both the agents' roles (as parties) and the institution's role (as guarantor of recognition).
claims.note: Asserts that contract-signing is an occurrent with a realization relation to roles.

claims.claim: Contracts generate and modify property relations through mutual recognition among agents.
claims.source_quote: Whereas registries stabilize recognition through institutional storage, contracts generate and modify property relations through mutual recognition among agents.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of contracts as generators/modifiers of property relations.

claims.claim: Enforcement processes such as litigation, execution, and repossession are repair occurrents.
claims.source_quote: Enforcement processes (litigation, execution, repossession) are repair occurrents: temporal events that restore coherence by reaffirming the underlying structure of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that enforcement processes are a subkind of occurrent (repair occurrents) with a restoration function.

claims.claim: Enforcement serves as the reactive maintenance mechanism of ownership.
claims.source_quote: Enforcement, in turn, serves as the reactive maintenance mechanism of ownership. It operates when recognition falters, when one party violates the dependencies that define property relations.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of enforcement with respect to ownership maintenance.

claims.claim: Theft temporarily displaces the realization of recognition without eliminating the dependent continuant of ownership.
claims.source_quote: Theft, for instance, does not merely deprive an owner of physical control, it temporarily displaces the realization of recognition. The thief possesses the object but not the dependent continuant of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of theft as a displacement of recognition realization.

claims.claim: A stolen object remains 'owned' as long as the institutional relations defining ownership persist.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the object remains 'owned' as long as the institutional relations that define ownership persist.
claims.note: Asserts a condition for ownership's persistence tied to institutional relations.

claims.claim: Ownership ceases to exist if the registry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or enforcement of the owner's claim ceases.
claims.source_quote: Only if recognition collapses, if the registry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim, does ownership cease to exist.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions under which ownership's existence terminates.

claims.claim: Failures in institutional maintenance such as theft, fraud, or corruption are ontological disruptions in the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Failures in institutional maintenance, such as theft, fraud, or systemic corruption, represent ontological disruptions in the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that these failures have an ontological character as disruptions in the recognition field.

claims.claim: A realizable dependent continuant is an entity that inheres in a bearer.
claims.source_quote: A realizable dependent continuant, in the framework of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), is an entity that inheres in a bearer and is fulfilled or manifested under certain conditions.
claims.note: Direct assertion of the ontological kind and its inherence relation to a bearer.

claims.claim: A realizable dependent continuant is fulfilled or manifested under certain conditions.
claims.source_quote: A realizable dependent continuant, in the framework of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), is an entity that inheres in a bearer and is fulfilled or manifested under certain conditions.
claims.note: Asserts a disposition/property of this kind of entity.

claims.claim: A legal norm has the capacity to structure behavior and recognition within an institutional framework.
claims.source_quote: A legal norm 'exists' insofar as it possesses the capacity to structure behavior and recognition within an institutional framework.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of legal norms as entities.

claims.claim: A legal norm continues to exist when unfulfilled as a potential for realization.
claims.source_quote: It does not vanish when unfulfilled; rather, it continues to exist as a potential for realization, ready to be instantiated when the relevant conditions arise.
claims.note: Asserts persistence and a property (potential for realization) of legal norms.

claims.claim: The capacity of a statute to obligate is an ontological parallel to the capacity of a knife to cut.
claims.source_quote: The capacity of a statute to obligate or of a right to empower operates in precisely the same way. These are not metaphors but ontological parallels.
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts these are ontological parallels, not merely analogies, committing to a structural identity claim.

claims.claim: A right has the capacity to empower.
claims.source_quote: The capacity of a statute to obligate or of a right to empower operates in precisely the same way.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of rights as entities.

claims.claim: A statute has the capacity to obligate.
claims.source_quote: The capacity of a statute to obligate or of a right to empower operates in precisely the same way.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of statutes as entities.

claims.claim: An object remains owned as long as the institutional relations defining ownership persist.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the object remains "owned" as long as the institutional relations that define ownership persist.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the conditions of ownership's existence.

claims.claim: Ownership ceases to exist when institutional maintenance fails.
claims.source_quote: Only if recognition collapses, if the registry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim, does ownership cease to exist.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions under which the entity 'ownership' goes out of existence.

claims.claim: Property has a physical aspect and a legal aspect.
claims.source_quote: Theft thus illustrates the duality of property's being: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts that property has two distinct ontological aspects or dimensions.

claims.claim: The physical aspect of property can change while its legal aspect remains constant.
claims.source_quote: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/structural property of property's two aspects.

claims.claim: Fraud is a fabrication of recognition through false appearances.
claims.source_quote: Fraud introduces a subtler form of disruption: the fabrication of recognition through false appearances.
claims.note: Asserts what fraud essentially is as an ontological kind—a fabricated recognition.

claims.claim: Theft is intelligible as a legal concept because ownership is an institutional relation.
claims.source_quote: is what makes theft intelligible as a legal concept.
claims.note: The author attributes the intelligibility of theft as a legal concept to the institutional nature of ownership; implies ownership is constitutively institutional.

claims.claim: Ownership ceases to exist when the legal order disintegrates or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim.
claims.source_quote: stry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim, does ownership cease to exist.
claims.note: Direct assertion about conditions under which a kind of entity (ownership) ceases to exist.

claims.claim: Property has a physical aspect and a legal aspect, forming a duality of being.
claims.source_quote: Theft thus illustrates the duality of property's being: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts that property has two distinct ontological aspects as properties/dimensions of its being.

claims.claim: A forged deed or fraudulent registration generates a spurious dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: A forged deed, counterfeit document, or fraudulent registration generates what might be called a spurious dependent continuant, an entity that mimics the structure of ownership but lacks ontological grounding within legitimate recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of a spurious dependent continuant, though hedged with 'what might be called'; the ontological commitment is clear enough to include.

claims.claim: A spurious dependent continuant mimics ownership but lacks ontological grounding in legitimate recognition.
claims.source_quote: an entity that mimics the structure of ownership but lacks ontological grounding within legitimate recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property (lack of ontological grounding) of a kind of entity (spurious dependent continuant).

claims.claim: Fraudulent ownership persists as an apparent fact within the institutional system for as long as institutions are deceived.
claims.source_quote: For as long as institutions are deceived, the fraudulent ownership persists as an apparent fact within the system.
claims.note: Asserts a property/condition of fraudulent ownership as an entity.

claims.claim: Discovery of fraud annihilates the false continuant and restores proper dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Once discovered, the repair process annihilates this false continuant, restoring coherence by reestablishing the proper dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts what happens to the fraudulent entity upon discovery — an ontological event of annihilation.

claims.claim: Destruction of a registry or falsification of records fragments the network of recognition that sustains ownership.
claims.source_quote: When a registry is destroyed in war, or when a corrupt bureaucracy falsifies records, the network of recognition that sustains ownership becomes fragmented.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/structural property: the network of recognition becomes fragmented under certain conditions.

claims.claim: Fragmented recognition produces contradiction debt: multiple incompatible ownership claims coexisting without resolution.
claims.source_quote: The result is contradiction debt: multiple, incompatible ownership claims coexisting without resolution.
claims.note: Asserts existence of a condition called 'contradiction debt' with specific ontological characteristics.

claims.claim: Property has the function of serving as a stabilizing relational structure.
claims.source_quote: as property ceases to serve its function as a stabilizing relational structure.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of property as an entity.

claims.claim: Post-conflict registry reconstitution is an act of ontological repair — restoration of coherence through reweaving of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Post-conflict reconstruction efforts frequently begin with reconstituting registries and reaffirming property rights, for these are not merely economic necessities but acts of ontological repair, the restoration of the world's coherence through the reweaving of recognition.
claims.note: Author endorses the view that these acts are ontological repair, not merely economic; asserts ontological function.

claims.claim: Institutions perform the function of transitive recognition, transferring ownership dependencies from one bearer to another.
claims.source_quote: institutions perform the function of transitive recognition, transferring ownership dependencies from one bearer to another without breaking coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of institutions as entities.

claims.claim: The continuity of ownership through death or dissolution is achieved because recognition is distributed across systems rather than confined to individuals.
claims.source_quote: The continuity of ownership through death or dissolution is a triumph of institutional ontology: recognition survives its bearers because it is distributed across systems rather than confined to individuals.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of recognition: it is distributed across systems.

claims.claim: Legal entities such as estates, trusts, and corporations are continuants of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The legal entity itself - the estate, trust, or corporation - acts as a continuant of recognition, absorbing and transmitting ownership through time.
claims.note: Asserts that legal entities are a subkind or instance of continuant, bearing the function of absorbing and transmitting ownership.

claims.claim: Institutions are ontological infrastructures that hold together the web of dependent continuants constituting the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are not merely procedural devices but ontological infrastructures. They hold together the web of dependent continuants that constitute the legal world.
claims.note: Direct assertion about what institutions are and their structural role.

claims.claim: Property depends on organized and enduring recognition for its existence.
claims.source_quote: Their breakdown reveals the fragility of this world and the dependence of property, and by extension, value, on organized and enduring recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property and recognition.

claims.claim: Value depends on organized and enduring recognition.
claims.source_quote: the dependence of property, and by extension, value, on organized and enduring recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between value and recognition.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: If property is a relational continuant sustained by recognition, then the commons represents a higher-order form of that same ontological pattern
claims.note: Author asserts this as a premise he endorses, establishing property's ontological kind and sustaining relation.

claims.claim: The commons is a higher-order form of the same ontological pattern as property.
claims.source_quote: the commons represents a higher-order form of that same ontological pattern, one in which ownership is distributed, and the field of recognition extends beyond individual bearers.
claims.note: Asserts the commons is a subkind/variant of the property pattern with specific structural properties.

claims.claim: The commons is not the negation of property but its generalization.
claims.source_quote: The commons is not the negation of property but its generalization.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/structural property of the commons with respect to property.

claims.claim: The commons emerges when the relation linking owner, object, and institution expands to include a community as the primary bearer of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It emerges when the relation linking owner, object, and institution expands to include a community or collective as the primary bearer of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological conditions of emergence and the bearer structure of the commons.

claims.claim: In the commons, the ownership relation inheres in a collective role — a distributed continuant realized through coordinated recognition among multiple agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: In the commons, by contrast, the ownership relation inheres in a collective role, a distributed continuant whose realization requires coordinated recognition among multiple agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts the inherence structure of ownership in the commons and the nature of the collective role as a distributed continuant.

claims.claim: The collective role functions as a bearer of rights and obligations not reducible to the sum of its participants.
claims.source_quote: This collective role (e.g., 'citizen,' 'member,' 'user') functions as a bearer of rights and obligations not reducible to the sum of its participants.
claims.note: Asserts a function and irreducibility property of the collective role entity.

claims.claim: The commons is an ontological ascent in which recognition attaches to a shared institutional identity rather than directly to individuals.
claims.source_quote: The commons thus represents an ontological ascent: a structure in which recognition no longer attaches to individuals directly but to a shared institutional identity through which individuals participate.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of the commons regarding how recognition is attached.

claims.claim: The dependent continuant 'public ownership' inheres in the collective institution of the polity.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuant 'public ownership' inheres in the collective institution of the polity, realized through procedures of management, funding, and protection.
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between public ownership (a dependent continuant) and the polity.

claims.claim: The commons is a recognitional field rather than a discrete relation.
claims.source_quote: The commons is thus a recognitional field rather than a discrete relation.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind/character of the commons.

claims.claim: The commons triad consists of a collective owner role, a shared resource object, and a recognizing institutional structure, each mutually dependent.
claims.source_quote: This relational structure can be modeled ontologically as a triadic dependency linking Owner (collective role), Object (shared resource), and Institution (recognizing structure). Each component depends on the others for existence.
claims.note: Asserts a triadic structure with mutual dependency relations among three kinds of entity.

claims.claim: The collective owner role cannot exist without institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: The collective owner role cannot exist without institutional recognition; the institution cannot realize its function without the resource; and the resource becomes 'common' only when recognized as such by the institution.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency/existential relation between the collective owner role and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: The institution cannot realize its function without the shared resource.
claims.source_quote: the institution cannot realize its function without the resource
claims.note: Asserts a functional dependency of the institution on the resource.

claims.claim: A resource becomes 'common' only when recognized as such by the institution.
claims.source_quote: the resource becomes 'common' only when recognized as such by the institution.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological condition for a resource acquiring the property of being common.

claims.claim: The commons is a positive ontological form — an organized structure of collective recognition.
claims.source_quote: the commons is not merely the absence of private ownership but a positive ontological form, an organized structure of collective recognition that defines how certain entities exist as shared rather than exclusive.
claims.note: Asserts that the commons is a positive ontological form with a specific structure.

claims.claim: Ownership ceases to exist when the legal order disintegrates or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim.
claims.source_quote: does ownership cease to exist. Theft thus illustrates the duality of property's being: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the conditions for existence of ownership as an entity.

claims.claim: Property has a dual being: a physical aspect and a legal aspect.
claims.source_quote: Theft thus illustrates the duality of property's being: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts that property has two distinct aspects as part of its ontological structure.

claims.claim: Fraud generates a spurious dependent continuant that mimics ownership but lacks legitimate ontological grounding.
claims.source_quote: A forged deed, counterfeit document, or fraudulent registration generates what might be called a spurious dependent continuant, an entity that mimics the structure of ownership but lacks ontological grounding within legitimate recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of a specific kind of entity (spurious dependent continuant) produced by fraud.

claims.claim: Fraudulent ownership persists as an apparent fact within the institutional system as long as institutions are deceived.
claims.source_quote: For as long as institutions are deceived, the fraudulent ownership persists as an apparent fact within the system.
claims.note: Asserts a property/state of the spurious entity relative to institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Discovery of fraud annihilates the false continuant and restores coherence by reestablishing proper dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Once discovered, the repair process annihilates this false continuant, restoring coherence by reestablishing the proper dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts what happens to the fraudulent dependent continuant upon discovery—ontological annihilation.

claims.claim: Destruction of registries or corruption of records fragments the network of recognition that sustains ownership.
claims.source_quote: When a registry is destroyed in war, or when a corrupt bureaucracy falsifies records, the network of recognition that sustains ownership becomes fragmented.
