claims.note: Asserts a relational/structural property of the recognition network under institutional failure.

claims.claim: Institutional failures create contradiction debt: multiple incompatible ownership claims coexisting without resolution.
claims.source_quote: The result is contradiction debt: multiple, incompatible ownership claims coexisting without resolution.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of a specific ontological condition (contradiction debt) resulting from institutional failure.

claims.claim: Property functions as a stabilizing relational structure.
claims.source_quote: as property ceases to serve its function as a stabilizing relational structure.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role that property bears.

claims.claim: Post-conflict reconstruction of registries and property rights are acts of ontological repair.
claims.source_quote: Post-conflict reconstruction efforts frequently begin with reconstituting registries and reaffirming property rights, for these are not merely economic necessities but acts of ontological repair, the restoration of the world's coherence through the reweaving of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature/function of reconstruction practices.

claims.claim: Institutions perform transitive recognition, transferring ownership dependencies from one bearer to another without breaking coherence.
claims.source_quote: institutions perform the function of transitive recognition, transferring ownership dependencies from one bearer to another without breaking coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role that institutions bear with respect to ownership dependencies.

claims.claim: Recognition survives its individual bearers because it is distributed across systems rather than confined to individuals.
claims.source_quote: The continuity of ownership through death or dissolution is a triumph of institutional ontology: recognition survives its bearers because it is distributed across systems rather than confined to individuals.
claims.note: Asserts a property of recognition—its distributed character enabling persistence beyond individual bearers.

claims.claim: The estate, trust, or corporation acts as a continuant of recognition, transmitting ownership through time.
claims.source_quote: The legal entity itself - the estate, trust, or corporation - acts as a continuant of recognition, absorbing and transmitting ownership through time.
claims.note: Asserts that legal entities are continuants of recognition with the function of transmitting ownership.

claims.claim: Institutions are ontological infrastructures that hold together the web of dependent continuants constituting the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are not merely procedural devices but ontological infrastructures. They hold together the web of dependent continuants that constitute the legal world.
claims.note: Asserts both the kind (ontological infrastructure) and function of institutions.

claims.claim: The legal world consists of a web of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: They hold together the web of dependent continuants that constitute the legal world.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological composition of the legal world.

claims.claim: Property depends ontologically on organized and enduring recognition.
claims.source_quote: the dependence of property, and by extension, value, on organized and enduring recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property and recognition.

claims.claim: Value depends ontologically on organized and enduring recognition.
claims.source_quote: the dependence of property, and by extension, value, on organized and enduring recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between value and recognition.

claims.claim: The persistence of property is a measure of the health of the institutions that sustain it.
claims.source_quote: The persistence of property, therefore, is a measure of the health of the institutions that sustain it.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between property-persistence and institutional health.

claims.claim: The commons is a relational continuant sustained by recognition in which ownership is distributed across a collective bearer.
claims.source_quote: If property is a relational continuant sustained by recognition, then the commons represents a higher-order form of that same ontological pattern, one in which ownership is distributed, and the field of recognition extends beyond individual bearers.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of the commons and its structural property.

claims.claim: The commons is not the negation of property but its generalization.
claims.source_quote: The commons is not the negation of property but its generalization.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological relationship between commons and property.

claims.claim: The commons emerges when the owner-object-institution relation expands to include a community as the primary bearer of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It emerges when the relation linking owner, object, and institution expands to include a community or collective as the primary bearer of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the structural condition for the commons as an entity.

claims.claim: In the commons, ownership is realized through collective roles and institutional mediation rather than exclusive possession.
claims.source_quote: the commons is property elevated to a higher order of dependency: a configuration in which ownership is realized through collective roles and institutional mediation rather than exclusive possession.
claims.note: Asserts a property/realization condition of commons ownership.

claims.claim: In ordinary ownership, the property relation inheres jointly in an individual agent and an institutional continuant, with a specific object as its third pole.
claims.source_quote: In ordinary ownership, the property relation inheres jointly in an individual agent and an institutional continuant, with a specific object as its third pole.
claims.note: Asserts the bearer structure of the private property relation as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: In the commons, the ownership relation inheres in a collective role, a distributed continuant requiring coordinated recognition among multiple agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: In the commons, by contrast, the ownership relation inheres in a collective role, a distributed continuant whose realization requires coordinated recognition among multiple agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts the bearer structure of commons ownership as a different kind of dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The collective role in the commons is a bearer of rights and obligations not reducible to the sum of its participants.
claims.source_quote: This collective role (e.g., 'citizen,' 'member,' 'user') functions as a bearer of rights and obligations not reducible to the sum of its participants.
claims.note: Asserts an irreducibility property of the collective role entity.

claims.claim: In the commons, recognition attaches to a shared institutional identity through which individuals participate, not to individuals directly.
claims.source_quote: a structure in which recognition no longer attaches to individuals directly but to a shared institutional identity through which individuals participate.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/relational property distinguishing commons recognition from private ownership recognition.

claims.claim: The dependent continuant 'public ownership' inheres in the collective institution of the polity.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuant 'public ownership' inheres in the collective institution of the polity, realized through procedures of management, funding, and protection.
claims.note: Asserts the bearer relation of the public ownership dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The commons is a recognitional field rather than a discrete relation.
claims.source_quote: The commons is thus a recognitional field rather than a discrete relation.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of the commons.

claims.claim: The commons triad consists of a collective owner role, a shared object, and a recognizing institution that are mutually dependent for existence.
claims.source_quote: The collective owner role cannot exist without institutional recognition; the institution cannot realize its function without the resource; and the resource becomes 'common' only when recognized as such by the institution.
claims.note: Asserts mutual existential dependencies among the three poles of the commons triad.

claims.claim: The commons is a positive ontological form—an organized structure of collective recognition defining how certain entities exist as shared.
claims.source_quote: the commons is not merely the absence of private ownership but a positive ontological form, an organized structure of collective recognition that defines how certain entities exist as shared rather than exclusive.
claims.note: Asserts the positive ontological status and defining function of the commons.

claims.claim: Creation is an occurrent through which a dependent continuant comes into existence.
claims.source_quote: Creation (C): an occurrent through which a dependent continuant (e.g., obligation) comes into existence.
claims.note: Direct assertion that creation is a type of occurrent with a specific ontological function.

claims.claim: Maintenance is the phase during which a dependent continuant exists, sustained by recognition and institutional context.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance (M): the phase during which the continuant exists, sustained by recognition and institutional context.
claims.note: Asserts that maintenance is a phase with specific sustaining conditions.

claims.claim: Extinction is a process that terminates a continuant's existence.
claims.source_quote: Extinction (E): the process that terminates the continuant's existence, either through fulfillment, repeal, or invalidation.
claims.note: Asserts extinction is a process and specifies its ontological role.

claims.claim: Creation and extinction are events; maintenance is endurance.
claims.source_quote: Creation and extinction are events; maintenance is endurance.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of the three lifecycle phases.

claims.claim: Legal reality is cumulative, growing by accretion rather than replacement.
claims.source_quote: This temporal modeling reveals that law's reality is cumulative... Legal reality grows not by replacement but by accretion, forming a complex stratigraphy of coexisting entities.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal reality regarding its mode of growth.

claims.claim: A constitution generates legislative powers, which generate statutes, which generate obligations, which generate rights and duties.
claims.source_quote: A constitution generates legislative powers; those powers generate statutes; statutes generate obligations; obligations generate rights and duties that persist until extinguished.
claims.note: Asserts generative causal-ontological relations among legal entities.

claims.claim: Obligations are realizable dependent continuants whose function is to constrain and guide behavior until realized.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, this is the realization of a realizable dependent continuant, the function of obligation is to constrain and guide behavior until it is realized, at which point it ceases to exist as a constraint.
claims.note: Asserts that obligations belong to a specific ontological category and have a specific function.

claims.claim: When an obligation is fulfilled, it ceases to exist as a constraint.
claims.source_quote: the function of obligation is to constrain and guide behavior until it is realized, at which point it ceases to exist as a constraint.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological change of state for obligations upon realization.

claims.claim: Breach transforms an obligation into a new entity: liability.
claims.source_quote: Other forms of extinction include annulment, breach, and repeal. Each operates differently... breach transforms it into a new entity (liability).
claims.note: Asserts that breach produces a distinct ontological entity, liability.

claims.claim: Annulment voids a legal relation retroactively.
claims.source_quote: annulment voids the relation retroactively
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological operation performed by annulment.

claims.claim: Repeal removes the institutional recognition that sustains a legal relation.
claims.source_quote: repeal removes the institutional recognition that sustains it.
claims.note: Asserts what repeal does ontologically to a legal continuant.

claims.claim: Extinction is always a transformation of structure, never mere negation.
claims.source_quote: What unites these cases is that extinction is never mere negation, it is always a transformation of structure.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the extinction process as such.

claims.claim: The repeal of a statute may dissolve thousands of dependent obligations.
claims.source_quote: the repeal of a statute may dissolve thousands of dependent obligations.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between statutes and obligations; modal phrasing lowers confidence slightly.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt is the accumulation of unresolved or conflicting continuants within a legal system's architecture.
claims.source_quote: leading to what this framework elsewhere calls contradiction debt: the accumulation of unresolved or conflicting continuants within the legal system's architecture.
claims.note: Author defines and endorses this concept as part of the framework's ontology.

claims.claim: Courts, legislatures, registries, and administrative bodies are temporal custodians of legal entities.
claims.source_quote: Institutions play the role of temporal custodians in this process. Courts, legislatures, registries, and administrative bodies maintain the continuity of legal entities by recording, interpreting, and updating their statuses.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function for these institutions in the ontology of law.

claims.claim: Institutional processes such as filing, adjudication, and publication constitute law's temporal metabolism.
claims.source_quote: Their procedures, filing, adjudication, publication, are the mechanisms through which the persistence and extinction of obligations are tracked and verified. These institutional processes constitute law's temporal metabolism.
claims.note: Asserts what these processes constitute in the ontological structure of law.

claims.claim: The formalization of time through legal mechanisms is an ontological necessity for law.
claims.source_quote: The formalization of time, through statutes of limitation, filing deadlines, or effective dates, is not a technical detail but an ontological necessity.
claims.note: Asserts that temporal formalization has ontological status, not merely technical.

claims.claim: Time is constitutive of law's being.
claims.source_quote: Time in law is codified precisely because it is constitutive of law's being.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive ontological relation between time and legal being.

claims.claim: A constitution creates a normative timeline within which subsequent legal entities come into being.
claims.source_quote: When a constitution is ratified... it creates a normative timeline, a horizon within which other entities come into being.
claims.note: Asserts that a constitution produces a specific ontological structure (normative timeline).

claims.claim: Law's temporality is recursive: each new legal act both depends on and reshapes the temporal structure it inherits.
claims.source_quote: Law's temporality is thus recursive: each new act both depends on and reshapes the temporal structure it inherits.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of legal temporality.

claims.claim: Retroactive legal acts change the structure of recognition regarding what counts as real in the legal past.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, such acts do not literally change the past; rather, they change the structure of recognition in the present regarding what counts as real in the legal past.
claims.note: Asserts what retroactive acts do ontologically.

claims.claim: Chronological time and recognitional time are distinct; recognitional time is proper to law.
claims.source_quote: This demonstrates the difference between chronological time and recognitional time: the latter is the temporality proper to law, measured not by duration but by the persistence of acknowledgment within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of two distinct kinds of time and attributes one to law.

claims.claim: Extinguished legal entities persist as records, precedents, or informational artifacts that influence future recognition.
claims.source_quote: When an obligation is fully discharged or repealed, it does not simply vanish; it transitions into the category of historical or archival being. It persists as a record, a precedent, or an informational artifact.
claims.note: Asserts a post-extinction ontological status for legal entities.

claims.claim: The archive of fulfilled or extinguished relations constitutes the memory of law.
claims.source_quote: The archive of fulfilled or extinguished relations constitutes the memory of law, allowing institutions to learn, analogize, and evolve.
claims.note: Asserts what the archive constitutes in the ontology of legal institutions.

claims.claim: Extinction of legal entities is transformation from active to inert, from living structure to memory.
claims.source_quote: Extinction, therefore, is never pure disappearance; it is transformation from active to inert, from living structure to memory within the broader system.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of legal extinction as transformation of state.

claims.claim: A legal system is a structure that stabilizes relations of recognition across agents, roles, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, a legal system is a structure that stabilizes relations of recognition across agents, roles, and institutions, preventing the collapse of social reality into contradiction or fragmentation.
claims.note: Direct ontological definition of a legal system.

claims.claim: The primary function of law is structural stabilization of relational dependencies among persons and norms over time.
claims.source_quote: Its primary function is not moral correction or coercive control, but structural stabilization: the maintenance of coherent relational dependencies among persons and norms over time.
claims.note: Asserts the primary function of law as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: Recognition is fragile and depends on mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Recognition, as earlier chapters established, is fragile. It depends on mutual acknowledgment, and mutuality is prone to rupture.
claims.note: Asserts a property of recognition as an ontological phenomenon.

claims.claim: Law functions as a repair mechanism that mitigates disruptions by formalizing and institutionalizing recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law functions as a repair mechanism that mitigates these disruptions by formalizing and institutionalizing recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of law in the social ontology.

claims.claim: Law is a temporally structured field of relations, an evolving ontology.
claims.source_quote: law is not merely an order of norms but a temporally structured field of relations, an evolving ontology whose stability lies not in stasis but in the patterned succession of creation and extinction.
claims.note: Asserts the fundamental ontological character of law.

claims.claim: Dormant or obsolete legal entities remain latent until formally repealed.
claims.source_quote: Some layers may be dormant, obsolete laws, suspended contracts, but they remain latent until formally repealed.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property (latency) of dormant legal entities.

claims.claim: Recognition is fragile.
claims.source_quote: Recognition, as earlier chapters established, is fragile.
claims.note: Direct property attribution to recognition.

claims.claim: Recognition depends on mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: It depends on mutual acknowledgment, and mutuality is prone to rupture.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between recognition and mutual acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Mutuality is prone to rupture.
claims.source_quote: It depends on mutual acknowledgment, and mutuality is prone to rupture.
claims.note: Asserts a disposition/property of mutuality.

claims.claim: Disagreements about meaning, legitimacy, and authority threaten the coherence of the social field.
claims.source_quote: Disagreements about meaning, legitimacy, and authority constantly threaten the coherence of the social field.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/threatening relation between disagreements and the social field's coherence.

claims.claim: Law functions as a repair mechanism that mitigates disruptions to recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law functions as a repair mechanism that mitigates these disruptions by formalizing and institutionalizing recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of law.

claims.claim: Law formalizes and institutionalizes recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law functions as a repair mechanism that mitigates these disruptions by formalizing and institutionalizing recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between law and recognition (formalization/institutionalization).

claims.claim: Law ensures recognition is structured rather than fleeting.
claims.source_quote: Through procedures, offices, and artifacts, it ensures that recognition is not fleeting but structured.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of law with respect to recognition.

claims.claim: Law sustains recognition through enduring forms rather than personal memory or goodwill.
claims.source_quote: not dependent on personal memory or goodwill but sustained through enduring forms.
claims.note: Asserts the means by which law maintains recognition.

claims.claim: Law operates through procedures, offices, and artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Through procedures, offices, and artifacts, it ensures that recognition is not fleeting but structured.
claims.note: Asserts that law has component parts or instruments (procedures, offices, artifacts).

claims.claim: Law is an apparatus of coherence.
claims.source_quote: The law, in this sense, is not primarily a set of prohibitions; it is an apparatus of coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership or essential character of law.

claims.claim: Law is a system that continuously reconstitutes the shared field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: a system that continuously reconstitutes the shared field of recognition upon which social reality depends.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of law.

claims.claim: Social reality depends on the shared field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: a system that continuously reconstitutes the shared field of recognition upon which social reality depends.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between social reality and the shared field of recognition.

claims.claim: Property is a dependent continuant relating an object to an owner.
claims.source_quote: Property is modelled as a dependent continuant relating an object to an owner and sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification: property is asserted to be a dependent continuant with specific relata.

claims.claim: Property relations are sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Property is modelled as a dependent continuant relating an object to an owner and sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Institutions recognize and maintain property relations.
claims.source_quote: Institutions recognize and maintain property relations while conferring ownership roles on agents or collectives.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/causal role of institutions with respect to property relations.

claims.claim: Institutions confer ownership roles on agents or collectives.
claims.source_quote: Institutions recognize and maintain property relations while conferring ownership roles on agents or collectives.
claims.note: Asserts that institutions have the function of role-conferral upon agents or collectives.

claims.claim: In commons regimes, ownership is a higher-order collective role realized through distributed recognition.
claims.source_quote: In commons regimes, ownership functions as a higher-order collective role realized through distributed recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of ownership in the commons: a higher-order collective role with a specific realization base.

claims.claim: Private property and the commons share the same ontological dependency pattern.
claims.source_quote: Both are sustained by the same dependency pattern, but the commons introduces an additional level of abstraction.
claims.note: Asserts structural ontological continuity between two kinds of property.

claims.claim: In the commons, a collective role replaces the individual agent as bearer of ownership.
claims.source_quote: The commons introduces an additional level of abstraction: the collective role replaces the individual agent as bearer of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a structural difference in who bears the ownership role in the commons vs. private property.

claims.claim: Recognition sustaining the commons is distributed across citizens, institutions, and juridical entities.
claims.source_quote: The recognition that sustains this relation is therefore multi-layered, distributed across citizens, institutions, and juridical entities.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the recognition relation in commons regimes: it is multi-layered and distributed.

claims.claim: The commons is an extension of property's ontological logic to collective bearers.
claims.source_quote: The commons is thus not a deviation from property but an extension of its ontological logic to collective bearers.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological relationship between the commons and property as a generalization of the same structure.

claims.claim: A river's ontological status as property shifts as recognition is redistributed.
claims.source_quote: The object remains the same in its material aspect, but its ontological status shifts as recognition is redistributed.
claims.note: Asserts that ontological status is a function of recognition distribution, not material constitution.

claims.claim: Ownership is not an attribute of objects but a relational configuration within a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: These transformations reveal that ownership is not an attribute of objects but a relational configuration within a system of recognition, an architecture of dependencies subject to institutional articulation.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the nature of ownership: relational, not intrinsic to objects.

claims.claim: Ownership is an architecture of dependencies subject to institutional articulation.
claims.source_quote: An architecture of dependencies subject to institutional articulation.
claims.note: Asserts the structural character of ownership as a dependency architecture.

claims.claim: Private property is a relation between one agent and the state.
claims.source_quote: As private property, it is a relation between one agent and the state.
claims.note: Asserts the relational ontological structure of private property.

claims.claim: State property is a relation between a public institution and the collective of citizens.
claims.source_quote: As state property, it is a relation between a public institution and the collective of citizens.
claims.note: Asserts the relational ontological structure of state property.

claims.claim: Common property is a relation among citizens mediated by institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: As common property, it is a relation among the citizens themselves, mediated by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the relational ontological structure of common property.

claims.claim: The commons occupies a delicate ontological equilibrium between inclusion and fragmentation.
claims.source_quote: The commons thus occupies a delicate ontological equilibrium between inclusion and fragmentation.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the commons as an ontological entity: its equilibrium condition.

claims.claim: Without ongoing maintenance, the commons devolves into privatization or anarchy.
claims.source_quote: Without such maintenance, the commons devolves into either privatization (when recognition contracts to individuals) or anarchy (when recognition dissolves entirely).
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional/causal property of the commons regarding what happens when recognition fails.

claims.claim: Open-source software, creative commons licensing, and public data repositories are forms of collective ownership realized through distributed recognition.
claims.source_quote: Open-source software, creative commons licensing, and public data repositories are contemporary expressions of collective ownership realized through distributed recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that these entities are instances of a specific ontological kind: collective ownership via distributed recognition.

claims.claim: An open-source license is an information artifact encoding conditions of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The open-source license, for example, functions as an information artifact encoding the conditions of recognition: it specifies who may use, modify, and distribute the software.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind (information artifact) and function of an open-source license.

claims.claim: In digital commons, the network of recognition among users and contributors sustains the property relation.
claims.source_quote: The network of recognition among users and contributors sustains the property relation.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: the property relation is sustained by the recognition network.

claims.claim: In digital commons, recognition is mediated by digital infrastructure rather than centralized authority.
claims.source_quote: Here, the commons is not merely public but networked: recognition is mediated by digital infrastructure rather than centralized authority.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of digital commons: the mediating entity of recognition is digital infrastructure.

claims.claim: The 'tragedy of the commons' is a breakdown of collective recognition.
claims.source_quote: The so-called 'tragedy of the commons' is, in ontological terms, a breakdown of collective recognition: when individual actions cease to align with the shared dependencies that define common ownership, the property relation disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of the tragedy of the commons as a recognition breakdown.

claims.claim: When individual actions cease to align with shared dependencies, the property relation disintegrates.
claims.source_quote: When individual actions cease to align with the shared dependencies that define common ownership, the property relation disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/structural claim about conditions under which the property relation ceases to exist.

claims.claim: Successful commons management depends on the resilience of its recognition network.
claims.source_quote: Successful commons management, whether ecological or digital, depends on the resilience of its recognition network, the capacity of its institutions to maintain coherence among distributed bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between commons management success and recognition network resilience.

claims.claim: In private property, the ownership relation is individualized and exclusive.
claims.source_quote: In private property, the relation is individualized and exclusive; in the commons, it is collective and inclusive.
claims.note: Asserts properties of the ownership relation in private property.

claims.claim: In the commons, the ownership relation is collective and inclusive.
claims.source_quote: In private property, the relation is individualized and exclusive; in the commons, it is collective and inclusive.
claims.note: Asserts properties of the ownership relation in the commons.

claims.claim: Law's reality is not material but relational.
claims.source_quote: Both forms demonstrate that law's reality is not material but relational: the world of ownership, whether private or public, exists only insofar as recognition persists.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property of law: its nature is relational rather than material.

claims.claim: The world of ownership exists only insofar as recognition persists.
claims.source_quote: The world of ownership, whether private or public, exists only insofar as recognition persists.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of ownership on recognition.

claims.claim: The triadic structure of owner, object, and institution is the ontological structure of both property and commons.
claims.source_quote: The same triadic structure - owner, object, institution - remains intact, but its bearers and dependencies evolve.
claims.note: Asserts that both property forms share an identical triadic ontological structure.

claims.claim: The positivist's social facts, the natural lawyer's moral order, and the realist's behavior all exist within a unified structure of dependence.
claims.source_quote: The positivist's social facts, the natural lawyer's moral order, and the realist's behavior all find their place within a unified structure of dependence.
claims.note: The author asserts that these three kinds of legal entities occupy a single unified structure of dependence — an ontological claim about their relational placement.

claims.claim: Law's meaning and authority emerge from the coherence of a unified dependence structure.
claims.source_quote: Law's meaning and authority emerge from the coherence of this structure, its capacity to sustain and realize relations among agents, institutions, and obligations.
claims.note: The author asserts a grounding/emergence relation: law's meaning and authority have their source in the coherence of the dependence structure.

claims.claim: The dependence structure has the capacity to sustain and realize relations among agents, institutions, and obligations.
claims.source_quote: its capacity to sustain and realize relations among agents, institutions, and obligations.
claims.note: The author attributes a functional/dispositional property to the dependence structure — sustaining and realizing relations. This is an ontological claim about the structure's role.

claims.claim: An ontology of norms describes the architecture of law's reality.
claims.source_quote: To speak of an ontology of norms is, therefore, to describe the architecture of law's reality, the lattice of possibilities that underlies every command, every principle, and every act of justice.
claims.note: The author asserts that law has a real architecture — a lattice of possibilities — which is an ontological claim about the structure of legal reality.

claims.claim: A lattice of possibilities underlies every legal command, every principle, and every act of justice.
claims.source_quote: the lattice of possibilities that underlies every command, every principle, and every act of justice.
claims.note: The author asserts that a lattice of possibilities stands in an underwriting relation to legal commands, principles, and acts of justice — a direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: Phenomenology and formal ontology converge in the study of law.
claims.source_quote: Phenomenology and formal ontology, though born from distinct intellectual traditions, converge in the study of law.
claims.note: The author asserts a convergence relation between two disciplines with respect to law. This is borderline methodological but also commits to a claim about the nature/scope of these fields relative to law.

claims.claim: Property is a dependent continuant relating an object to an owner.
claims.source_quote: Property is modelled as a dependent continuant relating an object to an owner and sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological kind and relational structure of property.

claims.claim: Property is sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Property is modelled as a dependent continuant relating an object to an owner and sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Institutions recognize and maintain property relations.
claims.source_quote: Institutions recognize and maintain property relations while conferring ownership roles on agents or collectives.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of institutions with respect to property.

claims.claim: Institutions confer ownership roles on agents or collectives.
claims.source_quote: Institutions recognize and maintain property relations while conferring ownership roles on agents or collectives.
claims.note: Asserts a relational role-conferring function of institutions.

claims.claim: In commons regimes, ownership is a higher-order collective role realized through distributed recognition.
claims.source_quote: In commons regimes, ownership functions as a higher-order collective role realized through distributed recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of ownership in commons regimes.

claims.claim: The commons and private property share the same dependency pattern.
claims.source_quote: Both are sustained by the same dependency pattern, but the commons introduces an additional level of abstraction.
claims.note: Asserts a shared ontological structure between two kinds of property regime.

claims.claim: In the commons, a collective role replaces the individual agent as bearer of ownership.
claims.source_quote: The commons introduces an additional level of abstraction: the collective role replaces the individual agent as bearer of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a structural difference in the bearer of ownership in commons versus private property.

claims.claim: Recognition sustaining the commons is distributed across citizens, institutions, and juridical entities.
claims.source_quote: The recognition that sustains this relation is therefore multi-layered, distributed across citizens, institutions, and juridical entities.
claims.note: Asserts a distributional property of the recognition relation in commons.

claims.claim: The commons is an extension of property's ontological logic to collective bearers.
claims.source_quote: The commons is thus not a deviation from property but an extension of its ontological logic to collective bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind/extension relation between commons and property ontology.

claims.claim: A river's ontological status as property shifts as recognition is redistributed.
claims.source_quote: The object remains the same in its material aspect, but its ontological status shifts as recognition is redistributed.
claims.note: Asserts that ontological status is dependent on the structure of recognition, not material constitution.

claims.claim: Ownership is not an attribute of objects but a relational configuration within a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: These transformations reveal that ownership is not an attribute of objects but a relational configuration within a system of recognition, an architecture of dependencies subject to institutional articulation.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the nature of ownership.

claims.claim: Ownership is an architecture of dependencies subject to institutional articulation.
claims.source_quote: An architecture of dependencies subject to institutional articulation.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of ownership as a dependency architecture.

claims.claim: Private property is a relation between one agent and the state.
claims.source_quote: As private property, it is a relation between one agent and the state.
claims.note: Asserts the relational structure of private property.

claims.claim: State property is a relation between a public institution and the collective of citizens.
claims.source_quote: As state property, it is a relation between a public institution and the collective of citizens.
claims.note: Asserts the relational structure of state property.

claims.claim: Common property is a relation among citizens themselves mediated by institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: As common property, it is a relation among the citizens themselves, mediated by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the relational structure of common property.

claims.claim: The commons is inherently dynamic due to multiple overlapping and conflicting dependencies.
claims.source_quote: This multiplicity makes the commons inherently dynamic. Its coherence depends on ongoing maintenance, legislation, governance, and participation.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional/structural property of the commons.

claims.claim: Without ongoing maintenance, the commons devolves into privatization or anarchy.
claims.source_quote: Without such maintenance, the commons devolves into either privatization (when recognition contracts to individuals) or anarchy (when recognition dissolves entirely).
claims.note: Asserts a causal/dependency relation regarding the commons' continued existence.

claims.claim: The commons occupies a delicate ontological equilibrium between inclusion and fragmentation.
claims.source_quote: The commons thus occupies a delicate ontological equilibrium between inclusion and fragmentation.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the commons' ontological situation.

claims.claim: Open-source licenses are information artifacts encoding conditions of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The open-source license, for example, functions as an information artifact encoding the conditions of recognition: it specifies who may use, modify, and distribute the software.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and function of open-source licenses.

claims.claim: In digital commons, the network of recognition among users sustains the property relation.
claims.source_quote: The network of recognition among users and contributors sustains the property relation.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between recognition network and property relation.

claims.claim: In digital commons, recognition is mediated by digital infrastructure rather than centralized authority.
claims.source_quote: Here, the commons is not merely public but networked: recognition is mediated by digital infrastructure rather than centralized authority.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/mediating property specific to digital commons.

claims.claim: The 'tragedy of the commons' is a breakdown of collective recognition.
claims.source_quote: The so-called 'tragedy of the commons' is, in ontological terms, a breakdown of collective recognition: when individual actions cease to align with the shared dependencies that define common ownership, the property relation disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological identity of a well-known phenomenon.

claims.claim: When collective recognition breaks down, the property relation of the commons disintegrates.
claims.source_quote: When individual actions cease to align with the shared dependencies that define common ownership, the property relation disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency/causal relation between recognition and the existence of the property relation.

claims.claim: Successful commons management depends on the resilience of its recognition network.
claims.source_quote: Successful commons management, whether ecological or digital, depends on the resilience of its recognition network, the capacity of its institutions to maintain coherence among distributed bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between commons management and recognition network resilience.

claims.claim: The triadic structure of owner, object, and institution is common to both private property and commons.
claims.source_quote: The same triadic structure - owner, object, institution - remains intact, but its bearers and dependencies evolve.
claims.note: Asserts a shared structural property across property forms.

claims.claim: In private property, the ownership relation is individualized and exclusive.
claims.source_quote: In private property, the relation is individualized and exclusive; in the commons, it is collective and inclusive.
claims.note: Asserts properties of the private property relation.

claims.claim: In the commons, the ownership relation is collective and inclusive.
claims.source_quote: In private property, the relation is individualized and exclusive; in the commons, it is collective and inclusive.
claims.note: Asserts properties of the commons ownership relation.

claims.claim: Law's reality is relational, not material.
claims.source_quote: Both forms demonstrate that law's reality is not material but relational: the world of ownership, whether private or public, exists only insofar as recognition persists.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental ontological property of law.

claims.claim: The world of ownership exists only insofar as recognition persists.
claims.source_quote: The world of ownership, whether private or public, exists only insofar as recognition persists.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of ownership on recognition.

claims.claim: The commons is a mode of being in which recognition itself becomes the shared object of care.
claims.source_quote: The commons, in its highest sense, is law's acknowledgment of interdependence, a mode of being in which recognition itself becomes the shared object of care.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological characterization of the commons as a mode of being; slightly interpretive but clearly the author's positive claim.

claims.claim: Evidence belongs to the class of information-bearing dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: evidence belongs to the class of information-bearing dependent continuants, entities that exist only through recognition and serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.note: Direct assertion of the ontological kind/class of evidence.

claims.claim: Information-bearing dependent continuants exist only through recognition.
claims.source_quote: evidence belongs to the class of information-bearing dependent continuants, entities that exist only through recognition and serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.note: Asserts a property/condition of existence for this class of entities.

claims.claim: Information-bearing dependent continuants serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.source_quote: entities that exist only through recognition and serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.note: Asserts the functional role of this class of entities.

claims.claim: Evidence is made through processes of recognition and contextualization, not simply found in the world.
claims.source_quote: Evidence, unlike raw data, is not simply found in the world; it is made through processes of recognition and contextualization.
claims.note: Ontological claim about the origin/constitution of evidence.

claims.claim: An act of interpretation transforms a physical or informational entity into a bearer of evidential force.
claims.source_quote: It is this act of interpretation, an occurrent of recognition, that transforms a physical or informational entity into a bearer of evidential force.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative relation between interpretation (occurrent) and evidential status.

claims.claim: The act of interpretation is an occurrent of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It is this act of interpretation, an occurrent of recognition, that transforms a physical or informational entity into a bearer of evidential force.
claims.note: Classifies the act of interpretation as a subkind of occurrent.

claims.claim: Evidence is a recognized information artifact.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, therefore, evidence is a recognized information artifact: a material or digital continuant carrying content that has been conferred a specific epistemic function within law's framework.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of evidence.

claims.claim: Evidence is a material or digital continuant carrying content conferred a specific epistemic function within law.
claims.source_quote: a material or digital continuant carrying content that has been conferred a specific epistemic function within law's framework.
claims.note: Asserts entity type (continuant) and its property (epistemic function conferred by law).

claims.claim: Data are information content entities that exist independently of their use or recognition.
claims.source_quote: Data are information content entities that exist independently of their use or recognition. They are mere representations or traces of events, measurements, recordings, or stored signals, whose significance is not yet defined.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status and defining property of data.

claims.claim: Testimony is a speech act occurrent.
claims.source_quote: Testimony, by contrast, is a speech act occurrent: a process through which an agent conveys information, intending recognition by others.
claims.note: Classifies testimony as a subkind of occurrent (speech act).

claims.claim: Testimony is transient, realized in time through performance.
claims.source_quote: Testimony may generate data (as in transcripts or recordings) but is itself transient, realized in time through performance.
claims.note: Asserts a property of testimony as an entity.

claims.claim: Testimony may generate data such as transcripts or recordings.
claims.source_quote: Testimony may generate data (as in transcripts or recordings) but is itself transient, realized in time through performance.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/generative relation between testimony and data.

claims.claim: Evidence arises when data or testimony are recognized as relevant to a legal issue and incorporated into an institutional process.
claims.source_quote: Evidence, finally, arises when data or testimony are recognized as relevant to a legal issue and incorporated into an institutional process.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions of existence for evidence as an entity.

claims.claim: Evidence is data with juridical status.
claims.source_quote: Evidence, in this sense, is data with juridical status: it bears a specific dependent continuant, evidential weight, that exists only within the system of recognition defined by procedural rules and institutional authority.
claims.note: Ontological classification relating evidence to data with an added property.

claims.claim: Evidential weight is a dependent continuant that exists only within the system of recognition defined by procedural rules and institutional authority.
claims.source_quote: it bears a specific dependent continuant, evidential weight, that exists only within the system of recognition defined by procedural rules and institutional authority.
claims.note: Classifies evidential weight as a dependent continuant with a specific mode of existence.

claims.claim: Proof is not an entity but a state of institutional coherence.
claims.source_quote: It is not an entity but a state of institutional coherence achieved when recognized evidence satisfies the criteria of persuasion set by the system.
claims.note: Explicit ontological claim denying proof entity-status and asserting it is a state.

claims.claim: Proof is an emergent configuration within the field of recognition in which evidential dependencies align to produce a coherent judgment.
claims.source_quote: Proof, therefore, is not an additional artifact but an emergent configuration within the field of recognition, a condition in which evidential dependencies align to produce a coherent judgment.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of proof as an emergent configuration.

claims.claim: Evidence denotes the recognized relation between information and event.
claims.source_quote: the former denotes the recognized relation between information and event, while the latter denotes the achieved coherence among such relations within an adjudicative context.
claims.note: Asserts the relational character of evidence ontologically.

claims.claim: Proof denotes the achieved coherence among evidential relations within an adjudicative context.
claims.source_quote: while the latter denotes the achieved coherence among such relations within an adjudicative context.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of proof as relational coherence.

claims.claim: In law, evidence ceases to exist the moment institutional recognition is withdrawn.
claims.source_quote: in law, evidence ceases to exist the moment recognition is withdrawn.
claims.note: Asserts a condition of existence for evidence as an entity dependent on recognition.

claims.claim: The ontology of evidence is inseparable from the institutional structures that confer and maintain its meaning.
claims.source_quote: This dependence on recognition means that the ontology of evidence is inseparable from the institutional structures that confer and maintain its meaning.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive dependence relation between evidence and institutional structures.

claims.claim: Evidence inheres in an information artifact such as a document, photograph, or recording.
claims.source_quote: Inheres in an information artifact (a physical or digital bearer, such as a document, photograph, or recording).
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between evidence (dependent continuant) and its bearer.

claims.claim: Evidence depends on an institutional continuant for its existence as evidence.
claims.source_quote: Depends on an institutional continuant (a court, tribunal, or agency) for its existence as evidence.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependence relation between evidence and institutional continuants.

claims.claim: Evidence is realized through procedural occurrents such as investigation, submission, and evaluation.
claims.source_quote: Is realized through procedural occurrents (investigation, submission, and evaluation).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between evidence and procedural occurrents.

claims.claim: Evidence gains persistence through record artifacts that embody institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Gains persistence through record artifacts (transcripts, exhibits, databases) that embody institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence-conferring relation between evidence and record artifacts.

claims.claim: Record artifacts such as transcripts, exhibits, and databases embody institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: record artifacts (transcripts, exhibits, databases) that embody institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of record artifacts as embodying institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Law is an apparatus of coherence that reconstitutes the shared field of recognition upon which social reality depends.
claims.source_quote: The law, in this sense, is not primarily a set of prohibitions; it is an apparatus of coherence, a system that continuously reconstitutes the shared field of recognition upon which social reality depends.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the nature and function of law as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: Contingent recognition arises in specific encounters, agreements, exchanges, and promises.
claims.source_quote: Contingent recognition arises in specific encounters, agreements, exchanges, promises.
claims.note: Author asserts properties and origins of contingent recognition as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: Institutional recognition embeds local recognition events within enduring structures, giving them generality and continuity.
claims.source_quote: Institutional recognition abstracts from these local events and embeds them within enduring structures, giving them generality and continuity.
claims.note: Asserts a property and relation of institutional recognition as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: A legal contract stabilizes a promise by inscribing it into an institutionally recognized form.
claims.source_quote: The legal contract, for example, stabilizes a promise by inscribing it into an institutionally recognized form.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between legal contract and promise, and a functional property of legal contracts.

claims.claim: Law converts ephemeral interpersonal acts into durable relations that persist independently of the original actors.
claims.source_quote: law converts ephemeral interpersonal acts into durable relations that persist independently of the original actors.
claims.note: Direct assertion about law's ontological function: a transformation relation producing durable entities.

claims.claim: Social coherence is the transformation of transitory acknowledgment into a reproducible structure of recognition.
claims.source_quote: This conversion is the essence of social coherence: the transformation of transitory acknowledgment into a reproducible structure of recognition.
claims.note: Author defines social coherence as an ontological kind constituted by this transformation.

claims.claim: Conflicts of rights, overlapping jurisdictions, and inconsistent precedents are potential ruptures in the network of dependencies that constitutes legal reality.
claims.source_quote: Conflicts of rights, overlapping jurisdictions, inconsistent precedents, each represents a potential rupture in the network of dependencies that constitutes legal reality.
claims.note: Asserts that legal reality is constituted by a network of dependencies and that certain conflicts are ruptures in it.

claims.claim: The institution of adjudication functions to repair ruptures in recognition, restoring coherence by reconciling competing recognitions.
claims.source_quote: The institution of adjudication functions precisely to repair such ruptures, restoring coherence by reconciling competing recognitions.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the institution of adjudication.

claims.claim: Courts realign relations rather than merely applying rules.
claims.source_quote: Courts do not simply apply rules; they realign relations.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of courts as ontological entities.

claims.claim: Judicial judgments are ontological adjustments that reweave the fabric of social reality.
claims.source_quote: Their judgments are ontological adjustments, acts that reweave the fabric of social reality to preserve its structural integrity.
claims.note: Author asserts that judgments are a specific kind of ontological act with a structural function.

claims.claim: Legal reasoning is a form of ontological maintenance.
claims.source_quote: Legal reasoning, in this sense, is a form of ontological maintenance.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind or property relation: legal reasoning is a kind of ontological maintenance.

claims.claim: Authority is a consequence of coherence, not its cause.
claims.source_quote: Authority is not the cause of coherence but its consequence.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/ontological ordering relation between authority and coherence.

claims.claim: An institution is authoritative because it reliably repairs contradictions and sustains recognition relations.
claims.source_quote: An institution is authoritative because it reliably repairs contradictions and sustains recognition relations.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological ground of institutional authority.

claims.claim: The legitimacy of law derives from its ontological efficacy in maintaining the intersubjective fabric of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The legitimacy of law thus derives not from power or tradition alone but from its ontological efficacy, its success in maintaining the intersubjective fabric of recognition upon which social life depends.
claims.note: Asserts that legitimacy has a specific ontological grounding.

claims.claim: A legal system that cannot repair itself ceases to be real in the ontological sense.
claims.source_quote: A legal system that cannot repair itself, that cannot realign fragmented recognitions, ceases to be real in the ontological sense. It becomes a shell, a residue of once-coherent relations.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological condition for the existence of a legal system.

claims.claim: Law is the order from within social life, not an order imposed from above.
claims.source_quote: Traditional theories describe law as enforcing order from above; ontology shows that law is the order from within.
claims.note: Author asserts law's ontological character as internally generated order.

claims.claim: Social stability is an emergent property of the ontological structure of law.
claims.source_quote: Social stability is thus an emergent property of the ontological structure of law.
claims.note: Asserts a property relation: social stability is emergent from and dependent on law's ontological structure.

claims.claim: Crises of legitimacy in legal and political systems are ontological crises of recognition coherence.
claims.source_quote: The crises of legitimacy that mark political and legal systems are therefore ontological crises, failures of recognition coherence that manifest as institutional decay.
claims.note: Asserts that legitimacy crises are a kind of ontological crisis.

claims.claim: Institutions exist to detect, mediate, and correct disruptions in recognition relations.
claims.source_quote: Institutions, in this light, can be understood as repair structures. They exist to detect, mediate, and correct disruptions in recognition relations.
claims.note: Asserts a function and role of institutions as a kind.

claims.claim: Legislatures repair gaps or ambiguities in norms.
claims.source_quote: Legislatures repair gaps or ambiguities in norms; courts repair conflicts of interpretation; administrative bodies repair mismatches between general norms and specific cases.
claims.note: Asserts functional roles of specific institutional kinds.

claims.claim: Courts repair conflicts of interpretation.
claims.source_quote: courts repair conflicts of interpretation
claims.note: Asserts a specific functional property of courts.

claims.claim: Administrative bodies repair mismatches between general norms and specific cases.
claims.source_quote: administrative bodies repair mismatches between general norms and specific cases.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of administrative bodies.

claims.claim: Enforcement agencies perform repair by aligning behavior with recognized obligations.
claims.source_quote: Even enforcement agencies perform repair by aligning behavior with recognized obligations.
claims.note: Asserts a function of enforcement agencies as a kind of repair structure.

claims.claim: Every act of legal repair produces new entities—judgments, precedents, amended statutes—that enter the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Every act of legal repair produces new entities, judgments, precedents, amended statutes, that enter the field of recognition as fresh continuants.
claims.note: Asserts that legal repair generates new ontological entities (continuants) within the recognition field.

claims.claim: Law repairs itself by creating new layers of coherence, building resilience through redundancy and interconnection.
claims.source_quote: Law repairs itself by creating new layers of coherence, building resilience through redundancy and interconnection.
claims.note: Asserts a self-repair property of law as an ontological system.

claims.claim: Contradictions occur when recognition relations become incompatible and cannot coexist.
claims.source_quote: Contradictions occur when recognition relations become incompatible, when two validly recognized obligations, rights, or authorities cannot coexist.
claims.note: Asserts a definition/property of contradiction as an ontological state within legal systems.

claims.claim: Contradiction is the ontological equivalent of logical inconsistency: a state in which dependencies defining entities cannot hold simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Contradiction is the ontological equivalent of conflict or inconsistency in logic: a state in which the dependencies that define entities can no longer hold simultaneously.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological characterization of contradiction.

claims.claim: Through adjudication, amendment, and reinterpretation, law continually converts contradiction into restored coherence.
claims.source_quote: Through adjudication, amendment, and reinterpretation, law continually converts contradiction into restored coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of law as an ongoing ontological process.

claims.claim: Public promulgation is an ontological requirement for law, not merely a procedural one.
claims.source_quote: Public promulgation is thus an ontological requirement, not merely a procedural one.
claims.note: Asserts that publicity is an ontological necessity for law to function as a recognition system.

claims.claim: Recognition depends on accessibility and must be shared to be sustained.
claims.source_quote: Recognition depends on accessibility; to be sustained, it must be shared.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition (property) of recognition as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: Law is a medium through which social recognition becomes collectively manifest.
claims.source_quote: Law is not only a system of norms but a medium through which social recognition becomes collectively manifest.
claims.note: Asserts that law has the ontological role of a medium for collective recognition.

claims.claim: Constitutions are ontological blueprints that specify the hierarchy of dependencies maintaining systemic coherence.
claims.source_quote: Constitutions, in this sense, are not just political instruments but ontological blueprints: they specify the hierarchy of dependencies that maintain systemic coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property/kind attribution for constitutions.

claims.claim: When institutional hierarchies collapse, the ontology of law destabilizes and social reality unravels.
claims.source_quote: When these hierarchies collapse, when institutions refuse to recognize one another's authority or when rules conflict beyond repair, the ontology of law destabilizes. The result is not mere disobedience but ontological disintegration.
claims.note: Asserts causal/ontological consequences of hierarchical collapse.

claims.claim: Ontological disintegration of law is the unraveling of the field of recognition that constitutes social being.
claims.source_quote: ontological disintegration: the unraveling of the field of recognition that constitutes social being.
claims.note: Asserts the nature of ontological disintegration as a specific ontological state.

claims.claim: Law's reality has an architecture composed of a lattice of possibilities underlying every command, principle, and act of justice.
claims.source_quote: to describe the architecture of law's reality, the lattice of possibilities that underlies every command, every principle, and every act of justice.
claims.note: The author asserts that law's reality has a specific architectural structure, an ontological claim about the nature of legal reality.

claims.claim: Phenomenology reveals how law is experienced and constituted through acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Phenomenology reveals how law is experienced and constituted through acts of recognition; ontology reveals the structures that make such recognition possible.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/function of phenomenology in relation to law and recognition—an ontological claim about the constitutive role of recognition.

claims.claim: Ontology reveals the structures that make recognition of law possible.
claims.source_quote: ontology reveals the structures that make such recognition possible.
claims.note: Asserts that law has underlying structures enabling recognition—an ontological claim about law's structural conditions.

claims.claim: Law is both experienced meaning and formal architecture—a structured field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: they offer a unified picture of law as both experienced meaning and formal architecture: a structured field of recognition that bridges subjective participation and objective order.
claims.note: The author asserts what kind of entity law is: a structured field bridging subjective and objective dimensions.

claims.claim: Social acts such as promising and commanding generate real, enduring entities: obligations, rights, and permissions.
claims.source_quote: Reinach extended this analysis to the juridical realm, demonstrating that social acts such as promising and commanding generate real, enduring entities, obligations, rights, permissions, that shape social reality.
claims.note: The author endorses Reinach's finding that obligations, rights, and permissions are real, enduring entities produced by social acts.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, and permissions are entities that shape social reality.
claims.source_quote: social acts such as promising and commanding generate real, enduring entities, obligations, rights, permissions, that shape social reality.
claims.note: Asserts that these normative entities have a causal/structural role in social reality—an ontological property claim.

claims.claim: Institutions are continuants that persist through time.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are continuants that persist through time; trials and legislative sessions are occurrents that realize functions; obligations and rights are dependent continuants inhering in persons and roles.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological category of institutions within BFO as a positive claim about legal ontology.

claims.claim: Trials and legislative sessions are occurrents that realize functions.
claims.source_quote: trials and legislative sessions are occurrents that realize functions
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and role-bearing property of legal processes.

claims.claim: Obligations and rights are dependent continuants inhering in persons and roles.
claims.source_quote: obligations and rights are dependent continuants inhering in persons and roles.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind (dependent continuant) and inherence relation of obligations and rights.

claims.claim: A statute is an information artifact that realizes a norm.
claims.source_quote: A statute, for instance, can be treated as an information artifact that realizes a norm
claims.note: Author presents this as how statutes are to be modeled, implying ontological commitment; 'can be treated' introduces slight hedging.

claims.claim: A court is an institutional continuant that performs adjudicative functions.
claims.source_quote: a court as an institutional continuant that performs adjudicative functions
claims.note: Asserted as part of the author's ontological modeling of law; slight hedging from modeling language.

claims.claim: A trial is an occurrent through which obligations are realized or extinguished.
claims.source_quote: a trial as an occurrent through which obligations are realized or extinguished.
claims.note: Asserted within the author's endorsed ontological framework for law.

claims.claim: Recognition is the constitutive act through which law comes into being.
claims.source_quote: From the phenomenological side, recognition is the constitutive act through which law comes into being
claims.note: The author asserts the constitutive ontological role of recognition for law's existence.

claims.claim: Law exists in the field generated by mutual acknowledgment among agents, roles, and rules.
claims.source_quote: Law exists not in isolated norms or institutions but in the field generated by mutual acknowledgment among agents, roles, and rules.
claims.note: A direct positive ontological claim about where and how law exists.

claims.claim: The field of law has both subjective and objective dimensions.
claims.source_quote: This field has both subjective and objective dimensions: it is experienced by participants as legitimacy and obligation, and it is modeled by ontologists as a structure of continuants and occurrents.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the legal field—that it has dual subjective and objective dimensions.

claims.claim: When a legislature enacts a statute, new dependent continuants (obligations, rights) enter the legal field.
claims.source_quote: When a legislature enacts a statute, it creates new dependent continuants (obligations, rights) that enter the field.
claims.note: Asserts that legislative acts create ontologically categorized entities—a claim about what legal acts produce.

claims.claim: Legal systems exist because of recognition, not independently of it.
claims.source_quote: Unlike physical systems, which persist independently of recognition, legal systems exist because of it.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the mode of existence of legal systems, contrasted with physical systems.

claims.claim: Legal structures possess stability through institutional embodiment.
claims.source_quote: unlike mere conventions, which dissolve when belief wanes, legal structures possess stability through institutional embodiment.
claims.note: Asserts a property (stability via institutional embodiment) of legal structures as entities.

claims.claim: Institutions are relatively independent continuants that endure as social structures.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are relatively independent continuants, enduring social structures that can sustain recognition even when individual beliefs vary.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and property of institutions.

claims.claim: Norms and obligations are dependent continuants that exist only as long as necessary relations among agents and institutions obtain.
claims.source_quote: Norms and obligations are dependent continuants, entities that exist only as long as the necessary relations among agents and institutions obtain.
claims.note: Asserts ontological kind and existential condition of norms and obligations.

claims.claim: Law's coherence is normative and relational rather than metabolic.
claims.source_quote: The difference is that law's coherence is normative and relational rather than metabolic.
claims.note: Asserts a distinctive property of law's coherence as an organized system.

claims.claim: Law is an organized system of dependencies oriented toward coherence.
claims.source_quote: Law, like life, is an organized system of dependencies oriented toward coherence.
claims.note: Direct ontological characterization of law as a kind of system with a telic orientation.

claims.claim: The entities modeled in legal ontology are formalizations of what participants in legal life actually live and recognize.
claims.source_quote: the entities we model are not abstractions detached from experience but formalizations of what participants in legal life actually live and recognize.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal ontological entities—that they are grounded in lived experience, not mere abstractions.

claims.claim: Evidence is an information-bearing dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: evidence belongs to the class of information-bearing dependent continuants, entities that exist only through recognition and serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of evidence as a kind of dependent continuant.

claims.claim: Information-bearing dependent continuants exist only through recognition.
claims.source_quote: evidence belongs to the class of information-bearing dependent continuants, entities that exist only through recognition and serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.note: Asserts a property (existence-dependence on recognition) of this class of entities.

claims.claim: Information-bearing dependent continuants serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.source_quote: entities that exist only through recognition and serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational role of the class.

claims.claim: Evidence is made through processes of recognition and contextualization, not simply found in the world.
claims.source_quote: Evidence, unlike raw data, is not simply found in the world; it is made through processes of recognition and contextualization.
claims.note: Asserts a property and genesis condition of evidence as an entity.

claims.claim: A physical or informational entity becomes evidence only when a legal institution interprets and integrates it within juridical relevance.
claims.source_quote: A fingerprint, a video recording, or a witness's statement becomes evidence only when a legal institution interprets and integrates it within the field of juridical relevance.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between evidence and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Evidence is a recognized information artifact carrying content conferred a specific epistemic function within law.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, therefore, evidence is a recognized information artifact: a material or digital continuant carrying content that has been conferred a specific epistemic function within law's framework.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification and property-ascription.

claims.claim: Data are information content entities that exist independently of their use or recognition.
claims.source_quote: Data are information content entities that exist independently of their use or recognition. They are mere representations or traces of events, measurements, recordings, or stored signals, whose significance is not yet defined.
claims.note: Ontological classification of data with a distinguishing property.

claims.claim: Testimony is a speech act occurrent.
claims.source_quote: Testimony, by contrast, is a speech act occurrent: a process through which an agent conveys information, intending recognition by others.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of testimony as a kind of occurrent.

claims.claim: Testimony is realized in time through performance.
claims.source_quote: Testimony may generate data (as in transcripts or recordings) but is itself transient, realized in time through performance.
claims.note: Asserts a property (temporal realization/transience) of testimony.

claims.claim: Evidence bears a dependent continuant called evidential weight that exists only within the system of institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Evidence, in this sense, is data with juridical status: it bears a specific dependent continuant, evidential weight, that exists only within the system of recognition defined by procedural rules and institutional authority.
claims.note: Asserts that evidential weight is a dependent continuant borne by evidence and dependent on institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Proof is not an entity but a state of institutional coherence.
