claims.claim: Recognition is the formative cause of law.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is not simply a prerequisite for law but its formative cause.
claims.note: Asserts a causal-constitutive relation between recognition and law's existence.

claims.claim: Recognition transforms potentialities into actualities.
claims.source_quote: It transforms potentialities into actualities, possibilities into realities.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition effects an ontological transition from potentiality to actuality.

claims.claim: Law is constructed through human acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law is constructed in the sense that it arises through human acts of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that human acts of recognition are the constructive origin of law.

claims.claim: Acts of recognition generate enduring entities that constrain future possibilities.
claims.source_quote: it is real in the sense that those acts generate enduring entities that constrain future possibilities.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition-generated entities have constraining causal power over future states.

claims.claim: A recognized institution exists independently of the individuals who recognized it.
claims.source_quote: The recognition of a court's jurisdiction, for instance, creates a continuing structure that exists independently of the individuals who recognized it.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological independence of institutions from their founding recognizers.

claims.claim: Institutions achieve temporal endurance through recursive recognition.
claims.source_quote: Institutions thus achieve temporal endurance not through physical permanence but through recursive recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the mechanism by which institutions persist through time.

claims.claim: Institutions stabilize momentary acts of recognition, embedding them in durable structures.
claims.source_quote: They stabilize the fragile, momentary acts through which obligations and authorities are created, embedding them in durable structures that outlast their founders.
claims.note: Asserts a stabilizing and embedding function of institutions with respect to recognition acts.

claims.claim: Institutions are repositories of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are the repositories of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of institutions with respect to recognition.

claims.claim: Institutions act as memory for recognition, preserving its effects across time.
claims.source_quote: Institutions thus act as memory for recognition, preserving its effects across time.
claims.note: Asserts that institutions have a memory-like function regarding recognition's ontological effects.

claims.claim: The institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes such as elections, sessions, and rulings.
claims.source_quote: The institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes, elections, sessions, rulings, that continually reaffirm its place in the ontology of the social world.
claims.note: Asserts that ongoing processes maintain institutional being.

claims.claim: Time is an intrinsic feature of law's ontology, not merely a background dimension.
claims.source_quote: Time, for law, is not a background dimension but an intrinsic feature of its ontology.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive property of law with respect to temporality.

claims.claim: An institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes such as elections, sessions, and rulings.
claims.source_quote: The institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes, elections, sessions, rulings, that continually reaffirm its place in the ontology of the social world.
claims.note: Direct assertion about what sustains the being/existence of institutions — an ontological claim about entities and their maintenance conditions.

claims.claim: Institutions occupy a place in the ontology of the social world.
claims.source_quote: The institution's being is maintained through ongoing processes, elections, sessions, rulings, that continually reaffirm its place in the ontology of the social world.
claims.note: The author asserts that institutions are genuine constituents of the social world's ontology.

claims.claim: Institutions act as memory for recognition, preserving its effects across time.
claims.source_quote: Institutions thus act as memory for recognition, preserving its effects across time.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/property of institutions — they function as memory that preserves recognition effects temporally.

claims.claim: Legal systems survive revolutions, reforms, and reinterpretations because core recognition structures persist.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems survive revolutions, reforms, and reinterpretations because certain core structures of recognition persist even as their material forms change.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal systems (continuity through change) and attributes a causal/explanatory relation to persisting recognition structures.

claims.claim: Core structures of recognition can persist even when their material forms change.
claims.source_quote: certain core structures of recognition persist even as their material forms change.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition structures are a distinct kind of entity separable from material forms, and that they can endure through material change.

claims.claim: The office of 'judge' exists as a recognized role that endures even as its function or authority evolves.
claims.source_quote: The office of 'judge,' for instance, may evolve in function or authority, but its existence as a recognized role endures.
claims.note: Asserts that the judge role is an entity (a recognized role) that has the property of enduring through functional changes.

claims.claim: Recognition links past, present, and future acts into a coherent temporal chain.
claims.source_quote: Recognition links past, present, and future acts into a coherent temporal chain.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of recognition — it connects temporally distinct acts into a unified chain, an ontological claim about relations between acts.

claims.claim: The trial is a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.source_quote: The trial thus functions as a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.note: Direct assertion that the trial bears a specific functional/ontological relation to law's epistemic architecture.

claims.claim: The trial is an ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge.
claims.source_quote: It is the ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge to produce determinate facts.
claims.note: Author asserts the trial has the property of being an ontological space with specific converging elements.

claims.claim: The trial produces determinate facts.
claims.source_quote: It is the ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge to produce determinate facts.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/productive relation between the trial and determinate facts.

claims.claim: Juridical truth has the property of institutional closure.
claims.source_quote: What distinguishes juridical truth from other epistemic forms is its institutional closure.
claims.note: Author plainly asserts that institutional closure is a defining property of juridical truth.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is a subkind of epistemic form.
claims.source_quote: What distinguishes juridical truth from other epistemic forms is its institutional closure.
claims.note: The phrase 'other epistemic forms' implies juridical truth is itself an epistemic form; direct implication of the author's framing.

claims.claim: Scientific and philosophical inquiry is open-ended and always subject to revision.
claims.source_quote: In scientific or philosophical inquiry, the process of verification is open-ended, always subject to revision through further evidence.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of scientific/philosophical inquiry as part of a contrast; stated as a positive claim about those inquiries.

claims.claim: The trial establishes closure through formal recognition.
claims.source_quote: In law, by contrast, the trial establishes closure through formal recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the trial has the function/role of establishing closure via formal recognition.

claims.claim: Once a verdict is rendered, juridical truth is fixed within that institutional world.
claims.source_quote: Once the trier of fact renders a verdict, the truth of the matter, within that institutional world, is fixed regardless of whether it corresponds to empirical reality.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of juridical truth after verdict: it is fixed within the institutional world.

claims.claim: Juridical truth need not correspond to empirical reality.
claims.source_quote: the truth of the matter, within that institutional world, is fixed regardless of whether it corresponds to empirical reality.
claims.note: Author asserts that juridical truth's fixity is independent of correspondence to empirical reality, implying non-necessary correspondence.

claims.claim: The epistemic architecture of law is realized through procedural acts of participants.
claims.source_quote: realized, brought into active expression through the procedural acts of the participants.
claims.note: Author asserts a realization relation between procedural acts and law's epistemic architecture.

claims.claim: The trier of fact's judgment is ontologically subordinate to the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The trier of fact's judgment is ontologically subordinate to the rule of recognition that defines the court's legitimacy, and yet it functions as the proximate source of factual truth within the system.
claims.note: Direct assertion of an ontological subordination relation between two entities.

claims.claim: The trier of fact's judgment is the proximate source of factual truth within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The trier of fact's judgment is ontologically subordinate to the rule of recognition that defines the court's legitimacy, and yet it functions as the proximate source of factual truth within the system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of the trier's judgment.

claims.claim: The verdict is a secondary dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: The verdict is a secondary dependent continuant: its existence depends on the sustained realization of multiple antecedent continuants, evidence, procedure, and institutional authority.
claims.note: Asserts that the verdict is an instance of a specific ontological kind.

claims.claim: The verdict's existence depends on the sustained realization of evidence, procedure, and institutional authority.
claims.source_quote: its existence depends on the sustained realization of multiple antecedent continuants, evidence, procedure, and institutional authority.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between the verdict and multiple antecedent continuants.

claims.claim: The verdict is a relational continuant linking the trier's role, the evidential record, and the institutional context.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, the verdict is a relational continuant linking the trier's role, the evidential record, and the institutional context.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and relational structure of the verdict.

claims.claim: The verdict endures as a recognized entity only as long as its triadic dependency remains coherent.
claims.source_quote: It endures as a recognized entity only as long as this triadic dependency remains coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a condition for the persistence of the verdict as an entity.

claims.claim: When a higher court overturns a verdict, it alters the dependency network that sustains its legal being.
claims.source_quote: When a higher court overturns a verdict, it does not erase the words spoken but alters the dependency network that sustains their legal being.
claims.note: Asserts what the act of overturning does ontologically.

claims.claim: An overturned verdict persists as a historical record but ceases to exist as juridical truth.
claims.source_quote: The earlier verdict persists as a historical record but ceases to exist as juridical truth.
claims.note: Asserts a distinction in modes of existence for the overturned verdict.

claims.claim: The trier of fact occupies the apex of law's epistemic hierarchy.
claims.source_quote: In this way, the trier of fact occupies the apex of law's epistemic hierarchy: it is the institution's capacity for meta-recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property (position) of the trier of fact within a hierarchy.

claims.claim: The trier of fact is the institution's capacity for meta-recognition.
claims.source_quote: it is the institution's capacity for meta-recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a functional identity between the trier of fact and a specific institutional capacity.

claims.claim: The trier of fact determines which recognized entities persist as components of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: The judge or jury does not generate new data but determines which recognized entities shall persist as components of legal reality.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological function of the trier of fact.

claims.claim: The judge is a role continuant whose being depends on the judiciary, the procedural framework, and public recognition.
claims.source_quote: As a role continuant, the judge's being depends on the institution of the judiciary, the procedural framework of adjudication, and the recognition of the public.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of the judge and the entities on which the judge's existence depends.

claims.claim: The judge realizes his role through occurrents of hearing, evaluating, and issuing judgment.
claims.source_quote: The judge realizes this role through occurrents of hearing, evaluating, and issuing judgment.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between the judge's role and specific occurrents.

claims.claim: Each judicial act (hearing, evaluation, judgment) functions as a recognition event.
claims.source_quote: Each of these acts functions as a recognition event: the hearing transforms evidence into deliberative content; evaluation transforms deliberation into finding; judgment transforms finding into legal fact.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological function of each type of judicial act.

claims.claim: The hearing transforms evidence into deliberative content.
claims.source_quote: the hearing transforms evidence into deliberative content
claims.note: Asserts a transformative relation realized by the occurrent of hearing.

claims.claim: Evaluation transforms deliberation into finding.
claims.source_quote: evaluation transforms deliberation into finding
claims.note: Asserts a transformative relational property of the act of evaluation.

claims.claim: Judgment transforms finding into legal fact.
claims.source_quote: judgment transforms finding into legal fact.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative relational property of the act of judgment.

claims.claim: The authority of each judicial transformation derives from the institutional continuant of the court.
claims.source_quote: The authority of each transformation derives from the institutional continuant of the court, which maintains the coherence of recognition across time and cases.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between judicial authority and the court as institutional continuant.

claims.claim: The judge's cognition is ontologically subsumed by the collective recognition that sustains it.
claims.source_quote: The judge's cognition, while individual, is ontologically subsumed by the collective recognition that sustains it.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological subordination relation between individual cognition and collective recognition.

claims.claim: The jury is a collective epistemic structure.
claims.source_quote: The jury, by contrast, represents the trier of fact as a collective epistemic structure.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind/nature of the jury.

claims.claim: The jury's being is the emergent dependent continuant of deliberation.
claims.source_quote: The jury's being is not the aggregate of its members' cognitions but the emergent dependent continuant of deliberation, a single collective role realized through interaction and institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of the jury's existence as emergent and dependent.

claims.claim: The jury exists only as a body constituted by the court.
claims.source_quote: The jury exists only as a body constituted by the court, guided by its instructions, and dissolved upon verdict.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of the jury on the court.

claims.claim: The jury's verdict is a collective realization of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Its verdict is thus a collective realization of recognition, not the expression of individual belief.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of the jury's verdict.

claims.claim: The jurors' private opinions cease to exist as juridical entities once the collective verdict is pronounced.
claims.source_quote: The jurors' private opinions cease to exist as juridical entities once the collective verdict is pronounced.
claims.note: Asserts a cessation of existence of a kind of entity at a particular moment.

claims.claim: The jury is a temporally bounded institution and a transient continuant.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the jury is a temporally bounded institution: a transient continuant whose sole function is to transform evidential relations into the singular fact of a verdict.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and temporal property of the jury.

claims.claim: The jury's sole function is to transform evidential relations into the singular fact of a verdict.
claims.source_quote: a transient continuant whose sole function is to transform evidential relations into the singular fact of a verdict.
claims.note: Asserts the function of the jury as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is a process of realization, not a static correspondence.
claims.source_quote: Both forms of the trier of fact, judicial and jury-based, demonstrate that juridical truth is a process of realization, not a static correspondence.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of juridical truth.

claims.claim: Verdicts rendered by unauthorized tribunals or improperly constituted juries lack legal existence.
claims.source_quote: This explains why verdicts rendered by unauthorized tribunals, corrupt judges, or improperly constituted juries lack legal existence.
claims.note: Asserts that a class of entities lacks a particular mode of existence.

claims.claim: Once rendered by a recognized trier of fact, the verdict becomes part of the enduring ontology of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: Once rendered by a recognized trier of fact, the verdict becomes part of the enduring ontology of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a part-whole relation between a verdict and the legal system's ontology.

claims.claim: Each verdict becomes evidence for future fact-finding.
claims.source_quote: each verdict becomes evidence for future fact-finding, integrating epistemic acts into the temporal fabric of legal being.
claims.note: Asserts a functional transformation of verdicts into evidence, a relational property.

claims.claim: Verdicts are nodes in a continuous network of recognition linking past and future acts of institutional cognition.
claims.source_quote: verdicts are not endpoints but nodes in a continuous network of recognition linking past and future acts of institutional cognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological role and relational position of verdicts within a network.

claims.claim: The trier of fact is the consciousness of law as a structure of being.
claims.source_quote: The trier of fact, in this sense, is the consciousness of law, not as a mind but as a structure of being that transforms the uncertain into the recognized.
claims.note: Asserts a metaphorical but intended ontological identification; qualified by 'not as a mind but as a structure of being.'

claims.claim: The trial is an occurrent that realizes the roles of trial judge, jury, counsel, and witness.
claims.source_quote: From the standpoint of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), the trial is an occurrent that realizes several dependent continuants simultaneously: the roles of trial judge, jury, counsel, and witness...
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of the trial and the realization relations it instantiates.

claims.claim: The trial realizes the functions of adjudication and defense.
claims.source_quote: the trial is an occurrent that realizes several dependent continuants simultaneously: the roles of trial judge, jury, counsel, and witness; the functions of adjudication and defense...
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between the trial and specific functions.

claims.claim: The trial realizes the procedural norms that define valid evidence and reasoning.
claims.source_quote: and the procedural norms that define what counts as valid evidence and reasoning. These dependent continuants exist as relational structures within the institutional continuant of the court.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between the trial and procedural norms.

claims.claim: The dependent continuants realized in a trial exist as relational structures within the institutional continuant of the court.
claims.source_quote: These dependent continuants exist as relational structures within the institutional continuant of the court.
claims.note: Asserts an existential location relation between dependent continuants and the court as institutional continuant.

claims.claim: The trial functions as a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.source_quote: The trial thus functions as a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological function of the trial.

claims.claim: The trial is the ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge to produce determinate facts.
claims.source_quote: It is the ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge to produce determinate facts.
claims.note: Asserts a relational and functional property of the trial as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: Juridical truth has the property of institutional closure that distinguishes it from other epistemic forms.
claims.source_quote: What distinguishes juridical truth from other epistemic forms is its institutional closure.
claims.note: Asserts a distinguishing property of juridical truth as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: The trial is a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.source_quote: The trial thus functions as a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.note: The author directly asserts the trial bears the realization relation to the epistemic architecture of law.

claims.claim: The trial is an ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge.
claims.source_quote: It is the ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge to produce determinate facts.
claims.note: The author asserts the trial is a kind of ontological space with specific converging elements.

claims.claim: The trial produces determinate facts.
claims.source_quote: It is the ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge to produce determinate facts.
claims.note: The author asserts a causal/productive relation between the trial and determinate facts.

claims.claim: Juridical truth has the property of institutional closure.
claims.source_quote: What distinguishes juridical truth from other epistemic forms is its institutional closure.
claims.note: The author asserts institutional closure as a distinguishing property of juridical truth.

claims.claim: Scientific and philosophical inquiry is open-ended and always subject to revision.
claims.source_quote: In scientific or philosophical inquiry, the process of verification is open-ended, always subject to revision through further evidence.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of scientific/philosophical inquiry as part of a direct ontological contrast.

claims.claim: The trial establishes closure through formal recognition.
claims.source_quote: In law, by contrast, the trial establishes closure through formal recognition.
claims.note: The author asserts formal recognition as the mechanism by which the trial produces closure.

claims.claim: Once a verdict is rendered, juridical truth is fixed within the institutional world regardless of correspondence to empirical reality.
claims.source_quote: Once the trier of fact renders a verdict, the truth of the matter, within that institutional world, is fixed regardless of whether it corresponds to empirical reality.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of juridical truth: it is fixed post-verdict and independent of empirical correspondence.

claims.claim: The epistemic architecture of law is realized through the procedural acts of trial participants.
claims.source_quote: realized, brought into active expression through the procedural acts of the participants.
claims.note: The author asserts a realization relation between procedural acts of participants and the epistemic architecture of law.

claims.claim: Valid authority arises when the exercise of power aligns with the institutional structures that confer it.
claims.source_quote: intact and coherent, where the exercise of power aligns with the institutional structures that confer it.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the nature and conditions of valid authority as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: Invalid authority arises when an agent acts outside or against institutional dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Invalid authority, by contrast, arises when an agent acts outside or against those dependencies, severing the relation between role and institution.
claims.note: Direct assertion defining invalid authority and its ontological conditions.

claims.claim: An act performed outside institutional dependencies lacks the ontological status of legality.
claims.source_quote: The act may still have material effects, but ontologically it lacks the status of legality; it fails to instantiate the dependent continuant 'authority.'
claims.note: Asserts a property (lack of legal ontological status) of acts performed outside institutional dependencies.

claims.claim: Authority is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: it fails to instantiate the dependent continuant 'authority.'
claims.note: Asserts that authority belongs to the ontological kind 'dependent continuant'.

claims.claim: Validity is a condition of ontological coherence within the field of recognition, not a moral judgment.
claims.source_quote: Validity, in this sense, is not a moral judgment but a condition of ontological coherence within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property of validity, distinguishing its ontological from moral character.

claims.claim: Authority consists in a set of relations among four entities: agent, role, institution, and norm.
claims.source_quote: we can model authority as a set of relations among four entities: agent, role, institution, and norm.
claims.note: Asserts the relational composition and constituent entities of authority.

claims.claim: An agent realizes a role.
claims.source_quote: The agent realizes a role, the role depends on an institution, and the institution is constrained by norms that define the limits of legitimate recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between agent and role.

claims.claim: A role depends on an institution.
claims.source_quote: The agent realizes a role, the role depends on an institution, and the institution is constrained by norms that define the limits of legitimate recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between role and institution.

claims.claim: An institution is constrained by norms that define the limits of legitimate recognition.
claims.source_quote: the institution is constrained by norms that define the limits of legitimate recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a constraining relation between norms and institution, and a function of norms.

claims.claim: The validity of authority depends on the consistency of the relations among agent, role, institution, and norm.
claims.source_quote: The validity of authority depends on the consistency of these relations.
claims.note: Asserts what authority's validity depends on — a relational consistency condition.

claims.claim: When any link among agent, role, institution, and norm is missing or contradictory, the exercise of power is ontologically defective.
claims.source_quote: When any link is missing or contradictory, the exercise of power becomes ontologically defective.
claims.note: Asserts a property (ontological defectiveness) that attaches to power exercised under broken relational links.

claims.claim: An ontologically defective exercise of power may exist as a social or physical event but not as a legal entity.
claims.source_quote: It may still exist as a social or physical event, but not as a legal entity.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim: defective exercises of power are events but not legal entities.

claims.claim: Authority persists through time even when individual bearers change.
claims.source_quote: Authority persists even when individual bearers change because it inheres in roles that are institutionally defined and reassignable.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of authority over time.

claims.claim: Authority inheres in roles that are institutionally defined and reassignable.
claims.source_quote: it inheres in roles that are institutionally defined and reassignable.
claims.note: Asserts that authority's location is in roles, and that roles have the properties of institutional definition and reassignability.

claims.claim: Authority is a structural continuant that exists by virtue of stable dependencies, not personal attributes.
claims.source_quote: authority, like obligation, is a structural continuant: it exists by virtue of stable dependencies, not personal attributes.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim (structural continuant) and its grounding conditions.

claims.claim: The endurance of authority depends on institutions' capacity to maintain coherence among dependencies across generations.
claims.source_quote: Its endurance depends on institutions' capacity to maintain coherence among these dependencies across generations.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between authority's endurance and institutional capacity.

claims.claim: Delegation is the mechanism of authority's propagation.
claims.source_quote: Delegation, as the mechanism of authority's propagation, is also the mechanism of law's scalability.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/role property of delegation.

claims.claim: Delegation is the mechanism of law's scalability.
claims.source_quote: Delegation, as the mechanism of authority's propagation, is also the mechanism of law's scalability.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of delegation with respect to legal systems.

claims.claim: Delegation distributes the burden of recognition, creating nested hierarchies of authority.
claims.source_quote: Delegation distributes the burden of recognition, creating nested hierarchies of authority that enable coherence at scale.
claims.note: Asserts that delegation has a distributing function and produces nested hierarchical structures.

claims.claim: Each delegation creates a new layer of recognition that extends the system's reach while preserving ontological alignment.
claims.source_quote: Each delegation creates a new layer of recognition, extending the system's reach while preserving ontological alignment.
claims.note: Asserts that delegations produce new recognition layers with specific properties.

claims.claim: Legal order arises from the recursive application of recognition producing authority, and authority enabling further recognition.
claims.source_quote: The complexity of legal order thus arises from the recursive application of the same principle: recognition producing authority, authority enabling further recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the generative ontological structure underlying legal order.

claims.claim: Authority is relational rather than intrinsic.
claims.source_quote: Because authority is relational rather than intrinsic, it is always susceptible to rupture.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental property of authority as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: Authority is always susceptible to rupture because it is relational.
claims.source_quote: Because authority is relational rather than intrinsic, it is always susceptible to rupture.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of authority grounded in its relational nature.

claims.claim: When recognition fails, the dependent continuant 'authority' loses ontological coherence.
claims.source_quote: When recognition fails, when subordinates disobey, citizens withdraw consent, or institutions contradict one another, the dependent continuant 'authority' loses coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a causal-ontological condition under which authority loses coherence.

claims.claim: Rule without recognition is domination, not authority.
claims.source_quote: The resulting condition, rule without recognition, is not authority but domination: the imposition of force without relational grounding.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim: rule without recognition instantiates domination, not authority.

claims.claim: Domination is the imposition of force without relational grounding.
claims.source_quote: rule without recognition, is not authority but domination: the imposition of force without relational grounding.
claims.note: Asserts a defining property of domination as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: Tyranny and anarchy are both failures arising from the disintegration of recognition structures that sustain authority.
claims.source_quote: tyranny and anarchy are mirror failures of ontology: both arise when the structures of recognition that sustain authority disintegrate.
claims.note: Asserts that tyranny and anarchy share a common ontological failure condition.

claims.claim: Judicial review, oversight committees, and chains of appeal function as recursive recognition processes.
claims.source_quote: Judicial review, oversight committees, and chains of appeal function as recursive recognition processes that ensure authority remains aligned with the structures that confer it.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role for legal institutions as recursive recognition processes.

claims.claim: A higher court's affirmation of a decision reasserts the coherence of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: When a decision is appealed, the higher court's affirmation reasserts the coherence of the system.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological function of appellate affirmation.

claims.claim: Overturning a decision repairs a rupture by restoring alignment between norm and institution.
claims.source_quote: when it is overturned, the act of reversal repairs a rupture by restoring alignment between norm and institution.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological function of reversal in legal review processes.

claims.claim: Legal authority is self-correcting due to recursive mechanisms of validation and review.
claims.source_quote: These recursive mechanisms make legal authority self-correcting.
claims.note: Asserts a property (self-correcting) of legal authority as a kind.

claims.claim: Institutions have a capacity called reflective recognition to monitor and repair their own ontological coherence.
claims.source_quote: They exemplify what we might call reflective recognition: the capacity of institutions to monitor and repair their own ontological coherence.
claims.note: Author introduces and endorses the concept, though hedged with 'what we might call'; still an ontological property claim about institutions.

claims.claim: Valid authority is power exercised through a recognized role within the bounds of institutional and normative dependence.
claims.source_quote: Valid authority = power exercised through a recognized role within the bounds of institutional and normative dependence.
claims.note: Direct definitional-ontological assertion summarizing valid authority's structural conditions.

claims.claim: Invalid authority is power exercised outside or against institutional dependencies, producing ontological contradiction.
claims.source_quote: Invalid authority = power exercised outside or against those dependencies, producing ontological contradiction (a breakdown in recognition).
claims.note: Direct definitional-ontological assertion summarizing invalid authority's structural conditions.

claims.claim: The verdict becomes part of law's ontology as an enduring dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: The resulting verdict becomes part of law's ontology, an enduring dependent continuant that anchors subsequent institutional acts such as sentencing, enforcement, or appeal.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts that the verdict is an enduring dependent continuant—a specific ontological claim about the kind of entity a verdict is.

claims.claim: The trial creates facts of law rather than revealing preexisting facts of nature.
claims.source_quote: The experiment seeks to reveal preexisting facts of nature; the trial creates facts of law.
claims.note: The author directly contrasts the ontological status of scientific experiments and legal trials, asserting that trials create new entities.

claims.claim: Each legal judgment constitutes a new entity within the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Each judgment constitutes a new entity within the legal world, a recognized fact with enduring effects.
claims.note: The author asserts that judgments are new entities with enduring effects—an ontological claim about entity creation.

claims.claim: The consensus achieved through trial is a relational continuant distributed across institutions, agents, and artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the consensus achieved through trial is a relational continuant distributed across institutions, agents, and artifacts (records, judgments, laws).
claims.note: The author explicitly makes an ontological claim, categorizing juridical consensus as a relational continuant.

claims.claim: The consensus achieved through trial is a socially instantiated field of coherence that endures through institutional reproduction.
claims.source_quote: It is a socially instantiated field of coherence that endures through institutional reproduction.
claims.note: The author asserts a property and persistence condition for juridical consensus as an ontological entity.

claims.claim: The roles of judge, jury, advocate, and witness are epistemic mechanisms.
claims.source_quote: Within this framework, the roles of participants, such as judge, jury, advocate, and witness, are themselves epistemic mechanisms.
claims.note: The author asserts that participant roles have a specific function (epistemic mechanism)—an ontological claim about the nature of those roles.

claims.claim: The advocate's task is to construct and challenge evidential continuants.
claims.source_quote: The advocate's task is to construct and challenge evidential continuants; the witness's role is to supply data that can be transformed into evidence.
claims.note: The author asserts functional roles for legal participants, with ontological commitment to evidential continuants as entities.

claims.claim: The witness's role is to supply data that can be transformed into evidence.
claims.source_quote: the witness's role is to supply data that can be transformed into evidence
claims.note: Asserts the function of the witness role—an ontological claim about role and function.

claims.claim: The judge's role is to maintain procedural integrity.
claims.source_quote: the judge's is to maintain procedural integrity; and the jury's is to synthesize recognition into a verdict.
claims.note: Asserts the function of the judge's role—an ontological claim about role and function.

claims.claim: The jury's role is to synthesize recognition into a verdict.
claims.source_quote: the jury's is to synthesize recognition into a verdict.
claims.note: Asserts the function of the jury's role—an ontological claim about role and function.

claims.claim: Miscarriages of justice are ontological ruptures—failures of recognition that produce entities that should not exist as legal truths.
claims.source_quote: Miscarriages of justice, in this view, are not simply factual errors but ontological ruptures: failures of recognition that produce entities (verdicts, records, precedents) that should not exist as legal truths.
claims.note: The author asserts that miscarriages of justice are a specific ontological kind (ontological ruptures) and that they produce entities of a defective sort.

claims.claim: Appellate decisions are secondary realization events designed to restore coherence when recognition fails.
claims.source_quote: Appeals, reviews, and retrials are not merely administrative safeguards; they are secondary realization events designed to restore coherence when recognition fails.
claims.note: The author categorizes appellate processes as secondary realization events—an ontological claim about their kind and function.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is conditionally stable, enduring as long as the network of recognition sustaining it remains coherent.
claims.source_quote: Truth in law is not immutable but conditionally stable, enduring as long as the network of recognition that sustains it remains coherent.
claims.note: The author asserts a persistence condition and property (conditional stability) of juridical truth as an ontological claim.

claims.claim: The ethical duty to testify honestly and judge impartially is an ontological condition for juridical truth's existence.
claims.source_quote: The ethical duty to testify honestly, to argue faithfully, and to judge impartially is not an external moral demand but an ontological condition for truth's existence.
claims.note: The author asserts that ethical duties function as ontological conditions—a claim about what juridical truth depends on for its existence.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is a distinct ontological achievement: the manifestation of coherence through procedural recognition.
claims.source_quote: juridical truth is neither illusion nor compromise but a distinct ontological achievement: the manifestation of coherence through procedural recognition.
claims.note: The author asserts that juridical truth is a specific ontological kind with a specific constitutive process.

claims.claim: Trials constitute one of the ways social reality is maintained.
claims.source_quote: Trials do not merely reflect reality; they constitute one of the ways reality is socially maintained.
claims.note: The author asserts that trials have a constitutive relation to social reality—an ontological claim about their role.

claims.claim: Law's ontology depends on recognition rather than direct correspondence with the world.
claims.source_quote: Because law's ontology depends on recognition rather than direct correspondence with the world, the possibility of error is built into its structure.
claims.note: The author asserts a foundational property of legal ontology—dependence on recognition rather than correspondence.

claims.claim: The possibility of error is built into law's ontological structure.
claims.source_quote: Because law's ontology depends on recognition rather than direct correspondence with the world, the possibility of error is built into its structure.
claims.note: The author asserts that fallibility is an intrinsic structural property of law's ontology.

claims.claim: A misrecognition is a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.source_quote: the result is a misrecognition: a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.note: The author defines and asserts misrecognition as a specific ontological failure-kind within legal epistemology.

claims.claim: Uncertainty is internal and necessary to law, not a flaw external to it.
claims.source_quote: we must therefore account for uncertainty not as a flaw external to law, but as an internal and necessary f[eature]
claims.note: The author asserts that uncertainty is an intrinsic property of juridical truth's ontological structure.

claims.claim: The trial is law's analogue to the experiment in science.
claims.source_quote: the trial is law's analogue to the experiment in science, but with a critical difference.
claims.note: The author asserts a structural-functional relation between trial and experiment; the analogy carries ontological commitment about the trial's role in law.

claims.claim: The trial functions as a socially distributed cognitive process producing juridical knowledge.
claims.source_quote: The trial thus functions as a socially distributed cognitive process, producing juridical knowledge through controlled interaction.
claims.note: The author asserts the trial's kind (socially distributed cognitive process) and its product (juridical knowledge).

claims.claim: Law's reality is sustained by collective commitment to recognition, not by discovery.
claims.source_quote: Law's reality is sustained not by discovery but by collective commitment to recognition.
claims.note: The author asserts what sustains legal reality—a direct ontological claim about dependence relations.

claims.claim: Legal systems persist through revolutions and reforms because core structures of recognition endure.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems survive revolutions, reforms, and reinterpretations because certain core structures of recognition persist even as their material forms change.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological basis of legal system persistence.

claims.claim: The office of 'judge' exists as a recognized role that endures despite functional evolution.
claims.source_quote: The office of 'judge,' for instance, may evolve in function or authority, but its existence as a recognized role endures.
claims.note: Asserts the existence and persistence of a specific institutional role.

claims.claim: Recognition links past, present, and future legal acts into a coherent temporal chain.
claims.source_quote: Recognition links past, present, and future acts into a coherent temporal chain.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of recognition connecting temporal acts.

claims.claim: The continuity of law is an ontological achievement consisting in the maintenance of recognition across generations.
claims.source_quote: The continuity of law is thus an ontological achievement: the maintenance of recognition across generations.
claims.note: Asserts what law's continuity fundamentally is, ontologically.

claims.claim: Recognition creates institutions, and institutions sustain recognition.
claims.source_quote: Recognition creates institutions, and institutions, in turn, sustain recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a bidirectional generative relation between recognition and institutions.

claims.claim: When recognition fails, legal entities begin to lose their being.
claims.source_quote: This decay is not merely political but ontological: the entities that depended on those relations begin to lose their being.
claims.note: Asserts that legal entities' existence depends on recognition relations.

claims.claim: A constitution unrecognized ceases to exist as law and becomes a historical artifact.
claims.source_quote: A constitution unrecognized ceases to exist as law; it becomes a historical artifact.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological transformation of a legal entity when recognition fails.

claims.claim: Ontological repair—restoration of coherence within the field of recognition—is the condition for legal renewal.
claims.source_quote: Ontological repair, the restoration of coherence within the field of recognition, is the condition for renewal.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition relation between ontological repair and legal renewal.

claims.claim: Recognition is an occurrent—a process that realizes the potential of agents to enter mutual acknowledgment relations.
claims.source_quote: It is an occurrent, a process that realizes the potential of agents to enter relations of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts recognition's ontological category (occurrent) and its functional role.

claims.claim: Obligations, rights, and offices are dependent continuants that persist after the recognition event.
claims.source_quote: The entities created, obligations, rights, offices, are dependent continuants that persist after the event.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category of these legal entities.

claims.claim: Institutions are independent continuants that house and stabilize dependent legal entities.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are independent continuants that house and stabilize these dependents.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and function of institutions.

claims.claim: Law is a dynamic interplay between occurrents of recognition and the continuants they produce and sustain.
claims.source_quote: The entire structure of law can thus be understood as a dynamic interplay between occurrents of recognition and the continuants they produce and sustain.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure of law in terms of occurrents and continuants.

claims.claim: Recognition is the generative event that gives law being.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is the generative event; institution is the enduring vessel; obligation is the relational product.
claims.note: Asserts recognition's ontological role as generative of legal being.

claims.claim: Institution is the enduring vessel that carries legal being forward in time.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is the generative event; institution is the enduring vessel; obligation is the relational product.
claims.note: Asserts the institution's ontological role as a temporal carrier of legal being.

claims.claim: Obligation is the relational product generated by recognition.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is the generative event; institution is the enduring vessel; obligation is the relational product.
claims.note: Asserts obligation's ontological character as a relational product.

claims.claim: Law's authority depends on enough actors performing relational acknowledgments that sustain its existence, not on unanimous belief.
claims.source_quote: The authority of law does not depend on everyone believing it is legitimate but on enough actors performing the relational acknowledgments that sustain its existence.
claims.note: Asserts what the authority of law ontologically depends on.

claims.claim: Law's durability reflects the density and regularity of recognition relations.
claims.source_quote: Law's durability, therefore, reflects the density and regularity of these recognition relations, not the purity of collective belief.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law—durability—and its ontological basis.

claims.claim: Recognition is the foundation of normativity from a phenomenological standpoint.
claims.source_quote: From a phenomenological standpoint, recognition is also the foundation of normativity.
claims.note: Asserts a foundational relational property: recognition grounds normativity.

claims.claim: Constraints of respect, reciprocity, and non-harm are built into the ontology of personhood.
claims.source_quote: These constraints are not moral ideals layered onto social life; they are built into the ontology of personhood.
claims.note: Asserts that normative constraints are intrinsic properties of the ontology of personhood.

claims.claim: Normativity emerges from being rather than being imposed upon it.
claims.source_quote: Normativity, in this sense, is not imposed upon being but emerges from it.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological relation between normativity and being.

claims.claim: Recognition is the point where the descriptive and the prescriptive converge, where ontology generates obligation.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is the point where the descriptive and the prescriptive converge, where ontology generates obligation.
claims.note: Asserts a convergence relation between ontology and obligation via recognition.

claims.claim: Statutes, court records, treaties, and constitutions serve as material anchors for recognition.
claims.source_quote: Statutes, court records, treaties, and constitutions serve as material anchors for recognition, ensuring that it can be reactivated by new generations.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of legal artifacts in relation to recognition.

claims.claim: Legal artifacts preserve the conditions under which law can continue to exist, but do not contain law by themselves.
claims.source_quote: These artifacts do not contain law by themselves; they preserve the conditions under which law can continue to exist.
claims.note: Asserts a property and a limitation of legal artifacts with respect to law's existence.

claims.claim: Law is a living archive of recognition that endures through renewal.
claims.source_quote: Law, therefore, is a living archive of recognition, a structure that endures through renewal.
claims.note: Asserts what law fundamentally is: a structure constituted by and enduring through recognition.

claims.claim: Every legal act is a crystallization of recognition—a moment when the fabric of relations thickens and takes shape.
claims.source_quote: Every legal act, legislation, judgment, contract, is a crystallization of recognition, a moment when the fabric of relations thickens and takes shape.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of legal acts as crystallizations of recognition.

claims.claim: Obligations attach to roles rather than to individuals as such.
claims.source_quote: Instead, obligations attach to roles. To act legally is to act in virtue of a role, and to bear a legal duty is to do so as the occupant of a structural position within an institution.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental ontological relation: obligation inheres in roles, not bare individuals.

claims.claim: Roles are the bearers of obligation through which institutions connect agents to norms.
claims.source_quote: Roles are the bearers of obligation, the nodes through which institutions connect agents to norms.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological function of roles as bearers and connectors.

claims.claim: Without roles, obligations would have no stable bearers and institutions would collapse into collections of individuals.
claims.source_quote: Without roles, obligations would have no stable bearers, and institutions would collapse into collections of individuals.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary dependence relation between roles and the stability of obligations and institutions.

claims.claim: A role is a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in an agent but depends on an institutional structure for its existence.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, a role is a specifically dependent continuant, an entity that inheres in an agent but depends on an institutional structure for its existence.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and dependency structure of roles.

claims.claim: The role of 'judge' depends on the institution of the judiciary for its existence.
claims.source_quote: The role of 'judge' depends on the institution of the judiciary; the role of 'buyer' depends on the institution of exchange; the role of 'citizen' depends on the political community that recognizes it.
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological dependency between a role and its institutional structure.

claims.claim: The role of 'buyer' depends on the institution of exchange for its existence.
claims.source_quote: The role of 'buyer' depends on the institution of exchange; the role of 'citizen' depends on the political community that recognizes it.
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological dependency between a role and its institutional structure.

claims.claim: The role of 'citizen' depends on the political community that recognizes it.
claims.source_quote: the role of 'citizen' depends on the political community that recognizes it.
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological dependency between a role and its recognizing community.

claims.claim: Roles are relational entities, not psychological identities.
claims.source_quote: These roles are not psychological identities but relational entities.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of roles as relational rather than psychological.

claims.claim: To occupy a role is to inhabit a position within a network of recognition that carries powers, responsibilities, and expectations.
claims.source_quote: To occupy a role is to inhabit a position within a network of recognition, one that carries with it certain powers, responsibilities, and expectations.
claims.note: Asserts properties borne by a role-occupant in virtue of the role.

claims.claim: Obligations inhere in roles rather than directly in agents.
claims.source_quote: Obligations, in turn, inhere in roles rather than directly in agents.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological locus of obligation as roles rather than agents.

claims.claim: When one official retires and another takes office, the obligation transfers because it belongs to the role, not the individual.
claims.source_quote: When one official retires and another takes office, the obligation does not disappear; it transfers seamlessly because it belongs to the role, not the individual.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological basis of obligation transfer between role-occupants.

claims.claim: Moral obligations attach to persons directly as moral agents; legal obligations attach to persons derivatively as role-occupants.
claims.source_quote: Moral obligations attach to persons directly, insofar as they are moral agents; legal obligations attach to them derivatively, insofar as they occupy roles within institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a distinction in ontological mode of attachment between moral and legal obligations.

claims.claim: A judge's decision derives its authority from the institutional relations defining her position, not from personal conviction.
claims.source_quote: Her decision's authority derives from the institutional relations that define her position, not from her personal conviction.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological source of judicial authority.

claims.claim: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.source_quote: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.note: Asserts specific ontological relations: inherence of role in agent, participation of agent in institution.

claims.claim: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.source_quote: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological dependency of obligation on role and institution.

claims.claim: The verdict is an enduring dependent continuant within law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: The resulting verdict becomes part of law's ontology, an enduring dependent continuant that anchors subsequent institutional acts such as sentencing, enforcement, or appeal.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts that the verdict is a kind of entity (enduring dependent continuant) within law's ontological domain.

claims.claim: The trial creates facts of law rather than revealing preexisting facts of nature.
claims.source_quote: The experiment seeks to reveal preexisting facts of nature; the trial creates facts of law. Each judgment constitutes a new entity within the legal world, a recognized fact with enduring effects.
claims.note: The author asserts that trials are fact-creating mechanisms, constituting new entities; this is a positive ontological claim about what trials do.

claims.claim: Each legal judgment constitutes a new entity within the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Each judgment constitutes a new entity within the legal world, a recognized fact with enduring effects.
claims.note: Direct assertion that judgments are entities with enduring effects in the legal world.

claims.claim: The consensus achieved through trial is a relational continuant distributed across institutions, agents, and artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the consensus achieved through trial is a relational continuant distributed across institutions, agents, and artifacts (records, judgments, laws).
claims.note: The author explicitly categorizes trial consensus as a relational continuant — a positive ontological classification.

claims.claim: The consensus achieved through trial is a socially instantiated field of coherence that endures through institutional reproduction.
claims.source_quote: It is a socially instantiated field of coherence that endures through institutional reproduction.
claims.note: Author asserts that trial consensus has a specific ontological character: a socially instantiated field with the property of enduring through institutional reproduction.

claims.claim: Participant roles in a trial (judge, jury, advocate, witness) are epistemic mechanisms.
claims.source_quote: The roles of participants, such as judge, jury, advocate, and witness, are themselves epistemic mechanisms. Each role carries specific functions designed to balance and verify recognition.
claims.note: The author asserts that roles are a kind of epistemic mechanism and bear the property of carrying specific functions.

claims.claim: The advocate's task is to construct and challenge evidential continuants.
claims.source_quote: The advocate's task is to construct and challenge evidential continuants; the witness's role is to supply data that can be transformed into evidence.
claims.note: Author asserts specific functional properties of the advocate role, referencing evidential continuants as entities.

claims.claim: The witness's role is to supply data that can be transformed into evidence.
claims.source_quote: the witness's role is to supply data that can be transformed into evidence
claims.note: Positive assertion about the function of the witness role within the trial's ontology.

claims.claim: The judge's role is to maintain procedural integrity.
claims.source_quote: the judge's is to maintain procedural integrity; and the jury's is to synthesize recognition into a verdict.
claims.note: Direct assertion of the judge's functional role within the institutional process.

claims.claim: The jury's role is to synthesize recognition into a verdict.
claims.source_quote: the jury's is to synthesize recognition into a verdict.
claims.note: Direct assertion of the jury's function as an epistemic mechanism producing verdicts.

claims.claim: Miscarriages of justice are ontological ruptures — failures of recognition that produce entities that should not exist as legal truths.
claims.source_quote: Miscarriages of justice, in this view, are not simply factual errors but ontological ruptures: failures of recognition that produce entities (verdicts, records, precedents) that should not exist as legal truths.
claims.note: Author positively asserts the ontological character of miscarriages of justice, classifying them as a kind (ontological rupture) and describing what entities they produce.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is conditionally stable, enduring as long as the supporting network of recognition remains coherent.
claims.source_quote: Truth in law is not immutable but conditionally stable, enduring as long as the network of recognition that sustains it remains coherent.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of juridical truth — conditional stability — and the relational condition on which it depends.

claims.claim: The ethical duty to testify honestly, argue faithfully, and judge impartially is an ontological condition for juridical truth's existence.
claims.source_quote: The ethical duty to testify honestly, to argue faithfully, and to judge impartially is not an external moral demand but an ontological condition for truth's existence.
claims.note: Author asserts that these duties bear a specific ontological relation to truth — they are conditions of its existence, not merely moral add-ons.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is a distinct ontological achievement: the manifestation of coherence through procedural recognition.
claims.source_quote: juridical truth is neither illusion nor compromise but a distinct ontological achievement: the manifestation of coherence through procedural recognition.
claims.note: The author positively classifies juridical truth as a kind of ontological achievement with a specific character.

claims.claim: Trials constitute one of the ways social reality is maintained.
claims.source_quote: Trials do not merely reflect reality; they constitute one of the ways reality is socially maintained.
claims.note: Direct assertion that trials bear a constitutive relation to social reality.

claims.claim: Misrecognition is a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.source_quote: the result is a misrecognition: a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.note: The author defines and asserts the ontological character of misrecognition as a specific kind of failure state within legal ontology.

claims.claim: Uncertainty in law is internal and necessary to law's structure, not an external flaw.
claims.source_quote: we must therefore account for uncertainty not as a flaw external to law, but as an internal and necessary f[eature]
claims.note: The author asserts a property of law's structure: that uncertainty is intrinsic and necessary to it.

claims.claim: Appeals and retrials are secondary realization events designed to restore coherence when recognition fails.
claims.source_quote: Appeals, reviews, and retrials are not merely administrative safeguards; they are secondary realization events designed to restore coherence when recognition fails.
claims.note: The author positively classifies appeals as a kind (secondary realization events) and asserts their function within the system's ontology.

claims.claim: The trial is a socially distributed cognitive process that produces juridical knowledge through controlled interaction.
claims.source_quote: The trial thus functions as a socially distributed cognitive process, producing juridical knowledge through controlled interaction.
claims.note: Author asserts both the kind (socially distributed cognitive process) and the functional property (producing juridical knowledge) of the trial.

claims.claim: The trial serves as a performative act of collective epistemic alignment.
claims.source_quote: The trial thus serves as a performative act of collective epistemic alignment.
claims.note: Author asserts the trial has the property of being a performative act and classifies its kind as collective epistemic alignment.

claims.claim: Juridical truth's fallibility is built into the structure of law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: Because law's ontology depends on recognition rather than direct correspondence with the world, the possibility of error is built into its structure.
claims.note: Author asserts a structural property of law's ontology — that fallibility is intrinsic to it.

claims.claim: A role inheres in an agent.
claims.source_quote: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts an inherence relation between role and agent as part of the ontological representation.

claims.claim: An agent participates in an institution.
claims.source_quote: The role inheres in the agent, who participates in the institution.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts a participation relation between agent and institution.

claims.claim: An obligation inheres in a role.
claims.source_quote: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts an inherence relation between obligation and role.

claims.claim: An obligation depends on an institution for its continuing validity.
claims.source_quote: The obligation inheres in the role and depends on the institution for its continuing validity.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts a dependency relation between obligation and institution.

claims.claim: The relation between agent, role, and institution forms a chain of ontological dependencies.
claims.source_quote: The relation between agent, role, and institution can be represented ontologically as a chain of dependencies.
claims.note: The author asserts this as an ontological representation, though 'can be represented' introduces slight qualification.

claims.claim: Law functions through roles rather than through the fluctuating intentions of individuals.
claims.source_quote: llows law to function objectively, to speak through roles rather than through the fluctuating intentions of individuals.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/dispositional property of law—that it operates via roles—which carries ontological commitment to roles as the locus of legal agency.

claims.claim: Misrecognition is a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.source_quote: the result is a misrecognition: a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.note: The author defines and asserts a property/functional failure of a kind of entity (misrecognition), constituting an ontological claim about what misrecognition is.

claims.claim: Uncertainty is an internal and necessary feature of law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: we must therefore account for uncertainty not as a flaw external to law, but as an internal and necessary feature of its ontology.
claims.note: The author asserts that uncertainty has a specific ontological status (internal, necessary feature) within law, not merely a methodological point.

claims.claim: Uncertainty arises whenever the dependencies that sustain a legal fact are incomplete or unstable.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, uncertainty arises whenever the dependencies that sustain a legal fact are incomplete or unstable.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological conditions under which uncertainty exists in relation to legal facts.

claims.claim: A verdict is constituted by dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority, must align coherently for juridical truth to exist.
claims.note: The author asserts that verdicts are constituted by dependent continuants, an ontological claim about the composition of a legal entity.

claims.claim: Recognition of evidence is constituted by dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority, must align coherently for juridical truth to exist.
claims.note: The author asserts that recognition of evidence is constituted by dependent continuants, an ontological claim about its composition.

claims.claim: Roles and institutional authority are constituted by dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority, must align coherently for juridical truth to exist.
claims.note: The author asserts that roles and institutional authority are constituted by dependent continuants, an ontological claim about their composition.

claims.claim: Juridical truth exists only when dependent continuants align coherently.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority, must align coherently for juridical truth to exist.
claims.note: The author asserts a necessary condition for the existence of juridical truth, an ontological claim about its dependency structure.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is an entity sustained by dependencies among institutional components.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, uncertainty arises whenever the dependencies that sustain a legal fact are incomplete or unstable.
claims.note: Implied by the claim that legal facts are sustained by dependencies; the author commits to legal facts (juridical truths) as ontologically dependent entities.

claims.claim: Misrecognition is a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.source_quote: the result is a misrecognition: a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.note: The author defines and asserts what misrecognition is as an entity/event with a specific nature.

claims.claim: Uncertainty is an internal and necessary feature of law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: we must therefore account for uncertainty not as a flaw external to law, but as an internal and necessary feature of its ontology.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of uncertainty with respect to legal ontology — it is internal and necessary, not external.

claims.claim: Uncertainty arises whenever the dependencies that sustain a legal fact are incomplete or unstable.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, uncertainty arises whenever the dependencies that sustain a legal fact are incomplete or unstable.
claims.note: The author asserts a causal/ontological condition for uncertainty's existence in the legal domain.

claims.claim: Legal facts are sustained by dependencies.
claims.source_quote: the dependencies that sustain a legal fact are incomplete or unstable.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal facts bear a dependency relation to other entities.

claims.claim: A verdict is constituted by dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority, must align coherently for juridical truth to exist.
claims.note: The author asserts that verdicts are constituted by dependent continuants — an ontological composition claim.

claims.claim: Recognition of evidence is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority...
claims.note: The author classifies recognition of evidence as a dependent continuant — a subkind/category claim.

claims.claim: Roles are dependent continuants within juridical truth.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority...
claims.note: The author classifies roles as dependent continuants — an ontological categorization claim.

claims.claim: Institutional authority is a dependent continuant within juridical truth.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority...
claims.note: The author classifies institutional authority as a dependent continuant — an ontological categorization claim.

claims.claim: Juridical truth exists only when dependent continuants align coherently.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority, must align coherently for juridical truth to exist.
claims.note: The author asserts a necessary condition for the existence of juridical truth — an ontological existence claim.

claims.claim: Valid authority is power exercised through a recognized role within institutional and normative dependence.
claims.source_quote: Valid authority = power exercised through a recognized role within the bounds of institutional and normative dependence.
claims.note: The author defines valid authority in structural/ontological terms, asserting what valid authority is.

claims.claim: Invalid authority is power exercised outside or against institutional dependencies, producing ontological contradiction.
claims.source_quote: Invalid authority = power exercised outside or against those dependencies, producing ontological contradiction (a breakdown in recognition).
claims.note: The author defines invalid authority ontologically, asserting what it is and what it produces.

claims.claim: Authority is justified by the coherence of the recognition structure that confers and sustains it.
claims.source_quote: Authority is not justified by consent alone nor by command alone, but by the coherence of the recognition structure that confers and sustains it.
claims.note: Positive assertion about the ground/property of authority.

claims.claim: Sovereignty is the uppermost level of the recognition hierarchy.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, however, sovereignty is not an isolated substance but the uppermost level of the recognition hierarchy: the meta-institution that organizes and sustains the entire network of dependent roles and norms.
claims.note: Asserts what sovereignty is ontologically — a relational position in a hierarchy.

claims.claim: Sovereignty is a meta-institution that organizes and sustains the network of dependent roles and norms.
claims.source_quote: sovereignty is not an isolated substance but the uppermost level of the recognition hierarchy: the meta-institution that organizes and sustains the entire network of dependent roles and norms.
claims.note: Asserts sovereignty's role/function as a meta-institution.

claims.claim: Sovereignty's legitimacy derives from coherence within the field of recognition, not metaphysical absoluteness.
claims.source_quote: Its legitimacy, like that of any institution, derives from coherence within the field of recognition, not from metaphysical absoluteness.
claims.note: Asserts a property (source of legitimacy) of sovereignty.

claims.claim: When sovereignty becomes detached from recognition, it ceases to be sovereign and becomes mere force.
claims.source_quote: When sovereignty becomes detached from recognition, when rulers claim power without relational grounding, it ceases to be sovereign in the ontological sense and becomes mere force.
claims.note: Asserts a conditional ontological transformation: detached sovereignty loses its kind-membership.

claims.claim: Authority is the connective tissue between obligation and institution.
claims.source_quote: Authority, then, is the connective tissue between obligation and institution.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/structural role for authority between two ontological categories.

claims.claim: Authority is a dependent continuant grounded in role recognition.
claims.source_quote: Understanding authority as a dependent continuant grounded in role recognition reveals law's true structure.
claims.note: Author endorses this characterization of authority as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: Obligations are dependent continuants — enduring relational entities that structure the legal world.
