claims.claim: Ontological resilience corresponds to the system's capacity for rapid, coherent repair.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, resilience corresponds to the system's capacity for rapid, coherent repair.
claims.note: Asserts an identity or correspondence relation between resilience and repair capacity as an ontological claim.

claims.claim: When contradictions outpace repair, the legal system's ontology begins to collapse.
claims.source_quote: When this capacity is lost, when contradictions outpace repair, the system's ontology begins to collapse, and with it, the lived reality of law.
claims.note: Asserts a condition under which a legal system loses ontological coherence.

claims.claim: Legal repair processes depend on public recognition as well as institutional processes.
claims.source_quote: Legal repair processes are not purely internal to institutions; they also depend on public recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between legal repair and public recognition.

claims.claim: A judgment or statute achieves repair only when recognized as valid by affected agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: A judgment or statute achieves repair only when it is recognized as valid by the agents and institutions it affects.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for the repair function of legal occurrents.

claims.claim: Recognition converts adjudication or legislation into a new stable configuration of continuants.
claims.source_quote: This recognition closes the repair loop, converting the occurrent (adjudication or legislation) into a new stable configuration of continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative relation: recognition converts occurrents into stable continuant configurations.

claims.claim: A judgment ignored or a statute unenforced is an incomplete occurrent and an unrealized repair.
claims.source_quote: a judgment ignored or a statute unenforced remains an incomplete occurrent, an unrealized repair.
claims.note: Asserts ontological kind membership: unrecognized legal acts are incomplete occurrents.

claims.claim: Recognition is both the starting and ending condition of legal repair.
claims.source_quote: recognition is both the starting and ending condition of legal repair, it defines the field within which contradictions arise and provides the medium through which coherence is restored.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition has a dual structural role (start and end condition) in the repair process.

claims.claim: Adjudication and legislation are ontological events through which law sustains its own being.
claims.source_quote: These processes are not merely functional or procedural; they are ontological events through which law sustains its own being.
claims.note: Asserts that adjudication and legislation are instances of the kind 'ontological event' with a self-sustaining function.

claims.claim: Each judgment and each act of legislation is a moment in the perpetual reconstitution of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: Each judgment, each act of legislation, is a moment in the perpetual reconstitution of legal reality.
claims.note: Asserts that individual legal acts are parts of the ongoing reconstitution process.

claims.claim: Law's endurance consists in continuous ontological labor—the ongoing repair of relations binding obligation, recognition, and authority.
claims.source_quote: Law's endurance, therefore, is not a matter of institutional inertia but of continuous ontological labor, the ongoing repair of the relations that bind obligation, recognition, and authority into a coherent whole.
claims.note: Asserts what law's endurance essentially is, an ontological characterization.

claims.claim: Law's persistence depends on the continued coherence of the recognition relations that constitute its ontology.
claims.source_quote: Its persistence depends on the continued coherence of the recognition relations that constitute its ontology.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between legal persistence and recognition-relation coherence.

claims.claim: Institutional collapse is the ontological disintegration of the field of recognition that sustains social being.
claims.source_quote: The result is institutional collapse: not merely the breakdown of governance, but the ontological disintegration of the field of recognition that sustains social being.
claims.note: Asserts what institutional collapse ontologically is.

claims.claim: Even amid collapse, traces of law persist, enabling continuity and repair.
claims.source_quote: Yet even amid collapse, traces of law persist, enabling continuity and repair.
claims.note: Asserts existence of persisting legal traces and their enabling function during collapse.

claims.claim: Institutional persistence depends on the stability of core continuants and the resilience of dependencies connecting them.
claims.source_quote: institutional persistence depends on the stability of certain core continuants and the resilience of the dependencies that connect them.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between institutional persistence and continuant stability.

claims.claim: Institutions exist as structured continuants composed of roles, obligations, and processes, each dependent on recognition.
claims.source_quote: Institutions exist as structured continuants composed of roles, obligations, and processes, each dependent on recognition within a broader system.
claims.note: Asserts ontological kind (structured continuant) and compositional relations for institutions.

claims.claim: Institutional collapse occurs when role-defining dependencies are no longer satisfied or mutual recognition ceases.
claims.source_quote: Collapse occurs when these dependencies are no longer satisfied, when the roles that define an institution lose their bearers or when mutual recognition among institutions ceases.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions under which institutions ontologically collapse.

claims.claim: Institutional continuity is achieved when recognition is maintained or successfully transferred to new bearers or structures.
claims.source_quote: Continuity, by contrast, is achieved when recognition is maintained or successfully transferred to new bearers or structures.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological condition for institutional continuity.

claims.claim: Law's durability depends on the ongoing realization of recognition relations at multiple levels of the institutional hierarchy.
claims.source_quote: Law's durability across time and upheaval thus depends less on material resources or political will than on the ongoing realization of recognition relations at multiple levels of the institutional hierarchy.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between legal durability and the realization of recognition relations.

claims.claim: A functioning institution requires recognized roles as dependent continuants inhering in agents.
claims.source_quote: Recognized roles (dependent continuants inhering in agents).
claims.note: Asserts that recognized roles are dependent continuants with an inherence relation to agents.

claims.claim: A functioning institution requires an institutional structure as a network of dependencies among roles.
claims.source_quote: Institutional structure (a network of dependencies among roles).
claims.note: Asserts that institutional structure is a network of dependency relations among roles.

claims.claim: A functioning institution requires active processes as occurrents that realize institutional functions.
claims.source_quote: Active processes (occurrents that realize institutional functions).
claims.note: Asserts that active institutional processes are occurrents bearing a realization relation to institutional functions.

claims.claim: A functioning institution requires sustaining recognition linking it to other institutions and to the public.
claims.source_quote: Sustaining recognition (a field of acknowledgment linking the institution to others and to the public).
claims.note: Asserts that sustaining recognition is a relational field connecting an institution to others and the public.

claims.claim: The trier of fact is an ontologically structured role.
claims.source_quote: It is an ontologically structured role, instantiated in persons who are empowered by institutions to generate legal truth under specified procedural conditions.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological category of the trier of fact.

claims.claim: The trier of fact role is instantiated in persons.
claims.source_quote: It is an ontologically structured role, instantiated in persons who are empowered by institutions to generate legal truth under specified procedural conditions.
claims.note: Asserts an instantiation relation between the role and persons.

claims.claim: Persons bearing the trier of fact role are empowered by institutions to generate legal truth.
claims.source_quote: instantiated in persons who are empowered by institutions to generate legal truth under specified procedural conditions.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional/functional property of role-bearers conferred by institutions.

claims.claim: Any legal system includes roles of those subject to the law.
claims.source_quote: any legal system is incomplete without the roles of those who are subject to the law. These include citizens, residents, offenders, and other categories of ruled persons.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of subject roles as necessary components of legal systems.

claims.claim: Citizens, residents, and offenders are kinds of ruled persons.
claims.source_quote: These include citizens, residents, offenders, and other categories of ruled persons, whose legal identity entails not only being governed, but also participating in institutional structures.
claims.note: Asserts subkind relations between specific roles and the category of ruled persons.

claims.claim: The legal identity of ruled persons entails participating in institutional structures through rights, responsibilities, protections, and vulnerabilities.
claims.source_quote: whose legal identity entails not only being governed, but also participating in institutional structures through rights, responsibilities, protections, and vulnerabilities.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive property of the legal identity of ruled persons.

claims.claim: The citizen role is a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in a person.
claims.source_quote: a role such as 'citizen' is modeled as a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in a person and is realized within a legal and institutional framework.
claims.note: Directly asserts ontological category and inherence relation for the citizen role.

claims.claim: The citizen role is realized within a legal and institutional framework.
claims.source_quote: a role such as 'citizen' is modeled as a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in a person and is realized within a legal and institutional framework.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between the citizen role and a legal-institutional framework.

claims.claim: The citizen role is not an intrinsic biological property.
claims.source_quote: It is not an intrinsic biological property, nor a transient behavior, but a status that exists in virtue of a social act.
claims.note: Asserts a negative ontological property distinguishing the citizen role from biological properties.

claims.claim: The citizen role exists in virtue of a social act such as birth, naturalization, or legal recognition.
claims.source_quote: a status that exists in virtue of a social act, for example, birth, naturalization, or recognition under immigration law.
claims.note: Asserts the grounding condition for the existence of the citizen role.

claims.claim: The citizen role confers normative powers and normative exposure.
claims.source_quote: The citizen role confers both normative powers and normative exposure: the power to vote, the protection of rights, the liability to prosecution.
claims.note: Asserts functional/dispositional properties conferred by the citizen role.

claims.claim: The offender role is a legally defined role instantiated through a verdict rendered by a trier of fact.
claims.source_quote: being an 'offender' does not refer to a psychological trait or past event alone, it is a legally defined role, typically instantiated through a verdict rendered by a trier of fact and made effective by a sentence.
claims.note: Asserts ontological category and instantiation conditions for the offender role.

claims.claim: The offender role is made effective by a sentence.
claims.source_quote: it is a legally defined role, typically instantiated through a verdict rendered by a trier of fact and made effective by a sentence.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between the offender role and a sentence as its activating condition.

claims.claim: A role is a specifically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: The role is a specifically dependent continuant.
claims.note: Direct assertion of ontological category for roles in BFO-based legal ontology.

claims.claim: A legal process is an occurrent involving institutional agents.
claims.source_quote: The process is an occurrent involving institutional agents.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category of legal processes.

claims.claim: A social act is a speech act or formal declaration.
claims.source_quote: The social act is a speech act or formal declaration (e.g., swearing-in).
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation between social acts and speech acts/formal declarations.

claims.claim: A legal fact is an information artifact.
claims.source_quote: The legal fact is an information artifact (e.g., ID card, verdict document, registry entry).
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category of legal facts as information artifacts.

claims.claim: A person may occupy different roles at different stages of life or legal process.
claims.source_quote: A person may occupy different roles at different stages of life or legal process: 'minor,' 'citizen,' 'defendant,' 'probationer,' 'expatriate.'
claims.note: Asserts a temporal variability property of persons with respect to role-bearing.

claims.claim: Role transitions are instantiated by institutional acts.
claims.source_quote: These transitions can be represented as role-lifecycle events, each instantiated by institutional acts and associated with specific normative consequences.
claims.note: Asserts that institutional acts are the instantiating conditions for role-lifecycle transitions.

claims.claim: Role transitions are associated with specific normative consequences.
claims.source_quote: each instantiated by institutional acts and associated with specific normative consequences.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between role transitions and normative consequences.

claims.claim: A criminal trial is an occurrent with temporal parts.
claims.source_quote: Trial: Occurrent (process with temporal parts)
claims.note: Directly asserts the ontological category of a criminal trial.

claims.claim: A court is an institutional aggregate.
claims.source_quote: Court: Institutional aggregate
claims.note: Directly asserts the ontological category of a court.

claims.claim: Testimony, evidence, and verdict are information artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Testimony, Evidence, Verdict: Information artifacts.
claims.note: Directly asserts the ontological category of testimony, evidence, and verdict.

claims.claim: The defendant becomes an offender upon conviction.
claims.source_quote: The defendant becomes an offender upon conviction.
claims.note: Asserts a role transition relation triggered by the event of conviction.

claims.claim: The jury ceases to be active upon delivery of the verdict.
claims.source_quote: The jury ceases to be active upon delivery of the verdict.
claims.note: Asserts a property change (deactivation) of the jury role upon a specific event.

claims.claim: The judge's role shifts from trial management to sentencing authority upon conviction.
claims.source_quote: The judge's role shifts from trial management to sentencing authority.
claims.note: Asserts a role-function transition for the judge within the trial process.

claims.claim: Role transitions involve realizable continuants being activated or deactivated via institutional action.
claims.source_quote: Each of these transitions involves realizable continuants being activated or deactivated in time, via institutional action.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological mechanism underlying legal role transitions.

claims.claim: Roles in a criminal trial are specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Roles: Specifically dependent continuants
claims.note: Directly asserts the ontological category of legal roles in trial context.

claims.claim: When relations among agents, norms, and institutions are coherent, responsive, and repairable, the system is just.
claims.source_quote: When the relations among agents, norms, and institutions are coherent, responsive, and repairable, the system is just.
claims.note: Direct assertion attributing the property of justice to a legal system based on relational coherence.

claims.claim: When relational structures fracture or ossify, injustice appears as ontological dissonance.
claims.source_quote: When those relations fracture or ossify, injustice appears as ontological dissonance.
claims.note: Asserts that injustice has the character of ontological dissonance and is caused by fractured relations.

claims.claim: Justice is immanent to law, not external or merely internal.
claims.source_quote: On the structural view, justice is neither external nor internal, it is immanent. It is the very condition of law's being.
claims.note: Asserts a property/relation: justice is the immanent condition of law's being.

claims.claim: Justice is the very condition of law's being.
claims.source_quote: It is the very condition of law's being.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive ontological relation between justice and law's existence.

claims.claim: Law cannot exist without coherence.
claims.source_quote: Law cannot exist without coherence, and coherence, when reflexive and repairable, is justice itself.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for law's existence: coherence.

claims.claim: Coherence, when reflexive and repairable, is justice itself.
claims.source_quote: coherence, when reflexive and repairable, is justice itself.
claims.note: Asserts an identity: reflexive, repairable coherence is identical to justice.

claims.claim: Justice is the integrity of recognition within a legal system.
claims.source_quote: The approach described in this book redefines justice as the integrity of recognition, the measure of how well a legal system sustains coherent relations among its dependent continuants.
claims.note: Direct definitional assertion identifying justice with a specific ontological property.

claims.claim: Justice measures how well a legal system sustains coherent relations among its dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: the measure of how well a legal system sustains coherent relations among its dependent continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of justice as a measure of relational coherence among dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Legal systems have dependent continuants as their constituents.
claims.source_quote: the measure of how well a legal system sustains coherent relations among its dependent continuants.
claims.note: Commits to dependent continuants as an ontological category present within legal systems.

claims.claim: Justice is what law is when it functions properly as a coherent, reflexive system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Justice is not something law ought to achieve; it is what law is when it functions properly as a coherent, reflexive system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts an identity: justice is the proper functioning state of law as a coherent, reflexive recognition system.

claims.claim: Injustice is the loss of structural integrity and the breakdown of recognition across institutions and roles.
claims.source_quote: injustice is the loss of structural integrity, the breakdown of recognition across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Asserts what injustice is: a specific ontological condition of structural breakdown.

claims.claim: An authoritarian system collapses into rigid closure, losing reflexivity and accumulating contradiction debt.
claims.source_quote: When a system becomes authoritarian, it collapses into rigid closure, losing reflexivity and accumulating contradiction debt.
claims.note: Asserts properties and conditions of authoritarian legal systems.

claims.claim: An anomic system dissolves into incoherence.
claims.source_quote: When it becomes anomic, it dissolves into incoherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property/condition of anomic legal systems.

claims.claim: Repair is ontological reconstruction, not merely moral correction.
claims.source_quote: Repair, therefore, is not moral correction but ontological reconstruction.
claims.note: Asserts the nature of legal repair as an ontological rather than moral act.

claims.claim: Repair restores the coherence that allows recognition and hence law to exist.
claims.source_quote: To repair is to restore the coherence that allows recognition, and hence law, to exist at all.
claims.note: Asserts a functional relation: repair restores coherence, which is necessary for law's existence.

claims.claim: Justice as structural integrity occupies a metaphysical middle ground between moral unity and procedural morality.
claims.source_quote: Justice, understood as structural integrity, therefore occupies a metaphysical middle ground between Dworkin's moral unity and Fuller's procedural morality.
claims.note: Asserts a locational/relational property of justice as structural integrity in the metaphysical landscape.

claims.claim: Justice is the organized coherence of being that allows law to persist, evolve, and remain real.
claims.source_quote: It is neither narrative nor norm but architecture, the organized coherence of being that allows law to persist, evolve, and remain real.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological identity and function of justice as organized coherence of being.

claims.claim: Justice is the equilibrium by which law continues to exist as law.
claims.source_quote: Justice, in this sense, is not the telos of law but its equilibrium: the form of balance by which law continues to exist as law.
claims.note: Asserts that justice is the equilibrium condition constitutive of law's continued existence.

claims.claim: Legal systems fail when their internal dependencies that constitute legal reality cease to cohere.
claims.source_quote: legal systems fail not merely when their rules are unjust or unpopular, but when the internal dependencies that constitute legal reality cease to cohere.
claims.note: Asserts that internal dependencies constitute legal reality and that their incoherence causes systemic failure.

claims.claim: Internal dependencies constitute legal reality.
claims.source_quote: the internal dependencies that constitute legal reality cease to cohere.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive relation: internal dependencies constitute legal reality.

claims.claim: Legal contradictions are violations of a legal system's ontological commitments concerning authority, validity, jurisdiction, recognition, and time.
claims.source_quote: this approach understands them as violations of a legal system's own ontological commitments concerning authority, validity, jurisdiction, recognition, and time.
claims.note: Asserts what legal contradictions are: violations of ontological commitments.

claims.claim: Coercion without authority is an exercise of legal power by an actor lacking valid authorization.
claims.source_quote: Coercion without authority: the exercise of legal power by an actor who lacks valid authorization to wield it.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type as an ontological condition of legal power without valid authorization.

claims.claim: Exercise of power after invalidation is continued use of legal power after it has been legally withdrawn or nullified.
claims.source_quote: Exercise of power after invalidation: the continued use of a legal power or competence after it has been legally withdrawn or nullified.
claims.note: Defines a contradiction type involving a temporal ontological failure of legal power.

claims.claim: Missing conferral chains occur when legal power cannot be traced through a valid sequence of grants and delegations.
claims.source_quote: Missing conferral chains: situations in which legal power cannot be traced back through a valid sequence of grants and delegations.
claims.note: Asserts the existence and nature of a structural defect in conferral relations.

claims.claim: Validity conflicts occur when a legal rule is simultaneously treated as both valid and invalid within the system.
claims.source_quote: Validity conflicts: cases in which a legal rule or regulation is simultaneously treated as both valid and invalid within the system.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving conflicting validity statuses.

claims.claim: Status conflicts occur when an entity occupies mutually exclusive legal statuses simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Status conflicts: circumstances in which an entity is made to occupy mutually exclusive legal statuses at the same time.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving incompatible legal statuses.

claims.claim: Persistence violations occur when legal facts meant to endure disappear without a terminating legal event.
claims.source_quote: Persistence violations: the disappearance of legal facts that are meant to endure, without any corresponding legal event to terminate them.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving the improper termination of persisting legal facts.

claims.claim: Ignored doctrinal blocks occur when legal power is exercised despite doctrines explicitly prohibiting such authorization.
claims.source_quote: Ignored doctrinal blocks: the exercise of legal power despite doctrines that explicitly prohibit or suspend such authorization.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving violation of prohibitive doctrines.

claims.claim: Doctrinal inconsistency is uneven application of doctrines to similar exercises of power, producing structurally unequal outcomes.
claims.source_quote: Doctrinal inconsistency: the uneven application of doctrines to similar exercises of power, producing structurally unequal legal outcomes.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving structural inequality from inconsistent doctrine.

claims.claim: Use of invalid legal bases involves legal actions relying on facts, rules, or determinations that no longer hold legal force.
claims.source_quote: Use of invalid legal bases: legal actions that rely on facts, rules, or determinations that no longer hold legal force.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving reliance on legally void bases.

claims.claim: Invalid delegations involve reliance on authority structures that are themselves legally defective or void.
claims.source_quote: Invalid delegations: reliance on authority structures that are themselves legally defective or void.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving defective authority structures.

claims.claim: Action without jurisdiction consists of institutional acts undertaken outside the legally defined scope of authority.
claims.source_quote: Action without jurisdiction: institutional acts undertaken outside the legally defined scope of authority.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving institutional acts beyond jurisdictional bounds.

claims.claim: Unrecorded legal effects are legally significant changes occurring without the required public or institutional record.
claims.source_quote: Unrecorded legal effects: legally significant changes that occur without the required public or institutional record.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving the absence of required records for legal changes.

claims.claim: Temporal incoherence occurs when legal effects are treated as occurring prior to the events that justify them.
claims.source_quote: Temporal incoherence: cases in which legal effects are treated as occurring prior to the events that are supposed to justify them.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological contradiction type involving inversion of causal-temporal order in legal effects.

claims.claim: Justice is immanent to law, not external or internal to it.
claims.source_quote: On the structural view, justice is neither external nor internal, it is immanent. It is the very condition of law's being.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological status of justice relative to law.

claims.claim: Law cannot exist without coherence.
claims.source_quote: Law cannot exist without coherence, and coherence, when reflexive and repairable, is justice itself.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary ontological condition for law's existence.

claims.claim: Coherence, when reflexive and repairable, is justice itself.
claims.source_quote: Law cannot exist without coherence, and coherence, when reflexive and repairable, is justice itself.
claims.note: Identity claim between reflexive, repairable coherence and justice.

claims.claim: Justice is the integrity of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The approach described in this book redefines justice as the integrity of recognition, the measure of how well a legal system sustains coherent relations among its dependent continuants.
claims.note: The author explicitly defines justice as a kind of structural integrity; this is an ontological identity claim.

claims.claim: Justice measures how well a legal system sustains coherent relations among its dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: justice as the integrity of recognition, the measure of how well a legal system sustains coherent relations among its dependent continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of justice in relation to dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Justice is what law is when it functions properly as a coherent, reflexive system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Justice is not something law ought to achieve; it is what law is when it functions properly as a coherent, reflexive system of recognition.
claims.note: Positive ontological identity claim about justice and law's functioning.

claims.claim: Injustice is the loss of structural integrity and the breakdown of recognition across institutions and roles.
claims.source_quote: injustice is the loss of structural integrity, the breakdown of recognition across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Asserts what injustice is ontologically—a loss of a structural property.

claims.claim: An authoritarian system collapses into rigid closure, losing reflexivity and accumulating contradiction debt.
claims.source_quote: When a system becomes authoritarian, it collapses into rigid closure, losing reflexivity and accumulating contradiction debt.
claims.note: Asserts properties and failure modes of authoritarian legal systems as ontological facts.

claims.claim: An anomic system dissolves into incoherence.
claims.source_quote: When it becomes anomic, it dissolves into incoherence.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property of anomic systems.

claims.claim: Repair is ontological reconstruction, not moral correction.
claims.source_quote: Repair, therefore, is not moral correction but ontological reconstruction. To repair is to restore the coherence that allows recognition, and hence law, to exist at all.
claims.note: Asserts what repair is as an ontological act, and its relation to law's existence.

claims.claim: Justice is the equilibrium of law—the form of balance by which law continues to exist as law.
claims.source_quote: Justice, in this sense, is not the telos of law but its equilibrium: the form of balance by which law continues to exist as law.
claims.note: Direct ontological identity claim about justice as law's equilibrium.

claims.claim: Justice is the organized coherence of being that allows law to persist, evolve, and remain real.
claims.source_quote: It is neither narrative nor norm but architecture, the organized coherence of being that allows law to persist, evolve, and remain real.
claims.note: Asserts what justice is ontologically—an architectural/structural property of being.

claims.claim: Legal systems fail when internal dependencies that constitute legal reality cease to cohere.
claims.source_quote: legal systems fail not merely when their rules are unjust or unpopular, but when the internal dependencies that constitute legal reality cease to cohere.
claims.note: Asserts a condition for legal system failure grounded in ontological dependence relations.

claims.claim: Legal breakdowns are violations of a legal system's ontological commitments concerning authority, validity, jurisdiction, recognition, and time.
claims.source_quote: this approach understands them as violations of a legal system's own ontological commitments concerning authority, validity, jurisdiction, recognition, and time.
claims.note: Positive assertion about the ontological nature of legal breakdowns.

claims.claim: Coercion without authority is the exercise of legal power by an actor lacking valid authorization.
claims.source_quote: Coercion without authority: the exercise of legal power by an actor who lacks valid authorization to wield it.
claims.note: Defines a type of structural contradiction as an ontological category.

claims.claim: Exercise of power after invalidation is the continued use of legal power after it has been withdrawn or nullified.
claims.source_quote: Exercise of power after invalidation: the continued use of a legal power or competence after it has been legally withdrawn or nullified.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type as an ontological category.

claims.claim: Missing conferral chains are situations where legal power cannot be traced through a valid sequence of grants and delegations.
claims.source_quote: Missing conferral chains: situations in which legal power cannot be traced back through a valid sequence of grants and delegations.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type involving relational ontology of authority.

claims.claim: Validity conflicts occur when a legal rule is simultaneously treated as both valid and invalid within the system.
claims.source_quote: Validity conflicts: cases in which a legal rule or regulation is simultaneously treated as both valid and invalid within the system.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type as an ontological category of status.

claims.claim: Status conflicts occur when an entity occupies mutually exclusive legal statuses simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Status conflicts: circumstances in which an entity is made to occupy mutually exclusive legal statuses at the same time.
claims.note: Defines a contradiction type involving incompatible ontological statuses.

claims.claim: Persistence violations are the disappearance of legal facts meant to endure without a terminating legal event.
claims.source_quote: Persistence violations: the disappearance of legal facts that are meant to endure, without any corresponding legal event to terminate them.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction involving the temporal persistence of legal facts.

claims.claim: Ignored doctrinal blocks are exercises of legal power despite doctrines explicitly prohibiting such authorization.
claims.source_quote: Ignored doctrinal blocks: the exercise of legal power despite doctrines that explicitly prohibit or suspend such authorization.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type as an ontological category.

claims.claim: Doctrinal inconsistency is the uneven application of doctrines to similar exercises of power, producing structurally unequal outcomes.
claims.source_quote: Doctrinal inconsistency: the uneven application of doctrines to similar exercises of power, producing structurally unequal legal outcomes.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type with ontological implications for legal equality.

claims.claim: Use of invalid legal bases involves legal actions relying on facts or rules that no longer hold legal force.
claims.source_quote: Use of invalid legal bases: legal actions that rely on facts, rules, or determinations that no longer hold legal force.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type involving dependence on void legal facts.

claims.claim: Invalid delegations involve reliance on authority structures that are themselves legally defective or void.
claims.source_quote: Invalid delegations: reliance on authority structures that are themselves legally defective or void.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type involving defective authority relations.

claims.claim: Action without jurisdiction consists of institutional acts undertaken outside the legally defined scope of authority.
claims.source_quote: Action without jurisdiction: institutional acts undertaken outside the legally defined scope of authority.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type as an ontological category.

claims.claim: Unrecorded legal effects are legally significant changes occurring without the required public or institutional record.
claims.source_quote: Unrecorded legal effects: legally significant changes that occur without the required public or institutional record.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction involving missing institutional documentation of legal facts.

claims.claim: Temporal incoherence occurs when legal effects are treated as occurring prior to the events that justify them.
claims.source_quote: Temporal incoherence: cases in which legal effects are treated as occurring prior to the events that are supposed to justify them.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction involving temporal relations among legal facts.

claims.claim: When relations among agents, norms, and institutions are coherent, responsive, and repairable, the system is just.
claims.source_quote: When the relations among agents, norms, and institutions are coherent, responsive, and repairable, the system is just.
claims.note: Asserts a property of just systems in terms of relational coherence among ontological kinds.

claims.claim: Injustice appears as ontological dissonance when relations among agents, norms, and institutions fracture or ossify.
claims.source_quote: When those relations fracture or ossify, injustice appears as ontological dissonance.
claims.note: Asserts that injustice has the ontological character of dissonance in structural relations.

claims.claim: A legal contradiction arises when standing normative relations persist at the Z2 level while effective realization diverges.
claims.source_quote: A legal contradiction arises when standing normative relations persist at the Z2 level while effective realization diverges, producing a stable misalignment across Z-levels.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the nature and conditions of legal contradiction as an entity with properties.

claims.claim: Legal contradiction produces a stable misalignment across Z-levels.
claims.source_quote: A legal contradiction arises when standing normative relations persist at the Z2 level while effective realization diverges, producing a stable misalignment across Z-levels.
claims.note: Asserts a property (stable misalignment) that legal contradiction has across Z-levels.

claims.claim: A frozen structure of misalignment underlies all crimes and torts.
claims.source_quote: This frozen structure underlies all crimes and torts, regardless of doctrinal surface differences.
claims.note: Asserts a relation: frozen structural contradiction underlies all crimes and torts.

claims.claim: The typology specifies structural conditions under which acts can count as crimes or legal wrongs.
claims.source_quote: it specifies the structural conditions under which acts can intelligibly count as crimes or other types of legal wrongs, and the failure modes through which criminalization itself becomes incoherent.
claims.note: Asserts that the typology has a function: specifying structural conditions for legal wrongs.

claims.claim: New contradiction types must take the form of violations of underlying dimensions of legal authority, validity, recognition, or temporal coherence.
claims.source_quote: new contradiction types, if they arise, must take the form of violations of these same underlying dimensions of legal authority, validity, recognition, or temporal coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary property of any possible legal contradiction type.

claims.claim: The typology of legal contradiction is a structural projection of the Minimum Legal Chain.
claims.source_quote: The typology of legal contradiction can now be seen as a structural projection of the Minimum Legal Chain rather than an independent classificatory scheme.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between the typology and the Minimum Legal Chain.

claims.claim: Each contradiction type corresponds to the failure or misalignment of one or more links within the Minimum Legal Chain.
claims.source_quote: Each contradiction type corresponds to the failure or misalignment of one or more links within that chain.
claims.note: Asserts a correspondence relation between contradiction types and chain link failures.

claims.claim: The persistence of contradiction reflects the accumulation of unresolved structural strain.
claims.source_quote: the persistence of contradiction reflects the accumulation of unresolved structural strain rather than isolated error.
claims.note: Asserts a property of persisting legal contradiction: it reflects accumulated structural strain.

claims.claim: The Square of Legal Contradiction functions as an entry point for legal diagnosis.
claims.source_quote: It functions as an entry point for diagnosis, guiding attention back to the specific structural conditions that must be restored for legality and justice to reemerge.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of the Square of Legal Contradiction.

claims.claim: Structural legal contradictions can be classified into diagnostic families based on recurring patterns of Z-level misalignment.
claims.source_quote: Structural legal contradictions can be classified into diagnostic families based on recurring patterns of Z-level misalignment.
claims.note: Asserts that structural legal contradictions have a classifiable structure into diagnostic families.

claims.claim: Diagnostic families capture distinct ways in which standing normative structures persist while effective legal realization diverges.
claims.source_quote: These families capture distinct ways in which standing normative structures persist while effective legal realization diverges, producing authority, validity, status, persistence, doctrinal, record, or temporal failures.
claims.note: Asserts that diagnostic families have a specific property: capturing modes of normative-realization divergence.

claims.claim: Authority, validity, status, persistence, doctrinal, record, and temporal failures are types of structural legal contradictions.
claims.source_quote: producing authority, validity, status, persistence, doctrinal, record, or temporal failures.
claims.note: Asserts that these named failure types are subtypes of structural legal contradiction.

claims.claim: A legal contradiction arises when standing normative relations persist at the Z2 level while effective realization diverges.
claims.source_quote: A legal contradiction arises when standing normative relations persist at the Z2 level while effective realization diverges, producing a stable misalignment across Z-levels.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the structural nature of legal contradiction as a Z-level misalignment — an ontological claim about what legal contradictions are.

claims.claim: Legal contradictions produce a stable misalignment across Z-levels.
claims.source_quote: A legal contradiction arises when standing normative relations persist at the Z2 level while effective realization diverges, producing a stable misalignment across Z-levels.
claims.note: Asserts a property (stability, cross-level misalignment) of legal contradictions as entities.

claims.claim: This frozen structure (stable misalignment) underlies all crimes and torts.
claims.source_quote: This frozen structure underlies all crimes and torts, regardless of doctrinal surface differences.
claims.note: Asserts a foundational relation: the structural misalignment is what grounds crimes and torts as a class.

claims.claim: Each contradiction type corresponds to a failure or misalignment of one or more links within the Minimum Legal Chain.
claims.source_quote: Each contradiction type corresponds to the failure or misalignment of one or more links within that chain, and the persistence of contradiction reflects the accumulation of unresolved structural strain rather than isolated error.
claims.note: Asserts a correspondence relation between contradiction types and components of the Minimum Legal Chain.

claims.claim: The persistence of legal contradiction reflects the accumulation of unresolved structural strain.
claims.source_quote: the persistence of contradiction reflects the accumulation of unresolved structural strain rather than isolated error.
claims.note: Asserts a property/cause of persisting legal contradictions — an ontological claim about the nature of their persistence.

claims.claim: The typology of legal contradiction is a structural projection of the Minimum Legal Chain.
claims.source_quote: The typology of legal contradiction can now be seen as a structural projection of the Minimum Legal Chain rather than an independent classificatory scheme.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between the typology and the Minimum Legal Chain — the typology is not independent but derived from that chain.

claims.claim: The Square of Legal Contradiction organizes legal failures according to whether authority, action, recognition, or repair has broken down.
claims.source_quote: the Square of Legal Contradiction provides a visual and analytic map of these failures, organizing them according to whether authority, action, recognition, or repair has broken down, and whether the breakdown arises from absence, excess, or conflict.
claims.note: Asserts structural properties and organizing dimensions of the Square of Legal Contradiction as an entity.

claims.claim: New contradiction types must take the form of violations of the dimensions of legal authority, validity, recognition, or temporal coherence.
claims.source_quote: new contradiction types, if they arise, must take the form of violations of these same underlying dimensions of legal authority, validity, recognition, or temporal coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary structural constraint on what legal contradiction types can be — an ontological claim about their essential nature.

claims.claim: Structural legal contradictions can be classified into diagnostic families based on recurring patterns of Z-level misalignment.
claims.source_quote: Structural legal contradictions can be classified into diagnostic families based on recurring patterns of Z-level misalignment.
claims.note: Asserts that structural legal contradictions form natural kinds (diagnostic families) grounded in Z-level misalignment patterns.

claims.claim: These diagnostic families capture distinct ways in which standing normative structures persist while effective legal realization diverges.
claims.source_quote: These families capture distinct ways in which standing normative structures persist while effective legal realization diverges, producing authority, validity, status, persistence, doctrinal, record, or temporal failures.
claims.note: Asserts properties of the diagnostic families — they correspond to real distinct modes of Z-level divergence.

claims.claim: Legal roles are ontologically real entities, not mere linguistic conventions or mental constructs.
claims.source_quote: a commitment to ontological realism about legal roles, the view that such roles are not mere linguistic conventions or mental constructs, but socially grounded, institutionally constrained, and ontologically real entities.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological status of legal roles.

claims.claim: Legal roles are socially constructed yet real.
claims.source_quote: Legal roles are real, even though they are socially constructed. This is not a contradiction.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts both social construction and ontological reality of legal roles.

claims.claim: Socially created entities can possess objective identity conditions, temporal persistence, and inter-agent salience.
claims.source_quote: entities can be socially created and maintained, but nonetheless possess objective identity conditions, temporal persistence, and inter-agent salience.
claims.note: Author endorses this as part of ontological realism, asserting properties of a kind of entity.

claims.claim: A judge is a bearer of a specifically dependent continuant that authorizes and constrains behavior within a legal framework.
claims.source_quote: a judge is someone who bears a specifically dependent continuant that authorizes and constrains behavior within a legal framework.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological nature of the judge role.

claims.claim: Legal roles have a structural presence in the social world.
claims.source_quote: It asserts that legal roles have a structural presence in the social world, they can be assigned, traced, transferred, and revoked.
claims.note: Author asserts this as part of his own realist commitment.

claims.claim: Legal roles play action-guiding functions, determining who can decide cases, initiate lawsuits, consent to contracts, or enforce rules.
claims.source_quote: They play action-guiding functions: determining who can decide cases, initiate lawsuits, consent to contracts, or enforce rules.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of legal roles.

claims.claim: Legal roles confer responsibilities and liabilities, not just powers or permissions.
claims.source_quote: they are normatively loaded: they confer responsibilities and liabilities, not just powers or permissions.
claims.note: Asserts a normative property belonging to legal roles as entities.

claims.claim: Legal roles can be instantiated only through specific processes such as appointment, registration, trial, and naturalization.
claims.source_quote: legal roles can be instantiated only through specific processes, appointment, registration, trial, naturalization.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological constraint on how legal roles come into being.

claims.claim: The processes through which legal roles are conferred are occurrent entities.
claims.source_quote: These processes are themselves occurrent entities, and the conditions under which a role is validly conferred are ontologically tractable.
claims.note: Asserts that role-conferring processes are a subkind of occurrents.

claims.claim: Becoming a defendant is the result of a filing, recognition, and response process.
claims.source_quote: becoming a defendant is not just a social fact; it is the result of a filing, recognition, and response process.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological account of how a particular role comes into existence.

claims.claim: Legal roles are structurally interdependent: a judge implies a court, a plaintiff implies a defendant, a police officer implies a jurisdiction.
claims.source_quote: A judge implies a court; a plaintiff implies a defendant; a police officer implies a jurisdiction.
claims.note: Asserts relational interdependence among legal role entities.

claims.claim: Legal roles exist within networks of recognition mediated by institutions and codified in legal norms.
claims.source_quote: roles do not float freely, but exist within networks of recognition, mediated by institutions and codified in legal norms.
claims.note: Asserts a relational and institutional grounding for legal roles.

claims.claim: The misassignment, denial, or arbitrary removal of legal roles constitutes a real harm.
claims.source_quote: their misassignment, denial, or arbitrary removal constitutes a real harm.
claims.note: Author asserts that because roles are real entities, actions against them produce real harms.

claims.claim: Legal systems are layered structures of norm-governed roles embedded in institutions and enacted through agent actions.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems are not collections of abstract rules floating in isolation; they are layered structures of norm-governed roles, embedded in institutions and enacted through the actions of agents.
claims.note: Author asserts what legal systems are as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Legal systems must be understood as role-based architectures where authority, responsibility, and participation are distributed through interlocking continuants and occurrents.
claims.source_quote: legal systems must be understood as role-based architectures, where legal authority, responsibility, and participation are distributed through a system of interlocking continuants and occurrents.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure of legal systems.

claims.claim: Governments are aggregates of institutions, each of which is a framework for producing and regulating roles.
claims.source_quote: governments themselves can be understood as aggregates of institutions, each of which exists not merely as a physical building or bureaucratic chart, but as a framework for producing and regulating roles.
claims.note: Author presents this with 'can be understood as,' slightly hedged, but contextually endorses it as the correct ontological account.

claims.claim: A legislature acts through persons who occupy roles such as speaker, member, clerk, and committee chair.
claims.source_quote: A legislature, for example, does not act qua legislature, it acts through persons who occupy the roles of speaker, member, clerk, committee chair, and so on.
claims.note: Asserts a relational structure: legislature acts via persons bearing specific roles.

claims.claim: Each institution is a composite entity composed of agentive continuants, specifically dependent continuants, information artifacts, and occurrents.
claims.source_quote: each institution can be modeled as a composite entity composed of: Agentive continuants (e.g., people, legal persons), Specifically dependent continuants (e.g., roles borne by those agents), Information artifacts (e.g., rules of procedure, statutes, charters), Occurrents (e.g., hearings, deliberations, decisions).
claims.note: Presented as a modeling claim but the author is asserting the ontological composition of institutions within his realist framework.

claims.claim: The role of the ruled—whether as citizen, subject, or offender—is ontologically rich and normatively significant.
claims.source_quote: the role of the ruled, whether as citizen, subject, or offender, is as ontologically rich and normatively significant as that of legal officials.
claims.note: Asserts properties (ontological richness, normative significance) of a kind of role entity.

claims.claim: Information artifacts such as statutes, charters, and rules of procedure are parts of institutions.
claims.source_quote: Information artifacts (e.g., rules of procedure, statutes, charters)
claims.note: Listed as a component of the composite institutional entity; author endorses this ontological decomposition.

claims.claim: Recognized roles are dependent continuants inhering in agents.
claims.source_quote: Recognized roles (dependent continuants inhering in agents).
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership and property relation: roles are dependent continuants and they inhere in agents.

claims.claim: Institutional structure is a network of dependencies among roles.
claims.source_quote: Institutional structure (a network of dependencies among roles).
claims.note: Asserts what institutional structure is as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: Active processes are occurrents that realize institutional functions.
claims.source_quote: Active processes (occurrents that realize institutional functions).
claims.note: Asserts kind membership (occurrents) and a realization relation to institutional functions.

claims.claim: A sustaining field of acknowledgment links institutions to others and to the public.
claims.source_quote: Sustaining recognition (a field of acknowledgment linking the institution to others and to the public).
claims.note: Asserts existence and relational structure of a field of acknowledgment.

claims.claim: When recognized roles, institutional structure, active processes, or sustaining recognition fail, institutional collapse begins.
claims.source_quote: When any of these conditions fail, institutional collapse begins.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: institutional existence depends on these four conditions.

claims.claim: Failures of recognition dissolve the continuants upon which law depends.
claims.source_quote: failures of recognition that dissolve the continuants upon which law depends.
claims.note: Asserts that law depends on continuants and that failed recognition dissolves them.

claims.claim: The postwar tribunals (Nuremberg, Tokyo) are instances of institutional reconstitution.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, they represent a case of institutional reconstitution: the creation of new continuants (tribunals, charters, offices) that restored coherence to a world of broken obligations.
claims.note: Asserts that these historical individuals are of the kind 'institutional reconstitution' and created new continuants.

claims.claim: Tribunals, charters, and offices created by postwar trials are new continuants.
claims.source_quote: the creation of new continuants (tribunals, charters, offices) that restored coherence to a world of broken obligations.
claims.note: Asserts that these entities exist as continuants.

claims.claim: In failed states, roles, obligations, and authority are extinguished when relations of recognition no longer obtain.
claims.source_quote: Their dependent continuants (roles, obligations, and authority) have been extinguished because the relations of recognition that defined them no longer obtain.
claims.note: Asserts that dependent continuants cease to exist when their defining recognition relations dissolve.

claims.claim: Failed states leave a residue of legal form without ontological being.
claims.source_quote: What remains is a residue of legal form without being, a field of unrealized continuants disconnected from the processes that give them life.
claims.note: Asserts that unrealized continuants exist as a residue disconnected from sustaining processes.

claims.claim: Institutional being is relational, not intrinsic.
claims.source_quote: The phenomenon of failed states reveals that institutional being is relational, not intrinsic.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental property of institutional being: it is essentially relational.

claims.claim: No institution exists independently; its reality depends on reciprocal recognition.
claims.source_quote: No institution exists independently; its reality depends on the reciprocal recognition of other institutions and the public.
claims.note: Asserts a universal ontological dependency for institutions.

claims.claim: When the recognition network dissolves, an institution ceases to exist as part of the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Once this network dissolves, the institution ceases to exist as part of the legal world, even if its material infrastructure remains.
claims.note: Asserts that institutional existence in the legal world requires the recognition network.

claims.claim: The collapse of Somalia (early 1990s) and Libya (after 2011) produced ontological fragmentation of legal entities.
claims.source_quote: The collapse of Somalia in the early 1990s, or of Libya after 2011, illustrates this ontological truth. Courts and ministries did not merely lose efficiency; they lost their status as legal entities.
claims.note: Asserts that these historical institutions lost their status as legal entities—an ontological claim about particular cases.

claims.claim: Competing factions in collapsed states produce overlapping and contradictory continuants.
claims.source_quote: Competing factions created conflicting systems of recognition, producing overlapping and contradictory continuants, multiple 'governments,' each claiming legitimacy but lacking universal recognition.
claims.note: Asserts existence of multiple contradictory continuants as a real ontological condition.

claims.claim: Collapse is a process, not an event—a gradual erosion of recognition coherence.
claims.source_quote: Collapse, therefore, is not an event but a process, a gradual erosion of recognition coherence across levels of the institutional network.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of collapse as a process-kind, not an event-kind.

claims.claim: Institutional continuity is relational, not material.
claims.source_quote: This demonstrates that continuity is not material but relational: it depends on maintaining coherence within the field of recognition, even if the physical or political context changes.
claims.note: Asserts a property of institutional continuity—it is constituted by relational coherence, not material substrate.

claims.claim: Institutional memory consists in the preservation of norms, procedures, and roles as informational continuants.
claims.source_quote: The capacity for such continuity depends on institutional memory, the preservation of norms, procedures, and roles as informational continuants that can be reactivated.
claims.note: Asserts that norms, procedures, and roles are informational continuants and that institutional memory is their preservation.

claims.claim: Constitutions, codes, and treaties are repositories of potential recognition.
claims.source_quote: Constitutions, codes, and treaties serve as repositories of potential recognition, awaiting renewal.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/dispositional property of these legal artifacts.

claims.claim: When agents acknowledge legal artifacts as authoritative, the dependent continuants those artifacts represent are reanimated.
claims.source_quote: When new agents or regimes acknowledge these artifacts as authoritative, the dependent continuants they represent are reanimated.
claims.note: Asserts a causal-ontological relation between acts of recognition and the reactivation of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The revival of German legal institutions after 1949 was a repair through selective continuity, not creation of an entirely new system.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this was not the creation of an entirely new system but a repair through selective continuity, a reconfiguration of existing dependencies to restore coherence at a new level.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of this historical transition as reconfiguration rather than creation ex nihilo.

claims.claim: Law's fragility lies in its dependence on recognition, which can dissolve through conflict or corruption.
claims.source_quote: Its fragility lies in its dependence on recognition, which can dissolve through conflict or corruption.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of law grounded in its ontological dependence on recognition.

claims.claim: Law's resilience lies in the distributed nature of recognition across institutions, roles, and agents.
claims.source_quote: Its resilience lies in the distributed nature of that recognition: because it is shared across institutions, roles, and agents, it can be reassembled even after partial collapse.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of law's recognition that grounds its resilience.

claims.claim: Law's ontology is both historical and recursive.
claims.source_quote: Law's ontology is thus both historical and recursive: it can rebuild itself from remnants, provided that some minimal field of recognition persists.
claims.note: Asserts two properties of law's ontological character.

claims.claim: Total collapse, where no shared recognition remains, marks the extinction of law as such.
claims.source_quote: At the limit, however, total collapse, where no shared recognition remains, marks the extinction of law as such.
claims.note: Asserts that law's existence is extinguished when shared recognition is entirely absent.

claims.claim: Without institutional structures that realize recognition, law's ontology cannot survive.
claims.source_quote: Law's ontology cannot survive without the institutional structures that realize recognition in enduring form.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for law's ontological persistence.

claims.claim: Collapse and continuity are phases in law's ontological cycle, not opposites.
claims.source_quote: In sum, collapse and continuity are not opposites but phases in law's ontological cycle.
claims.note: Asserts a structural relation between collapse and continuity within law's ontology.

claims.claim: Legal being depends on coherence among obligations, roles, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: that legal being depends on coherence among obligations, roles, and institutions, and that coherence, once lost, can only be restored through renewed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation constitutive of legal being.

claims.claim: Coherence lost in legal being can only be restored through renewed acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: coherence, once lost, can only be restored through renewed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for restoring legal ontological coherence.

claims.claim: Law has an ontology that is structured yet able to falter, rebuild, disintegrate, and repair.
claims.source_quote: a structure that can falter and rebuild, disintegrate and repair, yet endure so long as the human capacity for mutual recognition remains.
claims.note: The author asserts that law possesses a specific ontological structure with properties of resilience and reparability.

claims.claim: The persistence of law through history testifies to the resilience of its ontology.
claims.source_quote: The persistence of law through history, its ability to outlive empires, ideologies, and regimes, testifies to the resilience of its ontology
claims.note: The author asserts a property (resilience) of law's ontology, grounded in its historical persistence.

claims.claim: Law's coherence depends on acts of recognition and can be lost and restored through them.
claims.source_quote: coherence, once lost, can only be restored through renewed acts of recognition.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational dependency between law's coherence and acts of recognition.

claims.claim: Law exists through obligations, roles, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: ions, roles, and institutions, and that coherence, once lost, can only be restored through renewed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Though the text is truncated, the author asserts that law's being is constituted by (at minimum) roles and institutions, which is an ontological claim about law's constituents.

claims.claim: Law endures as long as the human capacity for mutual recognition remains.
claims.source_quote: yet endure so long as the human capacity for mutual recognition remains.
claims.note: The author asserts a conditional existential claim: law's endurance is dependent on the human capacity for mutual recognition.

claims.claim: Legal systems are networks of recognition sustained through structured relations among norms, agents, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Insofar as legal systems are networks of recognition sustained through structured relations among norms, agents, and institutions, they are already ontological architectures.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the nature of legal systems as relational ontological structures.

claims.claim: Legal systems are ontological architectures.
claims.source_quote: Insofar as legal systems are networks of recognition sustained through structured relations among norms, agents, and institutions, they are already ontological architectures.
claims.note: Author plainly asserts that legal systems constitute ontological architectures.

claims.claim: Every legal entity is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: every legal entity, whether an obligation, right, or institutional role, can be represented as a dependent continuant: an entity that exists only insofar as it inheres in a bearer (such as an agent, institution, or document) and depends on recognition for its persistence.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal entities are dependent continuants, a direct ontological classification.

claims.claim: A dependent continuant exists only insofar as it inheres in a bearer.
claims.source_quote: a dependent continuant: an entity that exists only insofar as it inheres in a bearer (such as an agent, institution, or document) and depends on recognition for its persistence.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological property of dependent continuants: existence via inherence in a bearer.

claims.claim: A dependent continuant depends on recognition for its persistence.
claims.source_quote: a dependent continuant: an entity that exists only insofar as it inheres in a bearer (such as an agent, institution, or document) and depends on recognition for its persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of dependent continuants: dependence on recognition for persistence.

claims.claim: An obligation is a subclass of DependentContinuant.
claims.source_quote: In OWL, an 'Obligation' can be formally declared as a subclass of 'DependentContinuant,' realized in 'LegalProcess,' and inhering in 'LegalAgent.'
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological classification of obligation as a subkind of dependent continuant.

claims.claim: An obligation inheres in a legal agent.
claims.source_quote: In OWL, an 'Obligation' can be formally declared as a subclass of 'DependentContinuant,' realized in 'LegalProcess,' and inhering in 'LegalAgent.'
claims.note: Asserts a relational property: obligation bears the inherence relation to a legal agent.

claims.claim: An obligation is realized in a legal process.
claims.source_quote: In OWL, an 'Obligation' can be formally declared as a subclass of 'DependentContinuant,' realized in 'LegalProcess,' and inhering in 'LegalAgent.'
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between obligation and legal process.

claims.claim: A role is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: a 'Role' can be modeled as a dependent continuant that specifies the conditions under which an agent participates in institutional continuants.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological classification of roles as dependent continuants.

claims.claim: A role specifies the conditions under which an agent participates in institutional continuants.
claims.source_quote: a 'Role' can be modeled as a dependent continuant that specifies the conditions under which an agent participates in institutional continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of roles with respect to agents and institutions.

claims.claim: A contract is a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants such as obligations and permissions.
claims.source_quote: A contract is not simply a text but a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants (obligations, permissions) that are realized through occurrents (signing, performance, enforcement).
claims.note: Asserts both the kind membership (legal continuant) and part-whole composition of contracts.

claims.claim: Obligations and permissions are dependent continuants that are parts of a contract.
claims.source_quote: A contract is not simply a text but a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants (obligations, permissions) that are realized through occurrents (signing, performance, enforcement).
claims.note: Asserts part-whole and kind relations among contract components.

claims.claim: Contracts are realized through occurrents such as signing, performance, and enforcement.
claims.source_quote: a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants (obligations, permissions) that are realized through occurrents (signing, performance, enforcement).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between contracts (and their dependent parts) and occurrents.

claims.claim: A contract is a subclass of LegalDocument, which is a continuant.
claims.source_quote: Contract (class) → subclass of LegalDocument (continuant).
claims.note: Explicit ontological subclass assertion in the author's formal model.

claims.claim: An obligation has the property of inhering in an agent (bearer) and being realized in a performance event.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) → subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Asserts relational properties of the obligation class in the author's formal ontology.

claims.claim: A signing event is a subclass of LegalOccurrent.
claims.source_quote: SigningEvent (class) → subclass of LegalOccurrent, linking Agent to Obligation through creates or activates property.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership: signing events are legal occurrents.

claims.claim: A signing event links an agent to an obligation through a creates or activates relation.
claims.source_quote: SigningEvent (class) → subclass of LegalOccurrent, linking Agent to Obligation through creates or activates property.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between signing events, agents, and obligations.

claims.claim: An institution is a subclass of InstitutionalContinuant.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) → subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership for institutions in the author's formal ontology.

claims.claim: An institution bears recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) → subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: Asserts relational properties of institutions toward other legal entities.

claims.claim: The entities encoded in OWL and RDF correspond to real ontological structures: continuants, occurrents, and their interdependencies.
claims.source_quote: The entities that OWL and RDF encode are not arbitrary symbols but correspond to real ontological structures: continuants, occurrents, and their interdependencies.
claims.note: Author plainly asserts ontological realism about the entities represented in legal knowledge systems.

claims.claim: Computational systems can participate in legal processes only insofar as they are embedded within recognized institutional roles.
claims.source_quote: The chapter argues that computational systems can participate in legal processes only insofar as they are embedded within recognized institutional roles.
claims.note: Asserts a condition on the participation relation between computational systems and legal processes.

claims.claim: Legal systems are networks of recognition sustained through structured relations among norms, agents, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Insofar as legal systems are networks of recognition sustained through structured relations among norms, agents, and institutions, they are already ontological architectures.
claims.note: The author asserts a positive ontological characterization of legal systems as relational networks.

claims.claim: Legal systems are ontological architectures.
claims.source_quote: Insofar as legal systems are networks of recognition sustained through structured relations among norms, agents, and institutions, they are already ontological architectures.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological nature of legal systems.

claims.claim: Law is a system of interdependent continuants whose coherence depends on formal relations of dependence, recognition, and realization.
claims.source_quote: law is a system of interdependent continuants whose coherence depends on formal relations of dependence, recognition, and realization.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts this as what formal languages make explicit, endorsing it as true.

claims.claim: Every legal entity is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: every legal entity, whether an obligation, right, or institutional role, can be represented as a dependent continuant: an entity that exists only insofar as it inheres in a bearer (such as an agent, institution, or document) and depends on recognition for its persistence.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal entities are dependent continuants, not merely that they can be modeled as such—the representational claim is grounded in the metaphysical one.

claims.claim: A dependent continuant exists only insofar as it inheres in a bearer and depends on recognition for its persistence.
claims.source_quote: an entity that exists only insofar as it inheres in a bearer (such as an agent, institution, or document) and depends on recognition for its persistence.
claims.note: The author defines and endorses this ontological characterization of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: An obligation inheres in a bearer and is realized in legal processes.
claims.source_quote: an 'Obligation' can be formally declared as a subclass of 'DependentContinuant,' realized in 'LegalProcess,' and inhering in 'LegalAgent.'
claims.note: Presented as a formal OWL declaration but the author endorses this as reflecting real ontological structure, not merely a modeling convention.

claims.claim: A role is a dependent continuant that specifies conditions under which an agent participates in institutional continuants.
claims.source_quote: a 'Role' can be modeled as a dependent continuant that specifies the conditions under which an agent participates in institutional continuants.
claims.note: Presented as a modeling claim but the author endorses formal models as corresponding to real ontological structures.

claims.claim: A contract is a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants such as obligations and permissions.
claims.source_quote: A contract is not simply a text but a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants (obligations, permissions) that are realized through occurrents (signing, performance, enforcement).
claims.note: The author explicitly contrasts this with the view that a contract is merely a text, asserting the ontological structure positively.

claims.claim: Obligations and permissions are dependent continuants that are parts of a contract.
claims.source_quote: A contract is not simply a text but a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants (obligations, permissions) that are realized through occurrents (signing, performance, enforcement).
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological composition of a contract.

claims.claim: Obligations and permissions are realized through occurrents such as signing, performance, and enforcement.
claims.source_quote: dependent continuants (obligations, permissions) that are realized through occurrents (signing, performance, enforcement).
claims.note: The author asserts a realization relation between dependent continuants and occurrents.

claims.claim: A contract is a subclass of LegalDocument and is a continuant.
claims.source_quote: Contract (class) ? subclass of LegalDocument (continuant).
