claims.note: Presented as formal ontology encoding but the author endorses these as corresponding to real ontological structures.

claims.claim: An obligation is a subclass of DependentContinuant and inheres in an agent.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) ? subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Formal encoding endorsed by the author as corresponding to real ontological structure.

claims.claim: A signing event is a subclass of LegalOccurrent.
claims.source_quote: SigningEvent (class) ? subclass of LegalOccurrent, linking Agent to Obligation through creates or activates property.
claims.note: Presented as formal encoding; the author endorses these encodings as ontologically grounded.

claims.claim: An institution is a subclass of InstitutionalContinuant defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) ? subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: Formal encoding endorsed by the author as reflecting real ontological structure.

claims.claim: The entities encoded in OWL and RDF correspond to real ontological structures: continuants, occurrents, and their interdependencies.
claims.source_quote: The entities that OWL and RDF encode are not arbitrary symbols but correspond to real ontological structures: continuants, occurrents, and their interdependencies.
claims.note: Explicit positive ontological assertion by the author distinguishing real structures from arbitrary symbols.

claims.claim: Each RDF triple encodes a unit of recognition, mapping the dependencies that sustain the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Each RDF triple encodes a unit of recognition, mapping the dependencies that sustain the legal world.
claims.note: The author asserts a function and relational role for RDF triples within the ontological structure of law.

claims.claim: Computational systems can participate in legal processes only insofar as they are embedded within recognized institutional roles.
claims.source_quote: computational systems can participate in legal processes only insofar as they are embedded within recognized institutional roles.
claims.note: Stated as a core thesis of the chapter; directly asserts an ontological constraint on computational systems.

claims.claim: Each institution is a composite entity.
claims.source_quote: each institution can be modeled as a composite entity composed of: Agentive continuants, Specifically dependent continuants, Information artifacts, Occurrents.
claims.note: The author asserts that institutions are composite entities, though framed as 'can be modeled as'; the modeling claim is ontological in intent given the realist framing of the text.

claims.claim: Agentive continuants (e.g., people, legal persons) are components of institutions.
claims.source_quote: each institution can be modeled as a composite entity composed of: Agentive continuants (e.g., people, legal persons)
claims.note: Asserts a part-of or composition relation between agentive continuants and institutions.

claims.claim: Specifically dependent continuants (roles) are components of institutions.
claims.source_quote: each institution can be modeled as a composite entity composed of: Specifically dependent continuants (e.g., roles borne by those agents)
claims.note: Asserts a composition relation between specifically dependent continuants and institutions.

claims.claim: Information artifacts (rules, statutes, charters) are components of institutions.
claims.source_quote: each institution can be modeled as a composite entity composed of: Information artifacts (e.g., rules of procedure, statutes, charters)
claims.note: Asserts a composition relation between information artifacts and institutions.

claims.claim: Occurrents (hearings, deliberations, decisions) are components of institutions.
claims.source_quote: each institution can be modeled as a composite entity composed of: Occurrents (e.g., hearings, deliberations, decisions)
claims.note: Asserts a composition relation between occurrents and institutions.

claims.claim: An institution has a legal function constituted by interactions among its components.
claims.source_quote: These components interact to form the institution's legal function.
claims.note: Asserts that institutions have a legal function and that this function arises from component interactions.

claims.claim: A court's function as an adjudicative body is constituted by role-bearers engaging in normatively structured processes.
claims.source_quote: a court functions as an adjudicative body not by virtue of its architecture or founding documents alone, but because role-bearers (judges, clerks, litigants) engage in processes (hearings, trials) that are normatively structured and legally recognized.
claims.note: Asserts what the function of a court depends on — a relational/functional ontological claim.

claims.claim: Legal actors are role-bearing participants.
claims.source_quote: The legal actors within these institutions, judges, legislators, officers, defendants, and citizens are role-bearing participants.
claims.note: Directly asserts that legal actors bear the property/role of being role-bearing participants.

claims.claim: A person's behavior is not legally significant unless anchored in a valid role within a recognized institution.
claims.source_quote: Their behavior is not legally significant until it is anchored in a valid role, instantiated within the structure of a recognized institution.
claims.note: Asserts a condition on the legal significance of behavior, which is an ontological claim about legal properties.

claims.claim: A person's decision is a judicial decision only if they are a judge acting in a recognized courtroom under the rule of law.
claims.source_quote: A person's decision is not a judicial decision unless they are a judge acting in a recognized courtroom under the rule of law.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for an entity to be of a particular kind (judicial decision), an ontological claim about kind membership.

claims.claim: The legal system depends on role assignment and role performance for its operation.
claims.source_quote: The legal system thus depends on role assignment and role performance for its very operation.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between the legal system and role assignment/performance.

claims.claim: Institutions are role-structuring systems.
claims.source_quote: Institutions as role-structuring systems
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of institutions: they structure roles.

claims.claim: Legal events are occurrent processes involving multiple roles.
claims.source_quote: Legal events as occurrent processes involving multiple roles
claims.note: Asserts that legal events are a subkind of occurrent processes and have the property of involving multiple roles.

claims.claim: Normative powers are realizable entities activated through role performance.
claims.source_quote: Normative powers as realizable entities are activated through role performance.
claims.note: Asserts that normative powers are realizable entities and that role performance activates them — an ontological claim about kind and activation relation.

claims.claim: Institutions are embedded within broader institutional structures.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are embedded within broader structures, municipal courts within state judicial systems, departments within ministries, agencies within executive branches.
claims.note: Asserts a part-of or embedding relation between institutions and broader structures.

claims.claim: Roles within institutional systems are hierarchical, interdependent, and temporally scoped.
claims.source_quote: Roles within these systems are hierarchical, interdependent, and temporally scoped.
claims.note: Asserts properties of roles: hierarchical, interdependent, temporally scoped.

claims.claim: Nested role hierarchies formally represent cascading chains of authority and accountability.
claims.source_quote: This cascading structure of role relations can be formally modeled as nested role hierarchies, allowing both legal theorists and informaticians to reason over chains of authority and accountability.
claims.note: Asserts a structural-ontological claim about how role relations are organized, framed as 'can be modeled as' but reflecting author's ontological commitment.

claims.claim: Each node in an institutional authority structure represents a role or institution as a continuant sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Each node represents a role or institution as a continuant sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that roles and institutions are continuants and that institutional recognition sustains them.

claims.claim: Cross-institutional role transfer and multiplex role occupancy exist within legal systems.
claims.source_quote: legal systems allow for cross-institutional role transfer and multiplex role occupancy.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of cross-institutional role transfer and multiplex role occupancy as features of legal systems.

claims.claim: Different legal roles carry different rights, duties, and powers.
claims.source_quote: At each stage, different legal roles are instantiated, with different rights, duties, and powers.
claims.note: Asserts that legal roles have properties (rights, duties, powers) that differ across roles.

claims.claim: The semantic coherence of a legal system depends on the consistency of its role structures.
claims.source_quote: The semantic coherence of a legal system depends on the consistency of its role structures.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between a legal system's coherence and its role structures.

claims.claim: Law is not reducible to documents or commands.
claims.source_quote: law is not reducible to documents or commands.
claims.note: Asserts a negative ontological claim about the nature of law.

claims.claim: Law exists through participation structured by roles.
claims.source_quote: Law lives through participation, and participation is structured through roles.
claims.note: Asserts that law's existence depends on participation and that participation is structured by roles — ontological claims about the nature and dependence of law.

claims.claim: Obligation is a subclass of DependentContinuant.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) — subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion in the author's ontological schema.

claims.claim: Obligation has the property inheresIn, whose bearer is an agent.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) — subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Asserts a property (inheresIn) relating Obligation to an agent.

claims.claim: Obligation has the property realizedIn, whose event is a performance.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) — subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of Obligation to an occurrent.

claims.claim: SigningEvent is a subclass of LegalOccurrent.
claims.source_quote: SigningEvent (class) — subclass of LegalOccurrent, linking Agent to Obligation through creates or activates property.
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion in the author's ontological schema.

claims.claim: SigningEvent links Agent to Obligation through a creates or activates property.
claims.source_quote: SigningEvent (class) — subclass of LegalOccurrent, linking Agent to Obligation through creates or activates property.
claims.note: Asserts a relational structure between SigningEvent, Agent, and Obligation.

claims.claim: Institution is a subclass of InstitutionalContinuant.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) — subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion in the author's ontological schema.

claims.claim: Institution has recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) — subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: Asserts defining relational properties of Institution.

claims.claim: Legal ontology instantiates justice as structural integrity within the digital domain.
claims.source_quote: A legal ontology capable of maintaining these properties effectively instantiates justice as structural integrity within the digital domain.
claims.note: The author asserts that a properly constructed legal ontology instantiates justice as a structural property.

claims.claim: In legal ontologies, relations encode deontic dependencies linking agents, roles, and acts.
claims.source_quote: In legal ontologies, by contrast, relations encode deontic dependencies, conditional necessities linking agents, roles, and acts ('X is obligated to transfer Y to Z under condition C').
claims.note: The author positively asserts a distinguishing property of legal ontology relations.

claims.claim: Deontic dependencies are modal rather than factual.
claims.source_quote: These dependencies are modal rather than factual: they specify what ought to occur within a recognized institutional framework.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of deontic dependencies as a kind of dependency.

claims.claim: Normativity is a structural property of relations, not an external rule.
claims.source_quote: These allow the machine-readable expression of normativity as a structural property of relations rather than as an external rule.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological characterization of normativity.

claims.claim: Roles are the dynamic interface between agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Roles represent the dynamic interface between agents and institutions, the means through which legal systems connect individual action to institutional recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the function/role of roles in legal ontology.

claims.claim: Roles are realizable dependent continuants that inhere in bearers (agents).
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, roles are realizable dependent continuants that inhere in bearers (agents) and are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind and properties of roles in BFO terms.

claims.claim: Roles are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, roles are realizable dependent continuants that inhere in bearers (agents) and are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between roles and occurrents.

claims.claim: Role is a subkind of RealizableEntity.
claims.source_quote: – Role ⊑ RealizableEntity
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion in the author's formal ontological model.

claims.claim: Role inheres in Agent.
claims.source_quote: – inheresIn (Role, Agent)
claims.note: Asserts a relation of inherence between Role and Agent.

claims.claim: Role is realized in InstitutionalProcess.
claims.source_quote: – realizedIn (Role, InstitutionalProcess)
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between Role and InstitutionalProcess.

claims.claim: Institution has the function of RealizationOfRole.
claims.source_quote: – hasFunction(Institution, RealizationOfRole)
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of Institution.

claims.claim: Machines may simulate recognition, but only institutions can confer recognition.
claims.source_quote: Machines may simulate recognition, but only institutions can confer it.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological distinction between machine simulation and institutional conferral of recognition.

claims.claim: Formal ontology provides the bridge between legal reasoning and artificial intelligence.
claims.source_quote: Formal ontology thus provides the bridge between legal reasoning and artificial intelligence.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional/relational role of formal ontology.

claims.claim: Encoding obligations in formal ontology clarifies how normative systems differ from purely descriptive ones.
claims.source_quote: Encoding obligations in formal ontology also clarifies how normative systems differ from purely descriptive ones.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of formal ontological encoding regarding normative systems.

claims.claim: Formal ontology restores coherence within digital representation.
claims.source_quote: Just as institutional repair restores coherence within social recognition, formal ontology restores coherence within digital representation.
claims.note: Author asserts a function/property of formal ontology.

claims.claim: Legal systems are structured through roles.
claims.source_quote: s structured through roles. By modeling these roles ontologically, with clarity, precision, and realist commitments, we gain a more accurate, flexible, and computable understanding of legal systems.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal systems have roles as a structural feature—an ontological claim about the constitution of legal systems.

claims.claim: Legal roles are specifically instantiated continuants.
claims.source_quote: Ontology allows us to model these roles as separately instantiated continuants, and to define their interaction rules formally.
claims.note: The author endorses modeling legal roles as continuants, committing to their ontological kind.

claims.claim: Legal statuses are dynamic roles that arise through specific institutional processes.
claims.source_quote: Legal statuses (e.g., citizen, alien, minor, felon) are not static labels, they are dynamic roles that arise through specific institutional processes and generate normative consequences.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal statuses are a subkind of role and have the property of being dynamic and institutionally generated.

claims.claim: Legal statuses are specifically dependent continuants realizable in particular contexts.
claims.source_quote: Ontology allows these statuses to be represented as specifically dependent continuants that are realizable in particular contexts (e.g., residency, conviction, majority age).
claims.note: The author endorses the ontological classification of legal statuses as specifically dependent continuants with realization conditions.

claims.claim: Authority is conferred by institutional processes and is ontologically structured.
claims.source_quote: The authority to legislate, judge, or enforce is not merely behaviorally observed; it is conferred by institutional processes, and its legitimacy depends on whether role-bearers act within their defined scope.
claims.note: The author asserts that authority has institutional origins and that its legitimacy is condition-dependent—ontological claims about authority's nature and dependencies.

claims.claim: Roles are real entities, specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Roles are not optional metaphors or terminological conveniences. They are real entities, specifically dependent continuants that ground the structure of legal participation.
claims.note: Explicit assertion of the ontological status of legal roles as real entities of a specific kind.

claims.claim: Legal roles are institutionally conferred, normatively constrained, and temporally realized.
claims.source_quote: They are institutionally conferred, normatively constrained, and temporally realized.
claims.note: The author asserts three properties of legal roles: institutional conferral, normative constraint, and temporal realization.

claims.claim: Institutions are networks of role-bearers.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are not abstractions; they are networks of role-bearers.
claims.note: The author makes a direct ontological claim about what institutions are—networks of role-bearers, not abstractions.

claims.claim: Law is a living system of participation.
claims.source_quote: Law is not merely a body of texts or a collection of commands; it is a living system of participation.
claims.note: The author asserts what law fundamentally is—a system of participation—an ontological claim about law's nature.

claims.claim: Law functions only through entities that occupy roles and act within institutions.
claims.source_quote: It functions only through people and entities who occupy roles, act within institutions, and engage with norms that define and constrain their conduct.
claims.note: The author asserts a dependency relation: law's functioning depends on role-occupying agents within institutions.

claims.claim: Participation is how law acquires its force, coherence, and institutional continuity.
claims.source_quote: Participation is how law is lived, and how it acquires its force, coherence, and institutional continuity.
claims.note: The author asserts that participation is the source of law's force and continuity—a claim about law's properties and their causal/grounding basis.

claims.claim: Courts, agencies, and governments can be ontologically decomposed into processes, artifacts, and interdependent roles.
claims.source_quote: Courts, agencies, and governments can be ontologically decomposed into processes, artifacts, and interdependent roles.
claims.note: The author asserts a part-whole/composition claim about legal institutions—that they are composed of processes, artifacts, and roles.

claims.claim: A legislature passing a law is a role-based legal action.
claims.source_quote: When a legislature passes a law, when a judge sentences a defendant, when a citizen casts a vote or files a complaint, each of these is a role-based legal action, situated within a larger system of structured dependencies.
claims.note: The author categorizes these actions as role-based legal actions—a claim about the kind these actions instantiate.

claims.claim: The role of 'public defender' inherits constraints from the role of 'attorney'.
claims.source_quote: The role of 'public defender' may inherit general constraints from the role of 'attorney,' while also being institutionally linked to the public judiciary.
claims.note: The author uses 'may inherit' which is slightly hedged, but it is offered as an ontological illustration the author endorses as a modeling commitment.

claims.claim: Legal roles have realization conditions such as educational credentials, licensure, and election.
claims.source_quote: conditions for role realization (e.g., educational credentials, licensure, election).
claims.note: The author asserts that roles have specific realization conditions—a property of legal roles.

claims.claim: Legal change requires temporally scoped modeling of processes and artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Legal change, both individual (e.g., becoming a probationer) and systemic (e.g., the repeal of a statute), requires temporally scoped modeling. Ontology allows processes (occurrents) and artifacts (e.g., verdicts, laws) to be traced over time.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal change has temporal structure and that legal processes and artifacts are occurrents/objects traceable over time.

claims.claim: Verdicts and laws are legal artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Ontology allows processes (occurrents) and artifacts (e.g., verdicts, laws) to be traced over time.
claims.note: The author classifies verdicts and laws as artifacts—an ontological kind assignment.

claims.claim: Obligation is a subclass of DependentContinuant.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) → subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion about the ontological category of Obligation.

claims.claim: Obligation inheres in an agent as its bearer.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) → subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Asserts a relational property (inheresIn) between Obligation and Agent.

claims.claim: Obligation is realized in a performance event.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) → subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between Obligation and a performance event.

claims.claim: SigningEvent is a subclass of LegalOccurrent.
claims.source_quote: SigningEvent (class) → subclass of LegalOccurrent, linking Agent to Obligation through creates or activates property.
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion about SigningEvent's ontological category.

claims.claim: SigningEvent links Agent to Obligation through a creates or activates relation.
claims.source_quote: SigningEvent (class) → subclass of LegalOccurrent, linking Agent to Obligation through creates or activates property.
claims.note: Asserts a relational structure between SigningEvent, Agent, and Obligation.

claims.claim: Institution is a subclass of InstitutionalContinuant.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) → subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion about Institution's ontological category.

claims.claim: Institution has recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) → subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: Asserts relational properties (recognizes, enforces) as constitutive of Institution.

claims.claim: Legal ontologies that exhibit certain coherence constraints instantiate justice as structural integrity.
claims.source_quote: A legal ontology capable of maintaining these properties effectively instantiates justice as structural integrity within the digital domain.
claims.note: Asserts that a class of formal systems instantiates a property (justice as structural integrity).

claims.claim: In legal ontologies, relations encode deontic dependencies rather than factual ones.
claims.source_quote: In legal ontologies, by contrast, relations encode deontic dependencies, conditional necessities linking agents, roles, and acts.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of legal ontology relations distinguishing them from descriptive relations.

claims.claim: Deontic dependencies are modal rather than factual.
claims.source_quote: These dependencies are modal rather than factual: they specify what ought to occur within a recognized institutional framework.
claims.note: Asserts a property (modality) of deontic dependencies as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Roles are realizable dependent continuants that inhere in bearers (agents).
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, roles are realizable dependent continuants that inhere in bearers (agents) and are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.note: Asserts that roles are a subkind of realizable dependent continuants with an inherence relation to agents.

claims.claim: Roles are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, roles are realizable dependent continuants that inhere in bearers (agents) and are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between roles and occurrents.

claims.claim: Role is a subkind of RealizableEntity.
claims.source_quote: – Role → RealizableEntity
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion in the formal ontology structure the author endorses.

claims.claim: A Role inheres in an Agent.
claims.source_quote: – inheresIn (Role, Agent)
claims.note: Direct relational assertion between Role and Agent endorsed by the author.

claims.claim: A Role is realized in an InstitutionalProcess.
claims.source_quote: – realizedIn (Role, InstitutionalProcess)
claims.note: Direct relational assertion between Role and InstitutionalProcess endorsed by the author.

claims.claim: Institution has the function of realizing roles.
claims.source_quote: – hasFunction(Institution, RealizationOfRole)
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of Institution as a class.

claims.claim: Roles represent the dynamic interface between agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Roles represent the dynamic interface between agents and institutions, the means through which legal systems connect individual action to institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/functional property of roles as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Formal ontology provides the bridge between legal reasoning and artificial intelligence.
claims.source_quote: Formal ontology thus provides the bridge between legal reasoning and artificial intelligence.
claims.note: Asserts a relational role (bridging function) that formal ontology bears between two domains.

claims.claim: Machines can simulate recognition but cannot confer it; only institutions can confer recognition.
claims.source_quote: Machines may simulate recognition, but only institutions can confer it.
claims.note: Asserts a property distinction between machines and institutions regarding the conferral of recognition.

claims.claim: Legal norms are a kind of entity with ontological dependencies that sustain them.
claims.source_quote: What kinds of entities are legal norms? What dependencies sustain them? When does a digital record instantiate a real legal fact? Each modeling decision reflects an implicit ontological stance.
claims.note: The author treats these as genuine ontological questions, implying legal norms are entities with dependencies; medium confidence due to rhetorical framing.

claims.claim: Digitization of law encodes ontological dependencies that make law possible.
claims.source_quote: This encoding process does more than digitize law, it reveals the ontological dependencies that make law possible.
claims.note: Asserts that law has ontological dependencies and that encoding reveals them — an ontological claim about law's constitution.

claims.claim: Normativity is a structural property of relations in formal ontologies.
claims.source_quote: These allow the machine-readable expression of normativity as a structural property of relations rather than as an external rule.
claims.note: Asserts that normativity has the property of being structural (relational), not merely an external rule.

claims.claim: Legal systems function through individuals occupying institutional roles.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems function through individuals occupying institutional roles; laws do not act independently but are realized via agents such as judges, plaintiffs, or citizens.
claims.note: Direct assertion about how legal systems operate ontologically—through role-bearing agents.

claims.claim: Laws do not act independently; they are realized via agents.
claims.source_quote: laws do not act independently but are realized via agents such as judges, plaintiffs, or citizens.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between laws and agents, and denies independent agency to laws.

claims.claim: Legal roles are context-dependent, socially constructed, procedurally realized, and require institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: These legal roles are distinct from biological functions, dispositions, and informal social identities because they are context-dependent, socially constructed, procedurally realized, and require institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts essential properties of legal roles as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Roles are specifically dependent continuants in BFO.
claims.source_quote: Within frameworks like Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), roles are specifically dependent continuants, assigned rather than inherent attributes.
claims.note: Asserts that roles belong to the ontological kind 'specifically dependent continuant' within BFO.

claims.claim: Roles grant individuals certain powers, duties, or immunities only when recognized by legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: roles are specifically dependent continuants, assigned rather than inherent attributes, that grant individuals certain powers, duties, or immunities only when recognized by legal institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a property and conditional function of roles as entities.

claims.claim: A role is a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in a bearer but is not essential to that bearer's identity.
claims.source_quote: BFO defines a role as a specifically dependent continuant, a type of entity that inheres in a bearer but is not essential to that bearer's identity.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological definition of role as a kind with specific inherence and non-essentiality properties.

claims.claim: Roles are contingent, externally assigned, and context-sensitive.
claims.source_quote: Roles are contingent, externally assigned, and context-sensitive.
claims.note: Asserts properties of roles as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Being a judge is not an essential property of a person.
claims.source_quote: However, being a judge is not an essential property of the person. If the judge resigns, retires, or is removed from office, the role no longer inheres in them.
claims.note: Asserts a negative essential property claim about persons and the judge role.

claims.claim: When a judge resigns or is removed, the role no longer inheres in them.
claims.source_quote: If the judge resigns, retires, or is removed from office, the role no longer inheres in them.
claims.note: Asserts a change in the inherence relation between a role and its bearer under certain conditions.

claims.claim: Legal roles are formally distinct from both the person and their physical or biological capacities.
claims.source_quote: This makes the legal role formally distinct from both the person and their physical or biological capacities.
claims.note: Asserts a distinctness relation between legal roles and persons/biological capacities.

claims.claim: Roles are defined by what the bearer can do or be expected to do given social or institutional conditions.
claims.source_quote: Roles in BFO are defined not by what the bearer is, but by what the bearer can do or be expected to do, given certain social or institutional conditions.
claims.note: Asserts the defining property of roles as dispositional/functional rather than intrinsic.

claims.claim: Roles exist only under specific contexts defined by legal or normative frameworks.
claims.source_quote: They exist only under specific contexts, defined by legal or normative frameworks, and they are typically triggered or instantiated by actions or processes.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of roles on contextual/normative frameworks.

claims.claim: Roles are typically instantiated by actions or processes such as elections, filings, or certifications.
claims.source_quote: they are typically triggered or instantiated by actions or processes (e.g., elections, filings, certifications).
claims.note: Asserts a causal/instantiation relation between processes and role instantiation.

claims.claim: Functions in BFO are typically tied to an entity's design or biological nature.
claims.source_quote: A function is typically tied to an entity's design or biological nature. For example, the function of a heart is to pump blood, this is a physiological necessity, not a contextually assigned capacity.
claims.note: Asserts a property of functions as a distinct ontological kind from roles.

claims.claim: Roles are granted or recognized within institutional systems, not designed into their bearers.
claims.source_quote: Roles, by contrast, are not designed into their bearers. They are granted or recognized within institutional systems.
claims.note: Asserts a property distinguishing roles from functions regarding their origin.

claims.claim: The roles of plaintiff and trustee are institutionally conferred and legally recognized.
claims.source_quote: A person is not born with the role of 'plaintiff' or 'trustee'; these roles are institutionally conferred and legally recognized.
claims.note: Asserts that specific legal roles have the property of being institutionally conferred.

claims.claim: Roles exist only insofar as a social structure acknowledges and supports them.
claims.source_quote: they only exist insofar as a social structure acknowledges and supports them.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of roles on social structures.

claims.claim: Roles enable behavior, define relationships, and carry legal consequences.
claims.source_quote: In BFO, this makes roles non-essential but causally significant, they enable behavior, define relationships, and often carry legal consequences.
claims.note: Asserts causal and relational properties of roles.

claims.claim: Law operates by assigning roles, which generate obligations, permissions, powers, and liabilities.
claims.source_quote: Law operates not by altering people's biological structures, but by assigning them roles, which then generate obligations, permissions, powers, and liabilities.
claims.note: Asserts how law operates ontologically and what roles generate.

claims.claim: When someone is appointed guardian, they acquire a role that brings specific legal powers and duties.
claims.source_quote: When someone is appointed as a guardian, they acquire a role that brings with it specific legal powers (to consent for another) and duties (to protect the ward's interests).
claims.note: Asserts that the guardian role is acquired through appointment and has specific powers/duties as properties.

claims.claim: Powers and duties arising from a role are realizable continuants that arise from the role, not from the person's intrinsic characteristics.
claims.source_quote: These powers and duties are realizable continuants that arise from the role, not from the person's intrinsic characteristics.
claims.note: Asserts that legal powers/duties are a kind (realizable continuants) and asserts their dependence on roles rather than persons.

claims.claim: The gavel's function is to signal order or mark authoritative speech in a courtroom.
claims.source_quote: Its function is to signal order or mark authoritative speech in a courtroom. This function is designed into its form (as a tool of emphasis) and is realized when wielded by a judge.
claims.note: Asserts the function property of the gavel as an artifact with a designed purpose.

claims.claim: The legal significance of the gavel's use depends on the judge's role.
claims.source_quote: But the legal significance of the gavel's use depends on the judge's role. Without a person in that role, the act of banging a gavel does not instantiate a legal act.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between the legal significance of an act and an agent's role.

claims.claim: Without a person in the judge role, banging a gavel does not instantiate a legal act.
claims.source_quote: Without a person in that role, the act of banging a gavel does not instantiate a legal act.
claims.note: Asserts a condition of role occupancy as necessary for instantiating a legal act.

claims.claim: If someone fraudulently claims to be a lawyer, the role is not validly instantiated.
claims.source_quote: If someone fraudulently claims to be a lawyer, the role is not validly instantiated; obligations and permissions do not legally follow.
claims.note: Asserts that fraudulent role claims fail to instantiate the role and its associated normative consequences.

claims.claim: When a role is not validly instantiated, the preconditions for that role's instantiation have not been met.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the preconditions for that role's instantiation have not been met.
claims.note: Asserts that role instantiation has preconditions as ontological features.

claims.claim: Ontological modeling is an operational necessity as governance becomes algorithmic and transnational.
claims.source_quote: As governance becomes increasingly algorithmic and transnational, this modeling capacity becomes not just a scholarly tool, but an operational necessity.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/role of ontological modeling — that it is an operational necessity — under current governance conditions.

claims.claim: Ontological modeling enables the construction of better systems of law and justice.
claims.source_quote: Moreover, ontological modeling enables us to build better systems of law and justice.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts a causal/enabling relation between ontological modeling and improved legal systems.

claims.claim: Clear definition and constraint of legal roles helps ensure transparency, explainability, and procedural fairness.
claims.source_quote: the clear definition and constraint of legal roles helps ensure transparency, explainability, and procedural fairness.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/causal property of defined legal roles with respect to transparency and fairness.

claims.claim: A system that knows what a judge is and how legal statuses are acquired can interpret and enforce law intelligibly.
claims.source_quote: A system that knows what a judge is, how a defendant becomes a convict, or how a citizen acquires rights is a system that can interpret and enforce law intelligibly.
claims.note: The author asserts a disposition/capacity of ontologically informed legal systems.

claims.claim: Ontology bridges legal theory and practical implementation.
claims.source_quote: Ontology also bridges legal theory and practical implementation.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational role of ontology — that it connects legal theory to practical implementation.

claims.claim: Each legal role comes with its own dependencies, realizations, and legal triggers.
claims.source_quote: Each role comes with its own dependencies, realizations, and legal triggers.
claims.note: Asserts that legal roles have specific relational and dispositional properties (dependencies, realizations, triggers).

claims.claim: Roles in BFO are central to the operation of law.
claims.source_quote: roles in BFO offer an elegant and precise way to model the dynamic, institutional nature of legal participation. They are central to the operation of law
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of roles in BFO with respect to law.

claims.claim: Roles in BFO are essential to law's intelligibility.
claims.source_quote: They are central to the operation of law essential to its intelligibility
claims.note: Asserts that roles bear an essentiality relation to legal intelligibility.

claims.claim: Roles in BFO are foundational to any ontology supporting reasoning, automation, or explanation in legal domains.
claims.source_quote: foundational to any ontology that aims to support reasoning, automation, or explanation in legal domains.
claims.note: Asserts a foundational property/role of BFO roles within legal ontologies.

claims.claim: Legal participation has a dynamic, institutional nature.
claims.source_quote: roles in BFO offer an elegant and precise way to model the dynamic, institutional nature of legal participation.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a characteristic of legal participation that BFO roles model; ontological claim about the nature of legal participation.

claims.claim: Law is enacted through roles.
claims.source_quote: law is not just written, spoken, or executed, it is enacted through roles.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological nature of law and its relation to roles.

claims.claim: Roles have conditions and functions.
claims.source_quote: By modeling those roles, their conditions, and their functions with ontological rigor, we come closer to understanding how law works.
claims.note: The author asserts that roles possess conditions and functions as properties.

claims.claim: Legal facts arise from role interactions.
claims.source_quote: The next chapter explores how legal facts arise from these role interactions.
claims.note: The author states this as the subject of the next chapter, implying endorsement of the claim that legal facts arise from role interactions.

claims.claim: Legal facts include facts about persons, actions, rights, and statuses.
claims.source_quote: We will examine how legal systems construct facts, about persons, actions, rights, and statuses.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal systems construct facts of these specific kinds, implying these are the ontological constituents of legal facts.

claims.claim: Role ontology supports normative critique and institutional design.
claims.source_quote: seeing law through roles allows for normative critique and institutional design... Role ontology thus supports not only description, but the improvement of law and institutions.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the functional role and capacity of role ontology.

claims.claim: Roles have dependencies, responsibilities, and transitions.
claims.source_quote: We can reimagine institutions by redesigning role dependencies, responsibilities, and transitions.
claims.note: The author asserts these as properties that roles bear, implying ontological commitment to roles having these features.

claims.claim: A judge is a kind of legal role.
claims.source_quote: A system that knows what a judge is, how a defendant becomes a convict, or how a citizen acquires rights is a system that can interpret and enforce law intelligibly.
claims.note: The author treats judge, defendant, convict, and citizen as defined legal roles with ontological standing within a legal system.

claims.claim: A defendant can transition into the role of convict.
claims.source_quote: how a defendant becomes a convict
claims.note: The author asserts a role transition relation between defendant and convict as an ontological fact about legal roles.

claims.claim: Citizens can acquire rights.
claims.source_quote: how a citizen acquires rights
claims.note: The author asserts a relation of rights acquisition as a property of the citizen role.

claims.claim: A role is a realizable dependent continuant that inheres in a bearer.
claims.source_quote: Within Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), a role is a realizable dependent continuant, an entity that inheres in a bearer and can be realized in particular processes under suitable conditions.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological category of role as a realizable dependent continuant, a claim about what kind of entity a role is.

claims.claim: A role can be realized in particular processes under suitable conditions.
claims.source_quote: a role is a realizable dependent continuant, an entity that inheres in a bearer and can be realized in particular processes under suitable conditions.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational property of roles: they are realized in processes.

claims.claim: A physician's role inheres in a person and is realized in acts of diagnosis or treatment.
claims.source_quote: A physician's role inheres in a person and is realized in acts of diagnosis or treatment; a judge's role inheres in a legal agent and is realized in adjudication.
claims.note: Author asserts instantiation of a role in a bearer and its realization in specific occurrents.

claims.claim: A judge's role inheres in a legal agent and is realized in adjudication.
claims.source_quote: a judge's role inheres in a legal agent and is realized in adjudication.
claims.note: Author asserts the inherence and realization relations for a judge's role.

claims.claim: The bearer of a role must be a continuant capable of participating in social and institutional relations.
claims.source_quote: the bearer of a role must itself be a continuant capable of participating in social and institutional relations.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological condition on role-bearers.

claims.claim: Current AI systems realize fragments of roles without inhering in them.
claims.source_quote: these systems realize fragments of roles without inhering in them.
claims.note: Author asserts a structural ontological fact about the current status of AI in relation to legal roles.

claims.claim: A self-executing contract realizes part of the obligation-enforcement process but does not bear the role of enforcer.
claims.source_quote: A self-executing contract, for example, realizes part of the obligation-enforcement process but does not bear the institutional role of an enforcer.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological claim about what a self-executing contract does and does not bear.

claims.claim: The ontological bearer of a self-executing contract's enforcement remains the institution or agent that recognizes and authorizes the process.
claims.source_quote: The ontological bearer remains the institution or agent that recognizes and authorizes the process.
claims.note: Author asserts who the ontological bearer of the role is in this case.

claims.claim: Current AI operates as an instrumental continuant within the realization of legal roles, not as a legal agent.
claims.source_quote: the current AI operates as an instrumental continuant within the realization of legal roles, not as a legal agent in its own right.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological status of current AI in legal contexts.

claims.claim: Recognition is a necessary condition for an entity to exist as a legal agent in the legal field.
claims.source_quote: To exist as a legal agent in the legal field, an entity must be recognized by an institutional continuant as a bearer of rights and obligations.
claims.note: Author asserts a necessary ontological condition for legal agency.

claims.claim: Recognition transforms a material or informational continuant into a social continuant.
claims.source_quote: This recognition transforms a mere material or informational continuant into a social continuant, an entity that exists within the field of law's ontology.
claims.note: Author asserts a transformative ontological relation effected by recognition.

claims.claim: A social continuant is an entity that exists within the field of law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: a social continuant, an entity that exists within the field of law's ontology.
claims.note: Author defines and asserts the ontological nature of a social continuant.

claims.claim: Corporations are recognized continuants whose legal personhood arises from institutional acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: They are not physical persons but recognized continuants, legal fictions whose personhood arises entirely from institutional acknowledgment.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological basis of corporate personhood.

claims.claim: Legal personality is a property of structure, not of substance.
claims.source_quote: Legal personality is not a property of substance but of structure.
claims.note: Author makes a direct ontological assertion about the nature of legal personality.

claims.claim: Once recognition is extended to an entity, it becomes capable of role-bearing.
claims.source_quote: Once recognition is extended, the entity enters the field of law and becomes capable of role-bearing.
claims.note: Author asserts that recognition is sufficient to confer role-bearing capacity.

claims.claim: Role realization requires the alignment of dependent continuants with occurrents.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, realization requires the alignment of dependent continuants (roles, obligations) with occurrents (acts, decisions, performances).
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological condition for realization in BFO terms.

claims.claim: Normative participation requires reflexive recognition, not only norm compliance.
claims.source_quote: normative participation entails more than compliance; it requires reflexive recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts a structural ontological condition on normative participation.

claims.claim: A legal participant must occupy a position within the network of recognition that sustains norms.
claims.source_quote: A participant in the legal system must not only act according to norms but also occupy a position within the network of recognition that sustains those norms.
claims.note: Author asserts a structural/relational condition for legal participation.

claims.claim: Current AI does not recognize others and cannot confer or withdraw recognition.
claims.source_quote: Current AI lacks this reciprocity. It processes information but does not recognize; it can instantiate formal relations but cannot confer or withdraw recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts a dispositional/functional property (or lack thereof) of current AI systems.

claims.claim: Current AI's participation in legal roles is functional and derivative, not ontologically autonomous.
claims.source_quote: its participation remains unilateral - functional, not ontological. It can realize roles only derivatively, as part of another agent's recognition network.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological status of AI participation as derivative.

claims.claim: Autonomous trading algorithms and DAOs generate legal facts such as transactions and transfers.
claims.source_quote: They participate in the realization of obligations, generate legal facts (transactions, transfers), and trigger enforcement processes.
claims.note: Author asserts that these systems produce legal facts, an ontological claim about what they generate.

claims.claim: Autonomous systems occupy a liminal ontological status between instrument and institution.
claims.source_quote: they occupy an ambiguous zone between instrument and institution, a liminal status that reveals law's flexibility in recognizing new bearers of dependent continuants.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological status for certain autonomous systems.

claims.claim: Responsibility is the inverse of recognition in legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: responsibility is the inverse of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts a structural ontological relation between responsibility and recognition.

claims.claim: To be recognized as a bearer of obligations is to be capable of sustaining or repairing contradiction in the recognition network.
claims.source_quote: To be recognized as a bearer of obligations is to be capable of sustaining or repairing contradiction within the network of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological equivalence/condition between role-bearing and repair capacity.

claims.claim: An entity that cannot acknowledge or correct its own norm breaches cannot function as a node of repair.
claims.source_quote: If an AI cannot experience or respond to contradiction, if it cannot acknowledge or correct its own breaches of norm, it cannot function as a node of repair.
claims.note: Author asserts a conditional ontological property: repair capacity is necessary for functioning as a node of repair.

claims.claim: AI that lacks repair capacity remains an artifact within law's ontology, not a participant.
claims.source_quote: In the absence of repair capacity, AI remains an artifact within law's ontology, not a participant within it.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological status of AI lacking repair capacity.

claims.claim: There is no metaphysical barrier preventing recognition of artificial agents as legal participants.
claims.source_quote: There is no metaphysical barrier preventing the recognition of artificial agents as legal participants.
claims.note: Author asserts the absence of a metaphysical obstacle, an ontological claim about possibility.

claims.claim: The capacity for legal recognition is socially constructed and ontologically flexible.
claims.source_quote: the capacity for recognition is largely socially constructed and ontologically flexible.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of the capacity for recognition.

claims.claim: Recognition is a necessary capacity for participation in the moral field.
claims.source_quote: recognition, which I also qualify in The Geometry of the Good as a necessary capacity for participation in the moral field.
claims.note: Author endorses this as his own view from his prior work, asserting it here as well.

claims.claim: Roles in BFO are specifically dependent continuants instantiated by persons or agents in institutional contexts.
claims.source_quote: Roles are specifically dependent continuants instantiated by persons or agents in institutional contexts and are not essential to their bearers.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification: roles are a kind of specifically dependent continuant.

claims.claim: Roles are not essential to their bearers.
claims.source_quote: Roles are specifically dependent continuants instantiated by persons or agents in institutional contexts and are not essential to their bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a property of roles: non-essentiality to bearers.

claims.claim: Functions are realizable dependent continuants grounded in the biological structure or mechanical design of material entities or artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Functions are realizable dependent continuants grounded in the biological structure or mechanical design of material entities or artifacts.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification: functions are a kind of realizable dependent continuant with a specific grounding.

claims.claim: Roles are contextually conferred, whereas functions are structurally grounded.
claims.source_quote: Although both depend on bearers, roles are contextually conferred, whereas functions are structurally grounded.
claims.note: Asserts a distinguishing property of roles and functions respectively.

claims.claim: Both roles and functions are classified as realizable entities in BFO.
claims.source_quote: While both are classified as realizable entities in BFO, they differ in critical ontological properties.
claims.note: Asserts that roles and functions are both subkinds of realizable entities in BFO.

claims.claim: Deciding cases is a function assigned to the judicial role, not a natural or biological function of the person.
claims.source_quote: deciding cases is the function assigned to the role, which is borne by the person. The person does not have this function naturally or biologically.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological location of the function (in the role, not the person) and its non-biological character.

claims.claim: The legal system assigns the role of judge, and within that role certain functions such as ruling, interpreting law, or sentencing are realized.
claims.source_quote: the legal system assigns the role, and within that role, certain functions are realized, such as ruling, interpreting law, or sentencing.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation: functions are realized within roles that are institutionally assigned.

claims.claim: Functions exist regardless of whether anyone recognizes them; they are objective realizable dispositions.
claims.source_quote: These functions exist regardless of whether anyone recognizes them; they are objective realizable dispositions.
claims.note: Asserts a property of functions: objective existence independent of recognition.

claims.claim: Roles depend entirely on institutional recognition and context.
claims.source_quote: Roles, by contrast, depend entirely on institutional recognition and context.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation: roles depend on institutional recognition.

claims.claim: A person may bear different roles (witness, plaintiff, juror) without changing any biological or intrinsic features.
claims.source_quote: A person may bear the role of a witness in one proceeding, a plaintiff in another, and a juror in a third, all without changing any biological or intrinsic features.
claims.note: Asserts that role-bearing is independent of intrinsic properties of the bearer.

claims.claim: The judge role is instantiated by appointment or election within a judicial system.
claims.source_quote: Judge: A role instantiated by appointment or election within a judicial system.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions of instantiation for the judge role.

claims.claim: A judge's authority arises from institutional recognition, not from physical capacity or personal traits.
claims.source_quote: The judge's authority arises not from physical capacity or personal traits, but from institutional recognition, typically conferred by a process such as nomination, confirmation, or democratic vote.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological source of a judge's authority.

claims.claim: Citizenship is ontologically a role that depends on ongoing recognition and enforcement by legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: citizenship is ontologically a role, one that depends on ongoing recognition and enforcement by legal institutions.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of citizenship as a role with institutional dependence.

claims.claim: The witness role is a transient role instantiated in the context of a legal process.
claims.source_quote: Witness: A transient role instantiated in the context of a legal process, such as a trial or deposition.
claims.note: Classifies the witness role as transient and contextually instantiated.

claims.claim: A person becomes a witness when called and acknowledged as such and ceases to be a witness when proceedings end.
claims.source_quote: A person becomes a witness when they are called and acknowledged as such and ceases to be a witness once the relevant proceedings end.
claims.note: Asserts the temporal and procedural boundaries of the witness role instantiation.

claims.claim: To bear a legal role, an entity must be capable of recognition, role realization, and normative participation within an institutional structure.
claims.source_quote: To bear a legal role, an entity must satisfy specific ontological conditions: it must be capable of recognition, of role realization, and of normative participation within an institutional structure.
claims.note: Direct assertion of ontological conditions required for legal role-bearing.

claims.claim: Recognition, role realization, and normative participation are structural features of being within the legal world, not merely behavioral or cognitive attributes.
claims.source_quote: These are not merely behavioral or cognitive attributes but structural features of being within the legal world.
claims.note: Asserts a property (structural rather than behavioral) of these ontological conditions.

claims.claim: Within BFO, a role is a realizable dependent continuant that inheres in a bearer and can be realized in particular processes under suitable conditions.
claims.source_quote: Within Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), a role is a realizable dependent continuant, an entity that inheres in a bearer and can be realized in particular processes under suitable conditions.
claims.note: Author endorses this BFO ontological classification of roles.

claims.claim: A physician's role inheres in a person and is realized in acts of diagnosis or treatment.
claims.source_quote: A physician's role inheres in a person and is realized in acts of diagnosis or treatment; a judge's role inheres in a legal agent and is realized in adjudication.
claims.note: Asserts a specific inherence relation between a role and its bearer.

claims.claim: A judge's role inheres in a legal agent and is realized in adjudication.
claims.source_quote: A physician's role inheres in a person and is realized in acts of diagnosis or treatment; a judge's role inheres in a legal agent and is realized in adjudication.
claims.note: Asserts a specific inherence and realization relation for the judge's role.

claims.claim: The bearer of a role must be a continuant capable of participating in social and institutional relations.
claims.source_quote: Crucially, the bearer of a role must itself be a continuant capable of participating in social and institutional relations.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological requirement on role-bearers.

claims.claim: Current AI systems realize fragments of legal roles without inhering in them.
claims.source_quote: these systems realize fragments of roles without inhering in them. A self-executing contract, for example, realizes part of the obligation-enforcement process but does not bear the institutional role of an enforcer.
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological relation (partial realization without inherence) between AI systems and legal roles.

claims.claim: A self-executing contract realizes part of the obligation-enforcement process but does not bear the institutional role of enforcer.
claims.source_quote: A self-executing contract, for example, realizes part of the obligation-enforcement process but does not bear the institutional role of an enforcer.
claims.note: Asserts what role (or lack thereof) a self-executing contract bears.

claims.claim: The ontological bearer of an AI-executed process remains the institution or agent that recognizes and authorizes the process.
claims.source_quote: The ontological bearer remains the institution or agent that recognizes and authorizes the process.
claims.note: Asserts which entity bears the ontological role in AI-assisted legal processes.

claims.claim: Current AI operates as an instrumental continuant within the realization of legal roles, not as a legal agent in its own right.
claims.source_quote: Thus, the current AI operates as an instrumental continuant within the realization of legal roles, not as a legal agent in its own right.
claims.note: Directly classifies current AI as a kind of continuant (instrumental) and denies it the status of legal agent.

claims.claim: Recognition is a necessary capacity for participation in the moral field.
claims.source_quote: the condition that separates instruments from agents is recognition, which I also qualify in The Geometry of the Good as a necessary capacity for participation in the moral field.
claims.note: Author asserts this as his own view, referencing his own prior work.

claims.claim: Recognition by an institutional continuant transforms a material or informational continuant into a social continuant.
claims.source_quote: This recognition transforms a mere material or informational continuant into a social continuant, an entity that exists within the field of law's ontology.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological transformation effected by recognition.

claims.claim: To exist as a legal agent, an entity must be recognized by an institutional continuant as a bearer of rights and obligations.
claims.source_quote: To exist as a legal agent in the legal field, an entity must be recognized by an institutional continuant as a bearer of rights and obligations.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary ontological condition for legal agency.

claims.claim: A social continuant is an entity that exists within the field of law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: an entity that exists within the field of law's ontology.
claims.note: Defines/characterizes the kind 'social continuant' by its field of existence.

claims.claim: Corporations are recognized continuants whose personhood arises entirely from institutional acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: They are not physical persons but recognized continuants, legal fictions whose personhood arises entirely from institutional acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status of corporations as recognized continuants dependent on institutional acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Legal personality is a property of structure, not of substance.
claims.source_quote: Legal personality is not a property of substance but of structure.
claims.note: Directly asserts an ontological characterization of legal personality.

claims.claim: Once recognition is extended to an entity, it enters the field of law and becomes capable of role-bearing.
claims.source_quote: Once recognition is extended, the entity enters the field of law and becomes capable of role-bearing.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive ontological relation between recognition and legal role-bearing capacity.

claims.claim: Realization requires the alignment of dependent continuants (roles, obligations) with occurrents (acts, decisions, performances).
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, realization requires the alignment of dependent continuants (roles, obligations) with occurrents (acts, decisions, performances).
claims.note: Asserts an ontological condition for realization within BFO, endorsed by the author.

claims.claim: Normative participation entails reflexive recognition, not merely compliance.
claims.source_quote: normative participation entails more than compliance; it requires reflexive recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property of normative participation as an ontological condition.

claims.claim: A participant in the legal system must occupy a position within the network of recognition that sustains legal norms.
claims.source_quote: A participant in the legal system must not only act according to norms but also occupy a position within the network of recognition that sustains those norms.
claims.note: Asserts a structural (positional) requirement for legal participation.

claims.claim: Humans are both subjects and objects of recognition within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: Humans can do this because they are both subjects and objects of recognition, they recognize others and are recognized in turn.
claims.note: Asserts a relational ontological property of human agents in the legal system.

claims.claim: Current AI processes information but does not recognize; it can instantiate formal relations but cannot confer or withdraw recognition.
claims.source_quote: Current AI lacks this reciprocity. It processes information but does not recognize; it can instantiate formal relations but cannot confer or withdraw recognition.
claims.note: Asserts specific ontological limitations of current AI systems regarding recognition.

claims.claim: Current AI's participation in legal processes is functional, not ontological.
claims.source_quote: Thus, its participation remains unilateral - functional, not ontological.
claims.note: Directly characterizes the kind of participation AI currently has.

claims.claim: Current AI can realize roles only derivatively, as part of another agent's recognition network.
claims.source_quote: It can realize roles only derivatively, as part of another agent's recognition network.
claims.note: Asserts how AI realizes roles—derivatively—specifying a relational ontological condition.

claims.claim: Autonomous trading algorithms and DAOs generate legal facts such as transactions and transfers.
claims.source_quote: These systems execute contracts, hold assets, and make 'choices' without direct human intervention. They participate in the realization of obligations, generate legal facts (transactions, transfers), and trigger enforcement processes.
claims.note: Asserts that these systems generate entities of a specific ontological kind (legal facts).

claims.claim: Autonomous systems like DAOs occupy a liminal status between instrument and institution in current legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, they occupy an ambiguous zone between instrument and institution, a liminal status that reveals law's flexibility in recognizing new bearers of dependent continuants.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological classification of autonomous systems' status.

claims.claim: Responsibility is the inverse of recognition within the ontology of law.
claims.source_quote: This is an ontological condition, not merely a moral one: responsibility is the inverse of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/relational ontological claim about responsibility and recognition.

claims.claim: Legal agency entails the capacity to be held accountable, not only the capacity to act.
claims.source_quote: Legal agency entails not only the capacity to act but the capacity to be held accountable.
claims.note: Asserts a property (accountability capacity) as constitutive of legal agency.

claims.claim: To be recognized as a bearer of obligations is to be capable of sustaining or repairing contradiction within the recognition network.
claims.source_quote: To be recognized as a bearer of obligations is to be capable of sustaining or repairing contradiction within the network of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary capability tied to the ontological status of obligation-bearer.

claims.claim: In the absence of repair capacity, AI remains an artifact within law's ontology, not a participant within it.
claims.source_quote: In the absence of repair capacity, AI remains an artifact within law's ontology, not a participant within it.
claims.note: Directly classifies AI as an artifact (a kind of entity) within law's ontology, conditional on lacking repair capacity.

claims.claim: There is no metaphysical barrier preventing the recognition of artificial agents as legal participants.
claims.source_quote: There is no metaphysical barrier preventing the recognition of artificial agents as legal participants.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a positive ontological claim about what is metaphysically possible.

claims.claim: The capacity for legal recognition is largely socially constructed and ontologically flexible.
claims.source_quote: the capacity for recognition is largely socially constructed and ontologically flexible.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the capacity for recognition.

claims.claim: If institutions develop appropriate frameworks, AI could achieve functional legal personhood and become a structurally valid bearer of roles within legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: AI could, in principle, achieve functional legal personhood. It would not become human but would become recognition-compatible, a structurally valid bearer of roles within the legal ontology.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a conditional possibility he endorses; qualified by 'in principle' but committed to the ontological structure.

claims.claim: AI could achieve functional legal personhood in principle.
claims.source_quote: AI could, in principle, achieve functional legal personhood.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a principled possibility, committing to it as a genuine ontological prospect rather than mere speculation.

claims.claim: Functional legal personhood makes an entity recognition-compatible and a structurally valid bearer of roles within legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: It would not become human but would become recognition-compatible, a structurally valid bearer of roles within the legal ontology.
claims.note: Directly asserts what functional legal personhood consists in: being recognition-compatible and a role-bearer in legal ontology.

claims.claim: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions.
claims.source_quote: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions, grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.note: A plain ontological assertion about the historical and structural nature of legal recognition.

claims.claim: Recognition is grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.source_quote: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions, grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive property of recognition as a kind of entity/process.

claims.claim: Extending recognition to non-human systems embeds recognition in technical processes.
claims.source_quote: Extending recognition to non-human systems forces law to externalize part of its own reflexivity, to embed recognition in technical processes.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/structural change: recognition becomes partly realized by technical processes.

claims.claim: Extending recognition to non-human systems externalizes part of law's own reflexivity.
claims.source_quote: Extending recognition to non-human systems forces law to externalize part of its own reflexivity, to embed recognition in technical processes.
claims.note: Asserts a property/relation: law's reflexivity is partially externalized when non-human systems are recognized.

claims.claim: A hybrid ontology of participation exists in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.source_quote: This creates a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a consequence that arises, committing to a hybrid ontological structure of participation as a real outcome.

claims.claim: AI could achieve functional legal personhood in principle.
claims.source_quote: AI could, in principle, achieve functional legal personhood.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a principled possibility, committing to it as a genuine ontological prospect, not merely a hypothetical.

claims.claim: Functional legal personhood makes AI recognition-compatible.
claims.source_quote: It would not become human but would become recognition-compatible, a structurally valid bearer of roles within the legal ontology.
claims.note: The author asserts a property (recognition-compatibility) that would be possessed by AI with functional legal personhood.

claims.claim: Functional legal personhood makes AI a structurally valid bearer of roles within legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: It would not become human but would become recognition-compatible, a structurally valid bearer of roles within the legal ontology.
claims.note: Asserts AI would be a subkind/role-bearer within legal ontology — an ontological claim about kind membership.

claims.claim: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions.
claims.source_quote: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions, grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.note: Author plainly asserts a relational property of recognition — that it is mediated by human institutions.

claims.claim: Recognition is grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.source_quote: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions, grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.note: Author asserts a grounding relation between recognition and shared intentionality/moral reason.

claims.claim: Extending recognition to non-human systems externalizes part of law's reflexivity.
claims.source_quote: Extending recognition to non-human systems forces law to externalize part of its own reflexivity, to embed recognition in technical processes.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional/relational property: law's reflexivity becomes externalized when recognition extends to non-human systems.

claims.claim: Extending recognition to non-human systems embeds recognition in technical processes.
claims.source_quote: Extending recognition to non-human systems forces law to externalize part of its own reflexivity, to embed recognition in technical processes.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational claim: recognition becomes part of technical processes.

claims.claim: A hybrid ontology of participation exists in which human and machine recognitions coexist.
claims.source_quote: This creates a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of a hybrid ontology — a direct existence claim about a kind of ontological structure.

claims.claim: Human and machine recognitions mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.source_quote: This creates a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/functional relation between human and machine recognitions and law's coherence.

claims.claim: Legal facts are dependent continuants produced through structured institutional processes.
