claims.source_quote: Legal facts are modeled as dependent continuants produced through structured processes rather than mere descriptions of reality.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological kind of legal facts.

claims.claim: Brute facts are physical or social events apprehensible by perception.
claims.source_quote: What begins as a brute fact, a physical or social event apprehensible by perception, becomes a legal fact only when it is incorporated into the network of recognition that constitutes the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts a property/definition of brute facts as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: A legal fact is a brute event incorporated into the network of recognition constituting the legal domain.
claims.source_quote: What begins as a brute fact, a physical or social event apprehensible by perception, becomes a legal fact only when it is incorporated into the network of recognition that constitutes the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts what a legal fact is and the condition for its existence.

claims.claim: Signed documents, spoken verdicts, and legislative decrees begin as brute occurrences in space and time.
claims.source_quote: A signed document, a spoken verdict, a legislative decree, all begin as brute occurrences in space and time, yet each acquires the status of a fact of law through a structured sequence of ontological transitions.
claims.note: Asserts the initial ontological status of these entities.

claims.claim: Legal status is acquired by brute entities through a structured sequence of ontological transitions.
claims.source_quote: each acquires the status of a fact of law through a structured sequence of ontological transitions.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/processual claim about how legal status is generated.

claims.claim: The transformation from brute to legal fact is the addition of a dependent continuant to an independent entity or process.
claims.source_quote: From the standpoint of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), the transformation from brute to legal fact can be described as the addition of a dependent continuant, a relational property sustained by recognition, to an independent entity or process.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure of the brute-to-legal transformation.

claims.claim: A dependent continuant is a relational property sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: the transformation from brute to legal fact can be described as the addition of a dependent continuant, a relational property sustained by recognition, to an independent entity or process.
claims.note: Asserts a property of dependent continuants as used in this legal ontology.

claims.claim: Brute facts as physical or social occurrences are independent continuants or occurrents.
claims.source_quote: The brute fact, as a physical or social occurrence, is an independent continuant or occurrent: it exists regardless of social acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological classification of brute facts within BFO.

claims.claim: Brute facts exist regardless of social acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: The brute fact, as a physical or social occurrence, is an independent continuant or occurrent: it exists regardless of social acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts a key property distinguishing brute facts from institutional facts.

claims.claim: When occurrences are recognized within an institutional framework, they acquire new properties such as legality, validity, and enforceability.
claims.source_quote: When these occurrences are recognized within an institutional framework, they acquire new properties such as legality, validity, and enforceability, that depend on ongoing recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that institutional recognition causes entities to bear new properties.

claims.claim: Properties like legality, validity, and enforceability depend on ongoing recognition.
claims.source_quote: they acquire new properties such as legality, validity, and enforceability, that depend on ongoing recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between these properties and recognition.

claims.claim: The act of recognition creates a new ontological layer by supervening on physical structure.
claims.source_quote: The act of recognition does not change the underlying physical structure but supervenes upon it, creating a new ontological layer.
claims.note: Asserts a supervenience relation and the production of a new ontological layer.

claims.claim: The legal status function is a dependent continuant that makes an entity part of the legal domain.
claims.source_quote: This additional layer, the legal status function, is what makes the entity part of the legal domain.
claims.note: Asserts the role/function of the legal status function as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: A valid signature is a dependent continuant that inheres in a physical mark.
claims.source_quote: This recognition introduces a new dependent continuant, the status of being a valid signature, which inheres in the physical mark and depends on the network of recognition that defines the relevant legal context.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status of a valid signature and its inherence relation.

claims.claim: A valid signature depends on the network of recognition defining the relevant legal context.
claims.source_quote: the status of being a valid signature, which inheres in the physical mark and depends on the network of recognition that defines the relevant legal context.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between a valid signature and its recognition network.

claims.claim: A legal signature status can persist even if the original signatory is absent or deceased.
claims.source_quote: That status can persist even if the original signatory is absent or deceased, as long as the institutional relations that sustain it remain intact.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of legal status as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The legal fact 'this document is signed' refers to a relational structure of recognition, not to physical lines.
claims.source_quote: The legal fact 'this document is signed' thus refers not to the physical lines themselves but to the relational structure of recognition that grants those lines their institutional meaning.
claims.note: Asserts what the legal fact refers to, i.e., its ontological referent.

claims.claim: A verdict is a legal occurrent that alters the configuration of dependent continuants within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The verdict is a paradigmatic legal occurrent: an event that alters the configuration of dependent continuants within the legal system by modifying recognition relations.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of a verdict and its causal/relational role.

claims.claim: A verdict, once entered into the record, becomes an enduring legal fact and a persistent part of institutional ontology.
claims.source_quote: Once entered into the record, it becomes an enduring legal fact, a persistent part of the institutional ontology that defines a person's status.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of verdicts as legal facts.

claims.claim: A verdict defines a person's status within institutional ontology.
claims.source_quote: Once entered into the record, it becomes an enduring legal fact, a persistent part of the institutional ontology that defines a person's status.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational role of verdicts with respect to persons.

claims.claim: Enactment of a statute or administrative order creates new dependent continuants: norms and obligations.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, this marks the creation of new dependent continuants, norms and obligations, that depend on the continued recognition of the decree's authority.
claims.note: Asserts that norms and obligations are dependent continuants produced by legal enactment.

claims.claim: Norms and obligations depend on the continued recognition of the decree's authority.
claims.source_quote: the creation of new dependent continuants, norms and obligations, that depend on the continued recognition of the decree's authority.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between norms/obligations and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: The ontological transformation of a decree proceeds in stages: from brute event to recognized act, to institutional continuant, to enduring legal system component.
claims.source_quote: The ontological transformation thus proceeds in stages: from brute event to recognized act, from recognized act to institutional continuant, and from institutional continuant to enduring component of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a staged ontological process with distinct entity types at each stage.

claims.claim: Recognition functions as the operator that generates new levels of dependence and coherence in legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: At each stage, recognition functions as the operator that generates new levels of dependence and coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of recognition in generating ontological structure.

claims.claim: Each legal fact involves a substrate (the brute fact or object), a status function, and a field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Each legal fact involves at least three entities: – A substrate (the brute fact or object), – A status function (the institutional property conferred), and – A field of recognition (the network of agents and institutions that sustain the status).
claims.note: Asserts the compositional ontological structure of every legal fact.

claims.claim: A status function is an institutional property conferred on a substrate.
claims.source_quote: A status function (the institutional property conferred)
claims.note: Asserts what a status function is as a kind of entity/property.

claims.claim: A field of recognition is a network of agents and institutions that sustain a status function.
claims.source_quote: A field of recognition (the network of agents and institutions that sustain the status).
claims.note: Asserts the composition and role of the field of recognition.

claims.claim: Witness is a transient role instantiated in the context of a legal process.
claims.source_quote: Witness: A transient role instantiated in the context of a legal process, such as a trial or deposition.
claims.note: Asserts that witness is a subkind of role with the property of being transient and context-dependent.

claims.claim: A witness role is accompanied by legal duties and legal protections.
claims.source_quote: This role is often accompanied by legal duties (e.g., to testify truthfully) and legal protections (e.g., immunity from certain reprisals).
claims.note: Asserts that the witness role has specific associated properties (duties and protections).

claims.claim: Legal roles are ontologically dependent on social institutions.
claims.source_quote: What they share is that they are all ontologically dependent on social institutions and not inherent to the person.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the dependence relation between legal roles and social institutions.

claims.claim: Legal roles are not inherent to the person who bears them.
claims.source_quote: What they share is that they are all ontologically dependent on social institutions and not inherent to the person.
claims.note: Asserts a negative property of roles: they are not intrinsic to persons.

claims.claim: A person (modeled as an independent continuant) bears multiple roles.
claims.source_quote: a single person (modeled as an independent continuant) bears multiple roles (modeled as specifically dependent continuants)
claims.note: Asserts the bearing relation between persons and roles, and their respective ontological categories.

claims.claim: Roles are specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Roles are therefore specifically dependent continuants, but they also require relational grounding.
claims.note: Asserts that roles belong to the ontological kind 'specifically dependent continuant'.

claims.claim: Roles are essentially relational entities.
claims.source_quote: roles are essentially relational entities. They are not properties of individuals in isolation but arise only in the context of social structures, practices, and expectations.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental property of roles: they are relational.

claims.claim: Roles exist because others acknowledge them and act in accordance with them.
claims.source_quote: they exist because others (individuals and institutions) acknowledge them and act in accordance with them.
claims.note: Asserts the grounding condition for the existence of roles.

claims.claim: A role arises from a position within an institutional system.
claims.source_quote: It arises from a position within an institutional system, and it is enacted through participation in structured social practices.
claims.note: Asserts the origin/source relation of roles to institutional systems.

claims.claim: A role is enacted through participation in structured social practices.
claims.source_quote: It arises from a position within an institutional system, and it is enacted through participation in structured social practices.
claims.note: Asserts how roles are enacted, a relational-process property.

claims.claim: Institutions are networks of interrelated roles governed by norms, rules, and functions.
claims.source_quote: Institutions like courts, legislatures, hospitals, and schools exist not as monolithic entities but as networks of interrelated roles, each governed by norms, rules, and functions.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological composition and structure of institutions.

claims.claim: A court is an ontologically structured system of roles and role-dependent processes.
claims.source_quote: The court is thus not only a building or an organization, but an ontologically structured system of roles and role-dependent processes.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of courts beyond physical or organizational description.

claims.claim: Institutions enable and constrain the realization of roles.
claims.source_quote: institutions do not simply 'assign' roles, they also enable and constrain their realization.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/causal relation between institutions and roles.

claims.claim: Roles are realized in processes.
claims.source_quote: Roles are realized in processes, and that these processes must be ontologically modeled as occurrents.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between roles and processes.

claims.claim: Role-realizing processes are occurrents bounded in time.
claims.source_quote: these processes must be ontologically modeled as occurrents, bounded in time, involving specific role-bearers, and producing observable outcomes.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and properties of role-realizing processes.

claims.claim: Some roles are mutually exclusive with other roles.
claims.source_quote: Some roles are mutually exclusive (e.g., judge and defendant in the same case)
claims.note: Asserts a constraint relation between certain role kinds.

claims.claim: Some roles are hierarchically ordered relative to other roles.
claims.source_quote: some are hierarchical (e.g., subordinate officer vs. commanding officer)
claims.note: Asserts a hierarchical relation between certain roles.

claims.claim: Some roles are logically dependent on other roles.
claims.source_quote: some are logically dependent (e.g., teacher requires student; buyer requires seller)
claims.note: Asserts a logical dependency relation between paired role kinds.

claims.claim: Roles are socially real, existing in virtue of institutional facts and shared expectations.
claims.source_quote: Roles are not simply mental constructs or linguistic conventions; they are socially real, existing in virtue of institutional facts and sustained by shared expectations.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status of roles as socially real entities.

claims.claim: Roles are as real as institutions themselves.
claims.source_quote: Roles are as real as institutions themselves, and they can and should be modeled accordingly in applied ontologies.
claims.note: Asserts parity of ontological status between roles and institutions.

claims.claim: Role transitions are temporally ordered processes that modify the rights, duties, and legal status of the individual.
claims.source_quote: role transitions (e.g., accused → convict → parolee) as temporally ordered processes that modify the rights, duties, and legal status of the individual.
claims.note: Asserts the nature and effect of role transitions as processes with ontological consequences.

claims.claim: Roles require institutional recognition, not just behavioral patterns.
claims.source_quote: roles require institutional recognition, not just actions. For example, acting like a judge does not confer legal authority without appointment.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition is a necessary condition for role instantiation.

claims.claim: Roles do not exist independently of the institutional structures that assign and define them.
claims.source_quote: Institutions assign and define roles which do not exist independently of these structures.
claims.note: Asserts ontological dependence of roles on institutions.

claims.claim: Behavior alone cannot instantiate a role.
claims.source_quote: Behavior alone cannot instantiate a role; legitimacy comes from institutional context.
claims.note: Asserts a negative causal/instantiation claim about the relationship between behavior and roles.

claims.claim: Role legitimacy derives from institutional context.
claims.source_quote: Behavior alone cannot instantiate a role; legitimacy comes from institutional context.
claims.note: Asserts the source of role legitimacy as a property of roles.

claims.claim: Roles are normatively structured and recognition-dependent entities.
claims.source_quote: Roles, therefore, are normatively structured and recognition-dependent, existing due to institutional assignment and societal acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts two key properties of roles: normative structure and recognition-dependence.

claims.claim: Loss of legal rights is best understood as loss of role-bearing status.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological standpoint, these situations are best understood as loss of role-bearing status.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological identification of what 'losing rights' amounts to.

claims.claim: A right exists as a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in an agent in virtue of a role.
claims.source_quote: The right in question exists as a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in the agent in virtue of a role.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of rights and their dependence on roles.

claims.claim: Loss of rights upon conviction or incompetency is best understood as loss of role-bearing status.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological standpoint, these situations are best understood as loss of role-bearing status.
claims.note: The author directly asserts an ontological characterization of rights loss.

claims.claim: A right exists as a specifically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: The right in question exists as a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in the agent in virtue of a role.
claims.note: Asserts what kind of entity a right is.

claims.claim: A right inheres in an agent in virtue of a role.
claims.source_quote: The right in question exists as a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in the agent in virtue of a role.
claims.note: Asserts a relation (inherence) between a right and an agent, grounded in role.

claims.claim: If an agent no longer instantiates the relevant role, the right is no longer realized.
claims.source_quote: If the agent no longer instantiates the relevant role (e.g., 'competent adult citizen'), the right is no longer realized.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between role instantiation and right realization.

claims.claim: Rights are not lost like physical objects; they are deactivated or suspended when conditions for their instantiation are unmet.
claims.source_quote: rights are not 'lost' like physical objects, they are deactivated or suspended because the conditions for their instantiation are no longer met.
claims.note: Asserts a property of rights regarding how they cease to obtain, distinguishing them from physical objects.

claims.claim: Role ontology enables formal tracking of the conditions for rights instantiation.
claims.source_quote: Role ontology enables us to track these conditions formally.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/dispositional property of role ontology; slightly methodological but commits to what role ontology does ontologically.

claims.claim: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions.
claims.source_quote: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions, grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the nature and mediation of recognition as a property of human institutions.

claims.claim: Extending recognition to non-human systems creates a hybrid ontology of participation.
claims.source_quote: Extending recognition to non-human systems forces law to externalize part of its own reflexivity, to embed recognition in technical processes. This creates a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: Author asserts existence of a hybrid ontology as a result of extending recognition.

claims.claim: Human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence in this hybrid ontology.
claims.source_quote: This creates a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between human and machine recognitions within law's structure.

claims.claim: Automated enforcement, algorithmic sentencing assistance, and AI-driven compliance systems participate in maintaining law's structure.
claims.source_quote: automated enforcement, algorithmic sentencing assistance, and AI-driven compliance systems all participate in maintaining law's structure.
claims.note: Author asserts participation relation between these systems and law's structure.

claims.claim: AI currently remains subordinate within law's ontology because it does not participate reflexively in recognition.
claims.source_quote: AI can simulate reasoning, perform adjudication, and execute contractual norms, but until it participates reflexively in recognition, until it becomes both subject and object of law's ontology, it remains subordinate.
claims.note: Asserts AI's current ontological status as subordinate due to lack of reflexive recognition.

claims.claim: AI can simulate reasoning, perform adjudication, and execute contractual norms.
claims.source_quote: AI can simulate reasoning, perform adjudication, and execute contractual norms, but until it participates reflexively in recognition...it remains subordinate.
claims.note: Author positively asserts capacities belonging to AI as properties/functions.

claims.claim: Algorithms, code, and decision engines function as realization mechanisms for institutional processes.
claims.source_quote: Algorithms, code, and decision engines function as realization mechanisms for institutional processes; they perform occurrents that instantiate legal effects.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/property of these entities within the legal domain.

claims.claim: Algorithms, code, and decision engines perform occurrents that instantiate legal effects.
claims.source_quote: they perform occurrents that instantiate legal effects.
claims.note: Asserts that these entities bear a realization relation to legal effects via occurrents.

claims.claim: A tax assessment algorithm realizes the function of calculation and compliance.
claims.source_quote: A tax assessment algorithm realizes the function of calculation and compliance; a sentencing recommender realizes aspects of judicial discretion; a blockchain contract realizes enforcement without intermediary authority.
claims.note: Author asserts realization relations between specific automated systems and legal functions.

claims.claim: A sentencing recommender realizes aspects of judicial discretion.
claims.source_quote: a sentencing recommender realizes aspects of judicial discretion
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between a specific system and a legal function.

claims.claim: A blockchain contract realizes enforcement without intermediary authority.
claims.source_quote: a blockchain contract realizes enforcement without intermediary authority.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation and a property of blockchain contracts.

claims.claim: Automated systems are instrumental continuants that participate in realizing dependent continuants without bearing those dependencies.
claims.source_quote: These automations can be represented ontologically as instrumental continuants: entities that participate in the realization of dependent continuants (obligations, duties, permissions) without themselves being bearers of those dependencies.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological kind and relational properties of automated systems.

claims.claim: Obligations, duties, and permissions are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: entities that participate in the realization of dependent continuants (obligations, duties, permissions)
claims.note: Author classifies these legal entities as a subkind (dependent continuants).

claims.claim: Automated systems enact but do not recognize.
claims.source_quote: They enact, but they do not recognize.
claims.note: Asserts a property (enacting) and the absence of a property (recognizing) in automated systems.

claims.claim: When automated systems are integrated without recognition structures, law's reflexivity weakens.
claims.source_quote: When such systems are integrated into the realization chain without corresponding recognition structures, law's reflexivity weakens, its ability to review, interpret, and repair its own acts diminishes.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/structural relation between automation without recognition and weakening of law's reflexivity.

claims.claim: Norm opacity is a loss of reflexivity in which normativity is concealed within technical structures.
claims.source_quote: Automation, by contrast, conceals normativity within technical structures: algorithmic parameters, training data, and decision rules invisible to both citizens and institutions.
claims.note: Author defines and asserts norm opacity as a real ontological condition of automated legal systems.

claims.claim: When legal functions are delegated to opaque systems, dependencies sustaining recognition become obscured.
claims.source_quote: When legal functions are delegated to opaque systems, the dependencies that sustain recognition become obscured.
claims.note: Asserts a relational consequence: delegation to opaque systems obscures recognition dependencies.

claims.claim: A system that generates legal effects without maintaining the trace of recognition is an ontological pathology.
claims.source_quote: The result is an ontological pathology, a system that generates legal effects without maintaining the trace of recognition that makes them law.
claims.note: Author asserts that this system type constitutes an ontological pathology—a property claim about such systems.

claims.claim: Algorithmic tools that produce obligations and outcomes without transparent institutional acknowledgment instantiate pseudo-recognition.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, they instantiate pseudo-recognition, processes that mimic the effects of legal recognition while bypassing its conditions.
claims.note: Author asserts that these tools instantiate a specific ontological kind: pseudo-recognition.

claims.claim: Unrecognized or unreviewable decisions introduce incoherent continuants into law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: Each unrecognized or unreviewable decision introduces incoherent continuants into law's ontology: obligations and rights that exist formally but without traceable dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts existence of incoherent continuants introduced by such decisions, and their property of lacking traceable dependencies.

claims.claim: Obligations and rights produced by opaque automated decisions exist formally but without traceable dependencies.
claims.source_quote: obligations and rights that exist formally but without traceable dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts a property of these legal entities—formal existence without traceable dependencies.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt accumulates invisibly within the digital substratum of legal practice over time.
claims.source_quote: Over time, contradiction debt accumulates invisibly within the digital substratum of legal practice.
claims.note: Author asserts existence of contradiction debt and its location/property within the digital substratum.

claims.claim: Norm loss is a deficit of ontological transparency.
claims.source_quote: The risk of norm loss can thus be expressed as a deficit of ontological transparency.
claims.note: Author identifies norm loss with a specific ontological property deficit.

claims.claim: Every legal system must preserve visible chains of recognition linking acts, agents, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: every legal system must preserve visible chains of recognition linking acts, agents, and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property/requirement of every legal system.

claims.claim: Ontological transparency has two dimensions: representational and institutional.
claims.source_quote: Ontological transparency has two dimensions: representational and institutional.
claims.note: Asserts a property (having two dimensions) of ontological transparency as an entity.

claims.claim: Representational transparency requires that formal ontologies encode dependencies of recognition, not just entities and relations.
claims.source_quote: Representational transparency demands that the formal ontologies used in legal AI, OWL schemas, RDF graphs, rule engines, encode not just entities and relations but their dependencies of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property/requirement of representational transparency as a dimension of ontological transparency.

claims.claim: Only human or institutional continuants can repair norms; machines may realize norms but cannot repair them.
claims.source_quote: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.note: Asserts a property distinguishing machine entities from human/institutional continuants regarding repair.

claims.claim: Accountability must be a structural property of law's ontology, not an afterthought.
claims.source_quote: Accountability must therefore be reintroduced at the ontological level, not as afterthought but as structural property.
claims.note: Asserts accountability as a structural property that must belong to law's ontological architecture.

claims.claim: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions.
claims.source_quote: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions, grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the nature and mediation of recognition as an ontological property.

claims.claim: Extending recognition to non-human systems creates a hybrid ontology of participation.
claims.source_quote: Extending recognition to non-human systems forces law to externalize part of its own reflexivity, to embed recognition in technical processes. This creates a hybrid ontology of participation.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of a new ontological kind—hybrid ontology of participation—resulting from this extension.

claims.claim: Human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence in this hybrid ontology.
claims.source_quote: This creates a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between human and machine recognitions within law's ontology.

claims.claim: Automated enforcement, algorithmic sentencing assistance, and AI-driven compliance systems participate in maintaining law's structure.
claims.source_quote: automated enforcement, algorithmic sentencing assistance, and AI-driven compliance systems all participate in maintaining law's structure.
claims.note: Asserts that these entities bear a participation relation to law's structure.

claims.claim: AI currently remains subordinate within law's ontology because it does not participate reflexively in recognition.
claims.source_quote: AI can simulate reasoning, perform adjudication, and execute contractual norms, but until it participates reflexively in recognition, until it becomes both subject and object of law's ontology, it remains subordinate.
claims.note: Author asserts a current ontological status (subordinate) grounded in a relational property (lack of reflexive recognition).

claims.claim: Full legal agency for AI requires that it be both subject and object of law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: until it becomes both subject and object of law's ontology, it remains subordinate.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for a kind of ontological status.

claims.claim: The ultimate test of AI's legal agency is whether it can repair, recognize contradiction, and restore coherence.
claims.source_quote: The ultimate test of AI's legal agency will not be whether it can act but whether it can repair, whether it can recognize contradiction, respond to it, and restore coherence within law's relational architecture.
claims.note: Asserts dispositional/functional properties required for legal agency.

claims.claim: Norm loss is the erosion of law's reflexive and interpretive structures through excessive delegation to algorithmic mechanisms.
claims.source_quote: Chief among them is norm loss: the erosion of law's reflexive and interpretive structures through excessive delegation to algorithmic mechanisms.
claims.note: Author defines and asserts norm loss as a real ontological risk/phenomenon with a specific character.

claims.claim: Automation without ontological transparency transforms law from a coherent field of recognition into a closed technical system.
claims.source_quote: When normative systems are automated without maintaining their ontological transparency...law risks transforming from a coherent field of recognition into a closed technical system.
claims.note: Author asserts this transformation as a real risk/consequence, slightly hedged by 'risks' but endorsed as author's own structural claim.

claims.claim: Algorithms, code, and decision engines function as realization mechanisms for institutional processes.
claims.source_quote: Algorithms, code, and decision engines function as realization mechanisms for institutional processes; they perform occurrents that instantiate legal effects.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/role property for a class of entities.

claims.claim: Algorithms perform occurrents that instantiate legal effects.
claims.source_quote: they perform occurrents that instantiate legal effects.
claims.note: Asserts that algorithms bear a realization relation to legal effects via occurrents.

claims.claim: A tax assessment algorithm realizes the function of calculation and compliance.
claims.source_quote: A tax assessment algorithm realizes the function of calculation and compliance.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between a specific kind of algorithm and a function.

claims.claim: A sentencing recommender realizes aspects of judicial discretion.
claims.source_quote: a sentencing recommender realizes aspects of judicial discretion.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between entity and function.

claims.claim: A blockchain contract realizes enforcement without intermediary authority.
claims.source_quote: a blockchain contract realizes enforcement without intermediary authority.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation and a property (absence of intermediary) for a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Automated legal systems are instrumental continuants that participate in realizing dependent continuants without bearing those dependencies themselves.
claims.source_quote: These automations can be represented ontologically as instrumental continuants: entities that participate in the realization of dependent continuants (obligations, duties, permissions) without themselves being bearers of those dependencies.
claims.note: Author positively asserts an ontological classification and relational property for automated systems.

claims.claim: Automated systems enact legal norms but do not recognize them.
claims.source_quote: They enact, but they do not recognize.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property (enactment without recognition) of automated legal systems.

claims.claim: Integration of automated systems without recognition structures weakens law's reflexivity.
claims.source_quote: When such systems are integrated into the realization chain without corresponding recognition structures, law's reflexivity weakens, its ability to review, interpret, and repair its own acts diminishes.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/structural relation between automated integration and a property of law.

claims.claim: Norm opacity exists as a pathological condition in which normativity is concealed within technical structures.
claims.source_quote: This loss of reflexivity manifests as what we may call norm opacity. In traditional legal processes, norms are enacted through visible, contestable acts...Automation, by contrast, conceals normativity within technical structures.
claims.note: Author introduces and asserts norm opacity as a real phenomenon with a specific character.

claims.claim: Opaque automated systems produce legal effects without maintaining the trace of recognition that makes them law.
claims.source_quote: The law continues to produce outcomes, but the relations that justify and validate them are hidden. The result is an ontological pathology, a system that generates legal effects without maintaining the trace of recognition that makes them law.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property (pathology) and a relational deficit of automated legal systems.

claims.claim: Algorithmic tools operate within law's realization layer but outside its recognition layer.
claims.source_quote: These tools operate within law's realization layer but outside its recognition layer: they produce obligations and outcomes without transparent institutional acknowledgment of how those outcomes are derived.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/locational property of algorithmic tools with respect to layers of law's ontology.

claims.claim: Algorithmic legal tools instantiate pseudo-recognition, mimicking legal recognition while bypassing its conditions.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, they instantiate pseudo-recognition, processes that mimic the effects of legal recognition while bypassing its conditions.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological kind (pseudo-recognition) and ascribes it to these systems.

claims.claim: Unrecognized or unreviewable algorithmic decisions introduce incoherent continuants into law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: Each unrecognized or unreviewable decision introduces incoherent continuants into law's ontology: obligations and rights that exist formally but without traceable dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts existence of a kind of entity (incoherent continuants) and their introduction into law's ontology.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt accumulates invisibly within the digital substratum of legal practice.
claims.source_quote: Over time, contradiction debt accumulates invisibly within the digital substratum of legal practice.
claims.note: Asserts existence and accumulation of contradiction debt as an ontological phenomenon in legal systems.

claims.claim: Every legal system must preserve visible chains of recognition linking acts, agents, and institutions to sustain coherence.
claims.source_quote: every legal system must preserve visible chains of recognition linking acts, agents, and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a structural requirement (relational property) of legal systems for coherence.

claims.claim: Ontological transparency requires that for every algorithmic decision, the underlying ontological structure must remain accessible and auditable.
claims.source_quote: Ontological transparency means that for every algorithmic decision, the underlying ontological structure...must remain accessible and auditable.
claims.note: Author defines and asserts a property (ontological transparency) as a structural requirement.

claims.claim: Only human or institutional continuants can repair norms; machines can only realize them.
claims.source_quote: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional/functional distinction between machine and human/institutional continuants.

claims.claim: Accountability must be a structural property of legal ontology, not an afterthought.
claims.source_quote: Accountability must therefore be reintroduced at the ontological level, not as afterthought but as structural property.
claims.note: Asserts that accountability is (or must be treated as) a structural ontological property of law.

claims.claim: Representational transparency requires that formal ontologies encode recognition dependencies, not just entities and relations.
claims.source_quote: Representational transparency demands that the formal ontologies used in legal AI...encode not just entities and relations but their dependencies of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a required property of formal ontologies used in legal AI.

claims.claim: Institutional transparency requires that social mechanisms surrounding automation remain active.
claims.source_quote: Institutional transparency requires that the social mechanisms surrounding automation, judicial review, public explanation, procedural appeal, remain active.
claims.note: Asserts a required property (activity) of social mechanisms as part of law's ontological structure.

claims.claim: Each legal fact involves at least three entities: a substrate, a status function, and a field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Each legal fact involves at least three entities: – A substrate (the brute fact or object), – A status function (the institutional property conferred), and – A field of recognition (the network of agents and institutions that sustain the status).
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the constituent entities of legal facts.

claims.claim: The field of recognition establishes a dependency relation between the substrate and the status function.
claims.source_quote: The transformation occurs when the field of recognition establishes a dependency relation between the substrate and the status function.
claims.note: Asserts a relational structure between entities constituting legal facts.

claims.claim: The dependency relation between substrate and status function is asymmetric.
claims.source_quote: This dependency relation is asymmetric and specifically dependent: the status cannot exist without the substrate and the field, but the substrate can exist without the status.
claims.note: Asserts a property (asymmetry) of the dependency relation.

claims.claim: The status function cannot exist without the substrate and the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: the status cannot exist without the substrate and the field, but the substrate can exist without the status.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of the status on substrate and field.

claims.claim: The substrate can exist without the status function.
claims.source_quote: the status cannot exist without the substrate and the field, but the substrate can exist without the status.
claims.note: Asserts the lack of existential dependency of the substrate on the status.

claims.claim: The legal fact 'this verdict is final' involves coexistence of a brute event, a status, and a sustaining field.
claims.source_quote: The legal fact 'this verdict is final' thus involves the coexistence of a brute event (the utterance), a status (finality), and a sustaining field (the judicial system that recognizes the verdict as binding).
claims.note: Asserts the ontological composition of a specific legal fact.

claims.claim: Legal facts are systematically embedded in hierarchical networks of recognition.
claims.source_quote: What distinguishes legal facts from other institutional facts is their systematic embedding in hierarchical networks of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a distinguishing structural property of legal facts.

claims.claim: The legal system provides a meta-field of recognition that organizes and stabilizes lower-level recognitions.
claims.source_quote: The legal system provides a meta-field of recognition that organizes and stabilizes lower-level recognitions.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of the legal system as a meta-field entity.

claims.claim: Each act of legal recognition draws its validity from the higher-order structure of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: Each act of legal recognition (signing, declaring, adjudicating) draws its validity from this higher-order structure.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between individual recognition acts and the higher-order institutional structure.

claims.claim: Legal facts possess a distinctive ontological robustness through multiply mediated dependence.
claims.source_quote: legal facts possess a distinctive kind of ontological robustness: their dependence is multiply mediated, sustained through layers of institutional coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property (ontological robustness via layered dependence) of legal facts.

claims.claim: The institutional field maintains the continuity of legal facts across time and circumstance.
claims.source_quote: the institutional field maintains the continuity of legal facts across time and circumstance.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of the institutional field in sustaining legal facts over time.

claims.claim: Brute facts are instantaneous or transient; legal facts endure.
claims.source_quote: Brute facts are instantaneous or transient; legal facts endure.
claims.note: Asserts a temporal property distinguishing brute facts from legal facts.

claims.claim: The persistence of legal facts arises because dependent continuants generated by recognition are temporally extended.
claims.source_quote: This persistence arises because the dependent continuants generated by recognition are temporally extended: they inhere in institutions that endure.
claims.note: Asserts the causal/ontological ground of legal fact persistence in temporally extended dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Dependent continuants generated by recognition inhere in institutions that endure.
claims.source_quote: the dependent continuants generated by recognition are temporally extended: they inhere in institutions that endure.
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between dependent continuants and enduring institutions.

claims.claim: Legal facts are temporally thickened versions of brute facts sustained by ongoing recognition.
claims.source_quote: legal facts are temporally thickened versions of brute facts, they retain a connection to their originating events but are sustained by ongoing recognition rather than physical continuity.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind/property relation: legal facts are a temporally extended form of brute facts.

claims.claim: Legal systems externalize recognition through documents, registries, and databases as durable artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems externalize recognition through documents, registries, and databases, creating durable artifacts that embody the continuity of legal facts.
claims.note: Asserts that legal systems produce artifact entities that embody institutional continuity.

claims.claim: Documents, registries, and databases serve as bearers for dependent continuants representing recognized legal relations.
claims.source_quote: These artifacts serve as bearers for dependent continuants representing recognized legal relations.
claims.note: Asserts a bearer relation between physical artifacts and dependent continuants.

claims.claim: A physical document carries the institutional relation of recognition that constitutes ownership.
claims.source_quote: we mean that the physical document carries the institutional relation of recognition that constitutes ownership.
claims.note: Asserts that a document bears the recognition relation constituting a legal status.

claims.claim: Ownership and important legal statuses are established by a system of institutional and social recognition.
claims.source_quote: Ownership and other important legal statuses are established by a system of institutional and social recognition itself.
claims.note: Asserts that legal statuses like ownership are constituted by institutional recognition, not by documents alone.

claims.claim: Documents act as enduring proof carrying official authority to counter opposing claims.
claims.source_quote: Documents act as enduring proof, carrying official authority to counter any opposing claims.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of documents within the legal ontology.

claims.claim: Law's objectivity arises from the stability of recognition across time, not from metaphysical independence.
claims.source_quote: Law's objectivity arises from the stability of recognition across time, not from metaphysical independence.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological ground of legal objectivity.

claims.claim: The legal fact is real because it is recognized, recorded, and reproduced within institutional networks.
claims.source_quote: The legal fact is real precisely because it is recognized, is often recorded, and publicly reproduced within the structured network of institutions that define the legal world.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions of reality for legal facts.

claims.claim: The truth conditions of legal facts are relational, depending on alignment of recognition among institutions.
claims.source_quote: The truth conditions of legal facts are thus relational: they depend on the alignment of recognition among institutions rather than on direct empirical correspondence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal fact truth conditions.

claims.claim: A brute fact such as physical occupancy does not constitute ownership without institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: a brute fact, such as A's physical occupancy of the land, does not constitute ownership without institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for ownership as a legal status.

claims.claim: Each recognition act generates a new dependent continuant inhering in an institutional continuant.
claims.source_quote: Each recognition act (signing, declaring, deciding) generates a new dependent continuant inhering in an institutional continuant.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition acts produce dependent continuants and specifies their inherence relation.

claims.claim: Each institutional continuant persists through time by realizing functions defined by its roles.
claims.source_quote: each institutional continuant persists through time by realizing functions defined by its roles.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for institutional continuants via function realization.

claims.claim: Legal facts are continuously regenerated through processes of recognition, realization, and recordkeeping.
claims.source_quote: legal facts are continuously regenerated through processes of recognition, realization, and recordkeeping, a recursive cycle that constitutes the ontology of legal reality.
claims.note: Asserts that legal facts are ontologically sustained by recursive processes.

claims.claim: Law creates a parallel layer of reality populated by entities that exist only through structured recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law does not merely describe or regulate the world; it creates a parallel layer of reality populated by entities that exist only through structured recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of a distinct ontological layer of legally constituted entities.

claims.claim: This layer of legally constituted reality exerts causal and normative effects on the brute world.
claims.source_quote: This layer, once constituted, exerts causal and normative effects on the brute world, it shapes behavior, distributes power, and mediates social life.
claims.note: Asserts causal and normative properties of the legally constituted layer of reality.

claims.claim: Brute facts depend on physical or causal relations; legal facts depend on recognition and institutional coherence.
claims.source_quote: Brute facts depend on physical or causal relations; legal facts depend on recognition and institutional coherence.
claims.note: Asserts the distinguishing dependency structures of brute facts versus legal facts.

claims.claim: The transition from brute to legal fact is an act of structured augmentation adding new relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: The transition from one to the other is not a leap into fiction but an act of structured augmentation: the world becomes more articulated through the addition of new relational continuants.
claims.note: Asserts that legal fact creation adds new relational continuants to reality.

claims.claim: Law is the organized practice of producing and maintaining augmentations of reality through recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law, in this view, is the organized practice of producing and maintaining these augmentations, of turning the flux of human action into the durable architecture of social reality.
claims.note: Asserts a defining function/role of law as an institutional practice.

claims.claim: Trials, hearings, filings, and administrative procedures are occurrents in the BFO sense.
claims.source_quote: These processes, trials, hearings, filings, and administrative procedures, constitute the ontological machinery through which law transforms events into enduring institutional entities. In the language of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), such processes are occurrents.
claims.note: Asserts that legal processes are instances of the BFO category of occurrents.

claims.claim: Legal processes bring about changes in the configuration of continuants.
claims.source_quote: such processes are occurrents: temporally bounded activities that bring about changes in the configuration of continu[ants].
claims.note: Asserts a causal/functional property of legal processes with respect to continuants.

claims.claim: A right inheres in the agent in virtue of a role.
claims.source_quote: nheres in the agent in virtue of a role. If the agent no longer instantiates the relevant role (e.g., 'competent adult citizen'), the right is no longer realized.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological grounding of rights in roles — a claim about the inhering relation between rights and agents.

claims.claim: Rights are deactivated or suspended when conditions for their instantiation are no longer met.
claims.source_quote: This account also clarifies why rights are not 'lost' like physical objects, they are deactivated or suspended because the conditions for their instantiation are no longer met.
claims.note: Asserts a property/state of rights entities — they undergo deactivation/suspension rather than loss.

claims.claim: Role ontology enables formal tracking of the conditions for right-instantiation.
claims.source_quote: Role ontology enables us to track these conditions formally.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/dispositional property of role ontology as a formal system.

claims.claim: Non-autonomous agents' legal action is best modeled as surrogate role occupancy.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this is best modeled as surrogate role occupancy: another agent (e.g., parent, guardian, corporate officer) performs legal actions on behalf of the role bearer.
claims.note: Author endorses this as the best ontological model — asserts a subkind/role relation for non-autonomous legal agents.

claims.claim: The child or corporate entity instantiates the principal role.
claims.source_quote: The child or corporate entity instantiates the principal role (e.g., 'ward' or 'corporation'), while the surrogate agent bears an institutionally authorized proxy role.
claims.note: Asserts instantiation relation between child/corporation and a principal role kind.

claims.claim: The surrogate agent bears an institutionally authorized proxy role.
claims.source_quote: while the surrogate agent bears an institutionally authorized proxy role (e.g., 'guardian' or 'executive director').
claims.note: Asserts that the surrogate bears a specific kind of role — ontological property/relation claim.

claims.claim: The surrogate is a role-realizer, not the right-holder.
claims.source_quote: The surrogate is not the right-holder; they are a role-realizer, empowered to act in specific ways under institutional constraints.
claims.note: Asserts ontological category distinction — surrogate is a role-realizer, not a right-holder.

claims.claim: The child or corporation is the target of legal effects and the anchor for rights and duties.
claims.source_quote: The child or corporation is not the actor in a direct biological sense, but they are the target of legal effects, the anchor for rights and duties, and the referent of institutional roles.
claims.note: Asserts relational properties of child/corporation entities with respect to legal effects and rights.

claims.claim: The ward holds the principal role of legal person with partial or suspended autonomy.
claims.source_quote: The ward (child or dependent adult) holds the principal role of legal person with partial or suspended autonomy.
claims.note: Asserts that the ward entity instantiates a specific role with specific properties.

claims.claim: The guardian bears an assigned surrogate role recognized by the state.
claims.source_quote: The guardian bears an assigned surrogate role, recognized by the state, allowing them to perform legal actions on behalf of the ward.
claims.note: Asserts a role-bearing relation between guardian and the surrogate role entity.

claims.claim: The guardian role is instantiated only by formal institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: The guardian role is instantiated only by formal institutional recognition, through appointment by court, state registry, or statute.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for instantiation of the guardian role — ontological dependency relation.

claims.claim: The guardian role entails specific powers and duties as realizable dependent continuants linked to the role.
claims.source_quote: The guardian role entails specific powers (e.g., to act) and duties (e.g., fiduciary care), which can be modeled as realizable dependent continuants linked to the role.
claims.note: Author endorses this modeling — asserts powers and duties are realizable dependent continuants linked to the guardian role.

claims.claim: The guardian role is a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in the person appointed as guardian.
claims.source_quote: The guardian role is a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in the person appointed as guardian.
claims.note: Direct ontological category and inhering-relation assertion about the guardian role in BFO terms.

claims.claim: The realization of the guardian role occurs during institutional processes like decision-making or court filings.
claims.source_quote: The realization of this role occurs during institutional processes like decision-making or court filings.
claims.note: Asserts when and through what the role is realized — a realization relation claim.

claims.claim: The institution (e.g., family court) acts as the role-granting authority for the guardian role.
claims.source_quote: The institution (e.g., family court) acts as the role-granting authority, with clear rules for activation and termination of the role.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/property of the institution entity in relation to role-granting.

claims.claim: An immigrant minor simultaneously occupies multiple roles, each conferring different rights and duties.
claims.source_quote: An immigrant minor may simultaneously occupy the roles of 'child,' 'asylum seeker,' and 'beneficiary of temporary protection.' Each role confers different rights and duties and is governed by distinct legal institutions.
claims.note: Author endorses this as an ontological fact about layered role occupancy and conferred normative statuses.

claims.claim: Each legal role is governed by distinct legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: Each role confers different rights and duties and is governed by distinct legal institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a governance relation between roles and legal institutions.

claims.claim: Institutions are systems for role assignment.
claims.source_quote: If we understand institutions as systems for role assignment, we can ask: Are the right roles being created?
claims.note: Author presents this as the basis for institutional design reasoning, implicitly endorsing the ontological characterization of institutions.

claims.claim: Primary rules instantiate obligations and rights as specifically dependent continuants inhering in legal subjects.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological perspective, primary rules are best understood as instantiating obligations and rights, types of specifically dependent continuants that inhere in legal subjects (persons or organizations) in virtue of the roles they occupy.
claims.note: Author endorses this as the best ontological understanding — asserts category and inhering-relation for obligations and rights.

claims.claim: Obligations and rights are specifically dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: primary rules are best understood as instantiating obligations and rights, types of specifically dependent continuants that inhere in legal subjects.
claims.note: Asserts ontological category membership for obligations and rights.

claims.claim: Obligations and rights inhere in legal subjects in virtue of the roles those subjects occupy.
claims.source_quote: types of specifically dependent continuants that inhere in legal subjects (persons or organizations) in virtue of the roles they occupy.
claims.note: Asserts the inhering relation and its grounding condition — directly ontological.

claims.claim: A tenant's obligation to pay rent and right to exclusive occupancy are institutionally instantiated entities.
claims.source_quote: These normative statuses are not physical properties of the person; they are institutionally instantiated entities that come into being through legal acts (e.g., contract signing) and persist within the constraints of legal processes.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological status of these normative entities as institutionally instantiated, not physical.

claims.claim: Normative statuses come into being through legal acts and persist within legal processes.
claims.source_quote: they are institutionally instantiated entities that come into being through legal acts (e.g., contract signing) and persist within the constraints of legal processes (e.g., eviction, renewal).
claims.note: Asserts temporal/causal properties of normative-status entities — ontological claim about their existence conditions.

claims.claim: Primary rules in legal ontology are realizable entities tied to bearers' roles and activated under institutional conditions.
claims.source_quote: Ontologies built on BFO can represent such rules as realizable entities tied to the bearers' roles and activated under specific institutional or procedural conditions.
claims.note: Author endorses this representation as accurate — asserts that primary rules are realizable entities with activation conditions.

claims.claim: Secondary rules are rules about rules.
claims.source_quote: Secondary rules, by contrast, are rules about rules.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a definitional ontological claim about the kind 'secondary rule' — a subkind or property assertion.

claims.claim: The Rule of Recognition is a shared standard among legal officials for identifying valid legal norms.
claims.source_quote: The Rule of Recognition: a shared standard among legal officials for identifying valid legal norms (e.g., statutes signed by the president, decisions from the supreme court).
claims.note: Author presents this description with endorsement in the context of building a formal ontology — asserts the nature of the Rule of Recognition entity.

claims.claim: Rules of Change confer authority to enact, amend, or repeal legal norms.
claims.source_quote: Rules of Change: rules that confer authority to enact, amend, or repeal legal norms (e.g., legislative procedures).
claims.note: Endorsed description of the functional/dispositional property of Rules of Change as entities that confer authority.

claims.claim: Rules of Adjudication establish procedures and allocate authority for resolving disputes.
claims.source_quote: Rules of Adjudication: rules that establish procedures and allocate authority for resolving disputes (e.g., jurisdictional doctrines, trial rules).
claims.note: Endorsed description of the functional property of Rules of Adjudication entities.

claims.claim: Trials, hearings, filings, and administrative procedures are ontological machinery through which law transforms events into enduring institutional entities.
claims.source_quote: These processes, trials, hearings, filings, and administrative procedures, constitute the ontological machinery through which law transforms events into enduring institutional entities.
claims.note: Direct assertion that these processes have the ontological role/function of transforming events into institutional entities.

claims.claim: Processes such as trials and hearings are occurrents: temporally bounded activities that bring about changes in continuants.
claims.source_quote: In the language of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), such processes are occurrents: temporally bounded activities that bring about changes in the configuration of continuants.
claims.note: The author asserts a subkind/classification claim: these processes are occurrents, with the defining property of being temporally bounded and causing change in continuants.

claims.claim: These processes are mechanisms by which potentialities become actualities.
claims.source_quote: They are the mechanisms by which potentialities become actualities, turning the abstract conditions of recognition into concrete instances of legal facticity.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of these processes: they instantiate potentialities as actualities.

claims.claim: Abstract conditions of recognition become concrete instances of legal facticity through these processes.
claims.source_quote: They are the mechanisms by which potentialities become actualities, turning the abstract conditions of recognition into concrete instances of legal facticity.
claims.note: Asserts a transformation relation between abstract recognition conditions and concrete legal facts, mediated by procedural processes.

claims.claim: Procedural realization of facts bridges law's dynamic dimension and its static dimension.
claims.source_quote: The procedural realization of facts is thus the bridge between law's dynamic and static dimensions, between the lived temporality of adjudication and the enduring reality of institutional record.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/structural claim about procedural realization: it connects two ontological dimensions of law.

claims.claim: Law has both a dynamic dimension (lived temporality of adjudication) and a static dimension (enduring institutional record).
claims.source_quote: The procedural realization of facts is thus the bridge between law's dynamic and static dimensions, between the lived temporality of adjudication and the enduring reality of institutional record.
claims.note: Implied by the bridge metaphor; the author commits to law having these two distinct ontological dimensions.

claims.claim: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.source_quote: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about what kinds of entities can perform norm-repair.

claims.claim: Accountability is a structural property of law, not an afterthought.
claims.source_quote: Accountability must therefore be reintroduced at the ontological level, not as afterthought but as structural property.
claims.note: Asserts that accountability has the property of being structurally constitutive of law's ontology.

claims.claim: Ontological closure is a condition where legal effects are generated but not recognized within the proper relational field.
claims.source_quote: Automation without accountability leads to what might be called ontological closure: a condition where legal effects are generated but not recognized within the proper relational field.
claims.note: Defines and asserts the existence of a condition called ontological closure with specific properties.

claims.claim: An unaccountable automated system suppresses reflexivity and forecloses recognition loops.
claims.source_quote: In both cases, a system suppresses reflexivity, foreclosing the loops of recognition that sustain coherence.
claims.note: Asserts that unaccountable automated systems have the property of suppressing reflexivity.

claims.claim: Recognition loops sustain the coherence of a legal system.
claims.source_quote: foreclosing the loops of recognition that sustain coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property: recognition loops bear the relation of sustaining coherence.

claims.claim: An unaccountable automated system is consistent but not coherent.
claims.source_quote: Its processes are consistent but not coherent; it cannot adjust when contradictions arise.
claims.note: Asserts a property distinction between consistency and coherence as applied to unaccountable automated systems.

claims.claim: Unaccountable automated systems redefine normativity from a relational state of recognition to a technical state of output.
claims.source_quote: The danger is not that such systems will misapply norms, but that they will silently redefine what normativity is: from a relational state of recognition to a technical state of output.
claims.note: Asserts that unaccountable systems transform the nature of normativity itself.

claims.claim: Ontological transparency is the metaphysical condition of accountability.
claims.source_quote: Ontological transparency is the metaphysical condition of accountability: it is what allows law to continue recognizing itself, even when parts of its operation are no longer human.
claims.note: Directly asserts an ontological relation: transparency is a condition that accountability depends on.

claims.claim: Law is a world of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Without visible recognition chains, law ceases to be a world of mutual acknowledgment and becomes a system of technical enforcement.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law: it is constituted by mutual acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Traditional contracts are institutional continuants grounded in shared recognition.
claims.source_quote: Traditional contracts are institutional continuants grounded in shared recognition: they exist because parties, and the legal institutions overseeing them, acknowledge the validity of their terms.
claims.note: Asserts that traditional contracts are a subkind of institutional continuant with a grounding relation to shared recognition.

claims.claim: Traditional contracts are realized through occurrents such as signing, performance, breach, or adjudication.
claims.source_quote: Their realization occurs through occurrents, acts of signing, performance, breach, or adjudication, each embedded within a wider field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that occurrents realize contracts, and specifies kinds of occurrents involved.

claims.claim: Smart contracts collapse the distinction between obligation and execution.
claims.source_quote: By contrast, the smart contract collapses the distinction between obligation and execution.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of smart contracts: they eliminate the obligation/execution distinction.

claims.claim: Smart contracts convert relational dependencies into automated occurrences.
claims.source_quote: It converts what was once a relational dependency sustained through recognition into an automated occurrence.
claims.note: Asserts a transformation in ontological kind: relational dependency becomes automated occurrence.

claims.claim: Smart contracts eliminate the temporal and interpretive interval in which recognition and repair normally occur.
claims.source_quote: In doing so, it eliminates the temporal and interpretive interval in which recognition and repair normally occur.
claims.note: Asserts that smart contracts remove the temporal interval that enables recognition and repair.

claims.claim: Ontological compression is a condition where obligations are transformed into executable conditions and recognition is replaced by verification.
claims.source_quote: The result is a form of ontological compression: obligations are transformed into executable conditions, and recognition is replaced by verification.
claims.note: Defines and asserts the existence of ontological compression with specific structural properties.

claims.claim: In smart contracts, law becomes a closed causal system.
claims.source_quote: The normative distinction between 'ought' and 'is' vanishes; law becomes a closed causal system.
claims.note: Asserts a property that smart-contract-based law acquires: being a closed causal system.

claims.claim: A smart contract realizes an obligation that no longer exists or should have been modified.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the smart contract realizes an obligation that no longer exists or that should have been modified.
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological relation between smart contracts and obligations they realize.

claims.claim: The blockchain's immutability enforces ontological permanence in a domain that requires adaptability.
claims.source_quote: The blockchain's immutability compounds the problem: it enforces ontological permanence in a domain that depends on adaptability.
claims.note: Asserts a property of blockchain (immutability) and its ontological consequence for law.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt can be embedded directly into the digital substrate of law.
claims.source_quote: The result is contradiction debt embedded directly into the digital substrate of law.
claims.note: Asserts that contradiction debt exists as an entity that can be located within law's digital substrate.

claims.claim: Contract-as-Text is an institutional continuant sustained by recognition and capable of reinterpretation.
claims.source_quote: Contract-as-Text: an institutional continuant sustained by recognition and capable of reinterpretation.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership and properties for one ontological category of contract.

claims.claim: Contract-as-Code is an executable specification that realizes obligations mechanically without recognition.
claims.source_quote: Contract-as-Code: an executable specification that realizes obligations mechanically without recognition.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership and functional property for the code-based contract category.

claims.claim: Contract-as-Institutional Process is the relational complex of recognition, enforcement, and repair mediating between text and code.
claims.source_quote: Contract-as-Institutional Process: the relational complex of recognition, enforcement, and repair that mediates between text and code.
claims.note: Asserts that contract-as-institutional-process is a relational complex with specific constitutive relations.

claims.claim: Recognition nodes function as repair agents within the digital ontology of law.
claims.source_quote: In effect, these nodes function as repair agents within the digital ontology of law, ensuring that automation remains embedded within the broader field of human recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role (repair agents) borne by recognition nodes within law's digital ontology.

claims.claim: Automation must remain embedded within the broader field of human recognition.
claims.source_quote: ensuring that automation remains embedded within the broader field of human recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural relational requirement: automation bears an embedding relation to human recognition.

claims.claim: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.source_quote: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the properties and limitations of machines versus human/institutional continuants—ontological claim about what kinds of entities can perform repair.

claims.claim: Accountability is a structural property of law, not an afterthought.
claims.source_quote: Accountability must therefore be reintroduced at the ontological level, not as afterthought but as structural property.
claims.note: Asserts that accountability has a specific ontological status (structural property) within law.

claims.claim: Ontological closure is a condition where legal effects are generated outside the proper relational field.
claims.source_quote: Automation without accountability leads to what might be called ontological closure: a condition where legal effects are generated but not recognized within the proper relational field.
claims.note: Defines and asserts the existence of ontological closure as a real condition with specific properties.

claims.claim: An unaccountable automated system suppresses reflexivity and forecloses recognition loops.
claims.source_quote: In both cases, a system suppresses reflexivity, foreclosing the loops of recognition that sustain coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of unaccountable automated systems—they suppress reflexivity and foreclose recognition loops.

claims.claim: An unaccountable automated system's processes are consistent but not coherent.
claims.source_quote: Its processes are consistent but not coherent; it cannot adjust when contradictions arise.
claims.note: Asserts a quality distinction (consistent vs. coherent) as a property of such systems.

claims.claim: Unaccountable automated systems redefine normativity from a relational state of recognition to a technical state of output.
claims.source_quote: The danger is not that such systems will misapply norms, but that they will silently redefine what normativity is: from a relational state of recognition to a technical state of output.
claims.note: Asserts that such systems have the property of transforming the ontological character of normativity.

claims.claim: Ontological transparency is both an epistemic and ethical property.
claims.source_quote: Ontological transparency then becomes both epistemic and ethical: it allows participants to trace the conditions under which legal entities are created, challenged, or extinguished.
claims.note: Asserts two properties (epistemic, ethical) of ontological transparency.
