claims.claim: Institutions generate, maintain, and terminate obligations through ongoing practices of acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Institutions generate, maintain, and terminate these dependent continuants through ongoing practices of acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts causal/constitutive roles institutions play with respect to obligations.

claims.claim: A legal obligation exists in virtue of an institution's recognition.
claims.source_quote: The obligation exists in virtue of the institution's recognition, just as the institution is capable of such recognition in virtue of its own role within the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding/constitutive relation between institutional recognition and legal obligation.

claims.claim: Moral obligations do not necessarily depend on institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Moral obligations arise from evaluative relations among agents that do not necessarily depend on institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property distinguishing moral obligations from legal ones.

claims.claim: Legal obligations require institutional recognition to exist as legal entities.
claims.source_quote: Legal obligations, by contrast, require institutional recognition to exist as legal entities.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary existential condition for legal obligations.

claims.claim: Legal obligations are embedded in a structure of roles and stabilized by institutions.
claims.source_quote: They are embedded in a structure of roles and stabilized by institutions capable of acknowledging, enforcing, and repairing them.
claims.note: Asserts structural properties and relations of legal obligations.

claims.claim: The difference between moral and legal obligations is a difference of ontological constitution.
claims.source_quote: This is not a difference of 'strength' or 'importance'; it is a difference of ontological constitution.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological (not merely normative) distinction between moral and legal obligations.

claims.claim: LegalObligation is a subkind of Obligation.
claims.source_quote: law:LegalObligation rdfs:subClassOf law:Obligation
claims.note: Author endorses this formalization as reflecting the conceptual distinction.

claims.claim: MoralObligation is a subkind of Obligation.
claims.source_quote: law:MoralObligation rdfs:subClassOf law:Obligation
claims.note: Author endorses this formalization as reflecting the conceptual distinction.

claims.claim: Moral obligations may persist even when legal recognition fails.
claims.source_quote: Moral obligations may persist even when legal recognition fails, generating tension.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of moral obligations independent of legal recognition.

claims.claim: Legal obligations may be extinguished or altered through institutional acts.
claims.source_quote: Legal obligations, meanwhile, may be extinguished or altered through institutional acts even when their moral counterparts remain unchanged.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal obligations—susceptibility to institutional modification/extinction.

claims.claim: Institutions are aggregated continuants endowed with the authority to recognize roles, obligations, claims, and permissions.
claims.source_quote: Institutions, in the sense employed throughout this book, are aggregated continuants endowed with the authority to recognize roles, obligations, claims, and permissions.
claims.note: Asserts the kind and essential property of institutions.

claims.claim: Institutions are independent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Institutions, by contrast, are independent continuants: they possess a unity and endurance that are not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.note: Asserts that institutions belong to the ontological category of independent continuants.

claims.claim: Institutions possess a unity and endurance not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.source_quote: they possess a unity and endurance that are not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.note: Asserts a property of institutions distinguishing them from mere collections of persons.

claims.claim: Institutions are a subkind of ObjectAggregate.
claims.source_quote: law:Institution a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:ObjectAggregate .
claims.note: Author endorses this OWL representation as capturing the ontological category of institutions.

claims.claim: Institutional acts of recognition are constitutive rather than merely descriptive.
claims.source_quote: These acts of recognition are constitutive rather than merely descriptive. Through them, institutions bring legal relations into existence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of recognition acts—they are constitutive of legal relations.

claims.claim: Institutions bring legal relations into existence through recognition acts.
claims.source_quote: Through them, institutions bring legal relations into existence.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive relation between institutional recognition and legal relations.

claims.claim: A legal norm (N) becomes a legal fact when recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Validation: N? becomes a legal fact when it is recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition (R?).
claims.note: Direct assertion about what makes a norm a legal fact — an ontological claim about the conditions of existence of legal facts.

claims.claim: A legal norm persists as long as dependencies linking it to its primary norm, secondary rule, and rule of recognition remain coherent.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance: The norm persists as long as the dependencies linking N?, P?, R?, and R? remain coherent.
claims.note: Asserts the persistence conditions (ontological dependencies) of a norm — a claim about what sustains a continuant's existence.

claims.claim: When its dependencies are broken, a norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.source_quote: Termination: When these dependencies are broken, through repeal, invalidation, or loss of recognition, the norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.note: Asserts that termination of dependencies entails the cessation of existence — an ontological claim about legal continuants.

claims.claim: Law's validity is a dynamic equilibrium sustained by ontological dependencies among rules and institutions.
claims.source_quote: law's validity is a dynamic equilibrium sustained by ontological dependencies among rules and institutions.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of legal validity — it is a dynamic equilibrium grounded in ontological dependencies.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the organizing principle that coordinates dependencies across the legal system's processes.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition is the organizing principle that coordinates these dependencies across the system's processes of creation, adjudication, and change.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational role of the rule of recognition — an ontological claim about its organizing function.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the metaphysical condition of legality itself.
claims.source_quote: the rule of recognition is not merely a sociological convention but the metaphysical condition of legality itself.
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts that the rule of recognition has a metaphysical role as the condition for legality — a strong ontological claim.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the structure that allows law to exist as a self-identifying domain of reality.
claims.source_quote: It is the structure that allows law to exist as a self-identifying domain of reality, a world of norms sustained by recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property and function of the rule of recognition in grounding law's existence.

claims.claim: The authority of the rule of recognition derives from ontological coherence, not from force or moral obligation.
claims.source_quote: Its authority derives not from force or moral obligation but from ontological coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the rule of recognition regarding the source of its authority — an ontological claim.

claims.claim: When the rule of recognition collapses, law disintegrates.
claims.source_quote: When the rule of recognition collapses, when institutions no longer share a unified structure of validation, law disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: law's existence depends on the rule of recognition; its collapse entails law's dissolution.

claims.claim: A constitutional crisis is the dissolution of the meta-structure that sustains legal being.
claims.source_quote: This is the ontological meaning of A constitutional crisis: the dissolution of the meta-structure that sustains legal being.
claims.note: Asserts that constitutional crises are instances of a specific ontological kind — dissolution of the sustaining meta-structure.

claims.claim: Restoration of law occurs when a new rule of recognition emerges and reorganizes the dependencies defining the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: the restoration of law occurs when a new rule of recognition emerges, reorganizing the dependencies that define the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts conditions under which law comes back into existence — an ontological claim about law's re-emergence.

claims.claim: Law's reality consists in the dependencies that bind its rules together, not in the commands it issues.
claims.source_quote: It implies that law's reality consists not in the commands it issues but in the dependencies that bind its rules together.
claims.note: Author asserts what constitutes law's reality — a direct ontological claim about the nature of law.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition, as meta-structure, embodies the highest level of ontological dependence in the legal world.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition, as meta-structure, embodies the highest level of ontological dependence in the legal world, it is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the rule of recognition — that it is law's highest-level ontological dependency and its principle of unity.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.source_quote: it is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of the rule of recognition within the legal ontology.

claims.claim: Law is an evolving ontological system: a network of roles, rules, and processes that continually realizes itself through maintenance of its dependencies.
claims.source_quote: we can see law as an evolving ontological system: a network of roles, rules, and processes that continually realizes itself through the maintenance of its dependencies.
claims.note: Author asserts the kind of entity law is — an evolving ontological system with a specific structure.

claims.claim: A fact-making failure occurs when the dependencies required for the existence of a legal fact are not satisfied, or when incompatible dependencies coexist without repair.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, a fact-making failure occurs when the dependencies required for the existence of a legal fact are not satisfied, or when incompatible dependencies coexist without repair.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological definition of fact-making failure — a claim about what conditions produce this kind of failure.

claims.claim: A fact-making failure corresponds to a breakdown in the chain linking occurrents (procedural events) to dependent continuants (recognized relations and statuses).
claims.source_quote: In the Basic Formal Ontology framework, this corresponds to a breakdown in the chain that links occurrents (procedural events) to dependent continuants (recognized relations and statuses).
claims.note: Asserts the ontological characterization of fact-making failure in terms of BFO categories — a relational ontological claim.

claims.claim: A pseudo-entity is an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The result is a pseudo-entity: an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of a kind of entity (pseudo-entity) and its defining property — lacking ontological integrity.

claims.claim: Law's existence is continuously contingent on the proper functioning of its institutional and relational machinery.
claims.source_quote: law's existence is neither metaphysically secure nor automatically self-sustaining, but continuously contingent on the proper functioning of its institutional and relational machinery.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law's existence — its contingency on institutional functioning — a direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: The role is anchored in the institution that recognizes it, not in the individual.
claims.source_quote: The diagram shows that the role is anchored not in the individual but in the institution that recognizes it.
claims.note: Direct assertion about where a role's ontological grounding lies.

claims.claim: The institution's stability underwrites the role's persistence.
claims.source_quote: The institution's stability underwrites the role's persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding/sustaining relation between institution and role persistence.

claims.claim: Obligations, claims, and permissions are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: They are dependent continuants; entities whose existence depends on the roles and institutional recognitions that sustain them.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim for obligations, claims, and permissions.

claims.claim: Obligations, claims, and permissions exist only by depending on roles and institutional recognitions.
claims.source_quote: entities whose existence depends on the roles and institutional recognitions that sustain them.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation between these entities and roles/institutions.

claims.claim: An obligation introduces a directed requirement linking one agent to another, mediated through a role.
claims.source_quote: it introduces a directed requirement linking one agent to another, mediated through a role.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/relational property of obligations.

claims.claim: A permission expands the space of possible actions.
claims.source_quote: A permission expands the space of possible actions.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/structural property of permissions.

claims.claim: A claim provides the correlative position that makes an obligation intelligible and enforceable.
claims.source_quote: A claim provides the correlative position that makes an obligation intelligible and enforceable.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/property of claims.

claims.claim: Obligation is a subkind of NormativeRelationalEntity.
claims.source_quote: law:Obligation rdfs:subClassOf law:NormativeRelationalEntity .
claims.note: The author endorses this classification as reflecting a conceptual truth.

claims.claim: Permission is a subkind of NormativeRelationalEntity.
claims.source_quote: law:Permission rdfs:subClassOf law:NormativeRelationalEntity .
claims.note: Endorsed as part of the author's own ontological framework.

claims.claim: Claim is a subkind of NormativeRelationalEntity.
claims.source_quote: law:Claim rdfs:subClassOf law:NormativeRelationalEntity .
claims.note: Endorsed as part of the author's own ontological framework.

claims.claim: NormativeRelationalEntity is a subkind of SpecificallyDependentContinuant.
claims.source_quote: law:NormativeRelationalEntity a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:SpecificallyDependentContinuant
claims.note: Author endorses this as capturing a 'conceptual truth' about these entities.

claims.claim: Obligations, claims, and permissions depend on bearers, roles, and institutions for their persistence and normative force.
claims.source_quote: obligations, claims, and permissions depend on the existence of bearers, roles, and institutions for their persistence and their normative force.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation.

claims.claim: Roles, not agents, are the primary bearers of normative load.
claims.source_quote: This depiction underscores that roles, not agents, are the primary bearers of normative load.
claims.note: Asserts a property/role of roles versus agents in bearing obligations etc.

claims.claim: Obligations are constituted through acts of institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: They are constituted through acts of recognition, typically institutional, that bind a role to a directed requirement.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive relation between recognition acts and obligations.

claims.claim: Recognition is the bridge between structural position and normative relation.
claims.source_quote: recognition is the bridge between the structural position and the normative relation.
claims.note: Asserts a mediating relational role for recognition in the ontology.

claims.claim: Without institutional recognition, there is no legal obligation.
claims.source_quote: Without recognition, explicit or implicit, there is no obligation in the legal sense.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for the existence of legal obligations.

claims.claim: Institutions generate, maintain, and terminate obligations through ongoing practices of acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Institutions generate, maintain, and terminate these dependent continuants through ongoing practices of acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts causal/generative relations between institutions and dependent continuants.

claims.claim: An obligation exists in virtue of the institution's recognition.
claims.source_quote: The obligation exists in virtue of the institution's recognition, just as the institution is capable of such recognition in virtue of its own role within the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding relation between institutional recognition and obligation existence.

claims.claim: Moral obligations arise from evaluative relations among agents that do not necessarily depend on institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Moral obligations arise from evaluative relations among agents that do not necessarily depend on institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts origin and independence conditions for moral obligations.

claims.claim: Legal obligations require institutional recognition to exist as legal entities.
claims.source_quote: Legal obligations, by contrast, require institutional recognition to exist as legal entities.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary existence condition for legal obligations.

claims.claim: Legal obligations are embedded in a structure of roles and stabilized by institutions.
claims.source_quote: They are embedded in a structure of roles and stabilized by institutions capable of acknowledging, enforcing, and repairing them.
claims.note: Asserts structural properties and relational embeddings of legal obligations.

claims.claim: The difference between moral and legal obligations is a difference of ontological constitution, not of strength or importance.
claims.source_quote: This is not a difference of 'strength' or 'importance'; it is a difference of ontological constitution.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological (not merely normative) distinction between the two kinds.

claims.claim: A legal obligation cannot exist without institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: A legal obligation cannot exist without institutional recognition.
claims.note: Plain assertion of a necessary existence condition.

claims.claim: A moral obligation does not depend on any institution for its existence.
claims.source_quote: A moral obligation does not depend on any institution for its existence.
claims.note: Plain assertion of independence from institutions for moral obligations.

claims.claim: Moral obligations may persist even when legal recognition fails.
claims.source_quote: Moral obligations may persist even when legal recognition fails, generating tension.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a structural consequence, though framed slightly as a modal possibility it is treated as a real ontological feature.

claims.claim: Legal obligations may be extinguished or altered through institutional acts even when their moral counterparts remain unchanged.
claims.source_quote: Legal obligations, meanwhile, may be extinguished or altered through institutional acts even when their moral counterparts remain unchanged.
claims.note: Author treats this as a real structural consequence of the ontological distinction.

claims.claim: Institutions are aggregated continuants endowed with the authority to recognize roles, obligations, claims, and permissions.
claims.source_quote: Institutions, in the sense employed throughout this book, are aggregated continuants endowed with the authority to recognize roles, obligations, claims, and permissions.
claims.note: Asserts the kind and essential properties of institutions.

claims.claim: Institutions possess recognitive power that anchors the relational field.
claims.source_quote: Their recognitive power anchors the relational field, giving it coherence and endurance.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property and relational role of institutions.

claims.claim: Institutions' recognitive acts are constitutive rather than merely descriptive.
claims.source_quote: These acts of recognition are constitutive rather than merely descriptive. Through them, institutions bring legal relations into existence.
claims.note: Asserts a property (constitutive nature) of institutional recognition acts.

claims.claim: Institutions are independent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Institutions, by contrast, are independent continuants: they possess a unity and endurance that are not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership for institutions.

claims.claim: Institutions possess a unity and endurance not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.source_quote: they possess a unity and endurance that are not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.note: Asserts a property of institutions distinguishing them from their members.

claims.claim: Institution is a subkind of ObjectAggregate.
claims.source_quote: law:Institution a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:ObjectAggregate .
claims.note: Author endorses this classification as capturing the ontological nature of institutions.

claims.claim: Legal roles are ontologically real entities, not mere linguistic conventions or mental constructs.
claims.source_quote: a commitment to ontological realism about legal roles, the view that such roles are not mere linguistic conventions or mental constructs, but socially grounded, institutionally constrained, and ontologically real entities.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological status of legal roles.

claims.claim: Legal roles are socially constructed yet ontologically real.
claims.source_quote: Legal roles are real, even though they are socially constructed. This is not a contradiction.
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts both properties as compatible and true.

claims.claim: Socially created entities can possess objective identity conditions, temporal persistence, and inter-agent salience.
claims.source_quote: Ontological realism, as articulated by Barry Smith and others, affirms that entities can be socially created and maintained, but nonetheless possess objective identity conditions, temporal persistence, and inter-agent salience.
claims.note: Author endorses this view as part of the realist commitment being advanced.

claims.claim: A judge bears a specifically dependent continuant that authorizes and constrains behavior within a legal framework.
claims.source_quote: a judge is someone who bears a specifically dependent continuant that authorizes and constrains behavior within a legal framework.
claims.note: Asserts a relational and property claim about the entity 'judge' in ontological terms.

claims.claim: Legal roles have a structural presence in the social world.
claims.source_quote: It asserts that legal roles have a structural presence in the social world, they can be assigned, traced, transferred, and revoked.
claims.note: Direct assertion of a property of legal roles.

claims.claim: Legal roles play action-guiding functions, determining who can decide cases, initiate lawsuits, consent to contracts, or enforce rules.
claims.source_quote: They play action-guiding functions: determining who can decide cases, initiate lawsuits, consent to contracts, or enforce rules.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of legal roles.

claims.claim: Legal roles are normatively loaded, conferring responsibilities and liabilities as well as powers and permissions.
claims.source_quote: And they are normatively loaded: they confer responsibilities and liabilities, not just powers or permissions.
claims.note: Asserts a normative property of legal roles.

claims.claim: Legal roles can be instantiated only through specific processes such as appointment, registration, trial, and naturalization.
claims.source_quote: legal roles can be instantiated only through specific processes, appointment, registration, trial, naturalization.
claims.note: Asserts a restriction on how legal roles come into being—an ontological claim about instantiation conditions.

claims.claim: The processes through which legal roles are conferred are occurrent entities.
claims.source_quote: These processes are themselves occurrent entities, and the conditions under which a role is validly conferred are ontologically tractable.
claims.note: Classifies legal processes as occurrents—an ontological subkind claim.

claims.claim: Becoming a defendant is the result of a filing, recognition, and response process.
claims.source_quote: becoming a defendant is not just a social fact; it is the result of a filing, recognition, and response process.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive relation between specific processes and the role of defendant.

claims.claim: Legal roles are structurally interdependent: a judge implies a court, a plaintiff implies a defendant, a police officer implies a jurisdiction.
claims.source_quote: A judge implies a court; a plaintiff implies a defendant; a police officer implies a jurisdiction.
claims.note: Asserts structural relational dependencies among legal roles—ontological relational claims.

claims.claim: Legal roles exist within networks of recognition mediated by institutions and codified in legal norms.
claims.source_quote: roles do not float freely, but exist within networks of recognition, mediated by institutions and codified in legal norms.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of legal roles regarding their embedding in institutional structures.

claims.claim: The misassignment, denial, or arbitrary removal of legal roles constitutes a real harm.
claims.source_quote: their misassignment, denial, or arbitrary removal constitutes a real harm.
claims.note: Asserts that certain events involving roles have real-world harmful consequences—ontological and normative claim.

claims.claim: Legal systems are layered structures of norm-governed roles embedded in institutions and enacted through the actions of agents.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems are not collections of abstract rules floating in isolation; they are layered structures of norm-governed roles, embedded in institutions and enacted through the actions of agents.
claims.note: Asserts what kind of entity a legal system is—an ontological classification claim.

claims.claim: Legal systems must be understood as role-based architectures where authority, responsibility, and participation are distributed through interlocking continuants and occurrents.
claims.source_quote: legal systems must be understood as role-based architectures, where legal authority, responsibility, and participation are distributed through a system of interlocking continuants and occurrents.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological composition and structure of legal systems.

claims.claim: Governments are aggregates of institutions that exist as frameworks for producing and regulating roles.
claims.source_quote: governments themselves can be understood as aggregates of institutions, each of which exists not merely as a physical building or bureaucratic chart, but as a framework for producing and regulating roles.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature and function of governments and their constituent institutions.

claims.claim: A legislature acts through persons who occupy specific roles such as speaker, member, clerk, and committee chair.
claims.source_quote: A legislature, for example, does not act qua legislature, it acts through persons who occupy the roles of speaker, member, clerk, committee chair, and so on.
claims.note: Asserts a relational claim about how legislative institutions are ontologically realized through role-bearing agents.

claims.claim: Each institution is a composite entity composed of agentive continuants, specifically dependent continuants, information artifacts, and occurrents.
claims.source_quote: each institution can be modeled as a composite entity composed of: Agentive continuants (e.g., people, legal persons), Specifically dependent continuants (e.g., roles borne by those agents), Information artifacts (e.g., rules of procedure, statutes, charters), Occurrents (e.g., hearings, deliberations, decisions).
claims.note: Asserts the ontological composition of institutions in terms of BFO categories.

claims.claim: The roles of the ruled—citizen, subject, offender—are as ontologically rich and normatively significant as those of legal officials.
claims.source_quote: the role of the ruled, whether as citizen, subject, or offender, is as ontologically rich and normatively significant as that of legal officials.
claims.note: Asserts a property (ontological richness and normative significance) of the roles borne by those governed by law.

claims.claim: Institutions are independent continuants.
claims.source_quote: s, by contrast, are independent continuants: they possess a unity and endurance that are not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.note: Direct assertion that institutions belong to the ontological category of independent continuants.

claims.claim: Institutions possess unity and endurance not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.source_quote: they possess a unity and endurance that are not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.note: Asserts a property (unity, endurance) and a non-reducibility relation of institutions to their members.

claims.claim: Institutions are a subkind of ObjectAggregate (in BFO terms).
claims.source_quote: law:Institution a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:ObjectAggregate .
claims.note: The OWL fragment is presented as expressing a 'core commitment of the ontology,' making it an endorsed ontological claim about kind membership.

claims.claim: Institutions possess recognitive powers that individual agents as such do not.
claims.source_quote: This fragment expresses a core commitment of the ontology: institutions possess recognitive powers that individual agents, as such, do not.
claims.note: Explicit assertion of a property (recognitive powers) held by institutions but not individual agents.

claims.claim: Individual officials perform recognitive acts in virtue of occupying a role within an institution.
claims.source_quote: Even when individual officials perform recognitive acts, they do so in virtue of occupying a role within an institution whose authority grounds those acts.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding relation: the institutional role, not the individual per se, grounds recognitive acts.

claims.claim: Institutional authority grounds the recognitive acts of individual officials.
claims.source_quote: they do so in virtue of occupying a role within an institution whose authority grounds those acts.
claims.note: Asserts that institutional authority bears a grounding relation to recognitive acts.

claims.claim: The institution is the stabilizing source of recognition for roles and normative entities.
claims.source_quote: The institution stands as the stabilizing source of recognition for both roles and their associated normative entities.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational property of institutions as sources of recognition.

claims.claim: Institutional persistence gives the legal system continuity across time.
claims.source_quote: It is the institution's persistence that gives the legal system continuity across time.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/grounding relation between institutional persistence and legal system continuity.

claims.claim: Institutions serve as stabilizing anchors of legal relations.
claims.source_quote: Because institutions serve as the stabilizing anchors of legal relations, their failures create fractures that spread across the relational field.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of institutions within the relational structure of law.

claims.claim: Institutional failures create fractures that spread across the relational field.
claims.source_quote: their failures create fractures that spread across the relational field.
claims.note: Asserts a causal property of institutional failures: they produce fractures in the relational field.

claims.claim: Obligations that depend on institutional recognition lose their grounding when recognition fails.
claims.source_quote: When an institution fails to recognize a role properly, obligations that depend on that recognition lose their grounding.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: obligations are grounded in institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Conflicting institutional recognitions produce contradictions agents cannot resolve within the existing structure.
claims.source_quote: When an institution recognizes conflicting obligations, it produces contradictions that agents cannot resolve within the existing structure.
claims.note: Asserts a property of conflicting recognitions: they generate unresolvable contradictions.

claims.claim: Unaddressed disruptions accumulate as contradiction debt that eventually destabilizes the system.
claims.source_quote: These disruptions accumulate as contradiction debt, which, if left unaddressed, eventually destabilizes the system.
claims.note: Asserts that contradiction debt is a real accumulating entity with a destabilizing effect on the system.

claims.claim: Recognition failure is a form of institutional failure in which an institution fails to acknowledge a role or obligation it is charged to maintain.
claims.source_quote: Recognition failure: An institution fails to acknowledge a role or obligation it is charged to maintain.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind of institutional failure and its defining property.

claims.claim: Recognition conflict is a form of institutional failure in which two institutions recognize incompatible obligations or permissions.
claims.source_quote: Recognition conflict: Two institutions recognize incompatible obligations or permissions concerning the same role.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind of institutional failure involving incompatible recognitions.

claims.claim: Diminished recognitive capacity is a form of institutional failure in which recognitive acts become inconsistent or unreliable.
claims.source_quote: Diminished recognitive capacity: Institutional procedures erode, and recognitive acts become inconsistent or unreliable.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind of institutional failure defined by degraded recognitive function.

claims.claim: Institutional drift is a form of institutional failure in which an institution ceases to fulfill its designed role.
claims.source_quote: Institutional drift: The institution ceases to fulfill the role it was designed for, altering the structure without explicit reconfiguration.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind of institutional failure with a specific defining property.

claims.claim: Conflicting institutional recognitions produce contradictions at the structural level.
claims.source_quote: This representation exposes a contradiction at the structural level: RoleX is simultaneously obligated and permitted in incompatible ways, each grounded in an institutional act of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property of conflicting recognitions: they generate structural-level contradictions.

claims.claim: Contradictions propagate through the network of roles and obligations, creating instability.
claims.source_quote: When such contradictions arise, they propagate through the network of roles and obligations, creating instability.
claims.note: Asserts a propagation relation: contradictions spread through the relational network and cause instability.

claims.claim: Repair is an institutional act that realigns recognitions and resolves incompatibility.
claims.source_quote: The system requires repair, an institutional act that realigns recognitions and resolves the incompatibility.
claims.note: Asserts that repair is a subkind of institutional act with a specific function.

claims.claim: Justice is a property of a well-ordered relational field, not an outcome or distributive condition.
claims.source_quote: Justice, in the structural ontology developed throughout this book, is not an outcome or a distributive condition but a property of a well-ordered relational field.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category of justice: a property, not an outcome or distributive condition.

claims.claim: A legal system is just when its roles, obligations, permissions, and institutional recognitions form a coherent and mutually supporting architecture.
claims.source_quote: A legal system is just when its roles, obligations, permissions, and institutional recognitions form a coherent and mutually supporting architecture.
claims.note: Asserts a structural condition for justice: coherence among legal entities and relations.

claims.claim: Coherence is the structural fit among all entities and relations composing legal life.
claims.source_quote: Coherence in this sense is not merely logical consistency; it is the structural fit among all the entities and relations that compose legal life.
claims.note: Asserts what coherence is: a structural fit property of the relational field.

claims.claim: Coherence is the structural condition that makes justice possible.
claims.source_quote: Coherence thus becomes the structural condition that makes justice possible.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary grounding relation between coherence and justice.

claims.claim: Justice is an emergent structural property of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: we gain a clearer view of justice as an emergent structural property.
claims.note: Asserts that justice has the ontological character of an emergent structural property.

claims.claim: Repair is an internal rebalancing mechanism, not an external correction.
claims.source_quote: Repair is not an external correction but an internal rebalancing.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of repair: internal to the system, not external.

claims.claim: Repair consists of institutional acts that realign roles, adjust obligations, clarify permissions, or resolve incompatible recognitions.
claims.source_quote: It consists of institutional acts that realign roles, adjust obligations, clarify permissions, or resolve incompatible recognitions.
claims.note: Asserts that repair is composed of institutional acts with specific relational functions.

claims.claim: Through repair, the legal architecture regains coherence and recovers its capacity to function justly.
claims.source_quote: Through repair, the architecture regains coherence, and the system recovers its capacity to function justly.
claims.note: Asserts that repair bears a restorative causal relation to coherence and just functioning.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt is a structural stress that accumulates in legal systems.
claims.source_quote: These disruptions create structural stresses, what earlier chapters described as contradiction debt, that accumulate until addressed.
claims.note: Asserts that contradiction debt is a real entity (structural stress) with an accumulative property.

claims.claim: Obligations must be grounded in institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Obligations must be grounded in institutional recognition and appropriately directed.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding relation between obligations and institutional recognition as a structural requirement.

claims.claim: Claims must correspond to obligations in a reciprocal pattern.
claims.source_quote: Claims must correspond to obligations in a reciprocal and intelligible pattern.
claims.note: Asserts a correlative relation between claims and obligations as part of the structural ontology.

claims.claim: Institutions are the primary agents of repair in the legal system.
claims.source_quote: institutions emerge as the primary agents of repair.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of institutions: they are the primary agents responsible for structural repair.

claims.claim: Misrecognition produces a false positive: a dependent continuant instantiated without necessary structural support.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this produces a false positive: a dependent continuant (the supposed legal fact) instantiated without the necessary structural support.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about what misrecognition produces—a dependent continuant without proper grounding.

claims.claim: Misrecognition creates ontologically unstable entities that exist in a state of suspended legitimacy.
claims.source_quote: Such misrecognition creates entities that are ontologically unstable, they exist in a state of suspended legitimacy, subject to annulment or correction once the error is discovered.
claims.note: Asserts a property (ontological instability, suspended legitimacy) of entities produced by misrecognition.

claims.claim: In epistemic error, the legal fact exists but is misunderstood; in ontological defect, the fact itself fails to exist.
claims.source_quote: In epistemic error, the fact exists, but our understanding of it is mistaken; in ontological defect, the fact itself fails to exist within the legal field.
claims.note: Asserts a distinction about the existence status of facts under two different failure modes.

claims.claim: When an impostor signs a contract using another's name, no genuine legal obligation is instantiated.
claims.source_quote: When an impostor signs a contract using another's name, the brute event of writing occurs... The act does not instantiate a genuine legal obligation, even if it temporarily appears to.
claims.note: Author asserts that the act fails to instantiate a genuine legal obligation—an ontological claim about non-existence.

claims.claim: An act signed by an impostor is void, not merely voidable—a non-being clothed in the appearance of law.
claims.source_quote: It is not merely voidable but void: a non-being clothed in the appearance of law.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status (void, non-being) of the resulting pseudo-entity.

claims.claim: Misrecognition is an act that generates entities without the dependencies required for their persistence.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition, then, is the ontological equivalent of a false creation, an act that generates entities without the dependencies required for their persistence.
claims.note: Asserts the nature and product of misrecognition as an ontological claim about entity-generation without proper dependencies.

claims.claim: Fraudulent legal entities are dependent continuants without proper grounding.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, such entities are dependent continuants without proper grounding: they borrow their apparent being from genuine institutional processes but lack alignment with the system's rule of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and deficiency of fraudulent legal entities.

claims.claim: Fraudulent entities are ontologically parasitic, depending on concealment of their own invalidity.
claims.source_quote: Fraud operates by manipulating recognition processes to produce entities that appear valid but are ontologically parasitic. A fraudulent deed or forged judicial order... depends on the concealment of its own invalidity.
claims.note: Asserts a property (ontological parasitism) and a dependency relation of fraudulent entities.

claims.claim: Once fraud is exposed, recognition collapses and no legal entity ever truly existed.
claims.source_quote: Once exposed, their recognition collapses, revealing that no legal entity ever truly existed.
claims.note: Asserts that fraudulent legal entities have no genuine existence—an ontological claim about non-being.

claims.claim: The nullification of fraud is an ontological repair restoring coherence in the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The nullification of fraud, therefore, is not merely a moral correction but an ontological repair: the restoration of coherence in the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that nullification has an ontological function (repair/restoration), not merely a moral one.

claims.claim: During fraud, the system tolerates temporary zones of incoherence in which contradictions persist.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, these moments constitute temporary zones of incoherence in which contradiction is tolerated.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the legal ontological field during fraud—temporary incoherence.

claims.claim: Jurisdictional voids are cases of non-recognition where brute events lack institutional dependencies to become legal facts.
claims.source_quote: A third form of failure arises in jurisdictional voids, where recognition cannot attach because no competent institution exists to confer it... brute events that could be legally significant occur outside any established field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of jurisdictional voids as a failure of recognition attachment.

claims.claim: Acts in jurisdictional voids exist in a liminal state between legality and non-being—recognitional indeterminacy.
claims.source_quote: They exist in a liminal state between legality and non-being, a condition we might call recognitional indeterminacy.
claims.note: Author asserts this ontological status, though the label 'recognitional indeterminacy' is introduced as a proposed term.

claims.claim: Recognition is always localized within a network of institutions defining territorial or functional domains.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is always localized within a network of institutions that define territorial or functional domains.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of recognition as an ontological claim about its localized nature.

claims.claim: When institutional domains fail to overlap or are contested, the ontological field of law fragments.
claims.source_quote: When these domains fail to overlap or are contested, the ontological field of law fragments.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/structural claim about what happens to law's ontological field under jurisdictional failure.

claims.claim: Creating new legal spaces is an act of ontological reconstruction that establishes conditions for recognition.
claims.source_quote: Creating new legal spaces is an act of ontological reconstruction, it establishes the boundaries within which recognition can once again attach to brute facts, converting chaos into order.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological function of establishing new jurisdictions/tribunals.

claims.claim: Misrecognition, fraud, and jurisdictional voids each represent a distinct mode of ontological breakdown.
claims.source_quote: These anomalies - misrecognition, fraud, and jurisdictional voids - illustrate that law's creation of facts is neither automatic nor infallible. Each reveals a distinct mode of ontological breakdown.
claims.note: Asserts that each anomaly is a subkind of ontological breakdown with distinct character.

claims.claim: Misrecognition corrupts referential alignment between recognition and its object.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition corrupts the referential alignment between recognition and its object.
claims.note: Asserts a property/effect of misrecognition on the recognition relation.

claims.claim: Fraud subverts the dependency structure of legal fact-making itself.
claims.source_quote: fraud subverts the dependency structure itself
claims.note: Asserts that fraud attacks the dependency structure—an ontological claim about what fraud does.

claims.claim: Jurisdictional voids eliminate the conditions of recognition altogether.
claims.source_quote: jurisdictional voids eliminate the conditions of recognition altogether.
claims.note: Asserts that jurisdictional voids remove the preconditions for recognition to occur.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt is a state in which the system's dependencies are violated but not yet repaired.
claims.source_quote: What unites them is the presence of contradiction debt: a state in which the system's dependencies are violated but not yet repaired.
claims.note: Asserts the existence and definition of contradiction debt as an ontological state of the legal system.

claims.claim: Unresolved contradiction debt accumulates, leading to systemic fragility and eventual collapse.
claims.source_quote: If left unresolved, such debt accumulates, leading to systemic fragility and eventual collapse.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/dispositional property of unresolved contradiction debt.

claims.claim: Procedural correctness is an ontological requirement, not merely a formal one.
claims.source_quote: Anomalies in fact-making also clarify why procedural correctness is an ontological, not merely formal, requirement.
claims.note: Asserts that procedural correctness has an ontological status and function.

claims.claim: Procedural errors are breaches in the chain of recognition that sustains law's being.
claims.source_quote: Procedural errors are not trivial technicalities but breaches in the chain of recognition that sustains law's being.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of procedural errors as disruptions to recognition's chain.

claims.claim: A judgment rendered without jurisdiction cannot exist as a valid legal entity.
claims.source_quote: A judgment rendered without jurisdiction, even if substantively just, cannot exist as a valid legal entity because it fails to satisfy its dependency conditions.
claims.note: Asserts the non-existence (as valid legal entity) of jurisdictionally defective judgments.

claims.claim: A contract without consent lacks the recognition necessary to instantiate obligation.
claims.source_quote: Similarly, a contract without consent lacks the recognition necessary to instantiate obligation.
claims.note: Asserts that consent is a dependency condition for a contract to instantiate a legal obligation.

claims.claim: Ontological correction modifies the structure of recognition in the present rather than undoing past brute events.
claims.source_quote: The act of correction does not travel backward in time to undo the brute events; rather, it modifies the structure of recognition in the present, redefining which entities are acknowledged as valid continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal correction as an ontological operation on the recognition structure, not on past events.

claims.claim: Once a fraudulent deed is annulled, its dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) are extinguished.
claims.source_quote: The fraudulent deed, once annulled, remains as a historical artifact, a record of misrecognition, but its dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) are extinguished.
claims.note: Asserts that annulment extinguishes dependent continuants—an ontological claim about what ceases to exist.

claims.claim: Law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality.
claims.source_quote: In this way, law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality: what once seemed real may persist as record but not as law.
claims.note: Asserts a structural distinction within law's ontology between historical record and current legal existence.

claims.claim: A pseudo-entity is an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The result is a pseudo-entity: an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the existence and defining property of pseudo-entities as a kind of deficient legal entity.

claims.claim: Institutions are independent continuants.
claims.source_quote: institutions, by contrast, are independent continuants: they possess a unity and endurance that are not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.note: Direct assertion that institutions belong to the ontological category of independent continuants.

claims.claim: Institutions possess unity and endurance not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.source_quote: they possess a unity and endurance that are not reducible to the persons who staff them.
claims.note: Asserts a property (unity, endurance) and a non-reduction relation between institutions and persons.

claims.claim: Institutions persist even as the individuals acting within them change.
claims.source_quote: This distinction allows us to understand how institutions persist even as the individuals acting within them come and go.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of institutions across membership change.

claims.claim: Institutions are a subkind of ObjectAggregate.
claims.source_quote: law:Institution a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:ObjectAggregate .
claims.note: The author presents this as a core ontological commitment: institutions are subclasses of BFO ObjectAggregate.

claims.claim: Institutions possess recognitive powers that individual agents as such do not.
claims.source_quote: institutions possess recognitive powers that individual agents, as such, do not.
claims.note: Asserts a distinctive property (recognitive powers) belonging to institutions but not individual agents.

claims.claim: When officials perform recognitive acts, they do so in virtue of occupying a role within an institution.
claims.source_quote: Even when individual officials perform recognitive acts, they do so in virtue of occupying a role within an institution whose authority grounds those acts.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding relation: institutional role-occupancy is the basis of an official's recognitive acts.

claims.claim: The institution's authority grounds recognitive acts performed by officials.
claims.source_quote: they do so in virtue of occupying a role within an institution whose authority grounds those acts.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding relation between institutional authority and individual recognitive acts.

claims.claim: The institution is the stabilizing source of recognition for roles and normative entities.
claims.source_quote: The institution stands as the stabilizing source of recognition for both roles and their associated normative entities.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational role of institutions as sources of recognition.

claims.claim: The institution's persistence gives the legal system continuity across time.
claims.source_quote: It is the institution's persistence that gives the legal system continuity across time.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/grounding relation between institutional persistence and legal system continuity.

claims.claim: Institutions serve as the stabilizing anchors of legal relations.
claims.source_quote: Because institutions serve as the stabilizing anchors of legal relations, their failures create fractures that spread across the relational field.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of institutions in the relational field of law.

claims.claim: When an institution fails to recognize a role, obligations depending on that recognition lose their grounding.
claims.source_quote: When an institution fails to recognize a role properly, obligations that depend on that recognition lose their grounding.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: obligations are grounded by institutional recognition.

claims.claim: When an institution recognizes conflicting obligations, it produces contradictions agents cannot resolve within the existing structure.
claims.source_quote: When an institution recognizes conflicting obligations, it produces contradictions that agents cannot resolve within the existing structure.
claims.note: Asserts a causal property of institutional recognition conflicts generating irresolvable contradictions.

claims.claim: Unaddressed contradiction debt eventually destabilizes the legal system.
claims.source_quote: These disruptions accumulate as contradiction debt, which, if left unaddressed, eventually destabilizes the system.
claims.note: Asserts that contradiction debt has a destabilizing property/effect on the system.

claims.claim: Contradictions propagate through the network of roles and obligations, creating instability.
claims.source_quote: When such contradictions arise, they propagate through the network of roles and obligations, creating instability.
claims.note: Asserts a propagation relation between contradictions and the role-obligation network.

claims.claim: Repairing contradictions requires an institutional act that realigns recognitions.
claims.source_quote: The system requires repair, an institutional act that realigns recognitions and resolves the incompatibility.
claims.note: Asserts that repair is an institutional act with a specific relational function (realigning recognitions).

claims.claim: Justice is a property of a well-ordered relational field.
claims.source_quote: Justice, in the structural ontology developed throughout this book, is not an outcome or a distributive condition but a property of a well-ordered relational field.
claims.note: Asserts that justice belongs to the category of properties and is a property of a relational field.

claims.claim: A legal system is just when its roles, obligations, permissions, and institutional recognitions form a coherent and mutually supporting architecture.
claims.source_quote: A legal system is just when its roles, obligations, permissions, and institutional recognitions form a coherent and mutually supporting architecture.
claims.note: Asserts a structural condition constituting justice in a legal system.

claims.claim: Coherence is the structural fit among all entities and relations composing legal life.
claims.source_quote: Coherence in this sense is not merely logical consistency; it is the structural fit among all the entities and relations that compose legal life.
claims.note: Asserts what coherence is as an ontological property of legal systems.

claims.claim: Coherence is the structural condition that makes justice possible.
claims.source_quote: Coherence thus becomes the structural condition that makes justice possible.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding or enabling relation between structural coherence and justice.

claims.claim: Justice is an emergent structural property.
claims.source_quote: we gain a clearer view of justice as an emergent structural property.
claims.note: Asserts that justice belongs to the ontological category of emergent structural properties.

claims.claim: Obligations must be grounded in institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Obligations must be grounded in institutional recognition and appropriately directed.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding relation between obligations and institutional recognition as a structural requirement.

claims.claim: Claims must correspond to obligations in a reciprocal pattern.
claims.source_quote: Claims must correspond to obligations in a reciprocal and intelligible pattern.
claims.note: Asserts a correlative relation between claims and obligations as part of structural ontology.

claims.claim: Institutions must sustain the recognitions that bring legal relations into being.
claims.source_quote: Institutions must sustain the recognitions that bring these relations into being.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive function of institutions with respect to legal relations.

claims.claim: Repair is an internal rebalancing mechanism, not an external correction.
claims.source_quote: Repair is not an external correction but an internal rebalancing.
claims.note: Asserts a property of repair distinguishing it from external correction—it is ontologically internal to the system.

claims.claim: Repair consists of institutional acts that realign roles, adjust obligations, clarify permissions, or resolve incompatible recognitions.
claims.source_quote: It consists of institutional acts that realign roles, adjust obligations, clarify permissions, or resolve incompatible recognitions.
claims.note: Asserts what repair is composed of—its ontological constituents as institutional acts.

claims.claim: Repair is the mechanism by which equilibrium is restored in a legal system.
claims.source_quote: Repair is the mechanism by which equilibrium is restored.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/causal role of repair in restoring structural equilibrium.

claims.claim: Institutions emerge as the primary agents of repair.
claims.source_quote: institutions emerge as the primary agents of repair.
claims.note: Asserts that institutions have the role/function of primary agents of repair.

claims.claim: A fraudulent deed, once annulled, persists as a historical artifact and record of misrecognition.
claims.source_quote: fraudulent deed, once annulled, remains as a historical artifact, a record of misrecognition
claims.note: Asserts a property/status of an annulled fraudulent deed—it remains as a historical artifact.

claims.claim: Annulment extinguishes the dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) of a fraudulent deed.
claims.source_quote: its dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) are extinguished
claims.note: Asserts that dependent continuants such as ownership, rights, and obligations cease to exist upon annulment.

claims.claim: Ownership, rights, and obligations are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: its dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) are extinguished
claims.note: Classifies ownership, rights, and obligations as a subkind of entity—dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality.
claims.source_quote: law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality: what once seemed real may persist as record but not as law
claims.note: Asserts a structural distinction within law between two kinds of reality.

claims.claim: What once seemed institutionally real may persist as record without persisting as law.
claims.source_quote: what once seemed real may persist as record but not as law
claims.note: Asserts a property of certain institutional entities—they can persist as historical record while losing legal existence.

claims.claim: Law adapts by extending its ontology to encompass irregularities that become normalized.
claims.source_quote: law adapts by extending its ontology to encompass these irregularities
claims.note: Asserts a functional/dispositional property of law—it can incorporate ontological anomalies.

claims.claim: Sufficiently widespread recognition generates its own coherence.
claims.source_quote: Recognition, once widespread enough, generates its own coherence, even if born in contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/generative property of recognition as an institutional phenomenon.

claims.claim: Each institution is a composite entity.
claims.source_quote: each institution can be modeled as a composite entity composed of: Agentive continuants (e.g., people, legal persons), Specifically dependent continuants (e.g., roles borne by those agents), Information artifacts (e.g., rules of procedure, statutes, charters), Occurrents (e.g., hearings, deliberations, decisions).
claims.note: The author asserts that institutions are composite entities with specific components—an ontological claim about the kind and structure of institutions.

claims.claim: Institutions are composed of agentive continuants.
claims.source_quote: each institution can be modeled as a composite entity composed of: Agentive continuants (e.g., people, legal persons)
claims.note: Direct assertion that agentive continuants are parts of institutional composite entities.

claims.claim: Institutions are composed of specifically dependent continuants (roles).
claims.source_quote: Specifically dependent continuants (e.g., roles borne by those agents)
claims.note: Asserts a part-of relation between specifically dependent continuants and institutions.

claims.claim: Institutions are composed of information artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Information artifacts (e.g., rules of procedure, statutes, charters)
claims.note: Asserts information artifacts as component parts of institutional entities.

claims.claim: Institutions are composed of occurrents.
claims.source_quote: Occurrents (e.g., hearings, deliberations, decisions).
claims.note: Asserts occurrents as component parts of institutional entities.

claims.claim: A court has the function of an adjudicative body.
claims.source_quote: a court functions as an adjudicative body not by virtue of its architecture or founding documents alone, but because role-bearers (judges, clerks, litigants) engage in processes (hearings, trials) that are normatively structured and legally recognized.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of courts as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: A court's adjudicative function is realized through role-bearers engaging in normatively structured processes.
claims.source_quote: a court functions as an adjudicative body not by virtue of its architecture or founding documents alone, but because role-bearers (judges, clerks, litigants) engage in processes (hearings, trials) that are normatively structured and legally recognized.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between the institution's function and the participation of role-bearing agents in processes.

claims.claim: Legal actors are role-bearing participants in institutions.
claims.source_quote: The legal actors within these institutions, judges, legislators, officers, defendants, and citizens are role-bearing participants.
claims.note: Asserts that legal actors bear the property of being role-bearing participants—an ontological claim about their nature.

claims.claim: A person's behavior is legally significant only when anchored in a valid role within a recognized institution.
claims.source_quote: Their behavior is not legally significant until it is anchored in a valid role, instantiated within the structure of a recognized institution.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between legal significance and role instantiation within recognized institutions.

claims.claim: A judicial decision requires the decision-maker to be a judge acting in a recognized courtroom under rule of law.
claims.source_quote: A person's decision is not a judicial decision unless they are a judge acting in a recognized courtroom under the rule of law.
claims.note: Asserts necessary conditions for an entity to be of the kind 'judicial decision'—an ontological claim about kinds.

claims.claim: The legal system depends on role assignment and role performance for its operation.
claims.source_quote: The legal system thus depends on role assignment and role performance for its very operation.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between the legal system and role assignment/performance.

claims.claim: Institutions are role-structuring systems.
claims.source_quote: Institutions as role-structuring systems
claims.note: Direct assertion about the nature/kind of institutions in ontological terms.

claims.claim: Legal events are occurrent processes involving multiple roles.
claims.source_quote: Legal events as occurrent processes involving multiple roles
claims.note: Asserts that legal events are a subkind of occurrent processes and have the property of involving multiple roles.

claims.claim: Normative powers are realizable entities activated through role performance.
claims.source_quote: Normative powers as realizable entities are activated through role performance.
claims.note: Asserts that normative powers are realizable entities and that role performance activates them—an ontological claim about the kind and activation conditions.

claims.claim: Roles within institutional systems are hierarchical, interdependent, and temporally scoped.
claims.source_quote: Roles within these systems are hierarchical, interdependent, and temporally scoped.
claims.note: Asserts properties (hierarchical, interdependent, temporally scoped) of roles as entities within institutional systems.

claims.claim: Institutions are embedded within broader institutional structures.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are embedded within broader structures, municipal courts within state judicial systems, departments within ministries, agencies within executive branches.
claims.note: Asserts a part-of or containment relation between institutions and broader structures.

claims.claim: Cascading role relations can be formally modeled as nested role hierarchies.
claims.source_quote: This cascading structure of role relations can be formally modeled as nested role hierarchies, allowing both legal theorists and informaticians to reason over chains of authority and accountability.
claims.note: Asserts the structure of role relations as nested hierarchies—an ontological claim about the structure of role relations, though the modeling framing slightly hedges direct assertion.

claims.claim: Legal systems allow for cross-institutional role transfer and multiplex role occupancy.
claims.source_quote: legal systems allow for cross-institutional role transfer and multiplex role occupancy.
claims.note: Asserts properties of legal systems as entities—specifically that they permit cross-institutional role transfer and multiple simultaneous role occupancy.

claims.claim: Different legal roles have different rights, duties, and powers.
claims.source_quote: At each stage, different legal roles are instantiated, with different rights, duties, and powers.
claims.note: Asserts that rights, duties, and powers are properties that differ across legal role kinds.

claims.claim: Role transitions in legal systems must be tracked with temporal logic and procedural semantics.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, these transitions must be tracked with temporal logic and procedural semantics to ensure clarity and prevent role conflicts or procedural error.
claims.note: Asserts a normative-ontological requirement about temporal and procedural properties of role transitions; primarily ontological but partly methodological.

claims.claim: The semantic coherence of a legal system depends on the consistency of its role structures.
claims.source_quote: The semantic coherence of a legal system depends on the consistency of its role structures.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between a property of legal systems (semantic coherence) and a property of their role structures (consistency).

claims.claim: Law is not reducible to documents or commands.
claims.source_quote: viewing legal systems as role-structured networks reinforces the idea that law is not reducible to documents or commands.
claims.note: Asserts a negative ontological claim about the nature of law—it cannot be reduced to documents or commands.

claims.claim: Law exists through participation structured through roles.
claims.source_quote: Law lives through participation, and participation is structured through roles.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological claim about how law exists—its mode of being is participatory and role-structured.

claims.claim: Each node in institutional authority structures represents a role or institution as a continuant sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Each node represents a role or institution as a continuant sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that roles and institutions are continuants and that institutional recognition sustains them—ontological claims about kind and sustaining relation.

claims.claim: Repair is an occurrent — an event that reconfigures the dependent continuants of a system.
claims.source_quote: repair is an occurrent, an event that reconfigures the dependent continuants of a system. It restores the pattern that allows obligations, claims, and permissions to cohere.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts the ontological category of repair as an occurrent with a specific function.

claims.claim: Repair restores the pattern that allows obligations, claims, and permissions to cohere.
claims.source_quote: It restores the pattern that allows obligations, claims, and permissions to cohere.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the function/role of repair in a legal system.

claims.claim: Justice is not a static property but a state of equilibrium.
claims.source_quote: Justice, then, is not a static property but a state of equilibrium continually maintained through acts of repair.
claims.note: Author asserts what kind of thing justice is — a state of equilibrium, not a static property.

claims.claim: Justice is continually maintained through acts of repair.
claims.source_quote: Justice, then, is not a static property but a state of equilibrium continually maintained through acts of repair.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between justice (as equilibrium) and acts of repair as its sustaining cause.

claims.claim: Justice is a quality of legal architecture — its coherence, responsiveness, and capacity for self-correction.
claims.source_quote: The structural lens positions justice as a quality of the architecture itself, its coherence, its responsiveness, and its capacity for self-correction.
claims.note: Author presents this as the conclusion of the structural lens, endorsing it as the correct framing of justice's ontological status.

claims.claim: Obligations depend on recognitive acts.
claims.source_quote: modeling shows how obligations depend on recognitive acts, how permissions align with roles, and how institutional authority underwrites the coherence of the normative field.
claims.note: Author asserts a dependence relation between obligations and recognitive acts as part of his own ontological framework.

claims.claim: Permissions align with roles.
claims.source_quote: modeling shows how obligations depend on recognitive acts, how permissions align with roles, and how institutional authority underwrites the coherence of the normative field.
claims.note: Asserts a structural relation between permissions and roles.

claims.claim: Institutional authority underwrites the coherence of the normative field.
claims.source_quote: how institutional authority underwrites the coherence of the normative field.
claims.note: Asserts that institutional authority has the function/role of underwriting normative coherence.

claims.claim: Legal relations are structured.
claims.source_quote: They underscore that legal relations are structured, and that their structure can be examined, questioned, and understood.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature of legal relations.

claims.claim: A municipal citation event contains an agent (the officer) bearing an enforcement role.
claims.source_quote: There is an agent, the officer, and a role, their authority to enforce the ordinance.
claims.note: Asserts that the officer is an agent and that their authority constitutes a role — ontological claims about kinds and role-bearing.

claims.claim: The driver bears an obligation in virtue of the role 'vehicle operator'.
claims.source_quote: There is an obligation borne by the driver in virtue of the role 'vehicle operator'
claims.note: Asserts that an obligation is borne by an individual in virtue of a role — a claim about role-obligation relations.

claims.claim: The city holds a claim as the entity responsible for maintaining safe public spaces.
claims.source_quote: a claim held by the city as the entity responsible for maintaining safe public spaces.
claims.note: Asserts that the city holds a claim and has a responsibility — ontological claims about an entity's properties and relations.

claims.claim: The officer holds a permission conferring authority to issue a citation.
claims.source_quote: there are permissions, such as the officer's authority to issue the citation
claims.note: Asserts that the officer holds a permission, which is a relation between an agent and a normative element.

claims.claim: The municipality's recognition anchors the ordinance, the role, and the related obligations.
claims.source_quote: there is an institution, the municipality, whose recognition anchors the ordinance, the role, and the related obligations.
claims.note: Asserts a grounding/anchoring relation between institutional recognition and normative elements.

claims.claim: The system's coherence depends on the alignment of obligations, roles, and institutional recognitions.
claims.source_quote: how the system's coherence depends on the alignment of these elements.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between systemic coherence and the alignment of specific ontological elements.

claims.claim: Justice emerges from the structure of a legal system.
claims.source_quote: how justice emerges, or fails to emerge, from the structure itself.
claims.note: Author endorses that justice has a structural origin; the 'or fails to emerge' introduces slight qualification but the positive claim is asserted.

claims.claim: Municipal parking enforcement involves roles, obligations, institutional recognitions, administrative processes, and opportunities for contradiction and repair.
claims.source_quote: dense with structural features: roles, obligations, institutional recognitions, administrative processes, and opportunities for contradiction and repair.
claims.note: Author asserts the structural composition of a concrete institutional arrangement.

claims.claim: Law adapts by extending its ontology to encompass irregularities.
claims.source_quote: law adapts by extending its ontology to encompass these irregularities. Recognition, once widespread enough, generates its own coherence, even if born in contradiction.
claims.note: Direct assertion about law's ontological property of adaptability and extension.

claims.claim: Widespread recognition generates coherence, even when originating in contradiction.
claims.source_quote: Recognition, once widespread enough, generates its own coherence, even if born in contradiction.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/generative relation between recognition and coherence.

claims.claim: Law can stabilize itself by incorporating its own anomalies, turning exceptions into new norms.
claims.source_quote: law can stabilize itself by incorporating its own anomalies, turning exceptions into new norms.
claims.note: Asserts a disposition/function of law as an institution.

claims.claim: Law's ontology is historically plastic despite being formally structured.
claims.source_quote: The transformation of unconstitutional acts into legitimate precedents illustrates how law's ontology, while formally structured, remains historically plastic.
claims.note: Asserts a property (historical plasticity) of law's ontological structure.

claims.claim: The field of recognition is self-referential and adaptive.
claims.source_quote: The field of recognition is self-referential and adaptive; it can reconstitute coherence even from initial incoherence.
