claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation and that are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.note: The author asserts a positive ontological characterization of virtual/intangible entities as information-and-code structures.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.note: The author asserts a dependency relation: these entities' persistence is constitutively dependent on institutional and technological mediation.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.source_quote: structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation and that are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.note: The author asserts a realization relation between intangible entities and material forms.

claims.claim: Ownership is a recognized dependency relation.
claims.source_quote: ownership as a recognized dependency, adapts across these layered domains of being.
claims.note: The author characterizes ownership ontologically as a form of recognized dependency, not merely as a legal category.

claims.claim: Tangible property belongs to the domain of material continuants.
claims.source_quote: At the most fundamental level, tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.note: The author asserts a categorical ontological classification: tangible property is situated in the domain of material continuants.

claims.claim: Being is layered into distinct domains.
claims.source_quote: ownership as a recognized dependency, adapts across these layered domains of being.
claims.note: The author's reference to 'layered domains of being' implies an ontological commitment to a stratified or layered ontology.

claims.claim: Justice is the inner logic of law, not external to it.
claims.source_quote: They come to see that justice is not external to the law but its inner logic, its measure of coherence with the world it orders.
claims.note: Author asserts a property/role of justice in relation to law.

claims.claim: Unjust institutions become ontologically incoherent.
claims.source_quote: When institutions become unjust, it is not only because they have violated moral norms, but because they have become ontologically incoherent, detached from the recognition that once sustained them.
claims.note: Author asserts a property (ontological incoherence) that unjust institutions have.

claims.claim: Unjust institutions are detached from the recognition that once sustained them.
claims.source_quote: When institutions become unjust, it is not only because they have violated moral norms, but because they have become ontologically incoherent, detached from the recognition that once sustained them.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational property of unjust institutions — detachment from recognition.

claims.claim: Recognition relations sustain institutions.
claims.source_quote: Which recognition relations sustain this institution, and where are they failing?
claims.note: Framed as a question for students but the author commits to recognition relations as sustaining entities for institutions.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and institutions are mechanisms through which people live together.
claims.source_quote: Students learn that the abstractions of law, rights, duties, institutions, are not distant constructs but the very mechanisms through which people live together.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional role of legal abstractions in human social existence.

claims.claim: Contract law is the formalization of reciprocal obligations.
claims.source_quote: Contract law as the formalization of reciprocal obligations.
claims.note: Author asserts a nature/kind relation: contract law is a kind of formalization of reciprocal obligations.

claims.claim: Ownership relations are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Property law as the management of dependent continuants (ownership relations) within institutional continuants (registries, markets, states).
claims.note: Author asserts a subkind/ontological category membership for ownership relations.

claims.claim: Registries, markets, and states are institutional continuants.
claims.source_quote: Property law as the management of dependent continuants (ownership relations) within institutional continuants (registries, markets, states).
claims.note: Author asserts ontological category membership for these entities.

claims.claim: Property law manages dependent continuants within institutional continuants.
claims.source_quote: Property law as the management of dependent continuants (ownership relations) within institutional continuants (registries, markets, states).
claims.note: Author asserts a functional/relational role for property law.

claims.claim: Constitutional law is the meta-ontology of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Constitutional law as the meta-ontology of recognition, governing the coherence of all other institutional relations.
claims.note: Author asserts a kind/nature claim about constitutional law.

claims.claim: Constitutional law governs the coherence of all other institutional relations.
claims.source_quote: Constitutional law as the meta-ontology of recognition, governing the coherence of all other institutional relations.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional role and relational property of constitutional law.

claims.claim: Justice is the coherence of relations among beings who exist only in relation.
claims.source_quote: that we exist only in relation, and that justice is the name we give to the coherence of those relations.
claims.note: Author asserts a definition/nature of justice as a property (coherence) of relations.

claims.claim: Human beings exist only in relation.
claims.source_quote: that we exist only in relation, and that justice is the name we give to the coherence of those relations.
claims.note: Author asserts a fundamental ontological property of human existence.

claims.claim: Law is the medium of justice.
claims.source_quote: law regains its unity with philosophy and its role as the medium of justice.
claims.note: Author asserts a role/function of law in relation to justice.

claims.claim: Law is the architecture of justice — a living, dynamic structure.
claims.source_quote: It becomes, once again, what it has always been at its highest sense: the architecture of justice, the living, dynamic structure through which human beings, together, create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.note: Author asserts a nature/kind claim about law as a dynamic structure.

claims.claim: Every courtroom, constitution, and code is an expression of the ontological truth that we exist only in relation.
claims.source_quote: every courtroom, constitution, and code is an expression of the same ontological truth: that we exist only in relation, and that justice is the name we give to the coherence of those relations.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational/expressive property of legal institutions.

claims.claim: Social reality is a shared structure that can be designed and repaired.
claims.source_quote: the ongoing design and repair of our shared social reality.
claims.note: Author commits to social reality as a kind of entity with the property of being designable and repairable.

claims.claim: Structural ontology provides an epistemic infrastructure for the study of justice.
claims.source_quote: structural ontology offers not just a theory of law but a new epistemic infrastructure for the study of justice itself.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional role of structural ontology — it has the property of being an epistemic infrastructure.

claims.claim: Law is the architecture of justice.
claims.source_quote: It becomes, once again, what it has always been at its highest sense: the architecture of justice, the living, dynamic structure through which human beings, together, create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.note: The author plainly asserts a property/role of law: that it is the architecture of justice.

claims.claim: Law is a living, dynamic structure.
claims.source_quote: the architecture of justice, the living, dynamic structure through which human beings, together, create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of law: that it is a living, dynamic structure.

claims.claim: Law is the medium through which human beings create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.source_quote: the living, dynamic structure through which human beings, together, create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional relation: law is the medium/structure enabling the creation and sustaining of a coherent world.

claims.claim: Law is a medium of justice.
claims.source_quote: law regains its unity with philosophy and its role as the medium of justice.
claims.note: The author asserts a role for law: being the medium of justice.

claims.claim: Law has unity with philosophy.
claims.source_quote: law regains its unity with philosophy and its role as the medium of justice.
claims.note: The author asserts a relation between law and philosophy: unity. Phrased as 'regains' implying this is the author's positive view of the proper relationship.

claims.claim: Justice is the inner logic of law, not external to it.
claims.source_quote: They come to see that justice is not external to the law but its inner logic, its measure of coherence with the world it orders.
claims.note: Author asserts a property/relation of justice with respect to law.

claims.claim: Justice is law's measure of coherence with the world it orders.
claims.source_quote: justice is not external to the law but its inner logic, its measure of coherence with the world it orders.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional/relational property of justice.

claims.claim: Unjust institutions are ontologically incoherent.
claims.source_quote: When institutions become unjust, it is not only because they have violated moral norms, but because they have become ontologically incoherent, detached from the recognition that once sustained them.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of unjust institutions—ontological incoherence.

claims.claim: Unjust institutions are detached from the recognition that once sustained them.
claims.source_quote: they have become ontologically incoherent, detached from the recognition that once sustained them.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational property of unjust institutions.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and institutions are mechanisms through which people live together.
claims.source_quote: Students learn that the abstractions of law, rights, duties, institutions, are not distant constructs but the very mechanisms through which people live together.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional role for these legal entities.

claims.claim: Contract law is the formalization of reciprocal obligations.
claims.source_quote: Contract law as the formalization of reciprocal obligations.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological characterization/role of contract law.

claims.claim: Property law manages dependent continuants (ownership relations) within institutional continuants.
claims.source_quote: Property law as the management of dependent continuants (ownership relations) within institutional continuants (registries, markets, states).
claims.note: Author asserts a functional and ontological characterization of property law.

claims.claim: Constitutional law is the meta-ontology of recognition governing coherence of all other institutional relations.
claims.source_quote: Constitutional law as the meta-ontology of recognition, governing the coherence of all other institutional relations.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological kind/role for constitutional law.

claims.claim: Structural ontology is a new epistemic infrastructure for the study of justice.
claims.source_quote: structural ontology offers not just a theory of law but a new epistemic infrastructure for the study of justice itself.
claims.note: Author asserts a role/function for structural ontology.

claims.claim: Justice is the living coherence of being-with.
claims.source_quote: Their task is to sustain justice as the living coherence of being-with.
claims.note: Author asserts a definition/property of justice.

claims.claim: Every courtroom, constitution, and code expresses the ontological truth that we exist only in relation.
claims.source_quote: every courtroom, constitution, and code is an expression of the same ontological truth: that we exist only in relation, and that justice is the name we give to the coherence of those relations.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological property shared by legal institutions.

claims.claim: Justice is the coherence of the relations through which we exist.
claims.source_quote: justice is the name we give to the coherence of those relations.
claims.note: Author asserts a definitional/ontological property of justice.

claims.claim: Human existence is fundamentally relational.
claims.source_quote: that we exist only in relation, and that justice is the name we give to the coherence of those relations.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological property of human beings—their mode of existence is relational.

claims.claim: Law is the architecture of justice—a living, dynamic structure.
claims.source_quote: It becomes, once again, what it has always been at its highest sense: the architecture of justice, the living, dynamic structure through which human beings, together, create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological characterization of law.

claims.claim: Law is the medium through which human beings create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.source_quote: the living, dynamic structure through which human beings, together, create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional/relational role of law.

claims.claim: Institutions have structures of recognition that give them life.
claims.source_quote: It invites those who study law to look beyond the surface of institutions and perceive the structures of recognition that give them life.
claims.note: Author asserts a constitutive relation between recognition structures and institutions.

claims.claim: Law is a living structure requiring continuous stewardship.
claims.source_quote: treat law as a living structure requiring continuous stewardship.
claims.note: Author asserts a property/disposition of law.

claims.claim: The practice of justice is architectural, systemic, and moral.
claims.source_quote: The practice of justice thus becomes architectural, systemic, and moral all at once.
claims.note: Author asserts properties of the practice of justice.

claims.claim: Artificial beings, humans, and institutions can potentially participate in recognition and bear obligations.
claims.source_quote: Understanding law ontologically enables them to ask what kinds of beings, human, artificial, institutional, can participate in recognition, bear obligations, and contribute to repair.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a genuine ontological question about kinds of beings, implying these are real categories of potential participants.

claims.claim: Social reality is a shared structure that can be designed and repaired.
claims.source_quote: the ongoing design and repair of our shared social reality.
claims.note: Author asserts ontological properties of social reality—it is shared and amenable to design and repair.

claims.claim: Law is the architecture of justice.
claims.source_quote: It becomes, once again, what it has always been at its highest sense: the architecture of justice, the living, dynamic structure through which human beings, together, create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/role of law: that law is (functions as) the architecture of justice. This is an ontological claim about law's nature and role.

claims.claim: Law is a living, dynamic structure.
claims.source_quote: the architecture of justice, the living, dynamic structure through which human beings, together, create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.note: The author asserts that law has the property of being a living, dynamic structure — an ontological claim about law's character.

claims.claim: Law is the medium through which human beings create and sustain a coherent world.
claims.source_quote: the living, dynamic structure through which human beings, together, create and sustain the possibility of a coherent world.
claims.note: The author asserts a relational/functional role for law with respect to human beings and social reality.

claims.claim: Law has unity with philosophy.
claims.source_quote: law regains its unity with philosophy and its role as the medium of justice.
claims.note: The author asserts that law and philosophy stand in a relation of unity, and that law has a role as medium of justice — ontological claims about law's relations and properties.

claims.claim: Law has the role of being the medium of justice.
claims.source_quote: law regains its unity with philosophy and its role as the medium of justice.
claims.note: The author asserts a functional/relational property of law: it is the medium of justice.

claims.claim: Tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.source_quote: At the most fundamental level, tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.note: Direct ontological categorization of tangible property as belonging to the domain of material continuants.

claims.claim: Material continuants are independent continuants in BFO terms.
claims.source_quote: These are independent continuants in BFO terms: physical objects that exist regardless of recognition, though their status as property depends on it.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation: material continuants are independent continuants in BFO.

claims.claim: Land, buildings, and artifacts are paradigmatic cases of tangible property.
claims.source_quote: Land, buildings, and artifacts are paradigmatic cases.
claims.note: Asserts that specific entities are instances of tangible property.

claims.claim: The property relation links the owner, the thing owned, and the institutional framework sustaining recognition.
claims.source_quote: The property relation here links the agent (owner), the object (thing owned), and the institutional framework that sustains recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relational structure constitutive of property.

claims.claim: Tangible property has distinctive stability due to the persistence of the object's material substrate.
claims.source_quote: The persistence of the object's material substrate gives tangible property a distinctive stability: even if recognition lapses, the physical entity remains available for reappropriation.
claims.note: Asserts a property (stability) of tangible property grounded in material persistence.

claims.claim: Intangible property occupies the domain of informational and conceptual continuants.
claims.source_quote: Intangible property, by contrast, occupies the domain of informational and conceptual continuants, entities that exist not as physical things but as structured content or form.
claims.note: Asserts ontological categorization of intangible property.

claims.claim: Copyrights, patents, trademarks, and debts are information content entities embedded in institutional recognition structures.
claims.source_quote: Copyrights, patents, trademarks, and debts are not objects in the material sense but information content entities (ICEs) embedded in institutional recognition structures.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of specific intangible property types.

claims.claim: Intangible property exists only through registries, ledgers, databases, and enforcement mechanisms.
claims.source_quote: They exist only through the systems that encode and sustain them: registries, ledgers, databases, and enforcement mechanisms.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: intangible property depends on institutional systems for existence.

claims.claim: A patent inheres in the institutional continuant of the patent office and the legal system.
claims.source_quote: A patent, for example, exists as a recognized right to exclude others from using a specific innovation; it inheres in the institutional continuant of the patent office and the legal system that enforces it.
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between a patent and an institutional continuant.

claims.claim: A patent's being depends on recognition distributed across institutions, realized through procedural occurrents.
claims.source_quote: Its being depends on recognition distributed across these institutions, realized through procedural occurrents such as filing, examination, and granting.
claims.note: Asserts ontological dependence and realization relations for patents.

claims.claim: When recognition ceases, intangible property ceases to exist as law.
claims.source_quote: When recognition ceases, through lapse, expiration, or legal invalidation, the intangible property ceases to exist as law, though its informational substrate may remain.
claims.note: Asserts a condition for the cessation of existence of intangible property.

claims.claim: Digital property includes software licenses, cryptocurrency tokens, domain names, and virtual goods.
claims.source_quote: Digital property includes software licenses, cryptocurrency tokens, domain names, and virtual goods in online environments.
claims.note: Asserts that specific entities are instances of digital property.

claims.claim: Digital property entities are computational continuants sustained by technological and institutional dependencies.
claims.source_quote: They are computational continuants, structured states of digital systems sustained by both technological and institutional dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts ontological kind and dependency relations for digital property entities.

claims.claim: Digital property entities are generically dependent continuants realized through coordinated functioning of hardware, software, and institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, they are generically dependent continuants realized through the coordinated functioning of hardware, software, and institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts BFO categorization and realization relations for digital property.

claims.claim: A digital token exists only as long as the blockchain encoding it remains operational and recognized as authoritative.
claims.source_quote: A digital token, for instance, exists only as long as the blockchain that encodes it remains operational and recognized as authoritative.
claims.note: Asserts an existence condition (dependency) for digital tokens.

claims.claim: Ownership of a digital token is defined by control over cryptographic credentials.
claims.source_quote: Its ownership is defined by control over cryptographic credentials, which serve as procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.note: Asserts what constitutes ownership in the digital token case.

claims.claim: Cryptographic credentials serve as procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.source_quote: Its ownership is defined by control over cryptographic credentials, which serve as procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/realization role for cryptographic credentials.

claims.claim: Technical recognition of cryptocurrencies achieves legal reality only when acknowledged by institutional systems.
claims.source_quote: Yet this technical recognition only achieves legal reality when it is acknowledged by institutional systems, when courts, regulators, or markets accept blockchain records as evidence of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency condition: technical recognition requires institutional acknowledgment for legal reality.

claims.claim: The ontological chain for digital assets runs from algorithmic recognition to institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: The ontological chain thus runs from algorithmic recognition to institutional recognition, forming a hybrid system of dependence.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/dependency structure constituting digital asset ontology.

claims.claim: Law and technology together sustain the being of digital assets.
claims.source_quote: Law and technology together sustain the being of digital assets, each contributing distinct but interlocking layers of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a co-sustaining relation between law, technology, and digital assets.

claims.claim: A software program is both a work of authorship (intangible property) and a functional system (digital property).
claims.source_quote: A software program is both a work of authorship (intangible property protected by copyright) and a functional system (digital property realized through execution on computational hardware).
claims.note: Asserts dual ontological categorization of software.

claims.claim: The same software entity exists simultaneously across different ontological layers, each sustained by its own recognition structure.
claims.source_quote: The same entity exists simultaneously across different ontological layers, each sustained by its own recognition structure.
claims.note: Asserts multi-layer ontological existence for software.

claims.claim: Data are information artifacts: structured representations of entities, events, or relations.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, data are information artifacts, structured representations of entities, events, or relations.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of data.

claims.claim: Data are generically dependent continuants that can exist in multiple copies simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Because data are generically dependent continuants that can exist in multiple copies simultaneously, property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.note: Asserts BFO categorization and a distinctive property of data.

claims.claim: Property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.source_quote: Because data are generically dependent continuants that can exist in multiple copies simultaneously, property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.note: Asserts what constitutes property over data given its ontological nature.

claims.claim: Data ownership is a right to control relational configurations rather than physical possession.
claims.source_quote: The legal innovation of data ownership thus consists in redefining property as a right to control relational configurations rather than physical possession.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of data ownership.

claims.claim: A virtual sword or digital land exists only as an aggregation of code instantiated within a software platform.
claims.source_quote: A virtual sword or parcel of digital land exists only as an aggregation of code instantiated within a software platform.
claims.note: Asserts the constitution and existence condition of virtual property entities.

claims.claim: Virtual property is recognized within one ontological layer (the virtual environment) and further sustained by another (the legal system).
claims.source_quote: Virtual property therefore exemplifies nested recognition: an entity recognized within one ontological layer (the virtual environment) whose reality is further sustained by another (the legal system).
claims.note: Asserts a nested recognition/dependency structure for virtual property.

claims.claim: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is their relational form, not their substance.
claims.source_quote: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is not their substance but their relational form.
claims.note: Asserts a unifying ontological feature (relational form) across property types.

claims.claim: In each case, ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object, and a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: In each case, ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object (physical, informational, or virtual), and a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the relational/dependency structure of ownership across all property types.

claims.claim: A procedural act (trial, filing, enactment) is an occurrent through which a legal fact is created.
claims.source_quote: Occurrent: The procedural act (trial, filing, enactment) through which a fact is created.
claims.note: Asserts that procedural acts are a kind of occurrent entity with the function of creating legal facts.

claims.claim: A legal relation or status (right, obligation, decision) is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: Dependent Continuant: The legal relation or status generated (right, obligation, decision).
claims.note: Asserts that legal relations and statuses are a subkind of dependent continuant.

claims.claim: An information artifact is a material or digital bearer that embodies a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: Information Artifact: The material or digital bearer that embodies the dependent continuant.
claims.note: Asserts a realization/embodiment relation between information artifacts and dependent continuants.

claims.claim: An institutional continuant is the system (court, registry, agency) that maintains recognition of an artifact.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Continuant: The system (court, registry, agency) that maintains recognition of the artifact.
claims.note: Asserts that courts, registries, and agencies are institutional continuants with the function of maintaining recognition.

claims.claim: Legal facts endure by linking transient events to enduring material supports within stable institutions.
claims.source_quote: This chain ensures the endurance of legal facts by linking transient events to enduring material supports within stable institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a structural relation between occurrents and continuants that explains the persistence of legal facts.

claims.claim: Digital artifacts are continuants bearing information content entities.
claims.source_quote: digital artifacts are continuants bearing information content entities; their legal significance arises from institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that digital artifacts are a kind of continuant with information content entities as a property/bearer relation.

claims.claim: The legal significance of digital artifacts arises from institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: digital artifacts are continuants bearing information content entities; their legal significance arises from institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between legal significance and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: A digital signature or electronic court order has the same ontological structure as its physical counterpart.
claims.source_quote: A digital signature or electronic court order is no less real than its physical counterpart because its being depends on the same structure of dependencies, authority, recognition, record.
claims.note: Asserts that digital and physical legal artifacts share the same ontological dependencies.

claims.claim: Law's reality resides in the relations that confer and sustain recognition of artifacts, not in their substance.
claims.source_quote: law's reality resides not in the substance of its artifacts but in the relations that confer and sustain their recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a positive ontological claim about where legal reality is grounded.

claims.claim: Filing deadlines, effective dates, and statutes of limitation are temporal constraints on legal occurrents.
claims.source_quote: Filing deadlines, effective dates, and statutes of limitation are not arbitrary technicalities; they are temporal constraints that ensure coherence across the system's occurrents.
claims.note: Asserts that these legal mechanisms are temporal constraints—an ontological property—not mere technicalities.

claims.claim: Temporal order is an ontological principle of law, realized through procedural regulation.
claims.source_quote: Temporal order, in this sense, is an ontological principle of law, realized through procedural regulation.
claims.note: Asserts that temporal order has the property of being an ontological principle of law.

claims.claim: Procedures connect local acts of recognition to the broader architecture of law.
claims.source_quote: They connect local acts of recognition to the broader architecture of law, ensuring that new entities are properly instantiated and aligned.
claims.note: Asserts a relational function of procedures within legal ontology.

claims.claim: An improperly filed motion may not exist as a legal entity.
claims.source_quote: an improperly filed motion may not exist as a legal entity, even if its content is known.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological consequence of procedural defect—the entity fails to exist.

claims.claim: A verdict rendered by an unauthorized tribunal lacks the status of a legal fact.
claims.source_quote: a verdict rendered by an unauthorized tribunal lacks the status of a legal fact, regardless of its substantive accuracy.
claims.note: Asserts that an unauthorized verdict does not instantiate a legal fact—an ontological status claim.

claims.claim: Ontological validity of legal entities depends on procedural realization.
claims.source_quote: Ontological validity depends on procedural realization, because only through procedure does recognition acquire enduring institutional form.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between ontological validity and procedural realization.

claims.claim: Procedural processes realize the functions of legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: In biology, physiological processes realize the functions of organs; in law, procedural processes realize the functions of institutions.
claims.note: Author endorses this parallel as an ontological claim about law, asserting a realization relation.

claims.claim: Legal functions depend on recognition rather than causal mechanisms.
claims.source_quote: The difference lies in the basis of dependence. Biological functions depend on causal mechanisms, while legal functions depend on recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that recognition is the ontological basis of dependence for legal functions.

claims.claim: Law endures through the continuous realization of its structures in procedural time.
claims.source_quote: Law, therefore, is not metaphorically but ontologically alive: it endures through the continuous realization of its structures in procedural time.
claims.note: Asserts that law's persistence is ontologically grounded in procedural realization.

claims.claim: The archive of law is the ontological memory that sustains the continuity of legal facts.
claims.source_quote: The archive of law, the cumulative record of trials, decrees, filings, and decisions, is not merely historical; it is ontological memory.
claims.note: Asserts that legal archives have the property of being ontological memory sustaining continuity of legal facts.

claims.claim: Each procedural occurrent generates continuants such as records, judgments, and statutes.
claims.source_quote: Each procedural occurrent generates continuants that populate the legal world, such as records, judgments, statutes.
claims.note: Asserts a generative relation between procedural occurrents and dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Information artifacts serve as vehicles of the recursive process of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Information artifacts serve as the vehicles of this recursive process, ensuring that recognition survives the passage of time.
claims.note: Asserts that information artifacts have the function/role of carrying recognition across time.

claims.claim: The procedural domain is the temporal field in which recognition becomes legal reality.
claims.source_quote: The procedural domain is thus the engine of legal being: the temporal field in which recognition becomes reality.
claims.note: Asserts a positive ontological characterization of the procedural domain.

claims.claim: Law is composed of primary and secondary rules.
claims.source_quote: law is not a mere collection of commands or isolated norms but a structured system composed of primary and secondary rules.
claims.note: Author endorses Hart's structural claim as an ontological description of law's composition.

claims.claim: Primary rules impose duties; secondary rules confer powers.
claims.source_quote: Primary rules impose duties, prescribing what must or must not be done, while secondary rules confer powers, specifying how primary rules may be recognized, altered, or adjudicated.
claims.note: Asserts property/function distinctions between two kinds of legal rules.

claims.claim: Secondary rules form the infrastructure of legal being.
claims.source_quote: Secondary rules form the infrastructure of legal being; they are the mechanisms by which norms acquire, retain, and lose their validity within a system of interdependent recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that secondary rules have the structural property of constituting legal infrastructure.

claims.claim: Secondary rules correspond to structural continuants that define the conditions of existence for obligations, rights, and legal facts.
claims.source_quote: secondary rules correspond to the structural continuants that define the conditions of existence for dependent entities such as obligations, rights, and legal facts.
claims.note: Asserts a correspondence/identity between secondary rules and structural continuants in BFO terms.

claims.claim: Secondary rules inhere in institutions and in the relations among them, not in individual agents.
claims.source_quote: secondary rules function as meta-level dependent continuants: they inhere not in individual agents but in institutions and in the relations among them.
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation locating secondary rules in institutions rather than individuals.

claims.claim: The secondary rule is an ontological operator that defines dependence relations determining when legal entities can exist.
claims.source_quote: The secondary rule is thus an ontological operator; it defines the dependence relations that determine when and how legal entities can exist.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/role property of secondary rules within legal ontology.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition specifies the ultimate criteria by which legal norms are validated within a system.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition specifies the ultimate criteria by which legal norms are validated within a system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition defines the boundary of legal reality—what counts as law and what does not.
claims.source_quote: It is the meta-structure that delineates the boundary of legal reality itself: what counts as law, and what does not.
claims.note: Asserts that the rule of recognition has the property of delimiting the domain of legal reality.

claims.claim: Every legal entity (statute, contract, judgment, obligation) derives its ontological status from alignment with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Everything that exists within a legal system - statutes, contracts, judgments, obligations - derives its ontological status from alignment with this rule.
claims.note: Asserts a universal dependence relation between legal entities and the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition functions as the system's ontological anchor.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition functions as the system's ontological anchor, ensuring coherence by maintaining a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function property of the rule of recognition within the legal system.

claims.claim: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is their relational form, not their substance.
claims.source_quote: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is not their substance but their relational form.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological basis of unity across property types.

claims.claim: Ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object, and a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object (physical, informational, or virtual), and a system of recognition.
claims.note: Explicit ontological claim about the nature and relational structure of ownership.

claims.claim: The persistence and transfer of property depend on the stability of these dependencies.
claims.source_quote: The persistence and transfer of property depend on the stability of these dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property's persistence/transfer and structural stability.

claims.claim: The transition from land and goods to software and data does not alter property's ontological nature.
claims.source_quote: The transition from land and goods to software and data does not alter property's ontological nature; it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the invariance of property's nature across domains.

claims.claim: The transition to digital property multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.source_quote: it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Asserts that digital property introduces new kinds of continuants as relata of property relations.

claims.claim: There is a stratified ontology of ownership spanning multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.source_quote: The result is a stratified ontology of ownership, in which legal recognition spans multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.note: Explicit ontological assertion about the layered structure of the ownership domain.

claims.claim: Legal recognition spans multiple layers of both material and immaterial being.
claims.source_quote: legal recognition spans multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.note: Asserts that immaterial being exists as a domain to which legal recognition extends.

claims.claim: Statutes, contracts, judgments, and obligations derive their ontological status from alignment with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Everything that exists within a legal system - statutes, contracts, judgments, obligations - derives its ontological status from alignment with this rule.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological grounding of legal entities.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition functions as the ontological anchor of a legal system.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition functions as the system's ontological anchor, ensuring coherence by maintaining a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of the rule of recognition within the legal system.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition maintains a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.source_quote: ensuring coherence by maintaining a unified structure of validation across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of the rule of recognition regarding institutional relations.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition provides law with closure as a self-sustaining field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It provides law with its closure as a self-sustaining field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the rule of recognition and a property of law (self-sustaining field).

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.source_quote: it is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.note: Directly asserts the ontological kind and relational role of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Asserts that the rule of recognition belongs to the ontological category of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition inheres in the system of institutions collectively, not in any single agent.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Asserts the locus of inherence of the rule of recognition as a relational/ontological claim.

claims.claim: The transition from land to software does not alter property's ontological nature.
claims.source_quote: The transition from land and goods to software and data does not alter property's ontological nature; it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Direct authorial assertion about the ontological nature of property across substrate types.

claims.claim: Property relations can attach to multiple types of continuants.
claims.source_quote: it merely multiplies the types of continuants to which property relations can attach.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property: property relations bear on continuants of various types.

claims.claim: Ownership has a stratified ontology spanning multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.source_quote: The result is a stratified ontology of ownership, in which legal recognition spans multiple layers of material and immaterial being.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of ownership's ontology.

claims.claim: Law is an ontological system with adaptive capacity.
claims.source_quote: The proliferation of digital and informational property also reveals law's adaptability as an ontological system.
claims.note: Asserts that law is an ontological system and has the property of adaptability.

claims.claim: Cryptographic assets, AI models, and virtual personas are entities that challenge traditional legal categories.
claims.source_quote: New technologies continually generate new entities, including cryptographic assets, artificial intelligence models, and virtual personas, that challenge traditional categories.
claims.note: Asserts existence of these entities and their relation to traditional categories.

claims.claim: Law extends recognition to novel entities through analogy and formal innovation.
claims.source_quote: law responds not by abandoning its framework but rather by extending recognition to these entities through analogy and formal innovation.
claims.note: Asserts a functional relation: law bears a recognition-extending relation to novel entities.

claims.claim: Law continuously expands the range of what can exist as property.
claims.source_quote: thereby expanding the range of what can exist as property.
claims.note: Asserts that law has the function of expanding the domain of property existence.

claims.claim: The expansion of legal recognition is expansion of recognition fields, not creation of new categories.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this is not the creation of new categories but the expansion of recognition fields, a process through which law continuously refines its map of social and material reality.
claims.note: Direct ontological distinction asserted by the author.

claims.claim: Property is a manifestation of relational dependence.
claims.source_quote: At every layer, property remains a manifestation of relational dependence.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive property of property: it is relational dependence.

claims.claim: Ownership exists only through the coordinated interplay of agents, institutions, and media of recognition.
claims.source_quote: ownership exists only through the coordinated interplay of agents, institutions, and media of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: ownership depends on agents, institutions, and recognition media.

claims.claim: The ontology of property mirrors the ontology of law itself.
claims.source_quote: The ontology of property thus mirrors the ontology of law itself: a hierarchy of dependent continuants sustained by networks of recognition that evolve with the structures of social life.
claims.note: Asserts a structural analogy/identity between property's ontology and law's ontology.

claims.claim: Law is a hierarchy of dependent continuants sustained by networks of recognition.
claims.source_quote: a hierarchy of dependent continuants sustained by networks of recognition that evolve with the structures of social life.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure of law.

claims.claim: Ownership persists only through the stable functioning of institutional mechanisms.
claims.source_quote: Property persists only through the stable functioning of institutional mechanisms that maintain and reaffirm recognition over time.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency: ownership's persistence depends on institutional mechanisms.

claims.claim: Ownership exists solely within a web of continuous institutional affirmation.
claims.source_quote: ownership exists solely within a web of continuous institutional affirmation.
claims.note: Asserts existential dependence of ownership on institutional affirmation.

claims.claim: Institutions serve as ontological stabilizers of property.
claims.source_quote: Institutions, in this sense, serve as ontological stabilizers of property: they ensure that the dependencies linking agents, objects, and rights remain coherent, traceable, and enforceable.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of institutions in relation to property.

claims.claim: Property relations are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Property relations, as dependent continuants, require persistent bearers in both agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a kind membership: property relations are a subkind of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Property relations require persistent bearers in both agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Property relations, as dependent continuants, require persistent bearers in both agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: property relations depend on agents and institutions as bearers.

claims.claim: Registries, contracts, and courts are institutional continuants.
claims.source_quote: The registry, the contract, and the court each function as institutional continuants, entities whose role is to instantiate and help maintain the relations that define ownership.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership of registries, contracts, and courts as institutional continuants.

claims.claim: Registries, contracts, and courts have the role of instantiating and maintaining ownership relations.
claims.source_quote: entities whose role is to instantiate and help maintain the relations that define ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/property of these institutional continuants.

claims.claim: Recording, verifying, adjudicating, and enforcing are occurrents that realize ownership's dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: They do so through a series of occurrents, procedural acts such as recording, verifying, adjudicating, and enforcing, which continually realize and reaffirm the dependent continuants of ownership and entitlement.
claims.note: Asserts that these procedural acts are occurrents and that they realize dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Without recurring institutional realizations, property would collapse into mere possession.
claims.source_quote: Without these recurring realizations, property would collapse back into mere possession and fragile memories, its ontological stability lost with the withdrawal of formal recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency: property's ontological stability depends on recurring institutional realizations.

claims.claim: A land registry or patent database is an institutional continuant that holds together the network of recognition.
claims.source_quote: A land registry, corporate register, or patent database is not merely a repository of information but an institutional continuant helping to hold together the network of recognition itself.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership and function of registries.

claims.claim: Each registry entry is a recorded dependent continuant sustained by institutional memory.
claims.source_quote: Each entry in such a registry represents a recorded dependent continuant, a legal fact sustained by institutional memory and procedural validation.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership: registry entries are dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Registration transforms transient recognition into a persistent institutional fact.
claims.source_quote: The act of registration transforms transient recognition (the acknowledgment of a transaction or ownership claim) into a persistent institutional fact.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative relation: registration changes the ontological status of recognition.

claims.claim: Once registered, ownership becomes part of the legal system's enduring ontology.
claims.source_quote: Once entered into the registry, ownership becomes part of the legal system's enduring ontology, capable of surviving changes in agents, institutions, or physical conditions.
claims.note: Asserts that registered ownership is part of the legal system's ontology.

claims.claim: Titles, deeds, and certificates are information artifacts embedded within institutional structures.
claims.source_quote: This persistence is achieved through the embedding of information artifacts, titles, deeds, certificates, within an institutional structure that ensures their ongoing validity.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership: titles, deeds, certificates are information artifacts.

claims.claim: The registry transforms ephemeral acts of acknowledgment into durable components of the legal order.
claims.source_quote: The registry thereby bridges temporal scales: it transforms ephemeral acts of acknowledgment into durable components of the legal order.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of registries: temporal transformation of ontological status.

claims.claim: Ownership survives through its representation in institutional memory, not through possession.
claims.source_quote: While possession can be lost with a gesture, ownership survives through the persistence of its representation in institutional memory.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive difference between ownership and possession regarding persistence.

claims.claim: The ownership relation continues to exist as long as the registry remains coherent and recognized.
claims.source_quote: As long as the registry remains coherent and recognized, the ownership relation continues to exist, even if the owner dies, the property is vacant, or the document itself is destroyed.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency: ownership's existence depends on registry coherence.

claims.claim: The registry is the metaphysical anchor of modern property systems.
claims.source_quote: The registry is thus the metaphysical anchor of modern property systems, law's apparatus for making recognition permanent.
claims.note: Asserts a structural role of registries in property ontology.

claims.claim: A contract is an information artifact that records the creation of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: A contract is an information artifact that records the creation of dependent continuants, including rights, obligations, and transfers, whose validity depends on institutional acceptance.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership of contracts as information artifacts bearing a recording relation.

claims.claim: Rights, obligations, and transfers are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: A contract is an information artifact that records the creation of dependent continuants, including rights, obligations, and transfers.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership of rights, obligations, and transfers.

claims.claim: The signing of a contract is an occurrent that realizes the agents' and institution's roles.
claims.source_quote: The signing of a contract is an occurrent that realizes both the agents' roles (as parties) and the institution's role (as guarantor of recognition).
claims.note: Asserts kind membership of contract-signing as an occurrent and its realization relations.

claims.claim: A contract creates a new property relation by encoding dependencies between agents and objects.
claims.source_quote: The contract thus creates a new property relation by encoding the dependencies that bind the agents and the object of exchange within the institutional field.
claims.note: Asserts a creative/generative function of contracts with respect to property relations.

claims.claim: Enforcement processes are repair occurrents that restore coherence in the network of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Enforcement processes (litigation, execution, repossession) are repair occurrents: temporal events that restore coherence by reaffirming the underlying structure of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts kind membership of enforcement processes as repair occurrents.

claims.claim: Theft temporarily displaces the realization of the recognition dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: Theft, for instance, does not merely deprive an owner of physical control, it temporarily displaces the realization of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that theft has an ontological effect: it displaces recognition realization.

claims.claim: The thief possesses the object but does not possess the dependent continuant of ownership.
claims.source_quote: The thief possesses the object but not the dependent continuant of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a distinction between possession and ownership as distinct ontological statuses.

claims.claim: An object remains owned as long as the institutional relations defining ownership persist.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the object remains 'owned' as long as the institutional relations that define ownership persist.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency: being-owned persists so long as institutional relations persist.

claims.claim: Ownership ceases to exist if the registry is destroyed or the legal order disintegrates.
claims.source_quote: Only if recognition collapses, if the registry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim, does ownership cease to exist.
claims.note: Asserts conditions under which ownership ceases to exist.

claims.claim: Failures of institutional maintenance such as theft and fraud are ontological disruptions in the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Failures in institutional maintenance, such as theft, fraud, or systemic corruption, represent ontological disruptions in the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that these events have a specific ontological character: they disrupt recognition fields.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a shared structural dependency organizing relations among institutions.
claims.source_quote: its ontological status is more precise: it is a shared structural dependency that organizes relations among institutions.
claims.note: Direct authorial assertion about the ontological nature of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition exists as a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Explicit ontological categorization of the rule of recognition as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition inheres in the system of institutions collectively, not in any one agent.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a dependent continuant that inheres not in any one agent but in the system of institutions collectively.
claims.note: Asserts a specific inherence relation for the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is realized whenever institutions recognize one another's acts as legally valid.
claims.source_quote: Its realization occurs whenever institutions recognize one another's acts as legally valid, when a court accepts a statute as binding, or when a legislature enacts a rule recognized by the judiciary.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between institutional acts and the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Each act of mutual recognition realizes the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Each act of mutual recognition realizes the rule of recognition and thereby reinforces its persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between acts of mutual recognition and the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition has a distributed and recurrent mode of being.
claims.source_quote: The rule's being is thus distributed and recurrent; it exists as long as its network of realizations continues across time.
claims.note: Asserts a property (distributed and recurrent being) of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition exists as long as its network of realizations continues across time.
claims.source_quote: it exists as long as its network of realizations continues across time.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Primary rules depend on secondary rules for their validity and normative force.
claims.source_quote: Primary rules depend on secondary rules for their validity and for the persistence of their normative force.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between primary and secondary rules.

claims.claim: Without secondary rules, primary norms cannot exist as components of a coherent legal system.
claims.source_quote: Without secondary rules, primary norms could exist as moral or customary directives but not as components of a coherent legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for primary norms' existence within a legal system.

claims.claim: Secondary rules provide the relational architecture that binds primary norms into an integrated structure.
claims.source_quote: Secondary rules provide the relational architecture that binds primary norms into an integrated structure.
claims.note: Asserts a structural role/function of secondary rules.

claims.claim: Secondary rules are the meta-conditions of legal being.
claims.source_quote: They are the meta-conditions of legal being, the relations that make norms real within a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that secondary rules occupy the ontological role of meta-conditions for norms' existence.

claims.claim: Secondary rules make norms real within a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: the relations that make norms real within a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive/grounding relation of secondary rules to the reality of norms.

claims.claim: A primary norm is a dependent continuant that inheres in an institution or agent role.
claims.source_quote: Primary Norm (Dependent Continuant) inheres in ? Institution or Agent Role.
claims.note: Explicit BFO-based ontological categorization asserted by the author.

claims.claim: A secondary rule is a dependent continuant that depends on a system of institutions for realization.
claims.source_quote: Secondary Rule (Dependent Continuant) depends on ? System of Institutions for realization.
claims.note: Explicit BFO-based ontological categorization asserted by the author.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is a meta-level continuant that organizes dependencies among all other rules.
claims.source_quote: Rule of Recognition (Meta-level Continuant) organizes dependencies among all other rules.
claims.note: Explicit ontological categorization and relational role asserted by the author.

claims.claim: Institutional processes are occurrents that realize dependencies defined by secondary rules.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Processes (Occurrents) realize the dependencies defined by secondary rules through enactment, adjudication, or amendment.
claims.note: Asserts ontological categorization and realization relation for institutional processes.

claims.claim: The validity of a primary norm is the result of its alignment with the dependency structure, not a property it possesses in isolation.
claims.source_quote: The validity of a primary norm, then, is not a property it possesses in isolation but the result of its alignment with this dependency structure.
claims.note: Asserts the relational (non-intrinsic) nature of legal validity.

claims.claim: A statute's validity is an ontological condition, not merely a sociological one.
claims.source_quote: The statute's validity is an ontological condition, not merely a sociological one, it exists within the system because its dependencies are coherently satisfied.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of a statute's validity.

claims.claim: A statute participates in a chain of dependence that traces back to the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: To say that a statute 'is law' is to say that it participates in a chain of dependence that traces back, through institutions and secondary rules, to the rule of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a participation/dependence relation between statute and rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of change defines the temporal dependencies of legal entities.
claims.source_quote: It specifies the temporal dependencies of legal entities, how one set of norms can succeed another without disrupting institutional continuity.
claims.note: Asserts a function/property of the rule of change regarding temporal dependencies.

claims.claim: The rule of adjudication defines repair dependencies that allow the system to maintain coherence.
claims.source_quote: It defines the repair dependencies that allow the system to maintain coherence in the face of contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property/role of the rule of adjudication.

claims.claim: Secondary rules are the ontological equivalents of homeostatic mechanisms in biological systems.
claims.source_quote: They are the ontological equivalents of homeostatic mechanisms in biological systems: processes that preserve stability amid constant transformation.
claims.note: Asserts an analogical ontological equivalence; medium confidence as it is comparative/analogical.

claims.claim: Legal systems are stratified networks of dependency with the rule of recognition at the apex.
claims.source_quote: Legal systems are stratified networks of dependency, with the rule of recognition at the apex.
claims.note: Asserts the structural/ontological character of legal systems.

claims.claim: Constitutions, statutes, regulations, and decisions each derive validity from the levels above them in the hierarchy.
claims.source_quote: Constitutions, statutes, regulations, and decisions all occupy different levels within this hierarchy, each deriving validity from the levels above.
claims.note: Asserts dependence relations among levels of the legal hierarchy.

claims.claim: Validity is a relational property: a norm is valid if it exists within the appropriate dependency network.
claims.source_quote: Validity is not an empirical property but a relational one: a norm is valid if it exists within the appropriate dependency network.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of validity as relational.

claims.claim: When a norm ceases to align with the rule of recognition, it loses its ontological grounding within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The moment a norm ceases to align with the rule of recognition...it loses its ontological grounding within the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a condition under which a norm loses its ontological status as law.

claims.claim: An invalid norm may still exist as a historical artifact but no longer exists as law.
claims.source_quote: The norm may still exist as a historical artifact, but it no longer exists as law.
claims.note: Asserts that invalidity entails a change in ontological category (artifact vs. law).

claims.claim: When a norm ceases to be law, its dependent continuants—obligations, rights, permissions—are extinguished or transformed.
claims.source_quote: Its dependent continuants, obligations, rights, permissions, are extinguished or transformed.
claims.note: Asserts that obligations, rights, and permissions are dependent continuants of valid norms.

claims.claim: Invalidity is the dissolution of recognition that sustains an entity's existence within the legal field.
claims.source_quote: invalidity is a kind of ontological death: the dissolution of recognition that sustains an entity's existence within the legal field.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of invalidity as loss of sustaining recognition.

claims.claim: Physical and social events such as signing, voting, and declaring serve as substrates of recognition.
claims.source_quote: At the base are physical and social events (signing, voting, declaring) that serve as the substrates of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts ontological role/function of physical and social events in the legal ontology.

claims.claim: Rules, rights, and duties are dependent continuants that inhere in institutions.
claims.source_quote: above them are dependent continuants (rules, rights, duties) that inhere in institutions.
claims.note: Asserts ontological categorization and inherence relation for rules, rights, and duties.

claims.claim: Secondary rules are meta-level continuants that define and coordinate dependencies among lower-level legal entities.
claims.source_quote: above these are meta-level continuants (secondary rules) that define and coordinate the dependencies among lower levels.
claims.note: Asserts ontological categorization and relational role of secondary rules.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition occupies the highest level as the organizing principle of the entire legal structure.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition occupies the highest level as the organizing principle of the entire structure.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological position and function of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: A new norm is created through an institutional process that realizes a secondary rule.
claims.source_quote: Generation: A new norm (N?) is created through an institutional process (P?) that realizes a secondary rule (R?).
claims.note: Asserts a generation/realization relation in norm ontology.

claims.claim: A norm becomes a legal fact when it is recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Validation: N? becomes a legal fact when it is recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition (R?).
claims.note: Asserts the condition under which a norm acquires the status of a legal fact.

claims.claim: A norm persists as long as the dependencies linking it to its institutional process, secondary rule, and rule of recognition remain coherent.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance: The norm persists as long as the dependencies linking N?, P?, R?, and R? remain coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition for norms in terms of dependency coherence.

claims.claim: When dependencies are broken, a norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.source_quote: Termination: When these dependencies are broken, through repeal, invalidation, or loss of recognition, the norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.note: Asserts a termination condition for norms' legal existence.

claims.claim: Social order arises from coherent recognition, obligation fulfillment, and institutional repair.
claims.source_quote: Social order is not imposed solely by coercion but arises from coherent recognition, obligation fulfillment, and institutional repair.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological sources/constituents of social order.

claims.claim: Social order is produced by sustained legal and moral structures.
claims.source_quote: produced by sustained legal and moral structures. Social order is not imposed solely by coercion but arises from coherent recognition, obligation fulfillment, and institutional repair.
claims.note: Asserts a productive/causal relation between legal/moral structures and social order.

claims.claim: Law is a relational, layered architecture of continuants, occurrents, and recognition structures.
claims.source_quote: An approach that understands law as a relational, layered architecture of continuants, occurrents, and recognition structures, rather than as a mere system of rules or commands.
claims.note: The definition of SOoL is the author's own ontological characterization of law's nature.

claims.claim: Law is not merely a system of rules or commands.
claims.source_quote: rather than as a mere system of rules or commands.
claims.note: Explicit denial of a reductive characterization, asserting what law is not.

claims.claim: Agent is a subkind of continuant.
claims.source_quote: law:Agent a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:Continuant .
claims.note: The OWL formalization expresses the author's endorsed ontological taxonomy; Agent is classified as a continuant.

claims.claim: Institution is a subkind of continuant.
claims.source_quote: law:Institution a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:Continuant ; rdfs:comment "Aggregated continuant composed of interrelated roles and norms."
claims.note: Ontological classification of Institution within BFO continuant hierarchy.

claims.claim: Institution is an aggregated continuant composed of interrelated roles and norms.
claims.source_quote: rdfs:comment "Aggregated continuant composed of interrelated roles and norms."
claims.note: The author's comment asserts the mereological/compositional structure of institutions.

claims.claim: Role is a subkind of realizable entity.
claims.source_quote: law:Role a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:RealizableEntity .
claims.note: Ontological classification of Role within BFO hierarchy.

claims.claim: Obligation is a subkind of dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: law:Obligation a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:DependentContinuant ;
claims.note: Ontological classification of Obligation within BFO hierarchy.

claims.claim: Obligation is a dependent continuant that constrains an agent's possible actions.
claims.source_quote: rdfs:comment "A dependent continuant that constrains an agent's possible actions."
claims.note: Author asserts the functional/dispositional property of obligations.

claims.claim: Recognition is a subkind of relational quality.
claims.source_quote: law:Recognition a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:RelationalQuality .
claims.note: Ontological classification of Recognition within BFO hierarchy.

claims.claim: RepairProcess is a subkind of process.
claims.source_quote: law:RepairProcess a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:Process .
claims.note: Ontological classification of RepairProcess within BFO hierarchy.

claims.claim: Agents bear roles.
claims.source_quote: law:bearsRole a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain law:Agent ; rdfs:range law:Role .
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between agents and roles as part of the endorsed ontology.

claims.claim: Institutions confer recognition on agents.
claims.source_quote: law:confersRecognition a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain law:Institution ; rdfs:range law:Agent .
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between institutions and agents.

claims.claim: Repair processes realize obligations.
claims.source_quote: law:realizesObligation a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain law:RepairProcess ; rdfs:range law:Obligation .
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between repair processes and obligations.

claims.claim: Agents sustain recognition of institutions.
claims.source_quote: law:sustainsRecognition a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain law:Agent ; rdfs:range law:Institution .
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between agents and institutions.

claims.claim: A Court of Law is an institution.
claims.source_quote: law:CourtOfLaw a law:Institution .
claims.note: Individual assertion: Court of Law is an instance of the Institution kind.

claims.claim: A Judge is an agent.
claims.source_quote: law:Judge a law:Agent .
claims.note: Individual assertion: Judge is an instance of the Agent kind.

claims.claim: Judicial Role is a role.
claims.source_quote: law:JudicialRole a law:Role .
claims.note: Individual assertion: JudicialRole is an instance of the Role kind.

claims.claim: Adjudication is a repair process.
claims.source_quote: law:Adjudication a law:RepairProcess .
claims.note: Individual assertion: Adjudication is an instance of the RepairProcess kind.

claims.claim: A judge bears the judicial role.
claims.source_quote: law:Judge law:bearsRole law:JudicialRole .
claims.note: Individual relational assertion between Judge and JudicialRole.

claims.claim: A Court of Law confers recognition on a judge.
claims.source_quote: law:CourtOfLaw law:confersRecognition law:Judge .
claims.note: Individual relational assertion between Court of Law and Judge.

claims.claim: Adjudication realizes legal obligation.
claims.source_quote: law:Adjudication law:realizesObligation law:LegalObligation .
claims.note: Individual relational assertion between Adjudication and LegalObligation.

claims.claim: Recognition, obligation, and repair are abstract relations expressible as computable entities.
claims.source_quote: showing how abstract relations (recognition, obligation, repair) become computable entities for simulation and verification.
claims.note: Author asserts these abstract relations have a computable entity status, implying ontological commitment to them as entities.

claims.claim: An object remains owned as long as the institutional relations defining ownership persist.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the object remains "owned" as long as the institutional relations that define ownership persist.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the conditions under which ownership exists.

claims.claim: Ownership ceases to exist when the registry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or enforcement of the owner's claim fails.
claims.source_quote: Only if recognition collapses, if the registry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim, does ownership cease to exist.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions under which ownership (an entity/relation) ceases to exist—an ontological claim about its persistence conditions.

claims.claim: Property has a dual being: a physical aspect and a legal aspect.
claims.source_quote: Theft thus illustrates the duality of property's being: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts that property has two distinct ontological aspects (physical and legal), a claim about property's nature.

claims.claim: The physical aspect of property can shift independently of its legal aspect.
claims.source_quote: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
