claims.note: Asserts a relation of independence between the physical and legal aspects of property—an ontological claim about their separability.

claims.claim: The legal aspect of property remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.source_quote: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts a property/disposition of the legal aspect of ownership regarding its persistence conditions.

claims.claim: Fraud involves the fabrication of recognition through false appearances.
claims.source_quote: Fraud introduces a subtler form of disruption: the fabrication of recognition through false appearances.
claims.note: Asserts what fraud is (its nature/function)—an ontological claim about a kind of entity/act.

claims.claim: Theft is intelligible as a legal concept because ownership is constituted by institutional relations.
claims.source_quote: is what makes theft intelligible as a legal concept. Ontologically, the object remains "owned" as long as the institutional relations that define ownership persist.
claims.note: Implies that the institutional constitution of ownership grounds theft's legal intelligibility—an ontological claim about the grounding relation, though partly inferential.

claims.claim: Social order arises from coherent recognition, obligation fulfillment, and institutional repair.
claims.source_quote: Social order is not imposed solely by coercion but arises from coherent recognition, obligation fulfillment, and institutional repair.
claims.note: Asserts that social order has specific constitutive sources/properties, an ontological claim about what produces social order.

claims.claim: Social order is not imposed solely by coercion.
claims.source_quote: Social order is not imposed solely by coercion but arises from coherent recognition, obligation fulfillment, and institutional repair.
claims.note: Asserts a property (or lack thereof) of social order — that coercion alone does not constitute it.

claims.claim: Law is a relational, layered architecture of continuants, occurrents, and recognition structures.
claims.source_quote: An approach that understands law as a relational, layered architecture of continuants, occurrents, and recognition structures, rather than as a mere system of rules or commands.
claims.note: The author's own structural ontology of law (SOoL) is defined here as a positive ontological characterization of what law is.

claims.claim: A legal Agent is a kind of Continuant.
claims.source_quote: law:Agent a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:Continuant .
claims.note: Subkind assertion: Agent is classified as a subclass of Continuant in the author's own ontology.

claims.claim: A legal Institution is a kind of Continuant.
claims.source_quote: law:Institution a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:Continuant ; rdfs:comment "Aggregated continuant composed of interrelated roles and norms."
claims.note: Subkind assertion: Institution is a subclass of Continuant.

claims.claim: A legal Institution is an aggregated continuant composed of interrelated roles and norms.
claims.source_quote: rdfs:comment "Aggregated continuant composed of interrelated roles and norms."
claims.note: Asserts a structural property/composition of Institution in the author's ontology.

claims.claim: A legal Role is a kind of RealizableEntity.
claims.source_quote: law:Role a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:RealizableEntity .
claims.note: Subkind assertion: Role is a subclass of RealizableEntity.

claims.claim: A legal Obligation is a kind of DependentContinuant.
claims.source_quote: law:Obligation a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:DependentContinuant ; rdfs:comment "A dependent continuant that constrains an agent's possible actions."
claims.note: Subkind assertion: Obligation is a subclass of DependentContinuant.

claims.claim: A legal Obligation constrains an agent's possible actions.
claims.source_quote: rdfs:comment "A dependent continuant that constrains an agent's possible actions."
claims.note: Asserts a functional/dispositional property of Obligation in the author's ontology.

claims.claim: Legal Recognition is a kind of RelationalQuality.
claims.source_quote: law:Recognition a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:RelationalQuality .
claims.note: Subkind assertion: Recognition is a subclass of RelationalQuality.

claims.claim: A legal RepairProcess is a kind of Process.
claims.source_quote: law:RepairProcess a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:Process .
claims.note: Subkind assertion: RepairProcess is a subclass of Process.

claims.claim: An Agent bears a Role.
claims.source_quote: law:bearsRole a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain law:Agent ; rdfs:range law:Role .
claims.note: Asserts a relational structure between Agent and Role in the author's ontology.

claims.claim: An Institution confers Recognition on an Agent.
claims.source_quote: law:confersRecognition a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain law:Institution ; rdfs:range law:Agent .
claims.note: Asserts a relational structure between Institution and Agent via recognition.

claims.claim: A RepairProcess realizes an Obligation.
claims.source_quote: law:realizesObligation a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain law:RepairProcess ; rdfs:range law:Obligation .
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between RepairProcess and Obligation.

claims.claim: An Agent sustains an Institution.
claims.source_quote: law:sustainsRecognition a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain law:Agent ; rdfs:range law:Institution .
claims.note: Asserts a relational property: agents sustain institutions through recognition.

claims.claim: A CourtOfLaw is a legal Institution.
claims.source_quote: law:CourtOfLaw a law:Institution .
claims.note: Individual assertion: CourtOfLaw is an instance of the Institution kind.

claims.claim: A Judge is a legal Agent.
claims.source_quote: law:Judge a law:Agent .
claims.note: Individual assertion: Judge is an instance of the Agent kind.

claims.claim: A JudicialRole is a legal Role.
claims.source_quote: law:JudicialRole a law:Role .
claims.note: Individual assertion: JudicialRole is an instance of the Role kind.

claims.claim: Adjudication is a legal RepairProcess.
claims.source_quote: law:Adjudication a law:RepairProcess .
claims.note: Individual assertion: Adjudication is an instance of the RepairProcess kind.

claims.claim: A Judge bears a JudicialRole.
claims.source_quote: law:Judge law:bearsRole law:JudicialRole .
claims.note: Asserts a specific relational fact between the individual Judge and JudicialRole.

claims.claim: A CourtOfLaw confers Recognition on a Judge.
claims.source_quote: law:CourtOfLaw law:confersRecognition law:Judge .
claims.note: Asserts a specific relational fact between CourtOfLaw and Judge.

claims.claim: Adjudication realizes a LegalObligation.
claims.source_quote: law:Adjudication law:realizesObligation law:LegalObligation .
claims.note: Asserts a specific realization relation between Adjudication and LegalObligation.

claims.claim: Recognition, obligation, and repair are abstract relations in law that can be formalized as computable entities.
claims.source_quote: showing how abstract relations (recognition, obligation, repair) become computable entities for simulation and verification.
claims.note: Asserts that these relations have a computable/entity status; author endorses this characterization as part of the structural ontology.

claims.claim: Social order is produced by sustained legal and moral structures.
claims.source_quote: produced by sustained legal and moral structures.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive relation between legal/moral structures and social order.

claims.claim: A legal norm becomes a legal fact when recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Validation: N? becomes a legal fact when it is recognized by other institutions in accordance with the rule of recognition (R?).
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about what makes something a legal fact—a recognition relation.

claims.claim: A legal norm persists as long as its dependencies among norm, process, primary rule, and secondary rule remain coherent.
claims.source_quote: Maintenance: The norm persists as long as the dependencies linking N?, P?, R?, and R? remain coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition grounded in ontological dependencies—a property of legal norms.

claims.claim: A legal norm ceases to exist when its dependencies are broken through repeal, invalidation, or loss of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Termination: When these dependencies are broken, through repeal, invalidation, or loss of recognition, the norm ceases to exist as a legal continuant.
claims.note: Asserts a termination condition for a kind of entity (legal continuant).

claims.claim: Law's validity is a dynamic equilibrium sustained by ontological dependencies among rules and institutions.
claims.source_quote: law's validity is a dynamic equilibrium sustained by ontological dependencies among rules and institutions.
claims.note: Author asserts this in his own voice as what Hart intuited; a property of law's validity.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the organizing principle that coordinates dependencies across the legal system's processes.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition is the organizing principle that coordinates these dependencies across the system's processes of creation, adjudication, and change.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the metaphysical condition of legality itself.
claims.source_quote: the rule of recognition is not merely a sociological convention but the metaphysical condition of legality itself.
claims.note: Author asserts this positively—a property/role claim about the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the structure that allows law to exist as a self-identifying domain of reality.
claims.source_quote: It is the structure that allows law to exist as a self-identifying domain of reality, a world of norms sustained by recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a structural role of the rule of recognition in constituting law's existence.

claims.claim: The authority of the rule of recognition derives from ontological coherence, not force or moral obligation.
claims.source_quote: Its authority derives not from force or moral obligation but from ontological coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property (source of authority) of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: When the rule of recognition collapses, law disintegrates.
claims.source_quote: When the rule of recognition collapses, when institutions no longer share a unified structure of validation, law disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: law's existence depends on the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: A constitutional crisis is the dissolution of the meta-structure that sustains legal being.
claims.source_quote: This is the ontological meaning of A constitutional crisis: the dissolution of the meta-structure that sustains legal being.
claims.note: Asserts what a constitutional crisis is—an ontological identity claim about a kind of event.

claims.claim: The restoration of law occurs when a new rule of recognition emerges.
claims.source_quote: the restoration of law occurs when a new rule of recognition emerges, reorganizing the dependencies that define the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a condition for law's re-existence—an ontological dependency claim.

claims.claim: Law's reality consists in the dependencies that bind its rules together, not in the commands it issues.
claims.source_quote: It implies that law's reality consists not in the commands it issues but in the dependencies that bind its rules together.
claims.note: Author endorses this as what Hart's distinction implies—an ontological claim about the nature of law.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is the meta-structure that embodies the highest level of ontological dependence in the legal world.
claims.source_quote: The rule of recognition, as meta-structure, embodies the highest level of ontological dependence in the legal world.
claims.note: Asserts a property and role of the rule of recognition within the ontological hierarchy.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.source_quote: it is law's principle of unity and persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/ontological role of the rule of recognition.

claims.claim: Law is an evolving ontological system: a network of roles, rules, and processes that continually realizes itself through maintenance of dependencies.
claims.source_quote: we can see law as an evolving ontological system: a network of roles, rules, and processes that continually realizes itself through the maintenance of its dependencies.
claims.note: Author asserts this as the result of modeling law in these terms—a kind claim about law.

claims.claim: A fact-making failure occurs when the dependencies required for the existence of a legal fact are not satisfied.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, a fact-making failure occurs when the dependencies required for the existence of a legal fact are not satisfied, or when incompatible dependencies coexist without repair.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological condition defining a kind of failure event.

claims.claim: A fact-making failure corresponds to a breakdown in the chain linking occurrents to dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: In the Basic Formal Ontology framework, this corresponds to a breakdown in the chain that links occurrents (procedural events) to dependent continuants (recognized relations and statuses).
claims.note: Asserts a relational breakdown between ontological categories as the nature of fact-making failure.

claims.claim: A pseudo-entity is an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The result is a pseudo-entity: an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of a kind (pseudo-entity) and its defining property.

claims.claim: Law's existence is continuously contingent on the proper functioning of its institutional and relational machinery.
claims.source_quote: law's existence is neither metaphysically secure nor automatically self-sustaining, but continuously contingent on the proper functioning of its institutional and relational machinery.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency property of law's existence.

claims.claim: Ownership ceases to exist when institutional maintenance fails.
claims.source_quote: only when the registry is destroyed, the legal order disintegrates, or the system ceases to enforce the owner's claim, does ownership cease to exist.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the conditions under which a kind of entity (ownership) ceases to exist.

claims.claim: Theft shifts property's physical aspect while its legal aspect remains constant.
claims.source_quote: Theft thus illustrates the duality of property's being: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts a property/quality of ownership under theft: the duality of physical and legal aspects.

claims.claim: Property has a physical aspect and a legal aspect.
claims.source_quote: Theft thus illustrates the duality of property's being: its physical aspect may shift, but its legal aspect remains constant until institutional maintenance fails.
claims.note: Asserts that property (as a kind of entity) has two distinct aspects.

claims.claim: A forged deed or fraudulent registration generates a spurious dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: A forged deed, counterfeit document, or fraudulent registration generates what might be called a spurious dependent continuant, an entity that mimics the structure of ownership but lacks ontological grounding within legitimate recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of a spurious dependent continuant produced by fraud; hedged slightly by 'what might be called' but the ontological commitment is made.

claims.claim: A spurious dependent continuant mimics ownership but lacks ontological grounding in legitimate recognition.
claims.source_quote: an entity that mimics the structure of ownership but lacks ontological grounding within legitimate recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the spurious dependent continuant: it lacks ontological grounding.

claims.claim: Fraudulent ownership persists as an apparent fact within the institutional system while institutions are deceived.
claims.source_quote: For as long as institutions are deceived, the fraudulent ownership persists as an apparent fact within the system.
claims.note: Asserts a temporal property of fraudulent ownership entities.

claims.claim: Discovery of fraud annihilates the false continuant and restores proper dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Once discovered, the repair process annihilates this false continuant, restoring coherence by reestablishing the proper dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts what happens to the spurious continuant entity upon discovery: it is annihilated.

claims.claim: Destruction of registries or falsification of records fragments the recognition network that sustains ownership.
claims.source_quote: When a registry is destroyed in war, or when a corrupt bureaucracy falsifies records, the network of recognition that sustains ownership becomes fragmented.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/relational outcome: the recognition network (an entity) becomes fragmented.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt is a condition in which multiple incompatible ownership claims coexist without resolution.
claims.source_quote: The result is contradiction debt: multiple, incompatible ownership claims coexisting without resolution.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of a kind of condition ('contradiction debt') and characterizes it.

claims.claim: Property functions as a stabilizing relational structure.
claims.source_quote: property ceases to serve its function as a stabilizing relational structure.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of property as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Post-conflict registry reconstruction constitutes ontological repair.
claims.source_quote: Post-conflict reconstruction efforts frequently begin with reconstituting registries and reaffirming property rights, for these are not merely economic necessities but acts of ontological repair, the restoration of the world's coherence through the reweaving of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts that registry reconstruction is an act of ontological repair, not merely economic.

claims.claim: Institutions perform the function of transitive recognition in succession and inheritance.
claims.source_quote: institutions perform the function of transitive recognition, transferring ownership dependencies from one bearer to another without breaking coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of institutions as entities.

claims.claim: Recognition survives its individual bearers because it is distributed across institutional systems.
claims.source_quote: The continuity of ownership through death or dissolution is a triumph of institutional ontology: recognition survives its bearers because it is distributed across systems rather than confined to individuals.
claims.note: Asserts a property of recognition: its distribution across systems enables persistence beyond individuals.

claims.claim: The legal entity (estate, trust, corporation) is a continuant of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The legal entity itself - the estate, trust, or corporation - acts as a continuant of recognition, absorbing and transmitting ownership through time.
claims.note: Asserts that legal entities are (a subkind of) continuants of recognition.

claims.claim: Institutions are ontological infrastructures.
claims.source_quote: Institutions are not merely procedural devices but ontological infrastructures. They hold together the web of dependent continuants that constitute the legal world.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological kind/role of institutions.

claims.claim: Institutions hold together the web of dependent continuants that constitute the legal world.
claims.source_quote: They hold together the web of dependent continuants that constitute the legal world.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/functional role of institutions with respect to dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The legal world is constituted by a web of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: They hold together the web of dependent continuants that constitute the legal world.
claims.note: Asserts the composition of the legal world as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: The persistence of property is a measure of the health of the institutions that sustain it.
claims.source_quote: The persistence of property, therefore, is a measure of the health of the institutions that sustain it.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between property persistence and institutional health.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: If property is a relational continuant sustained by recognition, then the commons represents a higher-order form of that same ontological pattern
claims.note: Though embedded in a conditional, the author endorses this as the established position being built upon.

claims.claim: The commons is a higher-order form of the same ontological pattern as property.
claims.source_quote: the commons represents a higher-order form of that same ontological pattern, one in which ownership is distributed, and the field of recognition extends beyond individual bearers.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind/relation of commons to property.

claims.claim: The commons is not the negation of property but its generalization.
claims.source_quote: The commons is not the negation of property but its generalization.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological relation between commons and property.

claims.claim: The commons emerges when the owner-object-institution relation expands to include a community as primary bearer of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It emerges when the relation linking owner, object, and institution expands to include a community or collective as the primary bearer of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a condition for the existence of the commons as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: In the commons, the ownership relation inheres in a collective role rather than an individual agent.
claims.source_quote: In the commons, by contrast, the ownership relation inheres in a collective role, a distributed continuant whose realization requires coordinated recognition among multiple agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts the bearer structure of the ownership relation in commons regimes.

claims.claim: The collective role in commons is a distributed continuant.
claims.source_quote: the ownership relation inheres in a collective role, a distributed continuant whose realization requires coordinated recognition among multiple agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of the collective role entity.

claims.claim: The collective role functions as a bearer of rights and obligations not reducible to the sum of its participants.
claims.source_quote: This collective role (e.g., 'citizen,' 'member,' 'user') functions as a bearer of rights and obligations not reducible to the sum of its participants.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the collective role entity.

claims.claim: In the commons, recognition attaches to a shared institutional identity through which individuals participate, not to individuals directly.
claims.source_quote: recognition no longer attaches to individuals directly but to a shared institutional identity through which individuals participate.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of recognition in commons regimes.

claims.claim: The dependent continuant 'public ownership' inheres in the collective institution of the polity.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuant 'public ownership' inheres in the collective institution of the polity, realized through procedures of management, funding, and protection.
claims.note: Asserts the bearer relation of a specific dependent continuant (public ownership).

claims.claim: The commons is a recognitional field rather than a discrete relation.
claims.source_quote: The commons is thus a recognitional field rather than a discrete relation.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind/nature of the commons.

claims.claim: The commons triad links Owner (collective role), Object (shared resource), and Institution (recognizing structure) as mutually dependent.
claims.source_quote: This relational structure can be modeled ontologically as a triadic dependency linking Owner (collective role), Object (shared resource), and Institution (recognizing structure). Each component depends on the others for existence.
claims.note: Asserts mutual ontological dependencies among the three poles of the commons triad.

claims.claim: The collective owner role cannot exist without institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: The collective owner role cannot exist without institutional recognition; the institution cannot realize its function without the resource; and the resource becomes 'common' only when recognized as such by the institution.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency relation between collective owner role and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: An institution cannot realize its function without the shared resource.
claims.source_quote: the institution cannot realize its function without the resource
claims.note: Asserts a dependency of the institution on the resource for functional realization.

claims.claim: A resource becomes 'common' only when recognized as such by the institution.
claims.source_quote: the resource becomes 'common' only when recognized as such by the institution.
claims.note: Asserts the condition under which a resource acquires the property of being common.

claims.claim: The commons is a positive ontological form, an organized structure of collective recognition.
claims.source_quote: the commons is not merely the absence of private ownership but a positive ontological form, an organized structure of collective recognition that defines how certain entities exist as shared rather than exclusive.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of the commons as a positive, organized structure.

claims.claim: In ordinary ownership, the property relation inheres jointly in an individual agent and an institutional continuant.
claims.source_quote: In ordinary ownership, the property relation inheres jointly in an individual agent and an institutional continuant, with a specific object as its third pole.
claims.note: Asserts the bearer structure of the property relation in private ownership.

claims.claim: Law's broader metaphysical function is the stabilization of social being through management of relational continuity.
claims.source_quote: law's capacity to maintain ownership demonstrates its broader metaphysical function: the stabilization of social being through the management of relational continuity.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of law as an entity.

claims.claim: Misrecognition produces a false positive: a dependent continuant instantiated without necessary structural support.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this produces a false positive: a dependent continuant (the supposed legal fact) instantiated without the necessary structural support.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the product of misrecognition as a dependent continuant without proper grounding.

claims.claim: Misrecognition creates ontologically unstable entities that exist in a state of suspended legitimacy.
claims.source_quote: Such misrecognition creates entities that are ontologically unstable, they exist in a state of suspended legitimacy, subject to annulment or correction once the error is discovered.
claims.note: Asserts a property (ontological instability, suspended legitimacy) of entities created by misrecognition.

claims.claim: In epistemic error, the fact exists but our understanding is mistaken; in ontological defect, the fact fails to exist.
claims.source_quote: In epistemic error, the fact exists, but our understanding of it is mistaken; in ontological defect, the fact itself fails to exist within the legal field.
claims.note: Asserts a distinction between two kinds of failure, with ontological claims about existence in each case.

claims.claim: When an impostor signs a contract, the necessary dependencies of intention, authority, and recognized identity are absent.
claims.source_quote: Yet the necessary dependencies (intention, authority, and recognized identity) are absent. The act does not instantiate a genuine legal obligation, even if it temporarily appears to.
claims.note: Asserts that certain dependency relations are absent, making the entity a non-being.

claims.claim: An impostor's signing of a contract does not instantiate a genuine legal obligation.
claims.source_quote: The act does not instantiate a genuine legal obligation, even if it temporarily appears to. It is not merely voidable but void: a non-being clothed in the appearance of law.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the non-existence of a legal obligation in this case.

claims.claim: Misrecognition is an act that generates entities without the dependencies required for their persistence.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition, then, is the ontological equivalent of a false creation, an act that generates entities without the dependencies required for their persistence.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of misrecognition as a kind of entity-generating act lacking proper dependency grounding.

claims.claim: Fraudulent entities are dependent continuants without proper grounding.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, such entities are dependent continuants without proper grounding: they borrow their apparent being from genuine institutional processes but lack alignment with the system's rule of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation and a property: fraudulent entities are a kind of dependent continuant lacking proper grounding.

claims.claim: Fraudulent entities borrow their apparent being from genuine institutional processes.
claims.source_quote: they borrow their apparent being from genuine institutional processes but lack alignment with the system's rule of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between fraudulent entities and genuine institutional processes.

claims.claim: Once fraud is exposed, no legal entity ever truly existed.
claims.source_quote: Once exposed, their recognition collapses, revealing that no legal entity ever truly existed.
claims.note: Asserts that the fraudulent entity's existence was always null, an ontological claim about non-being.

claims.claim: Nullification of fraud is an ontological repair restoring coherence in the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The nullification of fraud, therefore, is not merely a moral correction but an ontological repair: the restoration of coherence in the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that nullification has the ontological role/function of repair and coherence restoration.

claims.claim: During fraud, the system temporarily tolerates zones of incoherence in which contradictory dependencies coexist.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, these moments constitute temporary zones of incoherence in which contradiction is tolerated.
claims.note: Asserts a property of certain temporal states within the legal ontological field.

claims.claim: Jurisdictional voids are cases of non-recognition, not misrecognition.
claims.source_quote: These are not cases of misrecognition but of non-recognition, situations in which brute events that could be legally significant occur outside any established field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a categorical distinction between two kinds of ontological failure.

claims.claim: Acts in jurisdictional voids exist in a liminal state of recognitional indeterminacy between legality and non-being.
claims.source_quote: They exist in a liminal state between legality and non-being, a condition we might call recognitional indeterminacy.
claims.note: Author names and characterizes a state of recognitional indeterminacy; slightly hedged by 'we might call' but the ontological characterization is asserted.

claims.claim: Recognition is always localized within a network of institutions defining territorial or functional domains.
claims.source_quote: Recognition is always localized within a network of institutions that define territorial or functional domains.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of recognition: its localization within institutional networks.

claims.claim: When institutional domains fail to overlap or are contested, the ontological field of law fragments.
claims.source_quote: When these domains fail to overlap or are contested, the ontological field of law fragments.
claims.note: Asserts a property/consequence of institutional fragmentation on the ontological field of law.

claims.claim: Establishing new legal spaces is an act of ontological reconstruction.
claims.source_quote: Creating new legal spaces is an act of ontological reconstruction, it establishes the boundaries within which recognition can once again attach to brute facts.
claims.note: Asserts a role/function for the creation of new legal spaces: ontological reconstruction.

claims.claim: Misrecognition corrupts the referential alignment between recognition and its object.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition corrupts the referential alignment between recognition and its object; fraud subverts the dependency structure itself; jurisdictional voids eliminate the conditions of recognition altogether.
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological property/effect of misrecognition on the recognition relation.

claims.claim: Fraud subverts the dependency structure of legal fact-making.
claims.source_quote: fraud subverts the dependency structure itself
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological effect of fraud on dependency structures.

claims.claim: Jurisdictional voids eliminate the conditions of recognition altogether.
claims.source_quote: jurisdictional voids eliminate the conditions of recognition altogether.
claims.note: Asserts that jurisdictional voids destroy the preconditions for recognition to exist.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt is a state in which the system's dependencies are violated but not yet repaired.
claims.source_quote: What unites them is the presence of contradiction debt: a state in which the system's dependencies are violated but not yet repaired.
claims.note: Defines and asserts the existence and nature of contradiction debt as an ontological state.

claims.claim: Unresolved contradiction debt accumulates, leading to systemic fragility and eventual collapse.
claims.source_quote: If left unresolved, such debt accumulates, leading to systemic fragility and eventual collapse.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/dispositional property of unresolved contradiction debt.

claims.claim: Procedural correctness is an ontological, not merely formal, requirement for legal facts.
claims.source_quote: Anomalies in fact-making also clarify why procedural correctness is an ontological, not merely formal, requirement.
claims.note: Asserts a property of procedural correctness: it is ontologically necessary, not merely conventional.

claims.claim: Procedural errors are breaches in the chain of recognition that sustains law's being.
claims.source_quote: Procedural errors are not trivial technicalities but breaches in the chain of recognition that sustains law's being.
claims.note: Asserts what procedural errors are (a kind of breach) and what recognition does (sustains law's being).

claims.claim: A judgment rendered without jurisdiction cannot exist as a valid legal entity.
claims.source_quote: A judgment rendered without jurisdiction, even if substantively just, cannot exist as a valid legal entity because it fails to satisfy its dependency conditions.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the non-existence of a particular kind of legal entity.

claims.claim: A contract without consent lacks the recognition necessary to instantiate obligation.
claims.source_quote: Similarly, a contract without consent lacks the recognition necessary to instantiate obligation.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: consent is necessary for recognition, which in turn instantiates obligation.

claims.claim: The act of correction modifies the structure of recognition in the present, redefining which entities are valid continuants.
claims.source_quote: The act of correction does not travel backward in time to undo the brute events; rather, it modifies the structure of recognition in the present, redefining which entities are acknowledged as valid continuants.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological mechanism and effect of legal correction acts.

claims.claim: Once a fraudulent deed is annulled, its dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) are extinguished.
claims.source_quote: The fraudulent deed, once annulled, remains as a historical artifact, a record of misrecognition, but its dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) are extinguished.
claims.note: Asserts that annulment extinguishes specific dependent continuants; ontological claim about the cessation of legal entities.

claims.claim: Law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality.
claims.source_quote: In this way, law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality: what once seemed real may persist as record but not as law.
claims.note: Asserts a structural distinction within law's ontology between two different modes of persistence.

claims.claim: A pseudo-entity is an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The result is a pseudo-entity: an apparent legal fact that lacks ontological integrity within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Defines and asserts the existence of pseudo-entities as a kind of apparent legal fact with a specific lack.

claims.claim: A fraudulent deed, once annulled, persists as a historical artifact and record of misrecognition.
claims.source_quote: fraudulent deed, once annulled, remains as a historical artifact, a record of misrecognition
claims.note: Asserts a property/mode of persistence of an annulled fraudulent deed as a historical artifact.

claims.claim: Annulment extinguishes the dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) of a fraudulent deed.
claims.source_quote: its dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) are extinguished
claims.note: Asserts that ownership, rights, and obligations are dependent continuants and that they cease to exist upon annulment.

claims.claim: Ownership, rights, and obligations are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: its dependent continuants (ownership, rights, obligations) are extinguished
claims.note: Asserts a subkind/category relation: ownership, rights, obligations are kinds of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality.
claims.source_quote: law distinguishes between ontological history and institutional reality: what once seemed real may persist as record but not as law
claims.note: Asserts a property of law: that it makes a distinction between two ontological domains.

claims.claim: What once seemed institutionally real may persist as record without persisting as law.
claims.source_quote: what once seemed real may persist as record but not as law
claims.note: Asserts a property distinguishing record-existence from legal existence.

claims.claim: Sufficiently widespread recognition generates its own coherence even when born in contradiction.
claims.source_quote: Recognition, once widespread enough, generates its own coherence, even if born in contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/generative property of recognition: it produces coherence once it reaches a threshold of breadth.

claims.claim: Law can extend its ontology to encompass irregularities such as fraudulent elections or unauthorized tribunals.
claims.source_quote: law adapts by extending its ontology to encompass these irregularities
claims.note: Asserts that law has an ontology and that this ontology has the property of being extendable to include anomalies.

claims.claim: Unauthorized tribunals can acquire de facto recognition.
claims.source_quote: unauthorized tribunals gain de facto recognition
claims.note: Asserts a possible relational property (de facto recognition) that unauthorized tribunals can bear; author presents this as a real case, not merely hypothetical.

claims.claim: Property is a dependent continuant relating an object to an owner.
claims.source_quote: Property is modelled as a dependent continuant relating an object to an owner and sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the kind and relational structure of property.

claims.claim: Property is sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Property is modelled as a dependent continuant relating an object to an owner and sustained by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Institutions recognize and maintain property relations.
claims.source_quote: Institutions recognize and maintain property relations while conferring ownership roles on agents or collectives.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational role of institutions with respect to property.

claims.claim: Institutions confer ownership roles on agents or collectives.
claims.source_quote: Institutions recognize and maintain property relations while conferring ownership roles on agents or collectives.
claims.note: Asserts that institutions bear the function of conferring ownership roles.

claims.claim: In commons regimes, ownership is a higher-order collective role.
claims.source_quote: In commons regimes, ownership functions as a higher-order collective role realized through distributed recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property/role of ownership specifically in commons regimes.

claims.claim: In commons regimes, ownership is realized through distributed recognition.
claims.source_quote: In commons regimes, ownership functions as a higher-order collective role realized through distributed recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between collective ownership and distributed recognition.

claims.claim: Both private property and commons are sustained by the same dependency pattern.
claims.source_quote: Both are sustained by the same dependency pattern, but the commons introduces an additional level of abstraction.
claims.note: Asserts a shared ontological dependency structure across two kinds of property.

claims.claim: In the commons, the collective role replaces the individual agent as bearer of ownership.
claims.source_quote: The commons introduces an additional level of abstraction: the collective role replaces the individual agent as bearer of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a structural difference in the bearer of the ownership role in the commons.

claims.claim: Recognition sustaining the commons is distributed across citizens, institutions, and juridical entities.
claims.source_quote: The recognition that sustains this relation is therefore multi-layered, distributed across citizens, institutions, and juridical entities.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the recognition relation in the commons: its distributed, multi-layered character.

claims.claim: The commons is an extension of property's ontological logic to collective bearers.
claims.source_quote: The commons is thus not a deviation from property but an extension of its ontological logic to collective bearers.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological continuity/extension relation between property and the commons.

claims.claim: A river can exist as private, state, or common property depending on the structure of recognition attached to it.
claims.source_quote: A river, for example, can exist as private property, state property, or common property depending on the structure of recognition that attaches to it.
claims.note: Asserts that the ontological status of an object is determined by recognition structure.

claims.claim: Private property is a relation between one agent and the state.
claims.source_quote: As private property, it is a relation between one agent and the state.
claims.note: Asserts a relational ontological structure for private property.

claims.claim: State property is a relation between a public institution and the collective of citizens.
claims.source_quote: As state property, it is a relation between a public institution and the collective of citizens.
claims.note: Asserts a relational ontological structure for state property.

claims.claim: Common property is a relation among citizens themselves, mediated by institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: As common property, it is a relation among the citizens themselves, mediated by institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relational ontological structure for common property.

claims.claim: The ontological status of an object shifts as recognition is redistributed.
claims.source_quote: The object remains the same in its material aspect, but its ontological status shifts as recognition is redistributed.
claims.note: Asserts that ontological status is a function of recognition distribution, not material constitution.

claims.claim: Ownership is not an attribute of objects but a relational configuration within a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: These transformations reveal that ownership is not an attribute of objects but a relational configuration within a system of recognition, an architecture of dependencies subject to institutional articulation.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature of ownership.

claims.claim: Ownership is an architecture of dependencies subject to institutional articulation.
claims.source_quote: Ownership is not an attribute of objects but a relational configuration within a system of recognition, an architecture of dependencies subject to institutional articulation.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/dispositional property of ownership.

claims.claim: The commons is inherently dynamic.
claims.source_quote: This multiplicity makes the commons inherently dynamic.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the commons as an ontological kind.

claims.claim: The coherence of the commons depends on ongoing maintenance, legislation, governance, and participation.
claims.source_quote: Its coherence depends on ongoing maintenance, legislation, governance, and participation, that continually reaffirms its structure.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between the commons' coherence and ongoing institutional activity.

claims.claim: Without maintenance, the commons devolves into privatization or anarchy.
claims.source_quote: Without such maintenance, the commons devolves into either privatization (when recognition contracts to individuals) or anarchy (when recognition dissolves entirely).
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional/causal property of the commons regarding its dissolution conditions.

claims.claim: The commons occupies a delicate ontological equilibrium between inclusion and fragmentation.
claims.source_quote: The commons thus occupies a delicate ontological equilibrium between inclusion and fragmentation.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/positional ontological property of the commons.

claims.claim: Open-source software, creative commons licensing, and public data repositories are expressions of collective ownership realized through distributed recognition.
claims.source_quote: Open-source software, creative commons licensing, and public data repositories are contemporary expressions of collective ownership realized through distributed recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that these digital entities instantiate collective ownership realized via distributed recognition.

claims.claim: In digital commons, the institutional continuant is often minimal, such as a license text or shared protocol.
claims.source_quote: In these contexts, the institutional continuant is often minimal, sometimes no more than a license text or shared protocol.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the institutional continuant in digital commons contexts.

claims.claim: The network of recognition among users and contributors sustains the property relation in digital commons.
claims.source_quote: The network of recognition among users and contributors sustains the property relation.
claims.note: Asserts a sustaining dependency relation between recognition network and property relation.

claims.claim: An open-source license is an information artifact encoding the conditions of recognition.
claims.source_quote: The open-source license, for example, functions as an information artifact encoding the conditions of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind (information artifact) and function of an open-source license.

claims.claim: In digital commons, recognition is mediated by digital infrastructure rather than centralized authority.
claims.source_quote: Here, the commons is not merely public but networked: recognition is mediated by digital infrastructure rather than centralized authority.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property distinguishing digital commons in terms of the mediator of recognition.

claims.claim: The 'tragedy of the commons' is a breakdown of collective recognition.
claims.source_quote: The so-called 'tragedy of the commons' is, in ontological terms, a breakdown of collective recognition: when individual actions cease to align with the shared dependencies that define common ownership, the property relation disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological characterization of the tragedy of the commons as recognition breakdown.

claims.claim: When individual actions cease to align with shared dependencies of common ownership, the property relation disintegrates.
claims.source_quote: When individual actions cease to align with the shared dependencies that define common ownership, the property relation disintegrates.
claims.note: Asserts a conditional ontological claim about the dissolution of property relations.

claims.claim: Successful commons management depends on the resilience of its recognition network.
claims.source_quote: Successful commons management, whether ecological or digital, depends on the resilience of its recognition network, the capacity of its institutions to maintain coherence among distributed bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between commons management success and recognition network resilience.

claims.claim: In private property, the ownership relation is individualized and exclusive.
claims.source_quote: In private property, the relation is individualized and exclusive; in the commons, it is collective and inclusive.
claims.note: Asserts properties of the ownership relation in private property.

claims.claim: In the commons, the ownership relation is collective and inclusive.
claims.source_quote: In private property, the relation is individualized and exclusive; in the commons, it is collective and inclusive.
claims.note: Asserts properties of the ownership relation in the commons.

claims.claim: Law's reality is not material but relational.
claims.source_quote: Both forms demonstrate that law's reality is not material but relational: the world of ownership, whether private or public, exists only insofar as recognition persists.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature of legal reality.

claims.claim: The world of ownership exists only insofar as recognition persists.
claims.source_quote: The world of ownership, whether private or public, exists only insofar as recognition persists.
claims.note: Asserts an existence-dependency relation between ownership and recognition.

claims.claim: The commons is a mode of being in which recognition becomes the shared object of care.
claims.source_quote: The commons, in its highest sense, is law's acknowledgment of interdependence, a mode of being in which recognition itself becomes the shared object of care.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological characterization of the commons; slightly metaphorical but the author plainly endorses it as an ontological description.

claims.claim: Law can stabilize itself by incorporating its own anomalies, turning exceptions into new norms.
claims.source_quote: law can stabilize itself by incorporating its own anomalies, turning exceptions into new norms.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about law's capacity and its property of self-stabilization through anomaly incorporation.

claims.claim: Law's ontology is historically plastic despite being formally structured.
claims.source_quote: The transformation of unconstitutional acts into legitimate precedents illustrates how law's ontology, while formally structured, remains historically plastic.
claims.note: Asserts a property (historical plasticity) of law's ontology.

claims.claim: The field of recognition is self-referential and adaptive.
claims.source_quote: The field of recognition is self-referential and adaptive; it can reconstitute coherence even from initial incoherence.
claims.note: Asserts properties (self-referential, adaptive) of the field of recognition as an entity.

claims.claim: The field of recognition can reconstitute coherence even from initial incoherence.
claims.source_quote: The field of recognition is self-referential and adaptive; it can reconstitute coherence even from initial incoherence.
claims.note: Asserts a functional capacity of the field of recognition.

claims.claim: Fact-making failures and anomalies perform a diagnostic function within legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: Fact-making failures and anomalies thus perform a diagnostic function within legal ontology.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of fact-making failures and anomalies within legal ontology.

claims.claim: Validity requires proper referential grounding.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition shows that validity requires proper referential grounding
claims.note: The author endorses this as a condition for validity, revealed by the case of misrecognition.

claims.claim: The appearance of recognition is not sufficient for validity without structural coherence.
claims.source_quote: fraud shows that the appearance of recognition is not sufficient without structural coherence
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for validity—structural coherence beyond mere appearance.

claims.claim: Law's ontology depends on a spatial and institutional field capable of sustaining recognition.
claims.source_quote: jurisdictional voids show that law's ontology depends on the existence of a spatial and institutional field capable of sustaining recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: law's ontology depends on a spatial and institutional field.

claims.claim: Law is a network of dependencies that can fray, repair, and evolve.
claims.source_quote: law, though systematic, remains a living structure, a network of dependencies that can fray, repair, and evolve.
claims.note: Asserts that law is a network of dependencies—an ontological characterization with properties.

claims.claim: Law has the ability to absorb contradiction and reconstruct coherence without abandoning its ontological foundation.
claims.source_quote: its ability to absorb contradiction and reconstruct coherence without abandoning its ontological foundation.
claims.note: Asserts a disposition/capacity of law as an entity.

claims.claim: Law's reality is not merely prescriptive but performative.
claims.source_quote: these anomalies demonstrate that law's reality is not merely prescriptive but performative.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law's reality—that it is performative in nature.

claims.claim: Legal facts do not preexist their creation; they are brought into being through processes.
claims.source_quote: Legal facts do not preexist their creation; they are brought into being through processes that can succeed or fail.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status and origin of legal facts—they are created, not pre-existing.

claims.claim: Legal fact-creation processes can succeed or fail.
claims.source_quote: they are brought into being through processes that can succeed or fail.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the processes by which legal facts are created.

claims.claim: Misrecognition, fraud, and jurisdictional voids are expressions of law's limits, not aberrations from its ontology.
claims.source_quote: They are not aberrations from law's ontology but expressions of its limits, moments when the dependence of law on recognition becomes visible.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status of these anomalies—they are expressions of law's limits.

claims.claim: Law depends on recognition.
claims.source_quote: moments when the dependence of law on recognition becomes visible.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between law and recognition.

claims.claim: Law's deepest task is the continual restoration of coherence that makes its world possible.
claims.source_quote: law performs its deepest task: the continual restoration of the coherence that makes its world possible.
claims.note: Asserts a function/role of law as an entity.

claims.claim: Widespread recognition generates its own coherence.
claims.source_quote: Recognition, once widespread enough, generates its own coherence, even if born in contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/generative property of widespread recognition.

claims.claim: Evidence is a member of the class of information-bearing dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: evidence belongs to the class of information-bearing dependent continuants, entities that exist only through recognition and serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.note: Direct assertion of the ontological kind to which evidence belongs.

claims.claim: Information-bearing dependent continuants exist only through recognition.
claims.source_quote: evidence belongs to the class of information-bearing dependent continuants, entities that exist only through recognition and serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.note: Asserts a defining property of the kind: existence conditional on recognition.

claims.claim: Information-bearing dependent continuants serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.source_quote: entities that exist only through recognition and serve as mediators between brute occurrences and institutional judgment.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational role of this class of entities.

claims.claim: Evidence is made through processes of recognition and contextualization, not simply found in the world.
claims.source_quote: Evidence, unlike raw data, is not simply found in the world; it is made through processes of recognition and contextualization.
claims.note: Asserts a property/origin of evidence as an entity.

claims.claim: A physical or informational entity becomes evidence only when a legal institution interprets and integrates it within juridical relevance.
claims.source_quote: A fingerprint, a video recording, or a witness's statement becomes evidence only when a legal institution interprets and integrates it within the field of juridical relevance.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions under which an entity acquires the status of evidence.

claims.claim: The act of institutional interpretation is an occurrent of recognition.
claims.source_quote: It is this act of interpretation, an occurrent of recognition, that transforms a physical or informational entity into a bearer of evidential force.
claims.note: Asserts that the interpretive act is an occurrent (a kind of entity in BFO-style ontology).

claims.claim: Evidence is a recognized information artifact.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, therefore, evidence is a recognized information artifact: a material or digital continuant carrying content that has been conferred a specific epistemic function within law's framework.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of evidence as a subkind of information artifact.

claims.claim: Evidence is a material or digital continuant carrying content conferred a specific epistemic function within law.
claims.source_quote: evidence is a recognized information artifact: a material or digital continuant carrying content that has been conferred a specific epistemic function within law's framework.
claims.note: Asserts properties and kind-membership of evidence as a continuant.

claims.claim: Data are information content entities that exist independently of their use or recognition.
claims.source_quote: Data are information content entities that exist independently of their use or recognition.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of data and assertion of their independence from recognition.

claims.claim: Testimony is a speech act occurrent realized in time through performance.
claims.source_quote: Testimony, by contrast, is a speech act occurrent: a process through which an agent conveys information, intending recognition by others... is itself transient, realized in time through performance.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind (occurrent/process) to which testimony belongs and its temporal property.

claims.claim: Testimony may generate data such as transcripts or recordings.
claims.source_quote: Testimony may generate data (as in transcripts or recordings) but is itself transient, realized in time through performance.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/generative relation between testimony and data.

claims.claim: Evidence arises when data or testimony are recognized as relevant to a legal issue and incorporated into an institutional process.
claims.source_quote: Evidence, finally, arises when data or testimony are recognized as relevant to a legal issue and incorporated into an institutional process.
claims.note: Asserts the conditions of existence for evidence as an entity.

claims.claim: Evidential weight is a dependent continuant that exists only within the system of recognition defined by procedural rules and institutional authority.
claims.source_quote: it bears a specific dependent continuant, evidential weight, that exists only within the system of recognition defined by procedural rules and institutional authority.
claims.note: Asserts that evidential weight is a dependent continuant and specifies its dependence relation.

claims.claim: Proof is not an entity but a state of institutional coherence.
claims.source_quote: Proof, therefore, is not an additional artifact but an emergent configuration within the field of recognition, a condition in which evidential dependencies align to produce a coherent judgment.
claims.note: Directly asserts what proof is (and is not) ontologically.

claims.claim: Proof is an emergent configuration within the field of recognition in which evidential dependencies align to produce a coherent judgment.
claims.source_quote: Proof, therefore, is not an additional artifact but an emergent configuration within the field of recognition, a condition in which evidential dependencies align to produce a coherent judgment.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character and relational structure of proof.

claims.claim: Evidence denotes the recognized relation between information and event.
claims.source_quote: the former denotes the recognized relation between information and event, while the latter denotes the achieved coherence among such relations within an adjudicative context.
claims.note: Asserts that evidence is fundamentally a relation between information and event.

claims.claim: Proof denotes the achieved coherence among evidential relations within an adjudicative context.
claims.source_quote: the latter denotes the achieved coherence among such relations within an adjudicative context.
claims.note: Asserts proof's ontological structure as a coherence among relations.

claims.claim: In law, evidence ceases to exist the moment institutional recognition is withdrawn.
claims.source_quote: in law, evidence ceases to exist the moment recognition is withdrawn.
claims.note: Asserts a defining existential dependency of evidence on recognition.

claims.claim: The ontology of evidence is inseparable from the institutional structures that confer and maintain its meaning.
claims.source_quote: This dependence on recognition means that the ontology of evidence is inseparable from the institutional structures that confer and maintain its meaning.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary relational dependency between evidence and institutional structures.

claims.claim: Evidence inheres in an information artifact such as a document, photograph, or recording.
claims.source_quote: Inheres in an information artifact (a physical or digital bearer, such as a document, photograph, or recording).
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between evidence and its material/digital bearer.

claims.claim: Evidence depends on an institutional continuant for its existence as evidence.
claims.source_quote: Depends on an institutional continuant (a court, tribunal, or agency) for its existence as evidence.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependence relation between evidence and institutional continuants.

claims.claim: Evidence is realized through procedural occurrents such as investigation, submission, and evaluation.
claims.source_quote: Is realized through procedural occurrents (investigation, submission, and evaluation).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between evidence and procedural processes.

claims.claim: Evidence gains persistence through record artifacts such as transcripts, exhibits, and databases.
claims.source_quote: Gains persistence through record artifacts (transcripts, exhibits, databases) that embody institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between evidence and record artifacts that sustains its persistence.

claims.claim: Record artifacts embody institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Gains persistence through record artifacts (transcripts, exhibits, databases) that embody institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of record artifacts as bearers of institutional recognition.

claims.claim: A legal fact is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: initiating institutional processes that create a legal fact as a dependent continuant.
claims.note: Directly asserts the ontological category membership of legal facts.

claims.claim: Legal facts are embodied in record artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Legal facts are embodied in record artifacts, validated, and stored within institutional archives.
claims.note: Asserts a bearing relation between legal facts and record artifacts.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a relational continuant: a network of dependencies linking agents, institutions, and objects through recognized rights and obligations.
claims.note: Directly asserts the ontological category of property.

claims.claim: Property is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: Within the framework of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), property belongs to the category of dependent continuants, more specifically, to the subclass of relational continuants.
claims.note: Explicitly asserts the BFO category membership of property.

claims.claim: Relational continuants are a subkind of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: property belongs to the category of dependent continuants, more specifically, to the subclass of relational continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation between relational continuants and dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Ownership is a relation that inheres jointly among an owner, an owned object, and the institutional structure recognizing it.
claims.source_quote: Ownership is a relation that inheres jointly among an owner, an owned object, and the institutional structure that recognizes that relation.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure and bearers of the ownership relation.

claims.claim: If recognition of ownership is withdrawn, the property relation dissolves.
claims.source_quote: If any of these bearers ceases to exist or if recognition is withdrawn, the property relation dissolves.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation: the property relation's existence depends on ongoing recognition.

claims.claim: The ontological unity of property arises from the stability of recognition linking persons, objects, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: The ontological unity of property thus arises not from the material continuity of things but from the stability of recognition linking persons, objects, and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts what grounds the ontological unity of property.

claims.claim: Possession is a brute relation between an agent and an object.
claims.source_quote: Possession is a brute relation, an agent's physical control over an object.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of possession as a brute (non-institutional) relation.

claims.claim: Ownership is an institutional relation.
claims.source_quote: Ownership, by contrast, is an institutional relation: it transforms possession into a recognized right and extends it beyond the physical domain.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category of ownership as institutional.

claims.claim: Ownership is not reducible to physical fact.
claims.source_quote: This distinction reveals that ownership is not reducible to physical fact; it is sustained by social recognition encoded in institutional form.
claims.note: Asserts an irreducibility claim about ownership's ontological status.

claims.claim: Property is sustained by legal institutions.
claims.source_quote: It is the recognition through the social sphere of law that some brute object has acquired some new meaning, the creation of a new norm that inheres in the object, sustained by legal institutions, thus turning it into property.
claims.note: Asserts that legal institutions are the sustaining bearer of property.

claims.claim: A norm inheres in the property object.
claims.source_quote: the creation of a new norm that inheres in the object, sustained by legal institutions, thus turning it into property.
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between a norm and a physical object when it becomes property.

claims.claim: Use-rights (usus, fructus, abusus) are dependent continuants inhering in both the agent and the object.
claims.source_quote: Each right corresponds to a dependent continuant inhering in both the agent and the object, realized through institutional processes such as contracts, registration, or inheritance.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and bearers of use-rights.

claims.claim: The bundle of property rights is a complex structure of relations, not a monolithic entity.
claims.source_quote: The bundle of rights associated with a property object thus constitutes not a monolithic entity but a complex structure of relations, each maintained by distinct legal mechanisms.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure of property rights as plural and relational.

claims.claim: Property mediates between the world of material substances and the world of legal relations.
claims.source_quote: property mediates between the world of material substances and the world of legal relations.
claims.note: Asserts a distinctive mediating function/role of property.

claims.claim: A property object is a compound entity: a physical continuant bearing a dependent continuant of ownership.
claims.source_quote: The object 'as property' is thus a compound entity: a physical continuant bearing, in addition to its material qualities, a dependent continuant of ownership recognized by legal institutions.
claims.note: Asserts the compound ontological structure of an object-as-property.

claims.claim: Property exists only where institutional recognition confers and sustains the relevant relations.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological perspective, property exists only where institutional recognition confers and sustains the relevant relations.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological condition for property's existence.

claims.claim: Title is an information artifact that embodies the relation of ownership.
claims.source_quote: Title is the record or symbol of recognition, the information artifact that embodies the relation of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts that title is an information artifact and specifies its function as embodying ownership.

claims.claim: A right (ownership) is a dependent continuant sustained by the network of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Right, by contrast, is the dependent continuant itself, the ontological relation sustained by the network of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category of a right as a dependent continuant.

claims.claim: The validity of a title depends on the persistence of institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: The validity of the title depends on the persistence of institutional recognition: if the deed is forged, voided, or annulled, the right it purports to represent ceases to exist.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between title validity and institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Information artifacts such as registers, deeds, and digital ledgers sustain property recognition.
claims.source_quote: The register, the deed, and the digital ledger are all means of sustaining the recognition that keeps property real by recording duly instantiated legal facts.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological function/role of information artifacts in sustaining property.

claims.claim: Obligations and authority are continuants sustained by institutional relations.
claims.source_quote: Each is a continuant sustained by institutional relations.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and grounding of obligations and authority alongside property.

claims.claim: Law and morality operate at different ontological levels regarding property.
claims.source_quote: Law and morality thus operate at different ontological levels: the former concerns the existence of property, the latter its ethical legitimacy.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological distinction between the levels at which law and morality relate to property.

claims.claim: Evidence depends on an institutional continuant (a court, tribunal, or agency) for its existence.
claims.source_quote: Depends on an institutional continuant (a court, tribunal, or agency) for its existence as evidence.
claims.note: Direct assertion of an ontological dependency relation between evidence and institutional continuants.

claims.claim: Evidence is realized through procedural occurrents such as investigation, submission, and evaluation.
claims.source_quote: Is realized through procedural occurrents (investigation, submission, and evaluation).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between evidence and procedural occurrents.

claims.claim: Evidence gains persistence through record artifacts that embody institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Gains persistence through record artifacts (transcripts, exhibits, databases) that embody institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property (persistence) and a relation between evidence and record artifacts.

claims.claim: The material substrate of evidence carries informational content.
claims.source_quote: The material substrate carries informational content; institutional recognition confers relevance.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the material substrate layer of evidential being.

claims.claim: Institutional recognition confers relevance on evidence.
claims.source_quote: The material substrate carries informational content; institutional recognition confers relevance.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of institutional recognition in the ontological structure of evidence.

claims.claim: Procedural realization transforms relevance into juridical standing.
claims.source_quote: Procedural realization transforms relevance into juridical standing.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative functional relation between procedural realization and juridical standing.

claims.claim: Recording ensures the continuity of evidence.
claims.source_quote: Recording ensures continuity.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of recording in sustaining evidential being.

claims.claim: An evidentiary system is a network of recognition processes and artifacts that collectively produce juridical truth.
claims.source_quote: The coherence of these layers constitutes what we call an evidentiary system, a network of recognition processes and artifacts that collectively produce juridical truth.
claims.note: Asserts what an evidentiary system is and what it produces.

claims.claim: Evidence is inherently relational rather than substantial.
claims.source_quote: This framework also reveals why evidence is inherently relational rather than substantial.
claims.note: Asserts a fundamental ontological property of evidence.

claims.claim: A blood sample has no evidential significance in itself.
claims.source_quote: A blood sample, for instance, has no evidential significance in itself.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property (lack of intrinsic evidential significance) of a blood sample.

claims.claim: An object's existence as an evidential continuant ceases when its chain of dependency is broken.
claims.source_quote: The object may remain physically intact, but its existence as an evidential continuant ceases.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological condition under which evidential being is destroyed.

claims.claim: Truth within legal systems depends on the integrity of recognition relations that sustain it.
claims.source_quote: Truth within legal systems depends not merely on facts but on the integrity of recognition relations that sustain them.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between legal truth and recognition relations.

claims.claim: Information artifacts are independent continuants bearing informational content.
claims.source_quote: As independent continuants bearing informational content, they provide the medium through which recognition persists over time.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership and property of information artifacts.

claims.claim: Documents, exhibits, recordings, and digital files are vehicles through which evidence exists as law.
claims.source_quote: Documents, exhibits, recordings, and digital files are not mere containers of evidence but the vehicles through which evidence exists as law.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of information artifacts in the existence of evidence.

claims.claim: A photograph of a crime scene carries a dependent continuant of evidential force.
claims.source_quote: A photograph of a crime scene, for example, is not just an image but an institutionalized representation, it carries a dependent continuant of evidential force, maintained by the authenticity procedures of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts that a photograph bears a dependent continuant (evidential force) as a property.

claims.claim: Once introduced into the record, an artifact becomes part of the enduring ontology of the case.
