claims.source_quote: Once introduced into the record, such an artifact becomes part of the enduring ontology of the case: it exists as a legal entity long after the events it depicts have passed.
claims.note: Asserts a part-of relation and legal entity status for introduced artifacts.

claims.claim: An artifact introduced into the legal record exists as a legal entity.
claims.source_quote: It exists as a legal entity long after the events it depicts have passed.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership: the artifact is a legal entity.

claims.claim: In contemporary systems, evidence increasingly exists as data stored in digital repositories.
claims.source_quote: In contemporary systems, evidence increasingly exists as data stored in digital repositories, where authenticity and chain of custody depend on metadata, timestamps, and cryptographic signatures.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological form of evidence in contemporary systems.

claims.claim: Metadata, timestamps, and cryptographic signatures function as automated recognition processes.
claims.source_quote: These mechanisms function as automated recognition processes: algorithmic proxies for institutional verification.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of digital mechanisms in the ontology of evidence.

claims.claim: A hash value or digital certificate acts as an institutional stand-in encoding recognition into the artifact.
claims.source_quote: A hash value or digital certificate, for instance, acts as an institutional stand-in, encoding recognition into the artifact itself.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/property of hash values and digital certificates.

claims.claim: Law and technology co-produce evidential being.
claims.source_quote: Law and technology co-produce evidential being, binding informational continuants to institutional authority through recursive validation.
claims.note: Asserts a co-production relation between law, technology, and evidential being.

claims.claim: Evidence declared as such becomes a bearer of potential truth within a public and coercive system.
claims.source_quote: To declare something 'evidence' is to confer upon it a specific kind of ontological privilege, it becomes a bearer of potential truth within a public and coercive system.
claims.note: Asserts a property/role conferred on entities recognized as evidence.

claims.claim: Misrecognition of evidence produces ontological distortion: false facts institutionalized as truth.
claims.source_quote: Misrecognition at this level produces not merely epistemic error but ontological distortion, false facts institutionalized as truth.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/productive relation between misrecognition and a specific ontological outcome.

claims.claim: Evidence is the bridge between ontology and epistemology in law.
claims.source_quote: Evidence becomes the bridge between ontology and epistemology, the way law constructs truth from relation.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of evidence in relating ontology and epistemology.

claims.claim: The being of evidence is processual, not static.
claims.source_quote: Its being is not static but processual: an ongoing interplay among data, institutions, and interpretation.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property of evidence.

claims.claim: The courtroom is a site where legal entities are created, validated, and sustained.
claims.source_quote: The courtroom, in this view, is not a stage for the display of facts but a factory of ontology, where entities are created, validated, and sustained as the building blocks of juridical reality.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of the courtroom in producing ontological entities.

claims.claim: The trier of fact is an epistemic structure, not merely a person or group.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological perspective, the trier of fact is not merely a person or group but an epistemic structure: a complex role-bearing configuration through which the legal system realizes the function of determining fact.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim about the trier of fact.

claims.claim: The trier of fact's authority arises from institutional recognition of a specific role within a procedural context.
claims.source_quote: Its authority does not arise from individual cognition but from institutional recognition of a specific role within a procedural context.
claims.note: Asserts the source/basis of a property (authority) of the trier of fact.

claims.claim: The trier of fact is a dependent continuant realized in agents and sustained by institutions.
claims.source_quote: In Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) terms, the trier of fact is a dependent continuant realized in agents and sustained by institutions.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership and realization/sustenance relations for the trier of fact.

claims.claim: The trier of fact is a role, not a substance.
claims.source_quote: It is a role, not a substance, a structured relation that exists only when borne by an individual or collective within a recognized legal process.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim distinguishing the trier of fact from substance.

claims.claim: The trier of fact role exists only when borne by an individual or collective within a recognized legal process.
claims.source_quote: A structured relation that exists only when borne by an individual or collective within a recognized legal process.
claims.note: Asserts an existence condition (dependency) for the trier of fact role.

claims.claim: The trier of fact role is functionally dependent on institutional continuants and procedural occurrents.
claims.source_quote: This role is defined by its functional dependence on both institutional continuants (the court, tribunal, or administrative body) and procedural occurrents (the trial, hearing, or inquest).
claims.note: Asserts dependency relations between the trier of fact role and institutional/procedural entities.

claims.claim: A verdict is a dependent continuant inhering in the institutional configuration that authorizes it.
claims.source_quote: A verdict is not merely a conclusion about events but a dependent continuant inhering in the institutional configuration that authorizes it.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership and an inherence relation for verdicts.

claims.claim: The verdict's being depends on the trier's recognized role within the institutional structure.
claims.source_quote: The verdict's being, therefore, depends on the trier's recognized role within this structure.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between the verdict's existence and the trier's recognized role.

claims.claim: Artifacts such as registers, deeds, and digital ledgers are vehicles of property's ontology.
claims.source_quote: on artifacts serve as vehicles of property's ontology, just as they do for other legal facts. The register, the deed, and the digital ledger are all means of sustaining the recognition that keeps property real
claims.note: The author asserts that these artifacts bear a specific ontological role (vehicle of property's ontology), which is a property/function claim.

claims.claim: Registers, deeds, and digital ledgers sustain the recognition that keeps property real.
claims.source_quote: The register, the deed, and the digital ledger are all means of sustaining the recognition that keeps property real by recording duly instantiated legal facts.
claims.note: Asserts a functional relation between these artifacts and the sustaining of property's reality.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant.
claims.source_quote: Understanding property as a relational continuant also explains its transferability.
claims.note: The author endorses this ontological classification of property as a subkind (relational continuant).

claims.claim: Ownership does not inhere in the physical object alone but in a network of recognition linking object to owner.
claims.source_quote: Ownership can change bearers because it does not inhere in the physical object alone but in the network of recognition that links the object to an owner.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological locus of ownership—a relational network rather than the physical object.

claims.claim: A transfer of ownership occurs when the network of recognition is reconfigured.
claims.source_quote: A transfer occurs when this network is reconfigured, when recognition is withdrawn from one agent and extended to another.
claims.note: Asserts what constitutes a transfer event ontologically—a reconfiguration of a relational structure.

claims.claim: During a transfer, the physical object itself remains unchanged; only the relational structure surrounding it changes.
claims.source_quote: The object itself remains unchanged; what changes is the relational structure surrounding it.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the physical object (unchanged) and distinguishes it from the relational structure (changed) during transfer.

claims.claim: The jury's utterance occurs within a chain of recognition including empanelment, instruction, deliberation, and court validation.
claims.source_quote: The jury's utterance occurs within a chain of recognition: empanelment, instruction, deliberation, and validation by the court.
claims.note: Asserts a structural relation: the jury's utterance is part of a chain of recognition with specific stages.

claims.claim: Each stage of the chain of recognition realizes the dependencies that confer juridical status on the final judgment.
claims.source_quote: Each stage realizes the dependencies that confer juridical status on the final judgment.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between stages and the dependencies that produce juridical status.

claims.claim: The verdict's being depends on the trier's recognized role within the juridical structure.
claims.source_quote: The verdict's being, therefore, depends on the trier's recognized role within this structure.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependence relation between the verdict's existence and the trier's recognized role.

claims.claim: Without recognized role, a verdict collapses into a mere utterance with no legal existence.
claims.source_quote: Remove or corrupt that recognition, and the verdict collapses into a mere statement, a brute utterance without legal existence.
claims.note: Asserts that removal of recognition eliminates the verdict's legal existence, implying legal existence is a genuine ontological property.

claims.claim: Epistemic authority in law has a hierarchical nature.
claims.source_quote: This dependency structure illustrates the hierarchical nature of epistemic authority in law.
claims.note: Asserts a property (hierarchical structure) of epistemic authority in law.

claims.claim: The trier of fact's judgment is ontologically subordinate to the rule of recognition that defines the court's legitimacy.
claims.source_quote: The trier of fact's judgment is ontologically subordinate to the rule of recognition that defines the court's legitimacy.
claims.note: Directly asserts an ontological subordination relation between two entities.

claims.claim: The trier of fact's judgment functions as the proximate source of factual truth within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: yet it functions as the proximate source of factual truth within the system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of the trier's judgment within the system.

claims.claim: The rule of recognition defines the court's legitimacy.
claims.source_quote: the rule of recognition that defines the court's legitimacy
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive relation: the rule of recognition is what defines court legitimacy.

claims.claim: Ownership does not inhere in the physical object alone but in a network of recognition linking object to owner.
claims.source_quote: Ownership can change bearers because it does not inhere in the physical object alone but in the network of recognition that links the object to an owner.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological location of ownership as a property of a relational network.

claims.claim: A transfer of ownership occurs when the network of recognition is reconfigured.
claims.source_quote: A transfer occurs when this network is reconfigured, when recognition is withdrawn from one agent and extended to another.
claims.note: Asserts what a transfer of ownership is, ontologically.

claims.claim: Legal formalities such as signature and registration are procedural realizations through which recognition is reoriented.
claims.source_quote: signature, delivery, registration, or notarization are procedural realizations through which recognition is reoriented.
claims.note: Asserts that legal formalities have the ontological role of realizing the reorientation of recognition.

claims.claim: Without legal formalities, a transfer of ownership is ontologically incomplete.
claims.source_quote: Without these formalities, the transfer remains ontologically incomplete; the relation cannot shift coherently within the field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property of informal transfers.

claims.claim: Intangible property such as intellectual works is an information content entity.
claims.source_quote: the object of ownership is an information content entity, a generically dependent continuant that can exist on multiple bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim about the object of intangible ownership.

claims.claim: An information content entity is a generically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: the object of ownership is an information content entity, a generically dependent continuant that can exist on multiple bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation: information content entity is a generically dependent continuant.

claims.claim: A generically dependent continuant can exist on multiple bearers.
claims.source_quote: the object of ownership is an information content entity, a generically dependent continuant that can exist on multiple bearers.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of generically dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Copyright is a legally recognized relation between the author (or assignee) and the work's expression.
claims.source_quote: the copyright to a novel...is...the legally recognized relation between the author (or assignee) and the work's expression.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of copyright as a relational entity.

claims.claim: Ownership of a digital token consists solely in recognized control within an institutionalized computational system.
claims.source_quote: ownership of a digital token, blockchain entry, or virtual good consists solely in recognized control within an institutionalized computational system.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological constitution of digital asset ownership.

claims.claim: Property is an architecture of recognition sustained by informational and procedural continuants.
claims.source_quote: property, far from being tied to material substance, is increasingly an architecture of recognition sustained by informational and procedural continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of property as a kind.

claims.claim: Each right and obligation in a collective ownership arrangement is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: Each right and obligation in this arrangement is a dependent continuant inhering in specific configurations of agents and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership and inherence relation for rights and obligations.

claims.claim: A legal entity such as an association is a higher-order continuant.
claims.source_quote: The legal entity 'association' serves as a higher-order continuant maintaining coherence among these relations.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim about legal entities.

claims.claim: Collective ownership is a more complex configuration of dependencies among multiple agents, institutions, and shared objects.
claims.source_quote: collective ownership is not a different kind of property but a more complex configuration of dependencies: multiple agents jointly recognized as bearers of rights and obligations relative to shared objects.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological constitution of collective ownership.

claims.claim: When recognition lapses, ownership ceases to exist.
claims.source_quote: When recognition lapses, through expropriation, nationalization, or legal collapse, ownership ceases to exist.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological condition for the existence of ownership.

claims.claim: Property is as fragile as the institutions that sustain it.
claims.source_quote: property is as fragile as the institutions that sustain it, its being is always conditional on the coherence of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional/modal property of property regarding its dependence on institutions.

claims.claim: The being of property is conditional on the coherence of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: its being is always conditional on the coherence of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation between property and the legal system.

claims.claim: Registers, cadasters, and ledgers are information artifacts that distribute recognition over time and space.
claims.source_quote: Registers, cadasters, and ledgers serve as information artifacts that distribute recognition over time and space.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership and functional role of registration systems.

claims.claim: Registration converts private relations into public facts.
claims.source_quote: They convert private relations into public facts, enabling third parties to orient their behavior accordingly.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative relational function of registration.

claims.claim: Registration transforms property from a bilateral relation into a multilateral relation encompassing all potential recognizers.
claims.source_quote: This publicity transforms property from a bilateral relation between owner and object into a multilateral relation encompassing all potential recognizers within the system.
claims.note: Asserts a structural change in the relational structure of property effected by registration.

claims.claim: The value of property resides in the structure of relations that law sustains, not in things themselves.
claims.source_quote: The value of property does not reside in things themselves but in the structure of relations that law sustains.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological claim about where value inheres.

claims.claim: Property is a node in a larger field of social coordination where value is expressed through recognition.
claims.source_quote: Property is not merely a relation among agents and objects but a node in a larger field of social coordination where value, economic, symbolic, and moral, is expressed through recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relational and functional property of property within social ontology.

claims.claim: Property is a fundamental ontological mechanism through which law gives stable relational form to value.
claims.source_quote: Property is thus not only a legal category but a fundamental ontological mechanism: it is how law gives stable relational form to value.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/ontological role for property as a mechanism.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant, a structured dependency among agents, institutions, and things.
claims.source_quote: Property, as previously established, is not a substance but a relational continuant, a structured dependency among agents, institutions, and things that persists through recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and constitution of property.

claims.claim: Value emerges only within networks of exchange and assessment.
claims.source_quote: Just as ownership exists only within a field of recognition, so too does value emerge only within networks of exchange and assessment.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological condition for the existence of value.

claims.claim: A piece of land, a painting, or a patent possesses no intrinsic worth.
claims.source_quote: A piece of land, a painting, or a patent possesses no intrinsic worth; its value is the manifestation of recognition distributed across social and institutional relations.
claims.note: Asserts a property (or lack thereof) of material and intellectual objects.

claims.claim: Value is the manifestation of recognition distributed across social and institutional relations.
claims.source_quote: its value is the manifestation of recognition distributed across social and institutional relations.
claims.note: Asserts what value is ontologically.

claims.claim: Value belongs to the class of dependent continuants within BFO.
claims.source_quote: Within the framework of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), value belongs to the class of dependent continuants, but of a distinctive sort.
claims.note: Asserts kind-membership of value in BFO ontology, endorsed by the author.

claims.claim: Value is a relational disposition that exists only insofar as certain kinds of interactions are possible.
claims.source_quote: it is a relational disposition that exists only insofar as certain kinds of interactions, like market exchange, legal transfer, or institutional appraisal, are possible.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of value as a relational disposition with conditions of existence.

claims.claim: The ontological condition for value is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.source_quote: The ontological condition for value, therefore, is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between value and the legal system.

claims.claim: Stability and recognition transform material or informational objects into participants in the social field of exchange.
claims.source_quote: Stability and recognition transform material or informational objects into participants in the social field of exchange.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about what stability and recognition do to objects—changes their kind or status to 'participants in the social field of exchange'.

claims.claim: The ontological condition for value is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.source_quote: The ontological condition for value, therefore, is the legal system's capacity to sustain property relations across time and participants.
claims.note: Explicit assertion of an ontological condition: value depends on the legal system's sustaining power over property relations.

claims.claim: Property depends on institutional recognition; without it, ownership cannot exist.
claims.source_quote: On the first level, property depends on recognition: without institutional acknowledgment, ownership cannot exist.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between property/ownership and institutional recognition—an ontological dependency claim.

claims.claim: Value depends on stable, recognized ownership; without it, no coherent field for valuation exists.
claims.source_quote: On the second level, value depends on property: without stable, recognized ownership, there can be no coherent field for valuation.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence relation between value and property—an ontological dependency claim.

claims.claim: Recognition and value together form a hierarchy of ontological dependence.
claims.source_quote: Together, these layers form a hierarchy of ontological dependence:
claims.note: Asserts that the two-tiered relation constitutes a structured hierarchy—an ontological structural claim.

claims.claim: Property depends on recognition for its existence.
claims.source_quote: On the first level, property depends on recognition: without institutional acknowledgment, ownership cannot exist.
claims.note: Direct assertion of an ontological dependence relation between property and recognition.

claims.claim: Value depends on property for its existence.
claims.source_quote: On the second level, value depends on property: without stable, recognized ownership, there can be no coherent field for valuation.
claims.note: Direct assertion of an ontological dependence relation between value and property.

claims.claim: Recognition is a social/institutional continuant.
claims.source_quote: Level 1: Recognition (social/institutional continuants).
claims.note: Author categorizes recognition as a kind of entity (social/institutional continuant).

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant sustained by recognition.
claims.source_quote: Level 2: Property (relational continuants sustained by recognition).
claims.note: Author categorizes property as a relational continuant and asserts it is sustained by recognition.

claims.claim: Value consists in relational dispositions realized through exchange.
claims.source_quote: Level 3: Value (relational dispositions realized through exchange).
claims.note: Author categorizes value as relational dispositions, asserting what kind of entity it is and how it is realized.

claims.claim: Each level in the hierarchy of dependence presupposes the coherence of the level below it.
claims.source_quote: Each level presupposes the coherence of the one below it. When recognition fails, property dissolves; when property collapses, value disappears.
claims.note: Author asserts a structural ontological relation of presupposition between the hierarchy's levels.

claims.claim: Economic crises and legal ruptures are ontological failures of recognition cascaded through the hierarchy.
claims.source_quote: economic crises and legal ruptures alike can be understood as ontological failures of recognition cascaded through the hierarchy of dependence.
claims.note: Author endorses this characterization, though the framing 'can be understood as' introduces slight qualification.

claims.claim: Exchange is a realization occurrent—a process that brings relational capacities embedded in property to manifestation.
claims.source_quote: exchange is not merely the transfer of goods or titles but a realization occurrent: a process that brings to manifestation the relational capacities embedded in property.
claims.note: Author asserts what kind of entity/process exchange is and what it does ontologically.

claims.claim: When agents exchange property, they reconfigure the network of ownership relations through mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: When two agents exchange property, each recognizes the other's entitlement and, through mutual acknowledgment, reconfigures the network of ownership relations.
claims.note: Author asserts what exchange does to the relational structure of ownership.

claims.claim: Exchange is a realization of recognition symmetry.
claims.source_quote: Exchange, therefore, is a realization of recognition symmetry.
claims.note: Author directly asserts what exchange is in ontological terms.

claims.claim: Exchange creates value by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: It does not merely measure value; it creates it by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/constitutive ontological claim about the role of exchange in producing value.

claims.claim: Markets are ontological engines of equivalence that produce and stabilize value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: markets are ontological engines of equivalence, continuously producing and stabilizing value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Author directly asserts what markets are and what function they perform ontologically.

claims.claim: The trier of fact's judgment is ontologically subordinate to the rule of recognition that defines the court's legitimacy.
claims.source_quote: The trier of fact's judgment is ontologically subordinate to the rule of recognition that defines the court's legitimacy, and yet it functions as the proximate source of factual truth within the system.
claims.note: Direct ontological hierarchy claim asserting a subordination relation between two entities.

claims.claim: The trier of fact's judgment functions as the proximate source of factual truth within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The trier of fact's judgment is ontologically subordinate to the rule of recognition that defines the court's legitimacy, and yet it functions as the proximate source of factual truth within the system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/property of an entity.

claims.claim: The verdict is a secondary dependent continuant whose existence depends on evidence, procedure, and institutional authority.
claims.source_quote: The verdict is a secondary dependent continuant: its existence depends on the sustained realization of multiple antecedent continuants, evidence, procedure, and institutional authority.
claims.note: Asserts the verdict's ontological kind and its dependency relations.

claims.claim: The verdict is a relational continuant linking the trier's role, the evidential record, and the institutional context.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, the verdict is a relational continuant linking the trier's role, the evidential record, and the institutional context.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind and relational structure for the verdict as an entity.

claims.claim: When a higher court overturns a verdict, it alters the dependency network that sustains the verdict's legal being.
claims.source_quote: When a higher court overturns a verdict, it does not erase the words spoken but alters the dependency network that sustains their legal being.
claims.note: Asserts what overturning a verdict ontologically consists in—a change in dependency relations.

claims.claim: An overturned verdict persists as a historical record but ceases to exist as juridical truth.
claims.source_quote: The earlier verdict persists as a historical record but ceases to exist as juridical truth.
claims.note: Asserts two distinct ontological statuses of the same entity after overturning.

claims.claim: The trier of fact is the institution's capacity for meta-recognition.
claims.source_quote: In this way, the trier of fact occupies the apex of law's epistemic hierarchy: it is the institution's capacity for meta-recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a functional identity/property of the trier of fact as an entity.

claims.claim: The trier of fact determines which recognized entities shall persist as components of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: The judge or jury does not generate new data but determines which recognized entities shall persist as components of legal reality.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/disposition of the trier of fact.

claims.claim: The judge is a role continuant whose being depends on the judiciary, the procedural framework, and public recognition.
claims.source_quote: As a role continuant, the judge's being depends on the institution of the judiciary, the procedural framework of adjudication, and the recognition of the public.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of the judge and its dependency relations.

claims.claim: The judge realizes his role through occurrents of hearing, evaluating, and issuing judgment.
claims.source_quote: The judge realizes this role through occurrents of hearing, evaluating, and issuing judgment.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between a role continuant and specific occurrents.

claims.claim: Hearing transforms evidence into deliberative content; evaluation transforms deliberation into finding; judgment transforms finding into legal fact.
claims.source_quote: the hearing transforms evidence into deliberative content; evaluation transforms deliberation into finding; judgment transforms finding into legal fact.
claims.note: Asserts transformation relations between ontological entities through specific acts.

claims.claim: The authority of each judicial transformation derives from the institutional continuant of the court.
claims.source_quote: The authority of each transformation derives from the institutional continuant of the court, which maintains the coherence of recognition across time and cases.
claims.note: Asserts a dependence/derivation relation between authority and the court as institutional continuant.

claims.claim: The judge's cognition is ontologically subsumed by the collective recognition that sustains it.
claims.source_quote: The judge's cognition, while individual, is ontologically subsumed by the collective recognition that sustains it.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological subordination relation between individual cognition and collective recognition.

claims.claim: The jury is an emergent dependent continuant of deliberation realized through interaction and institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: The jury's being is not the aggregate of its members' cognitions but the emergent dependent continuant of deliberation, a single collective role realized through interaction and institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and constitution of the jury.

claims.claim: The jury exists only as a body constituted by the court, guided by its instructions, and dissolved upon verdict.
claims.source_quote: The jury exists only as a body constituted by the court, guided by its instructions, and dissolved upon verdict.
claims.note: Asserts existence conditions and temporal boundaries of the jury as an entity.

claims.claim: The jury's verdict is a collective realization of recognition, not an expression of individual belief.
claims.source_quote: Its verdict is thus a collective realization of recognition, not the expression of individual belief.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character of the jury's verdict.

claims.claim: Jurors' private opinions cease to exist as juridical entities once the collective verdict is pronounced.
claims.source_quote: The jurors' private opinions cease to exist as juridical entities once the collective verdict is pronounced.
claims.note: Asserts cessation of existence of a category of entity upon a specific occurrent.

claims.claim: The jury is a temporally bounded institution whose sole function is to transform evidential relations into a verdict.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the jury is a temporally bounded institution: a transient continuant whose sole function is to transform evidential relations into the singular fact of a verdict.
claims.note: Asserts ontological kind, temporal property, and functional role of the jury.

claims.claim: Verdicts rendered by unauthorized tribunals or improperly constituted juries lack legal existence.
claims.source_quote: This explains why verdicts rendered by unauthorized tribunals, corrupt judges, or improperly constituted juries lack legal existence.
claims.note: Asserts absence of a property (legal existence) for a category of entity.

claims.claim: A verdict without a coherent dependency structure does not instantiate juridical truth.
claims.source_quote: Their statements may describe reality accurately, but they do not instantiate juridical truth because the dependency structure is incomplete or incoherent.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for instantiating juridical truth.

claims.claim: Once rendered, a verdict becomes part of the enduring ontology of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: Once rendered by a recognized trier of fact, the verdict becomes part of the enduring ontology of the legal system.
claims.note: Asserts that verdicts become parts of a larger ontological structure.

claims.claim: Each verdict becomes evidence for future fact-finding, integrating epistemic acts into the temporal fabric of legal being.
claims.source_quote: This persistence exemplifies the recursive structure of law: each verdict becomes evidence for future fact-finding, integrating epistemic acts into the temporal fabric of legal being.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of verdicts within the legal system's temporal structure.

claims.claim: Verdicts are nodes in a continuous network of recognition linking past and future acts of institutional cognition.
claims.source_quote: In this sense, verdicts are not endpoints but nodes in a continuous network of recognition linking past and future acts of institutional cognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological role and relational position of verdicts within a network.

claims.claim: The trier of fact is the consciousness of law as a structure of being, not as a mind.
claims.source_quote: The trier of fact, in this sense, is the consciousness of law, not as a mind but as a structure of being that transforms the uncertain into the recognized.
claims.note: Author explicitly qualifies the metaphor but asserts an ontological identification of the trier with law's recognitive structure.

claims.claim: The trial is a procedural occurrent that realizes dependent continuants including roles, functions, and procedural norms.
claims.source_quote: From the standpoint of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), the trial is an occurrent that realizes several dependent continuants simultaneously: the roles of trial judge, jury, counsel, and witness; the functions of adjudication and defense.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind of the trial and its realization relations.

claims.claim: Dependent continuants realized in the trial exist as relational structures within the institutional continuant of the court.
claims.source_quote: These dependent continuants exist as relational structures within the institutional continuant of the court.
claims.note: Asserts a parthood/containment relation between dependent continuants and the court as institutional continuant.

claims.claim: The trial functions as a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.source_quote: The trial thus functions as a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role of the trial as an occurrent.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is institutionally realized coherence, not metaphysical or scientific truth.
claims.source_quote: What emerges from this process is not 'truth' in the metaphysical or scientific sense but a distinct ontological mode of truth: institutionally realized coherence.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological character and kind of juridical truth.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is distinguished from other epistemic forms by its institutional closure.
claims.source_quote: What distinguishes juridical truth from other epistemic forms is its institutional closure.
claims.note: Asserts a distinguishing property of juridical truth as an entity/kind.

claims.claim: The trial is a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.source_quote: The trial thus functions as a realization event for the entire epistemic architecture of law.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/ontological role of the trial: it realizes the epistemic architecture of law.

claims.claim: The trial is an ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge.
claims.source_quote: It is the ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge to produce determinate facts.
claims.note: Asserts that the trial is a kind of ontological space with specific converging elements.

claims.claim: The trial produces determinate facts.
claims.source_quote: It is the ontological space in which recognition, evidence, and authority converge to produce determinate facts.
claims.note: Asserts that determinate facts are produced by the trial process.

claims.claim: Juridical truth has institutional closure as a distinguishing property.
claims.source_quote: What distinguishes juridical truth from other epistemic forms is its institutional closure.
claims.note: Asserts a distinctive property of juridical truth: institutional closure.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is a kind of epistemic form.
claims.source_quote: What distinguishes juridical truth from other epistemic forms is its institutional closure.
claims.note: Implied by contrasting juridical truth with 'other epistemic forms'; it is itself an epistemic form.

claims.claim: Scientific and philosophical inquiry is open-ended and always subject to revision.
claims.source_quote: In scientific or philosophical inquiry, the process of verification is open-ended, always subject to revision through further evidence.
claims.note: The author asserts this as a characterizing property of scientific/philosophical inquiry in contrast to law.

claims.claim: The trial establishes closure through formal recognition.
claims.source_quote: In law, by contrast, the trial establishes closure through formal recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of the trial: it establishes institutional closure via formal recognition.

claims.claim: Once a verdict is rendered, the institutional truth is fixed regardless of correspondence to empirical reality.
claims.source_quote: Once the trier of fact renders a verdict, the truth of the matter, within that institutional world, is fixed regardless of whether it corresponds to empirical reality.
claims.note: Asserts a property of juridical truth: fixity within the institutional world independent of empirical correspondence.

claims.claim: The procedural acts of participants realize the epistemic architecture of law.
claims.source_quote: realized, brought into active expression through the procedural acts of the participants.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between procedural acts and the epistemic architecture of law.

claims.claim: Exchange is a realization of recognition symmetry.
claims.source_quote: Exchange, therefore, is a realization of recognition symmetry. It does not merely measure value; it creates it by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological nature of exchange as a kind of realization relation.

claims.claim: Exchange creates value by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.source_quote: It does not merely measure value; it creates it by generating coherence between relational continuants.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/generative ontological relation between exchange and value.

claims.claim: Markets are ontological engines of equivalence.
claims.source_quote: In this sense, markets are ontological engines of equivalence, continuously producing and stabilizing value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/ontological property of markets.

claims.claim: Markets continuously produce and stabilize value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.source_quote: markets are ontological engines of equivalence, continuously producing and stabilizing value through distributed acts of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of markets regarding how value is produced.

claims.claim: Property consists of dependent continuants that vary with the density and stability of recognition.
claims.source_quote: the dependent continuants that constitute property are subject to variations in the density and stability of recognition they receive.
claims.note: Asserts that property is constituted by dependent continuants and that these have a property of being subject to recognition variations.

claims.claim: Market value is a dependent continuant sustained by a field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Economic volatility is thus ontological volatility: a fluctuation in the field of recognition that sustains the dependent continuant 'market value.'
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts market value is a dependent continuant and names the field of recognition as what sustains it.

claims.claim: Economic volatility is ontological volatility.
claims.source_quote: Economic volatility is thus ontological volatility: a fluctuation in the field of recognition that sustains the dependent continuant 'market value.'
claims.note: Author asserts identity/equivalence between economic and ontological volatility.

claims.claim: Price is the quantification of recognition.
claims.source_quote: price appears as the quantification of recognition. It is the numerical form in which the degree of collective acknowledgment is expressed.
claims.note: Asserts a property/identity of price in relation to recognition.

claims.claim: Price is a representation of the equilibrium achieved through exchange.
claims.source_quote: A price is not identical to value but a representation of the equilibrium achieved through exchange.
claims.note: Asserts what price is ontologically (a representation), distinguishing it from value.

claims.claim: Price is a public signal of recognition coherence.
claims.source_quote: It serves as a public signal of recognition coherence, a token indicating that, within the current configuration of property and institution, a given object is acknowledged as possessing a specific relational worth.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/property of price.

claims.claim: Value belongs to the domain of ontology, while price belongs to the domain of measurement.
claims.source_quote: while price belongs to the domain of measurement, value belongs to the domain of ontology.
claims.note: Asserts a categorical distinction between value and price in ontological terms.

claims.claim: Price is an information artifact; value is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: The two are related as information artifact to dependent continuant: the former records the latter's realization in a form transmissible across agents and systems.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kinds that price and value respectively belong to.

claims.claim: Value arises from socially sustained recognition.
claims.source_quote: Because value arises from socially sustained recognition, it is susceptible to asymmetry and exclusion.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the genesis/dependence relation of value.

claims.claim: The ontology of value is inseparable from the politics of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Thus, the ontology of value is inseparable from the politics of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive/inseparability relation between ontological and political dimensions of value.

claims.claim: Redistribution, market regulation, and cultural change are processes of ontological recalibration.
claims.source_quote: Redistribution, market regulation, and even cultural change are, at their core, processes of ontological recalibration, attempts to reshape the dependencies that produce and maintain value.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind/nature of these social processes.

claims.claim: When agents lack a shared field of recognition, exchange becomes ontologically impossible.
claims.source_quote: When two agents do not share a coherent field of recognition, when their systems of property, currency, or obligation do not align, exchange becomes ontologically impossible.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for exchange as an ontological matter.

claims.claim: Without reciprocal recognition, no value is realized in a transfer.
claims.source_quote: The objects may still change hands, but no value is realized because the transfer lacks reciprocal recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for value realization.

claims.claim: Use-value and exchange-value are both realizations of property's relational capacities.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, however, both are realizations of property's relational capacities.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological status and shared nature of use-value and exchange-value.

claims.claim: Use-value and exchange-value are different modes of relation, not different substances.
claims.source_quote: The two are not different substances but different modes of relation: one internal, the other intersubjective.
claims.note: Asserts a categorical claim about the ontological nature of use-value and exchange-value.

claims.claim: Value is the institutional realization of phenomenological potential.
claims.source_quote: Thus, value is the institutional realization of phenomenological potential.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between value and phenomenological potential.

claims.claim: Value is the structured possibility of meaningful interaction among things, sustained by collective recognition encoded in law.
claims.source_quote: It is the structured possibility of meaningful interaction among things, sustained not by individual consciousness but by collective recognition encoded in law.
claims.note: Asserts what value is ontologically and what sustains it.

claims.claim: Property transforms subjective intentionality into objective social reality.
claims.source_quote: In this respect, property transforms subjective intentionality into objective social reality.
claims.note: Asserts a transformative causal/ontological function of property.

claims.claim: Digital assets, trademarks, and data sets possess value because they are embedded in networks of institutional and social recognition.
claims.source_quote: Digital assets, trademarks, data sets, and even social media 'influence' possess value because they are embedded in networks of institutional and social recognition that assign and sustain rights over them.
claims.note: Asserts the source and condition of value for immaterial entities.

claims.claim: The worth of immaterial entities is relational, not intrinsic.
claims.source_quote: Their worth is not intrinsic but relational, deriving from the coherence and scope of the recognition field that supports them.
claims.note: Asserts a property of immaterial entities regarding the nature of their worth.

claims.claim: When recognition falters, value dissipates.
claims.source_quote: When recognition falters, when a platform collapses or legal rights expire, the value dissipates.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: value depends on recognition for its continued existence.

claims.claim: Collapses of value are the dissolution of dependent continuants no longer sustained by institutional acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, such collapses are not mysterious market events but the dissolution of dependent continuants no longer sustained by institutional acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of value collapses.

claims.claim: Value is not an emergent property of matter but of relation.
claims.source_quote: value is not an emergent property of matter but of relation.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological category from which value emerges.

claims.claim: The world of value is the world of recognized dependency.
claims.source_quote: The world of value is the world of recognized dependency: of institutions maintaining coherence among agents, norms, and things.
claims.note: Asserts an identity/characterization of the domain of value.

claims.claim: Law furnishes the conditions for the realization of value.
claims.source_quote: Law does not create value ex nihilo, but it furnishes the conditions for its realization.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/relational role of law with respect to value realization.

claims.claim: Through recognition, registration, and enforcement, law renders property capable of bearing value.
claims.source_quote: Through recognition, registration, and enforcement, law renders property capable of functioning as a bearer of value.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/enabling relation between law and property's capacity to bear value.

claims.claim: The economic system is an ontological extension of the legal system.
claims.source_quote: The economic system is thus not an independent sphere but an ontological extension of the legal system, a dynamic field in which law's structures of recognition generate, distribute, and sustain value.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive ontological relation between the economic and legal systems.

claims.claim: Property is a foundational mechanism through which social value is generated and maintained.
claims.source_quote: Property is not merely a juridical category but a foundational mechanism through which social value is generated and maintained.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/ontological role of property.

claims.claim: Property is a relational continuant.
claims.source_quote: Property, as a relational continuant, is not confined to a single ontological domain.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind that property belongs to.

claims.claim: Property exists across multiple layers of reality: material, informational, and digital.
claims.source_quote: It exists across multiple layers of reality, including material, informational, and digital, each with its own modes of recognition, realization, and persistence.
claims.note: Asserts that property has existence across multiple ontological layers.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence condition and ontological characterization of intangible entities.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities are not material objects but structures of information and code.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation and that are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.note: The author directly asserts what intangible/virtual entities are ontologically: structures of information and code, not material objects.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities persist only through institutional and technological mediation.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation and that are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.note: The author asserts a property/condition of these entities: their persistence depends on institutional and technological mediation.

claims.claim: Intangible or virtual entities are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.source_quote: These entities are not material objects but structures of information and code that persist only through institutional and technological mediation and that are realized in a variety of material forms.
claims.note: The author asserts a realization relation between intangible/virtual entities and material forms.

claims.claim: Ownership is a recognized dependency relation.
claims.source_quote: one must trace how the same relational form, ownership as a recognized dependency, adapts across these layered domains of being.
claims.note: The author characterizes ownership ontologically as a relational form — a recognized dependency — asserting its nature as a relation.

claims.claim: Tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.source_quote: At the most fundamental level, tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.note: The author asserts a domain-membership claim: tangible property belongs to the ontological category of material continuants.

claims.claim: The verdict is a dependent continuant that anchors subsequent institutional acts.
claims.source_quote: The resulting verdict becomes part of law's ontology, an enduring dependent continuant that anchors subsequent institutional acts such as sentencing, enforcement, or appeal.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the verdict's kind and relational function.

claims.claim: The trial creates facts of law rather than revealing preexisting facts of nature.
claims.source_quote: The experiment seeks to reveal preexisting facts of nature; the trial creates facts of law.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive property distinguishing the trial as an entity-creating mechanism.

claims.claim: Each judgment constitutes a new entity within the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Each judgment constitutes a new entity within the legal world, a recognized fact with enduring effects.
claims.note: Asserts existence of a new entity produced by judgment.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is a recognized fact with enduring effects.
claims.source_quote: Each judgment constitutes a new entity within the legal world, a recognized fact with enduring effects.
claims.note: Asserts a property (enduring effects) of the kind 'recognized fact' that is juridical truth.

claims.claim: The consensus achieved through trial is a relational continuant distributed across institutions, agents, and artifacts.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, the consensus achieved through trial is a relational continuant distributed across institutions, agents, and artifacts (records, judgments, laws).
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of trial consensus as a relational continuant.

claims.claim: The consensus achieved through trial is a socially instantiated field of coherence.
claims.source_quote: It is a socially instantiated field of coherence that endures through institutional reproduction.
claims.note: Asserts a kind and property of the trial consensus entity.

claims.claim: The trial is a socially distributed cognitive process that produces juridical knowledge.
claims.source_quote: The trial thus functions as a socially distributed cognitive process, producing juridical knowledge through controlled interaction.
claims.note: Asserts the trial's kind (distributed cognitive process) and its function.

claims.claim: The judge, jury, advocate, and witness are epistemic mechanisms within the trial.
claims.source_quote: Within this framework, the roles of participants, such as judge, jury, advocate, and witness, are themselves epistemic mechanisms.
claims.note: Asserts that participant roles are a subkind of epistemic mechanism.

claims.claim: The advocate's function is to construct and challenge evidential continuants.
claims.source_quote: The advocate's task is to construct and challenge evidential continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the advocate role.

claims.claim: The witness's role is to supply data that can be transformed into evidence.
claims.source_quote: the witness's role is to supply data that can be transformed into evidence.
claims.note: Asserts the functional property of the witness role.

claims.claim: The judge's role is to maintain procedural integrity.
claims.source_quote: the judge's is to maintain procedural integrity.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the judge role.

claims.claim: The jury's role is to synthesize recognition into a verdict.
claims.source_quote: and the jury's is to synthesize recognition into a verdict.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of the jury role.

claims.claim: Malfunction of participant roles results in epistemic collapse—a failure of the trial's ontological function.
claims.source_quote: When they malfunction, through bias, corruption, or incompetence, the result is epistemic collapse, a failure of the trial's ontological function to produce recognized coherence.
claims.note: Asserts that role malfunction produces an ontological failure state (epistemic collapse).

claims.claim: Appeals, reviews, and retrials are secondary realization events designed to restore coherence.
claims.source_quote: Appeals, reviews, and retrials are not merely administrative safeguards; they are secondary realization events designed to restore coherence when recognition fails.
claims.note: Asserts a kind (secondary realization events) and function of appellate processes.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is conditionally stable, enduring as long as the network of recognition remains coherent.
claims.source_quote: Truth in law is not immutable but conditionally stable, enduring as long as the network of recognition that sustains it remains coherent.
claims.note: Asserts a property (conditional stability) of juridical truth as an entity.

claims.claim: The ethical duty to testify honestly, argue faithfully, and judge impartially is an ontological condition for juridical truth's existence.
claims.source_quote: The ethical duty to testify honestly, to argue faithfully, and to judge impartially is not an external moral demand but an ontological condition for truth's existence.
claims.note: Asserts these duties bear the relation of ontological condition to juridical truth.

claims.claim: Miscarriages of justice are ontological ruptures that produce entities that should not exist as legal truths.
claims.source_quote: Miscarriages of justice, in this view, are not simply factual errors but ontological ruptures: failures of recognition that produce entities (verdicts, records, precedents) that should not exist as legal truths.
claims.note: Asserts a kind (ontological ruptures) and a constitutive property of miscarriages of justice.

claims.claim: Trials allow communities to stabilize truth, as language stabilizes meaning and markets stabilize value.
claims.source_quote: Just as language allows communities to stabilize meaning, and markets allow them to stabilize value, trials allow them to stabilize truth.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of trials as truth-stabilizing institutions.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is a distinct ontological achievement: the manifestation of coherence through procedural recognition.
claims.source_quote: Thus, juridical truth is neither illusion nor compromise but a distinct ontological achievement: the manifestation of coherence through procedural recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a kind and constitutive description of juridical truth.

claims.claim: Trials constitute one of the ways social reality is maintained.
claims.source_quote: Trials do not merely reflect reality; they constitute one of the ways reality is socially maintained.
claims.note: Asserts that trials bear a constitutive relation to social reality.

claims.claim: Juridical truth is fallible because it depends on recognition rather than direct correspondence with the world.
claims.source_quote: Because law's ontology depends on recognition rather than direct correspondence with the world, the possibility of error is built into its structure.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property (built-in fallibility) of juridical truth.

claims.claim: A misrecognition is a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it describes.
claims.source_quote: the result is a misrecognition: a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.note: Defines misrecognition as an entity-kind with a specific relational failure property.

claims.claim: Uncertainty is an internal and necessary feature of juridical truth, not an external flaw.
claims.source_quote: we must therefore account for uncertainty not as a flaw external to law, but as an internal and necessary f[eature].
claims.note: Asserts a property (internal necessity) of uncertainty within law's ontology.

claims.claim: Law's reality is sustained by collective commitment to recognition rather than by discovery.
claims.source_quote: Law's reality is sustained not by discovery but by collective commitment to recognition.
claims.note: Asserts what sustains law's reality—a claim about the ontological ground of legal entities.

claims.claim: The trial is law's analogue to the experiment in science.
claims.source_quote: In this sense, the trial is law's analogue to the experiment in science, but with a critical difference.
claims.note: Asserts a structural analogy-relation between trial and experiment; the 'critical difference' qualifies but does not negate the relational claim.

claims.claim: Institutional closure is necessary for law's function of providing a stable domain of recognized facts.
claims.source_quote: This closure is not arbitrary but necessary for law's function: society requires a stable domain of recognized facts upon which obligations and rights can rest.
claims.note: Asserts a functional necessity property of institutional closure.

claims.claim: Misrecognition is a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.source_quote: the result is a misrecognition: a failure of the system to maintain coherence between the field of recognition and the events it purports to describe.
claims.note: The author defines misrecognition as a specific kind of failure, asserting what misrecognition is—an ontological claim about its nature.

claims.claim: Uncertainty is an internal and necessary feature of law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: we must therefore account for uncertainty not as a flaw external to law, but as an internal and necessary feature of its ontology.
claims.note: The author asserts a property of law's ontology: uncertainty belongs to it necessarily and internally.

claims.claim: Uncertainty arises whenever the dependencies that sustain a legal fact are incomplete or unstable.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, uncertainty arises whenever the dependencies that sustain a legal fact are incomplete or unstable.
claims.note: The author asserts a causal/constitutive relation: incomplete or unstable dependencies produce uncertainty in legal facts.

claims.claim: Legal facts are sustained by dependencies.
claims.source_quote: the dependencies that sustain a legal fact are incomplete or unstable.
claims.note: The author commits to the existence of dependencies that sustain legal facts—an ontological claim about the structure of legal facts.

claims.claim: A verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority, must align coherently for juridical truth to exist.
claims.note: The author categorizes these entities as dependent continuants—a subkind claim within a formal ontology.

claims.claim: Juridical truth exists only when dependent continuants constituting it align coherently.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority, must align coherently for juridical truth to exist.
claims.note: The author asserts a necessary condition for the existence of juridical truth—an ontological claim about what constitutes it.

claims.claim: Dependent continuants constitute juridical truth.
claims.source_quote: The dependent continuants that constitute a verdict, recognition of evidence, roles, and institutional authority, must align coherently for juridical truth to exist.
claims.note: The author asserts a constitution relation between dependent continuants and juridical truth.

claims.claim: Tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.source_quote: At the most fundamental level, tangible property occupies the domain of material continuants.
claims.note: Direct assertion that a kind of property belongs to a particular ontological domain.

claims.claim: Material continuants are independent continuants in BFO terms.
claims.source_quote: These are independent continuants in BFO terms: physical objects that exist regardless of recognition, though their status as property depends on it.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation: material continuants are independent continuants.

claims.claim: Physical objects exist regardless of recognition.
claims.source_quote: These are independent continuants in BFO terms: physical objects that exist regardless of recognition, though their status as property depends on it.
claims.note: Asserts a property of physical objects regarding their mode of existence.

claims.claim: The status of a physical object as property depends on recognition.
claims.source_quote: physical objects that exist regardless of recognition, though their status as property depends on it.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between property status and recognition.

claims.claim: The property relation links an owner, a thing owned, and an institutional framework.
claims.source_quote: The property relation here links the agent (owner), the object (thing owned), and the institutional framework that sustains recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the relational structure of the property relation with its three relata.

claims.claim: The material substrate of tangible property gives it distinctive stability.
claims.source_quote: The persistence of the object's material substrate gives tangible property a distinctive stability: even if recognition lapses, the physical entity remains available for reappropriation.
claims.note: Asserts a property (stability) of tangible property grounded in its material substrate.

claims.claim: Even if recognition lapses, the physical entity of tangible property remains available for reappropriation.
claims.source_quote: even if recognition lapses, the physical entity remains available for reappropriation and is susceptible to occupation or physical control.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of physical entities.

claims.claim: Intangible property occupies the domain of informational and conceptual continuants.
claims.source_quote: Intangible property, by contrast, occupies the domain of informational and conceptual continuants, entities that exist not as physical things but as structured content or form.
claims.note: Asserts a domain-membership claim for intangible property.

claims.claim: Informational and conceptual continuants exist as structured content or form, not as physical things.
claims.source_quote: entities that exist not as physical things but as structured content or form.
claims.note: Asserts a property distinguishing informational continuants from physical objects.

claims.claim: Copyrights, patents, trademarks, and debts are information content entities embedded in institutional recognition structures.
claims.source_quote: Copyrights, patents, trademarks, and debts are not objects in the material sense but information content entities (ICEs) embedded in institutional recognition structures.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim for specific legal entities.

claims.claim: Intangible property exists only through systems that encode and sustain it.
claims.source_quote: They exist only through the systems that encode and sustain them: registries, ledgers, databases, and enforcement mechanisms.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of intangible property on institutional systems.

claims.claim: A patent inheres in the institutional continuant of the patent office and the legal system.
claims.source_quote: A patent, for example, exists as a recognized right to exclude others from using a specific innovation; it inheres in the institutional continuant of the patent office and the legal system that enforces it.
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between a patent and an institutional continuant.

claims.claim: A patent's being depends on recognition distributed across institutions.
claims.source_quote: Its being depends on recognition distributed across these institutions, realized through procedural occurrents such as filing, examination, and granting.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency relation for patents.

claims.claim: Filing, examination, and granting are procedural occurrents that realize patent recognition.
claims.source_quote: realized through procedural occurrents such as filing, examination, and granting.
claims.note: Asserts that these procedures are occurrents and that they realize recognition.

claims.claim: When recognition of intangible property ceases, the intangible property ceases to exist as law.
claims.source_quote: When recognition ceases, through lapse, expiration, or legal invalidation, the intangible property ceases to exist as law, though its informational substrate may remain.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency: cessation of recognition causes cessation of legal existence.

claims.claim: Digital property includes software licenses, cryptocurrency tokens, domain names, and virtual goods.
claims.source_quote: Digital property includes software licenses, cryptocurrency tokens, domain names, and virtual goods in online environments.
claims.note: Asserts that these entities are instances of the kind 'digital property'.

claims.claim: Digital property entities are computational continuants sustained by technological and institutional dependencies.
claims.source_quote: they are computational continuants, structured states of digital systems sustained by both technological and institutional dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership and dependency property for digital property entities.

claims.claim: Digital property entities are generically dependent continuants realized through coordinated functioning of hardware, software, and institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, they are generically dependent continuants realized through the coordinated functioning of hardware, software, and institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a BFO kind-membership and realization relation for digital property.

claims.claim: A digital token exists only as long as the blockchain encoding it remains operational and recognized as authoritative.
claims.source_quote: A digital token, for instance, exists only as long as the blockchain that encodes it remains operational and recognized as authoritative.
claims.note: Asserts an existential dependency of a digital token on its blockchain.

claims.claim: Ownership of a digital token is defined by control over cryptographic credentials.
claims.source_quote: Its ownership is defined by control over cryptographic credentials, which serve as procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive property of digital token ownership.

claims.claim: Cryptographic credentials are procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.source_quote: which serve as procedural realizations of recognition within the digital system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/realization role for cryptographic credentials.

claims.claim: Technical recognition in cryptocurrencies achieves legal reality only when acknowledged by institutional systems.
claims.source_quote: this technical recognition only achieves legal reality when it is acknowledged by institutional systems, when courts, regulators, or markets accept blockchain records as evidence of ownership.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between technical and institutional recognition for legal existence.

claims.claim: The being of digital assets depends on both algorithmic and institutional recognition forming a hybrid system.
claims.source_quote: The ontological chain thus runs from algorithmic recognition to institutional recognition, forming a hybrid system of dependence. Law and technology together sustain the being of digital assets.
claims.note: Asserts a complex dependency structure sustaining the existence of digital assets.

claims.claim: A software program is both a work of authorship and a functional system realized through computational hardware.
claims.source_quote: A software program is both a work of authorship (intangible property protected by copyright) and a functional system (digital property realized through execution on computational hardware).
claims.note: Asserts that software simultaneously instantiates two ontological kinds.

claims.claim: The same software entity exists simultaneously across different ontological layers, each sustained by its own recognition structure.
claims.source_quote: The same entity exists simultaneously across different ontological layers, each sustained by its own recognition structure.
claims.note: Asserts a property of software entities regarding multi-layer ontological existence.

claims.claim: Data are information artifacts: structured representations of entities, events, or relations.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, data are information artifacts, structured representations of entities, events, or relations.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership claim for data.

claims.claim: Data are generically dependent continuants that can exist in multiple copies simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Because data are generically dependent continuants that can exist in multiple copies simultaneously, property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.note: Asserts a BFO kind-membership and a dispositional property for data.

claims.claim: Property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.source_quote: property over data must be defined by recognition of authority rather than exclusivity.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive property of data ownership.

claims.claim: The owner of data is the agent recognized as controlling its flow within institutional systems.
claims.source_quote: The owner of data is, in effect, the agent recognized as controlling its flow within these systems.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive identity claim about the owner of data.

claims.claim: A virtual sword or parcel of digital land exists only as an aggregation of code instantiated within a software platform.
claims.source_quote: A virtual sword or parcel of digital land exists only as an aggregation of code instantiated within a software platform.
claims.note: Asserts the constitutive composition and existential dependency of virtual property.

claims.claim: Virtual property exemplifies nested recognition: recognition within a virtual environment further sustained by the legal system.
claims.source_quote: Virtual property therefore exemplifies nested recognition: an entity recognized within one ontological layer (the virtual environment) whose reality is further sustained by another (the legal system).
claims.note: Asserts a structural property (nested recognition) of virtual property as an ontological claim.

claims.claim: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is their relational form, not their substance.
claims.source_quote: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is not their substance but their relational form.
claims.note: Asserts a unifying relational property across different kinds of property.

claims.claim: Ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object, and a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: In each case, ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object (physical, informational, or virtual), and a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the fundamental relational structure of ownership as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Tangible, intangible, and digital property are unified by their relational form, not their substance.
claims.source_quote: What unifies tangible, intangible, and digital property is not their substance but their relational form.
claims.note: Direct assertion about what unifies kinds of property—an ontological claim about their nature.

claims.claim: Ownership exists as a dependency relation linking an agent, an object, and a system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: In each case, ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object (physical, informational, or virtual), and a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological structure of ownership as a specific relational dependency.

claims.claim: Objects in ownership relations can be physical, informational, or virtual.
claims.source_quote: ownership exists as a dependency linking an agent, an object (physical, informational, or virtual), and a system of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that the object-relatum of ownership can be of three distinct kinds.
