claims.claim: Every legal entity exists only insofar as it inheres in a bearer and depends on recognition for its persistence.
claims.source_quote: every legal entity, whether an obligation, right, or institutional role, can be represented as a dependent continuant: an entity that exists only insofar as it inheres in a bearer (such as an agent, institution, or document) and depends on recognition for its persistence.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological structure of legal entities as dependent continuants with specific existence conditions.

claims.claim: Every legal entity is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: every legal entity, whether an obligation, right, or institutional role, can be represented as a dependent continuant
claims.note: The author uses 'can be represented as' but the surrounding argument commits to this as a genuine ontological claim, not merely a representational convenience.

claims.claim: Obligations are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: In OWL, an 'Obligation' can be formally declared as a subclass of 'DependentContinuant,' realized in 'LegalProcess,' and inhering in 'LegalAgent.'
claims.note: The author endorses this formal modeling as reflecting real ontological structure, not merely arbitrary symbolism.

claims.claim: Obligations are realized in legal processes.
claims.source_quote: an 'Obligation' can be formally declared as a subclass of 'DependentContinuant,' realized in 'LegalProcess,' and inhering in 'LegalAgent.'
claims.note: The author endorses the realization relation between obligations and legal processes as ontologically grounded.

claims.claim: Obligations inhere in legal agents.
claims.source_quote: an 'Obligation' can be formally declared as a subclass of 'DependentContinuant,' realized in 'LegalProcess,' and inhering in 'LegalAgent.'
claims.note: The author endorses the inherence relation as reflecting genuine ontological dependence.

claims.claim: A legal role is a dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: a 'Role' can be modeled as a dependent continuant that specifies the conditions under which an agent participates in institutional continuants.
claims.note: The author endorses this model as ontologically accurate, not merely representational.

claims.claim: A contract is a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants such as obligations and permissions.
claims.source_quote: A contract is not simply a text but a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants (obligations, permissions) that are realized through occurrents (signing, performance, enforcement).
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts this as an ontological fact, contrasting it with the naive view that a contract is merely a text.

claims.claim: Obligations and permissions are parts of a contract.
claims.source_quote: a legal continuant composed of dependent continuants (obligations, permissions)
claims.note: Direct assertion of a part-whole or composition relation between contracts and their normative components.

claims.claim: Contracts are realized through occurrents such as signing, performance, and enforcement.
claims.source_quote: that are realized through occurrents (signing, performance, enforcement).
claims.note: The author asserts a realization relation between contractual continuants and legal occurrents.

claims.claim: A contract is a subclass of LegalDocument, which is a continuant.
claims.source_quote: Contract (class) ? subclass of LegalDocument (continuant).
claims.note: The author presents this as part of a formal ontological model that corresponds to real ontological structures.

claims.claim: A signing event is a legal occurrent that links agents to obligations.
claims.source_quote: SigningEvent (class) ? subclass of LegalOccurrent, linking Agent to Obligation through creates or activates property.
claims.note: The author asserts this classification and relational role as reflecting genuine ontological structure.

claims.claim: An institution is an institutional continuant defined by recognition and enforcement relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) ? subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: The author asserts the ontological kind and defining relational properties of institutions.

claims.claim: The entities encoded in OWL and RDF correspond to real ontological structures.
claims.source_quote: The entities that OWL and RDF encode are not arbitrary symbols but correspond to real ontological structures: continuants, occurrents, and their interdependencies.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts ontological realism about the entities represented in formal legal ontologies.

claims.claim: Computational systems can participate in legal processes only when embedded within recognized institutional roles.
claims.source_quote: computational systems can participate in legal processes only insofar as they are embedded within recognized institutional roles.
claims.note: The author asserts a condition on the legal participation of computational systems—an ontological constraint on their role.

claims.claim: Human-institutional mediation is necessary in any legitimate legal AI system.
claims.source_quote: the necessity of human-institutional mediation in any legitimate legal AI system.
claims.note: The author asserts a necessary property or condition that any legitimate legal AI system must satisfy.

claims.claim: Obligation is a subclass of DependentContinuant.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) ? subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion in the author's ontological schema.

claims.claim: Obligation inheres in an agent as its bearer.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) ? subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Asserts a relation (inheresIn) between Obligation and Agent.

claims.claim: Obligation is realized in a performance event.
claims.source_quote: Obligation (class) ? subclass of DependentContinuant, with properties inheresIn (bearer: agent) and realizedIn (event: performance).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between Obligation and a performance event.

claims.claim: SigningEvent is a subclass of LegalOccurrent.
claims.source_quote: SigningEvent (class) ? subclass of LegalOccurrent, linking Agent to Obligation through creates or activates property.
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion in the author's ontological schema.

claims.claim: Institution is a subclass of InstitutionalContinuant.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) ? subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion in the author's ontological schema.

claims.claim: Institution has the properties of recognizing and enforcing obligations and rights.
claims.source_quote: Institution (class) ? subclass of InstitutionalContinuant, defined by recognizes and enforces relations toward obligations and rights.
claims.note: Asserts functional/relational properties of Institution as an entity kind.

claims.claim: A properly constructed legal ontology instantiates justice as structural integrity.
claims.source_quote: A legal ontology capable of maintaining these properties effectively instantiates justice as structural integrity within the digital domain.
claims.note: Asserts that a legal ontology (an entity) bears the property of instantiating justice as structural integrity.

claims.claim: Legal ontologies encode deontic dependencies rather than factual dependencies.
claims.source_quote: In legal ontologies, by contrast, relations encode deontic dependencies, conditional necessities linking agents, roles, and acts.
claims.note: Asserts a distinguishing property of legal ontologies as entity kinds.

claims.claim: Deontic dependencies are modal rather than factual.
claims.source_quote: These dependencies are modal rather than factual: they specify what ought to occur within a recognized institutional framework.
claims.note: Asserts a property (modal) of deontic dependencies as entities.

claims.claim: Roles are realizable dependent continuants in BFO terms.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, roles are realizable dependent continuants that inhere in bearers (agents) and are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.note: Asserts a subkind relation: roles are a kind of realizable dependent continuant.

claims.claim: Roles inhere in agents as their bearers.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, roles are realizable dependent continuants that inhere in bearers (agents) and are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between roles and agents.

claims.claim: Roles are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, roles are realizable dependent continuants that inhere in bearers (agents) and are realized through occurrents (acts).
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between roles and acts/occurrents.

claims.claim: Role is a subkind of RealizableEntity.
claims.source_quote: – Role ? RealizableEntity
claims.note: Direct subkind assertion in the author's formal ontological schema.

claims.claim: A Role inheres in an Agent.
claims.source_quote: – inheresIn (Role, Agent)
claims.note: Asserts an inherence relation between Role and Agent in the author's schema.

claims.claim: A Role is realized in an InstitutionalProcess.
claims.source_quote: – realizedIn (Role, InstitutionalProcess)
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between Role and InstitutionalProcess.

claims.claim: Institution has the function of realizing roles.
claims.source_quote: – hasFunction(Institution, RealizationOfRole)
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of Institution as an entity.

claims.claim: Roles represent the dynamic interface between agents and institutions.
claims.source_quote: Roles represent the dynamic interface between agents and institutions, the means through which legal systems connect individual action to institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/functional property of roles as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Machines can simulate recognition but cannot confer it.
claims.source_quote: Machines may simulate recognition, but only institutions can confer it.
claims.note: Asserts a property of machines (simulate but not confer recognition) and a distinguishing property of institutions.

claims.claim: Only institutions can confer legal recognition.
claims.source_quote: Machines may simulate recognition, but only institutions can confer it.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/causal property exclusive to institutions.

claims.claim: Formal ontology provides the bridge between legal reasoning and artificial intelligence.
claims.source_quote: Formal ontology thus provides the bridge between legal reasoning and artificial intelligence.
claims.note: Asserts a relational/functional property of formal ontology as an entity kind.

claims.claim: Digitization of law is an extension of the project of justice.
claims.source_quote: In this sense, the ongoing digitization of law is an extension of the very project of justice.
claims.note: Asserts a relation (extension of) between digitization of law and the project of justice.

claims.claim: Legal authority, jurisdiction, institutional roles, procedure, temporal ordering, legal effects, correlativity between rights and duties, and remedies are elements of legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: Legal authority, jurisdiction, institutional roles, procedure, temporal ordering, legal effects, correlativity between rights and duties, and the availability of remedies have been treated thus far as distinct elements of legal ontology.
claims.note: The author positively asserts these as elements of legal ontology, not merely as topics under discussion.

claims.claim: The Minimum Legal Chain specifies necessary conditions under which legal acts come into being as law.
claims.source_quote: This structure, which I will refer to as the Minimum Legal Chain, specifies the necessary conditions under which legal acts can come into being as law rather than as mere exercises of power.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological role and function of the Minimum Legal Chain.

claims.claim: Institutional failure and injustice arise from breakdowns within the Minimum Legal Chain.
claims.source_quote: Institutional failure and injustice arise not simply from bad outcomes or moral error, but from breakdowns within this chain that prevent legal relations from being coherently sustained over time.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/structural relation between chain breakdowns and institutional failure.

claims.claim: Contradiction is a structural feature of social being, not merely logical or moral inconsistency.
claims.source_quote: Within the framework developed throughout this work, contradiction is not merely meant to indicate logical or moral inconsistency but rather a structural feature of social being.
claims.note: Author defines and asserts the ontological nature of contradiction in his own voice.

claims.claim: Contradiction consists in tension among overlapping obligations, rights, and recognitions that cannot all be simultaneously satisfied.
claims.source_quote: ...the tension among overlapping obligations, rights, and recognitions that cannot all be satisfied simultaneously.
claims.note: Author gives a positive ontological definition of contradiction as a specific kind of structural tension.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt is a latent imbalance within the network of recognition that threatens systemic coherence if unresolved.
claims.source_quote: These tensions accumulate as what I described in The Geometry of the Good as contradiction debt, a latent imbalance within the network of recognition that, if unresolved, threatens systemic coherence.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence and nature of contradiction debt as an ontological condition.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt arises when dependent continuants bear incompatible realization conditions.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, contradiction debt arises whenever dependent continuants, such as obligations, permissions, or property rights, bear incompatible realization conditions.
claims.note: Explicit positive ontological assertion about the conditions of contradiction debt.

claims.claim: Obligations, permissions, and property rights are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: ...dependent continuants, such as obligations, permissions, or property rights, bear incompatible realization conditions.
claims.note: Author asserts obligations, permissions, and property rights are instances of the ontological category of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Contradiction exists within the network of relations that constitute law's ontology, not merely epistemically.
claims.source_quote: The contradiction is not epistemic but structural: it exists within the network of relations that constitute law's ontology.
claims.note: Author positively asserts the ontological (not merely epistemic) location of contradiction.

claims.claim: Each conflicting obligation continues to exist as a recognized entity while contradiction debt accumulates.
claims.source_quote: Each conflicting obligation continues to exist as a recognized entity, and the debt between them accumulates until resolved through repair.
claims.note: Author asserts that conflicting obligations persist as entities and that debt accumulates between them.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt is measurable by the degree to which recognition dependencies overlap without coherence.
claims.source_quote: ...contradiction is a form of ontological tension, measurable not in moral terms but in the degree to which recognition dependencies overlap without coherence.
claims.note: Author asserts a property (measurability) and a measure (overlap of recognition dependencies) of contradiction debt.

claims.claim: Repair processes are occurrents that restore coherence by recalibrating dependencies among legal continuants.
claims.source_quote: ...these are not merely cognitive acts but repair processes: occurrents that restore coherence by recalibrating dependencies among legal continuants.
claims.note: Author categorizes repair processes as occurrents and asserts their function ontologically.

claims.claim: Repair transforms the structure of recognition, redefining which entities continue to exist as valid within the legal world.
claims.source_quote: Repair transforms the structure of recognition, redefining which entities continue to exist as valid within the legal world.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological effect of repair on the structure of legal recognition and entity existence.

claims.claim: Laws that persist despite the withdrawal of social legitimacy become ontologically hollow.
claims.source_quote: Laws that persist despite the withdrawal of social legitimacy...become ontologically hollow: they exist formally but lack coherent support within the wider field of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological property (hollowness) of laws that lack social recognition support.

claims.claim: Misalignment between social and legal recognition generates instability manifesting as dissent, noncompliance, or crisis.
claims.source_quote: This misalignment generates instability, manifesting as public dissent, noncompliance, or institutional crisis.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal relation between ontological misalignment and social phenomena.

claims.claim: Legislative amendment and judicial reinterpretation are ontological necessities through which law sustains its being.
claims.source_quote: Thus, legislative amendment and judicial reinterpretation are not merely pragmatic tools but ontological necessities, mechanisms through which law sustains its being in a changing world.
claims.note: Author positively asserts the ontological status and function of legislative and judicial actions.

claims.claim: Two obligations inhering in the same agent as dependent continuants create structural inconsistency when their realizations are incompatible.
claims.source_quote: Both O₁ and O₂ inhere in A as dependent continuants and depend on distinct institutional recognitions. Their coexistence creates a structural inconsistency within A's role realization.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological relation (inherence) and a structural property (inconsistency) arising from it.

claims.claim: Courts, legislatures, and administrative agencies are repair organs within the ontological organism of law.
claims.source_quote: Courts, legislatures, and administrative agencies are therefore not merely decision-making bodies but repair organs within the ontological organism of law.
claims.note: Author asserts a role/function of these institutions within legal ontology.

claims.claim: The function of courts, legislatures, and agencies is to manage contradiction debt through iterative recognition and correction.
claims.source_quote: Their collective function is to manage contradiction debt through iterative recognition and correction, ensuring that the network of legal dependencies remains coherent despite internal strain.
claims.note: Author asserts the collective function of legal institutions in ontological terms.

claims.claim: The magnitude of contradiction debt within a system correlates with its capacity for pluralism.
claims.source_quote: The magnitude of contradiction debt within a system correlates with its capacity for pluralism.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational property between contradiction debt magnitude and pluralism capacity.

claims.claim: Pluralist systems generate more contradiction but also possess greater repair capacity.
claims.source_quote: Pluralist systems, those that tolerate overlapping norms, jurisdictions, and values, necessarily generate more contradiction but also possess greater repair capacity.
claims.note: Author asserts properties of pluralist systems regarding contradiction generation and repair capacity.

claims.claim: Authoritarian systems minimize contradiction by suppressing alternative recognitions, at the cost of rigidity and fragility.
claims.source_quote: Authoritarian systems, by contrast, minimize contradiction by suppressing alternative recognitions, but at the cost of rigidity and fragility.
claims.note: Author asserts properties and mechanisms of authoritarian systems in ontological terms.

claims.claim: Justice is the structural integrity of a legal system: its capacity to recognize, correct, and absorb contradiction without collapse.
claims.source_quote: Justice is defined not as distributive fairness or moral correctness, but as structural integrity: the capacity of a system to recognize, correct, and absorb contradiction without collapse.
claims.note: Author provides a positive ontological definition of justice as a structural property of legal systems.

claims.claim: Justice is a dynamic property of legal architecture rather than an external evaluative standard.
claims.source_quote: This analysis reframes justice as a dynamic property of legal architecture rather than an external evaluative standard.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological status of justice as an internal, dynamic property of legal systems.

claims.claim: Pluralist systems tolerate overlapping norms, jurisdictions, and values.
claims.source_quote: Pluralist systems, those that tolerate overlapping norms, jurisdictions, and values, necessarily generate more contradiction but also possess greater repair capacity.
claims.note: Asserts a defining property of pluralist systems as entities.

claims.claim: Pluralist systems necessarily generate more contradiction than non-pluralist systems.
claims.source_quote: Pluralist systems, those that tolerate overlapping norms, jurisdictions, and values, necessarily generate more contradiction but also possess greater repair capacity.
claims.note: Asserts a property (contradiction generation) of pluralist systems.

claims.claim: Pluralist systems possess greater repair capacity than authoritarian systems.
claims.source_quote: Pluralist systems, those that tolerate overlapping norms, jurisdictions, and values, necessarily generate more contradiction but also possess greater repair capacity.
claims.note: Asserts a comparative property (repair capacity) of pluralist systems.

claims.claim: Authoritarian systems minimize contradiction by suppressing alternative recognitions.
claims.source_quote: Authoritarian systems, by contrast, minimize contradiction by suppressing alternative recognitions, but at the cost of rigidity and fragility.
claims.note: Asserts a property and mechanism of authoritarian systems as entities.

claims.claim: Authoritarian systems have the properties of rigidity and fragility.
claims.source_quote: Authoritarian systems, by contrast, minimize contradiction by suppressing alternative recognitions, but at the cost of rigidity and fragility.
claims.note: Asserts qualitative properties belonging to authoritarian systems.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt in authoritarian systems tends to culminate in collapse.
claims.source_quote: When contradiction debt arises in such systems, it cannot be easily dissipated through institutional repair and instead tends to culminate in collapse.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of contradiction debt in authoritarian systems.

claims.claim: Pluralism is a condition of ontological resilience in sustainable legal systems.
claims.source_quote: pluralism is not a political preference but a condition of ontological resilience in sustainable legal systems.
claims.note: Author explicitly asserts pluralism bears the role/property of being a condition of ontological resilience.

claims.claim: Pluralism is not merely a political preference.
claims.source_quote: pluralism is not a political preference but a condition of ontological resilience in sustainable legal systems.
claims.note: Author explicitly denies a property (being a political preference) of pluralism.

claims.claim: Systems capable of integrating and repairing contradiction maintain coherence over time.
claims.source_quote: Systems capable of integrating and repairing contradiction maintain coherence over time; those that cannot, disintegrate.
claims.note: Asserts a property (coherence maintenance) of systems with contradiction-repair capacity.

claims.claim: Systems incapable of integrating and repairing contradiction disintegrate.
claims.source_quote: Systems capable of integrating and repairing contradiction maintain coherence over time; those that cannot, disintegrate.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional outcome (disintegration) for systems lacking repair capacity.

claims.claim: To bear a legal role, an entity must be capable of recognition, role realization, and normative participation within an institutional structure.
claims.source_quote: To bear a legal role, an entity must satisfy specific ontological conditions: it must be capable of recognition, of role realization, and of normative participation within an institutional structure.
claims.note: Direct assertion of ontological conditions for legal role-bearing.

claims.claim: Recognition, role realization, and normative participation are structural features of being within the legal world.
claims.source_quote: These are not merely behavioral or cognitive attributes but structural features of being within the legal world.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological nature of these conditions.

claims.claim: Within BFO, a role is a realizable dependent continuant that inheres in a bearer.
claims.source_quote: Within Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), a role is a realizable dependent continuant, an entity that inheres in a bearer and can be realized in particular processes under suitable conditions.
claims.note: Author endorses this BFO-based ontological classification of roles.

claims.claim: A physician's role inheres in a person and is realized in acts of diagnosis or treatment.
claims.source_quote: A physician's role inheres in a person and is realized in acts of diagnosis or treatment; a judge's role inheres in a legal agent and is realized in adjudication.
claims.note: Author asserts a specific instance of role-inhering relation.

claims.claim: A judge's role inheres in a legal agent and is realized in adjudication.
claims.source_quote: A physician's role inheres in a person and is realized in acts of diagnosis or treatment; a judge's role inheres in a legal agent and is realized in adjudication.
claims.note: Author asserts a specific instance of role-inhering relation.

claims.claim: The bearer of a role must be a continuant capable of participating in social and institutional relations.
claims.source_quote: Crucially, the bearer of a role must itself be a continuant capable of participating in social and institutional relations.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological requirement for role-bearers.

claims.claim: Current AI systems realize fragments of roles without inhering in them.
claims.source_quote: In ontological terms, these systems realize fragments of roles without inhering in them.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the status of current AI relative to roles.

claims.claim: A self-executing contract realizes part of the obligation-enforcement process but does not bear the institutional role of an enforcer.
claims.source_quote: A self-executing contract, for example, realizes part of the obligation-enforcement process but does not bear the institutional role of an enforcer.
claims.note: Asserts a specific ontological relation between smart contracts and roles.

claims.claim: The ontological bearer of a self-executing contract's enforcement process is the institution or agent that recognizes and authorizes it.
claims.source_quote: The ontological bearer remains the institution or agent that recognizes and authorizes the process.
claims.note: Asserts which entity is the proper ontological bearer.

claims.claim: Current AI operates as an instrumental continuant within the realization of legal roles, not as a legal agent.
claims.source_quote: Thus, the current AI operates as an instrumental continuant within the realization of legal roles, not as a legal agent in its own right.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of current AI.

claims.claim: Recognition is a necessary capacity for participation in the moral field.
claims.source_quote: The condition that separates instruments from agents is recognition, which I also qualify in The Geometry of the Good as a necessary capacity for participation in the moral field.
claims.note: Author endorses this as his own view.

claims.claim: Recognition transforms a material or informational continuant into a social continuant.
claims.source_quote: This recognition transforms a mere material or informational continuant into a social continuant, an entity that exists within the field of law's ontology.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological transformation effected by recognition.

claims.claim: A social continuant is an entity that exists within the field of law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: a social continuant, an entity that exists within the field of law's ontology.
claims.note: Author defines and endorses this ontological category.

claims.claim: Corporations are recognized continuants whose personhood arises entirely from institutional acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: They are not physical persons but recognized continuants, legal fictions whose personhood arises entirely from institutional acknowledgment.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological basis of corporate personhood.

claims.claim: Legal personality is a property of structure, not of substance.
claims.source_quote: Legal personality is not a property of substance but of structure.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature of legal personality.

claims.claim: Once recognition is extended, an entity enters the field of law and becomes capable of role-bearing.
claims.source_quote: Once recognition is extended, the entity enters the field of law and becomes capable of role-bearing.
claims.note: Asserts ontological consequence of recognition.

claims.claim: Role realization requires the alignment of dependent continuants with occurrents.
claims.source_quote: In BFO terms, realization requires the alignment of dependent continuants (roles, obligations) with occurrents (acts, decisions, performances).
claims.note: Author endorses this BFO-grounded ontological requirement for realization.

claims.claim: For human agents, the coupling of roles and occurrents is mediated by cognition, intention, and moral accountability.
claims.source_quote: For human agents, this coupling is mediated by cognition, intention, and moral accountability.
claims.note: Asserts a property of human agents regarding role realization.

claims.claim: For AI systems, role realization is mediated by computational processes, data flows, and algorithmic optimization.
claims.source_quote: For AI systems, it is mediated by computational processes, data flows, and algorithmic optimization.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of AI systems regarding realization.

claims.claim: Normative participation entails reflexive recognition.
claims.source_quote: From the standpoint of structural ontology, normative participation entails more than compliance; it requires reflexive recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological requirement for normative participation.

claims.claim: A participant in the legal system must occupy a position within the network of recognition that sustains legal norms.
claims.source_quote: A participant in the legal system must not only act according to norms but also occupy a position within the network of recognition that sustains those norms.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological condition for legal participation.

claims.claim: Human agents are both subjects and objects of recognition within a reciprocal architecture.
claims.source_quote: Humans can do this because they are both subjects and objects of recognition, they recognize others and are recognized in turn. Their roles, obligations, and rights exist within a reciprocal architecture.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of human agents in the recognition network.

claims.claim: Current AI lacks reciprocity of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Current AI lacks this reciprocity. It processes information but does not recognize; it can instantiate formal relations but cannot confer or withdraw recognition.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about the limits of current AI.

claims.claim: Current AI's participation in law is unilateral—functional, not ontological.
claims.source_quote: Thus, its participation remains unilateral - functional, not ontological.
claims.note: Author directly asserts this ontological distinction.

claims.claim: Current AI can realize roles only derivatively, as part of another agent's recognition network.
claims.source_quote: It can realize roles only derivatively, as part of another agent's recognition network.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological relational property of current AI.

claims.claim: Autonomous trading algorithms and DAOs generate legal facts such as transactions and transfers.
claims.source_quote: These systems execute contracts, hold assets, and make 'choices' without direct human intervention. They participate in the realization of obligations, generate legal facts (transactions, transfers), and trigger enforcement processes.
claims.note: Author asserts these systems generate legal facts, committing to their ontological status.

claims.claim: Autonomous trading algorithms and DAOs occupy an ambiguous ontological zone between instrument and institution.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, they occupy an ambiguous zone between instrument and institution, a liminal status that reveals law's flexibility in recognizing new bearers of dependent continuants.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of these systems.

claims.claim: Responsibility is the inverse of recognition.
claims.source_quote: This is an ontological condition, not merely a moral one: responsibility is the inverse of recognition.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological relation between responsibility and recognition.

claims.claim: Legal agency entails the capacity to be held accountable.
claims.source_quote: Legal agency entails not only the capacity to act but the capacity to be held accountable.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological condition constitutive of legal agency.

claims.claim: To be recognized as a bearer of obligations is to be capable of sustaining or repairing contradiction within the recognition network.
claims.source_quote: To be recognized as a bearer of obligations is to be capable of sustaining or repairing contradiction within the network of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological implication of being an obligation-bearer.

claims.claim: Current AI cannot function as a node of repair in the recognition network.
claims.source_quote: If an AI cannot experience or respond to contradiction, if it cannot acknowledge or correct its own breaches of norm, it cannot function as a node of repair.
claims.note: Asserts a functional/ontological incapacity of current AI.

claims.claim: In the absence of repair capacity, AI remains an artifact within law's ontology, not a participant.
claims.source_quote: In the absence of repair capacity, AI remains an artifact within law's ontology, not a participant within it.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification of AI lacking repair capacity.

claims.claim: There is no metaphysical barrier preventing the recognition of artificial agents as legal participants.
claims.source_quote: There is no metaphysical barrier preventing the recognition of artificial agents as legal participants.
claims.note: Author directly asserts this ontological claim.

claims.claim: The capacity for legal recognition is largely socially constructed and ontologically flexible.
claims.source_quote: the capacity for recognition is largely socially constructed and ontologically flexible.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of the capacity for recognition.

claims.claim: If appropriate institutional conditions are met, AI could achieve functional legal personhood as a recognition-compatible role-bearer.
claims.source_quote: AI could, in principle, achieve functional legal personhood. It would not become human but would become recognition-compatible, a structurally valid bearer of roles within the legal ontology.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a real in-principle possibility; hedged by 'in principle' but constitutes an ontological claim about what AI could be.

claims.claim: An AI achieving functional legal personhood would become recognition-compatible.
claims.source_quote: It would not become human but would become recognition-compatible, a structurally valid bearer of roles within the legal ontology.
claims.note: Author asserts a property (recognition-compatibility) that AI would bear under the specified condition; directly committed to as the nature of such an outcome.

claims.claim: An AI achieving functional legal personhood would be a structurally valid bearer of roles within legal ontology.
claims.source_quote: It would not become human but would become recognition-compatible, a structurally valid bearer of roles within the legal ontology.
claims.note: Author asserts a role/kind relation: such an AI would be a bearer of roles within legal ontology—an ontological claim about kind membership and role-bearing.

claims.claim: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions.
claims.source_quote: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions, grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.note: Plain positive assertion about a property/relation of recognition: it is mediated by human institutions.

claims.claim: Recognition is grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.source_quote: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions, grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.note: Author directly asserts the grounding relation of recognition to shared intentionality and moral reason.

claims.claim: Extending recognition to non-human systems embeds recognition in technical processes.
claims.source_quote: Extending recognition to non-human systems forces law to externalize part of its own reflexivity, to embed recognition in technical processes.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational/structural claim: recognition becomes embedded in technical processes when extended to non-human systems.

claims.claim: Extending recognition to non-human systems externalizes part of law's own reflexivity.
claims.source_quote: Extending recognition to non-human systems forces law to externalize part of its own reflexivity, to embed recognition in technical processes.
claims.note: Author asserts that law's reflexivity is (partially) externalized—an ontological claim about a property/process of law.

claims.claim: A hybrid ontology of participation exists in which human and machine recognitions coexist.
claims.source_quote: This creates a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of a hybrid ontology of participation as a result of extending recognition—an existence claim about a kind of ontological structure.

claims.claim: Human and machine recognitions mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.source_quote: This creates a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: Author asserts a functional/relational claim: both human and machine recognitions bear the function of sustaining law's coherence.

claims.claim: Pluralism is a condition of ontological resilience in sustainable legal systems.
claims.source_quote: pluralism is not a political preference but a condition of ontological resilience in sustainable legal systems.
claims.note: The author explicitly asserts this as an ontological argument advanced throughout the work, attributing a property (ontological resilience) to legal systems via pluralism.

claims.claim: Legal systems capable of integrating and repairing contradiction maintain coherence over time.
claims.source_quote: Systems capable of integrating and repairing contradiction maintain coherence over time; those that cannot, disintegrate.
claims.note: Direct assertion about a property of legal systems — their capacity for coherence maintenance — as a positive ontological claim.

claims.claim: Legal systems that cannot integrate contradiction disintegrate.
claims.source_quote: Systems capable of integrating and repairing contradiction maintain coherence over time; those that cannot, disintegrate.
claims.note: Asserts a dispositional property of legal systems lacking repair capacity.

claims.claim: Every unfulfilled obligation or unresolved injustice is a residue of incoherence within the structure of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Every unfulfilled obligation or unresolved injustice represents a residue of incoherence within the structure of recognition, a moral tension awaiting repair.
claims.note: Attributes an ontological property (incoherence/residue) to unfulfilled obligations and unresolved injustices.

claims.claim: Transitional justice, reparations, and truth commissions are large-scale repair mechanisms.
claims.source_quote: Transitional justice, reparations, and truth commissions all function as large-scale repair mechanisms, designed to reconcile past contradictions between law and moral recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/kind for these entities.

claims.claim: Transitional justice mechanisms retroactively redefine which entities continue to exist as valid within the reconstructed ontology of justice.
claims.source_quote: They operate by retroactively redefining which entities, verdicts, laws, or acts, continue to exist as valid within the reconstructed ontology of justice.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property and relation these mechanisms bear to the ontology of legal entities.

claims.claim: The annulment of unjust laws and posthumous exonerations extinguish incoherent continuants, restoring integrity to law's being.
claims.source_quote: The annulment of unjust laws or the posthumous exoneration of the wrongly convicted exemplify this process: the legal system repairs its own history by extinguishing incoherent continuants, thereby restoring integrity to its being.
claims.note: Asserts that these legal acts bear the relation of extinguishing incoherent continuants, a direct ontological claim about their effect.

claims.claim: Justice is the ongoing equilibrium between contradiction and repair.
claims.source_quote: justice itself can be defined as the ongoing equilibrium between contradiction and repair.
claims.note: The author proposes a definition of justice as an ontological state — equilibrium between two processes.

claims.claim: A just system is one that can transform conflict into coherence through structured recognition.
claims.source_quote: A just system is not one without conflict but one that can transform conflict into coherence through structured recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a defining property of just legal systems.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt becomes destructive only when repair ceases.
claims.source_quote: Contradiction is inevitable, but debt is manageable; it becomes destructive only when repair ceases.
claims.note: Asserts a conditional dispositional property of contradiction debt.

claims.claim: Law's ontological vocation includes preserving the world of recognition by absorbing and resolving contradiction debt.
claims.source_quote: A vital part of law's ontological vocation, therefore, is to preserve the world of recognition by absorbing and resolving contradiction debt through procedural and institutional means.
claims.note: Asserts a functional role/property of law as an entity.

claims.claim: Each act of interpretation, judgment, or reform is an act of continuous ontological maintenance.
claims.source_quote: Each act of interpretation, judgment, or reform contributes to this continuous ontological maintenance, a process by which law not only orders society but perpetually reconstructs the very conditions of its existence.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of legal acts — they constitute ontological maintenance.

claims.claim: Law perpetually reconstructs the very conditions of its own existence.
claims.source_quote: a process by which law not only orders society but perpetually reconstructs the very conditions of its existence.
claims.note: Asserts a reflexive property of law as an entity — it reconstructs its own conditions of existence.

claims.claim: Contradiction is an inevitable feature of law's relational ontology.
claims.source_quote: Contradiction, as established in the preceding section, is not a defect in law's design but an inevitable feature of its relational ontology.
claims.note: Asserts a property of contradiction with respect to law's ontology.

claims.claim: Processes of adjudication, amendment, and reinterpretation are acts of ontological maintenance.
claims.source_quote: These processes of adjudication, amendment, and reinterpretation are not merely procedural devices but acts of ontological maintenance: they restore the integrity of the network of dependent continuants that constitutes law's being.
claims.note: Asserts a functional identity/role for these legal processes.

claims.claim: Law's being is constituted by a network of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: they restore the integrity of the network of dependent continuants that constitutes law's being.
claims.note: Asserts that law's being consists of a network of dependent continuants — a direct ontological claim about law's constitution.

claims.claim: Every mechanism of legal correction is a form of ontological repair.
claims.source_quote: every mechanism of legal correction is a form of ontological repair, through which law reasserts its capacity to remain coherent despite constant tension and change.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind or functional identity: legal correction mechanisms are ontological repair processes.

claims.claim: Repair mechanisms are occurrents that act upon existing continuants to restore coherence among their dependencies.
claims.source_quote: repair mechanisms can be modeled as occurrents, temporal processes that act upon existing continuants (laws, obligations, roles, or rights) to restore coherence among their dependencies.
claims.note: The author presents this within a BFO framework as the correct ontological modeling, asserting it as the author's own view. Medium because 'can be modeled' introduces slight hedging.

claims.claim: Each repair mechanism operates by reconfiguring relations of recognition to dissolve contradiction debt.
claims.source_quote: Each mechanism operates by reconfiguring relations of recognition, thereby dissolving contradiction debt.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property and function of repair mechanisms.

claims.claim: Repair is the continuous realization of law's reflexivity.
claims.source_quote: Repair, in this sense, is the continuous realization of law's reflexivity: its ability to recognize, critique, and reconstruct itself as a system of interdependent continuants.
claims.note: Asserts an identity/property: repair realizes law's reflexivity, which is a property of law.

claims.claim: Adjudication is the most immediate and frequent mechanism of legal repair.
claims.source_quote: Adjudication is the most immediate and frequent mechanism of repair.
claims.note: Asserts a comparative property of adjudication among repair mechanisms.

claims.claim: Adjudication is a localized repair process — an occurrent that identifies and resolves incompatible dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, adjudication functions as a localized repair process: an occurrent that identifies incompatible dependencies within a specific case and resolves them by privileging one recognition relation over another.
claims.note: Asserts a kind membership (occurrent) and functional property for adjudication.

claims.claim: A losing legal claim in adjudication continues to exist as a potential dependency in future recognition contexts.
claims.source_quote: The losing claim is not annihilated but subordinated, it continues to exist as a potential dependency in future recognition contexts.
claims.note: Asserts persistence of a legal entity (the losing claim) and its relational status after adjudication.

claims.claim: Amendment restructures the ontological architecture of recognition itself.
claims.source_quote: amendment restructures the ontological architecture of recognition itself.
claims.note: Asserts a function/property of legislative amendment as an ontological operation.

claims.claim: Amendment alters the dependencies among institutional continuants such as statutes, constitutions, and regulatory bodies.
claims.source_quote: Legislative amendment alters the dependencies among institutional continuants, statutes, constitutions, and regulatory bodies, thereby recalibrating the parameters within which future contradictions will be managed.
claims.note: Asserts a relational effect of amendment on institutional continuants.

claims.claim: Reinterpretation is a form of semantic repair that alters the meaning of existing dependent continuants without changing their formal identity.
claims.source_quote: Reinterpretation functions as semantic repair: it alters the meaning of existing dependent continuants without changing their formal identity.
claims.note: Asserts a functional identity and property of reinterpretation as an ontological process.

claims.claim: Reinterpretation exemplifies continuant adaptation — the persistence of an entity through internal modification of its dependent relations.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, this process exemplifies continuant adaptation: the persistence of an entity (the law) through internal modification of its dependent relations.
claims.note: Asserts a subkind or instance relation: reinterpretation instantiates continuant adaptation.

claims.claim: Transitional justice is the macro-ontological repair of entire systems of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Transitional justice is the macro-ontological repair of entire systems of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a functional identity/kind for transitional justice.

claims.claim: After periods of violence or repression, the existing legal ontology is saturated with contradiction debt.
claims.source_quote: After periods of violence or repression, the existing legal ontology is saturated with contradiction debt: laws that sanctioned atrocities, verdicts grounded in coercion, and institutions complicit in moral collapse.
claims.note: Asserts a property (saturation with contradiction debt) of legal ontologies following repression.

claims.claim: Truth commissions, amnesties, reparations, and constitutional re-foundings are processes of ontological restoration.
claims.source_quote: Truth commissions, amnesties, reparations, and constitutional re-foundings all operate as processes of ontological restoration.
claims.note: Asserts a functional kind/role for these transitional justice mechanisms.

claims.claim: Transitional justice mechanisms determine which prior legal entities continue to exist as valid and which must be extinguished as incoherent remnants.
claims.source_quote: They determine which prior legal entities, laws, judgments, or records, continue to exist as valid within the reconstituted legal order, and which must be extinguished as incoherent remnants of a broken system.
claims.note: Asserts a functional relation these mechanisms bear to the persistence or extinction of legal entities.

claims.claim: The apartheid legal system generated massive contradiction debt.
claims.source_quote: The apartheid legal system generated massive contradiction debt: its laws were internally coherent but externally incoherent with the evolving global and moral ontology of justice.
claims.note: The author asserts a property ('contradiction debt') of the apartheid legal system as an entity.

claims.claim: Apartheid laws were internally coherent but externally incoherent with the moral ontology of justice.
claims.source_quote: its laws were internally coherent but externally incoherent with the evolving global and moral ontology of justice.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property (coherence/incoherence) of the laws with respect to the moral ontology of justice.

claims.claim: There exists an evolving global and moral ontology of justice.
claims.source_quote: externally incoherent with the evolving global and moral ontology of justice.
claims.note: The author's claim presupposes and asserts the existence of a moral ontology of justice as a real entity.

claims.claim: The TRC reconstituted the field of recognition by acknowledging victims, documenting truth, and redefining legitimacy.
claims.source_quote: it reconstituted the field of recognition by acknowledging victims, documenting truth, and redefining legitimacy.
claims.note: Asserts an action of the TRC that changed an entity (the field of recognition), attributing a transformative relation.

claims.claim: The TRC's process created new dependent continuants: recognitions of harm, forgiveness, and restoration.
claims.source_quote: This process created new dependent continuants, recognitions of harm, forgiveness, and restoration, that replaced the invalid entities of prior law.
claims.note: Directly asserts the existence of new dependent continuants as a kind of entity brought into being by the TRC process.

claims.claim: Recognitions of harm, forgiveness, and restoration are dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: This process created new dependent continuants, recognitions of harm, forgiveness, and restoration
claims.note: Asserts a subkind/classification: recognitions of harm, forgiveness, and restoration are instances of dependent continuants.

claims.claim: The new dependent continuants replaced the invalid entities of prior law.
claims.source_quote: new dependent continuants, recognitions of harm, forgiveness, and restoration, that replaced the invalid entities of prior law.
claims.note: Asserts a replacement relation between new entities and prior invalid legal entities.

claims.claim: The entities of prior apartheid law were invalid.
claims.source_quote: that replaced the invalid entities of prior law.
claims.note: Asserts a property (invalidity) of the entities produced by prior apartheid law.

claims.claim: The result of the TRC process was the creation of a new coherence, not a return to a preexisting one.
claims.source_quote: The result was not a return to a preexisting coherence but the creation of a new one, more consistent with the moral and institutional conditions of the post-apartheid order.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the outcome: a newly created coherence exists, distinct from any prior coherence.

claims.claim: The new coherence is consistent with the moral and institutional conditions of the post-apartheid order.
claims.source_quote: the creation of a new one, more consistent with the moral and institutional conditions of the post-apartheid order.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between the new coherence and the post-apartheid moral/institutional conditions.

claims.claim: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions.
claims.source_quote: Recognition has always been mediated by human institutions, grounded in shared intentionality and moral reason.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the nature and mediation of recognition as an ontological property.

claims.claim: Extending recognition to non-human systems creates a hybrid ontology of participation.
claims.source_quote: This creates a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of a hybrid ontological category arising from extending recognition.

claims.claim: Human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.source_quote: a hybrid ontology of participation, in which human and machine recognitions coexist and mutually sustain law's coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between human and machine recognitions and law's coherence.

claims.claim: Automated enforcement, algorithmic sentencing assistance, and AI-driven compliance systems participate in maintaining law's structure.
claims.source_quote: automated enforcement, algorithmic sentencing assistance, and AI-driven compliance systems all participate in maintaining law's structure.
claims.note: Author asserts that these systems bear a participation relation to law's structure.

claims.claim: AI can simulate reasoning, perform adjudication, and execute contractual norms.
claims.source_quote: AI can simulate reasoning, perform adjudication, and execute contractual norms, but until it participates reflexively in recognition...
claims.note: Author asserts AI's capacities as ontological properties/functions.

claims.claim: Until AI participates reflexively in recognition, it remains subordinate within law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: until it participates reflexively in recognition, until it becomes both subject and object of law's ontology, it remains subordinate.
claims.note: Asserts a conditional ontological status (subordination) for AI within legal ontology.

claims.claim: AI must become both subject and object of law's ontology to fully participate in it.
claims.source_quote: until it becomes both subject and object of law's ontology, it remains subordinate.
claims.note: Asserts a relational ontological condition for AI's full legal participation.

claims.claim: The extension of recognition to artificial systems may be a necessary evolution.
claims.source_quote: Yet the extension of recognition to artificial systems may be a necessary evolution.
claims.note: Author asserts this as a genuine possibility with normative weight, though hedged with 'may'.

claims.claim: Algorithms, code, and decision engines function as realization mechanisms for institutional processes.
claims.source_quote: Algorithms, code, and decision engines function as realization mechanisms for institutional processes; they perform occurrents that instantiate legal effects.
claims.note: Asserts that algorithms bear the functional role of realization mechanisms—a direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: Algorithms perform occurrents that instantiate legal effects.
claims.source_quote: they perform occurrents that instantiate legal effects.
claims.note: Asserts that algorithms are entities that perform occurrents with legal ontological consequences.

claims.claim: A tax assessment algorithm realizes the function of calculation and compliance.
claims.source_quote: A tax assessment algorithm realizes the function of calculation and compliance; a sentencing recommender realizes aspects of judicial discretion; a blockchain contract realizes enforcement without intermediary authority.
claims.note: Asserts realization relations between specific automated systems and legal functions.

claims.claim: A sentencing recommender realizes aspects of judicial discretion.
claims.source_quote: a sentencing recommender realizes aspects of judicial discretion
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation between a sentencing recommender and judicial discretion.

claims.claim: A blockchain contract realizes enforcement without intermediary authority.
claims.source_quote: a blockchain contract realizes enforcement without intermediary authority.
claims.note: Asserts a realization relation and a property (lack of intermediary) for blockchain contracts.

claims.claim: Automated systems are instrumental continuants that participate in the realization of dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: These automations can be represented ontologically as instrumental continuants: entities that participate in the realization of dependent continuants (obligations, duties, permissions) without themselves being bearers of those dependencies.
claims.note: Author asserts a specific ontological kind (instrumental continuant) for automated legal systems.

claims.claim: Automated systems enact norms but do not recognize them.
claims.source_quote: They enact, but they do not recognize.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property (enacting) and a missing property (recognition) for automated systems.

claims.claim: Obligations and duties are dependent continuants within law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: entities that participate in the realization of dependent continuants (obligations, duties, permissions)
claims.note: Asserts that obligations, duties, and permissions are instances of the kind 'dependent continuant'.

claims.claim: When automated systems lack corresponding recognition structures, law's reflexivity weakens.
claims.source_quote: When such systems are integrated into the realization chain without corresponding recognition structures, law's reflexivity weakens, its ability to review, interpret, and repair its own acts diminishes.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/structural relation between absence of recognition structures and weakening of law's reflexivity.

claims.claim: Norm opacity is a loss of reflexivity caused by concealing normativity within technical structures.
claims.source_quote: Automation, by contrast, conceals normativity within technical structures: algorithmic parameters, training data, and decision rules invisible to both citizens and institutions.
claims.note: Author defines and asserts the existence of norm opacity as an ontological pathology.

claims.claim: Algorithmic legal systems generate legal effects without maintaining the trace of recognition that makes them law.
claims.source_quote: The result is an ontological pathology, a system that generates legal effects without maintaining the trace of recognition that makes them law.
claims.note: Asserts a property of algorithmic systems (generating effects without recognition trace) and names it an ontological pathology.

claims.claim: Algorithmic risk assessments and automated determinations operate within law's realization layer but outside its recognition layer.
claims.source_quote: These tools operate within law's realization layer but outside its recognition layer: they produce obligations and outcomes without transparent institutional acknowledgment of how those outcomes are derived.
claims.note: Asserts a structural location (realization layer, not recognition layer) for these tools within law's ontology.

claims.claim: Algorithmic tools instantiate pseudo-recognition, mimicking legal recognition while bypassing its conditions.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, they instantiate pseudo-recognition, processes that mimic the effects of legal recognition while bypassing its conditions.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of a kind 'pseudo-recognition' and assigns it to algorithmic legal tools.

claims.claim: Unrecognized algorithmic decisions introduce incoherent continuants into law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: Each unrecognized or unreviewable decision introduces incoherent continuants into law's ontology: obligations and rights that exist formally but without traceable dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts that a kind of entity (incoherent continuant) is introduced into legal ontology by unrecognized decisions.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt accumulates invisibly within the digital substratum of legal practice.
claims.source_quote: contradiction debt accumulates invisibly within the digital substratum of legal practice.
claims.note: Author asserts the existence and accumulation of contradiction debt as an ontological feature of automated legal systems.

claims.claim: Every legal system must preserve visible chains of recognition linking acts, agents, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: every legal system must preserve visible chains of recognition linking acts, agents, and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property (chains of recognition) that legal systems must have.

claims.claim: Ontological transparency requires that for every algorithmic decision, the underlying ontological structure remain accessible and auditable.
claims.source_quote: Ontological transparency means that for every algorithmic decision, the underlying ontological structure...must remain accessible and auditable.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary property (accessibility, auditability) of ontological transparency in legal AI.

claims.claim: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.source_quote: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.note: Asserts a differential property: machines realize norms; only human/institutional continuants can repair norms.

claims.claim: Accountability must be a structural property of legal ontology, not an afterthought.
claims.source_quote: Accountability must therefore be reintroduced at the ontological level, not as afterthought but as structural property.
claims.note: Asserts accountability as a structural property of legal ontology.

claims.claim: Representational transparency requires that formal legal AI ontologies encode recognition dependencies, not merely entities and relations.
claims.source_quote: Representational transparency demands that the formal ontologies used in legal AI...encode not just entities and relations but their dependencies of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a required property of formal legal AI ontologies.

claims.claim: An AutomatedDecision class in legal ontology should specify which Institution recognizes its validity and under what Norm it operates.
claims.source_quote: an 'AutomatedDecision' class should specify which 'Institution' recognizes its validity, under what 'Norm' it operates, and how its outcomes can be reviewed or revoked.
claims.note: Asserts required relational properties of the AutomatedDecision ontological class.

claims.claim: The Truth and Reconciliation process created new dependent continuants: recognitions of harm, forgiveness, and restoration.
claims.source_quote: This process created new dependent continuants, recognitions of harm, forgiveness, and restoration, that replaced the invalid entities of prior law.
claims.note: Direct assertion that certain entities (dependent continuants) were created by the TRC process.

claims.claim: The post-apartheid legal order achieved a new coherence rather than restoring a prior one.
claims.source_quote: The result was not a return to a preexisting coherence but the creation of a new one, more consistent with the moral and institutional conditions of the post-apartheid order.
claims.note: Asserts a property (new coherence) of the post-apartheid legal order as an entity.

claims.claim: Systemic legal repair involves both destruction and creation of legal entities.
claims.source_quote: repair at the systemic level involves both the destruction and creation of legal entities, a dual movement of ontological pruning and regeneration.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of systemic repair as an ontological process involving creation and destruction of entities.

claims.claim: The Nuremberg and Tokyo Tribunals redefined dependencies linking individuals, states, and international institutions.
claims.source_quote: By prosecuting crimes against humanity, these tribunals redefined the dependencies linking individuals, states, and international institutions.
claims.note: Asserts that relations (dependencies) among entities were changed by these tribunals.

claims.claim: The post-WWII tribunals recognized individuals as subjects of international law.
claims.source_quote: They recognized new kinds of bearers (individuals as subjects of international law)
claims.note: Asserts a new kind of entity (individual as subject of international law) was recognized/created.

claims.claim: The post-WWII tribunals recognized crimes that transcend jurisdictional boundaries as new dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: and new dependent continuants (crimes that transcend jurisdictional boundaries).
claims.note: Asserts existence of a new kind of dependent continuant (transjurisdictional crimes).

claims.claim: The post-WWII juridical repair established a more coherent global ontology of justice.
claims.source_quote: This repair process established a more coherent global ontology of justice, one capable of sustaining recognition across nations and generations.
claims.note: Asserts a property (coherence) of the global ontology of justice as resulting from this process.

claims.claim: Repair can be generative: through resolving contradiction, law expands its own field of being.
claims.source_quote: It also demonstrated that repair can itself be generative: through resolving contradiction, law expands its own field of being.
claims.note: Asserts a disposition/function of repair and a property of law (capacity to expand its being).

claims.claim: Transitional contexts contain ontological residue of false recognition persisting as records, verdicts, or property relations.
claims.source_quote: repair mechanisms must also address the ontological residue of false recognition, the persistence of records, verdicts, or property relations derived from injustice.
claims.note: Asserts that certain entities (records, verdicts, property relations) persist as ontological residue.

claims.claim: Lustration, restitution, and legal nullification extinguish incoherent continuants incompatible with the restored order.
claims.source_quote: Mechanisms such as lustration (removal of compromised officials), restitution (return of confiscated property), and legal nullification (declaration of invalidity) serve to extinguish incoherent continuants that cannot be reconciled with the restored order.
claims.note: Asserts a function of these mechanisms: extinguishing specific types of entities (incoherent continuants).

claims.claim: Lustration, restitution, and nullification perform ontological purification, not merely symbolic acts.
claims.source_quote: These acts are not mere symbolic gestures; they perform the necessary work of ontological purification.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of these acts as ontologically real rather than symbolic.

claims.claim: Formal withdrawal of recognition eliminates entities whose existence would compromise coherence.
claims.source_quote: By formally withdrawing recognition, the system eliminates entities whose continued existence would compromise coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a causal ontological relation: withdrawal of recognition causes elimination of entities.

claims.claim: Justice is a dynamic process of continuous repair rather than a static condition.
claims.source_quote: Justice, in this view, is not a static condition but a dynamic process of continuous repair, the perpetual balancing of contradiction debt through institutional evolution.
claims.note: Asserts a property of justice as an entity: it is a dynamic process, not a static state.

claims.claim: Law endures as a living system where repair persists; where repair fails, law fractures into incoherence.
claims.source_quote: Where repair persists, law endures as a living system; where repair fails, the world of law fractures into incoherence and decay.
claims.note: Asserts a conditional property of law as an entity: its continued existence depends on repair.

claims.claim: When contradiction debt accumulates beyond repair capacity, law ceases to function as a coherent field of recognition.
claims.source_quote: When contradiction debt accumulates beyond a system's repair capacity, law ceases to function as a coherent field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property of law that changes under certain conditions—an ontological claim about law's nature.

claims.claim: Legal entities (rights, duties, offices, verdicts) can persist in name while losing ontological grounding.
claims.source_quote: Its entities, rights, duties, offices, verdicts, persist in name but lose ontological grounding.
claims.note: Asserts a property state of legal entities: nominal persistence without ontological grounding.

claims.claim: Authoritarian failure is a metaphysical crisis: a disintegration of law's being as organized dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: signals not merely a political or moral crisis but a metaphysical one: the disintegration of law's being as an organized structure of dependent continuants.
claims.note: Asserts that this failure mode constitutes a metaphysical/ontological crisis, not merely political.

claims.claim: Legal systems depend on continuous and coherent functioning of recognition and repair for their existence.
claims.source_quote: their dependence on the continuous and coherent functioning of recognition and repair.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: legal systems' existence depends on recognition and repair.

claims.claim: In authoritarian systems, dependent continuants (rights, obligations, roles) are forced into rigid hierarchies preventing adaptive repair.
claims.source_quote: dependent continuants (rights, obligations, and institutional roles) are forced into rigid hierarchies that prevent adaptive repair.
claims.note: Asserts a property of dependent continuants in authoritarian systems: forced rigidity.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt in authoritarian systems becomes latent and internalized within a brittle order.
claims.source_quote: Contradiction debt does not disappear; it becomes latent, internalized within a brittle order incapable of adjustment.
claims.note: Asserts a property of contradiction debt under authoritarianism: latent persistence.

claims.claim: Authoritarianism represents a closed recognition field in which all entities derive existence from a single institutional node.
claims.source_quote: authoritarianism represents a closed recognition field... all entities derive their existence from a single institutional node.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property (closed recognition field, unidirectional dependencies) of authoritarian legal systems.

claims.claim: Law has an ontological requirement for distributed recognition.
claims.source_quote: This closure violates law's ontological requirement for distributed recognition, transforming what should be a network into a monolithic structure.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary property of law: it requires distributed recognition to function as an ontological structure.

claims.claim: In authoritarian systems, the state's recognition ceases to map the reality it purports to govern.
claims.source_quote: The state continues to recognize itself, but its recognition ceases to map the reality it purports to govern.
claims.note: Asserts a failed relational property: recognition loses correspondence with social/moral reality.

claims.claim: Anomic failure is a state in which recognition persists in fragments but no longer constitutes a coherent world.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, anomy is the state in which recognition persists in fragments but no longer constitutes a coherent world.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological definition/property of the anomic failure mode.

claims.claim: In anomic systems, legal entities are created but their dependencies are inconsistent or overlapping, producing systemic incoherence.
claims.source_quote: Legal entities continue to be created, but their dependencies are inconsistent or overlapping, producing systemic incoherence.
claims.note: Asserts a property of legal entities in anomic systems: inconsistent dependency relations.

claims.claim: In anomic collapse, the field of law dissolves into competing micro-ontologies.
claims.source_quote: The field of law dissolves into competing micro-ontologies, each sustaining its own partial truth without connection to the whole.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of anomic collapse: fragmentation into incommensurable partial ontologies.

claims.claim: Anomic collapse results in contradiction saturation where every recognition conflicts with another and no repair process remains.
claims.source_quote: The result is a condition of contradiction saturation, a state where every recognition conflicts with another, and no higher-order repair process remains to arbitrate.
claims.note: Asserts a property (contradiction saturation) characterizing anomic legal systems.

claims.claim: In collapsed systems, legal entities (laws, offices, procedures) persist as historical artifacts lacking living recognition.
claims.source_quote: Their entities, laws, offices, procedures, persist as historical artifacts, lacking the living recognition necessary for their realization.
claims.note: Asserts a property of entities in collapsed systems: they exist as artifacts without the recognition needed for ontological realization.

claims.claim: A state that exists only nominally has already undergone ontological collapse.
claims.source_quote: The state exists only nominally; its ontology has already collapsed.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property: nominal existence is distinguished from genuine ontological existence.

claims.claim: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.source_quote: Machines may realize norms, but only human or institutional continuants can repair them.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the capacities of machines versus human/institutional continuants — an ontological claim about kinds and their properties.

claims.claim: Accountability is a structural property of law, not an afterthought.
claims.source_quote: Accountability must therefore be reintroduced at the ontological level, not as afterthought but as structural property.
claims.note: Asserts that accountability has a particular ontological status (structural property) within law.

claims.claim: Ontological closure is a condition where legal effects are generated outside the proper relational field.
claims.source_quote: Automation without accountability leads to what might be called ontological closure: a condition where legal effects are generated but not recognized within the proper relational field.
claims.note: Defines and asserts the existence of a condition (ontological closure) with specific properties.

claims.claim: An unaccountable automated system suppresses reflexivity and forecloses recognition loops.
claims.source_quote: In both cases, a system suppresses reflexivity, foreclosing the loops of recognition that sustain coherence.
claims.note: Asserts that unaccountable automated systems have the property of suppressing reflexivity and blocking recognition loops.

claims.claim: An unaccountable automated system rigidifies recognition through code.
claims.source_quote: Just as an authoritarian state rigidifies recognition through hierarchy, an unaccountable automated system rigidifies it through code.
claims.note: Asserts a property of unaccountable automated systems — that they rigidify recognition through code.

claims.claim: Unaccountable automated systems are consistent but not coherent.
claims.source_quote: Its processes are consistent but not coherent; it cannot adjust when contradictions arise.
