claims.note: Asserts properties of unaccountable automated systems distinguishing consistency from coherence.

claims.claim: Unaccountable automated systems redefine normativity from a relational state of recognition to a technical state of output.
claims.source_quote: The danger is not that such systems will misapply norms, but that they will silently redefine what normativity is: from a relational state of recognition to a technical state of output.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological transformation wrought by unaccountable automation on the nature of normativity.

claims.claim: Ontological transparency is the metaphysical condition of accountability.
claims.source_quote: Ontological transparency is the metaphysical condition of accountability: it is what allows law to continue recognizing itself, even when parts of its operation are no longer human.
claims.note: Directly asserts an ontological relation: ontological transparency is a condition for accountability.

claims.claim: Law is a world of mutual acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Without visible recognition chains, law ceases to be a world of mutual acknowledgment and becomes a system of technical enforcement.
claims.note: Asserts a property/nature of law — it is constituted by mutual acknowledgment.

claims.claim: Traditional contracts are institutional continuants grounded in shared recognition.
claims.source_quote: Traditional contracts are institutional continuants grounded in shared recognition: they exist because parties, and the legal institutions overseeing them, acknowledge the validity of their terms and consent to their obligations.
claims.note: Asserts that traditional contracts are a subkind of institutional continuant and have grounding in shared recognition.

claims.claim: Traditional contracts exist because parties and legal institutions acknowledge their validity and consent to obligations.
claims.source_quote: they exist because parties, and the legal institutions overseeing them, acknowledge the validity of their terms and consent to their obligations.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological dependency relation: contracts exist in virtue of recognition by parties and institutions.

claims.claim: The realization of traditional contracts occurs through occurrents such as signing, performance, breach, or adjudication.
claims.source_quote: Their realization occurs through occurrents, acts of signing, performance, breach, or adjudication, each embedded within a wider field of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that realization of contracts is via occurrents — an ontological claim about the realization relation.

claims.claim: Smart contracts collapse the distinction between obligation and execution.
claims.source_quote: By contrast, the smart contract collapses the distinction between obligation and execution.
claims.note: Asserts a property of smart contracts — they eliminate the ontological gap between obligation and its execution.

claims.claim: Smart contracts eliminate the temporal and interpretive interval in which recognition and repair normally occur.
claims.source_quote: In doing so, it eliminates the temporal and interpretive interval in which recognition and repair normally occur.
claims.note: Asserts a property of smart contracts regarding what they remove from the ontological structure of legal obligation.

claims.claim: Smart contracts produce ontological compression, transforming obligations into executable conditions.
claims.source_quote: The result is a form of ontological compression: obligations are transformed into executable conditions, and recognition is replaced by verification.
claims.note: Asserts that a specific condition (ontological compression) is produced by smart contracts, with a specific transformation.

claims.claim: In smart contracts, recognition is replaced by verification.
claims.source_quote: obligations are transformed into executable conditions, and recognition is replaced by verification.
claims.note: Asserts a substitution relation between recognition and verification as properties of smart contracts.

claims.claim: Smart contracts introduce ontological rigidity, realizing obligation without recognition.
claims.source_quote: A contract that executes automatically, even when one party is incapacitated or when terms become unjust, produces ontological rigidity, it realizes obligation without recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a property (ontological rigidity) of smart contracts and the absence of recognition in their realization structure.

claims.claim: Smart contracts lack the capacity for repair when unforeseen circumstances arise.
claims.source_quote: When unforeseen circumstances arise...the system lacks the capacity for repair. The code executes regardless, because recognition has been removed from the ontological chain.
claims.note: Asserts a property of smart contracts — absence of repair capacity — grounded in the removal of recognition.

claims.claim: In smart contracts, there is no institutional continuant capable of withdrawing or suspending the obligation once embedded in code.
claims.source_quote: There is no institutional continuant capable of withdrawing or suspending the obligation once it is embedded in code.
claims.note: Asserts a negative existential claim about the absence of a certain kind of entity in the smart contract ontology.

claims.claim: The blockchain's immutability enforces ontological permanence in a domain that depends on adaptability.
claims.source_quote: The blockchain's immutability compounds the problem: it enforces ontological permanence in a domain that depends on adaptability.
claims.note: Asserts a property of blockchain (ontological permanence) in tension with the properties of the legal domain.

claims.claim: Contradiction debt is embedded directly into the digital substrate of law by smart contracts.
claims.source_quote: The result is contradiction debt embedded directly into the digital substrate of law.
claims.note: Asserts that contradiction debt (a specific condition) is embedded in the digital substrate — an ontological location claim.

claims.claim: Contract-as-Text is an institutional continuant sustained by recognition and capable of reinterpretation.
claims.source_quote: Contract-as-Text: an institutional continuant sustained by recognition and capable of reinterpretation.
claims.note: Asserts that one form of contract is an institutional continuant with specific properties.

claims.claim: Contract-as-Code is an executable specification that realizes obligations mechanically without recognition.
claims.source_quote: Contract-as-Code: an executable specification that realizes obligations mechanically without recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that Contract-as-Code is a subkind of executable specification with the property of realizing obligations without recognition.

claims.claim: Contract-as-Institutional Process is the relational complex of recognition, enforcement, and repair mediating between text and code.
claims.source_quote: Contract-as-Institutional Process: the relational complex of recognition, enforcement, and repair that mediates between text and code.
claims.note: Asserts that one form of contract is a relational complex with specific components and a mediating function.

claims.claim: Smart contracts are self-executing code segments deployed on distributed ledgers that perform transactions automatically when specified conditions are met.
claims.source_quote: Smart contracts are self-executing code segments deployed on distributed ledgers, typically blockchains, designed to perform transactions automatically when specified conditions are met.
claims.note: Asserts the nature/kind and properties of smart contracts as a category of entity.

claims.claim: Repair agents within the digital ontology of law ensure automation remains embedded within the broader field of human recognition.
claims.source_quote: these nodes function as repair agents within the digital ontology of law, ensuring that automation remains embedded within the broader field of human recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that certain nodes have the role/function of repair agents and that automation has a relation of embeddedness in human recognition.

claims.claim: A state that exists only nominally has an ontology that has already collapsed.
claims.source_quote: the state exists only nominally; its ontology has already collapsed.
claims.note: Direct assertion about the ontological status of a nominally existing state.

claims.claim: Between full dysfunction and nominal existence lies a spectrum of intermediate dysfunctions.
claims.source_quote: Between these two extremes lies a spectrum of intermediate dysfunctions, each reflecting a distinct configuration of recognition failure.
claims.note: Asserts the existence of a spectrum of intermediate dysfunctional states.

claims.claim: Each intermediate dysfunction reflects a distinct configuration of recognition failure.
claims.source_quote: each reflecting a distinct configuration of recognition failure.
claims.note: Asserts a property (reflecting a distinct configuration of recognition failure) of each intermediate dysfunction.

claims.claim: In hybrid regimes or transitional societies, contradiction debt oscillates between rigidity and disintegration.
claims.source_quote: In hybrid regimes or transitional societies, contradiction debt oscillates between rigidity and disintegration.
claims.note: Asserts a property (oscillation between rigidity and disintegration) of contradiction debt in hybrid/transitional contexts.

claims.claim: Law in hybrid or transitional contexts exists in a metastable state.
claims.source_quote: Law in these contexts exists in a metastable state: coherent enough to function but unable to resolve accumulated contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts that law in these contexts has the property of being metastable.

claims.claim: Law in a metastable state is coherent enough to function but unable to resolve accumulated contradiction.
claims.source_quote: Law in these contexts exists in a metastable state: coherent enough to function but unable to resolve accumulated contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts two properties of metastable law: functional coherence and inability to resolve contradictions.

claims.claim: Conditions of chronic instability are ontologically precarious.
claims.source_quote: These conditions are ontologically precarious, for they depend on the constant exertion of compensatory effort.
claims.note: Directly asserts an ontological property (precariousness) of these conditions.

claims.claim: Ontologically precarious conditions depend on the constant exertion of compensatory effort.
claims.source_quote: These conditions are ontologically precarious, for they depend on the constant exertion of compensatory effort.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property: such conditions bear a dependence relation on compensatory effort.

claims.claim: Contract-as-Text is an institutional continuant sustained by recognition and capable of reinterpretation.
claims.source_quote: Contract-as-Text: an institutional continuant sustained by recognition and capable of reinterpretation.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification: asserts what kind of entity Contract-as-Text is and its properties.

claims.claim: Contract-as-Code is an executable specification that realizes obligations mechanically without recognition.
claims.source_quote: Contract-as-Code: an executable specification that realizes obligations mechanically without recognition.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification: asserts what kind of entity Contract-as-Code is and how it functions.

claims.claim: Contract-as-Institutional Process is the relational complex of recognition, enforcement, and repair that mediates between text and code.
claims.source_quote: Contract-as-Institutional Process: the relational complex of recognition, enforcement, and repair that mediates between text and code.
claims.note: Direct ontological classification: asserts the nature and relational role of this kind of entity.

claims.claim: When code replaces text and institutional process, law becomes a field of mechanical causation rather than recognition.
claims.source_quote: When the second replaces the first and third, law ceases to be a field of recognition and becomes a field of mechanical causation.
claims.note: Asserts a property change in law's ontological character under certain conditions.

claims.claim: True legal smart contracts must incorporate a recognition layer into the digital system.
claims.source_quote: True legal smart contracts must therefore reincorporate the recognition layer into the digital system, through 'oracle' mechanisms, arbitration nodes, or institutional gateways capable of intervening, interpreting, and repairing incoherent outcomes.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive property of what makes a smart contract a legal entity.

claims.claim: Smart contracts function as legal entities only when they incorporate reflexive recognition and the possibility of repair.
claims.source_quote: Only then can smart contracts function as legal entities rather than merely technical ones. Their ontological legitimacy depends not on code correctness but on the presence of reflexive recognition and the possibility of repair.
claims.note: Asserts conditions for ontological legitimacy and legal entity status of smart contracts.

claims.claim: Algorithmic adjudication systems occupy the domain of realization within law's architecture.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, they occupy the domain of realization within law's architecture: they perform acts that instantiate legal facts (verdicts, sentences, or classifications).
claims.note: Asserts the ontological location/role of algorithmic adjudication systems within law's structure.

claims.claim: Algorithmic adjudication systems simulate recognition without actually performing it.
claims.source_quote: Yet their operation exposes a deeper problem: they often simulate recognition without actually performing it.
claims.note: Asserts a property of algorithmic adjudication systems—that their recognition is simulated, not genuine.

claims.claim: Legal adjudication is an act of recognition that creates or extinguishes dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: Legal adjudication is an act of recognition par excellence. A court declares that a set of facts constitutes a breach... Each act of judgment creates or extinguishes dependent continuants, rights, duties, and legal facts.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature and causal role of legal adjudication.

claims.claim: Rights, duties, and legal facts are dependent continuants that persist only through institutional acknowledgment.
claims.source_quote: Each act of judgment creates or extinguishes dependent continuants, rights, duties, and legal facts, that persist only through institutional acknowledgment.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological kind and dependency condition of rights, duties, and legal facts.

claims.claim: Algorithmic output lacks the reflexivity that gives recognition ontological weight.
claims.source_quote: The algorithm does not see itself as recognizing; it merely outputs classifications. The recognition is therefore pseudo-recognition, formally consistent but ontologically inert until a human or institutional agent confers validation.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological property-deficit in algorithmic output compared to genuine recognition.

claims.claim: Algorithmic recognition is ontologically inert until a human or institutional agent confers validation.
claims.source_quote: The recognition is therefore pseudo-recognition, formally consistent but ontologically inert until a human or institutional agent confers validation.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: algorithmic outputs depend on human/institutional validation for ontological force.

claims.claim: Legal entities produced by unrecognized algorithmic decisions exist in a liminal state: enacted but unrecognized.
claims.source_quote: The resulting entities (revocations, penalties) exist in a liminal state: they are enacted but unrecognized, real in their consequences but unreal in law's ontology.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological status for entities produced by algorithmic systems lacking institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Algorithmic adjudication without oversight generates norm drift—the decoupling of institutional norms from their operational realizations.
claims.source_quote: The system's failure is thus ontological rather than merely technical. It produces legal outcomes that lack coherence with the broader field of recognition, generating norm drift: the gradual decoupling of institutional norms from their operational realizations.
claims.note: Asserts a systemic ontological failure mode (norm drift) as a property of unrecognized algorithmic adjudication.

claims.claim: AI systems inherit the recognition patterns—including biases and inconsistencies—of past institutions.
claims.source_quote: Because AI systems learn from historical data, they inherit the recognition patterns of past institutions, including their biases and inconsistencies.
claims.note: Asserts a property of AI systems regarding what they inherit from historical data.

claims.claim: Automation freezes the field of recognition at a particular historical moment, preventing repair and evolution.
claims.source_quote: In effect, automation 'freezes' the field of recognition at a particular historical moment, preventing repair and evolution.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of automation as it affects the ontological structure of recognition.

claims.claim: Ontological fossilization is the persistence of outdated dependencies in a system that no longer reflects society's living recognition structure.
claims.source_quote: Over time, this leads to ontological fossilization: the persistence of outdated dependencies in a system that no longer reflects the living structure of society's recognition.
claims.note: Asserts the nature of ontological fossilization as a real ontological condition caused by algorithmic automation.

claims.claim: Law in contexts of partial reform exists in a metastable state.
claims.source_quote: Law in these contexts exists in a metastable state: coherent enough to function but unable to resolve accumulated contradiction.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the state of law in certain contexts.

claims.claim: Metastable legal conditions are ontologically precarious.
claims.source_quote: These conditions are ontologically precarious, for they depend on the constant exertion of compensatory effort.
claims.note: Author directly asserts the ontological status of these conditions.

claims.claim: Authoritarian rigidity and anomic collapse share a structural affinity.
claims.source_quote: Authoritarian rigidity and anomic collapse share a deeper structural affinity: both reflect breakdowns in the reflexivity of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property (structural affinity) between two kinds of system failure.

claims.claim: Both authoritarianism and anomy are breakdowns in the reflexivity of recognition.
claims.source_quote: both reflect breakdowns in the reflexivity of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a shared property of two kinds of legal system failure.

claims.claim: In authoritarianism, reflexivity is suppressed so law cannot see or correct itself.
claims.source_quote: In authoritarianism, reflexivity is suppressed, law cannot see or correct itself.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of authoritarian legal systems.

claims.claim: In anomy, reflexivity is dispersed so law loses focus and authority.
claims.source_quote: In anomy, reflexivity is dispersed, law sees itself everywhere and nowhere, losing focus and authority.
claims.note: Author asserts a property of anomic legal systems.

claims.claim: Both authoritarianism and anomy cause law to lose the capacity for self-repair.
claims.source_quote: In both cases, the system loses the capacity to engage in self-repair.
claims.note: Asserts a loss of functional capacity in both types of system.

claims.claim: The incapacity for self-repair marks the ontological boundary of law's existence.
claims.source_quote: This incapacity marks the ontological boundary of law's existence.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim about what defines the limit of law's existence.

claims.claim: When recognition ceases to be reflexive, the world of law ceases to be self-sustaining.
claims.source_quote: Once recognition ceases to be reflexive, either because it is monopolized or dissipated, the world of law ceases to be self-sustaining.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive ontological relation between reflexive recognition and law's self-sustainability.

claims.claim: Ontological entropy is the gradual decay of coherence and reversion to brute relations of power.
claims.source_quote: What follows is ontological entropy: the gradual decay of coherence and the reversion of social life to brute relations of power, habit, or force.
claims.note: Defines and asserts the nature of ontological entropy as a real process.

claims.claim: In authoritarian systems, legal order becomes performative rather than functional.
claims.source_quote: The legal order becomes performative rather than functional, mimicking coherence through procedural spectacle.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the legal order under authoritarian conditions.

claims.claim: Citizens in decayed legal systems no longer experience law as a stable framework of meaning.
claims.source_quote: Citizens no longer experience law as a stable framework of meaning but as either a façade or a void.
claims.note: Asserts a changed relational property between citizens and law under decay.

claims.claim: Authoritarian rigidity embodies the moral failure of closure.
claims.source_quote: Authoritarian rigidity embodies the moral failure of closure, the refusal to acknowledge contradiction or to recognize the autonomy of others.
claims.note: Asserts a moral-ontological property of authoritarian rigidity.

claims.claim: Anomic collapse embodies the moral failure of dissolution.
claims.source_quote: Anomic collapse embodies the moral failure of dissolution, the abandonment of shared recognition and the retreat into self-interest or despair.
claims.note: Asserts a moral-ontological property of anomic collapse.

claims.claim: Both authoritarianism and anomy are failures of relational being.
claims.source_quote: Both are failures of relational being, in which the capacity for recognition that constitutes law is lost.
claims.note: Author directly asserts the ontological category of these failures.

claims.claim: Recognition constitutes law.
claims.source_quote: the capacity for recognition that constitutes law is lost.
claims.note: Asserts a constitutive ontological relation between recognition and law.

claims.claim: Authoritarianism destroys pluralism; anomy destroys coherence.
claims.source_quote: The former destroys pluralism; the latter destroys coherence.
claims.note: Asserts distinct destructive properties of each pathological form.

claims.claim: The ontology of law contains within it the seeds of both order and decay.
claims.source_quote: Thus, the ontology of law contains within it the seeds of both order and decay.
claims.note: Asserts a structural property of law's ontology.

claims.claim: Law endures not by eliminating contradiction but by sustaining the machinery of repair.
claims.source_quote: Law endures not by eliminating contradiction but by sustaining the delicate machinery of repair.
claims.note: Asserts what is constitutive of law's endurance as an ontological claim.

claims.claim: Repair is the ontological process by which contradiction debt is absorbed and coherence restored.
claims.source_quote: Repair, as developed throughout this work, is the ontological process by which contradiction debt is absorbed and coherence restored within law's relational architecture.
claims.note: Defines repair as a specific kind of ontological process with a function.

claims.claim: Repair acts upon dependent continuants such as conflicting obligations, roles, and institutional recognitions.
claims.source_quote: this process can be modeled as a dynamic sequence of occurrents that act upon dependent continuants, specifically, upon conflicting obligations, roles, and institutional recognitions.
claims.note: Asserts the relata and structure of the repair process in ontological terms.

claims.claim: Obligations, roles, and rights are dependent continuants that structure law's being.
claims.source_quote: Dependent Continuants (Obligations, Roles, Rights): enduring relations that structure law's being.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category membership and function of these entities.

claims.claim: Contradictory realizations are occurrents in which legal relations come into conflict.
claims.source_quote: Occurrents (Contradictory Realizations): processes in which these relations come into conflict.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and nature of contradictory realizations.

claims.claim: Courts, legislatures, and administrative bodies are institutional continuants bearing repair capacity.
claims.source_quote: Institutional Continuants (Courts, Legislatures, Administrative Bodies): bearers of repair capacity.
claims.note: Asserts ontological category membership and a functional property of these entities.

claims.claim: Adjudication, amendment, and reinterpretation are repair occurrents that realign dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Repair Occurrents (Adjudication, Amendment, Reinterpretation): mechanisms that realign dependencies.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological category and function of these processes.

claims.claim: The repair process produces a new dependent continuant (a Resolution) that reestablishes coherence.
claims.source_quote: The process modifies or extinguishes one or both obligations, creating a new dependent continuant, a Resolution, that reestablishes coherence.
claims.note: Asserts that the repair process generates a new entity with the function of restoring coherence.

claims.claim: Resolution is recorded in institutional memory to ensure persistence of coherence.
claims.source_quote: This resolution is then recorded in institutional memory (case law, statute, archive), ensuring the persistence of coherence and preventing reemergence of the same contradiction.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between resolution and institutional memory with a functional role.

claims.claim: Repair is a recurring ontological process, not a one-time correction.
claims.source_quote: repair is not a one-time correction but a recurring ontological process, a self-referential loop that maintains the identity of law across change.
claims.note: Asserts a property of repair as an ontological process.

claims.claim: Law maintains its identity by continuously reconstituting its own coherence.
claims.source_quote: embodying what may be called reflexive persistence: the ability of law to remain itself by continuously reconstituting its own coherence.
claims.note: Author introduces 'reflexive persistence' as a property of law; medium because hedged with 'what may be called'.

claims.claim: High detection latency allows contradiction debt to accumulate, increasing systemic fragility.
claims.source_quote: Ontological implication: delayed recognition allows contradiction debt to accumulate, increasing systemic fragility.
claims.note: Author asserts an ontological implication: a causal relation between delayed recognition and systemic fragility.

claims.claim: Repair efficiency measures the system's capacity to realign dependencies without structural rupture.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, RE measures the system's capacity to realign dependencies without structural rupture.
claims.note: Asserts what repair efficiency is ontologically measuring—a functional capacity of the system.

claims.claim: Algorithmic adjudication risks collapsing law's ontological distinction between realization and recognition.
claims.source_quote: Without these mechanisms, algorithmic adjudication risks collapsing law's ontological distinction between realization and recognition, producing an illusion of coherence while silently eroding justice's structural integrity.
claims.note: Asserts a property/risk of algorithmic adjudication as an ontological collapse of two distinct categories.

claims.claim: Smart contracts and algorithmic adjudication share the structural pathology of substituting execution for recognition.
claims.source_quote: Both smart contracts and algorithmic adjudication illustrate the same structural pathology: the substitution of execution for recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that two kinds of systems bear a shared property (structural pathology) defined as substituting execution for recognition.

claims.claim: Automation compresses law's ontological field, reducing relational complexity that sustains justice.
claims.source_quote: In each case, automation compresses law's ontological field, reducing the relational complexity that sustains justice.
claims.note: Asserts a property of automation with respect to law's ontological field.

claims.claim: Where recognition is removed, contradiction cannot be repaired.
claims.source_quote: Where recognition is removed, contradiction cannot be repaired; where repair is absent, incoherence accumulates until the system fractures.
claims.note: Asserts a structural dependency relation: recognition is a condition for repair of contradiction.

claims.claim: Where repair is absent, incoherence accumulates until the system fractures.
claims.source_quote: Where recognition is removed, contradiction cannot be repaired; where repair is absent, incoherence accumulates until the system fractures.
claims.note: Asserts a property/causal role of the absence of repair within law's ontological field.

claims.claim: These failures are ontological ruptures in which law's world ceases to align with itself.
claims.source_quote: These failures are not technical errors but ontological ruptures, instances in which law's world ceases to align with itself.
claims.note: Asserts that automation failures are a subkind of ontological rupture, not merely technical error.

claims.claim: Every algorithmic process must be treated as a participant within law's ontology.
claims.source_quote: Every algorithmic process must therefore be treated as a participant within law's ontology, explicitly modeled as a realization mechanism dependent on institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that algorithmic processes are participants in law's ontology and are realization mechanisms.

claims.claim: Every algorithmic process is a realization mechanism dependent on institutional recognition.
claims.source_quote: Every algorithmic process must therefore be treated as a participant within law's ontology, explicitly modeled as a realization mechanism dependent on institutional recognition.
claims.note: Asserts that algorithmic processes bear a dependency relation on institutional recognition.

claims.claim: Justice in the digital domain depends on coherence through reflexive recognition.
claims.source_quote: Justice, when transposed into the digital domain, depends on the same principle that sustains it in the human one: coherence through reflexive recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation: justice has the property of depending on reflexive recognition for coherence.

claims.claim: Automation that conceals its own ontological dependencies undermines the reality of law.
claims.source_quote: Automation that conceals its own ontological dependencies undermines the very reality of law it seeks to serve.
claims.note: Asserts a property/effect of a kind of automation on the reality of law.

claims.claim: Law is a field of recognition populated by continuants and occurrents whose coherence must be maintained through ongoing repair.
claims.source_quote: Structural jurisprudence treats law as a field of recognition populated by continuants and occurrents whose coherence must be maintained through ongoing repair.
claims.note: Author endorses this characterization of law's ontological nature as part of structural jurisprudence.

claims.claim: Algorithms can calculate, classify, and trigger, but only recognized institutions can confer, withdraw, or repair legal status.
claims.source_quote: Algorithms can calculate, classify, and trigger, yet only recognized institutions can confer legal status, withdraw it, or repair it when contradictions appear.
claims.note: Asserts distinct functional properties of algorithms versus recognized institutions within law's ontology.

claims.claim: Machine processes are occurrents that realize functions over dependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: In Basic Formal Ontology terms, machine processes are occurrents that realize functions over dependent continuants, while courts, agencies, and legislatures are institutional continuants that authorize and record that realization.
claims.note: Asserts that machine processes are a subkind of occurrent with the function of realizing dependent continuants.

claims.claim: Courts, agencies, and legislatures are institutional continuants that authorize and record realization.
claims.source_quote: courts, agencies, and legislatures are institutional continuants that authorize and record that realization.
claims.note: Asserts that courts, agencies, and legislatures are instances of institutional continuants bearing authorization and recording functions.

claims.claim: The distinction between realization and recognition is the heart of legal ontology and the basis for repair capacity.
claims.source_quote: These designs preserve the distinction between realization and recognition, which is the heart of legal ontology and the basis for repair capacity.
claims.note: Asserts that the distinction between realization and recognition has a foundational role in legal ontology.

claims.claim: Centralizing recognition in a single algorithm or office invites authoritarian closure.
claims.source_quote: Centralizing recognition in a single algorithm or a single office invites authoritarian closure.
claims.note: Asserts a property/risk of centralizing recognition: it constitutes or enables authoritarian closure.

claims.claim: Dispersing recognition without coordination risks anomic fragmentation.
claims.source_quote: Dispersing it without coordination risks anomic fragmentation.
claims.note: Asserts a property/risk of uncoordinated dispersal of recognition.

claims.claim: Pluralism is a precondition of resilience in hybrid legal orders.
claims.source_quote: Pluralism remains a precondition of resilience. Hybrid legal orders will be healthiest where authority is distributed across multiple recognition sources.
claims.note: Asserts that pluralism bears a precondition relation to resilience, which is a structural ontological dependency.

claims.claim: Whether an AI should bear a legal role turns on recognition and responsibility, not metaphysical essence.
claims.source_quote: Whether an AI should bear a role turns on recognition and responsibility. If institutions can attribute obligations, provide oversight, and route repair through reviewable processes, functional personhood becomes a question of architectural fit rather than metaphysical essence.
claims.note: Asserts that the relevant property for legal personhood is architectural/recognition-based, not metaphysical essence.

claims.claim: Any participant in law's ontology must be locatable in the network of recognition and capable of being recalled into repair.
claims.source_quote: It insists that any participant must be locatable in the network of recognition and capable, through its designers and governors, of being recalled into repair.
claims.note: Asserts necessary properties of any legal participant: locatability in recognition network and reparability.

claims.claim: Human judgment remains primary where recognition and repair require prudence, mercy, and equity.
claims.source_quote: Human judgment stays primary where recognition and repair require prudence, mercy, and equity.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of human judgment within the ontological architecture of law.

claims.claim: Artificial systems extend reach, regularity, and speed where calculation and pattern detection help.
claims.source_quote: Artificial systems extend reach, regularity, and speed where calculation and pattern detection help.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property/role of artificial systems within the legal ontological field.

claims.claim: Resolution Efficiency measures a system's capacity to realign dependencies without structural rupture.
claims.source_quote: Ontologically, RE measures the system's capacity to realign dependencies without structural rupture.
claims.note: Author explicitly states an ontological function of RE as a property of the system.

claims.claim: High Resolution Efficiency reflects adaptive repair mechanisms such as flexible adjudication and open amendment procedures.
claims.source_quote: High RE reflects adaptive repair mechanisms (flexible adjudication, open amendment procedures).
claims.note: Author asserts a property relation between high RE and adaptive repair mechanisms.

claims.claim: Low Resolution Efficiency correlates with institutional paralysis or political obstruction.
claims.source_quote: Low RE correlates with institutional paralysis or political obstruction.
claims.note: Author asserts a relational property between low RE and institutional states.

claims.claim: Coherence Retention quantifies how well repair processes maintain law's self-identity through change.
claims.source_quote: Ontological function: CR quantifies how well repair processes maintain law's self-identity through change, the 'Ship of Theseus' condition of institutional persistence.
claims.note: Author asserts the ontological function of CR as measuring law's identity-preservation.

claims.claim: Law has a self-identity that persists through change via repair processes.
claims.source_quote: CR quantifies how well repair processes maintain law's self-identity through change, the 'Ship of Theseus' condition of institutional persistence.
claims.note: Author commits to law having a self-identity subject to persistence conditions.

claims.claim: High Coherence Retention corresponds to incremental adaptation such as reinterpretation and jurisprudential evolution.
claims.source_quote: High CR = incremental adaptation (reinterpretation, jurisprudential evolution).
claims.note: Author asserts a property relation between high CR and incremental adaptation.

claims.claim: Low Coherence Retention corresponds to discontinuous reform such as revolution or collapse.
claims.source_quote: Low CR = discontinuous reform (revolution, collapse).
claims.note: Author asserts a property relation between low CR and discontinuous reform.

claims.claim: Contradiction Density reflects the ontological balance between diversity and coherence in law.
claims.source_quote: CD thus reflects the ontological balance between diversity and coherence, the living tension that sustains law's vitality.
claims.note: Author asserts CD as an ontological measure of the balance between two properties of legal systems.

claims.claim: Law's vitality is sustained by a living tension between diversity and coherence.
claims.source_quote: CD thus reflects the ontological balance between diversity and coherence, the living tension that sustains law's vitality.
claims.note: Author asserts a causal/sustaining relation between the diversity-coherence tension and law's vitality.

claims.claim: An optimal Contradiction Density is nonzero because pluralism requires some contradiction to remain dynamic.
claims.source_quote: Optimal CD is nonzero; pluralism requires some contradiction to remain dynamic.
claims.note: Author asserts a normative-ontological property: the optimal state of CD for a plural legal system.

claims.claim: Excessive Contradiction Density overwhelms repair capacity, leading to legal incoherence (anomy).
claims.source_quote: Excessive CD overwhelms repair capacity, leading to incoherence (anomy).
claims.note: Author asserts a causal relation between excessive CD and incoherence/anomy.

claims.claim: Zero Contradiction Density implies authoritarian overclosure, erasing pluralism and suppressing reflexivity.
claims.source_quote: Zero CD implies authoritarian overclosure, erasing pluralism and suppressing reflexivity.
claims.note: Author asserts that zero CD entails specific ontological conditions in the legal system.

claims.claim: The Institutional Resilience Index is a composite measure of institutional resilience.
claims.source_quote: Together, these metrics yield a composite measure of Institutional Resilience Index (IRI), expressible as: IRI = (RE × CR) / (DL × CD).
claims.note: Author asserts the existence of this composite entity as a measure of a system property.

claims.claim: High IRI values indicate a system capable of rapid recognition, efficient repair, and continuity of coherence despite pluralism.
claims.source_quote: High IRI values indicate a system capable of rapid recognition, efficient repair, and continuity of coherence despite pluralism.
claims.note: Author asserts a property relation between high IRI and specific capacities of legal systems.

claims.claim: Low IRI values denote institutional fragility, whether from rigidity or chaos.
claims.source_quote: Low IRI values denote fragility, whether from rigidity (low CD but high DL) or chaos (high CD but low RE).
claims.note: Author asserts that low IRI is a property indicating fragility in legal systems.

claims.claim: Human judgment is primary where recognition and repair require prudence, mercy, and equity.
claims.source_quote: Human judgment stays primary where recognition and repair require prudence, mercy, and equity.
claims.note: Asserts a property/role of human judgment in the legal order being described.

claims.claim: Artificial systems extend reach, regularity, and speed where calculation and pattern detection help.
claims.source_quote: Artificial systems extend reach, regularity, and speed where calculation and pattern detection help.
claims.note: Asserts a function/disposition of artificial systems in the described legal architecture.

claims.claim: Explicit ontologies keep dependencies visible and corrigible.
claims.source_quote: The two are bound together by explicit ontologies that keep dependencies visible and corrigible.
claims.note: Asserts a functional property of explicit ontologies in the legal system.

claims.claim: Human judgment and artificial systems are bound together by explicit ontologies.
claims.source_quote: The two are bound together by explicit ontologies that keep dependencies visible and corrigible.
claims.note: Asserts a relation between human judgment, artificial systems, and explicit ontologies.

claims.claim: Law has always integrated new media and new institutions while defending the integrity of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law has always integrated new media and new institutions while defending the integrity of recognition.
claims.note: Asserts a historical property/disposition of law as an entity.

claims.claim: The future of structural jurisprudence is continuous with its past.
claims.source_quote: Seen in this light, the future of structural jurisprudence is continuous with its past.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property between future and past structural jurisprudence; medium because framed by 'seen in this light' but still endorsed by the author.

claims.claim: Law has always integrated new media and new institutions while defending the integrity of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Law has always integrated new media and new institutions while defending the integrity of recognition.
claims.note: A positive assertion about the nature and history of law as an entity with a property/function.

claims.claim: Justice is the structural integrity of a living architecture that can absorb contradiction without losing itself.
claims.source_quote: Justice will then remain what it has been throughout this book, the structural integrity of a living architecture that can absorb contradiction without losing itself.
claims.note: The author directly defines justice as a kind of structural integrity, asserting what justice is as an ontological claim.

claims.claim: Justice is a living architecture with the capacity to absorb contradiction.
claims.source_quote: the structural integrity of a living architecture that can absorb contradiction without losing itself.
claims.note: Asserts that justice (as living architecture) has the disposition/property of absorbing contradiction while maintaining identity.

claims.claim: Law is an organized structure of interlocking relations that persists through time.
claims.source_quote: we have approached law not as a system of commands or a repository of doctrines, but as an organized structure of interlocking relations that persists through time.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the nature of law as a kind of entity with structural properties.

claims.claim: Law is constituted by relations among agents, roles, obligations, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: we have treated law not as an accumulation of texts or a sequence of commands, but as a material structure constituted by relations among agents, roles, obligations, and institutions.
claims.note: Asserts the constitutive relations of law as an entity.

claims.claim: Legal phenomena include obligations, rights, permissions, and violations.
claims.source_quote: every legal phenomenon, an obligation, a right, a permission, a violation, exists within a wider pattern of interdependencies.
claims.note: Asserts that these are kinds of entities that exist within legal systems.

claims.claim: Every legal phenomenon exists within a wider pattern of interdependencies.
claims.source_quote: every legal phenomenon, an obligation, a right, a permission, a violation, exists within a wider pattern of interdependencies.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of all legal phenomena.

claims.claim: Every obligation is borne by an agent in virtue of a role.
claims.source_quote: No obligation ever stands alone; it is borne by an agent in virtue of a role, arises from a form of recognition, persists through institutional support, and terminates through acknowledgment or repair.
claims.note: Asserts a structural relation between obligations, agents, and roles.

claims.claim: Every obligation arises from a form of recognition.
claims.source_quote: it is borne by an agent in virtue of a role, arises from a form of recognition, persists through institutional support, and terminates through acknowledgment or repair.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/generative relation between recognition and obligations.

claims.claim: Every obligation persists through institutional support.
claims.source_quote: it is borne by an agent in virtue of a role, arises from a form of recognition, persists through institutional support, and terminates through acknowledgment or repair.
claims.note: Asserts that institutions bear a sustaining relation to obligations.

claims.claim: Every obligation terminates through acknowledgment or repair.
claims.source_quote: it is borne by an agent in virtue of a role, arises from a form of recognition, persists through institutional support, and terminates through acknowledgment or repair.
claims.note: Asserts the termination conditions of obligations as ontological facts.

claims.claim: Every legal act both presupposes and alters the relational field in which it occurs.
claims.source_quote: Every legal act both presupposes and alters the relational field in which it occurs.
claims.note: Asserts a two-directional relation between legal acts and the relational field.

claims.claim: Law generates and maintains a network of directed dependencies.
claims.source_quote: it does so by generating and maintaining a network of directed dependencies. These dependencies form the architecture within which persons act, claim, recognize, and repair.
claims.note: Asserts that directed dependencies are entities generated and maintained by law.

claims.claim: Law is relational before it is conceptual, and structured before it is doctrinal.
claims.source_quote: Law, in this sense, is relational before it is conceptual, and structured before it is doctrinal.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological priority of law's relational and structural character over its conceptual and doctrinal character.

claims.claim: The stability of a legal system depends on the fit among its relations.
claims.source_quote: The stability of a legal system depends on the fit among these relations: how well obligations align with authority, how consistently institutions recognize the claims they are charged to maintain.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between system stability and relational fit.

claims.claim: Structural realism treats relations as central to the existence of legal phenomena.
claims.source_quote: Structural realism, as adopted in this book, treats relations as central to the existence of legal phenomena.
claims.note: The author adopts structural realism, committing to this ontological claim about the centrality of relations.

claims.claim: Law is constituted through directed dependencies among agents.
claims.source_quote: If law is constituted through directed dependencies among agents and recognized through institutional acts, then understanding law requires the capacity to 'see' these dependencies.
claims.note: Author endorses this conditional's antecedent as the basis for the ontological project.

claims.claim: Law is recognized through institutional acts.
claims.source_quote: If law is constituted through directed dependencies among agents and recognized through institutional acts...
claims.note: Stated as an if-clause the author endorses as the grounding premise; high commitment but framed conditionally.

claims.claim: Agents occupy roles within legal systems.
claims.source_quote: it is to draw attention to the relations that constitute a legal world: the roles that agents occupy, the obligations they bear, the institutions that anchor those obligations
claims.note: Asserts a relation of occupation between agents and roles.

claims.claim: Agents bear obligations within legal systems.
claims.source_quote: the roles that agents occupy, the obligations they bear, the institutions that anchor those obligations
claims.note: Asserts a bearing relation between agents and obligations.

claims.claim: Institutions anchor obligations within legal systems.
claims.source_quote: the roles that agents occupy, the obligations they bear, the institutions that anchor those obligations
claims.note: Asserts a structural anchoring relation between institutions and obligations.

claims.claim: Law is not merely a set of rules or discrete acts.
claims.source_quote: law is not merely a set of rules, nor a set of discrete acts, but an organized field whose coherence depends on recognitions, obligations, and institutional continuity.
claims.note: Negative ontological assertion clarifying what law is not, paired with a positive characterization.

claims.claim: Law's coherence depends on recognitions, obligations, and institutional continuity.
claims.source_quote: an organized field whose coherence depends on recognitions, obligations, and institutional continuity.
claims.note: Asserts a dependency relation between legal coherence and specific ontological kinds.

claims.claim: Institutional resilience is the structural correlate of justice.
claims.source_quote: Institutional resilience, in this model, is the structural correlate of justice.
claims.note: Direct ontological identification of institutional resilience with justice's structural correlate.

claims.claim: A just system can detect contradiction quickly, repair it effectively, and retain coherence without annihilating plurality.
claims.source_quote: A just system is one that can detect contradiction quickly, repair it effectively, and retain coherence without annihilating plurality.
claims.note: Asserts a property of the entity 'just system' — a direct ontological claim about what justice is.

claims.claim: Repair is a literal ontological function of law.
claims.source_quote: repair is not a metaphor but a literal ontological function: the process through which law endures as a living structure of interdependent continuants.
claims.note: Explicitly asserts that repair is an ontological function, not merely a metaphor.

claims.claim: Law endures as a living structure of interdependent continuants.
claims.source_quote: the process through which law endures as a living structure of interdependent continuants.
claims.note: Asserts a kind-membership and structural property of law as composed of interdependent continuants.

claims.claim: Where repair mechanisms are suppressed or overloaded, contradiction debt accumulates.
claims.source_quote: Where repair mechanisms are suppressed or overloaded, contradiction debt accumulates; where they are active and adaptive, law renews itself continuously.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/structural relation between repair mechanisms and contradiction debt — an ontological claim about law's dynamics.

claims.claim: Institutional resilience is the measure of justice's metaphysical vitality.
claims.source_quote: Institutional resilience, in this sense, is the measure of justice's metaphysical vitality, the capacity of recognition to survive its own contradictions.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological relation between institutional resilience and justice's metaphysical vitality.

claims.claim: Justice is a state of ontological coherence — the equilibrium of law's relational architecture.
claims.source_quote: justice is not conceived as a transcendental or purely moral ideal, but as a state of ontological coherence, the equilibrium of law's relational architecture.
claims.note: Directly asserts what justice is — an ontological identification.

claims.claim: A legal system is composed of dependent continuants including obligations, rights, roles, and institutional recognitions.
claims.source_quote: the network of dependent continuants that compose a legal system, including obligations, rights, roles, and institutional recognitions
claims.note: Asserts that obligations, rights, roles, and institutional recognitions are dependent continuants composing the legal system.

claims.claim: A just legal order achieves structural integrity by sustaining coherence amid contradiction, continuity amid reform, and reflexivity amid change.
claims.source_quote: A just legal order is thus one that achieves structural integrity: it sustains coherence amid contradiction, preserves continuity amid reform, and retains reflexivity amid change.
claims.note: Asserts properties of a just legal order — an ontological claim about structural integrity.

claims.claim: Justice is the measure of law's ontological health.
claims.source_quote: This conception reframes justice as the measure of law's ontological health, rather than as the fulfillment of a moral or teleological aim.
claims.note: Direct ontological identification of justice with law's ontological health.

claims.claim: The structural judge is a repair agent within law's ontological field, not a moral author of law's narrative.
claims.source_quote: The structural judge is not the moral author of law's narrative but a repair agent within its ontological field.
claims.note: Asserts the role and function of the judge as a kind of entity within law's ontological field.

claims.claim: Interpretation is the act of restoring coherence to the network of dependent continuants that law sustains.
claims.source_quote: Interpretation is not the discovery of an underlying moral truth but the act of restoring coherence to the network of dependent continuants that law sustains.
claims.note: Asserts what interpretation is — an ontological claim about its function.

claims.claim: A just decision resolves contradiction debt by bringing conflicting obligations, rights, and recognitions into coherent structure.
claims.source_quote: A just decision, therefore, is one that resolves contradiction debt, bringing conflicting obligations, rights, and recognitions into a coherent structure.
claims.note: Asserts a property/function of a just decision — an ontological claim about what justice does structurally.

claims.claim: Fuller's eight principles are the metaphysical grammar of law's survival.
claims.source_quote: His eight principles are the metaphysical grammar of law's survival.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological role for Fuller's principles — they constitute the metaphysical conditions of law's existence.

claims.claim: Fuller's procedural morality corresponds ontologically to the maintenance of recognition coherence.
claims.source_quote: Fuller's procedural morality thus corresponds, in ontological language, to the maintenance of recognition coherence.
claims.note: Asserts an ontological correspondence between Fuller's procedural morality and recognition coherence.

claims.claim: Fidelity to legal form preserves law's ontological coherence.
claims.source_quote: fidelity to form is legitimacy, because it preserves law's ontological coherence.
claims.note: Asserts a causal/constitutive ontological relation between fidelity to form and law's coherence.

claims.claim: A law that ceases to maintain its internal structural dependencies ceases to be functional as law in a coherent system.
claims.source_quote: a law that ceases to maintain its internal structural dependencies ceases to be functional as law in a coherent system.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for law's functional existence — an ontological claim.

claims.claim: Dworkin's integrity corresponds to horizontal coherence — the alignment of norms and principles within the legal system.
claims.source_quote: Dworkin's integrity corresponds to horizontal coherence, the alignment of norms and principles within the legal system.
claims.note: Author endorses this mapping as part of his own structural framework, though it also characterizes Dworkin; the author asserts this correspondence positively.

claims.claim: Fuller's procedural morality corresponds to vertical coherence — the alignment of law's norms with the institutions that sustain them.
claims.source_quote: Fuller's procedural morality corresponds to vertical coherence, the alignment of law's norms with the institutions that create, apply, and sustain them.
claims.note: Author endorses this mapping as part of his own framework; asserts an ontological correspondence.

claims.claim: Justice arises from the structural fitness of law's relational architecture, not from the rightness of content or virtue of process.
claims.source_quote: Justice arises not from the rightness of law's content nor from the virtue of its process but from the structural fitness of its relational architecture.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion of what produces justice — an ontological claim about its source.

claims.claim: Law's reality depends on the sustained functioning of institutions that generate and maintain recognition relations across time.
claims.source_quote: The law's reality does not depend on agreement about moral principle but on the sustained functioning of institutions that generate and maintain those relations across time.
claims.note: Asserts what law's existence depends on — a direct ontological claim.

claims.claim: When laws are secret, retroactive, or contradictory, the system's recognition structure breaks down.
claims.source_quote: When these conditions fail, when laws are secret, retroactive, or contradictory, the system's recognition structure breaks down.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/ontological consequence of certain legal failures.

claims.claim: The generality of rules, their public recognition, and congruence between norm and enforcement are conditions of existence for legal entities.
claims.source_quote: The generality of rules, their public recognition, and the congruence between norm and enforcement are not merely ethical requirements but conditions of existence for legal entities.
claims.note: Asserts that these procedural features are ontological conditions of existence, not merely moral ones.

claims.claim: Legal systems have patterns that give them coherence.
claims.source_quote: When we model a legal system, even in the most preliminary and conceptual sense, we reveal the patterns that give the system its coherence.
claims.note: The author asserts that legal systems possess coherence-giving patterns as a structural property.

claims.claim: Legal systems have a directionality of obligations.
claims.source_quote: Modeling helps us notice the directionality of obligations, the dependencies that underlie institutional authority, and the flows of recognition that sustain legal life.
claims.note: The author asserts obligations in legal systems have a directional structure as an ontological feature.

claims.claim: Institutional authority has underlying dependencies.
claims.source_quote: Modeling helps us notice the directionality of obligations, the dependencies that underlie institutional authority, and the flows of recognition that sustain legal life.
claims.note: The author asserts that dependencies are a real structural feature underlying institutional authority.

claims.claim: Legal life is sustained by flows of recognition.
claims.source_quote: the flows of recognition that sustain legal life.
claims.note: The author asserts that recognition flows are a real feature that sustain legal life, an ontological claim about the constitution of legal existence.

claims.claim: Justice and injustice emerge from the structure of a legal system.
claims.source_quote: we also begin to see how justice and injustice emerge from the structure itself.
claims.note: The author asserts that justice and injustice are emergent properties of legal structure, an ontological claim about their origin.

claims.claim: Modeling is a continuation of ontological inquiry.
claims.source_quote: Modeling, therefore, is not an ancillary exercise. It is a continuation of the ontological inquiry already undertaken.
claims.note: The author asserts modeling bears a specific relation (continuation) to ontological inquiry, making a claim about its nature and role.

claims.claim: Legitimacy corresponds to vertical coherence between law's norms and its institutions.
claims.source_quote: ty corresponds to vertical coherence, the alignment of law's norms with the institutions that create, apply, and sustain them.
claims.note: The author asserts a correspondence relation between legitimacy and vertical coherence, an ontological relational claim.

claims.claim: Structural integrity synthesizes legitimacy and coherence within a broader ontological framework.
claims.source_quote: Structural integrity synthesizes both but situates them within a broader ontological framework.
claims.note: The author asserts that structural integrity is a synthesis situated within an ontological framework — a claim about the nature and relations of these concepts.

claims.claim: Justice arises from the structural fitness of law's relational architecture.
claims.source_quote: Justice arises not from the rightness of law's content nor from the virtue of its process but from the structural fitness of its relational architecture.
claims.note: The author positively asserts the ontological ground of justice as structural fitness of relational architecture.

claims.claim: A legal system is just when the relations among agents, norms, and institutions are coherent, responsive, and repairable.
claims.source_quote: When the relations among agents, norms, and institutions are coherent, responsive, and repairable, the system is just.
claims.note: The author asserts a constitutive condition for justice in a legal system — an ontological claim about what justice is.

claims.claim: Injustice is ontological dissonance resulting from fractured or ossified relations among agents, norms, and institutions.
claims.source_quote: When those relations fracture or ossify, injustice appears as ontological dissonance.
claims.note: The author asserts that injustice is (appears as) ontological dissonance — a claim about the nature of injustice.

claims.claim: Law is a structured field composed of entities with determinate ontological statuses.
claims.source_quote: it is a structured field composed of entities with determinate ontological statuses, agents, roles, obligations, institutions, and of relations that bind these entities together across time.
claims.note: Direct positive assertion about the ontological nature of law.

claims.claim: Law is not a disembodied set of propositions nor an abstract normative order.
claims.source_quote: law is not a disembodied set of propositions nor an abstract normative order.
claims.note: The author explicitly denies two alternative ontological characterizations of law, committing to their negation.

claims.claim: Agents, roles, obligations, and institutions are structural components of legal reality.
claims.source_quote: The ontological distinctions, agent, role, obligation, are not technical artifacts but structural components of legal reality.
claims.note: Explicit assertion that these entities are real structural components, not merely representational conveniences.

claims.claim: Legal systems attach obligations and permissions to roles, not directly to persons as biological individuals.
claims.source_quote: legal systems do not attach obligations and permissions directly to persons as biological individuals. Instead, they attach them to roles, positions within a relational structure, that agents occupy.
claims.note: Asserts a relational property of legal systems regarding how obligations attach.

claims.claim: A role is a structured position within a network of relations.
claims.source_quote: A role is not an intrinsic property of a person. It is a structured position within a network of relations.
claims.note: Defines the ontological kind of a role—a relational position, not an intrinsic property.

claims.claim: Roles exist independently of the individuals who fill them.
claims.source_quote: These positions exist independently of the individuals who fill them. Roles persist even as agents move into and out of them.
claims.note: Asserts that roles have independent existence from the agents who occupy them.

claims.claim: Roles persist even as agents move into and out of them.
claims.source_quote: Roles persist even as agents move into and out of them.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence property of roles as a kind of entity.

claims.claim: Roles mediate the connection between agents and the obligations they bear.
claims.source_quote: This diagram expresses a basic commitment of the ontology: roles mediate the connection between agents and the obligations they bear.
claims.note: Asserts a relational mediating function of roles between agents and obligations.

claims.claim: The agent is the bearer of the role.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological perspective, the agent is the bearer of the role, but the role is the bearer of the obligation.
claims.note: Asserts a bearing relation between agents and roles.

claims.claim: The role is the bearer of the obligation.
claims.source_quote: From an ontological perspective, the agent is the bearer of the role, but the role is the bearer of the obligation.
claims.note: Asserts a bearing relation between roles and obligations.

claims.claim: Obligations adhere to roles recognized within an institutional framework, not to individuals as such.
claims.source_quote: Obligations do not adhere to individuals as such; they adhere to roles recognized within an institutional framework.
claims.note: Asserts the proper locus of obligation attachment within the ontology.

claims.claim: A role survives the turnover of individuals who occupy it.
claims.source_quote: A role survives the turnover of individuals who occupy it.
claims.note: Asserts a persistence/continuity property of roles as entities.

claims.claim: Institutional authority of a role does not depend on the identity of any particular person occupying it.
claims.source_quote: The authority of a judge, for example, does not depend on the identity of any particular person. It persists as an institutional position with a determinate set of obligations, permissions, and powers.
claims.note: Asserts that authority is a property of an institutional role-position, independent of individual identity.

claims.claim: A role is an instance of specifically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: law:Role a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:SpecificallyDependentContinuant .
claims.note: The author presents this OWL fragment as mirroring the book's 'conceptual commitments already established,' endorsing the ontological classification.

claims.claim: An obligation is an instance of specifically dependent continuant.
claims.source_quote: law:Obligation a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:SpecificallyDependentContinuant .
claims.note: Same rationale: the author endorses this representation as reflecting established ontological commitments.

claims.claim: An agent is an instance of independent continuant.
claims.source_quote: law:Agent a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bfo:IndependentContinuant .
claims.note: Author endorses the RDF/OWL fragment as mirroring the book's conceptual commitments, placing agents in the independent continuant category.

claims.claim: The endurance of roles supports the endurance of legal systems.
claims.source_quote: Modeling allows us to see how the endurance of roles supports the endurance of the system itself.
claims.note: Asserts a structural/causal relation between role persistence and system stability.

claims.claim: Justice and injustice emerge from the structure of legal relations.
claims.source_quote: we also begin to see how justice and injustice emerge from the structure itself.
claims.note: Author positively asserts this causal/structural claim, though framed in terms of what modeling reveals.

claims.claim: A role is recognized by an institution.
claims.source_quote: roleType --> institution : recognizedBy
claims.note: The UML sketch is presented as expressing the author's ontological commitments about recognition relations between roles and institutions.

claims.claim: Justice is immanent to law, not external or internal to it.
claims.source_quote: On the structural view, justice is neither external nor internal, it is immanent. It is the very condition of law's being.
claims.note: Direct ontological assertion about the nature and location of justice relative to law.

claims.claim: Law cannot exist without coherence.
claims.source_quote: Law cannot exist without coherence, and coherence, when reflexive and repairable, is justice itself.
claims.note: Asserts a necessary condition for law's existence—an ontological claim about what constitutes law.

claims.claim: Coherence, when reflexive and repairable, is justice itself.
claims.source_quote: Law cannot exist without coherence, and coherence, when reflexive and repairable, is justice itself.
claims.note: Identity claim: reflexive, repairable coherence is identified with justice—a direct ontological assertion.

claims.claim: Justice is the integrity of recognition in a legal system.
claims.source_quote: The approach described in this book redefines justice as the integrity of recognition, the measure of how well a legal system sustains coherent relations among its dependent continuants.
claims.note: The author asserts a definition/identity claim about what justice is ontologically.

claims.claim: Justice is what law is when it functions properly as a coherent, reflexive system of recognition.
claims.source_quote: Justice is not something law ought to achieve; it is what law is when it functions properly as a coherent, reflexive system of recognition.
claims.note: Direct ontological identification of justice with law's functional integrity.

claims.claim: Injustice is the loss of structural integrity and breakdown of recognition across institutions and roles.
claims.source_quote: In both cases, injustice is the loss of structural integrity, the breakdown of recognition across institutions and roles.
claims.note: Ontological claim identifying injustice with a specific structural condition.

claims.claim: Repair of injustice is ontological reconstruction, not moral correction.
claims.source_quote: Repair, therefore, is not moral correction but ontological reconstruction. To repair is to restore the coherence that allows recognition, and hence law, to exist at all.
claims.note: Asserts the nature and kind of the act of legal repair—an ontological rather than moral act.

claims.claim: Justice occupies a metaphysical middle ground between moral unity and procedural morality.
claims.source_quote: Justice, understood as structural integrity, therefore occupies a metaphysical middle ground between Dworkin's moral unity and Fuller's procedural morality.
claims.note: Direct ontological placement of justice in a metaphysical category.

claims.claim: Justice is the architecture—the organized coherence of being—that allows law to persist, evolve, and remain real.
claims.source_quote: It is neither narrative nor norm but architecture, the organized coherence of being that allows law to persist, evolve, and remain real.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of justice as architecture/organized coherence of being.

claims.claim: Justice is the equilibrium of law, not its telos.
claims.source_quote: Justice, in this sense, is not the telos of law but its equilibrium: the form of balance by which law continues to exist as law.
claims.note: Ontological claim about the role/function of justice in relation to law.

claims.claim: Legal systems fail when their internal dependencies that constitute legal reality cease to cohere.
claims.source_quote: legal systems fail not merely when their rules are unjust or unpopular, but when the internal dependencies that constitute legal reality cease to cohere.
claims.note: Asserts that internal dependencies constitute legal reality—an ontological claim about what legal reality is made of.

claims.claim: Internal dependencies constitute legal reality.
claims.source_quote: when the internal dependencies that constitute legal reality cease to cohere.
claims.note: Direct ontological claim: legal reality is constituted by internal dependencies.

claims.claim: Authoritarian legal systems collapse into rigid closure, losing reflexivity and accumulating contradiction debt.
claims.source_quote: When a system becomes authoritarian, it collapses into rigid closure, losing reflexivity and accumulating contradiction debt.
claims.note: Ontological claim about the structural properties of authoritarian legal systems.

claims.claim: Anomic legal systems dissolve into incoherence.
claims.source_quote: When it becomes anomic, it dissolves into incoherence.
claims.note: Ontological claim about the structural condition of anomic legal systems.

claims.claim: Coercion without authority is an exercise of legal power by an actor lacking valid authorization.
claims.source_quote: Coercion without authority: the exercise of legal power by an actor who lacks valid authorization to wield it.
claims.note: Defines a structural contradiction type—an ontological category of legal failure.

claims.claim: Exercise of power after invalidation is continued use of legal power after it has been legally withdrawn.
claims.source_quote: Exercise of power after invalidation: the continued use of a legal power or competence after it has been legally withdrawn or nullified.
claims.note: Defines an ontological category of structural legal contradiction.

claims.claim: Missing conferral chains are situations where legal power cannot be traced through valid sequences of grants and delegations.
claims.source_quote: Missing conferral chains: situations in which legal power cannot be traced back through a valid sequence of grants and delegations.
claims.note: Defines an ontological category of structural legal contradiction.

claims.claim: Validity conflicts occur when a legal rule is simultaneously treated as both valid and invalid within the system.
claims.source_quote: Validity conflicts: cases in which a legal rule or regulation is simultaneously treated as both valid and invalid within the system.
claims.note: Ontological claim about a category of structural legal contradiction.

claims.claim: Status conflicts occur when an entity occupies mutually exclusive legal statuses simultaneously.
claims.source_quote: Status conflicts: circumstances in which an entity is made to occupy mutually exclusive legal statuses at the same time.
claims.note: Ontological claim about a structural contradiction type involving legal statuses.

claims.claim: Persistence violations are the disappearance of legal facts meant to endure without a terminating legal event.
claims.source_quote: Persistence violations: the disappearance of legal facts that are meant to endure, without any corresponding legal event to terminate them.
claims.note: Defines an ontological category of structural legal contradiction involving continuant legal facts.

claims.claim: Temporal incoherence occurs when legal effects are treated as occurring prior to the events that justify them.
claims.source_quote: Temporal incoherence: cases in which legal effects are treated as occurring prior to the events that are supposed to justify them.
claims.note: Ontological claim about a temporal structural contradiction in legal systems.

claims.claim: Legal contradictions are violations of a legal system's ontological commitments concerning authority, validity, jurisdiction, recognition, and time.
claims.source_quote: Rather than treating breakdowns in law as interpretive disputes or failures of legitimacy, this approach understands them as violations of a legal system's own ontological commitments concerning authority, validity, jurisdiction, recognition, and time.
claims.note: Asserts the ontological nature of legal contradictions and what legal systems are committed to.

claims.claim: A legal contradiction is a stable misalignment across Z-levels where normative relations persist at Z2 while effective realization diverges.
claims.source_quote: A legal contradiction arises when standing normative relations persist at the Z2 level while effective realization diverges, producing a stable misalignment across Z-levels.
claims.note: The author asserts a positive ontological characterization of what a legal contradiction is, attributing specific structural properties to it.

claims.claim: The frozen structure of legal contradiction underlies all crimes and torts.
claims.source_quote: This frozen structure underlies all crimes and torts, regardless of doctrinal surface differences.
claims.note: The author asserts a relation (underlies) between the structural legal contradiction and all crimes and torts.

claims.claim: All crimes and other legal wrongs are contradictions.
claims.source_quote: this typology does not define classes of torts or crimes by name (though all are contradictions)
claims.note: The author asserts that crimes and torts are a subkind of contradictions—a direct ontological classification claim.

claims.claim: Each contradiction type corresponds to the failure or misalignment of one or more links in the Minimum Legal Chain.
